title: Are British graduates being conned? | Opinion | UK news | The Guardian
description: Thousands of students are graduating into an employment crisis, leaving them feeling hopeless and overqualified, as well as dealing with enormous debts from tuition fees. The Guardian’s economics commentator Aditya Chakrabortty explains
Author: Kirsty Major
Headline: Thousands of students are graduating into an employment crisis, leaving them feeling hopeless and overqualified, as well as dealing with enormous debts from tuition fees. The Guardian’s economics commentator Aditya Chakrabortty explains
Content: Are British graduates being conned? | OpinionUK newsAre British graduates being conned? | OpinionThousands of students are graduating into an employment crisis, leaving them feeling hopeless and overqualified, as well as dealing with enormous debts from tuition fees. When higher education was transformed, teenagers were offered a deal - pay £9,000 a year and secure a ‘bright future’. But as the Guardian’s economics commentator Aditya Chakrabortty accurately predicted, for many the reality has been very different.Presented byAditya Chakrabortty; produced byBryony Moore; editorKirsty MajorThu 30 Jul 2026 09.28 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsUK newsUniversitiesHigher educationSocial mobility

title: Even GB News cringes as Reform turns dementia patients into a political football | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Honest Bob was rattled at the idea of joining cross-party talks on social care. Why bother behaving as a serious opposition?
Author: John Crace
Headline: Honest Bob was rattled at the idea of joining cross-party talks on social care. Why bother behaving as a serious opposition?
Content: ‘Few other media organisations could be bothered to engage with the half-arsed grandstanding.’Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Few other media organisations could be bothered to engage with the half-arsed grandstanding.’Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAThe politics sketchReform UKEven GB News cringes as Reform turns dementia patients into a political footballJohn CraceHonest Bob was rattled at the idea of joining cross-party talks on social care. Why bother behaving as a serious opposition?Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareWhen you’ve lost the trust ofGB News, when you’re too deranged, too extreme and too outright mendacious for your biggest fan, then you know you are in trouble. You can almost sense the panic beginning to set in at Reform HQ.No longer topping the opinion polls. A new prime minister resetting the dial, the public increasingly choosing optimism over grievance. A party mired in financial sleaze. A leader turning into a laughing stock in his head-to-head with a dustbin. It was never meant to be this way for Reform. They thought they were the winners.With Nigel Farage locked away on a self-imposed witness protection programme, Richard Tice on an Accountancy for Dummies summer course and Zia Yusuf on a never-ending anger management retreat, the Reform front-of-house recess duties have been left toRobert Jenrick. Which is just the way Honest Bob likes it.No one rates Honest Bob higher than Honest Bob. He believes himself to be a winner. Someone who connects with the ordinary people. Which, to be fair, he does. Because Honest Bob has the unique ability to get people to dislike him on sight. It saves time that way. Why waste time getting to know him before you find you can’t bear him? He is a man who radiates inauthenticity. An establishment politician through and through who poses as the voice of forgotten Britain. Who believes the rules don’t apply to him. Who can’t help patronising everyone he meets.Thursday morning brought Honest Bob’s latest exercise in self-destruction. Giving a speech in a large hall, rammed with about … er … eight people. The only person in the room who actually wanted to be there was Honest Bob himself. Sometimes you have to wonder if it’s all a game on his part. As if he knows just how hopeless he really is and has devoted his life’s work to parodying himself. Reform’s ultimate enemy within. The former Tory politician who switched allegiance merely to bring down Nige, one day to be acknowledged as a hero to the Conservative party.There again, that would assume a level of self-awareness and intelligence that Honest Bob has never previously shown. So best to work on the basis that what you see is what you get. A not-very-bright opportunist who has bounced his way through life from one bad choice to another. A man with nothing very much to say, who still needs a teleprompter to say it.What Honest Bob wanted to talk about today was Andy Burnham’s “death tax”, which doesn’t even exist yet other than as a vague possibility to be considered among other options. But for Bob it was as if it had already been implemented. Already HMRC inspectors were hovering around hospices, terrifying dying patients by stealing their wedding rings, confiscating their debit cards and laughing as they emptied their houses and their bank accounts. This was Honest Bob’s wish fulfilment. There’s nothing that excites him more than misery porn.Then a rare moment of honesty. “I want to level with you,” he said. It would only be the least well-off who would end up paying a death tax. The rich would find ways of avoiding it. And by the rich, he meant himself, Nige, Dicky, Zia and Posh George Cottrell. “That’s what offshore accounts are for,” he boasted. You wouldn’t find any of the Reform elite being dim enough to pay for someone else’s social care.Dementia and disability were for other people’s families, not his. What was it to do with him if someone got Alzheimer’s and needed full-time care for seven years? In Reform World it’s every person for themselves. Unless they happen to be a party donor and pornographer. Under those circumstances, Honest Bob was sure he would find a way ofsaving that person £45m in taxby granting an unlawful planning permission. The rich look after each other.Honest Bob droned on like this for the best part of 20 minutes. Making specious argument after specious argument. Knocking down countless straw men. Lacking the insight to realise he was embarrassing himself. When he finally stopped, not a single person in the room bothered to applaud. Not even the Reform press person who was there to control the complete lack of interest.The first question came from GB News, more in sorrow than in anger. Why had Honest Bob made such a fool of himself? Why not actually try to join in the cross-party talks to find a solution to such a serious problem? Why the scare tactics of a death tax that isn’t even government policy? If the Tories and the Lib Dems could behave as grownups and engage with Andy Burnham, why couldn’t Reform? Instead, Reform ended up looking like a deeply unserious party. One that didn’t even have a health and social care spokesperson.For the first time, Honest Bob looked rattled. It hadn’t occurred to him that GB News might desert him. He had believed them to be on the side of grievance and division. What was in it for Reform to behave like a proper opposition? After all, its leader isn’t even currently an MP. Far better to invent a government policy it can then attack than to try to reach a consensus. That was clearly the way forward. Dementia patients were best used as a political football.It was all downhill from there. Few other media organisations could be bothered to engage with the half-arsed grandstanding. They were more interested in following up the Guardian’s story ofPosh George transferring £2m to his mum, moments before she sent money to Thicky Dicky. Why were all the financial dealings of the Reform elite so opaque? Why the need to deal in crypto and offshore accounts? What was wrong with ordinary bank transfers? It was almost as if there was something to hide.Now Honest Bob got genuinely snappy and tetchy. Why couldn’t people ask him the questions he wanted them to? Where was the respect he deserved? He had nothing to say on the money other than he was sure everything was above board. Of course it was. We had his word for it. Daddy had just been indulging George. Much more of this and the wheels will come off entirely.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchSocial careRobert JenrickGB NewscommentShareReuse this content

title: Dedicated followers of passion: the Kinks’ 40 greatest songs – ranked! | The Kinks | The Guardian
description: To coincide with a new exhibition in London about the Davies brothers, we rate the best of a band who brought a sociologist’s eye to hard rock, gentle pastoralia and so much in between
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: To coincide with a new exhibition in London about the Davies brothers, we rate the best of a band who brought a sociologist’s eye to hard rock, gentle pastoralia and so much in between
Content: Peter Quaife, Dave Davies, Mick Amory and Ray Davies of the Kinks in a promotional image for Sunny Afternoon, painted by BEV (Douglas Binder, Dudley Edwards and David Vaughan) in 1967.View image in fullscreenPeter Quaife, Dave Davies, Mick Amory and Ray Davies of the Kinks in a promotional image for Sunny Afternoon, painted by BEV (Douglas Binder, Dudley Edwards and David Vaughan) in 1967.RankedThe KinksDedicated followers of passion: the Kinks’ 40 greatest songs – ranked!To coincide with a new exhibition in London about the Davies brothers, we rate the best of a band who brought a sociologist’s eye to hard rock, gentle pastoralia and so much in betweenAlexis PetridisThu 30 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google40. Scattered (1993)The quality of Kinks albums declined precipitously from the late 80s: you sensed their hearts weren’t really in it. Even so,Ray Daviescouldn’t stop himself writing the occasional gem: from their final studio album Phobia, Scattered is a sweet, sad reflection on the Davies family’s complexities, powered by jangling guitars.39. Rosy Won’t You Please Come Home (1966)The decision of Davies’s older sister Rose to emigrate to Australia “devastated” him: it lurked in the background of Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire) but took centre stage on this track from Face to Face: evidently heartfelt, it twists and turns, deploying everything from pleading to mockery to secure her return.38. You Can’t Stop the Music (1975)Originally the soundtrack to a Ray Davies TV special, Soap Opera nearly broke the Kinks: some members assumed it would be their last album. There’s certainly a sense of finality to its closing track, impressive though it is: despite the title, it sounds like a eulogy for rock’n’roll, spiked with personal bitterness.View image in fullscreenRay Davies, Pete Quaife, Dave Davies and Mick Avory of the Kinks in 1965.Photograph: Chris Walter/WireImage37. Two Sisters (1967)As an example of how out of step the Kinks were with the burgeoning counterculture in 1967, the harpsichord-led Two Sisters is hard to beat. Loving domesticity and parenthood trumps free-spirited bohemia: formerly jealous of her unencumbered sibling, the married sister ends the song delightedly running “round the house with her curlers on”.36. I Go to Sleep (1965)Never released by the Kinks – a demo version is on the deluxe version of Kinda Kinks – the fraught ballad I Go to Sleep was the most sophisticated song Ray Davies had written by this time. The most famous cover is by the Pretenders, but the best is the 1967 version byGerman singer Marion Maerz: lushly orchestrated, echo-laden, girl group-adjacent, magnificent.35. Lavender Lane (1971)Belatedly excavated for the 2013 deluxe edition of Muswell Hillbillies, Lavender Lane’s failure to make the cut in 1971 seems baffling. It’s fantastic, a broadside against what would now be called gentrification that pivots between nostalgic sadness and fury, aimed at “the old school tie and all the la-di-do-dahs”.34. I’m Not Like Everybody Else (1966)In the hands of the Chocolate Watchband, who covered it in 1968, I’m Not Like Everybody Else is a classic screw-you garage band sneer. The Kinks’ original has a menacing power, but feels more complicated and personal, its emotional temperature shifting from defiant to faintly distraught.33. Living on a Thin Line (1984)From the largely ho-hum Word of Mouth, this is an atmospheric, ominous and pessimistic survey of Thatcher’s Britain from the pen of Dave Davies – “there’s no England now,” he dolefully concludes – subsequently rescued from obscurity and brought to the wider audience it deserved by its inclusion on the soundtrack of The Sopranos.32. (Wish I Could Fly Like) Superman (1979)At their height of Britpop, it was common to compare Damon Albarn’s brand of social satire to that of Ray Davies, a fairly obvious influence. More bizarre is how much this impressive single from 1979’s Low Budget sounded like Blur’s Girls and Boys: disco beat, slashing guitars, mannered Cockney vocals.View image in fullscreenThe Kinks on British TV in 1967.Photograph: ITV/Rex Features31. Too Much on My Mind (1966)Easy to overlook amid the waspish character studies and social satires of Face to Face – the Kinks’ first entirely superb album – Too Much on My Mind feels like Ray Davies’s most personal song of the era: a plaintive depiction of a man teetering on the verge of a breakdown. Understated, but quietly devastating.30. Till the End of the Day (1965)The last of the Kinks’ riff-heavy garage rock anthems – although the fantastic She’s Got Everything belatedly slipped out as a B-side in 1968 – is more sophisticated than its predecessors: check the harmony vocals. But it’s just as thrilling, and – curiously for the Kinks – snottily optimistic in tone. But if you flipped the single over …29. Where Have All the Good Times Gone? (1965)… you got the first – but definitely not the last – example of Ray Davies in contrarian mode. The 60s are fully swinging, the Kinks are at the centre of the action, and yet he’s riven with angst, complaining that things ain’t what they used to be, suggesting his parents had it better.28. This Time Tomorrow (1970)Not all of Davies’s scabrous music business satire Lola Vs Powerman and the Moneygoround Pt 1 has aged well, but This Time Tomorrow still rings out: detached from the album’s concept, it ceases to be a song about touring, and instead becomes a hugely affecting study of a life turned aimless.27. Death of a Clown (1967)Dave Davies’s aborted late 60s solo album was doomed by the Kinks’ gradually declining commercial fortunes rather than a lack of strong material, evidenced by Death of a Clown, rhythmically jaunty but hauntingly eerie: a compelling solo hit that wound up on 1967’s Something Else By the Kinks.26. Sitting in My Hotel (1972)Songs in which rock stars complain about life on the road seldom elicit much sympathy from the listener – there are, far, far worse jobs, after all – but Sitting in My Hotel is among the few exceptions: a heartbreaking piano ballad that perfectly expresses a sense of homesick dislocation.25. Mr Pleasant (1967)Sometimes, Ray Davies could sound like a grumpy reactionary, sometimes like a revolutionary, seething with class rage. It isn’t entirely clear what Mr Pleasant has done to incur Davies’s wrath, beyond being middle class, but his downfall is brilliantly, wittily depicted, to a jolly music hall-inspired backing. The evident delight in Davies’s voice is quite unsettling.24. Sweet Lady Genevieve (1973)As Ray Davies’s theatrical ambitions got more elaborate, his songwriting genius seemed to flicker more fitfully: the Kinks’ 70s concept albums can be a longwinded slog. But persevere and you’re occasionally rewarded with a song like the gorgeous Sweet Lady Genevieve, entirely up to the standards he’d set himself. Perhaps the Kinks’ great lost classic.23. 20th Century Man (1971)It isn’t entirely clear if the character in 20th Century Man is a character, or an expression of Ray Davies’s increasing alienation and the precarious state of his mental health. “I don’t want to be here,” it offers. He would attempt suicide two years later. Ironically, the music that misery is set to is utterly charming.22. Victoria (1969)Victoria deals in the sort of ambiguity that had become one of Davies’s most striking trademarks. Is it a nostalgic celebration of a bygone era, or a biting satire on empire? Probably both. Whatever it is, it’s a great song, blessed with a wonderful middle eight and an exultant brass arrangement.21. See My Friends (1965)Depending on who you believe, the sound ofSee My Friendswas either inspired by a brief stopover in Mumbai, or the raga-influenced playing of folk guitarist Jon Mark. Either way, it was a hugely innovative pop single, both for its droning sound and its (admittedly oblique) lyrical treatment of homosexuality.20. Come Dancing (1983)The Kinks’ only UK hit in the final22 yearsof their career concerned their fraught origin story – the death of Ray Davies’s sister Rene in a dancehall, the same day she gave him his first guitar – and featured a sound that recalled their mid-60s hits: the synth hasn’t dated well, but the song itself is sweet, sad nostalgia.View image in fullscreenRay Davies in 1965.Photograph: David Magnus/Rex Features19. Big Black Smoke (1966)Sixties London not as the swinging epicentre of the world, but a dark, forbidding nightmare, ready to swallow the unwary, including the song’s increasingly speed-addled protagonist. Ferociously performed and emotionally complex, as empathy for the girl’s frantic mother battles it out with a certain native Londoner’s relish at her grim fate.18. Better Things (1981)The Kinks’ unexpected early 80s elevation into hard-rocking, arena-packing stars in the US sailed over British audiences’ heads. If their albums from that era aren’t up to 60s standards, they have their moments, of which Better Things’ unexpectedly optimistic – and richly melodic – reflection on a collapsing marriage is the most stellar.17. Celluloid Heroes (1972)Kinks fans can argue all night over whether 1972’s Everybody’s in Show-Biz represents their last soup-to-nuts classic album. Less contentious is how great its highlights are, as evidenced by Celluloid Heroes, an impossibly weary rumination on celebrity and posthumous reputation, provoked by a visit to Hollywood Boulevard’s Walk of Fame.16. Dead End Street (1966)Outside of the world of folk, mid-60s British pop wasn’t big on social realism or protest, which made Dead End Street’s depiction of working-class poverty, complete with mournful french horn and shouted chorus, all the more striking. It had more in common with contemporary TV dramas than it did the rest of the charts.15. Shangri-La (1969)Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire) was a much thornier exploration of Britishness than the preceding year’s The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society. The lengthy, episodic Shangri-La’s melody barely conceals a lyric livid about conformity, limited aspirations and social mobility, a country “too scared to complain”.14. Picture Book (1968)It’s hard to pick out individual tracks from The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society – it works best taken as a whole – but Picture Book’s interrogation of memory (“those days when you were happy, a long time ago”) is particularly great: sentimental but irreverent, and genuinely affecting.13. Oklahoma USA (1971)Muswell Hillbillies is a curious, fascinating album, packed with great songs drenched in Americana but lyrically rooted in north London. Oklahoma USA is its highlight: its tune among Ray Davies’s prettiest, the lyrics both wistful and sharp – its dreams of a more glamorous existence in Oklahoma are fuelled by the Hollywood musical rather than reality of life there.12. Lola (1970)The subject of some controversy in recent years, Lola’s depiction of a brief, confused dalliance with a trans woman was more or less uncharted territory for pop in 1970, a topic no one other than Lou Reed had ventured to touch. It seemed to energise Ray Davies, pulling one of his greatest tunes out of him.11. David Watts (1967)Partly inspired by the Kinks’ encounter with a gay Midlands promoter, this story of schoolboy rivalry is liberally sprinkled with homoeroticism. Does the narrator envy Watts’s wealth and accomplishments or is his fascination sparked more by Watts’s lack of interest in girls? The music fits perfectly: relentless, agitated, but deliberately mannered.10. Dedicated Follower of Fashion (1966)The Kinks, Marianne Faithfull subsequently opined, were “creepy and silent” and seemed “fearful of everyone”. Perhaps Ray Davies was taking notes, which would explain how perfectly he skewered the affectations of 60s hipsters here. Best moment: when the lyric slips into contemporary journalese: “This pleasure-seeking individual always looks his best.”View image in fullscreenThe Davies brothers on stage in the US in 1975.Photograph: Stephen Morley/Redferns9. God’s Children (1971)If you want an example of Ray Davies’s contrarian nature, consider God’s Children. Easily one of his finest early 70s songs – spellbinding melody, intriguing lyrics about the advance of technology – and he stuck it on the soundtrack to a sex comedy about a man rendered irresistible to women after a penis transplant.8. A Well Respected Man (1965)The song that introduced a sharp brand of social satire into 60s British pop and inspired a legion of contemporary imitators – Semi-Detatched Suburban Mr James, et al. But no one else was as nuanced a lyricist as Ray Davies: listen to the verse about the protagonist’s ghastly mother, and you can virtuallyseeher.7. You Really Got Me (1964)After 60 plus years, You Really Got Me is so familiar, it’s hard to picture the jolt it must have delivered in the summer of 1964, its distorted riff, unhinged guitar solo and Ray Davies’s vocal – alternately impassioned and slightly camp – sounding nothing like anything British pop had thus far produced. It still rocks.6. All Day and All of the Night (1964)That rarest of things: an attempt to follow up a huge hit with something similar that improves on the original. Cut from the same cloth as You Really Got Me, it succeeds by dialling everything up: it’s tougher, heavier, more exhilarating, and the mid-chorus key change is a masterstroke.5. The Village Green Preservation Society (1968)The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society flopped on release: perhaps a rock band singing in praise of the George cross and virginity was too confusing amid 1968’s revolutionary tumult. It was correctly reassessed as their masterpiece. The opening track demonstrates Davies’s songwriting firing on all cylinders: funny, sharp, provocative, warm.4. Sunny Afternoon (1966)How good a writer was Ray Davies at his zenith? Good enough to draw a pen portrait of a dissipated, abusive aristocrat and somehow manage to elicit a sense of empathy from the listener, helped by the irresistible melody and the song’s timelessness: its story could have been written in the 1920s but it’s not a nostalgic pastiche.3. Autumn Almanac (1967)At the close of the summer of love, Ray Davies was to be found lovingly hymning the mundane life of a suburban gardener. Far more than a mere dry run for The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society, Autumn Almanac is a lovely song: no snark or cynicism, just warmth and empathy.2. Days (1968)That Days failed to make the UK Top 10 tells you everything about the Kinks’ waning commercial fortunes and nothing about the song itself. In a just world, anything blessed with a tune this beautiful, so suffused with equal part sadness and reflective warmth, would have been No 1 for weeks. A masterpiece.1. Waterloo Sunset (1967)Critic Robert Christgau called Waterloo Sunset “the most beautiful song in the English language”: certainly it’s among the greatest singles of the 60s, quite possibly one of the greatest pop songs of all time and a remarkable example of the songwriter’s art. On top of an extraordinarily beautiful melody, the lyrics are perfectly balanced between love for London, affection for the lovers meeting outside Waterloo Station and aching sadness: ever the outsider, Davies looks on at it all from a distance, and complains about the cold. It’s his best song, but it isn’t head-and-shoulders over everything else he wrote, which says a great deal about his brilliance.The Kinks: Brothers, by Ray Davies, Dave Davies and Christian Furr, is at the Gibson Garage, London, until 6 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsThe KinksRankedPop and rockRay DaviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Europe burns: a visual guide to the wildfires | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Ferocious flames continue to rage in parts of France and Spain, with no sign of abating. We chart the destruction in graphics and pictures
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Ferocious flames continue to rage in parts of France and Spain, with no sign of abating. We chart the destruction in graphics and pictures
Content: Wildfires in Arès, south-west France, 25 July 2026. Photograph: Damien Rembert/EPAFerocious flames continue to rage in parts of France and Spain, with no sign of abating. We chart the destruction in graphics and picturesByDamian Carrington,Lucy Swan,Ana Lucía González Paz,Harvey SymonsThu 30 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe hellish infernos that have torn through parts of France and Spain have caused deaths, the evacuation of 330,000 people from their homes, widespread destruction and clouds of toxic smoke. Records have already been smashed and with the fourth heatwave of the European summer setting in, there are few signs of the waves of wildfires ending.France has already surpassed the worst previous year for the size of the area burned, with August, usually the hottest month, yet to come.Chart showing the cumulative area burned by fires in FranceInSpain, the cumulative number of fires in 2026 has also set a new record for this time of year, and the cumulative burnt area remains just below the level reached by late July during a devastating fire season in 2022.Chart showing the cumulative area burned by fires in SpainWhy have the wildfires been so bad?The extreme severity of the blazes is the result of “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather this year, supercharged by the climate crisis. Last winter and much of spring in western Europe was very wet, encouraging heavy growth of trees, shrubs and other vegetation.Chart showing how in February 2026 Spain had 241% of the normal average rainfall, while in April 2026 it had 58%However, by May the first of a series of heatwaves had hit Europe. All heatwaves are made more intense and more likely by the global heating caused by fossil fuel burning. The heatwave at the end of June was themost severe ever recorded in Europeand would have been impossible without the added heat from more than a century of carbon pollution.Western Europe’s hottest JuneChart showing how in June 2026 Western Europe had an average surface air temperature anomaly of 3.06CThe high temperatures meant the hot atmosphere strongly evaporated water from rivers and lakes and sucked plants and soil dry, with the conditions made80 times more likely by global heating. As a result of the drought conditions, vegetation became tinder and the risk of wildfires soared, leading to a series of wildfires scientists have described as “firewaves”.Map showing drought conditions in EuropeThe situation has been worsened by the unprecedented development of enormous “fire clouds” –pyrocumulonimbus– in France. These form from the heat from huge fires and become aself-feeding firestorm, spitting lightning bolts and sparking further blazes.View image in fullscreenA pyrocumulonimbus, or ‘fire cloud’, in the Fontainebleau forest region, about 37 miles south of Paris, France.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APView image in fullscreenFirefighters use controlled burning to halt a wildfire near Cebreros, Ávila province, Spain.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APThe severity of the fires has been extremely challenging for the fire-fighting authorities, who in the past would have expected to extinguish the fires. One firefighter, Javier García, told Associated Press he had never faced anything like it in his two decades in the job.“The evolution is alarming,” he said, adding that they were now prioritising evacuations and property protection because fast-moving walls of flames were too ferocious.Firefighters tackle wildfire in central SpainWhat have been the consequences?Many thousands of residents and holidaymakers have had toevacuate, often prompted by urgent alerts sent to their phones. Emergency shelters have been set up, including 78 by the Red Cross in Spain. “This is a pattern we are seeing more and more across Europe: heatwaves, drought and wildfires feeding into one another, and communities bearing the consequences,” said Maria Alcazar Castilla, from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.View image in fullscreenEvacuees at the Bordeaux exhibition centre in France.Photograph: Albert Llop/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAn evacuated woman with her dog in the exhibition centre in Bordeaux.Photograph: Ed Jones/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA sports centre in Boadilla del Monte, Madrid, Spain, has become a shelter for evacuated residents.Photograph: Víctor Lerena/EPAThe longer-term damage to homes and livelihoods is yet to be reckoned with, but will be large. The wildfires around Bordeaux have claimed some of the region’s famous vineyards, while the tourism and manufacturing industries around Valencia have been hard hit.View image in fullscreenThe winemakers Antoine Latipau and his wife, Yana-Cheyenne, have lost most of their farm to the fires in Trévillach, in the French Catalan south.Photograph: Antoine/Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenSheep search for food on a scorched pasture near Piedralaves, 60 miles west of Madrid.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA burnt car in Gironde, France.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersA further longer-term impact will be the damage to health caused by the toxic smoke from the fires. About1.5 million people a yearare estimated to have their lives shortened by wildfire smoke.View image in fullscreenResidents try to shield themselves from the toxi smoke in Avila, Spain.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesEmmanuel Macron, the French president, has described the wildfire emergency as the “toughest” situation the country had dealt with since the second world war. In Spain, Pedro Sánchez, the prime minister, said his country was suffering the effects of the climate crisis.View image in fullscreenA towering pyrocumulus in Castellón province, Spain.Photograph: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/ReutersDozens of emergency vehicles tackle fire in Gironde, FranceEurope is the fastest-warming of all continents, owing to an increase in heat dome conditions and the proximity of the Arctic, where reflective ice is melting rapidly.Chart showing that Europe has an average temperature anomaly relative to the baseline of 0.87CSimon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said: “The science on the cause is unequivocal: global heating, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making protracted heatwaves, severe floods and violent mega-storms more frequent, more intense and more costly.“The awful costs of this climate crisis – both human and economic – are now reaching national emergency levels. What needs to be done is equally clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”A map showing temperatures in western Europe.The EU has watered down a series of green measures in the past year in the face of political opposition and corporate lobbying. Hadja Lahbib, the European commissioner for crisis preparedness,told the Financial Times: “The commission can only be as ambitious as the member states want it to be. When member states drag their feet [on the climate crisis] … there is a real danger and an incalculable price.”The Guardian’s climate forum 2026. On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts – including Prof Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh, Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman – for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening.Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsWildfiresExtreme heatFranceSpainEuropeClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: A meat thermometer transformed my cooking – here are nine of the best for roasts and barbecues | Meat | The Guardian
description: Stop guessing and start probing with our writer’s pick of the top thermometers, including smart Bluetooth and leave-in models
Author: Rachel Ogden
Headline: Stop guessing and start probing with our writer’s pick of the top thermometers, including smart Bluetooth and leave-in models
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterMeatReviewA meat thermometer transformed my cooking – here are nine of the best for roasts and barbecuesStop guessing and start probing with our writer’s pick of the top thermometers, including smart Bluetooth and leave-in modelsReaders’ favourite barbecue tips and tricksRachel OgdenThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.While fewer of us are eating meat regularly – I refer you to the rise of“beef days”– if you’re going to cook it, it needs to be done properly. Overcooked beef with the texture of shoe leather, or undercooked poultry with a side of food poisoning, will put off even the most devoted carnivore.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.A reliable meat thermometer solves both problems. It takes the guesswork out of cooking, helping you achieve melt-in-the-mouth steak and the best of any cut, with no special skills required.As a bonus, it can even help you make modest energy-use savings by preventing overcooking. Buying one of the best meat thermometers isn’t about adding to a pile of gadgets – it’s about making the most of the meat you choose to eat. Personally, I’d choose a cheaper piece of meat cooked perfectly over a pricey one that’s dry and chewy.At a glanceBest meat thermometer overallNinjaProChef wireless thermometer WP100EU£89.99 at SharkNinjaBest budget meat thermometerSalterHeston Blumenthal Precision indoor/outdoor meat thermometer£17.99 at AmazonBest wireless smart meat thermometerTyphurSync Gold dual two-probe wireless meat thermometer£199.99 at AmazonBest wireless Bluetooth meat thermometerMeaterPro£129 at John LewisBest leave-in meat thermometerETIDot digital oven thermometer£32.50 at ETIWhy you should trust meI grew up believing that I didn’t like meat – I was vegetarian through my teens. Turns out, I just didn’t like how it was cooked. As an adult, I’ve always kept a meat thermometer at hand and have been testing them since I bought my first Meater wireless probe nine years ago. Since then, I’ve upgraded as the tech has improved. I test a lot ofair fryers, multicookers and ovens, so for me a meat thermometer isn’t just a nice-to-have – it’s an essential tool for assessing how well an appliance cooks.How I testedView image in fullscreenBoiling point … each thermometer underwent hot and cold calibration before testing.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianThere are unexpected side effects to testing meat thermometers. One is cooking so much meat that a slightly greasy fug lingers in the house for days. Another is temporarily altering my App Store algorithm, after downloading five meat thermometer apps in succession. That’s a lot of cooking, says the store. Would I enjoy these 10 grocery shopping apps? Or how about some hiking and cycling apps to balance out your burger binge?I tested 12 thermometers, but only nine made the cut. The first two tests used hot and cold calibration methods. I took the temperature of boiling water in a pan and ice water in a glass, alongside a thermocouple thermometer, and compared the readings. This was repeated three times for each. Since meat thermometers are designed for solids, liquid readings may not be degree-perfect, but they provided a guide to accuracy at the upper and lower limits of the scale.I started the cooking part of the tests by pan-frying thick beef burgers on a medium-to-high heat, noting when each thermometer said they were done, when I was advised to flip (if applicable), and if the burgers were still pink in the middle. Burgers were placed in a preheated pan straight out of the fridge, with just a small amount of oil. They were then fried for about six to seven minutes on each side with a three-minute rest, until cooked through and measuring a peak of 70-72C in the centre.This was followed by roasting chicken legs in a preheated air fryer at 190C. It normally takes about 25-28 minutes for the chicken to reach an internal temperature of 75-78C, with a three-minute rest. For each thermometer, I noted when it read that the chicken was done, then checked it by slicing open the leg to see if there was any pink remaining. I also noted whether the juices were running clear and whether the meat remained moist.Finally, I evaluated how easy each thermometer was to set up, use and maintain, and its battery life. All samples have been returned to their supplier or donated to charity.The best meat thermometers, testedView image in fullscreen‘Even provides guidance on when to flip food’: the Ninja ProChef wireless thermometer.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianBest meat thermometer overall:Ninja ProChef wireless thermometer WP100EUNinjaProChef wireless thermometer WP100EUfrom£89.99£89.99 at SharkNinja£90 at ArgosWhat we loveIt can handle high-heat flare-ups on a grillWhat we don’t loveThe connection can drop out briefly sometimesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£89.99 at SharkNinja£90 at ArgosCompared with other wireless thermometers, this Ninja unit has plenty going for it. First, if you’re looking for a brand you recognise, then price-wise, onlyMeater’s entry-level SEand thePlusare in the same ballpark. Its app is easy to use – particularly for smart meat thermometer newbies – even providing guidance on when to flip food. But where it stands out is its integration with Ninja’s other appliances. The app includes cooking charts and appliance-specific guidance, making it especially useful if you already own a Ninja air fryer, grill or outdoor oven.Why we love itThe probe connected to the app first time – not always a given with connected devices – and was easy to navigate. It can handle temperatures up to 370C, so it was no surprise that it did well in the hot-water test, reading only a degree lower than the thermocouple, but it was out by a few more degrees with ice water.It’s a thicker probe than theMeater Pro, so it can be tricky to insert, but it handled cooking well. Although there was a slight fluctuation in the estimated cooking time (dropping from 15 to 10 minutes in only two minutes), barbecue cooks that get easily distracted will welcome its alert to flip and that it factors in rest time, which resulted in a thoroughly cooked burger. Placement in chicken was problematic, playing havoc with the estimated cooking time and alerting me that it was cooked before it actually was – but reinserting solved the issue.It’s a shame that …it’s better for bigger items than small pieces of food.Water resistance?YesProbe length:8.5cm (6.5cm from tip to insertion line)Battery life:up to 30 hours (AAA battery supplied for charging case)Recycling and longevity:the Ninja ProChefcomes with a two-year warranty, and the brand advises that all its electrical products should be recycled at dedicated recycling points. It doesn’t offer a repair serviceNinjaProChef wireless thermometer WP100EUfrom£89.99£89.99 at SharkNinja£90 at ArgosWhat we loveIt can handle high-heat flare-ups on a grillWhat we don’t loveThe connection can drop out briefly sometimesBest budget meat thermometer:Heston Blumenthal Precision by Salter Indoor/Outdoor meat thermometerSalterHeston Blumenthal Precision indoor/outdoor meat thermometerfrom£17.99£20 at John Lewis£17.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGave a faster reading than others on testWhat we don’t loveTricky to manoeuvre it in an air fryer drawerView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£20 at John Lewis£17.99 at AmazonEqually at home in the kitchen as it is by the barbecue, this versatile instant-read thermometer can withstand temperatures from -45C to 200C. Unlike others, it’s also suitable for making jam and caramel and checking the temperature of deep-frying oil, while its silicone casing and probe cover keep it protected from the elements. It’s the long probe you’ll love most, though, letting you check bangers on the barbecue without reaching for the oven gloves.Why we love itIn testing, the Heston Precision was fantastically accurate, matching up with the thermocouple in the boiling- and ice-water tests most of the time. The probe was easy to use and insert, too. Salter’sPrecision meat thermometeris practically identical in spec and similar in price, and put in a similar performance in my testing – but the Heston made the list because of its extra cooking guidance.The slim probe made it easy to check multiple spots in burgers and chicken, ensuring they were cooked through with no pink remaining.It’s a shame that …at 30cm long with the cover on,it’s awkward to fit in a cutlery drawer – a hanging hook would be a useful addition.Water resistance?Yes, to IPX5Probe length:18cmBattery life:approximately one year (2xAAA batteries supplied)Recycling and longevity:the Heston Blumenthal thermometer comes with a one-year guarantee that can be extended to two ifregistered within 30 days of buying. It can be recycled at a local e-waste collection point or household recycling centre in the small WEEE container once the battery is removedSalterHeston Blumenthal Precision indoor/outdoor meat thermometerfrom£17.99£20 at John Lewis£17.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGave a faster reading than others on testWhat we don’t loveTricky to manoeuvre it in an air fryer drawerBest wireless smart meat thermometer:Typhur Sync Gold dual-probe wireless meat thermometerTyphurSync Gold dual two-probe wireless meat thermometer£199.99£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveYou can pop the probes in the dishwasher when you’re doneWhat we don’t loveThe app and base beep, which could be annoyingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£199.99 at AmazonTyphur is in the process of making a humanoid kitchen robot, Athena, so I was expecting great things from its Sync Gold Dual meat thermometer. And for the most part, it lived up to expectations. Its two probes live in a sleek base that not only charges them but also acts as a monitor and control hub, so you can track cooking without reaching for your phone.It also uses a stronger, longer-range signal (sub-1GHz for those radio frequency aficionados out there) – making it ideal if thick walls or a robust barbecue disrupt smart probe connections.Why we love itThe Sync Gold can withstand up to 500C and is waterproof, too, making it suitable for almost any type of cooking, including sous vide. Having said that, I was surprised to find it struggled during the boiling-water test, coming in 3C lower than the thermocouple, and read 0C in the ice-water test, when the thermocouple read 4C. Fortunately, its cooking performance was excellent.The app was easy to set up and use, while the base took more getting used to, although it’s useful if you’re avoiding your phone. I liked the cooking graph and frequent alerts, although it doesn’t remind you to turn the food. Both the burger and chicken were perfectly cooked without drying or overcooking. Great performance, then – as you’d expect at this price.It’s a shame that …the base is set with arrows to scroll through and a button to select, rather than being a touchscreen.Water resistance?Yes, probes to IPX8; base to IPX2Probe length:8.5cm (7.5cm from tip to insertion line)Battery life:24+ hours on a single charge/rechargeable baseRecycling and longevity:the thermometer’s sealed design means it’s not intended to be repaired, although it is covered by a two-year warranty. Typhur doesn’t offer a take-back or recycling schemeTyphurSync Gold dual two-probe wireless meat thermometer£199.99£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveYou can pop the probes in the dishwasher when you’re doneWhat we don’t loveThe app and base beep, which could be annoyingBest wireless Bluetooth meat thermometer:Meater ProMeaterProfrom£129£129 at John Lewis£129 at ArgosWhat we loveA compact, stylish base that isn’t plasticWhat we don’t lovePricey for a single probeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£129 at John Lewis£129 at ArgosMy fridge sits behind my kitchen door – but if yours is in a more visible location, you’ll appreciate that the Meater Pro’s magnetic bamboo base can be affixed to the fridge door for storing the thermometer, so it’s within easy reach when you’re next cooking steak. There’s plenty more to like, too.The probe is waterproof, dishwasher-safe for cleaning, and suitable for deep-frying orsous vide. It’s also heatproof up to 550C, and slimmer than most at just 0.5cm in diameter – making it easier to use with smaller cuts of meat. Meater claims its app is so friendly, you can leave it to your kids. While they’d probably rather be playing Pokémon Go, I did find it genuinely easy to use.Why we love itI use aMeater Plusin my kitchen, but it’s not as whizzy as the Pro, which charges rapidly and lasts a long time (a 15-minute charge will buy you about 12 hours of cooking), making it perfect for spur-of-the-moment meat feasts. In testing, I appreciated the ability to specify not only the meat being cooked and the level of cooking, but also how you’re cooking it – there’s an option for air fryers, for example.It didn’t perform so well in the water tests – fluctuating between 92C and 97C when the thermocouple read 99C, and 1.3C when the thermocouple was at 3C – although it did offer guidance for frozen meat. Cooking performance was better, although the burger was drier as a result of the preset being 2C higher than what I’d normally choose, and the chicken was a little pink. This could have been down to probe placement or the leg being thicker.It’s a shame that …estimated cooking time takes a while to appear. I was over halfway through cooking the burger by the time this popped up.Water resistance?YesProbe length:9.8cm (6.7cm from tip to insertion line)Battery life:24+ hours from a 30-minute charge, estimated two years of charging based on one steak a week (AAA battery supplied for charging case)Recycling and longevity:the Meater Pro isn’t recyclable at the end of its life, but it does come with atwo-year warrantyshould it need to be replaced or repairedMeaterProfrom£129£129 at John Lewis£129 at ArgosWhat we loveA compact, stylish base that isn’t plasticWhat we don’t lovePricey for a single probeBest leave-in meat thermometer:ETI Dot digital oven thermometerETIDot digital oven thermometerfrom£32.50£32.50 at ETI£36 at AmazonWhat we loveLarge display for keeping an eye on progressWhat we don’t loveNo cooking guidance, so you’re on your ownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£32.50 at ETI£36 at AmazonI enjoy the name of the Dot – both short for digital oven thermometer and a nod to its round shape – but it’s more than an appealing moniker that made me like this thermometer. Equipped with a wired probe, magnets for convenient placement on an oven door, and a light to brighten the LCD screen, this is a simple bit of kit, executed well.The stainless-steel braided lead is a generous 1.2m, and the probe will measure temperatures from as low as -50C up to 300C. There’s no ignoring its 70dB alarm for when it hits temperature – great for easily distracted cooks who have wandered off to another room.Why we love itIf you dislike apps or fiddly setup routines, the Dot will appeal. It has just three buttons: one on the back for power and adjusting screen brightness, and two on the front to set the target temperature. And that’s it.It did well in the water tests, only usually a degree out from the thermocouple, but pan cooking and air frying proved more awkward. Positioning the probe in smaller items was tricky, and the cable often got in the way, meaning I had to reinsert it for an accurate reading. Eventually, I got a juicy well-done burger and thoroughly cooked chicken, but it took some effort. That said, for its intended use in the oven, it’s better designed, more robust, and slimmer than Lakeland’s in-oven model below.It’s a shame that …its fold-up stand is flimsy and popped off in my hand. It didn’t break, but a more substantial structure would be an improvement.Water resistance?Yes, to IP65Probe length:11.4cmBattery life:5,000 hours (2xAAA batteries supplied)Recycling and longevity:it comes with only a one-year guarantee, but ETI offers arepair serviceand willrecyclereturned productsETIDot digital oven thermometerfrom£32.50£32.50 at ETI£36 at AmazonWhat we loveLarge display for keeping an eye on progressWhat we don’t loveNo cooking guidance, so you’re on your ownThe best of the restView image in fullscreenThe Weber Smart Probe is an affordable way to dip your toe into app-monitored cooking.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianWeber Connect smart probe and grate sensorWeberConnect smart probe and grate sensor£39.99£39.99 at WeberWhat we loveIt’s compact and winds up for easy storageWhat we don’t loveBattery type is less common (but it is included)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£39.99 at WeberBest for:barbecuingDesigned to work either as a probe or a grate sensor with anybarbecue, the Weber Connect smart probe is one for the alfresco cooks. It’ll withstand temperatures of up to 420C, attaches to your barbecue via magnets, has a 0.91m cable, and comes with a clip so it can measure ambient temperature. If you want to dip your toe into app-monitored cooking, the Smart Probe could be one of the most affordable ways to do it.Its performance in the water tests was mixed, coming in at 99C when the thermocouple read 100C, and 1C when the thermocouple read 3.7C. Indoors, it’s tricky to use, but not impossible. For example, the ambient heat of the pan tended to skew the reading when cooking the burger, registering it as cooked before it actually was, while the cable was too thick for the air fryer drawer to close properly. I had to reposition the probe a couple of times in the chicken, but once it was in the right spot, the readings were what I’d expect. Used in an oven or, as it’s intended, on a barbecue, it worked well for larger cuts, but it’s far from being an all-purpose meat thermometer.It didn’t make the final cut because …the choice for app-assisted cooking is limited – for example, chicken leg wasn’t listed.Water resistance?Weather resistant, but not waterproof;probe length:8.89cm;battery life:one year (1xCR2032 battery supplied);recycling and longevity:two-year limited warranty; no recycling or repair programme. It has a big, clear digital display, a button on the back flicks between celsius and fahrenheit readings, and the probe protector offers suggested temperatures for different meats and levels of doneness, along with resting advice. The display pivots 90 degrees so you can read it from any angle.It’s less versatile than some, though. While it has a temperature range of -40 to 150C, it was confused by the ice-water test, reading 1C when the water was actually at 4C. It was spot on for the boiling water, though. During cooking, it was slower to climb up to temperature than other units on test, although it got there in the end. Both the burger and chicken were well cooked, but not before the screen had become splashed with fat – a combination of waiting time and a short probe.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s powered by a button battery, which you’re less likely to have to hand for replacement – and the one supplied was almost flat.Water resistance?No;probe length:11.5cm;battery life:two years of moderate use(1xCR2032 battery supplied);recycling and longevity:the probe cover and battery can potentially be recycled, but the thermometer can’t, and Oxo doesn’t have a policy in place for recycling its products. However, it does offer a “better guarantee”, a lifetime warranty that promises to replace or refund products with material or manufacturing defectsOxoGood Grips Chef’s Precision digital instant read thermometerfrom£17£22.50 at John Lewis£17 at AmazonWhat we loveTurns off automatically to conserve battery lifeWhat we don’t loveYou’ll be cleaning the screen more frequentlyProCook meat thermometerProCookMeat thermometer grey fork£11£11 at ProCookWhat we loveA hanging hook saves drawer spaceWhat we don’t loveAAA batteries not includedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£11 at ProCookBest for:an easy-to-read displayIt’s unwieldy and won’t be for everyone, but I liked the simplicity of this affordable meat thermometer. There are just two buttons for scrolling through what you want to cook – meat and taste – plus you have the option to easily switch temperature readings between celsius and fahrenheit under the battery cover. An anti-slip handle, easy-to-read backlit LCD panel, safety caps for its menacing prongs, one-year guarantee, and presets for six meats complete the package.Its temperature range goes from -5 to 250C – although, like many others I tested, it did better with boiling water than cold. It was only one degree off for boiling water, but for ice water, this increased to two or three degrees. It worked well for the chicken leg in the air fryer, but I had issues with the burger. Not only did it leave a pair of large holes in the meat, but it also tended to hit the base of the pan when inserted from the top, throwing off the reading. I had more success piercing the burger from the side – awkward, but accurate. As such, it’s probably better for use with larger cuts of meat and joints.It didn’t make the final cut because …there are no real instructions for getting started or guidance on how far the probes need to be inserted.Water resistance?Yes, to IPX3;probe length:8cm;battery life:one to three years depending on batteries bought and frequency of use (2xAAA batteries, not included);recycling and longevity:one-year guarantee. At the end of its lifespan, ProCook will recycle it for free when you buy a new electrical item from it via itstrade-in/WEEE schemeProCookMeat thermometer grey fork£11£11 at ProCookWhat we loveA hanging hook saves drawer spaceWhat we don’t loveAAA batteries not includedLakeland digital in-oven kitchen thermometerLakelandDigital in-oven kitchen thermometer£27.99£27.99 at LakelandWhat we loveA loud alarm will definitely get your attentionWhat we don’t loveBatteries not includedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£27.99 at LakelandBest for:multifunctionalityIf you like your kitchen gadgets to do more than one thing, Lakeland’s digital in-oven kitchen thermometer should please you. When it’s not working as a thermometer, it doubles as a kitchen timer – just change it using the switch on the back. It also comes with a decent three-year guarantee, a handy leaflet of cooking guidance, a temperature range from -20C to 250C, and presets for different meats and doneness. It even has a fold-out stand on its rear, plus a small notch so you can hang it. However, the screen is hard to read – on a bright day, I found myself having to tilt it to see the display.Performance was mixed: it did well with boiling water, reading the same temperature as the thermocouple, although it was several degrees out with ice water. I struggled to position it in the chicken, and it shifted during cooking and needed reinsertion to get an accurate reading. The cable was too thick to use easily in the air fryer, too. It was awkward in a pan and slipped out of the burger when I flipped it, so it’s definitely one that’s just for the oven.It didn’t make the final cut because …a dim screen, even on full brightness, makes it almost impossible to read unless positioned at just the right angle.Water resistance?No;probe length:15cm;battery life:should last past the three-year guarantee depending on the batteries bought and frequency used(2xAAA batteries, not included);recycling and longevity:three-year guarantee. Lakeland doesn’t offer a repair service, and advises that the thermometer is thrown away in line with local waste disposal guidelinesLakelandDigital in-oven kitchen thermometer£27.99£27.99 at LakelandWhat we loveA loud alarm will definitely get your attentionWhat we don’t loveBatteries not includedThe rest of the testThose that didn’t make the cut in my testing include theSalter analogue meat thermometer(doesn’t require batteries or charging, but its dial didn’t offer as much information as others here, and it briefly malfunctioned in my test); plusSalter’s Precision meat thermometer, which performed brilliantly, but is identical in price and similar in spec to theHeston Blumenthal Precision meat thermometerabove. The Heston put in a similar performance but came with more guidance.Also missing is theETI RFXwireless. On a positive note, it uses radio frequency rather than wifi for a more stable connection, but it’s lacking in features compared with other wireless meat thermometers. The app is basic – there are no guided cooks, for example – and I didn’t find it especially user-friendly. It also requires exact placement in small items, or else it can give misleading data – I had to reinsert it mid-cook. I have includedETI’s Dot digital oven thermometer, though, and would always recommend itsThermapen, which is the thermometer I use for general cooking at home.What you need to knowView image in fullscreen‘Digital meat thermometers are more accurate than analogue and are quick to respond to temperature changes.’Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianWhat kind of meat thermometer do I need?The type of meat thermometer you choose will depend on what you might cook with it and how.Analogue or traditional meat thermometerswill be fine for infrequent users, or those who mainly cook joints of meat in the oven or on the barbecue. They’re durable, affordable, and don’t need to be recharged or have their batteries replaced. That said, they’re less precise than others and can be slow to respond to changes, which can lead to overcooking, plus the dial can get in the way under a grill or in a pan. They’re better than no meat thermometer at all, but could prove frustrating for a keen cook.Digital meat thermometersare more accurate than analogue, quick to respond to temperature changes, and may also come with extra features, such as a timer, alarm, or presets for different meats and levels of cooking. They’re available either as a stand-alone, instant-read probe or wired to a base, so that the probe can stay in an oven, pan, grill or barbecue – just always check the maximum temperature, particularly with wired models. Most cost less than £40 and are a good choice if you don’t need all the bells and whistles – and extra cost – of a smart wireless probe.Smart, wireless meat probesare designed to be used with a companion app for checking the temperature remotely. There may also be a separate base for monitoring, so you don’t always need to have your device to hand. They’re often pricey, but if you cook meat frequently, you’ll love the convenience of not being confined to the kitchen or grill. They’re the most versatile of the lot: many fit in smaller food items more easily; they work well in pans, grills and ovens; and apps will usually offer guidance for achieving the best results. Great for beginners and more confident cooks aiming to up their game.How to use a meat thermometerCorrect placement of a meat thermometer will return the most accurate reading, but this depends on what you’re cooking and the type of thermometer you’re using. Smart probes usually need to be inserted fully into the meat, up to a marked insertion line, while instant-read probes often only need the thin tip inserted so it reaches the centre of the food. Analogue meat thermometers typically need to be inserted deeper than instant-read models. Check the insertion guide for your particular model.The aim with most meats is to insert the probe into the thickest part, avoiding bone or gristle. For example, for a whole chicken, this would be through the thigh into the centre of the breast. While multiple insertion holes allow juices to leak out, don’t be afraid to take the meat thermometer out mid-cook and reinsert if the temperature looks too high too soon.How to clean a meat thermometerIt’s important to clean your meat thermometer when switching between pieces of meat to avoid cross-contamination. Wipe the probe with a hot, soapy cloth (don’t submerge), then rinse and dry with a kitchen towel to prevent bacteria growth. An alcohol wipe will do in a pinch.For stuck-on mess, soak the probe tip in hot soapy water to soften the residue before cleaning. Resist the temptation to scrub with harsh cleaners or pads – scratches on a probe create more places for bacteria to grow and can affect sensory accuracy.It’s advisable to clean a probe after every session: dip it in diluted bleach or distilled white vinegar (avoiding any electronic parts), then rinse under hot running water. Don’t forget to clean protective sheaths or covers since these can harbour bacteria, too.Can you use a meat thermometer for other foods?Yes, but not all foods. If you don’t have the budget for a cooking thermometer and a meat thermometer, the latter can be used for foods such as quiche, casseroles and desserts.However, they’re not usually suitable for liquids.Meatthermometer probes tend to be thicker and slower to react, which can lead to imprecise readings in liquids. In addition, they may not cover the temperature range.It’s also best to opt for a specialised thermometer for high-heat cooking, such as jam or caramel, or deep-frying. A meat thermometer may not have the upper range, plus high heat can damage sensors.Rachel Ogden has worked as a consumer journalist for decades, becoming an expert unboxer before it was a thing, although she is less successful at repacking. Her home has hosted hundreds of small appliances, fromair fryersand slow cookers to meat thermometers, while outside, you’ll find her messing about with barbecues andpizza ovens.
