title: ‘It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra’: why cinema loves the cello | Movies | The Guardian
description: From Audrey Hepburn to Pedro Pascal, cellists have become a movie shorthand for sensitivity, intensity and emotional depth. But why has Hollywood turned one orchestral instrument into a character in its own right?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Audrey Hepburn to Pedro Pascal, cellists have become a movie shorthand for sensitivity, intensity and emotional depth. But why has Hollywood turned one orchestral instrument into a character in its own right?
Content: Take a bow … Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenTake a bow … Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!Photograph: Album/AlamyMovies‘It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra’: why cinema loves the celloFrom Audrey Hepburn to Pedro Pascal, cellists have become a movie shorthand for sensitivity, intensity and emotional depth. But why has Hollywood turned one orchestral instrument into a character in its own right?Jonathan WellsThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a throwaway line in 2012’s The Avengers, after a character’s death, when his partner is alluded to. “There was a cellist, I think,” muses Robert Downey Jr’s Tony Stark. It’s a spot of pathos amid the punch-ups – but also rather telling. Because when even a superhero blockbuster reaches for the cello, you know the instrument is carrying more than just a melody.Earlier this month,a trailer droppedfor the upcoming Pedro Pascal drama Behemoth!, in which he plays a celebrated cellist returning to Hollywood to score films. Real-life cellist and film composer Hildur Guðnadóttir says the instrument “is definitely having a moment right now. But it’s always been present.”View image in fullscreenAudrey Hepburn in Love in the Afternoon.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIt’s true. And this cinematic love affair first found its rhythm almost 70 years ago, whenAudrey Hepburnplayed a witty young cellist in Love in the Afternoon. In the decades since, the instrument has become a marker for a certain type of character: cultured, intense, romantic, haunted. Think Alan Rickman in Truly, Madly, Deeply – or the titular cellist in the 1996 Czech drama Kolya, which won the Academy Award for best foreign language film. Even Woody Allen toyed with the stereotype; in Annie Hall, Carol Kane’s leftwing, liberal intellectual played the cello in a deleted scene.But why, out of every option in the orchestra, did the cello become the instrument of introspection? “It’s the cliche, but it’s probably because the cello comes closest to the human vocal range,” says Guðnadóttir. “It has this ability to play around with notes, too, like human intonation. Press a note on a keyboard and it’s straightforward, definitive. The cello – like our voices – can play with this intonation for expression.”Put an actor in a scene playing the cello, then, and they can deliver dialogue without words. Guðnadóttir says the only other instrument with this human timbre and “fluidity of intonation” is the bass clarinet. But you’re unlikely to see a protagonist reaching for one – nor a prestige biopic being made of a famous bass clarinettist. In fact, the cello has cornered the market on tragic orchestral stories – perhaps most notably in the Emily Watson-starring Hilary and Jackie.“That film, the story of cellist Jacqueline du Pré, is the cello film that has stuck with me most,” says Guðnadóttir. And it’s not the only cellist biopic to reach the screen. In 2009’s The Soloist,Jamie Foxxwas cast as musician Nathaniel Ayers, but the narrative was restrung, swapping his primary instrument – the double bass – for the cello.View image in fullscreenSuite soul … Emily Watson as Jacqueline du Pré in Hilary and Jackie.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyYou can see why. Not only does the cello have that uncannily human register, it’s also visually dynamic. A cellist’s bow strokes are physical and expressive, and the performer’s face is rarely obscured – making it a perfect screen partner.It’s probably why cellists tend to be the beating heart of musical dramas. Guðnadóttir also scored Cate Blanchett’s tour-de-force Tár, in which a cellist becomes the catalyst for the drama. Christopher Walken’s cellist, struggling with Parkinson’s, is the centrepiece of 2012’s A Late Quartet, and Dermot Mulroney (a real-life cellist who played on the scores of multiple Mission: Impossible films) frequently guest-starred in Prime Video series Mozart in the Jungle.View image in fullscreenHeartstrings … Jamie Foxx in The Soloist (2009).Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarBut cellist characters are not confined to musical dramas. The cello’s emotional shorthand has been transcribed across almost every genre: from Chloë Grace Moretz in sci-fi romance If I Stay, to Maryam d’Abo in 007 adventure The Living Daylights, to cellist love interests in sitcoms from Frasier to New Girl. And then there’s the darker side of the cello, whether channelled by Michelle Pfeiffer in supernatural thriller What Lies Beneath, Uma Thurman in neo-noir Jennifer 8 or Jenna Ortega in Netflix’s smash series Wednesday.“There is a gothic connection to the cello,” says Guðnadóttir, who won her Oscar for scoring Joker, a soundtrack that features the instrument prominently, with its neck being “choked”. “When it’s played in an ugly way – because we yearn for it to be this beautiful instrument – it feels uncomfortable.”Director Richard Shepard took that darker side one step further in 2018 with The Perfection, a horror set inside a prestigious music academy. When choosing the instrument his two leads would play, he wanted something both sinister and sensual.“I remember growing up on the Upper West Side of New York City, near Lincoln Center,” he says, “and seeing these young cellists on the subway, lugging these huge cases. It stuck with me. How big it is. How much effort it takes to not only play it, but just move it. When writing The Perfection, we felt that physicality could make a statement. It’s sexy. It’s a sexy instrument.”The film-makers behind the Allison Williams-starring horror film were determined to make the cello playing as convincing as the scares. “It was really hard work,” says Shepard, “but I’m proud there are only two shots of musicians’ hands rather than actors’ hands in the entire film.”View image in fullscreenHigh-toned … Alan Rickman in Truly, Madly, Deeply (1990).Photograph: BBC/AllstarThe cello is an instrument actors can’t bluff their way through – it’s harder to fake than hiding your hands behind a piano or overdubbing a singing voice. Ortega trained for Wednesday and earned Golden Globe and Emmy nominations. Watson trained for Hilary and Jackie and got an Oscar nod. Pascal recently told Vanity Fair that taking on the cello was “literally the hardest, hardest, hardest thing I’ve ever had to learn to do.” If he’s angling for awards, there are few better bets than a deep, introspective stringsman.And that perception extends beyond the screen. David Cohen, the principal cellist of the London Symphony Orchestra, says that “there’s definitely a stereotype that cellists are the orchestra’s empaths – warm, thoughtful and just a little bit intense. I’m not sure it’s entirely true, but it’s amusing that film-makers so often cast cellists as the emotionally intelligent ones. You rarely see the villain saying: ‘Just let me finish my Bach Suite …’”Cohen adds that the cello’s versatility often shapes the characters written around it. “It can sound noble, lonely, hopeful or quietly heroic – often within the same phrase,” he says. “It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra. And, because it has the depth to suggest sadness without wallowing in it, the cello is also film music’s favourite therapist.”Catherine Warner is a music therapy practitioner who has long watched the cello play its introspective, insular part on film. But she also points to the instrument’s role in memorable cinematic dialogues. In The Witches of Eastwick, a devilish Jack Nicholson seduces Susan Sarandon’s cellist during a duet, which Warner says “seemed to symbolise Sarandon’s character’s sexual awakening, as well as her discovery of authentic emotional expression – she had previously struggled to bring that into her playing”.In Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World, Paul Bettany plays a cello bass line under Russell Crowe’s virtuosic violin flourishes. Warner says this “symbolises a close supportive working relationship whereby the soloist can be freer to express their brilliance”. The cello, then, is a literal baseline: a “straight man” that performs whatever emotional function the story needs.View image in fullscreenDevilish … Jack Nicholson and Susan Sarandon in The Witches of Eastwick (1987).Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyWarner also returns to something she once wrote in a collection of essays: “Symbolically, the cello can evoke the sense of the instrument being rather like a person.” And this gets closest to explaining Hollywood’s obsession with the instrument. More than any other member of the orchestra, introducing a cello is like casting another actor in a scene. Guðnadóttir even says that “there’s something about the size of it being quite close to the human body – not to mention the shape of the cello almost looking like a torso.”Pair its resemblance to the human body with its similarity to our vocal range, and it’s no wonder cinema loves the instrument. It’s a character actor in and of itself. It can be embraced, fought, comforted or strangled. Now we just need to wait for the inevitable Oscar category: best bowed string instrument in a leading role. It’s either that, or Pascal runs the risk of having his cello nominated ahead of him.Explore more on these topicsFilmClassical musicPedro PascalAudrey HepburnJamie FoxxEmily WatsonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Labour says Reform ‘up to its neck in sleaze’ and demands investigation into donations | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Electoral Commission urged to look into donations made by mother of convicted fraudster
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Electoral Commission urged to look into donations made by mother of convicted fraudster
Content: Nigel Farage with George Cottrell (right, in sunglasses) in 2019.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyView image in fullscreenNigel Farage with George Cottrell (right, in sunglasses) in 2019.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyReform UKLabour says Reform ‘up to its neck in sleaze’ and demands investigation into donationsExclusive: Electoral Commission urged to look into donations made by mother of convicted fraudsterRevealed: George Cottrell transferred $2m to his mother days before her donations to Reform UKJessica ElgotDeputy political editorThu 30 Jul 2026 13.05 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour has accused Reform UK of being “up to its neck in sleaze” as it called on theElectoral Commissionto urgently investigate substantial donations made to the party by the mother of a convicted fraudster.Bridget Phillipson, Labour’s new chair, called on the commission to examine whether any rules had been broken, after revelations in the Guardian that George Cottrelltransferred more than $2m to his motherin the days before her donations to the party in 2024.ALabourspokesperson said Reform was “up to [its] neck in sleaze and dodgy money”.The commission has already made a referral to the Metropolitan police, who are looking into whether Reform may have been concealing or disguising donations derived from an “impermissible” donor.The Guardian has since reported that Cottrell’s mother, Fiona Cottrell, received several tranches of money adding up to more than $2m, which she attributed to her son, according to financial industry sources. Her son is a close ally and adviser toNigel Farage.Transfers were then made either directly to Reform or via Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle for the political party, according to sources.In her letter, Phillipson said the Guardian’s new revelations “may be relevant to the question of whether the true source of political donations made toReform UKhas been correctly identified and whether the statutory requirements governing permissible donors have been complied with”.A Labour spokesperson said it was now time for Reform to seriously address the allegations. “If these latest claims about George Cottrell are true, Reform may have taken money from a convicted fraudster who was the ultimate source of the donations,” the party said. “That would mean Reform accepted his money even though he has never shown he was legally allowed to donate to a political party at the time.“With every passing day it’s clearer that Reform think the rules don’t apply to them. They need to wake up and start treating these allegations with the seriousness they deserve and come clean about who is really bankrolling the party.”At a press conference on Thursday, Reform’s economics spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, ducked specific questions about the donations.In testy exchanges with reporters, he said the story “has been going on for a long time”, but he did not engage with the substance of the allegations.He told the BBC: “We are entirely confident that Reform followed all electoral rules at the time when the donations were made. Of course, we’ll participate with any inquiries. To the best of my knowledge, we haven’t even been contacted by the police, so I don’t think we have anything more to add to that.”Jenrick suggested that journalists should be questioning George Cottrell, and said they should return to the intended subject matter of the press conference, which was social care. “Reform is certain that all the electoral rules were followed,” he told ITV. “If you’ve got a question for Mr Cottrell then I think you have to direct that to him.”The Met’s investigation is examiningdonations to Reform, including those from Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle whose director is the party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice. The firm gave Reform two donations of £250,000 in the run-up to the 2024 general election. These were first revealed by the Guardian.Cottrell, who was convicted for fraud in the US, now lives in Montenegro but is seen often alongside Farage. He has previously been described as Farage’s chief of staff but Reform has maintained that he is only a volunteer.Asked about the transfers, lawyers for Cottrell said their client had no further comment.In previous legal correspondence, Cottrell has not denied giving his mother – who is understood to be of relatively modest means – large sums of money. Instead, he said via lawyers that “any political donations his mother has made have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”.Fiona Cottrell has not responded to several attempts by the Guardian to contact her.Asked on Wednesday for a response to the story, a Reform spokesperson said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with all donations.”Farage isfighting a byelectionafter resigning his seat of Clacton. All other mainstream parties have declined to stand a candidate against him, though there are 34 independents on the ballot paper, including novelty candidates such asCount Binface.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageParty fundingElectoral CommissionLabourBridget PhillipsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to free mayors from ‘Treasury death grip’ with new devolved powers | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Local leaders say plan will transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projects
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Local leaders say plan will transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projects
Content: Andy Burnham at the Submarine Academy for Skills and Knowledge at BAE Systems in Cumbria today. He will announce his devolution plan on Friday.Photograph: Chris Furlong/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the Submarine Academy for Skills and Knowledge at BAE Systems in Cumbria today. He will announce his devolution plan on Friday.Photograph: Chris Furlong/PADevolutionBurnham to free mayors from ‘Treasury death grip’ with new devolved powersLocal leaders say plan will transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projectsJosh HallidayNorth of England editorThu 30 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s regional mayors will be able to break out of the “death grip of the Treasury” by borrowing to invest in big projects under “transformational” plans to shift power out of Whitehall.For the first time, mayors will keep a share of income tax generated in their area from 2028, as well as business rates totalling tens of millions of pounds by April 2027.These will replace existing grants rather than being additional money, but local leaders said no longer relying on ringfenced Treasury handouts would “transform” their funding.Oliver Coppard, theLabourmayor of South Yorkshire, said: “It’s really important because it gets us out of the death grip of the Treasury and gives us that long-term certainty around income.”Andy Burnham will announce the measures on Friday as part of what he called “the biggest transfer of power from Westminster in a generation”.He said: “Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community. Soon, every local leader will have the power and resources to improve public transport, build homes and create jobs.“I know what it’s like to be ignored by politicians in Westminster. I’m not going to make that same mistake now I’m PM.”Under a new “local first” principle, Burnham will instruct ministers to justify why powers should remain in Whitehall rather than be devolved.As well asgreater control over technical education for teenagers, announced by the government this week, some of those close to the prime minister have called for mayors to oversee schools, GPs and childcare providers through health and education commissioners – a similar role to that played by police and crime commissioners.No 10 said Britain’s civil service of 520,000 would become “smaller and more strategic” as decision-making moves out of London, where one in five of these officials are based.England’s directly elected mayors, who control areas spanning three-quarters of the population, would be able to use the revenue generated from business rates and income tax as they wish, including tax breaks for important industries or rebates to residents.However, experts said one of the most significant consequences was that it would allow combined authorities to take out 30-year loans against their projected income to fund major projects that previously needed Treasury approval.Mayors said they were currently prevented from funding huge initiatives on housing and transport because they could not take out private loans on the basis of one-year funding settlements from Whitehall.Henri Murison, the chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the change “completely transforms” what combined authorities would be able to do.He said the ability for mayors to borrow against future income could unlock huge transport projects such as an underground station at Manchester Piccadilly.It is not yet clear what proportion of income tax or business rates would be retained by combined authorities, with officials still working on the numbers. John Healey, the chancellor, is expected to set out the detail in the autumn budget.Ben Houchen, the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley, suggested he would use the income tax to hand out tax rebates to local people.However, it is understood that this would be technically extremely difficult given mayors do not know how much individuals have paid in tax. Also, because the income tax revenue is not additional money for mayors but is replacing government grants, it is more likely to be spent on long-term projects than giveaways to residents.Ministers are considering ways to ensure less economically productive areas such as Humberside and north-east England are not left behind. If mayors received 2.5% of the 20p basic rate of income tax, London would get £2.3bn in 2026-27 while Hull and East Yorkshire would get £135m, according to areport last monthby the thinktank Re:State.The thinktank IPPR North described the move as “the most significant shift in how England is funded in a generation”.Policy experts previouslysaid rushing ahead with fiscal devolution risked creating a “two-tier England”, potentially leaving behind roughly a quarter of the country’s population that did not have a mayoral authority.The government is planning to encourage these areas – spanning millions of people in Dorset, Somerset, Oxfordshire, Gloucestershire, Wiltshire and parts of Kent – to form mayoral authorities in order to benefit from greater autonomy over their funding.Since 2024, only two combined authorities – Greater Manchester and West Midlands – have been able to keep all of the business rate income generated in their areas.In Greater Manchester, this amounted to £100m in 2024-25, the first year of operation. Three-quarters was retained by each of the 10 local authorities and £25m was kept by the mayoral authority and spent on projects.Explore more on these topicsDevolutionAndy BurnhamLabourTax and spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: French riot police used teargas on people trying to board small boat, charity claims | Migration | The Guardian
description: CRS officers funded by UK tried to stop boarding of boat, on day four asylum seekers died trying to cross Channel
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: CRS officers funded by UK tried to stop boarding of boat, on day four asylum seekers died trying to cross Channel
Content: Footage released by Utopia 56 purports to show migrants and police clashing in CalaisMigrationFrench riot police used teargas on people trying to board small boat, charity claimsCRS officers funded by UK tried to stop boarding of boat, on day four asylum seekers died trying to cross ChannelRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 30 Jul 2026 15.20 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench riot police funded by UK taxpayers used teargas on asylum seekers in an attempt to stop them from boarding a boat in which three women were later found dead, a charity has claimed.Footage and photographs seen by the Guardian show CS gas canisters being fired towards groups of people on Plage du Braek near Dunkirk at 4am on Thursday. At 6am, three women were found dead in a boat near the same beach.According to the charity Utopia 56, which took the images, staff witnessed French riot police firing the canisters at people who were trying to board the same boat in which the bodies were discovered.As part of a £660m agreement signed by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in May, 50 officers fromCompagnies Républicaines de Sécurité (CRS)“specially trained in the use of riot and crowd control tactics” have been deployed using UK public money.In a separate development, a fourth person – a man – also died on Thursday when his dinghy got into difficulty in a separate incident off the coast of Dannes.The incidents happened hours after the busiest day for small boat crossings so far this year, which totalled 752 arrivals in the UK.View image in fullscreenPeople thought to be migrants are rescued from the sea on Thursday after they attempted to board a small boat from the beach near Dunkirk.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAClashes between riot police and asylum seekers took place on roads leading to Plage du Braek from 4am, Utopia 56 said.Angèle Vettorello, a coordinator at the charity, said: “An hour before the boat carrying the women’s bodies was found, our team was right next to the beach. Riot officers from the CRS were there and were trying to stop 80 people, including families, from trying to access the beach and those people were trying to get inside the boat.“We saw them using teargas against people and later we found at least 35 teargas canisters there. We do not know if the women whose bodies were discovered were already in the boat or were part of the group trying to reach the beach. We can see police pressure on the beach is putting more people at risk. We saw it last week and we are seeing it now and we have seen it for some time. It is terrible.”The CRS has faced allegations of brutality and racism. In February, nine officers from the force were found guilty of beating peaceful protesters who were sheltering from teargas during the “gilets jaunes” anti-government demonstrations in 2018. Two years ago, leaked WhatsApp messages showed CRS officers had exchanged an image of a sinking small boat laden with migrants.The CRS, although paid for by the UK, maintains “operational independence” inFranceand are also authorised to use water cannon, stun grenades and batons.The French interior ministry and the Home Office have been approached for comment.View image in fullscreenPeople leave the sea after failing to board a small boat from the beach near Dunkirk on Thursday.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAThe boat on which the women’s bodies were found was brought into shore at 6am. The bodies were brought ashore after the French emergency services, including firefighters, police and paramedics, mounted a rescue.Attempts to resuscitate the women failed and all three were declared dead. They were reported to be aged about 20, 30 and 50. Their nationalities are as yet unknown.The man who died was in a dinghy that capsized as people attempted to board. It had arrived from Sainte-Cécile, a beach farther south, with people already aboard. It is believed to have departed from Berck, a further 13 miles south.Six other people, including a one-year-old child, suffered minor injuries, the French authorities said. Some of those onboard were taken to hospital and a man with burns over half of his body was airlifted by a navy helicopter.Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said: “Refugees are ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances, and those who risk dangerous small boat journeys do so only out of desperation. There is no legal way for somebody escaping the Taliban in Afghanistan or brutal civil war in Sudan to reach sanctuary in the UK.“The government has even shut down family reunion for refugees, which overwhelmingly helped women and children. Fewer refugees would risk crossings if the government created safe pathways.”On Wednesday Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, insisted the government’s plan to curb Channel crossings was working, although he admitted there was “more to do”.This week French police were recorded saying they had orders not to stop people getting into their boats and setting off for the UK. One told Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, as he stood on Hardelot beach, south of Boulogne-sur-Mer: “Our order is to let them go.”More than 900 people have crossed the Channel in the past week as people smugglers take advantage of a calm sea. A total of 13,376 migrants have crossed this year, down from 24,389 at the same point last year.A government spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened to hear about these deaths. Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit.“We will continue working relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys.”Explore more on these topicsMigrationImmigration and asylumFranceWater transportEuropeRefugeesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds evacuated after ‘apocalyptic’ wildfire near Suffolk nuclear power station | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: Major incident declared, with Sizewell B power station monitoring blaze and RSPB nature reserve badly hit
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Major incident declared, with Sizewell B power station monitoring blaze and RSPB nature reserve badly hit
Content: A helicopter lifts water from the sea to spread on the Dunwich Heath fire, with Sizewell B nuclear power station in the background.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA helicopter lifts water from the sea to spread on the Dunwich Heath fire, with Sizewell B nuclear power station in the background.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianSuffolkHundreds evacuated after ‘apocalyptic’ wildfire near Suffolk nuclear power stationMajor incident declared, with Sizewell B power station monitoring blaze and RSPB nature reserve badly hitPippa NeillandCaroline DaviesThu 30 Jul 2026 15.46 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 03.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of people have been evacuated and a major incident declared after a wildfire spread over more than 80 hectares (200 acres) on the coast ofSuffolk, just a few miles from the Sizewell B nuclear power station.The fire – which had been described by one witness as “apocalyptic” – was said to be stabilising on Thursday night. The statement was posted by Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service, which said at least 12 fire crews were remaining overnight in the area.Jon Lacey, the chief fire officer at Suffolk fire and rescue, said earlier in the evening: “The wind change has helped a little bit, unexpectedly, and also a helicopter [dropping water] is helping to dampen the fire down.”View image in fullscreenBathers watch the wildfire from Dunwich beach in Suffolk.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThe wildfire came a day after half of England was declared to beofficially in drought, including East Anglia and six other areas. On Thursday, Natural Resources Wales declared a drought across the whole of Wales, which is on course for itsdriest Julysince records began nearly 200 years ago.As the climate crisis supercharges “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather, the UK and Europe are seeing back-to-back heatwaves that encourage vegetation to grow but then dry it out, producing ideal fuel for fires.Firefighters have responded to 393 wildfires across England and Wales in July, making it the busiest month on record and placing significant pressure on crews and resources.Phil Garrigan, the chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council, said: “Wildfires are no longer isolated or seasonal events. They are becoming a recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities and emergency services.“As climate and environmental conditions continue to change, we must ensure our fire and rescue services are equipped to meet that challenge.”Map of the blaze showing the position of the nuclear power stationIn France, the fires around Bordeaux continued to smoulder on Thursday, while Spain and now Turkey are dealing with major blazes.In Suffolk, crews were called to reports of a fire at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, shortly after 5.30pm on Wednesday and that night a number of homes were evacuated.Rob Tucker, who has a cottage at Cliff House holiday park, said: “We were evacuated at 10pm. One of the guys that works at the holiday park came along and said we were being evacuated. Everything’s been left behind apart from my cars and the clothes that we were wearing.”A nearby caravan park was also evacuated on Thursday and residents opened up their homes to help. Andrew Turner, the chair of Westleton parish council, said: “I had two families in my house. Two families and two dogs. There are now pillows and stuff in the village hall but the objective is to get everyone into houses. The council is still taking names of people who are willing to put up rooms.“We’re a tightknit community, it’s great to see the community come together, I wouldn’t expect anything less.”View image in fullscreenEvacuees from homes and holiday parks gather at Westleton village hall in Suffolk.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThe damage to wildlife is expected to be considerable because the fire hit the RSPB’s Minsmere nature reserve.The charity’s area manager, Adam Rowlands, said: “The heathland habitat where the main fire is is home to really special and rare species in the UK, birds like nightjars, nightingales and Dartford warblers.“It’s absolutely devastating to see this damage compared to last night when the fire started, I saw a 20ft fireball burning through the trees, with nightjars flying away from the fireball. Last night I stood on the heath and it was apocalyptic, the sky was orange, the smoke was billowing, it could be seen and smelled 20 miles to the north.”Firefighters say there is not thought to be any danger to Sizewell B, which is a few miles from the blaze. A spokesperson for EDF, which operates the site, said the wildfire was not affecting operations and was being closely monitored. It is understood Sizewell B has an emergency plan that covers a range of scenarios including a fire on site.Freddie Gulliver, from the Suffolk Joint Emergency Planning Unit, said there was currently no concern that the fire might spread towards Sizewell B. “Sizewell is not a risk, a concern, currently at this stage,” he said. “From the meetings we’ve had at the moment, that hasn’t been a concern.”View image in fullscreenA fire engine returns from the Dunwich Heath blaze.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianPeople have been urged to avoid the area where possible and keep windows and doors closed.Andy Burnham promised support to firefighters on Thursday. Speaking to reporters during a visit to Cumbria, the prime minister said: “We’ve got the situation under close monitoring, and I’m receiving regular updates. It is a very serious incident.”Dr Zakary Campbell-Lochrie, a lecturer in fire science at the University of Edinburgh, said: “This wildfire is occurring at the same time as drought conditions have officially been declared in large parts ofEngland, including Suffolk.“The hot, dry weather conditions, including the multiple heatwave events across much of the UK in recent weeks, lead to strong drying conditions for vegetation, which can subsequently be highly susceptible to ignition and can present a much greater danger when fires do occur.”The climate crisis, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, is making heatwaves more intense and more frequent. A fortnight ago, the Reform-led Suffolk county councilvoted to rescinda climate emergency declaration that had been adopted in 2019 and removed references to the climate emergency from council policies, strategies and communications “where appropriate”.On Thursday, the UK Health Security Agency saidEngland was on trackto record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer.Explore more on these topicsSuffolkFirefightersWildfiresEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netflix sued for $105m over stolen Nicolas Cage war thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: Makers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles office
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Makers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles office
Content: Nicolas Cage.Photograph: Jeff Vespa/@portraits/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNicolas Cage.Photograph: Jeff Vespa/@portraits/ShutterstockMoviesNetflix sued for $105m over stolen Nicolas Cage war thrillerMakers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles officeBenjamin LeeThu 30 Jul 2026 15.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflixis being sued for $105m over the theft of a hard drive including an unreleasedNicolas Cagewar movie.The streamer’s Los Angeles office was the target of a theft involving a number of hard drives, one of which contained a copy of second world war spy thriller Fortitude.The makers of the $45m-budgeted film are now suingNetflixover the loss.“Netflix disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards,” a spokesperson said in a statement shared with theHollywood Reporter. “While we do not own the rights to Fortitude, we take content security seriously and have taken extra measures to support the film-maker and his team. This includes conducting a thorough investigation and offering to monitor known piracy sites for any unauthorized distribution or sale.”Netflix reportedly received a copy of the film in June after expressing interest in promotional materials at the end of last year. A digital copy was then sent so the film could be screened internally with the film’s producers instructing Netflix to delete the files afterward.Sean Berney, head of Netflix film acquisitions, wrote in an email that it was a first for the company to be the subject of such a theft. “We’ve been working through this with our security teams to no luck,” he added. “Our piracy teams are on high alert with the breach and will monitor.”Netflix is accused of failing to disclose details of whether a police report was initially filed as well as later declining a request by the film-makers to involve the LAPD after they filed their own report.The lawsuit claims that any future sale of the film has now been put in jeopardy with any international release strategy and awards campaign paused.“The resulting damage to plaintiffs is profound,” the lawsuit said, according toPage Six. “Through its mishandling of the film and subsequent dismissiveness, Netflix has jeopardized plaintiffs’ investment of over $45m and the significant value of the film itself. Netflix has also deprived the film, its cast and its creators of the opportunity to bring their work to market and receive recognition that a properly marketed worldwide release likely would have generated.”Fortitude is a London-set espionage thriller focused on British intelligence operatives changing the course of the second world war. Cage stars alongside Matthew Goode, Michael Sheen and Ben Kingsley. The film is directed by Simon West, whose previous credits include Tomb Raider and The General’s Daughter.Martin Scorsese was at one point attached to the project but was then the subject of alawsuitclaiming he took $500,000 from first-time screenwriter Simon Afram to help develop the film but failed to do so. Scorsese’s lawyers called it a “classic example of the novice film-maker who refuses to appreciate the stark difference between expectation and reality in the film-making business”. It was later settled.“I spent seven years of my life bringing this incredible true story to the screen,” Afram said in a statement. “But this film was never mine alone. It belongs to the extraordinary cast and their performances of a lifetime that deserve to be seen and recognized. It represents the moment these artists have earned.”Explore more on these topicsFilmNetflixNicolas CageUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian missile destroys US firm’s Kyiv drone factory | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Strike on Terminal Autonomy plant appears to be first time in the war that Moscow has targeted a US company
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Strike on Terminal Autonomy plant appears to be first time in the war that Moscow has targeted a US company
Content: A deep-strike drone. The plant hit by Russia made AQ-400 Scythe and AQ-100 Bayonet deep-strike drones (not pictured).Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenA deep-strike drone. The plant hit by Russia made AQ-400 Scythe and AQ-100 Bayonet deep-strike drones (not pictured).Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUkraineRussian missile destroys US firm’s Kyiv drone factoryStrike on Terminal Autonomy plant appears to be first time in the war that Moscow has targeted a US companyAram Rostonin WashingtonThu 30 Jul 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA drone factory in Kyiv destroyed by a Russian ballistic missile on Friday was owned by a US corporation registered in Delaware, in what appears to be the first time Moscow has targeted a US company in the conflict.Terminal Autonomy makes precision “deep-strike” drones with guidance systems that are resistant to Russian jamming signals, according to a person familiar with the company.The phrase “terminal autonomy” refers to the final phase of a kamikaze drone’s attack in which AI takes over control of the weapon after the defending force jams radio waves or mobile service.State records show that the corporation was registered in Delaware in 2023. The company’s website says: “We deploy AI-guided loitering munitions and precision munitions, which are already in active service against enemy assets on the frontline.”Terminal Autonomy did not reply to an emailed request for comment. The Ukrainian defence ministry also did not respond to an email.Anthony Vinci, a former senior US intelligence officer who wrote The Fourth Intelligence Revolution: The Future of Espionage and the Battle to Save America, said: “The Russians don’t care who owns the manufacturing facility. It’s still a target. They don’t care if it’s American or someone else’s.”Early in July, Donald Trump, who had previously been lukewarm to efforts to arm Ukraine, said the US would license Ukraine tomanufacture Patriot anti-aircraft missiles.Vinci said: “I do think if Patriot missiles or any American system was manufactured inUkraine, I think the Russians would target that manufacturing facility.”The Russian state news agency Tassfirst reportedon the attack on Sunday, citing the Russian defence ministry as its source. The report did not disclose that an American company owned the factory but mentioned that “specialists from a Ukrainian-American company” had worked there. Tass accurately reported that the plant made AQ-400 Scythe and AQ-100 Bayonet drones.Nobody was killed in the attack, according to a source familiar with the company.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa agrees to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceed | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Uefa nations have agreed to boycott all Fifa tournaments if the global governing body continues with its plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Uefa nations have agreed to boycott all Fifa tournaments if the global governing body continues with its plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup
Content: Spain’s Dani Olmo with the World Cup after their victory over Argentina in New York.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenSpain’s Dani Olmo with the World Cup after their victory over Argentina in New York.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoUefaUefa agrees to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceedUefa agrees stance at emergency meeting on ThursdayBoycott would begin with Under-20 Women’s World CupNick AmesandMatt HughesThu 30 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean countries have agreed to boycott all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino pushes forward with his proposals to sell chunks of the World Cup toUS-based private investment.In an extraordinary development all 55 Uefa members resolved not to participate in future World Cups or other Fifa-run events, saying in a statement that they “unanimously and unequivocally reject” the proposals. An emergency meeting that lasted just short of two hours ended with a united front despite earlier fears that smaller countries, attracted by the money on offer through Infantino’s scheme, would be swayed in favour.European FAs are expected to write toFifathis week with a formal notification of their threat to boycott future tournaments unless the planned World Cup sell-off is withdrawn.Fifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s gameRead moreIt means Infantino faces an uphill battle to push his plan forward. Countries had been given until 19 September to sign up but there will now be significant pressure to drastically revise his scheme or withdraw it completely. While the majority of European FAs had submitted letters of support in favour of his re-election next March, such a decisive line in the sand fromUefaweakens his position dramatically.Uefa’s statement confirmed the decision. “As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” it read.Thursday’s meeting was introduced by the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with executive committee members and Uefa’s Fifa council representatives also addressing delegates. Those early speeches are understood to have set the tone, with around 20 further FA heads taking the floor and multiple sources describing an atmosphere of “unity”. Among those to offer their view was Debbie Hewitt, the president of the FA, who one attendee said gave a “very tough” exposition in favour of a boycott.That was backed up in a statement by an FA spokesperson that read: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”Along the lines spelled out by Uefa, at senior level the proposed boycott would begin with next year’s Women’s World Cup, while the first age-group Fifa tournament to be boycotted is likely to be the Under-20 Women’s World Cup. It is due to take place in Poland from 5 September with six of the 24 competitors, including England, due to represent Uefa countries.England’s women’s team also have a two-legged World Cup qualifying playoff tie against Greece in October, which would be a major test of the FA’s resolve if Fifa refuse to back down.The European governing body invited other confederations to follow their lead. Uefa are understood to be confident that a number of Asian countries, in particular, are similarly minded. Infantino’s strongholds traditionally lie outside Europe and a collapse in support elsewhere could have severe consequences for the Fifa president.“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences,” Uefa said. “This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.”Sources within European football believe Uefa’s decision increases the chances of a Europe-backed candidate running against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, which he had been expected to sail through without opposition.The North, Central American and Caribbean confederation, Concacaf, also unanimously rejected Fifa’s proposal after an emergency meeting chaired by the president, Victor Montagliani, who is seen as a potential successor to Infantino, but stopped short of following Uefa’s lead by announcing a boycott.Despite this, it is understood that the majority of Concacaf’s 41 members are losing confidence in Infantino’s leadership of Fifa, raising the possibility that his own position could be in serious doubt for the first time since he took office in 2016.A number of European national associations are understood to have held talks with their respective governments over the matter, many of whom have backed a boycott in private.The new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was the first politician to criticise Fifa’s plan on Tuesday evening, writing on X that the World Cup “was never anyone’s to sell”.“This is a principled decision that we strongly support. Football belongs to the fans, not billionaire investors. Enough is enough. It’s time to take a stand to protect our game.”Explore more on these topicsUefaWorld CupFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content
