title: ‘It was a big shock’: new border rules left couple stuck in Kraków after living in UK for 80 years | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Maria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to Bury
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Maria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to Bury
Content: Maria and Czeslaw Krupa with two family members  outside the Tauron Arena in Kraków.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyView image in fullscreenMaria and Czeslaw Krupa with two family members  outside the Tauron Arena in Kraków.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyBrexit‘It was a big shock’: new border rules left couple stuck in Kraków after living in UK for 80 yearsMaria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to BuryLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Polish citizens who have lived in the UK for nearly 80 years after their parents fled the second world war have spoken of their terrifying experience after being told they did not have post-Brexit rights to return to the UK.In May, while visiting Poland, they learned that although they had been welcomed as refugees after the war, they now needed special post-Brexit paperwork to return to their home in Bury,Greater Manchester.Maria Krupa, 85, and her husband, Czeslaw, 92, who met in the UK and went on to marry and settle in Bury, were issued with “aliens’ registration cards” and have travelled extensively as adults without anyone asking them for their immigration status.View image in fullscreenMaria and Czeslaw Krupa in Kraków airport.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyCzeslaw, who came from Lviv which was then part ofPoland, and Maria, who left her home town in what is now Belarus as an infant, had travelled to Poland in May to meet surviving family members.But Ryanair refused to allow them to board the flight for their return journey on the grounds that they had neither proof of the right to live in the UK nor thenew electronic travel authorisation(ETA) now required for foreign tourists entering the UK.“It was a big shock,” said Maria. “We were very, very disappointed and a bit upset because my husband takes a lot of medicine because of a stroke to his spinal cord.”They had arrived in Southampton in 1947 and 1948 as the young dependants of displaced Polish service members who had been evacuated from their homes in 1940 and later became part of Gen Władysław Anders’s Polish army that served in Persia, India, the Middle East and Africa.Anders’s army played a key role in the defeat of the Third Reich and had integrated into the British military command structure after friction with the Soviets in 1942.“We tried to explain toRyanairthat our fathers fought for Poland and England in the war, but they refused to let us on the plane because they said they would have to pay a big fine,” said Maria.“My husband was really upset,” she said, explaining that Czeslaw used a mobility scooter and was on a lot of medication after the stroke. He has difficulty getting in and out of cars and “just wanted to get home”, she said.View image in fullscreenCzeslaw Krupa, left, with his brother and cousin in Africa in 1944.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyThey are speaking out to help others who might be in the same position. “It was a big, big shock because we never heard of this and we never thought for one minute that after nearly 80 years someone would tell us we couldn’t go home,” said Maria.Kate Smart, the chief executive of Settled, who helped the Krupas, said the charity was seeing “thousands of cases” like the Krupas’. “It is a really common occurrence, almost on a daily basis,” she said.The EU settlement scheme was launched in 2019 to give EU citizens living in the UK the documentary evidence needed to travel as they had done under the pre-Brexit, free-movement rules.Many of the people seen by Settled are elderly people who have British children and grandchildren. “They have nobody in their family circle who thinks like immigrants so they don’t talk about things like ‘settled status’,” said Smart.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMaria Krupa as a child in Karachi, then part of India, where her father was stationed in 1943. Displaced Polish people were housed in refugee camps.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyMaria said she had never thought to get a British passport as she had never needed it in the previous 80 years and it had never crossed her mind. “It was really important. I didn’t think of it as sort of weakening my identity. I love England. I mean, I always say, I’m very grateful to England, you know, to have taken so many people, you know thousands after the war. But I just thought it was important that we stay Polish,” she said.After being forced to leave the airport late on a Sunday night in May, they returned the next day with an ETA but the couple had to pose as tourists, claiming they lived in Poland as the online form would not accept their British address.View image in fullscreenMaria and Czeslaw Krupa celebrate Czeslaw’s 90th birthday in Bury.Photograph: Image courtesy of the Krupa familyMaria said: “When we arrived in England we were terrified. We had to be careful about what we said. We were terrified because they started asking questions and we thought we are not going to lie again and have to tell the truth.”After going to Citizens Advice in Bury, they were connected with Settled. Smart commended theHome Officeresolution centre for its swift action after the charity submitted a no-time-limit application that resulted in settled status for the Krupas last week.She appealed to the government to take note of the issues with the EU settlement scheme, arguing “a process should have kicked in at the airport” when an issue such as this one arose.A spokesperson said the Home Office would encourage people to check their immigration status before they travel, but anyone in a similar situation to the Krupas should makea no-time-limit applicationto get the paperwork they needed to travel in and out of the country.“Anyone settled in the UK without up-to-date evidence of their status is encouraged to make a no-time-limit application. This will give them access to an eVisa and facilitate seamless future travel,” they said.Explore more on these topicsBrexitHome OfficeImmigration and asylumEuropean UnionForeign policyEuropeSecond world warfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my brother stop hogging the living room while staying in my flat? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Daniella doesn’t want to go to bed early. Seamus says she shouldn’t offer the sofabed if she doesn’t want guests. Who has room for improvement?
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Daniella doesn’t want to go to bed early. Seamus says she shouldn’t offer the sofabed if she doesn’t want guests. Who has room for improvement?
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my brother stop hogging the living room while staying in my flat?Daniella doesn’t want to go to bed early. Seamus says she shouldn’t offer the sofabed if she doesn’t want guests. Who has room for improvement?Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prosecution: Danielladouble quotation markIt’s not that I don’t want him here, but he needs to understand that I am giving up my space to host himMy younger brother Seamus is staying with me in my flat for six weeks. He’s a teacher and lived with me for a bit last year, before moving to Dubai.When he lived with me before, we split the bills and mortgage, which was a great help as I was in a tricky spot as a freelancer. He needed somewhere to live after our parents sold their house, so I turned my living room into a bedroom for him.After he moved out, I used it as a living room again. Now, he’s come back to see friends and family. I bought a sofabed for his stay, which set me back £400. While I like having him here, there has been some tension.double quotation markI don’t feel it’s fair to ask him for a financial contribution, but I wouldn’t say no either if he offeredSeamus immediately started changing things around in the flat. He turned up the temperature in the shower and I burned myself. He moved the chopping boards back to where he used to store them. He took the spare keys I was using, so I got locked out.I like going to bed around midnight, but Seamus wants to go to sleep at 10.30. On the first night, he asked to go to bed at 9.55pm, which meant I had to leave the room and stop the show I was watching. I kicked off. He said: “I’m tired and deserve my own space too.” But it’s not really his room any more. And he wasn’t fresh off the plane – he’d been staying with friends.It’s not that I don’t want him here, but he needs to understand that I am giving up my space to host him. I do appreciate Seamus helping out around the flat when he’s staying with me. He waters my flowers and does odd jobs. He’s not messy, but I have to ask him to pack away the sofabed every morning so I can use the room in the evenings.He’s no longer a lodger, but he’s not quite a guest either. I don’t feel it’s fair to ask him for a financial contribution, but I wouldn’t say no if he offered. He has no bills or outgoings and his rent abroad is paid for.Going back to living with someone 24/7 is a big adjustment. I’m single, and I’d started to enjoy spending time on my own. Am I being selfish or is my irritation reasonable?You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThe defence: Seamusdouble quotation markIf you say someone can be a guest in your home, you can’t take it back when it doesn’t suit youI need somewhere to stay when I’m back and I’d rather stay with my sister than our parents, who have moved to the country. I think Daniella was a bit put out because I originally said I would move between the two homes, but it’s easier for me to stay in one place.I understand she is giving up her living room, so I make sure I leave it as I found it and put away the sheets and sofabed every morning. I’ve tried to make myself useful around the flat. I have cooked, bought food and done the gardening. I’ve bought things too – for example, I put up some shelves.I guess she wouldn’t be stressed if things were less tight for her financially, and as I don’t have any outgoings or bills I understand why she might appreciate a contribution. I don’t mind chipping in towards the bills, but she hasn’t said how much she wants.double quotation markI didn’t mean to change things around. I adjusted the water settings on the shower, then forgot to turn it back downLast year, moving in made sense for both of us: I didn’t have anywhere to go and she needed a flatmate to help pay the bills. I paid about £900, which was just under half of her monthly outgoings of £1,875 for her mortgage and bills.I didn’t mean to change things when I came back. I adjusted the water settings on the shower because I prefer it hot, then forgot to turn it back down – it was accidental. As for moving the chopping boards, I didn’t even think about it. How was I to know she had moved things about since the last time I was here?When she got upset with me for kicking her out of her living room so I could go to sleep, I was confused because she had said the room was mine during my stay. She either wants me here or she doesn’t. If you say someone can be a guest in your home, you can’t take it back when it doesn’t suit you.I have adjusted my bedtime to around 11pm, which works better. And Daniella has said that if she wants to watch something that goes on later, she will give me advance notice. I think that will help us live harmoniously for the next six weeks.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersIf Seamus wants his own space, he should pay for somewhere else to stay. Letting Daniella watch her TV shows is a small price to pay for free accommodation. He should make the effort to fit around her lifestyle – including finding out where the chopping boards live!Phoebe, 24Seamus needs to work on his communication. Even if he previously lived there, he doesn’t any more and should act accordingly. Changing the shower settings and taking keys without saying is a massive overstep. However, Daniella should compromise on the early bedtime.Aleah, 30Staying in someone’s home, even as a family member, is a privilege. It’s their home, not yours. The 11pm compromise sounds reasonable if you have different sleeping patterns. It’s fair for Daniella to be paid rent (discuss it together) and for Seamus not to change things around.Maggie, 59Daniella needs to remember that a kind gesture cannot be given with strings attached. Seamus asking for his own space in the evening is reasonable, and he’s doing what he can to be a good guest. Assuming Daniella’s shows are on a streaming service, she could always watch them on a different device.Ellie, 29Daniella has kindly welcomed her brother into her home, but it seems no discussion has been had about her expectations. Six weeks is a long time to have a guest, so it’s important they have their own space and set boundaries.Saeid, 38Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: should Seamus stop lounging around?The poll closes on Wednesday 5 August at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked ifFay should stop queuing for hours to get a good spot at concerts23%of you said yes –Fay is guilty77%of you said no –Fay is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgeFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shaboozey: The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales review – a striking addition to the rich canon of country concept albums | Music | The Guardian
description: Beneath the Hollywood narrators, Pink Floyd-y interludes and accompanying comic books lies songwriting that proves the Tipsy singer’s breakout success was no fluke
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Beneath the Hollywood narrators, Pink Floyd-y interludes and accompanying comic books lies songwriting that proves the Tipsy singer’s breakout success was no fluke
Content: Darkly atmospheric and powerful … Shaboozey.View image in fullscreenDarkly atmospheric and powerful … Shaboozey.Alexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewShaboozey: The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales review – a striking addition to the rich canon of country concept albums(American Dogwood/Empire)Beneath the Hollywood narrators, Pink Floyd-y interludes and accompanying comic books lies songwriting that proves the Tipsy singer’s breakout success was no flukeAlexis PetridisThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s fair to say that if Shaboozey never released another note of music, his place in history would still be assured.He wasn’t the only Black country-leaning artist brought to a wider audience by a guest appearance on Beyoncé’s 2024 album Cowboy Carter, but no one else capitalised on the exposure quite so remarkably. Released two weeks after his guest appearance on that album’s Spaghettii, his single A Bar Song (Tipsy) unexpectedly eclipsed Beyoncé’s success, becoming the biggest-selling country single of the year – more than 1.75bn streams and counting on Spotify – and for a time, the joint longest-running US No 1 of all time. He’s received three nominations at theCountryMusic awards, an event traditionally resistant to artists of colour. The accompanying album, Where I’ve Been, Isn’t Where I’m Going, was by far the most successful sustained attempt to fuse hip-hop and country, two genres that have been warily circling each other for some time, spawning the occasional novelty hit such as Nelly and Tim McGraw’s Over and Over Again, the Ludacris-featuring 2010 remix of Jason Aldean’s Dirt Road, and Lil Nas X’s Old Town Road; the baleful, rap-influenced spectre of bro country; and the deep underground sub-genre of hick-hop, a hidden world of Maga politics, confederate flags and festivals held at Georgia mud holes. The album is still on the US chart, 112 weeks after its release.View image in fullscreenShaboozey: The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales.Understandably, its success has led Shaboozey to swing for the fences two years on. The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales is a 20-track concept album, accompanied by a three-issue comic of the same name. It features scene-setting interstitial tracks: cinematic and orchestral, ambient and Pink Floyd-y, with weeping pedal steel subbing for David Gilmour’s trademark mournful string-bends. There’s narration by actors Jamie Foxx, Teyana Taylor and Sam Elliott, the latter going some way to ameliorate the traditional problem with concept albums: that the listener quickly loses the thread of the narrative and spends most of the album listening without a clue what’s supposed to be going on.Country got to concept albums long before rock did. Marty Robbins’ thematically linked Gunfighter Ballads and Trail Songs were released in 1959, Johnny Cash’s Bitter Tears in 1964 – and they loom large in the genre’s history. Willie Nelson’s Red Headed Stranger, the 1975 saga of a murderer on the run, is regularly voted the greatest country album of all time; many major artists, including Emmylou Harris, Kenny Rogers and Dolly Parton, have at least one in their catalogue. You could thus view The Outlaw Cherie Lee as a concerted effort to pivot away from pop into country’s heartlands, albeit while still featuring a heavily Auto-Tuned guest appearance by rapper Gunna on High Noon (“spent a hundred thou on clothes / I got bad hoes,” he offers, presumably not referencing farming equipment). Cowgirl and Born to Die are two obvious – and, it has to be said, remarkably charming – attempts to replicate the success of Shaboozey’s biggest hit: “Got another bar song for you,” he notes by way of introduction to the former. Bullets and Blades, meanwhile, is a big and strikingly beautiful ballad with Shaboozey duetting with R&B star Kehlani.Elsewhere, The Outlaw Cherie Lee is more purely country: If I Was an Outlaw has saloon-bar piano, Sweet Revenge goes country rock, while the closing track is a burst of the traditional cowboy ballad Streets of Laredo sung by Orville Peck. The album’s predominant mode is stark and brooding, driven by fingerpicked acoustic guitar and decorated with fiddle. At their best, these tracks are darkly atmospheric and powerful – as on Drunk – although it’s occasionally hard not to feel that part of Shaboozey’s USP has gone with his decision to dial down the rap influence in his vocals. He can certainly croon with a glowering power, but there’s a distinct leap in excitement when he reverts to a hip-hop-inspired delivery, the better to inhabit the character of a swaggering outlaw on Til Sunday.How gen Z women are conquering country music: ‘Fans are speaking louder than gatekeepers’Read moreStill, as a demonstration of his eclecticism – or, if you prefer, a desire to be all things to all people – The Outlaw Cherie Lee works well. The pop-facing tracks hit, the strike rate when he diversifies is higher than his naysayers would suggest, and there’s an impressive boldness about his evident desire to draw R&B, soul and hip-hop artists into his world – aside from Gunna and Kehlani, there’s an impressive turn from Leon Bridges on Burn It Down. The overarching storyline is tight and well handled. Perhaps most importantly, the album never feels like the work of an artist whose career has been destabilised by a huge, unexpected and unrepeatable hit, but rather the work of an artist digging in for the long haul.What Alexis listened to this weekMr Wa7t – Secrets (Richard Norris Fitness Mix)The original is great soulful, deep pop, but Richard Norris’s remix turns it into delightfully smooth, hot-afternoon Balearic: very much what is needed at the moment.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekCountryRapPop and rockHip-hopalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gunther von Hagens obituary | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: German anatomist who devised a system of ‘plastination’ to preserve cadavers that were exhibited all over the world
Author: Mick O'Hare
Headline: German anatomist who devised a system of ‘plastination’ to preserve cadavers that were exhibited all over the world
Content: Gunther von Hagens was known by some sections of the media as ‘Doctor Death’.Photograph: Agencja Fotograficzna Caro/AlamyView image in fullscreenGunther von Hagens was known by some sections of the media as ‘Doctor Death’.Photograph: Agencja Fotograficzna Caro/AlamyExhibitionsObituaryGunther von Hagens obituaryGerman anatomist who devised a system of ‘plastination’ to preserve cadavers that were exhibited all over the worldMick O'HareThu 30 Jul 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe German anatomist Gunther von Hagens, who has died aged 81 of a cerebral haemorrhage, following nearly two decades of living with Parkinson’s disease, was the creator of the international exhibition Body Worlds, which generated plaudits and revulsion in equal measure whenever and wherever it toured. Frequently accused of showmanship and self-aggrandisement, the theatrical Von Hagens, always seen wearing a black fedora, was known by some sections of the media as “Doctor Death” thanks to his use of a technique called “plastination”, which he had invented to preserve human corpses. Bodily fluids, fats and organs that usually decay after death were replaced with plastics, so tissues remained intact. The corpses could then be put on display, usually with the skin peeled away to reveal skeletons, organs and muscles.Plastinated corpses remain flexible, meaning they can be manipulated into lifelike poses – a basketball player or a trapeze artist – or sliced into cross sections. But Von Hagens often trod a fine line between scientific exposition and the macabre. Other exhibits included a dead expectant woman with her foetus still in her uterus and a man who had deliberately killed himself by driving into a tree at the place his wife had died previously. Both had donated their bodies for plastination and were exhibited along with the objects that caused their deaths.Unsurprisingly, Von Hagens and Body Worlds – which first went on display in Japan in 1995 – were considered somewhat contentious. Religious leaders denounced him. Churches in his native Germany held requiems for the corpses. The chief rabbi of Haifa described plastination as a violation of the Jewish principle ofkavod adam, or human dignity, while the Catholic archbishop of Miami deemed Von Hagens would, when arriving at the gates of hades, be treated as he had treated his subjects, unaware that the anatomist had already expressed a wish for his own body to be plastinated on death.He was also disparaged by secular critics who simply found his work repugnant, with the Nobel laureateGünter Grassreported to have compared him to the Nazi eugenicist Josef Mengele. The journalist Jasper Gerard wrote a particularly caustic article in the Sunday Times in 2002, concluding that “the moral problem is not how Von Hagens treats the dead, it’s what [his exhibition] says about his view of the living”.Others acclaimed Von Hagens as an emancipator and normaliser of the human physique. The Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio said he “illuminated physiology and helped us grasp the anatomical elegance of our species”. One visitor to Body Worlds, who had tried to take her own life, declared that the exhibits convinced her never to consider harming herself again. At the time of Von Hagens’s death, it was estimated more than 20,000 people had pledged to donate their bodies to him – including family members and his employees – while more than 58 million people have visited Body Worlds. The exhibition even featured in the 2006 James Bond film, Casino Royale, in which Von Hagens played a cameo role.Over the years many legal challenges were brought against him and Body Worlds in various countries over both his acquisition of cadavers and the morality of his exhibitions, including accusations that he received corpses from Kyrgyzstan without the permission of family members or the authorities. He insisted that all corpses in his possession were donated with full consent. However, in 2002 Von Hagens wasaccused of accepting 56 corpsesfrom a Russian pathologist who had apparently passed them on to him without approval. The bodies were impounded by German officials and returned to Russia. Von Hagens was not charged with an offence.View image in fullscreenVon Hagens with members of the audience who paid to watch him perform a public autopsy at the Atlantis gallery, London, in 2002.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMeanwhile, in 2002 Von Hagens held apublic postmortemof one of his subjects – the first public autopsy in the UK since the 1830s and broadcast in part by Channel 4 – in the Atlantis art gallery in east London before a sold-out audience of 500. This, it was argued, breached the Anatomy Act of 1832 introduced to regulate educational use of cadavers. Once again charges were never filed.Born in Alt-Skalden, which was then part of Germany, but is now in Poland, where the town is known as Skalmierzyce, Gunther was the third of five children. His father, Gerhard Liebchen, formerly a bank clerk, was a wartime sergeant in the Nazi SS, his mother, Gertrud, was a homemaker. Having fled the advancing Soviet army towards the end of the second world war, the family lived in Berlin before settling in Greiz, a town in what would become communist East Germany.Gunther was a haemophiliac – once given only days to live – and spent much of his childhood in and out of hospital. This stimulated an interest in medicine, specifically anatomy, and after leaving school in 1965 he studied medicine at Jena University, having witnessed his first human autopsy at the age of 17. While at university he began questioning the orthodoxy of communism and participated in protests against the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.The following January he made attempts to escape eastern Europe, twice failing to cross the Czech border into Austria. He was arrested and spent almost two years in prison.On his release, the West German government bought his freedom, alongside other political prisoners, and he continued his degree at Lübeck University, later earning a doctorate from Heidelberg University in 1975. This was where he met Cornelia von Hagens, another medical student, who became his wife that year, and whose surname he took. They had three children, Rurik, Bera and Tona, before divorcing in 1989.After graduating, Von Hagens became a lecturer at the Institutes of Pathology and Anatomy at Heidelberg where, between 1977 and 1982, he developed and patented the technology for infusing anatomical specimens with plastics. The technique had obvious practical medical uses. Students could view damaged hearts or scarred livers without waiting for somebody to donate their body, while entire corpses could also be sliced into slabs for study.Von Hagens subsequently set up a company to supply plastinated body parts to medical institutions and eventually began to realise his technique might have commercial value via exhibitions and practical demonstrations of his methods. In this he was aided by his second wife, Angelina Whalley, a German anatomist whom he met after she attended his anatomy classes, and whom British tabloids typically nicknamed “the Bride of Frankenstein”. She managed his Heidelberg-based business and later curated his exhibitions after they married in 1992.Despite being accused of unnecessary dramatic flair, Von Hagens, an avowed agnostic, insisted his sole intention was to educate the public about human anatomy and to end the squeamishness often associated with it. “It’s an honour to cause this controversy,” hetold the Guardian in 2002at the opening of his London exhibition. “Yes, some specimens are difficult to look at. But it has helped people discover new respect for their bodies.”In later life he divided his time between Berlin and Guben, on the Polish border, where he had set up a plastination laboratory. Beyond his medical and business life, his interests were limited, although he enjoyed playing and listening to violin music.Angelina and his children from his first marriage survive him.Gunther Gerhard von Hagens, anatomist and businessman, born 10 January 1945; died 24 July 2026Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsMedicineobituariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It makes you feel you’ve got a really dirty house’: what’s behind the UK’s plagues of flies? | Insects | The Guardian
description: From Leicestershire to Carmarthenshire, neighbourhoods are struggling with wave after wave of houseflies. Why are they suffering while others are spared? And is there no alternative to nets and zappers?
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: From Leicestershire to Carmarthenshire, neighbourhoods are struggling with wave after wave of houseflies. Why are they suffering while others are spared? And is there no alternative to nets and zappers?
Content: Short-term solution … Fly paper won’t tackle the source of an infestation.Composite: Arterra Picture Library/AlamyView image in fullscreenShort-term solution … Fly paper won’t tackle the source of an infestation.Composite: Arterra Picture Library/AlamyInsects‘It makes you feel you’ve got a really dirty house’: what’s behind the UK’s plagues of flies?From Leicestershire to Carmarthenshire, neighbourhoods are struggling with wave after wave of houseflies. Why are they suffering while others are spared? And is there no alternative to nets and zappers?Lucy KnightThu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrancesca Davies’s living room is absolutely teeming with flies. You can’t enter the contact centre worker’s home without a cluster of insects rising from the sofa or the floor to buzz around your face. Davies and her family live in West Heath, a suburb of the Cheshire town Congleton. Davies’s husband, Alex Andrew, a 29-year-old maintenance engineer, grew up in the market town and he used to think of West Heath as a desirable area, with its well-maintained houses and access to green space. When he and Davies were able to buy a new-build here in 2019 via a shared ownership scheme, they felt incredibly lucky. That is, until they moved in, and realised that every summer swarms of flies descend on their neighbourhood, an issue that is “getting worse”, Davies says.At the moment, the 27-year-old swats flies out of her young daughters’ bedroom every night before she puts them to bed, and keeps doors and windows closed or covered with fly nets as much as possible. She and Andrew have even bought an industrial fly killer (like the ones often found in fish and chip shops) for their kitchen, as it is impossible to start cooking without attracting even more insects. The pair have become used to the sound of flies “getting zapped throughout the night”, Davies says.View image in fullscreenFrancesca Davies outside her home in Congleton, Cheshire.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe family have considered moving out of the area because of the flies, and say some of their former neighbours already have. But Davies is reluctant to give up on the house that is her “pride and joy”, she says. “It is a wonderful place to live. West Heath is so pretty, and everyone’s so lovely.”Not to mention, “You would have to sell it in the winter,” Andrew points out, as prospective buyers would surely be put off by flies swarming around during a viewing. Instead, Davies is attempting to put pressure on the council and the Environment Agency to investigate bysetting up a petition, which now has more than 1,000 signatures, asking local authorities “to take this matter seriously and to prioritise our community’s wellbeing”.The petition has attracted a number of comments from other local people, including one who lives a 20-minute walk away from Andrew and Davies. “I’m shooing 40-plus flies out of my kitchen regularly throughout the day,” the commenter says. “It’s a constant battle.” Andrew says he has spoken to many neighbours who are struggling with the problem: one orders takeaways every day in the summer to avoid having to cook, while another has draped their newborn baby’s cot in a mosquito net. “They’ve all had enough,” Andrew and Davies’s neighbour Bryan Stahl says, when we walk over the road to his house, which the street’s residents generally consider to be the worst affected by the infestation.Fly infestation in Congleton - loopThough it’s hard to believe as we swat flies away while we chat, today is a relatively mild day for flies, Stahl tell me, because it is breezier than it has been in recent weeks. At the height of the recent heatwave, the 54-year-old and his partner stayed inside, or in garden chairs under a gazebo walled with fly nets. Davies and Andrew have a similar structure for their garden, which they set up when their daughters want to use their paddling pool. Stahl, a higher level teaching assistant in a school, has spent about £500 on the gazebo and numerous fly screens, he thinks – and is considering forking out thousands more for permanent fly shutters. “It makes you feel like you’ve got a really dirty house,” he says.Even though you would be hard-pressed to find anyone as anti-fly right now as the residents of West Heath, it’s not as if flies are popular with many people. Whether it’s Jeff Goldblum’s gruesome transformation into a fly in David Cronenberg’s 1986 horror film The Fly, or God sending swarms of flies as one of the 10 plagues inflicted on the Egyptians to persuade the Pharaoh to set the Israelites free in the Old Testament, the messaging is clear: flies are disgusting.But could they be due a rebrand? After all, bees can be just as buzzy and annoying, and even sting us, but that doesn’t seem to have damaged their “cute” reputation, their likeness printed on T-shirts or tablecloths. Like bees, flies are pollinators and “essential to a healthy planet,” says Andrew Whitehouse, head of operations at the invertebrate conservation charity Buglife. In fact, he adds, there are some plants that areonlypollinated by flies – including the cacao tree. “So if you didn’t have flies, you wouldn’t have chocolate.”And though we might find it gross that flies are so attracted to faeces or rotting matter, it is actually a good thing that they are. “Fly larvae or maggots will eat lots of dead organic material,” Whitehouse says. “In doing that, they’re recycling nutrients back into the soil, they’re getting rid of those things like dead bodies and dung. That prevents the spread of disease as well. So it’s incredibly important.”In addition, “loads and loads of other animals eat flies”, Whitehouse says. “Spiders spring to mind, but lots of vertebrates as well. So birds and bats and amphibians and reptiles and fish all feed on either adult flies or their larvae. And they’re a really important food source for lots of these animals.”View image in fullscreen‘Everyone’s had enough’ … Bryan Stahl.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThere are more than 7,000 species of fly found in the UK, including bluebottles, greenbottles, hoverflies, mosquitoes, fruit flies and crane flies (daddy longlegs). Houseflies (your classic chunky black fly; probably what comes to mind when most of us think of a fly) are generally considered the UK’s most common, although it is difficult to say for sure, because “weirdly, not enough people study flies”, says Erica McAlister, a fly expert and Natural History Museum curator.Houseflies are important pollinators all over the world – in fact, McAlister says, a cousin of the common houseflyis the dominant pollinatorin the Arctic. “People are stuck on bees being the most important pollinators – and they are good, I’m not going to deny that,” she says. But while bee larvae don’t do anything except consume food until they have grown into their adult form, flies are “kicked out at birth”, and as larvae “they’re out there already helping clean up our environment”. And for anyone stuck on the idea that flies aren’t as cute as bees, she urges them to “go andlook up a bee-fly”, which she says is “arguably one of the cutest species in the UK”.double quotation markIf insects die, we are on a downward spiral very quicklySure, a fly that has been “walking from faeces to food or decomposing food to another food” could be transporting pathogens, McAlister admits – but in “much the same way as if you handle money or if you go into a pub or if you shake hands with people”. As for flies “vomiting” on food, another complaint you often hear from fly-haters, it is not “vomiting” in the same way we think about humans throwing up, she says. “They’re not bringing up gut contents”, but releasing digestive enzymes on to food to break it down, “because they do not have biting mouth parts – they basically have a straw or a sponge with which they can suck up these ingredients.”Instead of dwelling on flies’ negative associations, she says, “I try to get people to think of them as like, ‘It’s amazing, you’ve got these wild animals roaming around in front of your face.’” McAlister encourages people to learn about flies’ “fascinating” metamorphosis from larvae to adult fly, or the fact that they can land upside down, or that their eyes consist of thousands of facets that act like individual cameras. Every second, “they are processing thousands upon thousands of images”, she says.It is all the more important to think positively about flies given that insects as a whole, including flies, are largely in decline. Although some migrant species are bucking the trend, the UK’s local species that rely on specific host plants or locations are “suffering badly” as the country becomes less accommodating to wildlife, McAlister says. “We need our politicians to really work at encompassing all of their decisions with an ecological framework,” she believes. And that’s in order to protect our own future, not just the future of flies: “If we die, insects won’t care,” McAlister says. “But if insects die, we are pretty much on a very downward spiral very quickly” – because of our reliance on their pollination services.View image in fullscreenAlex Andrew, who has swathed his daughters’ paddling pool in fly nets.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianMcAlister is not saying that we should all be living like Davies and Andrew. She is well aware that flies en masse can be a problem – but killing them, particularly in “a horrible and inhumane way” such as via fly tape, isn’t always the answer. Paradoxically, creating fly-friendly environments such as ponds in gardens, or even “a bucket on the veranda”, invites all kinds of wildlife, she says, including fly predators like birds and frogs, so flies actually get eaten and end up bothering humans less.“There is an argument” for pest control when it comes to fly infestations, she says, but the most important thing to do is to “find out why that’s happened. Because the flies are an indicator that maybe something else is going on.” When fly infestations are reported, as they are every summer (currently, residents inSileby, LeicestershireandLlanelli, Carmarthenshireare suffering along with those in West Heath), usually a link can be found “to some sort of waste event or some sort of environmental perturbation”, the curator says.Tick bites are on the rise in the US and UK. Here’s how to protect yourselfRead moreDavies and her neighbours think their fly problem is connected to a local recycling plant run by the company Tandom. In a statement sent to the Guardian, Tandom says it has “implemented a range of additional precautionary measures”, and is “working constructively with the Environment Agency, Cheshire East council and our independent pest control specialists”, but emphasised: “There is currently no evidence that flies are breeding on our site.” A spokesperson for the Environment Agency confirmed that it is in touch with Tandom, and says it has instructed the company “to take immediate steps to tackle the issue”, adding that it “will not hesitate to take appropriate enforcement action if required”.Rather than automatically blaming flies when they bother us, we should look for potential human involvement, McAlister thinks. While we often think of house flies as dirty because they feed on faeces and are found in dirty areas, they actually “have to be the absolute opposite – they have to be exceptionally clean because they are sometimes in a bad environment”, she says. “But it’s our environment; we’re the ones who’ve made this environment. So, you know, we’re throwing stones at an indicator that something has maybe gone wrong.”Perhaps it’s humans, then, not flies, who are the true pests.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsInsectsHousingCommunitiesAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have to become warriors’: the fight to save the world’s only women’s sculpture park | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With most monuments in London made by men, Claire Mander envisaged the Artist’s Garden as a way to redress the balance. Now, she says, it could be turned into a generic space for VIP events and cocktails
Author: Anita Chaudhuri
Headline: With most monuments in London made by men, Claire Mander envisaged the Artist’s Garden as a way to redress the balance. Now, she says, it could be turned into a generic space for VIP events and cocktails
Content: ‘It has never occurred to me not to work on a large scale’ …  Lakwena Maciver with her installation at the Artist’s Garden at Temple in London in 2021.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreen‘It has never occurred to me not to work on a large scale’ …  Lakwena Maciver with her installation at the Artist’s Garden at Temple in London in 2021.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAArt and design‘We have to become warriors’: the fight to save the world’s only women’s sculpture parkWith most monuments in London made by men, Claire Mander envisaged the Artist’s Garden as a way to redress the balance. Now, she says, it could be turned into a generic space for VIP events and cocktailsAnita ChaudhuriThu 30 Jul 2026 06.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years ago, when Claire Mander was studying for an art history MA at the Courtauld Institute inLondon, she stumbled upon the neglected roof terrace of nearby Temple underground station. She found herself strangely drawn to the overgrown expanse with its stunning views of the Thames and the London Eye.“It was dirty, abandoned and a magnet for antisocial behaviour,” recalls Mander, now director and curator of theColab, an arts charity and incubator specialising in large-scale outdoor sculptures. She researched the history of the abandoned space, which was built as part of the Victoria Embankment in 1870. Before that, the ground beneath the site housed a 17th-century sculpture garden created by the Countess of Arundel.“It inspired me to visualise how the roof terrace could become a really special women’s sculpture garden,” says Mander. “The ‘hidden in plain sight’ nature of the location felt to me like the perfect place to redress some of the gender disparity that we see in public artworks.”View image in fullscreen‘Hidden in plain sight’ … view over the the Artist’s Garden in central London.Photograph: theCOLABA survey byArtUK revealed that of almost 1,500 monuments in London, more than a fifth were dedicated to named men and only 4% were dedicated to women, half as many as those that celebrated animals. And of all the public sculptures in London, only 13% were created by women.Mander kept badgering Westminster council until eventually they gave her the go-ahead. With funding from donations and over £500,000 to date from the council, the Artist’s Garden opened in October 2021. It is the world’s first and only public sculpture garden devoted to the work of female artists. Since then they have attracted 100,000 visitors a year, commissioned 18 major works, and collaborated with 24 different emerging and established artists.But now, theColab has been informed by Places for London, Transport for London’s property arm, that their licence to occupy the site will not be renewed on 1 October and they must clear the garden.View image in fullscreenTechnicolor forest … Alice Wilson’s Savoy on show at the Artist’s Garden.Photograph: theCOLABA Places for London spokesperson said: “The terrace and station roof may now require essential repair and safety works, and the space needs to be cleared for the assessment of the extent of the works required. We are working with Westminster city council and local stakeholders to explore alternative locations nearby for the Artist’s Garden, while also developing future plans for the terrace at Temple. As a legally protected space, it will always remain accessible to the public.”Mander disputes this, stating that the repairs relate to upgrading the commercial property below the terrace, and that according to the scope of works, no large-scale overhaul of the roof is mentioned. She believes the space is at risk of being handed over to a private developer. “It’s a prime location with incredible views of the river, ideal for VIP events selling overpriced cocktails. They don’t understand that this is a landmark project. Their perception seems to be that we’re a small, pathetic female-led charity that’s doing some sort of nice little sculptural things. But we are prepared to take this to court if it comes to it.” They have launched a campaign and petition to save the garden.Alexandra Hodby, head of programmes at YorkshireSculpturePark and a trustee of the gardens, points out that such spaces are of vital cultural and economic value, both to artists and to the cities they inhabit. “Look at the High Line in New York. It wasn’t even a public space, then it was made public through art. Artists activated it. Now it’s one of the most visited places in the city.”Hodby believes that sculpture has a particular power to engage the public in a way that art on gallery walls does not. “There’s an immediacy about it, there’s no separation between the work and the world.” This is true. On the day I visit, London is in the grip of a heatwave. Office workers, builders on an early lunch, bemused tourists, all throng the space. A toddler crawls towards Mexican artist Adeline de Monseignat’s pebbled Croissant, no doubt spying a potential see-saw. In the distance, I spot people posing for selfies beside Alice Wilson’s Savoy, a giant forest of technicolor timbers.View image in fullscreenAdeline de Monseignat’s Up-Up showing at the Artist’s Garden.Photograph: theCOLAB“Obviously, seeing art made by women inspires other women who want to make art themselves. But it goes far beyond that,” says Hodby. “Representation is about being part of a public space and being seen. Visibility allows visitors to see themselves, be it the Artist’s Garden or Yorkshire Sculpture Park where we endeavour to show a broad range of artists including non-binary, queer practice and younger artists.”Lakwena Maciver created the site’s opening exhibit, a kaleidoscopic mural titled Back in the Air: A Meditation on Higher Ground. It unfurled across the entire 140 sq-metre space. For the British-Ugandan artist, the site holds particular emotional significance. “When I was a teenager, we would get the train up to town and I remember sitting in Embankment Gardens eating Skittles with my sister. I’d be thinking about my future but also feeling that, as a minority, London didn’t belong to me. To be asked to do the mural was very special because I was being invited to contribute something so monumental. It was like, I do belong! It has never occurred to me not to work on a large scale but I had so many positive interactions with visitors at that site, it gave me a lot of confidence.”View image in fullscreen‘A place to reflect’ … the Artist’s Shed at the Artist’s Garden.Photograph: theColabArtist Florence Peake created work for the site’s current show Sculpture in Three Acts. “It’s rare these days in London to find a public space that is free and doesn’t have a commercial agenda. It’s a place to reflect, take a breath and be with artworks that may draw you in, and hold space for a state of reflection.”She believes the garden has provided a much-needed space. “It allows visitors to see that women can make huge monolithic work. Of course we can! It’s just that so often we’re not trusted to be ambitious and do things to scale. Our visions are often rejected and considered naive. This is what I’ve encountered in my 30 years of being an artist anyway. A man comes along and says ‘I want to build a big steel thing sticking 18 metres up in the air’ and he’s hailed as a genius. A woman suggesting the same thing, there are anxious sideways glances.”At the heart of the garden is the artist’s hut, currently featuring a wraparound photomontage created by feminist artist Linder Sterling. “The Artist’s Garden is situated in Temple, once the province of the Knights Templar,” she says. “It seems that women have to become warriors now and defend our right to take up space there.”Presiding over the back wall of the montage is a portrait of the Countess of Arundel, reminding us of the lineage of women who have gone before. “On one of the walls of the hut, you can see the phrase ‘She Is Here’, the title of the work, writ large,” adds Sterling. “Now that the site is under threat, She Is Here has become a rallying cry - we’re not going anywhere.”Explore more on these topicsArt and designSculptureWomenArtLondonTfLfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The outlook gets better and better at Rolls-Royce | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: With fingers in various highly lucrative pies, maybe the firm becoming LSE’s most valuable isn’t as fanciful as it seems
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: With fingers in various highly lucrative pies, maybe the firm becoming LSE’s most valuable isn’t as fanciful as it seems
Content: Well beyond making engines for widebody aircraft, Rolls-Royce is squarely positioned in the defence, AI and nuclear energy sectors.Photograph: Nadja Wohlleben/ReutersView image in fullscreenWell beyond making engines for widebody aircraft, Rolls-Royce is squarely positioned in the defence, AI and nuclear energy sectors.Photograph: Nadja Wohlleben/ReutersNils Pratley on financeRolls-RoyceThe outlook gets better and better at Rolls-RoyceNils PratleyWith fingers in various highly lucrative pies, maybe the firm becoming LSE’s most valuable isn’t as fanciful as it seemsThu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareTufan Erginbilgiç, the chief executive of Rolls-Royce, seemed to be getting ahead himself when hesaid a year agothat the engine-maker had the potential to become the most valuable company on the London Stock Exchange.Yes, everyone knows about the remarkable turnaround. Rolls was a corporate calamity during the Covid shutdown of global aviation, then a tenfold increase in the share price followed under Erginbilgiç. But it still required a leap of imagination to think the firm could challenge the very top of the capitalisation charts one day.And it still requires work. Today’s valuation of £120bn puts Rolls roughly neck and neck with the miner Rio Tinto for fourth place in the Footsie, but there is still a big gap to Shell (£185bn), AstraZeneca (£198bn) and HSBC (£274bn), none of whom intend to stand still.Erginbilgiç’s long-term bullishness, however, sounds less fantastical with every set of results.Thursday’s half-year numberscame with the usual upgrade to financial forecasts. Cashflow over the full year will be £200m better than previously predicted at £3.8bn-£4bn; for operating profits, the increase was £700m to £4.7bn-£4.9bn. Those upgrades suggest there is still mileage in Erginbilgiç’s efforts to invest in the reliability of the engines to allow a “win-win” renegotiation of contracts with airlines.The long-term growth projections, however, rely on many other things – way beyond widebody-aircraft engines – going well. Defence looks a safe bet, naturally. The sight of the prime minister at Barrow-in-Furness on Thursday served as a reminder that Rolls makes the nuclear propulsion systems for the UK’s submarines. The rest of the country’s defence investment plan, whatever the wrangles over the precise budget, is unambiguously good news for Rolls too. There are possibilities in propulsion systems for uncrewed aircraft and much more.The division that is suddenly getting most attention, though, is power systems. It used to be seen as a maker of boring old-tech diesel systems for marine vessels and military tanks. But AI datacentres in the US also want the equipment. And they also want Rolls’s gas-fired turbines for primary power as they struggle to get hooked up to an under-invested US electricity grid. Rolls’s order book for power generation was up 55% in the half.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProfits boost for UK defence firms as governments increase spendingRead moreIt looks, too, as if there will be spillover AI benefits for Rolls’s small modular reactors (SMRs). At 470 megawatts, SMRs were originally intended only as sources of low-carbon power for national grids, but some hyper-scale datacentre projects in the US are so huge and power-hungry that they have become potential customers. It gives Rolls a foot in several AI power camps: diesel for back-up; gas for primary power; and SMRs when they arrive in the 2030s.The very big possibility is Rolls’s intendedre-entry into the market for engines for narrowbody aircraft. That is a slower story because Airbus and Boeing have yet to commit formally to new single-aisle models. Nor it is guaranteed that Rolls would win a place as an engine supplier given the competition from incumbents.But the potential market is enormous – many times the size of the widebody one – which is why Rolls’s requests for financial support from the UK Treasury will almost certainly be granted, never mind that corporate welfare for a company awash with cash-for-share buybacks sounds an aberration. In reality,subsidies are a fact of lifein the international aerospace business, a point that will surely not be lost on a reindustrialising prime minister. Think of the potential for 40,000 jobs in UK advanced manufacturing, runs the corporate pitch.If it all comes together, then, yes, Erginbilgiç’s projections for Rolls’s potential are not as wild as they seem. The company is positioned squarely at the centre of “major global trends”, as he puts it: defence, AI and energy transition via nuclear. One of these days, something will go wrong, just as it did regularly at Rolls for about two decades. But it is also impossible to name another major UK company with huge opportunities on various fronts.In retrospect, the Treasury missed a trick in 2020. Instead of granting loan guaranteesto help Rolls out of its Covid financial hole, the UK state could have made a few billion quid by insisting on bonds that converted into shares.Explore more on these topicsRolls-RoyceNils Pratley on financeAerospace industryAI (artificial intelligence)Energy industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham the crowd-pleaser knows how to make friends, but he’ll be defined by how he makes enemies | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The prime minister’s instinct to not upset people is set against a lifelong desire to effect transformative change. The two may not sit together easily, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The prime minister’s instinct to not upset people is set against a lifelong desire to effect transformative change. The two may not sit together easily, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Andy Burnham on a visit to Alstom Transport in Derby on Tuesday, as the government launches new technical educational routes for young people.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham on a visit to Alstom Transport in Derby on Tuesday, as the government launches new technical educational routes for young people.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/PAOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham the crowd-pleaser knows how to make friends, but he’ll be defined by how he makes enemiesAndy BeckettThe prime minister’s instinct to not upset people is set against a lifelong desire to effect transformative change. The two may not sit together easilyThu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.50 EDTShareAndy Burnham has always liked to be liked. Studying at secondary school near Liverpool in the 1980s, he writes in his autobiography and manifesto,Head North, “involved me walking something of a tightrope. Because of my mum and dad’s insistence that I should aim for university, I would largely try to keep up to date with my work. But … I realised I could often make the class laugh and that won me credit with the in-crowd. It was hard to be both a good student and one of the lads.”As the new leader of a divided country, he is still trying to appeal to opposing interests while establishing his own, upbeat brand. “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity,” he said in hisfirst speech outside 10 Downing Street. After a post-Brexit decade dominated by angry rightwing politics, Labour infighting, never-ending culture wars and online acrimony, Burnham’s affable, seemingly inclusive politics has a strong initial appeal. This week, for the first time in 18 months,Labour is ahead of Reform UKin the polls. It’s possible that some voters have finally had enough of divisive politics and would like to try something different.As an insecure party, temperamentally and electorally,Labouris periodically drawn towards a politics of national unity. “New Labour is the political arm of none other than the British people as a whole,” claimed its general election manifesto in 1997, managing to sound both wildly over-confident and anxiously self-justifying. Lacking the Tories’ right to rule aura and association with deep Englishness – even though those politically priceless qualities depend on a deliberately partial reading of history – Labour tries to make its governments seem more legitimate by using patriotic, non-partisan language. Yet only its most articulate and assured leaders, such as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and perhaps now Burnham, successfully pull this off.Yet unlike Blair in 1997 and Wilson in 1964, Burnham is not launching a fresh Labour project in relatively benign economic and political times, and aiming to keep the status quo broadly intact. Instead, he is trying to rescue a two-year-old administration by promising “a new political model and a new economic model”, and “the biggest changes [in Britain] in the last 40 years”. None of these can be done, it seems reasonable to assume, without challenging many of the old order’s beneficiaries. So how is his politics of unity likely to fare once he starts making lots of enemies?Those may include shareholders of privatised utilities, wealthy owners of under-taxed homes, people who like London’s national dominance, leaders of other parties who don’t want Burnham’s “more collaborative” politics, and journalists who prefer reporting on Westminster plots and rivalries rather than the progress of reforms in the rest of the country. The instantly hostile, sometimes hysterical reaction from much of the press and most other parties to his initial, relatively modest and non-partisan policy proposals gives a hint of the fury coming his way. As Gordon Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer all painfully learned, any Labour leadership even fractionally to the left of Blair’s in any policy areawill be widely presented as areturn to the supposedly bleak 1970sor the beginning of a socialist dictatorship – even though such comparisons are dependent on crude caricatures and huge exaggerations. Many voters, across multiple parties, from Labour to the Greens to Reform UK, have been saying for years that they want Britain to be governed in a new way; but heaven help any government that dares to try.Yet Burnham’s positivity may be less naive than it seems. As mayor of Greater Manchester and a candidate in Makerfield, his can-do air attracted support far beyond Labour’s shrunken strongholds. Many voters don’t pay close attention to government policies, to all their practical implications and precisely how they will be funded. If they did, Starmer would have got more credit for the painstaking and important improvements his government made toemployment rights, for instance.But voters do notice politicians with zest. “I think this might be the best day of my life,” said Burnhamat the opening of No 10 Northin Manchester. The apparent unguardedness, and the risk that it will come back to haunt him, both break the cautious rules of British politics as they have accumulated since the 1990s. The opening paragraphs of future articles about the rise and fall of the Burnham administration already write themselves. Yet successful governments put an appealing emotional and rhetorical frame around their unavoidably diffuse and incompleteactivities, which makes these activities resonate and seem part of a bigger story. These governments, in short, are greater than the sum of their parts.Burnham saw some of the pervasive impact of Margaret Thatcher’s premiership as a politically conscious teenager. His school bus passed the entrance to a local colliery, where striking miners were slowly but surely being defeated. As a junior minister, he served in the equally pivotal Blair government. As mayor, Burnham spent nine years away from Westminster, watching from a distance as several of Blair and Thatcher’s successors quickly failed. So it’s not surprising that Burnham gives the impression of having thought quite a lot about how to be an effective prime minister. “I am under no illusions about how hard this is all going to be,”he wrote last week, “but I have a clear plan and I know how to get things done.”We’ll see. So far, his plan includes several elements – a 10-year time span, tight immigration restrictions, increased defence spending and a focus on working class and non-metropolitan Britain – familiar from Starmer’s premiership and other failed governments since Brexit. Burnham also appears to believe that less-than-revolutionary figures such as his new chancellor, John Healey, can help achieve his ambitious goal of “ending neoliberalism” in Britain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch appointments could be a cunning ploy: seeking radical ends by deceptively moderate, reassuring means. Or they could show that Burnham’s bolder ideas, developed relatively recently, are still outweighed by his instinct not to upset people. But as his year-long, often dismissed, but precisely executed leadership coup has just demonstrated, his capacity to surprise should not be underestimated.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourManchestercommentShareReuse this content

title: The US public is fed up with RFK Jr. To really ‘make America healthy again’, it should look to Europe | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Americans are dying younger than Europeans, despite being the wealthiest people on the planet. Wellness fads won’t change that, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Americans are dying younger than Europeans, despite being the wealthiest people on the planet. Wellness fads won’t change that, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr at the inaugural Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington DC, November 2025.Photograph: Rod Lamkey/APView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr at the inaugural Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington DC, November 2025.Photograph: Rod Lamkey/APOpinionUS newsThe US public is fed up with RFK Jr. To really ‘make America healthy again’, it should look to EuropeDevi SridharAmericans are dying younger than Europeans, despite being the wealthiest people on the planet. Wellness fads won’t change thatThu 30 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTShareI’m just back from my home country, the United States. I always enjoy visiting, but every time I go between the US and my adopted home of Europe, I’m keenly aware of disparity in health: Americans live much shorter lives and spend more of their lifetime in poor health. This is despite Americansearning some of the highest salariesper capita in the world andspending twice as muchas comparable countries on healthcare.Arecent studyin the New England Journal of Medicine of 74,000 adults found that even the wealthiest Americans had higher mortality rates than the wealthiest Europeans – and that the richest Americans had mortality rates comparable to the poorest residents of northern and western Europe. Across every wealth category, Americans were more likely to die younger than Europeans, suggesting that even wealth doesn’t insulate from larger factors that impact life expectancy.That the US has a health problem isn’t controversial. TheMake America Healthy Againmovement, led by US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, has highlighted soaring rates of obesity, diabetes and chronic disease. The movement’s public face isn’t scientists or doctors, but influencers posting videos from saunas, gyms and parks talking about better choices and individual discipline. Eat more red meat. Do more push-ups. Drink raw milk. Avoid vaccines and boost your natural immunity. Sweat more. This health advice is given, while month by month,public health agencies are gutted, research is not funded and experts are sidelined and dismissed from advisory groups.Of course, the public aren’t stupid. Polling consistently finds that scientistsremain among the most trusted sourcesof information in the US, compared withpoliticians and influencers. RFK Jr himself isn’t popular,60% of voters disapproveof the job he’s doing. People might enjoy following entertaining social media accounts, but when Americans want reliable health information, they still largely turn to doctors and scientists.Why are Americans dying younger than Europeans? If we look at the data, several factors pop out. I’ll pick up a few here.The US is a uniquely violent high-income country, with guns theleading cause of death for children and adolescents, followed by road traffic collisions. For example, thefirearm death rateamong American children (age 0-17) is 72 times higher in the US than in the UK, with one mass shooting taking place per day, on average.Why? Because the US doesn’t regulate guns as tightly as the UK (which effectively banned handguns after the Dunblane shooting) and hasn’t addressed road safety as a government issue. No amount of cold plunges or protein shakes will prevent you from getting shot or being killed on the roads. Those are policy decisions that have to be addressed by government.Additionally, the US is the only high-income country that doesn’t guarantee healthcare: around26 million Americansremain uninsured while millions more carry insurance plans with loopholes or deductibles so high that it’s financially risky to access care. According to a Commonwealth Fund survey, an estimated 57% of underinsured adults delayed or avoided medical care because of cost. Diseases that could have been detected early become more serious and more expensive. Think of waiting with your asthmatic child outside an emergency room, hoping their breathing stabilises because otherwise you’ll face a $20,000-30,000 bill. As a result, Americans have substantially higher levels of preventable and treatable mortality than Europeans.How to solve those challenges? Looking to the UK and European countries helps. While these nations differ politically and economically, most share universal healthcare, strong regulation of guns, investment in public transport alongside road infrastructure and safety, and through EU legislation an emphasis onfood quality and safe ingredients.In contrast, rooted in libertarianism and “freedom”, the Maha movement pushes individual solutions to the US’s health challenges. Of course, personal behaviour matters in health. Diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol consumption affect how long we live. Yet many of the largest contributors to premature mortality in the US cannot be solved by individual discipline. They require policies and institutions capable of reducing collective risks across society.What does freedom even mean? It depends who you ask. I would define freedom as the ability to live a long and healthy life, and in that regard, public health policies can bring more freedom. People in the UK have given up their freedom to easily own a gun to gain the freedom for children to go to school safely without shooter drills. The UK has not had a school shooting since Dunblane – and not because individuals haven’t planned to carry one out. They justhaven’t been able to find a gun.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaha is right: Americans need to become healthier and live longer. But this won’t happen with influencers telling people to do pull-ups or increase sunlight exposure. Otherwise, the wealthiest Americans would be outliving us all. What the US needs is public policy that makes daily life healthier and less dangerous. Unfortunately, the Maha movement, through its leader RFK Jr, has done the opposite in diminishing key US public health agencies such as the CDC, the FDA and the NIH, and removing the US from the WorldHealthOrganization.How your community looks affects your health profoundly. Less me, more us. That’s the key health lesson the US could learn from Europe.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionHealthRobert F Kennedy JrUS gun controlUS healthcarecommentShareReuse this content

title: The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together | Zheng Zeguang | The Guardian
description: There is no point competing in isolation. There are so many benefits to be had, in manufacturing, healthcare, research and governance, says Zheng Zeguang, Chinese ambassador to the UK
Author: Zheng Zeguang
Headline: There is no point competing in isolation. There are so many benefits to be had, in manufacturing, healthcare, research and governance, says Zheng Zeguang, Chinese ambassador to the UK
Content: A visitor high-fives a humanoid robot at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, Shanghai, 18 July 2026.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersView image in fullscreenA visitor high-fives a humanoid robot at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, Shanghai, 18 July 2026.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working togetherZheng ZeguangThere is no point competing in isolation. There are so many benefits to be had, in manufacturing, healthcare, research and governanceZheng Zeguang is the Chinese ambassador to the UKThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.11 EDTShareArtificial intelligence is widely regarded as one of the defining technologies of our time. Like the steam engine, the harnessing of electricity and the internet before it, it has the potential to transform how we work, live and interact.But every technological revolution brings challenges as well as opportunities. As AI systems become more capable, people are asking legitimate questions. How can AI remain safe, accountable andunder human control? How should its development be governed? How can itsbenefits be sharedmore widely?These questions were at the heart of the 2026 World AI Conference, held last week in Shanghai. Representatives from more than 100 countries and international organisations gathered to discuss how AI could better serve humanity, and how a more inclusive and effective global governance framework could be built. I am glad the UK also sent a delegation to the conference.China’s president, Xi Jinping, delivered an important address calling on all countries to “boost innovation-driven development”, in a spirit of openness and mutual benefit, to strengthen risk-awareness and ensure that AI is secure and controllable. We must, he said, encourage inclusiveness and promote mutual learning between civilisations. He also stressed the importance of improving global AI governance together.Things are moving quickly. To further support global AI development, China has announced that in the next five years it will provide developing countries with 5,000 opportunities in AI training and seminar programmes. We will also develop international AI-application cooperation centres with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the League of Arab States, the African Union, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and our fellow Bric countries. Thirty nations will also be able to use the AI-powered, early-warning weather system,Mazu.View image in fullscreenXi Jinping delivering the keynote speech at the World AI Conference, Shanghai, China, 17 July 2026.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockTo ensure that AI is a trustworthy tool for humanity, legitimate concerns over data security, privacy protection and responsible use must be taken seriously. These challenges transcend national borders. They obviously require international collaboration, especially in areas such as developing common standards and practical governance. At the same time, security considerations should not become a blanket justification for restricting normal technological cooperation or fragmenting global innovation.China’s own experience reflects this approach. Through the AI Plus Initiative, AI is being integrated into manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, energy and consumer services, helping to build one of the world’s most dynamic AI ecosystems. In 2025, China’s core AI industry exceeded 1.2tn yuan (about £130bn) and a large number of AI companies are growing rapidly.Another notable feature of China’s AI development is its emphasis onopen-source and open-weightmodels. The success of models such as Qwen,DeepSeekand Kimi demonstrates that advanced AI capabilities can be developed at lower cost and made accessible to a much wider community of developers and users. Lowering the barriers to innovation allows more countries, researchers and smaller enterprises to participate in the AI revolution instead of being left behind.It is important to say that no country has a monopoly on innovation. Different nations bring different strengths to AI development, and lasting progress will depend on how well those strengths complement one another rather than compete in isolation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath RaghavanRead moreThis is where China and the UK have much to gain from working together. The UK has a competitive edge in frontier research, life sciences, financial services and AI innovation. China has well-recognised strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering and large-scale industrial deployment, plus one of the world’s largest markets for AI applications. These advantages are highly complementary.In healthcare, combining British strengths in biomedical research with China’s capacity to deploy AI at scale can acceleratedrug discovery, improve medical imaging and enhance healthcare delivery. In manufacturing, pairing British innovation with China’s industrial capabilities can speed up the adoption of smarter, cleaner and more efficient production. Joint research can also contribute to internationally applicable standards for AI safety, testing and evaluation, supporting innovation while strengthening public trust. Such cooperation would not only benefit our two countries but also generate solutions with wider global value.Policymakers, researchers and business leaders from China and the UK need to increase exchanges and translate dialogue into joint research, commercial partnerships and closer cooperation on AI governance.For China, for Britain and for the wider world, cooperation is not simply desirable. It is the right way forward to ensure that AI develops in a way that benefits us all.Zheng Zeguang is the Chinese ambassador to the UKDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
