title: I’ve seen what can confound Farage on his home turf: optimism. People need a politics that offers them that | Owen Jones in Clacton | The Guardian
description: You can’t blame his constituents in Clacton for their pessimism – because they have been let down for years, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: You can’t blame his constituents in Clacton for their pessimism – because they have been let down for years, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Clacton-on-Sea, on 7 July, the day Nigel Farage announced his resignation as MP.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClacton-on-Sea, on 7 July, the day Nigel Farage announced his resignation as MP.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOpinionNigel FarageI’ve seen what can confound Farage on his home turf: optimism. People need a politics that offers them thatOwen Jonesin ClactonYou can’t blame his constituents in Clacton for their pessimism – because they have been let down for yearsThu 30 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 06.39 EDTShareUnder battered England flags, cynicism, pessimism and exhaustion stalk the streets of Clacton.As the byelection called byNigel Farageapproaches, one young couple do not know which candidates are standing. Neither has ever voted. Living in Britain is “depressing”, says the woman in a black floral dress. “The cost of living these days is stupid,” says her partner, wearing a black and grey mechanic’s shirt and a black and red cap. They both work 40 or 50 hours a week, he says, yet “we’re still struggling to pay rent, food, electric, everything else”. They rarely get a day off, and time spent together is rarer still.No wonder they are not agonising over the£5m personal giftFarage received from a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, or thedonations in kindfrom a convicted fraudster. Life is already taking up all their time.Communities across Britain have endured stagnation and decline since the financial crash of 2008, but Clacton has more problems than most. Families still descend on the flashing arcades and fairground rides of Clacton pier, but nothing has replaced the economic world swept away by the decline of the English seaside holiday. Clacton is among thetop 10% of deprived English constituencies. One neighbourhood is ranked the most deprived in England.Yet the scandal over Farage’s income provokes precious little anger here. “I know how corrupt everything is,” says a former soldier, who served 22 years. “It’s just part and parcel of politics.” The belief that all politicians are on the take – and that Farage is therefore no different – is everywhere. Tell people that other politicians are not receiving £5m lump sums from foreign billionaires and many simply shrug. Contempt for politicians has become Farage’s protection.Some come up with their own comforting explanations. A flat cap-wearing man in a wheelchair, who arrived here from Cyprus six decades ago, assumes Farage might invest the £5m in the local community.There is concern, but it is crowded out by other grievances. “That’s the bit that bothers me,” says one elderly man, before adding something more revealing. “Do you want him as a prime minister? Probably not, but what choice do we have?”Farage continues to profit from the belief that both Labour and the Conservatives have failed in office. A middle-aged man in a navy polo shirt says he will vote Reform because “the others have just given me a load of rubbish”. The deceit of the toppled prime minister has left its mark. “That Keir Starmer was a complete liar,” he says.One thought on the Clacton contenders: the ‘establishment’ looks a bit different these days, doesn’t it? | Marina HydeRead moreFarage also benefits from what voters project on to him. When I approach one elderly couple, the man is promptly abandoned by his wife, who correctly anticipates that he will answer at length. He regrets voting for Boris Johnson’s Conservatives – and, before that, Margaret Thatcher. “She sold us off,” he says. “Water, telecoms.”Why, then, I ask, supportsomeone who regards Thatcheras a political hero? “You’ve got to give them a chance,” he replies, apparently without noticing that he has repeatedly regretted doing exactly that.Only around one in 20 residents herewas born abroad, and 96% are white, yet migration and race loom over the constituency. Economic grievance inevitably plays a part. When I suggest to one affable young man covered in tattoos that migrants are blamed for the country’s problems, he agrees. “It’s an easy route out, isn’t it?”He still intends to vote for Farage, because “I believe he does what he says he’s going to do”. Unfortunately, he cannot say what that is.But economics cannot explain everything. Disinformation about migrants and refugees – promoted by sections of the media and spread online – has cut through. One middle-aged couple told me they would have voted for the far-right Restore party, had it fielded a candidate. They grow increasingly agitated as we speak.“Eighty-five per cent of Muslim women can’t even speak English, and that’s a fact,” says the man. Where did he get this statistic? Annoyed at being asked for evidence, he eventually says it came “from news” and tells me to “go and look it up”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter they leave, I do. According to recentcensus data, two-thirds of Muslim women have English as their main language, with 87.7% speaking the language proficiently. Among British-born women, nearly all have English as their main language.This is what happens when real anger at a country in crisis collides with lies about who has caused it. “This country’s in a right mess,” says a bald, weather-beaten, middle-aged man, his sleeveless shirt open at the chest. When I ask what is wrong, he answers pithily: “Everything about it, everything.”Unless there is a secret army of shy Count Binface voters, the comedy writer turned “independent space warrior” – popular on social media – will not triumph here. I find only a couple of people intending to plump for him.The Guardian view on Nigel Farage’s byelection stunt: spectacle is not scrutiny | EditorialRead moreThat’s not to say there isn’t dissent. Outside a cafe, an elderly man with a wispy grey ponytail and sunglasses pushed back on his head nurses a drink from a white mug, an England flag hanging in the window behind him. He tells me he has Asperger’s and has “always known from a young age that we’re all the same”.Farage, he argues, is riding in “on a white charger to rescue them from the refugees”, even though “I don’t believe Nigel Farage is for the working man”. Politicians roll up their sleeves and affect the common touch, but “they’re a different class. They’re the ruling class, and it’s the same fucking ruling class all the time”.He has lost his soulmate and says he rarely leaves home. In a town where so many are resigned to cynicism, he has a simple prescription: “We’ve got one world,” he says. “Let’s look after it and let’s look after each other.”Clacton is not uniquely prejudiced, nor is it afflicted by mass stupidity. You can’t blame the people here for their prevailing pessimism. Neither the Tories nor Labour haverescued coastal townslike this from their pronounced decline – nor Britain as a whole from a generation of stagnation. The anger is real: work that doesn’t pay, public services that have been stripped back, communities not invested in. The people of Clacton have concluded that if the main parties have no answers, why not bet on something else?But acrypto billionaire-funded multimillionairewith multiple jobs who blames migrants for their ills is hardly the solution. Indeed, Farage wants to double down on the very economic policies that have caused so much pain. One young man intending to vote for Farage complains about Labour attacking disability benefits. “Yeah, but they’re all trying to do that,” he says bleakly. “Everyone’s trying to do it.” The only way out is surely a politics which ends people’s resignation to decline – and offers some optimism.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I’d never cried during a live broadcast – then three poignant words had me sobbing | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: I couldn’t help choking up when the writer Katriona O’Sullivan told me her life story. Now I’m on a mission to get everyone to read her memoir, writes Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: I couldn’t help choking up when the writer Katriona O’Sullivan told me her life story. Now I’m on a mission to get everyone to read her memoir, writes Adrian Chiles
Content: ‘Most people who start out in the world she knew never make it out’ … Katriona O’Sullivan.Photograph: Johnny Savage/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Most people who start out in the world she knew never make it out’ … Katriona O’Sullivan.Photograph: Johnny Savage/The GuardianOpinionPovertyI’d never cried during a live broadcast – then three poignant words had me sobbingAdrian ChilesI couldn’t help choking up when the writer Katriona O’Sullivan told me her life story. Now I’m on a mission to get everyone to read her memoirThu 30 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTShareIn more than 30 years of live broadcasting, I’ve only once sobbed on air. This was the other week, during a radio interview with a professor of psychology called Katriona O’Sullivan. That’s what she is now, a professor at Maynooth University in County Kildare. Before that, she was at Trinity College Dublin, where she also got her PhD. Before that, she was to be found on the access programme through which she got into Trinity. Before that she was living a life of chaos in Dublin, a single mother with next to nothing.She was in Dublin escaping an even more chaotic life in Birmingham, which had followed a childhood in Coventry, growing up in harrowing, grinding, distressing, miserable, terrifying poverty. No single adjective feels adequate here, so I’ve thrown in as many as I can think of.She’s better with words than me, as you’ll find if you read her memoir,which is called Poor. I’m buying so many copies of her book to give to people that she may soon have to write one called Rich.I’m on a mission to get everyone in the country to read it.O’Sullivan and her siblings were parented, if that’s the right word (it isn’t), by two heroin users. She went hungry, for food and for love. Her first real taste of either came at primary school. It was there she came across Ms Arkinson and Miss Hall. If Coventry can manage a statue of Lady Godiva atop a horse, I suggest it should also find a spot for one of Ms Arkinson and Miss Hall.Ms Arkinson, a teacher, was Irish and knew O’Sullivan’s heritage. “An Irish girl in my class – what a treat.” To have an adult pleased to have her in the room was a new sensation for O’Sullivan. “I loved Ms Arkinson and I knew she loved me,” she writes. “Her eyes said so. The way she helped me said so.”Miss Hall was the teacher’s assistant who, like Ms Arkinson, like every kid in the school, was aware that poor Katriona smelled. “Pissy pants”, some of her classmates called her. As children often do when they are in crisis, she wet the bed, every night. And she didn’t know how to wash. “There were no towels in our bathroom, barely any toilet paper. Never any soap. None of us owned a toothbrush.” Miss Hall took her to the toilets, locked the door and taught her how to wash. And she gave her clean pants that had the days of the week stamped on them. Words fail me.In a fairy story, this would have been the moment that things started to get better. Well, they did, but mainly they didn’t. Years of disarray lay ahead, horrific stuff I can’t bear to relate here. And even stuff, she told me, that she couldn’t bring herself to write. What that concerns I dread to think.Raised by addicts, abused, neglected, broke: how Katriona O’Sullivan escaped her fateRead moreShe tells an uplifting, if brutal, story so well. It helps that I love her voice, which is a mashup of my two favourite accents: my, erm, own accent, West Midlands, and Dublin. Listening to her, it struck me how much we know about the lives of all manner of ordinary and extraordinary people. Celebrities afford us blow-by-blow accounts of their every move. Athletes, actors, musicians, politicians; you name it. Some of their accounts are better than others, some more honest than others. But we have that insight. Important work is also done by film-makers, endeavouring to show what life looks like in far-flung corners of planet Earth.This is all to the good, but it’s bizarre that we know more about what it’s like to be Taylor Swift, or Cristiano Ronaldo, or what it’s like to live in Bangladesh or the Amazon basin, than we know about what life is like for millions of people in this country with childhoods like Katriona’s.Most of us probably have a clearer idea of what it’s like to live on the International Space Station than what it’s like to live in a tower block in the wrong part of Coventry, existing – just existing – as a member of the underclass. Underclass is a ghastly word, I know, which is possibly one reason we don’t like using it. More likely it’s just another excuse to look away and pretend that world doesn’t exist. There’s a good chance you haven’t even read this far.O’Sullivan’s story, in a turn of events that is nothing less than thrilling, has a happy ending. She landed in Dublin before the 2008 crash, when the Celtic tiger was still alive and kicking. There was money about – money to help people in her world. Help with childcare, treatment for addiction, counselling, access courses to higher education for those whose trajectories were never going to fly them close to any such thing. It all worked out wonderfully in the end. And it’s joyous to join her on that ride.double quotation markMost of us have a clearer idea of what it’s like to live in space than in a tower block in the wrong part of CoventryThen the epilogue, her afterword, is a thump to the solar plexus. It amounts to a stern bollocking from her to you if you happen to be drawing the wrong conclusions from this story. It’s fine to love the rags-to-riches ride – who doesn’t? – but if you’re taking it as proof that, if you just try hard enough, you can do it,you can be anything you want to be,then that, she says in so many words, is balls.Most people who start out in the world she knew never make it out. She insists she did so only because political decisions were made in a time of relative plenty to fund the kind of social services that were there to help her. Many of those services, inIrelandand the UK, have since been cut.As for the bit that had me choking up on live radio, it was talking about three words that jumped out of a sentence in her book describing her love, her need, for school dinners. It’s not her reference to the food that got me – it’s how, almost as an aside, she refers to her classmates: “Other kids, the loved ones, they sometimes complained, but I didn’t give a shit what was served. I’d have eaten anything.”The loved ones. What it must be like to think that everyone but you is loved.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on ‘kidulthood’: Britain prices young adults out of independent life | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: More young people live with parents as low wages, insecure work and unaffordable housing turn family support into another source of inequality
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: More young people live with parents as low wages, insecure work and unaffordable housing turn family support into another source of inequality
Content: ‘Britain appears to be slowly drifting towards a southern European experience without the family culture that makes this feel normal.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘Britain appears to be slowly drifting towards a southern European experience without the family culture that makes this feel normal.’Photograph: GettyOpinionHousingThe Guardian view on ‘kidulthood’: Britain prices young adults out of independent lifeEditorialMore young people live with parents as low wages, insecure work and unaffordable housing turn family support into another source of inequalityThu 30 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.12 EDTShareIn Britain, young people are expected to become independent in their 20s. Yet the UK’s economic model increasingly denies them the means to do so. Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), commissioned partly for theBBC, finds that the proportion of 25-year-olds living with their parents has risen from 25% in the 1990s to 42% today. The research says “co-residence” among those in their 20s and 30s has increased by more than a third over two decades. The rate in Britain remains well below Italy and Spain, where leaving home is frequently more about finding a partner than turning 18, going to university or starting work. But that is scant comfort: Britain appears to be slowly drifting towards a southern European experience without the family culture that makes this feel normal.Young Britons struggle to move out of “the hotel of mum and dad” for obvious reasons. Employment for those aged 25 has fallen for both women and men. Real earnings have barely progressed beyond the level reached around two decades ago. Hardly a surprise, then, that home ownership at 25 has dropped from 43% in the mid-1980s to 15% today. As the IFSnotes, the changing age, educational, ethnic or migrant composition of the population might have been expected to reduce rates of co-residence. Instead, the “declining affordability of housing” has driven them up. In short, young adults are not just opting for a cheaper domestic arrangement to save money. They are submitting to it because they have less control over their lives as the options narrow for housing and work.Britain’s economy risks turning a generation’s 20s into a depressingly prolonged “kidulthood”. Having your own home provides privacy, the ability to establish adult relationships and the space to experiment with identity. The dilemmas that not having a place of one’s own can create were highlighted by a 26-year-old man who moved back to live with his parents. He told the BBC’s Todayprogramme: “I’m not going to bring a girl back to my parents’ house. So it would have 100% affected that part of my life, which does get me low.”Richer parentsoften help their adult children to become independent; among the wealthiest fifth of households, about 15% gave or lent money to their children in 2018-20, compared with under 5% among the poorest fifth. Lower-income families help by keeping their adult children dependent in the home. The latter may save rent, but it can also mean less privacy and autonomy for young adults, and greater housing and living costs for their parents. The evidence is that the trend reproduces inequality not only in wealth but in the ability to establish an independent life.These financial outcomes are not the result of neutral markets. They reflect institutions that suppress wages, let landlords capture housing scarcity and allow the wealthy to buy opportunities denied to others. A social democratic programme should build more social housing, strengthen wages and job security, and shift taxation away from work towards rent extraction. “If you don’t give people a good home, what chance have they got of having a good life?” Andy Burnham hasargued. Before becoming prime minister, hepromised“the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”. Without bold change, the government will keep subsidising the consequences of social and economic failure while leaving the causes intact.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on sporting fair play: it was never quite cricket | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Saltburn’s alleged trickery caused outrage, but cricket’s moral code conceals a rich history of cheating and convenient national myth
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Saltburn’s alleged trickery caused outrage, but cricket’s moral code conceals a rich history of cheating and convenient national myth
Content: Cricket player seems to show fielder tricking umpire by clicking to imitate edgesOpinionCricketThe Guardian view on sporting fair play: it was never quite cricketEditorialSaltburn’s alleged trickery caused outrage, but cricket’s moral code conceals a rich history of cheating and convenient national mythThu 30 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.12 EDTShareOne incident has dominated this week’s sporting headlines, garnering even more column inches than Gianni Infantino’s apparentdesireto sell the football World Cup to the highest bidder. It occurred in a second XI cricket match last weekend between Saltburn and Norton in the North Yorkshire and South Durham League. A fielder at first slip was alleged to have clicked his fingers as the ball passed the batter’s bat, in anattemptto con the umpire into thinking that there had been an edge. The ball sank into the wicketkeeper’s gloves; bowler, keeper and fielder erupted in a full-throated appeal; and the umpire sent the disbelieving batter on his way for a duck.There the matter might have ended, but these days even second XI matches are recorded and there was footage of the alleged finger-clicking. Over the past few days, this footage has been analysed in minute detail. One writer on The Athletic bathetically likened theinterrogationof the video to the decoding of the Zapruder film of President John F Kennedy’s assassination. What precisely does it show? Could the sound have emanated from behind a grassy knoll at the Saltburn ground?The club and league have opened investigations, but, even without those inquiries being concluded, Saltburn have suspended the alleged clicker – 38-year-oldBrian Devine– and said that he will not play for the club for the foreseeable future. Sleepy Saltburn, worried about critics labelling it the “Argentina of village cricket”, are taking no chances. But is the footage really definitive? What will Devine’s teammates say? The story could run and run.View image in fullscreenWG Grace.Photograph: PA Photos“It’s not cricket” has been the hackneyed phrase rolled out in almost every iteration of this gloriously clickbaity story. But what is cricket? It’s one player hurling a dangerous projectile at another. An odd activity on which to base a moral code. Yet, at the same time as parroting “It’s not cricket”, pundits have been enumerating the sport’s numerous other falls from grace (and indeed the great WG Grace was a noted rule-bender) over the centuries. There was bribery and corruption in the early days, which led to games that both teams were trying to lose; numerous incidents of doctoring the ball to get it to behave in peculiar ways, the Australian “Sandpapergate” in 2018 being the most notorious; the time-honoured reluctance of batters to walk for catches even when they know they are out; and a host of modern-day match-fixingscandals. The “spirit of cricket” is a fragile flower.We have an especially rose-tinted view of village cricket, insisting that amateurs “Play up! Play up! And play the game!”, in the words of Henry Newbolt’spoemVitaï Lampada. We imagine village cricket as the bucolic dreamworld described in Siegfried Sassoon’s recollections of prewar games (the idyll before the nightmare of the trenches), Hugh de Sélincourt’s 1924 classic The Cricket Match and AG Macdonell’s 1933 England, Their England. Endless summer days, resplendent rural grounds, sumptuous teas and pastoral rivalry.But even if that vision once shimmered, it does so no longer: the beautiful old cricket ground is now a supermarket car park, English summers increasingly Saharan, and the winning-is-everything mentality that has seeped into amateur cricket all too often ends with volunteer umpires being abused and rival players exchanging jibes – orworse. It’s just not cricket, but then it probably never was.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Will Andy Burnham’s plan to retool education work? | Education policy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers on the prime minister’s attempt to put academic and technical education routes on an equal footing in England
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers on the prime minister’s attempt to put academic and technical education routes on an equal footing in England
Content: ‘Andy Burnham’s desire to revive vocational education … has no chance of long-term fulfilment without a complete overhaul of the 14-19 curriculum.’Photograph: Janine Wiedel Photolibrary/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Andy Burnham’s desire to revive vocational education … has no chance of long-term fulfilment without a complete overhaul of the 14-19 curriculum.’Photograph: Janine Wiedel Photolibrary/AlamyEducation policyLettersWill Andy Burnham’s plan to retool education work?Readers on the prime minister’s attempt to put academic and technical education routes on an equal footing in EnglandThu 30 Jul 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTShareI find the debate about the purported conflict between academic and technical education baffling and somewhat amusing (Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needs, 28 July).In the 1950s, I attended Northampton technical high school. I studied the sciences plus English, French and technical (engineering) drawing to GCE level. I also did hands-on workshops in woodwork, metalwork and leatherwork (Northampton being a traditional shoemaking town). At A-level, I passed physics, chemistry and double maths, and studied physics at Leeds University. I also sang in choirs.My subsequent career in international business systems took me through manufacturing companies, consultancy and ultimately university teaching. I also sang in a cathedral choir for 50 years. I never found the academic, practical and artistic worlds mutually exclusive.So a useful model that we’ve perhaps lost: back to the 1950s!Graham WarrenCoventryAndy Burnham’s desire to revive vocational education is very welcome and long overdue (Andy Burnham’s plans for technical education build on coalition’s UTC roots, 29 July), but has no chance of long-term fulfilment without a complete overhaul of the 14-19 curriculum and, crucially, the abandonment of the deep-rooted cultural assumptions that underlie the current desiccated model, with its dreary apparatus of nonstop tests and examinations.Chief of these assumptions is the idea that technical and vocational education are for “other people’s children” – an idea that can be traced back to the late 1860s, when industrial magnates began sending their children to be gentrified at public schools, and which will persist as long as technical and vocational education is presented chiefly as a solution to the problems posed by “non-academic” pupils.Burnham’s desire to establish parity of esteem between hard hat and mortar board is wholly admirable, but that parity has to be established while children are still at school and, in this regard, he could do worse than revisit the recommendations of the 2004Tomlinson report, which the then Labour government sadly lacked the courage to implement.Michael PykeThe Campaign for State EducationThe discussion on education, training and employment for young people seems to be devolving into the same apprenticeship or trade versus higher education debate, blaming young people as usual, without focusing on the actual problem. My children are in the 16-24 age group and the issue I’ve observed among them and their friends is that many young people would like to go down the apprenticeship or trades route, and there are plenty of courses in colleges, but there are vanishingly few opportunities available to be employed as apprentices to trades, or for those with basic college training.An exceptional few get an apprenticeship and a few more lucky ones have a relative who will take them on. Unless this is fixed urgently, the problem will continue.Pam DunnLeedsHere we go again. I am sureAndy Burnhamhas all the right intentions in wishing to develop a relevant curriculum for all pupils, especially those aged 14-plus. The problem is so may governments have tried this and consistently failed. This is due to the fact that it is simply back to the future of the outdated and divisive grammar/technical schooling system.It will fail for two clear reasons. The first is that how can the majority of pupils at 13 make rational decisions on their pathway without closing doors to future unfulfilled development? The second is that independent schools and parents using them will shun the direct employment study route for the university pathway to Russell group universities, particularly Oxbridge.Gary NethercottWoodbridge, SuffolkI have high hopes for Andy Burnham as prime minister. However, it seems that once again the point has been missed regarding how to equip young people for the workplace. Offering vocational and technical courses aligned to the job market makes sense. However, the root cause of why many young people are disengaged is what needs addressing.The skills needed in the workplace are generic: team building, creativity, resilience, flexibility, independent thinking, work ethic, communication, self-belief, cooperation and empathy. These skills not only provide readiness for work but also enjoyment of learning and, importantly, relevance.The demise of teaching in the performing arts has demoted these very skills that are paramount to the development of young people and readiness for the workplace.Come on Burnham, Powell et al … this is the chance to redress the balance in teaching and meaningful learning, not just to attempt to ready young people for the job market. It is how to enable young people to become fully rounded adults that is crucial.Helen ElliottRetired deputy headteacher, Taunton, SomersetBe good to know if Andy Burnham’s advice to state schools, “teach pupils for local jobs”, applies to private schools.Dr Mike SquiresLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The cost and burden of avoiding ‘forever chemicals’ should not fall on parents | Pfas | The Guardian
description: Letter: Kendal Archer says it is the government’s responsibility to legislate and big agriculture’s responsibility not to cover our food in chemicals
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Kendal Archer says it is the government’s responsibility to legislate and big agriculture’s responsibility not to cover our food in chemicals
Content: ‘Since my first pregnancy, I have grappled with the endless advice and contradictions on health.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Since my first pregnancy, I have grappled with the endless advice and contradictions on health.’Photograph: AlamyPfasLettersThe cost and burden of avoiding ‘forever chemicals’ should not fall on parentsKendal Archersays it is the government’s responsibility to legislate and big agriculture’s responsibility not to cover our food in chemicalsThu 30 Jul 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTShareI read your article (‘Forever chemicals’ linked to gut inflammation in children after early exposure, 24 July) on prenatal and early-life exposure to Pfas leading to higher levels of intestinal inflammation in children – and by extension colorectal cancer – with interest.I’m a mum of two. Since my first pregnancy, I have grappled with the endless advice and contradictions on health. Should I use glass bottles of non-organic milk, or plastic bottles of organic milk. Organic broccoli wrapped in plastic, or plastic-free non-organic broccoli.As I read the article, I also processed the solution: “Mothers can take some steps to protect themselves, including using water filtration systems that removePfas, buying organic, avoiding waterproof clothing, and avoiding stain guards.”My immediate reaction was of despair and rage. How can these huge, systemic issues be just another thing for us to solve? How many working families can afford to eat only organic food? How many of us can afford to fit water filter systems? How many of us can avoid getting wet during school pick ups?It is outrageous that these issues are now so commonplace and uncontested that the burden of solving them gets shunted on to the shoulders of parents.It is not our responsibility. It is the government’s responsibility to legislate. It is big agriculture’s responsibility not to cover our food in chemicals. It is the water companies’ responsibility to ensure we have clean water. As if these things even need to be said.I cannot read another article about how I am irreparably damaging my child’s long-term health, with the solution just to “buy x or y”. The solution is bigger and harder than this. And it is not our responsibility to shoulder it.Kendal ArcherExeterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Homelessness crisis starts at the prison gate | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: Letter: No government can credibly promise to end rough sleeping while one public institution keeps releasing people straight into it, writes Gary Teper
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: No government can credibly promise to end rough sleeping while one public institution keeps releasing people straight into it, writes Gary Teper
Content: Rough sleepers in Manchester.Photograph: Ashley van Dyck/AlamyView image in fullscreenRough sleepers in Manchester.Photograph: Ashley van Dyck/AlamyHomelessnessLettersHomelessness crisis starts at the prison gateNo government can credibly promise to end rough sleeping while one public institution keeps releasing people straight into it, writesGary TeperThu 30 Jul 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTShareWe should all applaud Andy Burnham’s commitment to end rough sleeping (‘It’s generations of decline’: can Andy Burnham really end rough sleeping?, 24 July). The ambition is right and overdue. But heset the same goalin Greater Manchester in 2017 and found, as anyone would, that you cannot clear people off the street faster than the system puts them there. Much of rough sleeping is manufactured upstream.Take prison. In 2024-25,around 1,000 peoplea month left prison in England and Wales homeless and went on to sleep rough. Homelessness feeds reoffending, reoffending feeds custody, and release feeds the street. No government can credibly promise to end rough sleeping while one public institution keeps releasing people straight into it.We run accommodation for prison leavers under the Ministry of Justice’s transitionalcommunity accommodation service tier 3 (Cas3) schemeand house more than 1,400 ex-offenders a night. What we see is simple: a bed alone is not enough. Many people leaving custody need housing alongside trauma-informed support, life skills and help to sustain a tenancy. Give them that continuity and the cycle can be broken. Without it, homelessness becomes a revolving door.The £340m to be spent at the street end will not fix a pipeline that starts at the prison gate. Until the government treats prison release as homelessness prevention, not homelessness management, the promise will stay a promise.Gary TeperManaging director, The Housing NetworkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Burnham must take international aid obligations seriously | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Letter: Desmond Whyms says a fundamental rethink of aid is necessary to ensure Britain can genuinely help countries improve their human and environmental outcomes in the long term
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Desmond Whyms says a fundamental rethink of aid is necessary to ensure Britain can genuinely help countries improve their human and environmental outcomes in the long term
Content: A programme aimed at keeping 1 million girls in school across Africa, Asia and the Middle East was recently axed by the British government two years after it was announced.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA programme aimed at keeping 1 million girls in school across Africa, Asia and the Middle East was recently axed by the British government two years after it was announced.Photograph: AlamyForeign policyLettersBurnham must take international aid obligations seriouslyDesmond Whymssays a fundamental rethink of aid is necessary to ensure Britain can genuinely help countries improve their human and environmental outcomes in the long termThu 30 Jul 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.03 EDTShareHalima Begum’s excellent article on the opportunities now facing our new prime minister (Andy Burnham could easily ignore the UK’s falling aid commitment. He would be wise not to, 23 July) sheds a harsh light on the UK’s recent performance in international development.Labour’samplificationof earlierTory cutsto the development budget is shortsighted, self-defeating and immoral, with evenmilitary leaders not supportiveof it. It highlights the weakening of Britain’s soft power as well as resulting in a more unstable world.As well as reinstating the aid budget, a fundamental rethink is needed, as currently much “aid” moneycomes backto the global north, benefiting wealthy countries,NGOs and institutions, but failing to build national orregional capacityand autonomy for reducing poverty, protecting the environment or improving health and education. The focus on short-term, UK-attributable “results” that accompanied the earlier 0.7% aid commitment often doeslittle to avertongoing aid dependency.The abolition of the Department for International Development, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Officeencouraging the departureof those with expertise and integrity, have further resulted in the FCDO being unfit for development purposes.A radical new mandate and structure is needed to genuinely assist southern governments and institutions to deliver their plans for improved human and environmental outcomes long term. That, and a recommitment to taking our international obligations seriously, is still what I hope for with the reset promised by Burnham and his team.Desmond WhymsFormer senior health adviser, Department for International DevelopmentExplore more on these topicsForeign policyAidAndy BurnhamLabourConservativesForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeGlobal healthlettersShareReuse this content

title: Emily Campbell cooks up weightlifting gold: ‘MasterChef was more nerve-racking’ | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Athlete set a new Commonwealth record in +86kg final before revealing she is to appear on cookery show
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Athlete set a new Commonwealth record in +86kg final before revealing she is to appear on cookery show
Content: Emily Campbell delivered a combined score of 278kg.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmily Campbell delivered a combined score of 278kg.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Emily Campbell cooks up weightlifting gold: ‘MasterChef was more nerve-racking’Athlete set a new Commonwealth record in +86kg final before revealing she is to appear on cookery showSean Ingleat SEC ArmadilloThu 30 Jul 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time Emily Campbell stepped on to the platform for a final time on Thursday, the women’s +86kg weightlifting final had all the fervour of a revivalist meeting.Everyone was cheering. There were loud shouts and exhortations. People who didn’t know a snatch from a clean and jerk two hours before had become instant converts. It was the Campbell Effect in action again. But the double Olympic medallist wasn’t finished there.Commonwealth Games 2026: England stun Australia on the track, weightlifting and netball on day seven – liveRead more“Emily is not satisfied with a gold medal,” said the announcer. “She’s not satisfied with a CWG [Commonwealth Games] record. She wants more!” The clean and jerk bar had been set to 160kg. But the army volunteers whose job it is to add more weights had barely moved, when the announcer piped up again. “Stop the clock! 163kg on the bar please loaders. Emily wants a Commonwealth record!”Then the 32-year-old with three lions on her England shirt, and six lions woven into her dyed-red hair, went out and got it. One striking display of force and timing got the bar on her shoulders. Another got it over the head. Then the SEC erupted in a sea of love and appreciation.View image in fullscreenA focused Emily Campbell makes her record breaking lift in the clean and jerk.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCampbell responded by blowing kisses to her adoring fans. “I couldn’t have asked them to be any louder,” she said. “I couldn’t really hear myself think.”But how she deserved it after lifting 115kg in the snatch and 163kg in the clean and jerk for a combined score of 278kg. That, incredibly, was 25kg clear of her nearest rival. As people waved St George flags and punched the air it was hard to imagine how she could be any more popular, but then she told us she would be appearing on Celebrity MasterChef next month.“It was a really fun experience,” she said. “It was really nice for me to do something without being Emily the weightlifter. Food is something I’ve always been massively passionate about.“MasterChef was definitely more nerve-racking than this, absolutely. MasterChef was very tough. It was a very tough competition, but I enjoyed it thoroughly. My signature dish is Caribbean and that’s all I’m going to give you because I want you to watch it.”The only moment that gave us pause afterwards came when Campbell intimated she wasn’t entirely sure whether she would go for a hat-trick of Olympic medals at the LA Games in 2028.View image in fullscreenEmily Campbell’s fans cheer her on.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“Do you want me to be dead honest with you?” she said. “It hurts everywhere. Everywhere. Your knees, your shoulders, your back, everywhere. We’re lifting serious weight and it is hard and that’s why you have to be really sensible.“So I’ve got some thinking to do. We’re going to go back with the team. We’re going to strategise. LA, we would like to go, but we’ve got to look at the practicalities. If they work, you will see me start qualification at the end of the year. But for now, we enjoy what just happened. We have some good food, maybe a few drinks, and then we move on from that.”As she spoke, the 18-year-old Etta Mae Love of Canada, who won bronze, was talking about how Britain’s finest lifter had been an inspiration when she first started.That made Campbell smile, even if it also made her feel a little strange. “It is lovely now that I’m at a stage where I’ve become so old that I’m sharing the stage with people that were inspired by me,” she said. “But it’s always very surreal when people go – you’re a role model – because you never set out to do that.“You just set out to do the thing that you love and you do it with grace. But if I can get someone to do something they’re passionate about, then I’ve done more than my job.”And this, certainly, was another job impeccably done.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesWeightliftingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Four crashes and a disqualification: chaotic Commonwealth Games race to be replayed | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Scotland’s Melanie Woods was originally awarded gold in Glasgow but the women’s T54 1500m final will now be held again on Friday
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Scotland’s Melanie Woods was originally awarded gold in Glasgow but the women’s T54 1500m final will now be held again on Friday
Content: Noemi Alphonse, of Mauritius, picks up her racing wheelchair after the crash.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenNoemi Alphonse, of Mauritius, picks up her racing wheelchair after the crash.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APCommonwealth Games 2026Four crashes and a disqualification: chaotic Commonwealth Games race to be replayedScotland’s Melanie Woods was originally awarded goldWomen’s T54 1500m final will now be restaged on FridaySean Inglein GlasgowThu 30 Jul 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt turned into Glasgow’s version of Wacky Races. After four crashes, three overturned wheelchairs, three appeals and a disqualification, the women’s T54 1500m final is to be rerun 39 hours after it first took place.The controversial decision was taken on Thursday after the extraordinary scenes at the Scotstoun track on Wednesday – and despite the medallists doing a lap of honour, posing for photographs together and going to bed thinking they were part of Commonwealth history.The drama started on the first bend when Canada’s Nandini Sharma cut across Noemi Alphonse of Mauritius, who then flipped spectacularly in the air.Racism claim by Idi Amin’s grandson groundless, insists Commonwealth chiefRead moreMoments later Australia’s Eliza Ault-Connell, who had also been impeded, was knocked to the floor. The chain reaction then led to Scotland’s Joanna Robertson skidding on one wheel across the Mondo track, while England’s Ellis Kottas crashed into a wall.While all this was happening, Scotland’s Melanie Woods took gold in a Commonwealth record of 3min 33.39sec. But it turned out the drama was just getting started.Shortly afterwards, Sharma was disqualified for causing the crash, leaving Kottas to take silver, having finished 50 seconds back, and Australia’s Mikaela Dingley to claim bronze.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHowever, after appeals from Australia and Mauritius, and a counter-claim from Canada, Para-athletics chiefs have now decided to run the race again at 10.24am on Friday - more than 39 hours after the official race began.Six of the seven athletes will be allowed to compete again. However, Sharma’s disqualification will stand. The ceremony was not due to be held until Thursday, so none of the athletes were actually presented with medals.In an Instagram post on Thursday Kottas said she accepted the decision. “While I really don’t want to rerun the race (lowkey traumatised) if I’m going to medal I want to do so on my own merit, so I will go out and give it all I’ve got,” she said. “If I don’t medal, so be it. I’ll still have the incredible memories of lifting that England flag.”However the decision was criticised by Jonny Riall, chef de mission for Team England, who said: “We are incredibly disappointed by the late decision to rerun the T54 1500m tomorrow morning.View image in fullscreenScotland’s Melanie Woods was declared the winner after the crash but it will be rerun on Friday morning.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters“While there is no formal protest process available to us, we have strongly challenged the decision,” he added. “The race officials did not halt the race at the time of the incident, nor was any immediate decision made to declare the race void or order a rerun.”Team Scotland also released a statement, which was rather more prosaic. “We note the decision of the Jury of Appeal regarding the Women’s T54 1500m final,” it said. “Melanie Woods and Joanna Robertson will now prepare to compete again on Friday in the rerun.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Perfect Pearson fires England into netball semi-final showdown with New Zealand | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lois Pearson bagged a perfect 17 goals from 17 shots as England defeated South Africa 58-54 to set up a semi-final with New Zealand at the Commonwealth Games
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lois Pearson bagged a perfect 17 goals from 17 shots as England defeated South Africa 58-54 to set up a semi-final with New Zealand at the Commonwealth Games
Content: Lois Pearson of England on the ball during the victory over South Africa.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenLois Pearson of England on the ball during the victory over South Africa.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PACommonwealth Games 2026Perfect Pearson fires England into netball semi-final showdown with New ZealandEngland 58-54 South AfricaLois Pearson scores 17 goals from 17 shotsPA MediaThu 30 Jul 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland stormed back from a six-goal deficit at the end of the first quarter to book their place in the netball semi-finals with a 58-54 win over South Africa.Anna Stembridge’s side went into the game knowing defeat would mean them failing to reach the last four of the competition for the first time since the sport was introduced to the Games in 1998.Australia dispatch England with ease in Commonwealth Games netball clashRead moreA thumping 66-47 defeat by Australia in their second Group A game had left their qualification hopes hanging by a thread and they started as slight underdogs against the South Africans, to whom they lost a bruising three-match series in January.England could not contain the towering South Africa goal shooter Elmerè van der Berg, who dominated the shooting circle in the opening quarter, with Stembridge’s side punished for failing to capitalise on their turnovers.The loss of centre Imogen Allison, who hobbled off with an ankle injury early in the second quarter, further threatened their chances, but England rallied with the help of eight from Lois Pearson to pull back to a single-goal deficit at half-time.The introduction of goal defence Halimat Adio made the difference in the third quarter as she shackled Van der Berg superbly while Pearson’s continued accuracy gave the Roses a 43-39 advantage.England maintained their advantage throughout a muscular fourth quarter and Pearson finished with a perfect 17 goals from 17 shots to set up a semi-final against New Zealand on Saturday.Stembridge said: “We spoke around not getting too many opportunities like this, where it’s the last game of the pool stages and ultimately it decides a semi-final position.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The girls leaned into that pressure and they really trusted one another. We did not catastrophise the first quarter. We knew we had more to give, and I’m just delighted that we gave enough to get ourselves into a semi-final.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesNetballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s game | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Fifa’s pitch to persuade members to approve sale of World Cup’s commercial rights includes more tournaments, higher ticket prices and debt financing
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa’s pitch to persuade members to approve sale of World Cup’s commercial rights includes more tournaments, higher ticket prices and debt financing
Content: Gianni Infantino proposed making the World Cup a biennial tournament five years ago.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino proposed making the World Cup a biennial tournament five years ago.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersFifaFifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s gameFifa’s 25-page sales deck produced by JP MorganReference made to doubling global tournamentsExclusive byMatt HughesThu 30 Jul 2026 10.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa’s sales pitch to persuade members to approvethe sale of the World Cup’s commercial rightsclearly states that its plans for financial growth will be achieved by staging more tournaments, having higher ticket prices and debt financing.A 25-page sales deck titled “Fifa Forward Enterprise Member Materials”, that has been seen by the Guardian, makes the case for the creation of a new company to run Fifa’s commercial operations, 20% of which would be sold to Joshua Kushner, a US investor who is the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.Fifa’s sale of the century: how Kushners and Trump are at centre of a tangled webRead moreThe prospectus has been produced by JP Morgan, the US bank that was also behind the failed European Super League breakaway five years ago.In addition to the previously reported $20m (£15m) sign-up payment Fifa has offered to all 211 member associations, which could be made available as soon as January, the document projects that the four-year Fifa Forward payments would increase to $24m for each member by the 2035-39 cycle.JP Morgan makes clear in the sales deck that such growth will come from “a growing tournament portfolio”, “third party sources of capital and debt financing”, and prioritising “high yield” partnerships and events.There is also a reference to more than doubling the number of global tournaments held each year, from 200 to 450, which if followed through would put a huge strain on player workload.Staging the World Cup more frequently would be the most obvious way of raising revenue, withGianni Infantinohaving previously proposed making it a biennial tournament five years ago.The bank also raises the prospect of TV coverage of the biggest events such as theWorld Cupbeing sold to subscription channels or streamers, by referring to a lan to “expand and optimize media rights monetization”.JP Morgan claims that Fifa is “undermonetized” but significantly makes comparisons with other sports leagues with the revenue figures based on club or franchise earnings, rather than with comparable governing bodies.Fifa’s stated annual revenue of $3.6bn therefore compares unfavourably with the NFL’s compared revenue of $21.2bn, Major League Baseball’s $13.1bn and the NBA’s $12.5bn.The document was sent to all 211 member associations on Wednesday night and immediately provoked a strong reaction.One senior figure queried why Fifa, which has cash reserves of around $4bn and accumulated revenues of $15bn over the current four-year cycle, would need to take on debt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnother highlighted the odd comparison of a world governing body with private, member-run leagues, while JP Morgan’s proposed timeline for completing the deal was also questioned.According to the document “Investors will be given access to a term sheet and select materials” in August before a vote of Fifa members has taken place.Significantly there is little mention of the investor group elsewhere in the prospectus, with no reference to its identity, projected returns or exit terms.There is one more major omission in the document, as there is not a single mention of women’s football anywhere across the 25 pages.Fifa was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsFifaWorld Cup 2026World CupFootball politicsGianni InfantinonewsShareReuse this content

title: Not so black and white: how Eddie Howe lost control at Newcastle in one summer | Newcastle United | The Guardian
description: Everything was looking rosy for Howe at St James’ Park until Alexander Isak’s departure led to rushed signings and a messy season
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Everything was looking rosy for Howe at St James’ Park until Alexander Isak’s departure led to rushed signings and a messy season
Content: Eddie Howe was popular during five years on Tyneside in which he delivered the club’s first domestic trophy since 1955.Photograph: Scott Heppell/PAView image in fullscreenEddie Howe was popular during five years on Tyneside in which he delivered the club’s first domestic trophy since 1955.Photograph: Scott Heppell/PANewcastle UnitedAnalysisNot so black and white: how Eddie Howe lost control at Newcastle in one summerLouise TaylorEverything was looking rosy for Howe at St James’ Park until Alexander Isak’s departure led to rushed signings and a messy seasonThu 30 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTShareLast September, David Hopkinson, just installed as Newcastle’s chief executive, perched on a stool at a downstairs corner table in Shearer’s Bar at St James’ Park and between sips of zero alcohol lager, likenedEddie Howeto Bruce Springsteen. According to Hopkinson, Newcastle’s manager was “the Boss” and “the talent”. He conjured up an imaginary scene involving Springsteen asking for M&M’s before a concert and being duly supplied with a dressing room overflowing with the brightly coloured confectionery. The same principle, he said, would apply to “Eddie”, who would e furnished with “whatever he wants”.Six months later, things had changed. In late March, Hopkinson sat around a heavy wooden table in a St James’ Park boardroom and, between sips of coffee, said he did not “have a stance on the manager’s future”. What he could tell assembled reporters was that arecent home defeatby Sunderland “hurt”. It “resonated” and was being taken “seriously”. Given that Newcastle had just lost aChampions League tie 8-3 to Barcelona on aggregateand were en route to finishing 12th in the Premier League, Howe admitted to “sleepless nights” before a summit with the club’s majority Saudi Arabian ownership at Matfen Hall hotel in Northumberland the following month.Football Daily | Thought leader Eddie Howe runs out of time and ideas at NewcastleRead moreThe 48-year-old, who only a year earlier had choreographedNewcastle’s Carabao Cup triumph, securing their first domestic trophy since 1955, would win that particular battle. Thanks to a convincing, typically articulate presentation detailing his future tactical plans, Howe was allowed by the visitors from Riyadh to remain in the job he had occupied since November 2021. Even then, however, he suspected he was losing a war that had begun long before Hopkinson’s installation.It was an often subliminal conflict about power and control that started when Amanda Staveley, the club’s former co-owner, was ousted in the summer of 2024. Howe had been very much Staveley’s appointment and, given that she was then responsible for running the club on a daily basis, he was permitted considerable say in buying and selling players.During his time in charge of Bournemouth, Howe exerted significant control over all spheres of the organisation, his unwillingness to delegate even extending to proof reading the match programme. In an era when sporting directors rather than managers invariably call the ultimate shots in the Premier League Howe, unusually, enjoyed similar authority at Newcastle. With Andy Howe, his nephew, occupying a senior recruitment role and invitations to visit the team’s training ground issued at Eddie’s discretion, Howe’s word was law.That regimen initially served him well. When Paul Mitchell, who succeeded Dan Ashworth as sporting director, suggested alterations to transfer policy and playing style, Howe made his displeasure plain. Within a year Mitchell left. It was June 2025 and with the League Cup won three months earlier the manager had never seemed more secure. Yet that exit of a second sporting director arguably prefaced Howe’s ownfall.View image in fullscreenAlexander Isak celebrates scoring the second goal in the Carabao Cup final against Liverpool at Wembley in March 2025. Three months later he asked to leave the club.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersAdmittedly, it was not his fault Alexander Isak forced a £125m move to Liverpool last summer, but Howe was heavily involved in Newcastle signing £240m of largely underachieving talent in a forlorn attempt to compensate for the Sweden striker’s defection. If neither the £69m Nick Woltemade nor the £55m Yoane Wissa were suitable replacements for Isak, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga often underwhelmed. Only the central defender Malick Thiaw impressed.Moreover, it had not gone unnoticed in Riyadh that Howe’s unwillingness to sell players exacerbated the ownership’s financial problems at a time when Newcastle’s comparatively low commercial revenues made it a struggle to remain within football’s spending rules. In May, the club entered a Uefa settlement agreement after breaching European investment rules last season. It dictates they must balance the books very carefully for the next three years and explains why their latest sporting director, Ross Wilson,sold Anthony Gordonand Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively this summer. Howe was reluctant to lose the pair and became dismayed at the prospect of seeing another key individual in Bruno Guimarães depart for Arsenal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionToon turnover: the stats behind Eddie Howe’s highs and lows at NewcastleRead moreWilson, who arrived from Nottingham Forest in October, has presided over a marked policy pivot involving signing young players possessing high resale potential. So far this close season Newcastle have acquired four promising yet inexperienced newcomers aged 20 or under in Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Touré, Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur. Hopkinson has boasted that Newcastle are aiming to be one “of the best clubs in the world” by 2030 but Howe is not the only one to have detected a disconnect between such lofty expectations and a bold experiment with youth that could easily go badly wrong. Well aware he had remained at Bournemouth a season too long before being sacked in 2020, it seems Howe decided it would be better to jump rather than be pushed, and leave on amicable terms.In five years on Tyneside, he improved some players almost beyond recognition – Joelinton and Jacob Murphy in particular – and choreographed an often thrilling brand of football during two Champions League campaigns. At their high tempo, hard-pressing best, Newcastle were gloriously entertaining, but Howe’s team became frequently poor in possession and adept at forfeiting leads. Pace and athleticism seemed prioritised ahead of vision and incision. Like their workaholic manager, Newcastle increasingly resembled a team that had forgotten how to relax and read the game’s nuances.Howe is gifted enough, intelligent enough and young enough to reach the highest echelons of coaching but first he needs to rest, reassess and, perhaps, remember why he once fell in love with Arsenal’s football during their Cesc Fàbregas-inspired tiki-taka phase. The irony of his Newcastle tenure is that a manager obsessed with off-field control came undone partly by its absence on the pitch.It is a paradox Howe may reflect on as he sits at his treasured piano and creates some new mood music of his own.Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UnitedEddie HoweanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘Outstanding leader’ Fleming backed to find calm among the chaos for England | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The New Zealander has won the County Championship and makes those around him better but is also not averse to mind games
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: The New Zealander has won the County Championship and makes those around him better but is also not averse to mind games
Content: Stephen Fleming has won titles in the Indian Premier League.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenStephen Fleming has won titles in the Indian Premier League.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAEngland cricket team‘Outstanding leader’ Fleming backed to find calm among the chaos for EnglandNew Zealander has won the County Championship and makes those around him better but is also not averse to mind gamesSimon BurntonThu 30 Jul 2026 13.18 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith two games of the 2005 season remaining Nottinghamshire, under the captaincy of Stephen Fleming, were sitting precariously at the top of the County Championship, still needing to visit their two main rivals. First up was Kent: Notts were 397 for five after the first day, but rain washed out most of the second and at the end of the third Kent were only five down. A draw looked inevitable, and with a Shane Warne-inspired Hampshire – Notts’ final opponents – on their way to victory at Glamorgan the title chase seemed to be turning. But Fleming had other plans.“He called a meeting of the senior players on the fourth morning to say he had an idea,” says Darren Bicknell, his Notts teammate. “If Kent didn’t win the game against us, they were dead, they’d have no way to win the title, so he recognised that he had them over a barrel a little bit.” Fleming offered Kent the chance to chase 420 in 70 overs, an unlikely target – but also the best they were going to get. “To take a calculated gamble in that game was a stroke of genius,” Bicknell says. “Some of the senior players were a bit anxious, thinking we didn’t need to take any risks because the draw was still a good result. But people went with him.”Root to captain England after Fleming confirmed as new men’s Test coachRead moreOn that final day Kent duly declared their first innings; Notts motored at seven an over until the agreed total was reached then declared also; then Kent, with no choice but to attack, were bowled out for 205. Notts won the title with a game to spare.England’s interim captain when New Zealand played them the previous year – Marcus Trescothick, now back in charge of England’s Test side in an interim role – had admitted his opposite number was “regarded as the best captain in the world”, and here was more proof. Kent’s first man out in that forlorn run chase? Rob Key, the man who has just appointed him England coach.“He was just very calm all the time, very unruffled,” Bicknell says of Fleming. “He worked out the game really well, worked out people very well, but overall he was just calm, even in the hottest of moments. Everyone trusted him to be on everything. I think in moments when things weren’t going well, there was a reflection from him that everything was still all right: just be patient, stay calm, and it will come right as long as we’re doing the right things. He was just a really good man and the sort of person you felt like you wanted to play for. I think he’ll be very good and he’ll bring a sense of common sense and calmness to the whole England set-up.”Fleming has notalwaysbeen calm in hot moments. There is another widely quoted example of his cricketing cunning: in the fifth of six ODIs in South Africa in 2004 the hosts, needing to win to keep the series alive, came out to chase an achievable, rain-affected target of 178 in 29 overs. As their captain, Graeme Smith, approached the crease Fleming unleashed a stream of invective.Just three days earlier Smith had described Fleming “changing his game plan against me in every match so far … I’m sure he’s just trying to get into my mind”. But as this normally gentle man showered him in abuse, that was all forgotten. Smith responded in kind and then, distracted, scored 15 off 33; New Zealand won by two runs. “Graeme is an emotional guy. That was one chink we thought we might explore and he took the bait,” Fleming later said. “It was never personal. I made it personal in one game to get the edge.”View image in fullscreenStephen Fleming walks back to the pavilion in his last Test, against England in Napier, New Zealand in March 2008.Photograph: Ross Setford/APThose who have worked with Fleming describe an empathetic man, a skilled reader of people – skills he can use to build you up, but perhaps also to destroy you. “He was quite simply an outstanding leader of men,” says David Alleyne, another member of that Nottinghamshire side. “He had a great way of communicating, and finding the right time and the right space to really empower you as an individual, and get you to think about your game in a way that was going to help the team. I found him quite remarkable in that sense. He was very calm, very calculated.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPraise for Fleming has not quite been universal, and most notably Hemang Badani, currently head coach of Delhi Capitals and Southern Brave, said the success he achieved at Chennai Super Kings in the Indian Premier League – where he reached 10 finals and won five titles – was all down to his long-time captain, MS Dhoni. “He’s never won anywhere outside the IPL,” Badani said in 2024. “If someone says he’s a great coach, I wouldn’t agree. Dhoni is the winner.”Chris Jordan, having played under Fleming at CSK and Southern Brave, disagrees. “He comes with a lot of empathy. He has a very relaxed aura about him but he’s still very, very detailed in his planning and his messaging. And he’s very, very good at creating role clarity within a team,” Jordan says. “One thing he identified about the Hundred, he was astute enough to realise that it can be quite chaotic. So he found a way of getting us to find simplicity within the chaos, just with his messaging and his tactical awareness. He’s just a very well-rounded coach, and when you start to spend time with him you really get the feeling that you not only want to do well for yourself, but you want to do it for him as well.”Jordan is one of just a handful of people to have played under Fleming and alongside Joe Root, who has returned as England captain. “I definitely think Joe and Flem as a combination will be quite excellent, and I actually think Flem could take Joe Root’s captaincy to the next level,” Jordan says. “He really has that knack of bringing out the best in players and making you really believe in yourself. He’s just a top human being.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamCricketfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Charley Hull refuses to apologise after £100,000 scratchcard prank on caddie | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: Charley Hull, who was two under after her first round, said: ‘I think people need to lighten up,’ while Atthaya Thitikul leads on -7
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Charley Hull, who was two under after her first round, said: ‘I think people need to lighten up,’ while Atthaya Thitikul leads on -7
Content: Charley Hull said her caddy, Adam Woodward, took the prank well.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenCharley Hull said her caddy, Adam Woodward, took the prank well.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAWomen's OpenCharley Hull refuses to apologise after £100,000 scratchcard prank on caddieHull: ‘I think people need to lighten up’Thitikul leads on -7; double major winner Ryu on -5Ewan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesThu 30 Jul 2026 15.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharley Hull has delivered an emphatic, unapologetic response towards those who criticised a prank on the eve of the Women’s Open.Hull used pre-tournament media duties to reveal she bought fake scratchcards in a Blackpool joke shop, before using one to trick her caddie, Adam Woodward, into believing he had won £100,000. Hull filmed Woodward’s initially euphoric and subsequently despondent reaction to the incident.While some onlookers saw the funny side of the stunt, Hull also drew harsh words for her treatment of Woodward. Many perceived it as unduly cruel. The caddie has worked for Hull for the vast majority of her professional career. Hull’s carefree, playful nature is well known within her sport.Charley Hull shooting for Open glory after multiple near misses at majorsRead moreIn this instance, Hull cares little about splitting opinion. “People that have complaints about it, I would say loosen up,” Hull said after a two-under-par 69 to start her challenge at Royal Lytham & St Annes. “I don’t have my social media on my phone on tournament weeks. I delete it and when I go home I’ll add it again. I don’t really like people seeing me and tagging me and stuff. I like to keep in the present moment. But I think people need to lighten up if they’re taking that too seriously because it was pretty funny.”Hull added she would “100%” participate in a similar scenario again. “He thought it was funny after, he is not uptight,” she said of Woodward. “It’s a joke. If people don’t like it they can lump it, do you know what I mean?“I felt bad for Adam but at the end of the day I have just got to have a good week. At the end of the week I’ll buy him 100 scratchcards.” A peculiar business.Hull trails the early leader, Atthaya “Jeeno” Thitikul, by five shots. The Thai player has been astonishingly consistent in majors – posting 11 top-10 finishes since 2021 – but is yet to win. Perhaps Lytham will be key – Thitikul won top amateur honours as a 15-year-old when the Women’s Open was staged here in 2018. Thitikul’s close shaves on the biggest stage are worthy of comparisons with Hull. Her 64 was the lowest score in a Lytham Women’s Open.Ryu Hae-ran’s ambition is not only to extinguish the hopes of her rivals but secure a little piece of history. Until Thitikul’s surge, Ryu topped the leaderboard. Victories at this year’s PGA and Evian Championships mean she is in the incredible position of seeking a third major win in a row. Only four female golfers have achieved the feat yet Ryu’s position is unique. She has not played in any other tournaments outside the majors in question.Unsurprisingly perhaps, the South Korean responded with a firm no when asked whether she has contemplated three from three. Fifty-four holes in a links environment provide the epitome of a long way to go. Still, her five-under-par 66 – which included half a dozen birdies and an outward half of 31 – felt significant.View image in fullscreenRyu Hae-ran has won the past two majors on the women’s tour and is going for a hat-trick at Lytham.Photograph: Jon Super/AP“I felt so hard on this type of course that I cannot focus on the win,” Ryu said. “I have to just enjoy my golf and not stress too much. Today’s score is pretty good but we have three more days and this is a major. I just keep thinking about myself, not winning, and keep enjoying myself on the golf course.”Ryu has always been an elite ball striker, with her greens in regulation statistics remarkable. Improvement in putting has elevated her game in 2026. “These days my golf is pretty good,” said the 25-year-old with more than a whiff of understatement. Shiho Kuwaki later matched Ryu’s first-round total.Lottie Woad’s 69 enhanced hopes of a home winner, eight years after England’s Georgia Hall prevailed at Lytham. Woad has quietly risen to fifth in the world rankings, little over a year since she turned professional. Her round owed much to avoiding every one of Lytham’s 174, highly penal bunkers. Woad’s approach is an aggressive one. “I think I hit the most drivers out of anyone in my group,” she said. “It’s one of my strengths, so I didn’t see the point in laying back.“Some of the par fives are pretty tight off the tee but they’re probably the only birdie opportunities you’re really going to get round here so I was just always trying to play driver for those.”Minjee Lee made birdie at the par-three 1st and bagged an eagle at the 6th but still slumped to a 75. The former champion Sophia Popov was 10 shots worse than that. The English duo of Mimi Rhodes and Annabell Fuller both signed for 71. Lydia Ko is also even par. Nelly Korda is far from out of this tournament but has significant work to do after opening with a two-over-par 73.Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches | The FA | The Guardian
description: The minimum ban for discriminatory behaviour is to be raised to 10 matches by the Football Association
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: The minimum ban for discriminatory behaviour is to be raised to 10 matches by the Football Association
Content: Preston’s Milutin Osmajic was banned for nine matches after he was found to have made racist remarks.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenPreston’s Milutin Osmajic was banned for nine matches after he was found to have made racist remarks.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersThe FAFA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matchesDiscrimination ‘continues to be challenge’Current minimum ban is six matchesPaul MacInnesThu 30 Jul 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.Premier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubsRead moreAcross the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted.
