If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.Explore more on these topicsThe FAFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Supreme court says Palestine Action co-founder can challenge ban on group | Palestine Action | The Guardian
description: UK’s highest court gives permission for Huda Ammori to challenge court of appeal ruling
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: UK’s highest court gives permission for Huda Ammori to challenge court of appeal ruling
Content: Huda Ammori has been fighting to have the ban on Palestine Action overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign.Photograph: Abdullah Bailey/AlamyView image in fullscreenHuda Ammori has been fighting to have the ban on Palestine Action overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign.Photograph: Abdullah Bailey/AlamyPalestine ActionSupreme court says Palestine Action co-founder can challenge ban on groupUK’s highest court gives permission for Huda Ammori to challenge court of appeal rulingHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 13.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe co-founder ofPalestine Actionhas won permission to challenge the ban against the group at the UK’s highest court.The direct action groupwas proscribedas a terrorist organisation in July last year but its co-founder, Huda Ammori, has been fighting to have the ban overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign.In February, the high court ruled that the ban wasdisproportionate and unlawfulbut its decision was overturned by the court of appeallast month.On Thursday, the supreme court said Ammori could appeal against the court of appeal’s decision and that the case would be heard in the final quarter of this year.It means the fate of more than 3,500 people who have been arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action since the ban remains in limbo as their cases are on hold until the legality of proscription has been definitely resolved.Ammori welcomed the supreme court’s decision, saying: “The proscription of Palestine Action has become a vehicle for a far broader crackdown on expressions of solidarity with the Palestinian people.“This unprecedented attack on free speech and the right to protest in this country is already having a chilling effect at a time when speaking out about Israel’s crimes could not be more urgent.”She appealed directly to the supreme court to hear the case after the court of appeal’s decision refused permission to appeal against its own decision within hours of the application.The court of appeal review was comprised of five judges, which is unusual as it normally consists of two or three. It included the country’s two most senior judges: the lady chief justice, Sue Carr, and the master of the rolls, Geoffrey Vos.The supreme court said it was arguable that the ban represented a disproportionate interference with articles 10 and 11 of the European convention on human rights, which protect the rights of freedom of speech and protest respectively.Ammori has pledged to challenge the ban, which has been widely condemned by civil liberties groups, as well as by UN experts and politicians from across the divide, at the European court of human rights if it is upheld by the UK courts.As the supreme court’s decision was published, dozens more people were arrested for allegedly supporting, being a member of and/or encouraging others to join Palestine Action.In a demonstration outside Westminster magistrates court in central London, protesters took turns to stand up and declare their support for or membership of Palestine Action.Many of the mainly elderly protesters lay down after speaking and were carried away by officers. Among those arrested was an 87-year-old woman in a wheelchair.Sir Jonathon Porritt was one of those arrested for showing support for Palestine Action, according to the activist group Defend Our Juries.Porritt, 76, is a former director of Friends of the Earth and was an adviser to the Prince of Wales – now King Charles – for more than 30 years.Dick Scroop, 79, from Wolverhampton, was one of those who was there to be arrested.He said: “There’s a genocide in which the British government is deeply implicated by its diplomatic efforts and the continuing supply of weapons to Israel, and the attempt to suppress legitimate protests by the wielding of anti-terrorism laws is simply unacceptable. It’s an assault on free speech.”By inviting support for Palestine Action, and expressing membership of the group, the protesters risk up to 14 years’ imprisonment in trials before a jury, a significant escalation from most of the previous arrests for holding placards which will be dealt with by magistrates and risk a maximum of six months in jail.Many arrested on Thursday had previously been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action.The Metropolitan Police said 117 people were arrested, most for “expressing support for a proscribed organisation”.Explore more on these topicsPalestine ActionUK supreme courtCourt of appealnewsShareReuse this content

title: US government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conference | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: State department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in Brazil
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: State department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in Brazil
Content: The map presented in Brazil on Sunday showed a landlocked Nigeria in the Sahara and placed Mozambique in the Horn of Africa.Photograph: Picture obtained by ReutersView image in fullscreenThe map presented in Brazil on Sunday showed a landlocked Nigeria in the Sahara and placed Mozambique in the Horn of Africa.Photograph: Picture obtained by ReutersUS foreign policyUS government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conferenceState department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in BrazilReutersThu 30 Jul 2026 18.48 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US government map ofAfricamislabeled every country during a state department presentation at a ⁠global conference in Brazil ⁠this week, ​causing a stir among attenders who took screenshots and posted them online.Reuters viewed a video of the presentation given at the Aids 2026 conference in ⁠Rio de Janeiro, which shows the errant map displayed halfway during a presentation about the state department’s new health agreements.A Reuters analysis found the image of the map included ⁠in the presentation contained an artificial intelligence watermark that signals it was made with OpenAI tools. The ​company said it was investigating the report.The state ‌department said it took “full responsibility” ‌for the confusion caused and that the map had been produced by a team member who hastily changed ‌the slide deck before the event.The map showed Nigeria, where the US currently has several hundred troops deployed, as landlocked in the Sahara desert. Mozambique, which is in south-eastern Africa, was relocated to the Horn of Africa, while Côte d’Ivoire in west Africa was placed on the other side of the continent.Screenshots of the map first appeared in a Substack post by the Aids expert Emily Bass and were widely ‌shared on LinkedIn, with one post garnering about 40,000 views.“Whoever created and approved this slide did not know where countries in Africa are and did not care to ​check their work,” wrote Matt Petit, who focuses on AI and geopolitics at the Atlantic Council, in the post.In a statement, the state department said: “We take full responsibility for the confusion and misrepresentation it caused for attendees, including our African partners.” The speaker at the conference was Jeff Graham, the ⁠top US health envoy who oversees the initiative known as the President’s Emergency Plan ​for Aids Relief, or Pepfar. He ​did not reply to requests for comment.The ​state department said the discussions at the conference were “substantive and constructive” despite the map ​and that it remained ‌committed to fighting Aids ​with real results. The ​Trump administration’s decision last year to pause funding pending a review disrupted aid programs worldwide, but Pepfar’s core work such as the provision of life-saving drugs has largely resumed. The US is scaling back other areas of its spending including on prevention and surveillance, and plans to fully phase out the program in South Africa.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyAfricaAids and HIVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Father of US teen school shooter sentenced to 15 years for providing gun | Georgia high school shooting | The Guardian
description: Colin Gray is the father of Colton, who was 14 when he opened fire at Apalachee high school in Georgia in 2024
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Colin Gray is the father of Colton, who was 14 when he opened fire at Apalachee high school in Georgia in 2024
Content: Colin Gray during his sentencing hearing at Barrow county superior court on 30 July 2026, in Winder, Georgia.Photograph: Hyosub Shin/Pool Atlanta Journal-Constitution/APView image in fullscreenColin Gray during his sentencing hearing at Barrow county superior court on 30 July 2026, in Winder, Georgia.Photograph: Hyosub Shin/Pool Atlanta Journal-Constitution/APGeorgia high school shootingFather of US teen school shooter sentenced to 15 years for providing gunColin Gray is the father of Colton, who was 14 when he opened fire at Apalachee high school in Georgia in 2024Richard Luscombeand agencyThu 30 Jul 2026 14.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe father of a teenage student who killed two teachers and two classmates in aGeorgia high school shootingtwo years ago was sentenced on Thursday to 15 years in prison for providing his son with the weapon used in the attack.Colin Gray’s offenses, the judge Nicholas Primm said during the sentencing hearing in Winder, were crimes of negligence “tethered to the tragedy committed by his son” Colton, who was 14 when he entered Apalachee high school on 4 September 2024 and opened fire.Primm said Gray, who was convicted in March on charges of second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter, shared responsibility for the attack, having gifted his son the assault-style rifle as a Christmas present.“My heart aches for everyone that was there that day, for all of you that have been impacted by it,” said Primm, a Barrow county superior court judge.“But the law requires that I set aside emotion. I don’t get to sentence with passion. I have the nearly impossible task of sentencing you without passion despite the immeasurable heartache that you caused.”On Tuesday, Primm sentenced Colton, now 16, tolife in prisonwithout parole for the murders of teachers Richard Aspinwall, 39; Cristina Irimie, 53; and 14-year-old students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo. Another teacher and eight students were hurt, seven of them wounded by gunfire.Colton had entered into a plea deal with prosecutors admitting guilt on 55 counts and avoiding a scheduled October trial while leaving sentencing up to the judge.Brian Hobbs, Gray’s defense attorney, asked Primm for a sentence of 10 years for his client followed by 10 more of probation; prosecutors said he deserved 80 years in prison.He is one of a handful of American parents who have been criminally charged after their children were accused in shootings. A jury in March found Gray guilty of second-degree murder in the deaths of the two students.Georgialaw defines second-degree murder as causing the death of a child by committing the crime of cruelty to children.Gray, 55, was also found guilty of involuntary manslaughter in the killings of Aspinwall and Irimie.In impact statements, family members of the people who died, and other victims of the shooting, condemned what they said were Gray’s failures as a parent.“This wasn’t unavoidable. This was preventable. Because of the choices made inside the Gray household, four families were handed life sentences of grief,” Breanna Schermerhorn, the mother of Mason, told the court.Shayna Aspinwall, whose husband was killed, said the sentence must take into account “the families left behind who must carry the grief and trauma for the rest of our lives”.“He did not pull the trigger but purchased and left a firearm accessible to a minor,” she said.Prosecutors said Gray gave his son the rifle as a Christmas gift along with ammunition, a gun sight and other shooting accessories.Jason Smith, an investigator with the Barrow county sheriff’s office, testified that Colton carried the semiautomatic rifle on to the school bus with the barrel sticking out and wrapped in poster board. The teenager left his second-period class and went to a bathroom, emerged with the rifle and shot people in the hallway and a classroom, he said.The teenager, prosecutors said, was immersed in an online “true crime community” in which he and other young people discussed their obsession with mass shooters – in Gray’s case, Nikolas Cruz, who murdered 14 students and three adults at Florida’s Marjory Stoneman Douglas high school in 2018.Gray, they said, had showed signs of deteriorating mental health in the weeks leading up to the shooting at the school about 45 miles east of Atlanta.Gray’s attorney said his son “actively hid the depth of his involvement” in the online community, and that a sentence for the father equal to the son’s would erase the line in Georgia law “between the harm a person intends to do and the harm a person fails to prevent”, Hobbs argued.But Brad Smith, the Barrow county district attorney, said Gray “was convicted for what he did know”. The father, Smith said, ignored “a substantial and unjustifiable risk” in giving his son the weapon despite being aware that Colton had adorned his bedroom walls with photographs and news articles about the Marjory Stoneman Douglas shooting.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsGeorgia high school shootingGun crimeUS crimeGeorgiaLaw (US)US justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Child pedestrian casualties are almost five times higher in England’s worst-off areas | Road safety | The Guardian
description: Official figures expose widening gap in road deaths and injuries between poor and wealthy postcodes
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Official figures expose widening gap in road deaths and injuries between poor and wealthy postcodes
Content: Official figures show 2,432 people under 16 were killed or seriously injured on Great Britain’s roads last year.Photograph: Crispin Hughes/AlamyView image in fullscreenOfficial figures show 2,432 people under 16 were killed or seriously injured on Great Britain’s roads last year.Photograph: Crispin Hughes/AlamyRoad safetyChild pedestrian casualties are almost five times higher in England’s worst-off areasOfficial figures expose widening gap in road deaths and injuries between poor and wealthy postcodesGwyn TophamTransport correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of children killed or injured crossing roads is almost five times higher in England’s most deprived areas than its wealthiest, official analysis suggests.Department forTransportfigures show a widening gap over the past 10 years in road casualties between those living in the poorest 10% of postcodes and the most affluent 10%.The number of people reported killed or seriously injured across Great Britain’s roads went up to 29,918 in 2025, 2,432 of whom were under 16. The total was 3% above the 2022-24 average while fatalities fell 4% to 1,538.DfT analysis of where the most serious accidents in England occurred showed stark differences in the proportion of casualties from poorer and wealthier areas, particularly among younger people.More than 20% of child pedestrians killed or injured lived in the most deprived 10% of areas, compared with 4% living in the least deprived, according tothe DfT reporton deprivation and road casualties in England.It found strong links between casualties and deprivation for all pedestrians and bus users. The difference is less stark for car occupants, but mileage is higher in wealthier postcodes, which the analysts said “suggests that the risk for car occupants is much higher for the most deprived income deciles even though they have less exposure”.Theoverall British figuresreleased by the government showed fatalities continued to rise for motorcycle users, countering the falling death toll for car drivers.Campaigners said the 14% rise – from 325 deaths in 2024 to 372 last year – needed a response.Rebecca Guy of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents said: “It is particularly concerning that the gap between the most and least deprived areas has widened over the last decade.“If the government is serious about reducing road deaths and serious injuries, tackling inequality must be at the heart of its approach.“That means targeting investment and prevention efforts toward the communities at greatest risk, ensuring everyone has access to safe roads, safe infrastructure and safe journeys.”Motorcyclists were one of the most vulnerable groups on the roads and the figures reinforced the need for targeted action to improve their safety, she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpeeding was a factor in 52% of recorded deaths on Great Britain’s roads last year. More than three-quarters of those killed across all types of accidents were male, the figures show.Motorways were statistically the safest roads per mile travelled in 2025 – accounting for only 6% of fatalities despite carrying 21% of traffic.A DfT spokesperson said: “Everyone should feel safe on our roads, no matter where they live.“Our road safety strategy, the first in over a decade, recognises that people from deprived areas can face higher risks on the road. That’s why it aims to reduce deaths and serious injuries for all road users. We will keep track of the strategy’s impact, including how it affects people in more deprived areas to make sure measures are fair to all communities.”The headline on this article was amended on 30 July 2026. An earlier version said that child pedestrian deaths were almost five times higher in England’s worst-off areas; it should have said casualties.Explore more on these topicsRoad safetyEnglandTransportInequalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: More prisoners in England and Wales are recalled than released for first time | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Returns for breaches of licence conditions rose 31% in the first quarter of 2026, adding to pressure on prison places
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Returns for breaches of licence conditions rose 31% in the first quarter of 2026, adding to pressure on prison places
Content: A man leaves HM Prison Liverpool. The rise in the recall rate since the first quarter of 2025 is probably due in part to early release schemes, the MoJ says.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenA man leaves HM Prison Liverpool. The rise in the recall rate since the first quarter of 2025 is probably due in part to early release schemes, the MoJ says.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyPrisons and probationMore prisoners in England and Wales are recalled than released for first timeReturns for breaches of licence conditions rose 31% in the first quarter of 2026, adding to pressure on prison placesJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore people were recalled to prison than were released during the first three months of 2026, the first time on record the “recall rate” has surpassed 100% inEnglandand Wales.Between January and March 2026, 12,977 people were released from prison while 13,193 people were returned to prison for breaching their licence conditions, up 31% from last year, new Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data showed.This means that for every 100 people released, 101 people were recalled to custody, creating a “recall rate” of over 100%.This rate has increased rapidly from about 30% a decade ago. Between January and March 2016, 17,923 people were released and 5,185 were recalled, meaning about 30 people were recalled for every 100 prisoners released.Prisons in England and Wales are close to capacity, and the government has recentlypaused its plans to release about 6,000 prisoners earlyto ease the crisis.Andy Keen-Downs, the chief executive of the Prison Advice and Care Trust, said: “The prison population crisis will not be solved if as many people are being sent back to prison as are leaving it.”He warned that if current circumstances don’t change, prison places may run out by Christmas.“Hundreds of people are recalled every month not because they have committed new offences, but because they have fallen foul of licence conditions,” he said. “This makes little sense at a time when the government is doing everything it can to reduce pressure on the prison system.”In total, 51,419 prisoners were recalled to jail in the year to March 2026 after breaching the terms of their licence, up 28% from the previous 12 months and the highest number since current records began in 2015.Of all recalls, 22% involved a further charge of offending, while the vast majority were for breaches of licence conditions, which have risen sharply over the past decade.Burnham stirs up political row with review of release plans for violent criminalsRead moreBreaches include failing to keep in touch with probation services or failing to reside at an approved address.The figures also showed 70,066 prisoners have been freed early since September 2024, when the government brought in emergency measures in response to the overcrowding crisis.Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said the number of recalls were “piling further pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate” and showed “a system that simply isn’t working”.“Thousands of people are being sent back to custody each year for licence breaches rather than new crimes, and we know from our work that many of these recalls are linked to homelessness after leaving prison, addiction to drugs and alcohol, and mental health issues,” he said.Almost 13,000 peopleleft prison homeless or as rough sleepers in the year to April 2025, a 39% rise from the previous year.Pavan Dhaliwal, the chief executive of the charity Revolving Doors, which works with people who are in repeat contact with the justice system, said the system needs reform so recall becomes a “genuine last resort”.“Sending people back to prison when they are struggling to rebuild their lives is costly, counterproductive and keeps the revolving door turning,” she said.The MoJ said the increase was probably due in part to early release schemes, under which more prisoners have been released on licence earlier in their sentences.Alex Hewson from the Prison Reform Trust said more people on short sentences being released on licence was creating “more opportunities for recall”.“We are now using recall far more frequently than in the recent past, and it is reasonable to ask whether every return to custody is necessary and proportionate,” he said. “Given the pressure on both prisons and probation, that question deserves serious attention.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifteen elephant deaths at Kenya park may be due to cyanide poisoning | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service
Content: A KWS investigation found 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and tests had detected a potential toxic substance.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA KWS investigation found 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and tests had detected a potential toxic substance.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockWildlifeFifteen elephant deaths at Kenya park may be due to cyanide poisoningAnalysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife ServiceCarlos Mureithiin NairobiThu 30 Jul 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe recent deaths of 15 elephants near a park in southern Kenya in the past month were likely caused by the animals ingesting pesticides used on nearby tomato farms, the KenyaWildlifeService (KWS) has said.Erustus Kanga, the agency’s director general, told Citizen TV that analysis of samples collected from the carcasses had found traces of cyanide, a chemical compound used in farming as a predator control poison and a pest fumigant, which hasalso been used by poachers.“Cyanide is a highly toxic chemical,” he said. “If elephants consume cyanide, they cannot survive a day or two.”The deaths occurred in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku Group ranch areas around Amboseli national park, an area covering 392 sq km (96,865 acres) and that, together with other neighbouring conservancies are home to more than 1,600 elephants.Kenya investigating unexpected deaths of 15 elephants in national parkRead moreKimana town is a leading tomato producer and a place where researchers at the Route to Food Initiative, a food rights programme, have previouslyreportedthe use of a cyanide substance on the crop.Isaac Lekolool, the head of veterinary and capture services at KWS, told Citizen TV that the stomach contents of one member of a herd that roamed Kimana sanctuary included “lots of tomatoes,” suggesting agrochemical poisoning.Kanga warned that the effects could reach a wider population, as livestock may also eat from farms in the area.“We have the goats, we have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this cyanide is truly the one that is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact.”On Tuesday, KWSannouncedit was investigating the deaths of the elephants from 24 June and 24 July in Amboseli. It said 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and that preliminary tests had detected a potential toxic substance.Benson Leyian, the CEO of Big Life Foundation, a conservation organisation that operates in the area surrounding Amboseli national park, said the elephant deaths were a cause for concern.“Thanks to decades of community-centred conservation, the Amboseli elephant population is one of the best protected inAfrica, and elephant poaching has been virtually eliminated here. Aside from losses during periods of severe drought, we haven’t seen a cluster of elephant deaths like this for some time,” he said.Ina statement, the International Fund for Animal Welfare described the deaths as “deeply alarming”, adding the incident “reinforces why we must continue investing in science, monitoring, and collaborative conservation efforts”.“Every elephant lost is significant – not only for the species, but for the health of the ecosystems they help sustain and the communities that live alongside them,” it said.Farmers and herders inKenyahave in the past poisoned wildlife in retaliation for eating their crops and livestock.In Zimbabwe, poachers have killed dozens of elephants bylacing watering holes and salt licks with the chemical compound.The Amboseli ecosystem is a major source of tourism revenue, but tensions have been building in recent months as local leaders demand the handover of the park’s management and operations to the government of Kajiado county, where it is located. Earlier this month, a court suspended the county government’s takeover.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeAnimalsKenyaAfricaFarmingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Grey lump with orange wings’: hummingbird hawk-moths descend on UK gardens | Insects | The Guardian
description: Boom in hummingbird hawk-moth sightings put down to hot weather, strong winds and food scarcity in Europe
Author: Chris Baraniuk
Headline: Boom in hummingbird hawk-moth sightings put down to hot weather, strong winds and food scarcity in Europe
Content: Luke Burstow spied the hummingbird hawk-moth enjoying buddleia flowers in his garden in Sussex.Photograph: Luke BurstowView image in fullscreenLuke Burstow spied the hummingbird hawk-moth enjoying buddleia flowers in his garden in Sussex.Photograph: Luke BurstowInsects‘Grey lump with orange wings’: hummingbird hawk-moths descend on UK gardensBoom in migrating moth sightings put down to hot weather, strong winds and food scarcity in EuropeChris BaraniukThu 30 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 05.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe had just sat down to dinner in the garden when a speedy visitor whizzed by – a “grey lump with orange wings”, recalled Luke Burstow, from Sussex. It was ahummingbird hawk-moth, a flying insect that migrates to the UK from continental Europe and north Africa.“I was like: ‘Wow!’,” said the software project manager. “I didn’t even know they existed.”Burstow is one of many UK wildlife watchers who have described seeing the moth on social media lately. “This made my day,”wrote one Reddit userafter their sighting.Butterfly and moth experts told the Guardian that 2026 could be a bumper year for hummingbird hawk-moths in the UK after a boom in sightings during recent weeks. Hot weather and strong winds appear to have brought many of the insects here from more southerly climes.Burstow, who, along with his wife, spied the hummingbird hawk-moth enjoying buddleia flowers on 30 June, said: “It was just so different to everything else you normally see.” After quickly Googling the species, Burstow ran inside to grab his camera and managed to take some photos of the creature. He marvelled at how, even with a very fast shutter speed, the moth’s wings –which beat roughly 80 times per second– still appeared slightly blurry in his photos.View image in fullscreenA hummingbird hawk-moth. ‘I was like: “Wow!”,’ said Luke Burstow. ‘I didn’t even know they existed.’Photograph: Luke Burstow“We’ve had a big increase in sightings and inquiries about the hummingbird hawk-moth sent to us this year,” said Richard Austin, a recording schemes officer at the charity Butterfly Conservation. “We expect it is going to be a great summer for them.” Austin cautioned, however, that it was too early to compare their numbers with previous years.Hummingbird hawk-moths may be spotted all around the UK, including in Northern Ireland and even northern Scotland. Warm southerly winds associated with recent heatwaves could have helped bring high numbers of the moths to the UK, said Richard Harrington, an honorary fellow of the Royal Entomological Society. “It may also be that their food plants are drying out in their Mediterranean breeding areas,” he added.Sunny weather in the UK has perhaps encouraged people to spend more time than usual in their gardens, raising the chances that they will spot one of the moths, said Ray Barnett, a council member at the British Entomological and Natural History Society. “I’m in Bristol and there’s lots of people recording it locally,” he said.There’s a chance the hummingbird hawk-moths could stick around, should the UK continue to experience milder winters due to global warming, Barnett added.Hibernating adults that make it through the British winter may go on to reproduce in the UK on a regular basis. Hummingbird hawk-moth larvae feed on plants includinglady’s bedstrawand hedge bedstraw, which are common wildflowers in the UK.“If these weather patterns continue, then [the moth] is going to survive winters regularly,” said Barnett. “It’s almost becoming a resident species rather than a purely migratory species.”Explore more on these topicsInsectsButterfliesEnglandWildlifeClimate crisisWild flowersEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: A rain festival with no rain: the Indian farmers bracing for a ‘super’ El Niño as monsoon arrives late | Global development | The Guardian
description: Raja is normally a celebration of the start of the monsoon, but in the eastern state of Odisha, the rains came so late the seeds were sown under clear skies
Author: Neelima Vallangi
Headline: Raja is normally a celebration of the start of the monsoon, but in the eastern state of Odisha, the rains came so late the seeds were sown under clear skies
Content: Farmers in Laxmipur village, Odisha state, say their crops failed during the last El Niño event in 2023-24View image in fullscreenFarmers in Laxmipur village, Odisha state, say their crops failed during the last El Niño event in 2023-24Global developmentA rain festival with no rain: the Indian farmers bracing for a ‘super’ El Niño as monsoon arrives lateRaja is normally a celebration of the start of the monsoon, but in the eastern state of Odisha, the rains came so late the seeds were sown under clear skiesSupported byAbout this contentWords and photographs byNeelima VallangiThu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKasturi Gamango and Pramila Sabar cannot contain their giggles as they explain one of the big attractions of the Raja festival, which they attended a few days earlier along with 20 other farmer families in Laxmipur, in Odisha’s Ganjam district.“We do no work for three days during the festival,” they say. “Our husbands cook and clean while we enjoy our free time.”Raja is a vibrant, agrarian celebration in the richly forested eastern Indian state of Odisha that celebrates fertility, womanhood and Basumati, the Hindu goddess of the Earth. Traditionally, the three-day event is held from 14 to 16 June to mark the start of the rainy season and the beginning of sowing crops.But this year the fields remained untouched, and the skies clear. The monsoon did not arrive until the end of the month.Global experts have officially declared that this year would see theonset of a “super” El Niño, an extreme version of the weather cycle, and expect it to intensify rapidly from July to September.View image in fullscreenSanjith Mandal says his family had to take out a loan at a high interest rate when his crops failed during the last El NiñoIn India, El Niño years are usually associated with a weak monsoon, delayed and uneven rainfall, dry spells and extreme temperatures, leading to agricultural droughts, increased energy use and water shortages as reservoirs are depleted.Juneended with a 40% shortfall in rainand even with the excess rainfall this month, the effects of drought have not been mitigated. The state has facedat least 19 droughts over the past 50 years.Despite the dry conditions and a lack of irrigation facilities, farmers in Laxmipur cautiously sowed seeds in their paddy fields in the last days of June, hoping it would rain in time for germination. Mangala Sabar, 45, remembers the 2023-24 El Niño years “when the transplanting attempts failed twice in each year, and we lost the entire crop”.Sanjith Mandal, 24, also remembers that time. “When the crops failed those two years, our family took a loan of 30,000 rupees [£235] from a moneylender at very high interest to manage expenses. Almost everyone here has taken on debt.”View image in fullscreenPramila Sabar, left, and Kasturi Gamango show pictures of the Raja festival celebrations in JuneDuring El Niño, the main concern is reduced rainfall and lower soil moisture, which adversely affect farming, says Nitin Bassi, a water management specialist at the Council on Energy, Environment andWater(CEEW), a Delhi-based thinktank.“Monsoon happens after a peak summer in our country, and the soil is dry. If the soil is not saturated enough when it rains, there won’t be any runoff going into the reservoirs, natural tanks and ponds, and there won’t be sufficient water to supply for winter crops either,” he says.2:58Could ‘Godzilla’ El Niño bring the hottest year on record? – video explainerAccording to Bassi, nearly 50% of the cultivated area in Odisha is largely rain-fed, where irrigation is not practised or available.A 2024 analysis by CEEWfound that the monsoon arrived up to a week late in Odisha over the past decade, and winter rainfall from October to December had increased.Mangala Sabar has been supporting his family of four by working daily-wage jobs in the local construction industry, supplemented by rice grown in his field. “With that, we only have to buy groceries, and household expenditure will be manageable. Otherwise, I have to work twice as hard to make up for the lost sustenance and earn extra income needed to buy rice for the entire year for my family,” he says. “I only find work for about 15 days a month, even that is highly uncertain.”View image in fullscreenThe Jarao River joins the Rushikulya River, which feeds a nearby reservoirIn Mali Jagannathpur village, on the banks of the Rushikulya River, farmers wait for canal water to be released from a nearby reservoir once rainfall picks up, so they can sow their seeds.However, not all fields have access to canal water. Widowed about four years ago, K Sukumari, 28, wanted to farm her husband’s plot, but has been unable to grow rice due to the water shortage.“Five years ago, when I worked in the field with my husband, I remember there was water in the borewell and even rainfall was adequate,” says Sukumari, who is raising her two children alone, one of whom needs special care.The borewell has dried up, and rainfall has often been delayed and deficient for the past few years, she says. She works in a brick kiln factory for half of the year and in other people’s fields during the growing season to earn a living.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenK Sukumari says her borewell has dried up and rainfall has been little and late in recent yearsIn many villages in Odisha, household income is a mix of daily-wage labour, sharecropping and remittances from migration, supplemented by subsistence paddy farming.“Drought is not an unknown hazard for Odia farmers,” says Chandni Singh, a lead author for theIntergovernmental Panel on Climate Changeand climate adaptation researcher at the Indian Institute for Human Settlements, referring to farmers living in Odisha.“We know that in any farming system, people are very smart,” says Singh. “They are not passive victims; they are innovating and adapting.“But you can’t expect a farming household to endlessly adapt in place,” she says. “The other thing farming households can do is diversify risk. So you start migrating.”“Distress migration” is occurring in some parts of Odisha but remittances have been a substantial source of income for many villages, improving livelihoods in the southern region, according to Liby Johnson, executive director of Gram Vikas, a development organisation working with Odisha’s rural communities for nearly five decades.However, at the heart of farming communities’ wellbeing and long-term resilience against the climate crisis is water security and weather certainty, he says. Gram Vikas has launched aslew of initiativesin Odisha’s villages, including hyperlocal weather forecasting, detailed aquifer mapping to understand groundwater availability, and the building of low-cost soil and water conservation structures to enhance water retention.Overlooking the hills of the Eastern Ghats, one of the 25 automatic weather stations installed by Gram Vikas stands on the roof of Mangala Sabar’s house, at the entrance to Laxmipur village. The outer wall has been turned into a huge blackboard where weekly weather conditions and a seven-day rain forecast are written in the local Odia language. He receives the processed weather forecast information via WhatsApp and is responsible for updating the board.View image in fullscreenMangala Sabar writes the conditions recorded by the weather station installed on his roof on a giant blackboardThe India Meteorological Department also launched an initiative last year to provide accurateforecasts of the monsoon’s arrivalup to 30 days in advance. Tailored forecasts are now being delivered to more than 38 million farmers via SMS and phone calls, including in Odisha.Similarly, several El Niño-related advisories were issued by the government recommending farmers delayed sowing, choose low-duration or other less water-intensive crops, and adopt drought-resilient varieties.However, uptake of this information remains limited. “The idea that data alone will influence a farmer’s decision is flawed. People don’t make decisions like that, especially farmers who are dealing with uncertainty every day,” says Singh.“The core information comes from their local knowledge, like reading the soil, the ants, the trees and the clouds. There’s also an outsized influence of peers – studies show that the uptake of that climate information is much higher when information comes through peers,” she says.Johnson says: “One has to really give space for an evolutionary process for cropping changes to happen.We have to instil confidence in the community that the information is accurate and valuable, and let the farmer choose what works best for them.”View image in fullscreenFarmers in Odisha are braced for a difficult year as a ‘super’ El Niño follows a brutal summerThis month the rating agencyS&P Global warnedthat a weak monsoon in India could drive up inflation, weaken rural demand and strain fiscal balances.With bursts of heavy rainfall across some parts of the country in the month of July, the overallmonsoon deficit has narrowedto 21%. But there remains deep uncertainty as El Niño strengthens.Farmers in Odisha, however, are pushng on. “How can we know if it will rain adequately or not? There is no point in worrying about that. We will sow the seeds regardless because we are farmers,” says Mangala Sabar. “We will farm, and let’s see what happens.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentEnvironmental sustainabilityIndiaEl Niño southern oscillationFarmingDroughtWaterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Weatherwatch: rainclouds are travelling farther in warmer world | Water | The Guardian
description: Climate crisis affects not only the amount of rain that falls but where, with implications for land use and water security
Author: Kate Ravilious
Headline: Climate crisis affects not only the amount of rain that falls but where, with implications for land use and water security
Content: Because warmer air holds more water vapour, scientists says it stays aloft longer and travels farther before falling as rain.Photograph: ANP/AlamyView image in fullscreenBecause warmer air holds more water vapour, scientists says it stays aloft longer and travels farther before falling as rain.Photograph: ANP/AlamyWeatherwatchWaterWeatherwatch: rainclouds are travelling farther in warmer worldClimate crisis affects not only the amount of rain that falls but where, with implications for land use and water securityKate RaviliousThu 30 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHave you ever wondered how far a raindrop has travelled before it lands on you? It may have journeyed thousands of kilometres from the ocean, sea or lake it evaporated from – and now research shows raindrops are travelling even farther than they used to.Warmer air can hold more water vapour, and that is changing not only how much rain we receive but also where it falls. Travis Aerenson, of the University of Wyoming, and his colleagues modelled atmospheric moisture movements in the US over more than three decades. Their research showed that in the southwestern and southern plains, moisture in the atmosphere travels 30 to 50 miles (50 to 80km) farther than it did 35 years ago, staying aloft for an extra two to four hours before falling as rain.Their findings, published inGeophysical Research Letters, also show that more evaporation is occurring from ocean surfaces and less from land surfaces. The change in atmospheric moisture pathways affects where and when precipitation occurs, with implications for land use. The researchers also note that the trend for moisture to travel farther will result in the water security of more countries and states falling increasingly outside their borders, requiring greater collaboration between neighbours.Explore more on these topicsWaterWeatherwatchClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK government reviews why police ceding criminal cases to US military | Police | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: ministers and police chiefs examining how cases involving US military personnel on UK soil are handled after Guardian revelations
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Exclusive: ministers and police chiefs examining how cases involving US military personnel on UK soil are handled after Guardian revelations
Content: Complainants are often not given the same protections in the US military court martial process as they would have got in a British court.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenComplainants are often not given the same protections in the US military court martial process as they would have got in a British court.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyBase justicePoliceUK government reviews why police ceding criminal cases to US militaryExclusive: ministers and police chiefs examining how cases involving US military personnel on UK soil are handled after Guardian revelationsHarry Davies,Rob Evans,Emine SinmazandLouisa LoveluckThu 30 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 02.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government and police chiefs are reviewing the process through whichUS militarypersonnel accused of committing serious crimes on UK soil are avoiding the British justice system.The effort, involving multiple government departments, is examining why UK police forces, which have primary responsibility for investigating such cases, have been ceding jurisdiction to US military investigators.Such decisions pave the way for alleged perpetrators to be tried in a US military court martial process, an alternative justice system in which victims are often not given the same protections as they would get in a British court.The government and police reviews were launched after the Guardian uncovered a series of casesin which British police forces allowed the American military to take over investigations into allegations of serious sexual offences.When thefirst case was revealedin June, Downing Street said it was “very concerning” that UK authorities were not involved in the prosecution of an American fighter pilot accused of raping and strangling a British woman, Sarah Steele, in his apartment after they met on a dating app.After Cambridgeshire police allowed US military police to take control of the case, the pilot, Capt Jacob Wulfson, was prosecuted in a court martial on a US airbase in Suffolk. The jury, an all-male panel of air force officers, convicted Wulfson of strangling an intimate partner butacquitted him of sexual assault.Victims of sexual attacks by US military personnel that would meet a common definition of rape in the UK are finding that their attackers are instead beingprosecuted for lesser offences.Under the set of laws that govern US forces, known as the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), the crime of rape carries a narrower definition than that adopted by the British courts, meaning many cases are charged instead as sexual assault.Wulfson was given a six-month sentence which he is serving at the US base RAF Lakenheath.View image in fullscreenCapt Jacob Wulfson, centre, pictured at the Dubai airshow in 2019.Photograph: Tech Sgt Joseph Pick/US air forces centralIn recent weeks, Home Office and justice ministers met Steele to discuss her case and whether changes should be made to how UK police and prosecutors handle cases involving US military personnel.A government spokesperson said Steele had “shown incredible bravery in coming forward” and ministers had“committed to identifying and learning any lessons from this case to ensure that victims are supported and treated with the seriousness, dignity and compassion they deserve”.The spokesperson said officials were working closely with the NationalPoliceChiefs’ Council (NPCC) “to look at the guidance in place to ensure that cases are correctly referred to the Crown Prosecution Service for advice”.Ministers have promised to press the US government for a full account of what happened in the Wulfson case. In a statement, the Foreign Office said it had “been engaging with the US on this matter”.How the US bypasses British courts to try its military over crimes in the UKRead moreThe Guardian has unearthed several other cases involving US air force personnel who avoided UK courts despite their alleged crimes occurring while off duty. In each, local police handed over the investigation to military prosecutors, sometimes within days of receiving a report of a crime on UK soil.Hannes Marschalekallegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girland four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He admitted a charge of indecent conduct after negotiating a plea bargain at a court martial. The conviction was later quashed on technical grounds.Tyrion Davisallegedly raped two British womanin Suffolk. He was convicted of one count of sexual assault when he was court martialled but acquitted of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.James Loubeau, who wasaccused of a “spree” of rapesand sexual assaults in East Anglia, drugging some women and breaking into the homes of others, also avoided the British courts.He was acquitted at a court martial where he was tried over allegations from just one of the six women who accused him of attacking them. He was later convicted in a court in Miami over another woman’s allegations, after an FBI investigation into his alleged attacks on women in England.Suffolk police had handed over the Loubeau case to military prosecutors just 11 days after two British women contacted the force to say he and another US airman had drugged and raped them after a meeting in a nightclub.In response to the Guardian’s reporting on such cases, Gavin Stephens, the chair of the NPCC, has written to all chief constables in England and Wales to ensure forces understand their legal obligations in cases involving visiting US forces.A source familiar with discussions in government said ministers were alarmed to learn that UK police forces may not be seeking advice from the CPS before handing over investigations to the US military.View image in fullscreenA sign on a fence outside the runway of RAF Lakenheath.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianUnder legislation dating back to the 1950s, visiting US armed forces in the UK can prosecute their own personnel if the offences were committed while they were on duty or against another member of the military, its property, or a dependant such as a spouse or child.In all other cases, the British police have the first option on whether to launch an investigation into visiting US military personnel. However, the cases uncovered by the Guardian suggest the US has pushed to take control of investigations over which it does not have primary jurisdiction. British police appear to be acquiescing to these requests.Two police forces – Suffolk and Cambridgeshire – areconducting their own reviewsof how they handle investigations involving US military personnel.Bunker busters and a Burger King: a visual guide to US military bases on British soilRead moreIn a statement, Cambridgeshire police said: “We are conducting a policy review being led by our investigation standards department.” The force added that the review was looking at cases going back to 2018, and it did not yet know how many there had been.Suffolk police said: “We are in the process of reviewing the decision-making surrounding the transfer of primacy to the US air force and around case transfer practices more generally.”More than 12,000US militarypersonnel are stationed in the UK, operating from at least 15 bases and facilities. The largest concentration of personnel is at two US military installations in Suffolk, RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall. Large numbers of US forces live in the surrounding areas, including in Norfolk and Cambridgeshire.Concern about US service personnel avoiding the British justice system has been raised by MPs from across the political parties. Nick Timothy, the Conservative justice spokesperson, said Wulfson “should have been fully investigated by the English police and prosecuted in our courts”.Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrats’ justice spokesperson, said: “The British public expect crimes committed in England to be prosecuted in the English courts under English law. That expectation should not change simply because the accused is a member of the foreign military.”Responding to a question in parliament about the Steele case earlier this month, the justice minister, Sarah Sackman, said: “Our thoughts are with the victim, and with the other victims whose experiences have subsequently come to light.”Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsPoliceBase justiceUK criminal justiceUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Raids across UK in crackdown on nuisance car finance texts | Spam | The Guardian
description: Laptops, phones and documents seized as information commissioner acts on messages about mis-selling scandal
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Laptops, phones and documents seized as information commissioner acts on messages about mis-selling scandal
Content: Phones seized during raids by the Information Commissioner's Office on nuisance phone calls.Photograph: Information Commissioner's OfficeView image in fullscreenPhones seized during raids by the Information Commissioner's Office on nuisance phone calls.Photograph: Information Commissioner's OfficeSpamRaids across UK in crackdown on nuisance car finance textsLaptops, phones and documents seized as information commissioner acts on messages about mis-selling scandalRupert JonesThu 30 Jul 2026 09.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaptops, mobile phones and documents have been seized after officials carried out search warrants in a crackdown on claims companies plaguing people with spam text messages about the car finance mis-selling scandal.The UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO)executed warrants at homes and businesseslinked to five companies in London, Liverpool, Bolton, Burnley and Swansea on Wednesday.More than 12m complaints about nuisance marketing text messages have been submitted by the public since September 2025 as claims management companies (CMCs) and other firms attempt to grab a share of the billions of pounds in compensation expected to be paid out to motorists who were mis-sold car loans.The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced a£7.5bn industry-wide compensation schemefor the millions of victims of the scandal in March.Legal challenges, however, forced the regulatorto partly suspend the scheme.The FCA had expected to start paying out £829 on average this year to those affected by the scandal – in which drivers were overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers between 2007 and 2024 – but a court ordered the regulator to suspend parts of the scheme until a hearing in December or February next year.The head of investigations at the ICO, Andy Curry, said: “People are fed up with being bombarded by unwanted calls, texts and emails about car finance claims, and we’re taking action.”This week’s raids “send a clear message to the claims management sector: comply with the law or expect to hear from us”, he said.The companies linked to the searches are subject to continuing investigation. They are believed to be responsible for sending a combined 170m texts to members of the public between September 2025 and May this year.The ICO is working with the FCA, the Advertising Standards Authority and the Solicitors Regulation Authority to tackle poor practices relating to motor finance claims by some CMCs, law firms and lead generation companies.The raids represent an escalation of the crackdown on rogue CMCs and other businesses. As a result of the FCA’s work, more than 1,200 misleading adverts have been removed or amended since January 2024.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome firms face enforcement investigations, while others have had to reduce their “unreasonable” fees or allow consumers to walk away from contracts free of charge.The ICO has the power to apply to the courts for a warrant to search premises as part of investigations under the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, where evidence may be seized. This can include mobile phones, laptops and sim farms: collections of devices that house hundreds or thousands of mobile phone sim cards.The FCA has said there is no need to use a CMC or law firm because people can complain for free using atemplate letteron its website. This week itlaunched a nationwide advertising campaignto direct people to the letter. It will run across TV, radio, print, billboards and social media until 6 September.Explore more on these topicsSpamMotor financeInformation commissionerFinancial Conduct AuthorityRegulatorsConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo calls himself pontiff who ‘happens to be American’  | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: First US pope says mission is to be pastor of a universal church but expresses ‘great love’ for his home country and its core principles
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: First US pope says mission is to be pastor of a universal church but expresses ‘great love’ for his home country and its core principles
Content: Pope Leo XIV says he thinks of himself as ‘the pope who happens to be American’.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersView image in fullscreenPope Leo XIV says he thinks of himself as ‘the pope who happens to be American’.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersPope Leo XIVPope Leo calls himself pontiff who ‘happens to be American’First US pope says mission is to be pastor of a universal church but expresses ‘great love’ for his home country and its core principlesAngela Giuffridain RomeThu 30 Jul 2026 10.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leo, the first US pontiff, has expressed “great love” for his home country and its core principles of freedom, opportunity and welcoming immigrants, but qualified that he just “happens to be American”.In an interview with the US broadcaster NBC on the sidelines of a prayer event in Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat near Rome, Leo, who has condemned the immigration policies of Donald Trump’s administration, spoke about his own family history in describing his relationship with the US.He said his grandparents were immigrants while on his mother’s side, “we have people who were both slaves and slave owners”.When asked how important being American was to him, Leo said: “I think of myself more as the pope who happens to be American. Not to belittle what it means to be an American.“I have great love for America but I understand my mission as having a very important dimension, which is precisely being pastor of a universal church and having a voice and an opportunity to speak to people throughout the world.”Asked what he loved about the US, he replied: “So many things. In a sense, speaking about principles, what America stands for, the sense of freedom, the sense of opportunity, the sense of having invited for generations people from around the world to be part of America.”Having grown up in the US, Leo, who spent two decades as a missionary in Peru, said he continued to hold the principles “that have been a part of being American for so many years”.Since being elected pontiff in May last year, Leo, 70, has repeatedly spoken up for migrants and called Trump’s immigration policies “inhuman”.Relations with the Trump administration worsened further afterthe pontiff strongly condemned the US-Israeli war against Iran.In hisfirst key address to the USon the eve of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, he praised the country’s history of ⁠welcoming migrants while urging Americans to live up to the ideals put forward in the ⁠declaration, in what was seen as another rebuke to Trump.The pontiff marked 4 July with a brief visit to the southern Italian island of Lampedusa, one of the main entry points to Europe for people making the perilous sea crossing from north Africa in search of refuge.Leo is yet to take upTrump’s invitationto the White House, made by the vice-president, JD Vance, during a meeting at the Vatican the day after his inaugural papal mass. Leo told NBC that no trip had been planned, but he hoped to visit the US soon.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVThe papacyReligionUS immigrationMigrationTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifty-three days and counting: 93-year-old leader’s record absence fuels health speculation | Cameroon | The Guardian
description: Cameroon’s Paul Biya has not made a statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 June
Author: Giovanni Wanneh
Headline: Cameroon’s Paul Biya has not made a statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 June
Content: Paul Biya giving a speech in Maroua, Cameroon, last October, with his wife, Chantal, sitting beside him.Photograph: Xinhua/AlamyView image in fullscreenPaul Biya giving a speech in Maroua, Cameroon, last October, with his wife, Chantal, sitting beside him.Photograph: Xinhua/AlamyCameroonFifty-three days and counting: 93-year-old leader’s record absence fuels health speculationCameroon’s Paul Biya has not made a statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 JuneGiovanni Wannehin Buea andEromo Egbejulein AccraThu 30 Jul 2026 08.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA record 53-day absence by the world’s oldest head of state has renewed speculation in his native Cameroon about whether he is dead or alive, even thoughdiscussing his health is illegal in the country.On 7 June, 93-year-old Paul Biya left for Switzerland for what officials described as a “brief private stay” alongside his wife, Chantal. Almost two months later, neither the president nor the first lady have addressed the country or been seen publicly.Biya, who took office in 1982 after a seven-year stint as prime minister, has taken increasingly long absences fromCameroonin recent years, spending much of his time at the five-star InterContinental hotel in Geneva.No official timetable has been announced for the president’s return from his latest trip abroad, leaving Cameroonians to rely on a succession of conflicting statements from government officials.The minister of communication, René Emmanuel Sadi, said Biya was in good health and “working from Geneva, where he currently resides”.“Reports claiming otherwise are pure fantasy and malicious manipulation aimed at destabilising opinion,” he added. Jacques Fame Ndongo, a senior official from the ruling party and the higher education minister, said Biya had been “meticulously following the files submitted to him by his aides … wherever he is”.The labour minister, Grégoire Owona, gave a different explanation, saying the president was on annual leave and comparing him to regular Cameroonian citizens. “Paul Biya, elected by the Cameroonian people and paid by them, is a worker who has the right to annual leave,” he said. “His employer is obliged to grant it. He informed his employer before leaving and will do the same upon his return.”View image in fullscreenA session of Cameroon’s national assembly this month.Photograph: Mengnjo Etienne/ReutersCameroonian authorities banned discussion of Biya’s health in October 2024, during another absence. Nevertheless, local media have published claims in recent weeks that he is critically ill, and jokes about Biya being a work-from-abroad president or a remote-work president have resurfaced on social media.Mamadou Mota, the vice-president of the opposition Cameroon Renaissance Movement party, said Biya’s latest absence had created a “glaring institutional vacuum”. “A country cannot be governed by remote control while critical socioeconomic challenges go unaddressed,” he said.Last November, Biya was sworn in for his eighth consecutive seven-year term, a month aftera presidential electionmarred by widespread allegations of irregularities and voter suppression. Although the Constitutional Council dismissed post-electoral complaints by opposition parties, many of them refused to recognise the outcome, arguing that the election had further eroded public confidence in Cameroon’s democratic institutions.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the opposition politician Issa Tchiroma protest in Douala after Biya’s re-election in October last year.Photograph: Zohra Bensemra/ReutersBiya has yet to name a government since being sworn in for his latest term. With parliamentary and municipal elections expected in early 2027, many are worried that the ripple effect of that and his prolonged absence could disrupt the electoral cycle.Cameroon has the largest economy in centralAfrica, but unemployment rates, high inflation and poor public infrastructure are stymieing the prospects of its young people, who make up about two-thirds of its estimated population of 30.6 million.“Politics should be about serving the people, but the [ruling] CPDM [party] appears more interested in holding on to power than addressing the concerns of Cameroonians,” said Kohtem Sambit, the secretary general of the opposition Movement for Patriotism and People’s Prosperity.“The minister of the economy borrowed more than 21bn [Central African francs] in the name of the Cameroonian people, saying it was approved by Mr Biya,” Sambit told the Guardian. “How do we justify this? You do not see the person who signed, nor do you know his whereabouts. That debt will be paid by the public.”Referring to Owona’s remarks, Sambit said: “If the president is on annual leave, he is still accountable to the Cameroonian people because he is paid with taxpayers’ money. His whereabouts should therefore be disclosed.”A tale of two Francks? World’s oldest leader creates deputy role – raising prospect of dynastic successionRead moreAnother opposition party, the Social Democratic Front, has argued that the issue is not whether the president has a constitutional right to travel, but rather the government’s failure to explain the extension of what had initially been described as a brief private visit. Another opposition leader, Patricia Tomaïno Ndam Njoya, of the Cameroon Democratic Union, has called for an impartial procedure to determine any “temporary or permanent incapacity of the head of state”.In April, parliament reintroduced the office of vice-president as part of a constitutional overhaul, but the position has yet to be filled, leaving Cameroon without a designated deputy should the president become incapacitated. As Biya’s son and stepsonreportedly jockey for position, public disagreements between cabinet ministers have become commonplace.Last week, the party’s secretary general, Jean Nkuete, convened a rare meeting of senior party officials. The CPDM described the gathering only as an “important working session” and did not release an agenda or further details. Attempts to obtain comment from senior party figures were unsuccessful. Several party officials have declined interview requests, citing personal reasons.For the businessman Nji Lucas, the president’s prolonged absence has become an economic concern. “I do not have confidence because it is almost as if the country is on autopilot,” he said. “No serious investor wants to commit resources in a country where there is uncertainty over political leadership. There is no trust, and investors require certainty before making long-term decisions.”Explore more on these topicsCameroonAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts | Japan | The Guardian
description: Soldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivors
Author: Gavin Blair
Headline: Soldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivors
Content: 0:43Police footage shows scale of damage inside Aeon mall after explosion cause by Japan quake – videoJapanDeath toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue effortsSoldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivorsEarthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in picturesGavin Blairin TokyoThu 30 Jul 2026 02.49 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 22.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death toll from the powerful earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday has risen to 30, as thesearch for survivorstrapped in a badly damaged shopping centre, paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country continues.‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquakeRead moreThe 6.8-magnitude quake, which struck Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu, injured at least 62 people, according to the prefectural government.Almost 5,000 Self-Defence Forces (SDF) personnel deployed to the region faced temperatures of up to 35C on Thursday, officials said, adding that a 5.8-magnitude aftershock overnight had further hampered the rescue efforts.Map of earthquake siteAbout 170 rescue workers were searching the Aeon shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake struck.The company said about 3,000 customers were evacuated to a car park before a gas explosion occurred in another part of the shopping centre. Six of the 12 people pulled from the rubble have died.All those caught in the explosion were shop workers who had returned to the building after the evacuation, Aeon said. The company’s president bowed in apology at a press conference on Wednesday, saying Aeon had failed to anticipate the explosion, the cause of which was being investigated.1:09Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – videoJapanese media footage from inside the shopping centre showed part of the ceiling had collapsed, with metal fragments and other debris scattered across the floor as helmeted, masked rescue workers searched the area.Police and SDF personnel were continuing to search for one worker in the debris at the Nippon Paper mill in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed. Of the 10 others who were trapped, eight died and two were injured.In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at the factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government.View image in fullscreenNippon Paper mill, where a chimney collapsed.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPANearly 23,000 homes had no electricity and 75,000 had no running water, Kumamoto officials said. About 15,000 people had been evacuated to 400 shelters.The defence minister said on Wednesday evening that the SDF was airlifting coolers to shelters in Kumamoto, while SDF vessels were delivering water and food.“We’re doing everything possible to make saving lives a priority, making efforts to deliver life-saving supplies, beginning with water,” Shinjiro Koizumi said.Aerial police footage showed several homes had been flattened, including some that had crumbled into a river.View image in fullscreenA collapsed house in Hikawa, Kumamoto.Photograph: Kyodo/ReutersThe earthquake registered the maximum level 7 on Japan’s seven-level shindo scale. “It was the strongest quake I have ever experienced,” Kanzo Matsumoto, 73, the operator of a luxury hot spring inn in Yatsushiro, told Agence France-Presse.The national Geospatial Information Authority said parts of the ground had shifted by 87cm during the quake.Yatsushiro town hall sustained damage to its base-isolation system, an earthquake-resistant technology designed to protect buildings by cushioning their foundations against intense shaking. The system was rebuilt after a deadly earthquake in 2016.View image in fullscreenVehicles are crushed under collapsed buildings in Yatsushiro, south-western Japan.Photograph: Hiro Komae/APSome car and semiconductor manufacturers with plants in Kyushu have halted production.Toyota said it would pause operations at three plants while it assessed the quake’s impact on suppliers and ⁠logistics. Honda suspended operations at a motorcycle plant until Friday.Taiwan’s TSMC has resumed operations at its Kumamoto facility, while Sony, Renesas Electronics and Tokyo Electron have halted production.Kyushu is ‌an important hub for Japan’s automotive and semiconductor industries, which account for about 20% of the region’s industrial output.Analysts said the shutdowns appeared to be driven largely by precaution than damage to production facilities.Kumamoto was struck by two devastatingearthquakes in 2016that killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.The archipelago, home to about 125 million people, usually experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18% of the world’s earthquakes.With Associated Press, Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsJapanEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The number of remains is difficult to determine’: civil war death site dug up for landfill in El Salvador | Global development | The Guardian
description: Despite a 2018 ruling to stop waste being dumped where civilians were executed in the country’s civil war, diggers are working at what campaigners call a place where ‘human life, biodiversity and the environment will be sacrificed’
Author: Camilo Freedman
Headline: Despite a 2018 ruling to stop waste being dumped where civilians were executed in the country’s civil war, diggers are working at what campaigners call a place where ‘human life, biodiversity and the environment will be sacrificed’
Content: View of crosses where remains from a war-era massacre where found less than 100 meters away from the work site for a landfill in Tecoluca, El Salvador, May 2026.Photograph: Camilo Freedman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenView of crosses where remains from a war-era massacre where found less than 100 meters away from the work site for a landfill in Tecoluca, El Salvador, May 2026.Photograph: Camilo Freedman/The GuardianSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanGlobal development‘The number of remains is difficult to determine’: civil war death site dug up for landfill in El SalvadorDiggers are working at what campaigners call a place where ‘human life, biodiversity and the environment will be sacrificed’Supported byAbout this contentWords and photographs byCamilo Freedmanin Tecoluca, El SalvadorThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the morning of 16 February,dozens of police officers arrivedat San Francisco Ángulo, a small rural community an hour south ofEl Salvador’s capital. They had come, residents were told, to escort heavy machinery belonging toCyeemsal, a Mexican-owned company hired to begin construction of a landfill on a site the community considers sacred.Félix Laínez, 58, president of the San Francisco Ángulo community association, had been warned that this would happen. The community has lost a series of legal appeals against the court rulings authorising the work, and construction is continuing. “It is clear that we will find no support in any state institution,” says Laínez, who has little hope of success in their final constitutional appeal, which is now before the supreme court.View image in fullscreenFélix Laínez, a community leader in San Francisco Ángulo, at the landfill site.What makes this more than a land dispute is what lies beneath the ground where the machines are digging. A 2018 ruling by El Salvador’s human rights ombudsman documented two military operations carried out at the site 45 years ago.In the first, on 19 June 1981, a group of women were interrogated, raped and murdered by soldiers. In the second, on 25 July, about 25 armed men entered homes and opened fire, killing about 45 civilians. Their remains are still being exhumed but most of the victims were women and children.Now, the community fears the authorities want to bury its history under tons of rubbish.Rafael Paz Narváez, a sociology professor at the University of El Salvador, says the place was used throughout the war as an execution site.“The army, the [national] guard, the police and the death squads made Lomas de Ángulo a place of execution of prisoners,” he says. “The number of remains is very difficult to determine precisely, but it is large. There are remains in many places.”The construction work has already disturbed some of those remains, according to one excavator operator. The man, who asked not to be identified, says he found six grave sites when work began. In the first, he found at least three bodies.“The smell was like a cemetery,” he says.He initially worked around the graves, but was ordered to remove and rebury the remains. When ordered to move them a second time, he refused, left the site and says he was threatened with a theft accusation – which he strongly denies.He says the project’s representatives later offered him money and a job on condition that he declared to the attorney general’s office that he had never seen any bodies.
