He refused.Laínez brought the allegation before a hearing in Guatemala of theInter-American Commission on Human Rightsin 2018, stating on record his concern about the removal of remains from the civil war era in the area where the landfill is to be located.View image in fullscreenThe landfill site, which is due to receive more than 265 tonnes of solid waste a dayOn the basis of those findings, the ombudsman’s office issued an interim ruling, requesting that the environment ministry and theAsociación de Municipios Los Nonualcos, the local authority promoting the project, halt all construction work at the site.However, the ombudsman’s office cannot enforce its rulings and can only request compliance. While its measures remain formally in force, construction began anyway.The landfill, promoted by Los Nonualcos, an association of 18 municipalities in the departments of La Paz and San Vicente, will receive more than 265 tonnes of solid waste a day, according to documents submitted by the community to the ombudsman’s office this year. A technical assessment of the soil, based on official government data, found the site lies above a critical water-catchment area with highly permeable volcanic soils, which experts say would accelerate pollution leaching underground and contaminating the water sources serving about 1,750 families across 24 communities.A previous landfill site nearby is already leaching contaminants into the Salamar River, which communities downstream depend on for drinking, bathing and irrigation.For Prof Paz Narváez, the landfill is not an isolated decision but part of a pattern in a country where the president, Nayib Bukele,promotes an authoritarian agendaand describes himself as the“world’s coolest dictator”.The San Vicente region, he says, is becoming what campaigners call “a sacrifice zone” – a place designated for environmental exploitation. “Human life, biodiversity and the environment will be sacrificed here,” says Paz Narváez.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA protest by the community against the landfill plans on Labour Day in the capital, San Salvador. The banner translates as: ‘San Francisco Angulo isn’t rubbish. Out with the machinery!’The community of San Francisco Ángulo was never formally consulted, in violation of the country’senvironmental law. Laínez says the municipal authorities have produced documents claiming community agreement, but adds: “Here, no one has signed anything, no one has agreed. How can we be in agreement when we are fighting?”The community has filed complaints with several government institutions andfiled a constitutional appealwith the supreme court in February. Cyeemsal says it does not consider itself the executive body directly responsible for the project.A former machine operator who wished to be identified only as Caín says he was contracted by El Salvador’snational solid waste authority, known as Andres, to carry out the earthworks. Local residents are already being charged through their utility bills for waste collection by Andres, even though they never agreed to the project.Javier Núñez, a spokesperson for the project, did not respond to detailed questions. Los Nonualcos and Andres did not respond to requests for comment.As Cyeemsal is asubsidiary of the Mexican holding companyCyeemex, community groups also wrote to the Mexican president, Claudia Sheinbaum, calling for an investigation into the embassy’s reported role in the project. Neither she nor the embassy responded.View image in fullscreenA mural in Tecoluca commemorating the victims of the civil war-era massacres that took place in San Francisco ÁnguloIn March, Laínez presented the community’s case before theInter-American Commission on Human Rights, where theWorld Organisation Against Torturecalled on the commission to urge El Salvador to refrain from reprisals against participants.On 18 May, after a request from the attorney general’s office, the lower court in Tecoluca dismissed the deforestation case against the company in a hearing lasting just seven minutes. Community members say they were notified of the ruling by WhatsApp.“We were not even given the opportunity to present our case,” says René Alfaro, a community member present at the hearing. “They just read the document, and it was over in minutes.”César Cañas, a leader of theMovement for the Defence of Land and Natural Resources of Tecoluca, calls the ruling a mockery and says the community will continue to use “every legal tool available” to fight for its rights.Laínez, who was outside the courthouse when the decision came through, regrets the impact the landfill is having on his community. “We were happy here. We lacked for nothing – water, firewood, fish. Today we have none of that,” he says.“I am over 50, and I have already lived. But look at the children in this community,” he says. “If we do not stop this, there is nothing good waiting for them here.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanEl SalvadorAmericasHuman rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Apple and Amazon report rising revenues as investors turn on some tech stocks | Technology | The Guardian
description: Both tech companies beat Wall Street predictions on revenue in their second quarters
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Both tech companies beat Wall Street predictions on revenue in their second quarters
Content: The Apple Store at Towson Town Center Mall in Maryland.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Apple Store at Towson Town Center Mall in Maryland.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesTechnologyApple and Amazon report rising revenues as investors turn on some tech stocksBoth tech companies beat Wall Street predictions on revenue in their second quartersNick Robins-EarlyThu 30 Jul 2026 17.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple andAmazonboth released their second quarter earnings on Thursday, a test of investor confidence in major tech companies amid growing concerns over exorbitant AI spending.Apple revealed quarterly revenue of $109.4bn, beating Wall Street expectations of $108.65bn in revenue. It also reported $2.02 earnings per share, driven by sales of its marquee products such as iPhones and laptops.Amazon reported that its revenue was $200.6bn compared with analyst predictions of $196.47bn. The company also grew its AWS cloud computing service and beat market expectations on advertising revenue, though free cash flow declined. Amazon’s stock jumped more than 8% in immediate after hours trading.It has been a tough month for several prominent tech companies, with shares in Tesla and Meta both plunging after they revealed huge spending on AI infrastructure in their latest earnings reports. A recent selloff in chip stocks like Nvidia, the result of loss in investor confidence and advances in Chinese chip manufacturing, has also rattled the market.View image in fullscreenAmazon’s fulfillment center in Robbinsville, New Jersey.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersInvestors have paid especially close attention in recent weeks to tech companies’ free cash flow after large capital expenditures – largely on AI – have caused concern. As the industry continues to plow money into building out AI capabilities in search of future profits, shareholders have become more jittery when earnings reports reveal larger-than expected AI spending.Apple, meanwhile, has benefitted from the chip stock selloff as investors viewed the company as a safe haven amid the broaderAI-driven volatility. The company’s stock is up around 23% this year, leading the so-called Magnificent Seven tech stocks, which include Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Tesla and Nvidia. Apple’s stock price dropped slightly on Thursday following earnings after it reported its revenue from its services division was below market expectations.Thursday’s earnings call was also CEO Tim Cook’s final report before he steps down after 15 years as Apple’s top executive. Apple’s market value grew immensely over Cook’s tenure as chief executive, from around $350bn in 2011 tosurpassing the $5tn markdays before Thursday’s earnings call. Earlier this month the company overtook Nvidia to become the world’s most valuable company.Cook will bereplaced by John Ternus, a longtime hardware engineering executive who has been at the company since 2001. Ternus stated earlier this week that he aims to expand the Apple’s entertainment business, which has had success with movies like the blockbuster F1 and streaming series such as The Studio.“As you know, this will be my final earnings call,” Cook said on Thursday. “I am beyond excited for John to step into his new role and lead Apple into its next era. He is truly one of a kind and there is no better person to take the helm of the company.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAppleAmazonStock marketsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% as inflation fears mount | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Split vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs close to $90 a barrel
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Split vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs close to $90 a barrel
Content: Governor of the Bank of England (BoE) Andrew Bailey addresses a press conference after today’s interest rate decisionPhotograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenGovernor of the Bank of England (BoE) Andrew Bailey addresses a press conference after today’s interest rate decisionPhotograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAInterest ratesBank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% as inflation fears mountSplit vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs close to $90 a barrelBusiness live – latest updatesOnly Middle East crisis is preventing drop in UK interest ratesRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 11.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBank of Englandhas kept UK interest rates on hold as it warned that a further escalation in the Iran war could drive inflation above 4% next year, adding to cost of living pressures on households.Against a volatile backdrop in the Middle East conflict, the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted by six to three to keep its key base rate at 3.75%.As Donald Trump’s renewed attacks on Iran drive up global energy prices, the Bank said an “adverse scenario” involving a drawn-out war and oil prices remaining above $100 a barrel could push UK inflation to a peak of 4.5% by the middle of 2027.However, on a day of fresh US strikes in the widening conflict, Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, played down suggestions among City traders that Threadneedle Street was edging closer to raising rates.In a press conference after the decision, he said there was little sign that inflationary pressures were becoming entrenched because the growth outlook for the UK economy remained weak.“Please do not leave this room thinking that the Bank of England is edging towards a [interest rate] hike because, frankly, there’s nothing in what I said, and I think any of us have said, along those lines,” Bailey said.Official figures showed inflation in the UKfell by more than expected in June to 2.6%, down from a peak of 3.8% last year. It had been on track to fall close to 2% before the outbreak of the Iran war.The Bank said a loose labour market and higher borrowing costs for households and businesses, compared with before the war, would reduce inflation over time. It added that conditions before the conflict were more “benign” than they had been before previous global shocks, including the Covid pandemic and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.The decision to keep interest rates unchanged is expected to giveAndy Burnhama boost in his push to lower the cost of living. He has announced a sweeping package of support for households in his first week as prime minister.Under his plans, electricity bills in Great Britain will be cut by an average of £45 a year from October by removing VAT from them. The Bank said it expected the policy, alongside a £2 cap on bus fares in England, to lower the headline inflation rate by 0.1 percentage point.However, the MPC said it stood “ready to act as necessary” to prevent inflationary pressures from becoming entrenched.Highlighting the risk of stubbornly high inflation, Catherine Mann, an external economist on the MPC, joined her fellow committee members Megan Greene and Huw Pill in dissenting against the majority of the panel with a vote to raise rates immediately to 4%.Greene, another external member, and Pill, the Bank’s chief economist, had previously been outvoted in pushing for a quarter-point rise at the previous MPC meeting amid concern about inflation.Financial markets had priced in a more than 90% probability of Threadneedle Street keeping borrowing costs on hold, with the outside chance of a rise. Investors expect a rise in borrowing costs to 4% before the end of the year.The news comes after the Federal Reserve held borrowing costs unchanged on Wednesday and its new chair, Kevin Warsh, unnerved some investors worried over the US central bank’s readiness to tackle high inflation – leading to a rise in US government borrowing costs to the highest level since 2007.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, briefly rose above $100 a barrel last week before falling back, amid fears that the violence across the Middle East could shatter the world economy’s earlier resilience to the Iran war. It was trading at a little below $90 on Thursday.The Bank of England said that under its central forecast – involving the oil price falling back to about $71 a barrel – it still expected UK inflation to peak at about 3.2% later this year as households came under pressure from higher energy prices.Under a milder scenario for the war, it said inflation would peak at about 3% before falling rapidly, leading the central bank to cut borrowing costs. However, economists said the situation remained highly dependent on how the conflict unfolded.Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at the consultancy CapitalEconomics, said: “Much depends on what happens to energy prices and whether or not that leads to the second-round inflation effects that could transform a temporary rise in inflation into a longer-lasting one.”While awaiting developments in the war, he said, “the BoE doesn’t seem to be moving closer to actually raising rates”.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandEconomicsEconomic policyInflationMonetary policy committeenewsShareReuse this content

title: Only the Middle East crisis is preventing a drop in UK interest rates  | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Bank’s wariness about inflationary pressures from the conflict lie behind decision to hold steady at 3.75%
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Bank’s wariness about inflationary pressures from the conflict lie behind decision to hold steady at 3.75%
Content: Journalists gather outside the Bank of England in preparation for the interest rate announcement.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenJournalists gather outside the Bank of England in preparation for the interest rate announcement.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAInterest ratesAnalysisOnly the Middle East crisis is preventing a drop in UK interest ratesPhillip InmanBank’s wariness about inflationary pressures from the conflict lie behind decision to hold steady at 3.75%Business live – latest updatesThu 30 Jul 2026 08.44 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareThere is a threat of high inflation coming to the UK but only from the conflict in the Middle East, which could keep oil prices high for much longer than was expected when Donald Trump first began attacking Iran.It is the war that makes the difference between a benign outlook for inflation and one that puts it back on a rising trajectory, senior UK central bankers believe.The Bank of England’s monetary policy committee was clear in its decision on Thursdayto hold interest rates at 3.75%that underlying pressures on inflation are almost entirely absent in the domestic economy. Prices are stable and, without the war, would be rising steadily at the central bank’s 2% target.Threadneedle Street officials are worried that retail prices will ratchet up if companies spot a way to increase them, taking advantage of a general expectation among consumers that the war has raised the costs of production. They also fear that workers will see another rise in inflation coming and pitch for a major increase in wages.They haven’t seen any of these trends yet. If anything, the opposite is true and the spillover, or second-round effects from rising energy and transport costs, remain muted.Supermarkets have proved resilient andkept food inflation low. Services companies – for so long after the pandemic a source of rising prices – have managed to restrict increases this year.As the Bank’s quarterly review says: “So far, there are few signs of second-round effects. But there is not enough evidence yet to rule out this risk, and the MPC will continue to monitor evidence closely.”Annual wage increases are low across the private sector, at 2.8% in the second quarter of this year. They are expected to rise to 3% in the third quarter, but that increase keeps wage increases at a level Bank officials are comfortable with.As for companies capitalising on a period of rising prices whether or not it actually affects them, the official data does not show that happening across the manufacturing, construction or services industries.The three MPC members who voted to increase the cost of borrowing this month acknowledge that neither workers nor firms have reacted to inflation. They argue that the figures we have seen – the latest being the drop in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 2.6% in June – are a reflection of cost pressures, or more precisely the lack of them, going into the conflict. Once prices begin to rise again, workers and companies are bound to react, they argue, embedding inflationary pressures into the UK economy even if the Middle East war is settled.The majority on the MPC focused more on the labour market anda rise in unemployment and sharp fall in vacanciesover the last three years. They also see that financial markets have reacted by raising mortgage and commercial lending rates, tightening the screw on homebuyers and firms without the Bank making a move itself.If anything, businesses that want to invest and with that employ more people could do with a boost from lower interest rates.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is only Donald Trump’s failure to confect an exit from the Middle East crisis that stands in the way of that.The Bank’s forecasters expect inflation to peak at 3.2% next spring, but say it could be much higher, at 4.1%, if the war persists and Brent crude prices go back above $100 a barrel and stay there.The National Institute of Economic and Social Research said this week that the UK had already lost theequivalent of £28bn in growth this yearas a result of the Middle East conflict.The Bank’s warning that it might need to raise rates if the war continues means the impact on businesses, consumers and mortgage borrowers could, unless Trump pulls back, be much more severe.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandEconomicsEconomic policyInflationMonetary policy committeenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shell’s profits more than double after jump in oil and gas prices | Shell | The Guardian
description: Environmentalists renew calls for windfall tax to support households after Q2 earnings rise to almost $10bn
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Environmentalists renew calls for windfall tax to support households after Q2 earnings rise to almost $10bn
Content: Environmental campaigners outside Shell UK’s London headquarters on Wednesday.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenEnvironmental campaigners outside Shell UK’s London headquarters on Wednesday.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAShellShell’s profits more than double after jump in oil and gas pricesEnvironmentalists renew calls for windfall tax to support households after Q2 earnings rise to almost $10bnLauren AlmeidaandJillian AmbroseThu 30 Jul 2026 03.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShell has posted its second highest quarterly earnings on record as the energy market surge caused by the Middle East crisis helped to double its net profit to almost $10bn in the three months to June.Europe’s biggest oil and gas company reported a quarterly profit of $9.8bn (£7.4bn), more than double the figure for the second quarter last year and the highest since its record-high earnings in the months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.The company behind plans to develop the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea revealed its earnings before a planned meeting between Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, and Shell’s chief executive, Wael Sawan, who is expected to urge the government to develop North Sea projects.Sawan told CNBC: “The prime minister’s office has reached out, and we’re hoping to schedule a discussion soon … The biggest thing that can be done at the moment is to continue to support the development of the North Sea, to continue to invest in renewables, to continue to provide targeted support to those who need it in these difficult times.“These are difficult times, undoubtedly, and I think the government, from everything we pick up publicly, is trying to do what it can to be able to support. And [the] UK is our headquarters, is our home, and we will offer any support that we can to the government as they try to navigate these difficult waters.”Robert Palmer, the deputy director at the campaign group Uplift, which opposes North Sea development, accused Shell of “maniacal behaviour” for “putting its profits ahead of the health of our planet”.Get in touchContact the Guardian Business teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject you can contact the Business team confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging.When asked who you wish to contact please select the ‘Business (UK & Global)’ team.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show more“As families and firefighters across Europe battledevastating wildfires, Shell is cashing in on Trump’s war and doubling down on oil and gas,” he said. “The world is literally on fire and Shell wants to add more fuel.”The severe disruption in global energy markets since the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February led to a 30% drop in Shell’s gas production in the last quarter compared with the same period a year ago, after its gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar was damaged by Iranian drones.The company was more than able to offset the lost earnings, however, as a result of higher global market prices and savvy trading. In its liquified natural gas business, earnings grew to $2.7bn in the second quarter, up 55% from last year. Its chemicals and products business, which is home to its oil trading desk, reported earnings of $2.3bn, up sharply from $118m a year ago and the division’s highest quarterly profit since 2021.“We have one of the world’s largest and strongest trading capabilities,” Sawan told CNBC. “And that allows us to deal with times like this.”The global oil price has climbed from about $61 a barrel in January to highs of $126 at the end of April, after Iran’s de facto blockade on flows of oil and gas through the strait of Hormuz. The market volatility has included some of the sharpest price swings on record, which traders are able to use to amplify their profits. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at just over $90 a barrel on Thursday.Shell’s oil rival BP has reportedly warned staff that a potential oversupply of oil and gas could lead to lower market prices to come, as it set out plans to cut another 700 jobs from its global operations following cuts of 7,000 last year.The Financial Times said it had seen an email to staff from BP’s production boss, Gordon Birrell, in which he set out plans to streamline the business and said BP had to be “competitive at the bottom of the cycle, not just the top”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShell’s surging profits reignited calls from environmental campaigners for taxes to fund support for the households hardest hit by the rise in energy costs.Climate campaigners attack Shell over ‘windfall’ profits from Iran warRead moreRudy Schulkind, a political campaigner at Greenpeace, said the environmental group was “running out of words to describe the obscenity” of huge profits at Shell.“Europe is engulfed by apocalyptic wildfires, communities across Asia are reeling from devastating floods, and the UK battles through drought and yet more dangerous heat,” he said. “These aren’t anomalies, they’re the defining story of the fossil fuel age. Shell takes the profits, and the rest of us pick up the catastrophic bill.”Schulkind called on the government to implement a windfall tax on big oil companies and to use the revenue “to help households with the cost of living, strengthen our resilience against extreme weather, and supercharge the transition to clean, affordable energy”.Shares in Shell rose 1.5% in early trading on Thursday to £33.72, the highest since early June.This article was amended on 30 July 2026. An earlier version misnamed Rudy Schulkind.Explore more on these topicsShellOil (Business)Oil and gas companiesEnergy industryFossil fuelsOil (Environment)CommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I had a really crippling break’: how author Michael Thomas lost 20 years to mania, depression and more | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: In 2006 the novel Man Gone Down made Thomas famous and won him a €100,000 prize. He expected to produce a follow-up within a year – but life had other plans
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: In 2006 the novel Man Gone Down made Thomas famous and won him a €100,000 prize. He expected to produce a follow-up within a year – but life had other plans
Content: ‘I could be living in my car’ … Michael Thomas.Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I could be living in my car’ … Michael Thomas.Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianAutobiography and memoirInterview‘I had a really crippling break’: how author Michael Thomas lost 20 years to mania, depression and moreSteve RoseIn 2006 the novel Man Gone Down made Thomas famous and won him a €100,000 prize. He expected to produce a follow-up within a year – but life had other plansThu 30 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt should be some kind of happy ending when, after years of poverty and graft, an aspiring writer publishes their debut novel and it is greeted with acclaim and awards – but that’s not how it happened for Michael Thomas. His 2006 novel Man Gone Down seemed to augur the arrival of a powerful new literary voice, the beginning of a brilliant career. He featured on the cover of the New York Times Book Review, hewon the €100,000 Dublin literary award– one of the most generous prizes in the book world – and he was promoted to assistant professor at Hunter College, New York, where he taught creative writing. But a follow-up would not arrive until now, 20 years later. Thomas’s new memoir, The Broken King, goes some way to explaining what happened in between. It also confirms his formidable talent.The Broken King is an extraordinary read – deeply personal and intimate, but also expansive and free-ranging, taking in everything from TS Eliot (the title comes from Eliot’s poemLittle Gidding) to James Baldwin, Brazilian football and the Rolling Stones. Thomas’s story runs through what he describes as a “perfect storm of conditions”: poverty, parental abandonment, racism, alcoholism, sexual violence, self-sabotage and mental illness. It would be tempting to classify it as some kind of misery memoir, but it is neither bleak nor generic – Thomas is simply too good a writer for that. Reviews in the US have been glowing: “Thomas has rendered beautifully an excruciating existence from which it is impossible to turn away,” raved the author Thomas Chatterton Williamsin the New York Times.Thomas did not “enjoy” literary success first time round. In fact, it contributed to his breakdown. Receiving the Dublin literary award did not make him think, “I am a great author,” he tells me via video call. His reaction was more relief that he could pay off some of his debts: “We were two months behind on our mortgage.” Nor did he revel in the attention: “When I started getting critical acclaim and showing up on the cover of things, I couldn’t feel it. And I kept trying to tell people that I couldn’t feel it, and they thought it was being smug or humble. I was really in a year-long descent.”View image in fullscreenThomas after winning the Impac Dublin literary award in 2009.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyHe’s sitting in his office at Hunter College. Behind him are books, artefacts, an acoustic guitar and a commanding view over Manhattan. “It’s in a state of construction. I’m making a floating birch wall over here,” he apologises, pointing off-camera. He speaks gently, with a musical lilt, and he looks much younger than his 58 years – partly because he’s as athletic as he is artistic. He enjoys exercise and physical labour, such as house-building and carpentry, as much as he does teaching and writing. To him, there’s nothing contradictory about “thinking of the poetry I want to write while doing an intense set of deadlifts”.In late 2007, less than a year after Man Gone Down was published, Thomas was planning his next step. “I had a proposal, six pages, and it was neat and clean and tidy. I gave it to my editor; I had a meeting with the publisher. They said: ‘Great, go off and do your thing.’ I was glib about it, like: ‘Yeah, I’ll knock this out in six months to a year. I can write about mental illness’ – not mine.” He pauses to laugh at the irony. “My father’s, and my brother’s. And then I had a break, a really crippling break.”double quotation markI hope this doesn’t seem insensitive: the book is autistic. It’s really just a study of someone with level-one autismPromoting his book, travelling, doing talks; trying to write, teach, read, parent; procrastinating, not sleeping well, drinking too much coffee, he became what he now characterises as “short-cycling manic depressive”. “I would have an ‘illumination’ for two hours, and then I wouldn’t have time to record it and I’d tumble into a depressive state. And I could have multiple states within a few days, and so the brilliant idea would become mundane or esoteric or fragmented, almost as though I was getting a narrative from a stranger.”Events came to a head when he was alone in Kansas City on his book tour, “seeing dragons and demons and all kinds of things”. Waiting to board a flight home, he had a breakdown at the airport. “I knew I was insane,” he writes. When his wife takes him to a psychiatric hospital back in New York, he tells the doctor: “It’s a curious thing, the phrase ‘out of your mind’ … My trouble now is that I’m in a way, in part, deep in it. More than I’ve ever been. It’s not a good environment, doctor.”As with the rest of the book, Thomas catalogues these events and experiences in uncanny, almost photographic detail, but the narrative also pans out across his memories and anxieties, and his vast cultural hinterland. He almost apologises for The Broken King’s expansiveness: “Part of it was realising how personal it was going to be, and trying to make it more intricate to really distance myself from the work.”Man Gone Down was a loosely fictionalised account of a small section of Thomas’s life, when he was in his 30s, desperately trying to keep his head above water, financially and psychically, and hold on to his marriage and his three young children. The Broken King expands on that narrative considerably, particularly Thomas’s male relationships: with his father (who abandoned the family when Thomas was eight, struggled with depression, drank heavily, and at times lived in his car); his older brother (who steals from his family and others, and is in and out of prison); and his two sons (he also has a daughter), whom he worries are destined to extend the lineage of troubled men.View image in fullscreenAs a kid Thomas struggled to fit in.Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianThere’s a moment halfway through the book when the penny almost drops: an occupational therapist diagnoses his second son, Miles, with a “non-specific cognitive disorder”, and even suggests: “Like father, like son.” That took him by “complete surprise”, Thomas says, but he did not act on it until much later. Until that point he had attributed his difficulties in life to all manner of factors – “race, class, artistic temperament, and just so many other things. Models from books and films and music, and just this kind of alienation and estrangement … but no, not neurodivergence.” As a child he was diagnosed with dyslexia, ADHD and other conditions, but it wasn’t until adulthood that it was defined as level 1 autism. As such, The Broken King is, among other things, a chronicle of neurodivergence from the inside. “I hope this doesn’t seem insensitive: the book is autistic,” Thomas says. “It’s really just a study of someone with level-one autism trying to tell a story.”double quotation markWe grew up in public housing with a single mom believing education was the great equaliser, and she just busted her assThomas’s story raises all kinds of questions about the relationship between neurodivergence and artistic talent, not to mention nature and nurture. How to square his diagnosis with other traumatic elements of his upbringing: the poverty, the alcoholism, the abandonment? Racism also plays a part. His great-grandfather was born enslaved, in Virginia, he tells me. He remembers his great-grandmother when he was a child – a living connection to that time. He shows me a photograph of his mother in Virginia, in 1951. She is looking at a burnt cross that was put up outside her high school. She migrated north to Boston, where she met his father, but largely raised him and his two older siblings singlehandedly. “We grew up in public housing with a single mom believing education was the great equaliser, and she just busted her ass.”As a kid Thomas struggled to fit in, socially as well as racially (he also has Irish and Native American ancestry). “I could read at an early age and could do my brother’s homework, but I couldn’t tie my shoes.” He connected with Black role models – Malcolm X, Martin Luther King, Stokely Carmichael, Frederick Douglass – but he also loved the Beatles and Bob Dylan and Greek mythology. “I was called an Oreo [Black on the outside, white on the inside, like the cookie], or a ‘honky nigger’ or ‘not really Black’.”At the same time, Thomas writes, “white people were dangerous because they were extreme. They tried to either aid or block my passage into their segregated world.Benevolentwhites didn’t think I was Black. Whatever native intelligence I possessed had nothing to do with my race. Blackness was something they were helping me overcome.” Meanwhile, he was “subject to most of the chronic and systemic, acute and arbitrary violence the republic or the individual believed I deserved”.View image in fullscreen‘I don’t want the things that happened to me to happen to my kids.’Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianThomas’s marriage to a relatively wealthy white woman complicates matters further, in terms of both fitting in with his white in-laws and raising mixed-race children. Their experience of the world will certainly be different from his, he says. “Just as my mother didn’t want her experience to be mine, I don’t want the things that happened to me to happen to my kids. I’m not worried about them ‘losing their Blackness’, though. They get to define who they are.” All of Black culture is theirs, he says, as is all of every other culture – as it was for him, as it should be for everyone.There is another challenging, complicating element to Thomas’s story: early on in the book he discloses that he was raped when he was seven years old. He doesn’t go into detail about the incident – except to say it happened when he was at a day camp in Boston. He didn’t tell anyone at the time; in fact, he strove to hide the incident from his parents, even burning his clothes afterwards. “I knew my pain would kill them,” he writes. He is open about how the incident warped his life. “Growing into a young man I was distant, wayward, wild, drunk. I could be cruel. I’d lie to everyone I knew.” He struggled with self-harm, alcoholism, depression, physical and emotional intimacy – “I lived in a perpetual post-trauma.” He told his future wife in his 20s after he was re-traumatised reading a passage about rape in a Baldwin novel. As soon as he finished reading it he went into a fever, was trapped in his apartment for days hallucinating, and was eventually hospitalised with pneumonia. As soon as he recovered, a dinner party conversation about sex caused him to shut down and not speak for three days.In this context, I hesitate to even bring the incident up. Thomas is comfortable talking about it right now, he says, but when he has told friends about it, he has often regretted it.“It didn’t bring any clarity to me and it hurt them,” he explains. “Like it was giving them too much to deal with. And watching people over the years or just over the weeks, wondering how to be with me and be with that information, they had to treat me differently.” These things can become a lens through which to judge others’ actions and behaviours, he suggests. You could say the same of race, or neurodivergence, or gender, or any number of factors.double quotation markI’m becoming acutely aware of my strangeness, but not self-conscious about it, or apologetic or aggressiveI was feeling apprehensive about interviewing Thomas, I tell him, given how honestly and openly he has written about his life. He felt the same, he admits, having not been in the public eye for decades, though he has been relaxed and talkative throughout our 90-minute conversation, which digresses at times into chat about sports teams or our favourite Beatles albums. Is there a worry, though, given how his last experience of literary success contributed to his breakdown, that the same thing could happen this time around?He seems less worried about it. A lot has happened in the intervening two decades. He got divorced in 2014, which inevitably affected his children. His mother died from Covid in 2020 (his next book will be about her life, he says). His eldest son, Alex, is now 30, and a social worker. His other son, Miles, is 27 and handling his own neurodivergence very differently from how Thomas did. “He doesn’t have as much invested in controlling the conventional world. He’s not angry.” Thomas also has an eight-year-old son with a new partner. He has no idea how he has been as a father, he says: “Sometimes I think I intensified some of the suffering … sometimes I feel like I gave them a lot … sometimes I just think I became my father with privilege and safety nets. Without growing up privilege-adjacent, and then having literary and academic success and a tenured position, and people saving my bacon over the years, I could be living in my car right now.”Lena Dunham on going to rehab: ‘It was like the first day of college, except many of the people had a problem with heroin’Read moreIn general, at present, it feels as if he has found some stability. “I’m trying to figure it out through Bowie right now,” he says, jokingly, quoting lines from Changes: “‘I turned myself to face me, but I never caught a glimpse …’ I’m becoming acutely aware of my strangeness, but not self-conscious about it, or apologetic or aggressive.”Is that liberating? “It calms some of the noise,” he replies. “This might sound cheesy: I don’t know if I’m OK with myself, but I think I’m starting to accept myself. I’m also about to turn 59, so I don’t have that younger man’s piss and vinegar. I think I’m a little more reflective and less impulsive. I don’t have the anger I used to have. I don’t have the fear I used to have – at least in this moment. I know it can come again. I feel incredibly lucid. There’s been a lot of loss in the last decade, so … today I feel OK.”The Broken King by Michael Thomas is published by Summit (£16.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsAutobiography and memoirNeurodiversityRaceFictionMental healthinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Love’s Labour’s Lost review – paella, bullfighting and flamenco make Shakespeare’s farce a fiesta | Stage | The Guardian
description: Choreographer Carmen Igarza deserves to take a bow as spectacular dance and movement add passion to the seemingly unfinished play
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Choreographer Carmen Igarza deserves to take a bow as spectacular dance and movement add passion to the seemingly unfinished play
Content: Show-stopping … Norah Lopez Holden and Pablo Egea in Love’s Labour’s Lost at Shakespeare’s Globe.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreenShow-stopping … Norah Lopez Holden and Pablo Egea in Love’s Labour’s Lost at Shakespeare’s Globe.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianStageReviewLove’s Labour’s Lost review – paella, bullfighting and flamenco make Shakespeare’s farce a fiestaShakespeare’s Globe, LondonChoreographer Carmen Igarza deserves to take a bow as spectacular dance and movement add passion to the seemingly unfinished playMark LawsonThu 30 Jul 2026 07.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fact that Love’s Labour’s Lost is relatively unloved by Shakespeare producers and scholars is due to this mid-16th-century comedy being an early example of his dramatic craft – anRSC online timelinelists it ninth in the 38 main attributed plays – and an unusually inconclusive ending: the typical act five marry-go-round is suddenly deferred for a year.These problems mean that even purists object less than usual to a solving directorial concept. Tom Littler, inalfresco stagingsplaying this summer in Guildford and Richmond, pairs the seemingly incomplete piece with Much Ado About Nothing (which some believe to be an otherwise lost Shakespeare piece called Love’s Labour’s Won), unifying the characters and plot lines.‘I just knew it would sound incredible!’: why the Globe is giving Shakespeare some flamenco fireRead moreApart from also being outdoors, Indiana Lown-Collins’s revival for Shakespeare’s Globe is an equally but differently radical revision. Shakespeare has the Spanish kingdom of Navarre – where three young men have signed up to an early detox scheme, renouncing sex and food for meditation – visited by a princess of France and her retinue, who threaten their pledges.In this version, everyone is Spanish – a translation helped, in the summer of 26, by there being as many fans flapping in the audience as in a high-season Madrid street cafe. On stage, adieu becomes adios with some other English words translated – a repast is specified to be paella – and the action punctuated and inflected by sequences of flamenco dance and song.The hunting of a deer in the original here becomes a choreographed bullfight, spectacularly danced by Pablo Egea as the tauran prey. Dance and movement routines – the romantic longing and underlying violence of flamenco reasonably reflecting the themes of the play – regularly stop the show. The programme bills Carmen Igarza as choreographer and Vanessa Guevara as pre-hispanic movement consultant; however this duet worked, they deserve to take a bow at the end of each performance.Less happily, substantial rewriting introduces the figure of Queen Elizabeth I to the masque staged amid the climactic anti-romantic interactions, including jokes about her sex life and vagina. Shakespeare’s play is filled with bawdy that this production always stands up: in the scene in which the three would-be abstinent men are disguised as Muscovites, they sport golden penile codpieces and nippled shoulder pads. However, had Shakespeare pricked his patron in the way this production adds, Love’s Labour’s Lost would have been his final play, the other 29 lost to us.Love’s Labour’s Lost / Much Ado About Nothing review – breezy double bill brings out the best in bothRead moreI would be concerned about students and tourists leaving the Globe admiring Shakespeare’s Elizabethan lèse-majesté, and such is the power of Littler’s double bill that Love’s Labour’s Lost played alone now feels even more half-hearted. But this production is, within its concept, generally a joy.The cast is multi-national, sometimes within a single performer. The Swiss-British-Turkish-Italian Philip Arditti also inflects his cocky reluctant-abstinent Berowne with libidinous dons from culture, and spars nicely with Bea Segura’s sparky Rosaline. Another Spanish actor, Andro Crespo, is an unusually authentic Don Adriano de Armado, while also beautifully leading Michael McMahon and Adrián Solá’s setting of the final song, “When daisies pied and violets blue”. Alongside those responsible for movement and music, casting director Becky Paris should also win applause.AtShakespeare’s Globe, London, until 13 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageShakespeare's GlobeWilliam ShakespearereviewsShareReuse this content

title: How Harlan Coben became the king of potboiler TV | Television | The Guardian
description: The prolific crime author’s latest Netflix thriller I Will Find You has become one of the streamer’s most-watched shows of all time – but what’s his secret?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The prolific crime author’s latest Netflix thriller I Will Find You has become one of the streamer’s most-watched shows of all time – but what’s his secret?
Content: Sam Worthington and Britt Lower in I Will Find You.Photograph: Christos Kalohoridis/Netflix © 2025View image in fullscreenSam Worthington and Britt Lower in I Will Find You.Photograph: Christos Kalohoridis/Netflix © 2025TelevisionHow Harlan Coben became the king of potboiler TVThe prolific crime author’s latest Netflix thriller I Will Find You has become one of the streamer’s most-watched shows of all time – but what’s his secret?Stuart HeritageThu 30 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix’s all-time top 10 English languageseries chartis starting to look like a stale old thing. It is topped by Wednesday, which is four years old, and includes dusty old hits including Stranger Things season four (four years old), Monster: The Jeffrey Dahmer Story (four years old), The Queen’s Gambit (six years old), and Bridgerton season one (six years old).I Will Find You review – seen one maddeningly watchable Harlan Coben adaptation? You’ve seen them allRead moreBut wait. Just before you write off Netflix as a platform half a decade past its peak, a plucky new entryhas entered the all-time top10 to liven things up. That show is I Will Find You, the latest belched out from the glistening ovipositor of Harlan Coben. If you’re a fan of Coben’s work – and we’ll get into that in due course – then I Will Find You will be instantly recognisable, since it bears many of the author’s hallmarks.Does it have a cast so confusing that your brain needs to take a few moments to adjust to it? Yes. Does it have a title that appears to be picked at random from a tombola barrel filled with the world’s least descriptive words? Absolutely. Do you have a sense when you’re watching it that your television has deliberately leftNetflixand put ITV3 on just to see if you’re paying attention? Oh heavens yes. But it is so popular that you end up worrying that you’re the only person alive who doesn’t actively enjoy it? The numbers speak for themselves.Functionally, there is not much separating I Will Find You from any of the previous 12 Netflix Coben adaptations, like Hold Tight or Fool Me Once or Stay Close or Run Away or Missing You (or even any of the shows he made with other platforms, like Sky’s The Five or Prime’s Harlan Coben’s Shelter). And, indeed, these were all extremely popular too. While the newest show leads with 101.9m worldwide views, 2024’s Fool Me Once gained 98.2m, with 2025’s Missing You and this year’s Run Away both getting over 50m views.This isn’t surprising, given that Coben is a phenomenally successful writer, who has sold more than 90m books in his 30-year career. What might be more surprising, though, is the fact that almost nobody professes to be a fan of his. Compare the reaction to his work to that of George RR Martin, or Lee Child, or even Anne Rice during her lifetime – authors who inspire fervent, noisy support in their fans – and you’ll see the difference.This might be Coben’s appeal, in fact. Rather than develop a cult of personality, he just unfussily gets on with the job of churning out one potboiler after another, and is presumably rewarded with riches beyond his wildest dreams. But this does nothing to change the assumption that people consume his shows without ever fully loving them.Part of this, I’m convinced, is down to the scattershot casting of his adaptations, which seem to hoover up whichever actor happens to be at a loose end at any given point in time. I Will Find You is a perfect case in point. It stars Britt Lower, brilliant in Severance, who until recently had been curating a career playing spiky oddballs in work that went out of its way to confound viewers. But here she is, playing a flat plot device in the sort of show that feels like it was designed to be the fourth thing you watch on a long haul flight.View image in fullscreenHarlan Coben.Photograph: Arnold Jerocki/WireImageThe glut of Netflix adaptations has made Coben extremely wealthy – in 2018 he signed a multimillion-dollar deal to see 14 of his novels developed into content – but he cannot write quickly enough to keep up with the pace of adaptation. He still has some unadapted books in the tank, like Play Dead and Miracle Cure and last year’s Gone Before Goodbye (although since that last one was apparently co-written with Reese Witherspoon, it has to be a matter of time). However, this all might be about to change with the news that an adaptation of his Myron Bolitar bookshas just started filming.This is potentially the lodestar. Despite having a name that sounds like someone choking on some fish, Myron Bolitar is Coben’s best-loved character. A hotheaded basketball player turned agent, who finds himself investigating murders on the side, Bolitar has been the subject of 12 books (along with a handful of young adult books about Myron’s nephew Mickey), and is essentially Coben’s Jack Reacher.If Bolitar lands with anything like the impact of I Will Find You, its recurring premise and cast (including Colin Woodell from Pulse, Chloe Fineman from Saturday Night Live and Griffin Dunne from being Griffin Dunne) will probably help it grow over the course of several years. In other words, don’t be surprised if it becomes Harlan Coben’s biggest hit yet. Just don’t be surprised if you can’t find anyone who will actually admit liking it.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionHarlan CobenUS televisionNetflixThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Don’t Date Brandon review – this lazy true-crime show doesn’t start to do justice to these women’s horrors | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The tale of the women who came together to unpick the destructive swathe that one man cut through his local dating pool is woefully lacking in the detail you need to understand their plight. It feels voyeuristic and misguided
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The tale of the women who came together to unpick the destructive swathe that one man cut through his local dating pool is woefully lacking in the detail you need to understand their plight. It feels voyeuristic and misguided
Content: Going public … Brandon’s first and second wives, Amber (left) and Athena.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenGoing public … Brandon’s first and second wives, Amber (left) and Athena.Photograph: Channel 4TV reviewTelevision & radioReviewDon’t Date Brandon review – this lazy true-crime show doesn’t start to do justice to these women’s horrorsThe tale of the women who came together to unpick the destructive swathe that one man cut through his local dating pool is woefully lacking in the detail you need to understand their plight. It feels voyeuristic and misguidedLucy ManganThu 30 Jul 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m beginning to suspect that the feminist movement is operating a covert psyops wing. I like to think that this is the motive force behind the slew of true-crime documentaries that show us, time and again, what bad men do and how they go about it. Perhaps the repeated stories of women – often unhappy with parts of their lives, or otherwise emotionally vulnerable – being love-bombed by apparent male saviours then finding themselves isolated, controlled, coerced, destabilised and battered into submission and sometimes killed that form the predominant subject of this popular modern genre are a way of teaching the young (especially) what is out there. Maybe it’s a way to help them spot the earliest signs of a predator’s approach and arm the innocent against them.Otherwise, you know, it’s just voyeuristic filler for the ever-gaping schedule maw.So, then, to the latest possibly instructive tool, possibly a piece of mindless rubbish: Don’t Date Brandon. It’s a strange title – both lazy and misguided, more suggestive of a 90s sitcom (ditzy roommates! Wild situations! One hot guy!) than an account of one man’s cutting of a destructive swathe through his local dating pool, which is what it is.But that is all of a piece with what is – at least on the basis of the one episode of the three that was made available for review – a lazy and misguided programme. It is based on the podcast Ex-Wives Undercover, which tells survivors’ stories about toxic relationships (gaslighters, catfishers, romance scammers, men leading double lives, those who threaten harm and those who carry it out). It is hosted by the two women around whose experiences with a man called Brandon Johnson the documentary is built.Amber Rasmussen met him online when she was 35 and became his second wife. He warned her to stay away from his ex-wife Athena Klingerman, with whom he had a four-year-old daughter Sydney, and – after he showed Amber the messages that proved Athena to be the “psycho” he said she was – Amber was happy to do so.That was until the red flags around her own relationship with Brandon – the woman claiming to be his girlfriend, the mystery job that required so much travel, the cancer diagnosis just as she was planning on moving out of the marital home, inexplicable bills and parking tickets – made her contact Athena. Whereupon they began unpicking the web of lies Brandon had been telling them both. He had of course been lying about his job, which was mostly the cover for an affair he was having with a woman called Avery (Sydney had a bedroom at her house and was told to keep everything secret from her mother and Amber), and his cancer claims (he had pretended to be ill while he was with Athena too), and about Athena’s nature. She had never run up $100,000 on his credit card, as he had told Amber, and the message threads he had shown his second wife had been completely fabricated by him over an entire year.Most of this information, however, is crammed into the last few minutes of the first episode. The rest of it is spent largely marking time. Amber outlines at length the facts of their relationship, but there is very little emphasis on the psychological effects of Brandon’s actions. Without that, the manipulation looks – to the outsider – so obvious, so blatant that you begin not to sympathise with Brandon’s victim but rather to roll your eyes at a naivety so profound.I am not saying Amber is in any way to blame, you understand. I’m saying that the programme’s pacing, and its lack of granular detail for so long, means that it does not even start to do justice to the gradual erosion of mind and spirit, the inexorable normalisation of the unacceptable, upon which perpetrators like Brandon depend. I imagine that the next two episodes concentrate on the escalation of Brandon’s behaviour (he was eventually charged with assault and attempted kidnapping with intention to commit rape, and accepted a plea agreement that means he is serving a 10-year sentence in a state prison and is eligible for parole next year) and on Amber and Athena going public with their stories. That in turn leads to the uniting of many other victims of Brandon, a man the women discover was served his first restraining order in 1997 at the age of 19. But those episodes will come on top of a shaky foundation that puts Amber (especially) and Athena in the position of effectively having something to prove about themselves, rather than about the man who hurt them.Don’t Date Brandon is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Freudian trip: how psychoanalysis and skydiving are helping Aurora orchestra open up Mahler’s First | Classical music | The Guardian
description: When Mahler premiered his first symphony, it left audiences baffled. For their latest Prom, Aurora are bringing it to life – with the help of Sigmund Freud
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When Mahler premiered his first symphony, it left audiences baffled. For their latest Prom, Aurora are bringing it to life – with the help of Sigmund Freud
Content: Flautist (and artistic director) Jane Mitchell is airborne in Aurora Orchestra’s Shostakovich’s Fifth by Heart at the BBC Proms in August 2025.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenFlautist (and artistic director) Jane Mitchell is airborne in Aurora Orchestra’s Shostakovich’s Fifth by Heart at the BBC Proms in August 2025.Photograph: Andy ParadiseClassical musicFreudian trip: how psychoanalysis and skydiving are helping Aurora orchestra open up Mahler’s FirstWhen Mahler premiered his first symphony, it left audiences baffled. For their latest Prom, Aurora are bringing it to life – with the help of Sigmund FreudJane MitchellThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2014, Aurora Orchestra did something that had never been done at the Proms before. We played Mozart’s 40th symphony – that has been done,many times– but from memory.It was terrifying. Orchestral musicians usually start getting out their instruments 10 minutes before they go on stage, but people started warming up nearly an hour before – endless repetitions of fragments of music as players tested what they thought they might forget. We didn’t know if we would get on stage and freeze or fall off. Thankfully, we did neither and fear turned into excitement. Ourbassoonist Amy Harmandescribed the feeling as “like skydiving without a parachute. But in a good way.”Even so, if someone had told me then that 12 years later we would be performing from memory Mahler’s First Symphony – a piece almost twice as long as the Mozart that uses more than double the number of musicians – I would have been surprised. And if I’d then been told that in the first half of the concert we’d be presenting a new play about Mahler, featuring choreography involving the entire orchestra alongside two actors and a complicated sound design (and written by me!), I’d have laughed. Butthis weekendwe will do exactly this.View image in fullscreenRehearsals earlier this week for Mahler’s First By Heart.Photograph: Aurora OrchestraAfter the Mozart, our performances from memory became a regular Proms feature. Then, three years ago, we upped the ante when we took on Stravinsky’sThe Rite of Spring. Memorising that enormously complex work was a challenge, but what felt especially scary was the fact we were dedicating the concert to a single piece.The second half would feature the performance; the first would introduce the work to the audience … somehow. It was my job to figure out what this actually meant – and it took a really long time.What emerged was a 40-minute first half that told the story of how the Rite was written and premiered, combining text, musical analysis, orchestral excerpts, choreography for the whole orchestra and video projection, and featuring performances by the actors Charlotte Ritchie and Karl Queensborough.It felt as if we had hit on something, so we have continued in this vein. At the following year’s Proms, we presented a first half dedicated to the creation ofBeethoven’s Ninth Symphonybefore performing the work itself; last year, we turned toShostakovich’s Fifth.It’s hard to know what to call these first halves. We used to use the word “presentation”, but it has become more than that. “Play” or “orchestral theatre” feel closer, but all suggestions are welcome.View image in fullscreenKarl Queensborough and Charlotte Ritchie with  Aurora Orchestra’s 2023 The Rite by Heart at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Andy ParadiseOur choice of repertoire tends to be as simple as what would be fun to perform from memory and which pieces have an interesting story to explore. The first question is especially important, as we are asking players to spend hours and hours with this music. Everyone will have their own process of memorising – some go for runs with the music on headphones, some play it over and over – and some get out highlighter pens.My own creative process always begins with reading. I’ll know the music from playing it (I’m Aurora’s principal flautist), but I’ll want to learn more about the composer and the historical context. It’s always the words that come directly from the composers and their contemporaries that tell me what we should do.When I researched The Rite of Spring, I was struck by the many collaborative voices clamouring to give their accounts of how they created the premiere production. For Beethoven’s Ninth, I read the composer’s conversation books: notebooks in which he asked friends to write down what they were saying, as an aide for his profound hearing loss, and realised we didn’t need any other words. With Shostakovich’s Fifth, I realised how few words exist from the composer himself – however much I read, he remained elusive.I work closely with our conductor, Nicholas Collon, to untangle the score and decide which passages to focus on and how to present the music in a way that shows physically what the score is doing. James Bonas co-directs – we often refer to him as our “bad audience member”, as he tells us what is working, what is not and what is too academic or music-jargony. I used to find this part of the process excruciating, but I’ve learned to enjoy it.I love the fact that every year I get to be completely immersed in a different composer’s world and music. This year has all been about Mahler. The first time I performed his music as a student flautist, I felt as if I had stepped inside a world I didn’t quite understand, but which was oddly familiar. I remember clinging on to the other more experienced instrumentalists and their phrasing and timing. Everything seemed exaggerated. Every melody carried so much emotion, with dynamics lurching from the quietest, highest held chord to the loudest eruption of the full orchestra. Daunting stuff when you’re just starting out, but also the adrenaline high orchestral players live for.Mahler, in stark contrast to Shostakovich, left us many words, and they reveal an artist constantly analysing his own feelings and emotions.double quotation mark…for as long as I can remember –my need to express myself musically begins at the point where the dark feelings hold sway, at the door which leads to the other world – the world in which things are no longer separated by time and space … For those that listen closely, everything about me is explained in my music.This is particularly the case with his First Symphony, into which he poured his lived experience: memories of soldiers in the forests of his childhood home, the sound of cuckoos outside his composing room, songs about problematic love affairs and children’s nursery rhymes.Little surprise, then, that when Mahler presented his First Symphony to the world, in Budapest in 1889, he felt as if he was baring his soul. But audiences were baffled. Reviewers described the music as “offensively trivial”, “a disaster” and “ridiculous”. In the months that followed, his friends described him as looking sick and feeling misunderstood. “For goodness sake, where do people put their ears and their hearts if they can’t understand this music?” he said.View image in fullscreenMax Revell (centre) as a silent Shostakovich in Aurora Orchestra’s Proms performance in 2025.Photograph: Andy ParadiseI began wondering what Mahler might have thought ofSigmund Freudand the groundbreaking work he was doing around this same time. I was fascinated to learn that the two had met: the composer made an appointment to talk to Freud in 1910. The accounts of their meeting tell us that they discussed exactly these ideas, why he felt he needed to write particular kinds of music and why he felt the public couldn’t understand him. I began to wonder if this meeting could become a framework through which to explore the symphony.And so my script follows Mahler’s journey, from conceiving and composing the symphony to premiering it to widespread bewilderment and then trying to get people to understand it.The programme notes he provided for the second performance read hilariously like someone overexplaining themselves. I love his attempts to describe his third movement, with which people had a particular problem:double quotation markI want you to imagineThe Hunter’s Funeral Procession, a picture from an old book of children’s fairytales: in this picture – the beasts of the forest accompany the dead woodsman’s coffin to the grave, with hares carrying a small banner, with a band of Bohemian musiciansin front, and the procession escorted by music-making cats, toads, crows etc …There’s plenty more. We have a script and we have a brilliant singer (Natalie Lewis) and two wonderful actors (Jack Bardoe and Sarah Twomey) who have been rehearsing with me, James and Nicholas this past week. But the orchestra will have only a day and a half to rehearse the first half, in which they are required to remember terribly confusing versions of bits of the symphony and lots of strictly choreographed moves around the stage.The only way this works is if we have a military plan mapped out. We call this flat-packing. The players need to trust us – which has taken time, I admit. Each year, I do wonder: perhaps this will be the year where we’ve pushed them too far? That thought is certainly in my head this week.View image in fullscreenAurora Orchestra, conducted by Nicholas Collon, perform Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring from memory at the 2023 Proms.Photograph: Andy ParadiseYou might ask: “Why bother?”For me, there are two main reasons. First, I am so aware of how lucky I am to have the best seat in the house at orchestral concerts. Flutes sit right in the middle of the orchestra and I can hear all the conversations between instruments and the shifting textures surrounding me. The aural experience is visceral and immersive. I want to find ways to give audiences the same breathtaking experience I have.Second, I am in a very small minority of people who have spent a lot of time studying music: at university, then music college, then for 20 years as a professional musician. Yet I still don’t feel I know much. Whenever a conductor or colleague talks to me about how a bit of a score works, or breaks apart a texture, or gives some historical context, it always enhances my understanding of the music and makes me listen more closely.Our plays are about giving audiences ways to feel closer to the music. Someone once described it to me as “giving the keys to the kingdom”, which I love. You may listen to the music differently because you know more about the composer, or the social context, or because you’ve seen musical textures brought to life; the players choreographed across the stage reflect this. We want to communicate the music to everyone, whether this is your first orchestral concert or you know and love the work. Come and see if we’ve got it right at the Royal Albert Hall in London this Saturday and Sunday.Jane Mitchell is Aurora Orchestra’s artistic director. Mahler’s First By Heart is at the BBC Proms at7pm on 1 Augustand at11am on 2 August.
