title: Helm by Sarah Hall audiobook review – a breath of fresh air from the Pennines  | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Louise Brealey teases out the playful and poetic moments of these shapeshifting stories, told from the perspective of the northeasterly wind and those it has wreaked chaos on through the ages
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Louise Brealey teases out the playful and poetic moments of these shapeshifting stories, told from the perspective of the northeasterly wind and those it has wreaked chaos on through the ages
Content: Lyrical prose … Sarah Hall.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/The ObserverView image in fullscreenLyrical prose … Sarah Hall.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/The ObserverAudiobook of the weekFictionReviewHelm by Sarah Hall audiobook review – a breath of fresh air from the PenninesLouise Brealey teases out the playful and poetic moments of these shapeshifting stories, told from the perspective of the northeasterly wind and those it has wreaked chaos on through the agesFiona SturgesThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe only named wind in the British Isles, Helm is a strong northeasterly gale that blows down the slopes of Cross Fell in the Pennines and is known for its unusual cloud formations. Helm has been known to dislodge roofs, haystacks, trees and riders from their horses.Twenty years in the writing, Sarah Hall’s Helm is an ambitious novel that tells stories from the perspective of the wind, and from the people on whom, through the ages, Helm has wreaked chaos. Those figures include a Neolithic tribeswoman and seer called NaNay who is building a stone circle; an astrologer and exorcist known as a “wizard priest”; a Victorian meteorologist who travels across the Pennines by train and later by carriage into Helm’s “onslaught”; and a climatologist measuring microplastics in the atmosphere from her observation hut in the fells. Separated by centuries, their stories are nonetheless woven together, each of them bonded by weather.Helm is a book of vast scope, lyrical prose and sharp shifts in style and tone, all of which makes it a tricky job for a narrator. Fortunately, the actor Louise Brealey – who has already read two of Hall’s books: The Wolf Border and Burntcoat – proves more than able, teasing out its playful and poetic moments and revelling in the flashes of coarseness.Helm is a slippery, shapeshifting phenomenon that Hall notes can be hard to visualise and explain, though that doesn’t stop her from trying. “Imagine a skater launching off a quarter pipe two-thousand feet high, then somersaulting. Again. And again. And again.”Available via Faber, 13hr 3minFurther listeningWhistlerAnn Patchett, Bloomsbury, 10hr 43minA fiftysomething English teacher notices an older man following her around New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and eventually recognises him as her former stepfather, Eddie. As they reconnect, old memories come to the surface. Read by the author.London FallingPatrick Radden Keefe, Picador, 12hr 59minBlending true crime and social history, the Empire of Pain author unravels the knotty story of a troubled teenager’s death by falling from a building into the River Thames.Explore more on these topicsFictionAudiobook of the weekreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Give respect to Africa and the bush people’: Mulatu Astatke on pioneering Ethio-jazz and honouring his roots  | Music | The Guardian
description: The musician faced resistance when he premiered his sound in the 60s, but audiences have fallen in love with it since. At 82, he’s still finding new directions – and wants more recognition for Africa’s indigenous artists
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: The musician faced resistance when he premiered his sound in the 60s, but audiences have fallen in love with it since. At 82, he’s still finding new directions – and wants more recognition for Africa’s indigenous artists
Content: ‘Ethio-jazz is a beautiful science’ … Mulatu Astatke.Photograph: Alexis MaryonView image in fullscreen‘Ethio-jazz is a beautiful science’ … Mulatu Astatke.Photograph: Alexis MaryonMusic‘Give respect to Africa and the bush people’: Mulatu Astatke on pioneering Ethio-jazz and honouring his rootsThe multi-instrumentalist faced resistance when he premiered his sound in the 60s but audiences have fallen in love with it since. Now aged 82, he’s still finding new directions – and wants recognition for Africa’s indigenous artistsGeneva AbdulThu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Do you know the Metro club?” I feign recognition to the 82-year-old father of Ethio-jazz, Mulatu Astatke, who knows the UK capital’s vanished haunts better than I do (the Soho venue closed down decades ago). By then, he had immersed himself in the city’s 60s jazz scene, befriending Ronnie Scott and the saxophonist Joe Harriott, with whom he occasionally jammed across Soho’s clubs, as well as musicians from Africa and the Caribbean.But when he returned to “Swinging Addis” years later with the new genre he’d innovated in England and the United States, the audience at one of his first performances weren’t so taken by his fusion of jazz riffs with the harp-likebegena. “Stop,” Astatke was told. “No more!” He didn’t say a word. Instead, he bowed, said his thanks and walked off. “I said: ‘I’ll show you,’” recalls Astatke in his smoky voice. “‘One day, I’ll come back and show you.’”True to his word, audiences around the world have since fallen under the spell of his otherworldly music. We meet days after Astatke’s performance at London’s Royal Festival Hall in June, which is expected to be his last performance in the UK. Like much of his music, he’s difficult to place at first. Dressed in all black, he blends into an armchair in the almost empty lounge of a north London hotel with art deco flourishes. It was beautiful to see the packed audience appreciating Ethiopian jazz, he tells me.But it wasn’t easy trying to do something new. The jazz he has built across more than a dozen albums is mesmeric, layering the distinct pentatonic scales of traditional Ethiopian music with western-style jazz and funk, and infectious Afro-Latin rhythms. He weaves in traditional instruments – thekrar,masenqoandkebero– as well as religious chants dating back to the fourth century. “Ethio-jazz is a beautiful science,” he says, leaning back into his chair. “You can hear jazz, you can hear 12th notes, you can hear the 5th notes and everything all combined together.”View image in fullscreenBig cheese in the Big Apple … Mulatu in Time Square in 1972.Photograph: Courtesy of Mulatu AstatkeLong before the Ethiopian giant honed his sound, he was sent by his parents to aboarding school in Wrexham, north Wales, at 16, set on studying aeronautical engineering. It was there he picked up the trumpet and was encouraged toward a career in music. Subsequent spells at London’s Trinity College of Music and Boston’s Berklee College of Music, as its first ever African student, followed.Throughout the late 60s, Astatke shuttled between New York – where his group, the Ethiopian Quintet, recorded the albums Afro-Latin Soul 1 & 2 – and Addis Ababa, where he began recording singles for Amha Records, the country’s first independent label, in 1969. “I really wanted to be different, I wanted to be myself, I wanted to be Mulatu,” he says of the years spent honing his sound. “Then once I created Ethio-jazz, I became myself.”double quotation markPromoting Ethiopia, promoting our cultural people to the world, that’s what makes me so great and happyHis Ethio-jazz is rooted within the musical culture of a country that, unlike many of its neighbours, has enjoyed independence for most of the last 2,000 years (with the exception of a brief Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941). Astatke had returned to Addis with his own vibraphone and electric keyboards, to a golden age of nightlife and music under Emperor Haile Selassie’s reign (think saxophonist Getatchew Mekurya, singer Mahmoud Ahmed and keyboardist Hailu Mergia, to name a few), which served as fertile ground for experimentation.With his reputation growing, in 1973 Astatke performed in Addis with Duke Ellington, who was touring Ethiopia and Zambia on a state-sponsored trip. He “never expected this from an African”, the US jazz legend told Astatke, as the saxophone section played Ethio-jazz. “He loved it,” he recalls today, wistfully. “It was so good, so beautiful.”View image in fullscreenGood vibes … Astatke in the late 1960s.Photograph: Courtesy of Mulatu AstatkeThe era of a famously wild nightlife under Selassie came to an end when the emperor was deposed by a Marxist regime in 1974, and a repressive period followed for nearly two decades in which hundreds of thousands of Ethiopians were killed, jailed or exiled.My questions about Astatke’s performances for Selassie and life under Ethiopia’s Communist junta are, however, met with reticence. “I have no involvement with the military, I have no involvement with politics, I have no involvement with nobody. I live peacefully. That’s how I survive,” he says firmly. Why the lack of interest in politics? “I don’t love it. You don’t respect politicians. I love my country, I love my culture, I love the people. That’s all. Nothing else.”Astatke wants to ensure that Ethiopia’s cultural contributions don’t go unnoticed. Speak with the musician long enough and each conversation will inevitably bend to the country’s “bush people”, who he feels have yet to receive credit for their musical contributions. Take, for example, the diminished scales used by American saxophonist Charlie Parker (imagine leaps or half-steps in sound); the Derashe tribe in southern Ethiopia, he says, play the same scale. “Who is first? Is it Charlie Parker or this tribe?” he says. “We never give respect to these people.”As he lists off other examples that speak to the forgotten African influence in western music, it feels like I’ve stumbled on to a gameshow. Which came first, themasenqoor the cello? The energised cha-cha and mambo music he heard in a visit to Cuba when he met Fidel Castro, or the similar sounds found in Nigerian, Ghanaian and Tanzanian rhythms?View image in fullscreenBass pleasures … a Mulatu of Ethiopia session in 1972.Photograph: Mulatu AstatkeAstatke jumps then to Japan, a country whose traditional music uses the same five-note scale as Ethiopia. (“Who was first? Who created? Where did this come from?”) Then he compares Beethoven and Tchaikovsky, who famously had distinct musical notations, to St Yared, a sixth-century Aksumite composer credited with creating his own musical notations (“How much respect do you give to him?”). Astatke recalls being invited to lecture at a university in Ethiopia, where students couldn’t name the mountain beyond the classroom but knew the German and Russian composers. “We don’t do any research, we go more to Europe instead of doing research on African people,” he says. “I feel sorry for the educational system in the world, culturally.”Mulatu Astatke review – father of Ethio-jazz still innovating during farewell tourRead moreIn the 1990s, Astatke visited various Ethiopian indigenous communities – the Derashe in the south and Gambella, home to the Nilotic Anuak people – where he was immediately welcomed. There he would have long discussions and, on occasion, stay in small huts. The high respect he holds for them is palpable: “The bush people created Mulatu, because I became a musician by listening to themasenqo.”His manager, sitting at the table with us, gets out his laptop and pulls up a joyous performance by Astatke with members of the Derashe tribe, one of the several communities he brought to the studio in the 1990s. A second video,from the 1970s, shows him performing with traditional musicians playing thekrar. “I became a musician by listening to these people,” he says, “they created me.”Astatke will soon return to Addis Ababa where he’s expecting an audience at the AfricanJazzVillage he opened in 2013, now run by his son. The venue still draws international visitors and spotlights local musicians today.What’s next? He toys with the idea of playing new music at the club in Addis. His most recent album, Mulatu Plays Mulatu, was a new arrangement of hisclassics with his UK band, but his next will feature musicians from “the bush” as well as those in Addis. But there is no name for the project yet, he insists – it is still a work in progress.“Promoting Ethiopia, promoting our cultural people to the world, that’s what makes me so great and happy,” he says. “It took me years and years, but finally we made it.” Only then, do I see a smile beneath Astatke’s serious demeanour. “Give respect to Africa,” he says again, “and the bush people.”Mulatu Astatke’s album Mulatu Plays Mulatu is out now on Strut Records.Explore more on these topicsMusicJazzEthiopiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Giordano: Marina album review – a fascinating resurrection of an unsung early opera | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The long-lost score, finally premiered 138 years after it was written, brims with melodic promise despite its dramatic shortcomings
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The long-lost score, finally premiered 138 years after it was written, brims with melodic promise despite its dramatic shortcomings
Content: Treasurable, thrilling … Eleonora Buratto at the world premiere of Umberto Giordano’s Marina in 2026.Photograph: Lorenza DaverioView image in fullscreenTreasurable, thrilling … Eleonora Buratto at the world premiere of Umberto Giordano’s Marina in 2026.Photograph: Lorenza DaverioClassical musicReviewGiordano: Marina album review – a fascinating resurrection of an unsung early operaBuratto/De Tommaso/Orchestra I Pomeriggi Musicali/Milletarì(Decca)The long-lost score, finally premiered 138 years after it was written, brims with melodic promise despite its dramatic shortcomingsClive PagetThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a bold move by the 21-year-old Umberto Giordano to enter the 1888 one-act opera competition won by Mascagni’s Cavalleria Rusticana. Marina, set in Montenegro during an unspecified conflict with Serbia, came sixth, the score languishing until 2026, when it received its belated premiere at Milan’s Teatro dal Verme. This recording reveals a composer with a keen ear for musical colour even if the opera is no masterpiece.View image in fullscreenGiordano: Marina.Photograph: DeccaWhen Marina, a Montenegrin, takes in Giorgio, a wounded Serb, the inevitable conflict with her brother and her bullish suitor precipitates a typical verismo catastrophe. After a militaristic opening, Marina takes centre stage with an aching ballad of lost opportunity. Her scene with the injured Giorgio follows abruptly, redeemed by Giordano’s knack for trotting out appealing melodies. It’s not the most sophisticated writing but it comes straight from the heart.There’s a drinking song that sounds like a crib from Verdi’s Otello and a patriotic Montenegrin ditty which, alongside a brief aria for Giorgio, is the show’s hit. The scene between Marina and her brother is decently judged, even if the one-act format prevents the kind of character development a longer work would permit.Eleonora Buratto is treasurable as Marina, her bright soprano thrilling at the top. As Giorgio, Freddie De Tommaso proves a classy verismo hero, his voice dark yet suitably Italianate. The Orchestra I Pomeriggi Musicali is supple and secure under the idiomatic baton of Vincenzo Milletarì.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Mario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin review – the Peruvian leftist who fell in love with Margaret Thatcher | Mario Vargas Llosa | The Guardian
description: This stylish biography of the author traces his journey from left to right, and from ‘posh Lima’ to Cricklewood
Author: Pratinav Anil
Headline: This stylish biography of the author traces his journey from left to right, and from ‘posh Lima’ to Cricklewood
Content: Mario Vargas Llosa in 1986.Photograph: Christopher Pillitz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMario Vargas Llosa in 1986.Photograph: Christopher Pillitz/Getty ImagesBook of the dayMario Vargas LlosaReviewMario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin review – the Peruvian leftist who fell in love with Margaret ThatcherThis stylish biography of the author traces his journey from left to right, and from ‘posh Lima’ to CricklewoodPratinav AnilThu 30 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Those words on the opening page of Conversation in the Cathedralannounced the arrival of a writer who understood that national history could become the organising principle of fiction. At precisely the moment when Latin America was discovering the intoxicating possibilities of magical realism – a form whose exuberance had an elective affinity with revolutionary politics, collapsing the distinction between the marvellous and the possible – Mario Vargas Llosa plumped for old-fashioned realism instead.It was a question of sensibility as much as politics, Gerald Martin suggests in this chatty yet coolly analytical biography. He traces the path of a novelist who began by dissecting oligarchy with surgical precision and ended happily dining among its ranks, completing one of literary history’s most spectacular political migrations – from the hard left to the hard right, over the course of half a century.Yet Martin’s revisionist point is that Vargas Llosa crossed a shorter ideological distance than is often imagined. He never truly belonged to the left. His brief flirtation was not with socialism so much as with a socialist: the dazzling, unattainable Lea Barba, whom he met at San Marcos University. Their undergraduate comradeship unfolded between bookshops and the smoky tables of a bohemian nightclub managed by Lea’s communist father. Beneath the guerrilla chic, Martin finds in Vargas Llosa an old patrician confidence in hierarchy. The “factory defect”, as one university contemporary put it, was congenital: Vargas Llosa never ceased to be a “Lima posh boy”.double quotation markHe wrote up the encounter with Thatcher in a piece titled The Lady Among the Wild BeastsVargas Llosa’s greatest novels were written under Jean-Paul Sartre’s spell, before the French philosopher’s indulgence towards revolutionary regimes finally alienated him. The break with Sartre in particular and the left in general came in 1971 with the “Padilla affair”, when the Cuban poet Heberto Padilla was arrested and compelled to perform a grotesque public confession renouncing his “counter-revolutionary” work and denouncing fellow dissidents. Vargas Llosa led an international campaign against Castro’s treatment of writers. Martin is strikingly unsentimental about this celebrated moment of liberal courage. He argues that Vargas Llosa’s comparison of Castro with Stalin was wildly overdrawn and that the campaign against Havana helped isolate the regime at precisely the moment the Latin American left most needed it.Many biographies are now exercises in rehabilitation. Happily, Martin has written a genuinely critical life. The occasional overworked oedipal reading of his subject’s affairs and an inexplicable fondness for the word “sexy” are minor irritants in a searching, stylish account whose real subject is not merely Vargas Llosa but the intellectual and political milieux that made and unmade him.Martin restores the women whom Vargas Llosa reduced to literary raw material. His scandalous marriage at 19 to his aunt-by-marriage, Julia Urquidi, 10 years his senior, became Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter – the sunniest, and by some distance the best loved, of his novels. Her own memoir, What Varguitas Didn’t Say exposes the gap between Vargas Llosa’s breezy romance and the less charming reality of adultery and abandonment. Alas, it never troubled the bestseller lists.Julia was discarded for Patricia Llosa, his first cousin, nine years his junior, with whom he had three children. Like so many writers’ wives of her generation, she was forever taking one for the team, quietly spiriting away the offending pram whenever he bellowed: “Patriiiicia! Take this baby away, I can’t woooork!”Half a century later, she too was replaced, this time by the Spanish society doyenne Isabel Preysler, the mother of the singer Enrique Iglesias, with whom the octogenarian finally exchanged the republic of letters for the pages of ¡Hola!.His move to England proved unexpectedly formative. Vargas Llosa settled in unswinging Cricklewood, which suited a pre-existing taste for suburban conservatism. The historian Hugh Thomas, another distinguished émigré from the left, played Virgil to Vargas Llosa’s Dante, escorting him into the circles of Tory respectability and, eventually, to Margaret Thatcher herself. He wrote up the encounter with fanboy adoration in a piece titled The Lady Among the Wild Beasts.The novelist who spent decades exposing the seductions of ideology proved remarkably susceptible to a new one. After Peru rejected his presidential ambitions when he ran on a neoliberal ticket against Alberto Fujimori in 1990, he increasingly revelled in precisely those circles where power congratulates itself upon its realism. Utopias, sources of aspiration on the left, became mere pathologies in his later fictions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the 2010 Nobel prize, Vargas Llosa increasingly lent his prestige to the hard right, backing Peru’s trigger-happy unelected ruler Dina Boluarte and Chile’s anti-gay, anti-abortion crusader José Antonio Kast; denouncing feminism as literature’s “staunchest enemy,” and treating every leftward electoral twitch as a “return tocaudillismo.”Gabriel García Márquez is the book’s foil: the magician to Vargas Llosa’s realist, the man who stayed with the leftist tribe while his lesser rival abandoned it. Martin, now thebiographer of both, is uniquely placed to reconstruct the most famous right hook in literary history. In 1976, Vargas Llosa floored García Márquez with a punch after allegedly accusing him of overstepping the mark by comforting Patricia during the collapse of their marriage.The punch marked more than a personal rupture. It sealed an ideological one. García Márquez later remarked that there were only “two soups on the menu”: capitalism and socialism. Vargas Llosa turned up his nose at one and spent the rest of his life gorging himself on the other.Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life by Gerald Martinis published by Bloomsbury (£35).Explore more on these topicsMario Vargas LlosaBook of the dayBiography booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Line Held Tight – miners, mechs and mismanagement on a distant planet | Games | The Guardian
description: Deep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on you
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Deep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on you
Content: Dark and satanic … A Line Held Tight.Photograph: Humble GroveView image in fullscreenDark and satanic … A Line Held Tight.Photograph: Humble GroveSummer games previewsGamesA Line Held Tight – miners, mechs and mismanagement on a distant planetDeep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on youKeith StuartThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is rare for video games to feature industrial action as a key theme, but it does happen. There’s the shady Dockworker’s Union in Disco Elysium and the Orbital Workers Union in space adventure Tacoma; then there is Lynx, the evil union-bashing corp in Hardspace: Shipbreaker. Soon we can add A Line Held Tight, a visual novel that puts workers’ rights – and workers’ lives – at the very centre of the narrative.In the distant future, a colony of miners digs far beneath the surface of an isolated planet, searching for veins of some exotic ore, protected from the poisonous atmosphere within giant mech suits. But the working conditions are woeful and as a strike looms, an unpopular employee named the Canary must decide whether or not to stand with colleagues and fight against suppression. The player, of course, takes on the role of the Canary, navigating personal as well as political struggles in a world rendered in stark monochrome.View image in fullscreenStark choices … A Line Held Tight.Illustration: Humble GroveAlthough there are clear parallels with the miners’ strike in 80s Britain, Humble Grove’s three-person team was inspired by a situation closer to home. “My interest in telling a story about a trade union comes from our own industry’s burgeoning union interest in the face of mass layoffs,” says co-founder Cel Davison. “People who write sci-fi generally speaking fall into one of two camps: those who are interested in writing speculative futures and those who use futuristic settings to tell stories that are reflections of our present. We tend to fall into the latter end of that spectrum.”Using the highly adaptable narrative game engineNarrat, the game provides a dynamic story guided by player choices. The Canary has a complicated personal connection with the mine, the union and its leaders, which the player has to make sense of. “We’re very interested in the internal workings and conflicts within a collective, how they can make or break a political movement. Our protagonist the Canary starts off as someone quite disinterested in politics, but finds themself in situations where they have to decide what and who they really care about. There’s a lot of variables behind the scenes tracking how the mine’s inhabitants feel about the Canary and the decisions they make.”Although the game is set in the distant future on an alien planet, elements of it are very grounded in British history. It has a traditional folk soundtrack, recorded by two of Humble Grove, Davison and Beck Michalak, who both play at folk sessions in Yorkshire where mining and union-related songs are common. The game’s visuals resemble charcoal sketches providing a stark, almost Victorian feel. “We first got the idea from some wonderful charcoal drawings at the Wakefield Coal Mining Museum,” says Davison. “Charcoal gives a great coal-like feel, and being a traditional medium gives it a grounded textural feel, but conversely when we worked with it we found it can create some very gauzy, ghostly imagery. This really mirrors the way the Canary processes the world as someone trapped in their own head, especially at the beginning of the game.”Humble Grove’s debut game No Longer Home was a thoughtful meditation on moving house and leaving a life behind; it looks like A Line Held Tight will take a similarly meditative approach. This time however, the themes are more prescient than Humble Grove may have intended. “I hope it helps people consider how their everyday actions can have political consequences,” says Davison. “If I’m being really honest I hope it convinces more people to join a union.”A Line Held Tighter is released onPCand Mac in late 2026Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Halo: Campaign Evolved review – they don’t make ‘em like this any more | Halo | The Guardian
description:
PC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game Studios
Halo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the time
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: PC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game StudiosHalo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the time
Content: Once more unto the breach … Halo: Campaign Evolved.Photograph: Halo StudiosView image in fullscreenOnce more unto the breach … Halo: Campaign Evolved.Photograph: Halo StudiosHaloReviewHalo: Campaign Evolved review – they don’t make ‘em like this any morePC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game StudiosHalo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the timeKeza MacDonaldThu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis 25th-anniversary remake of Xbox’s most iconic shooter comes loaded with symbolism. It arrives at a time when Xbox’s whole gaming division (and indeed the games business as a whole)is in turmoil. It’s been made by Halo Studios, an outfit that has arguably never quite recaptured the magic conjured by Halo: Combat Evolved’s original developer Bungie, a studio now owned by rival Sony. It has been polished and prettified using Unreal Engine 5, making it look and feel more modern at the expense of visual uniqueness: Halo now looks similar to hundreds of other games made with those same tools, where Bungie’s 2001 original, made with a bespoke engine, still looks austerely distinctive. I never wanted to become this person, but: perhaps thingswerebetter in the old days?I had my misgivings after the opening level, in which freshly defrosted supersoldier Master Chief fends off an alien attack on a disintegrating spaceship. Originally this was a masterclass in explosive action: you wake up, you look around (once a clever way to determine whether you needed to invert the controls), and you get right into it, firing gaming’s best pistol at chittering alien grunts who scatter from your bullets. Now it’s wrapped in needlessly expanded cutscenes and explanations. WhereHaloStudios has made changes to Combat Evolved’s pacing, it really feels noticeable.After that, however, I spent much less time thinking about what has been changed, and much more thinking about what hasn’t. Nobody really makes single-player shooters like Halo any more: tense, adaptable, challenging. In 2026, we have multiplayer shooters of every imaginable kind; there is little reason for computer-controlled enemies to be intelligent and unpredictable, because we mostly play against other humans, and they provide infinite variation. What we don’t have in abundance in 2026 is atmospheric single-player shooters like this, or Half-Life, or System Shock 2. Solo campaigns in shooters such as Call of Duty have been reduced to flashy “cinematic” shooting galleries. Halo: Campaign Evolved reminded me what we’ve been missing.The imposing Elites are still the probably cleverest foes I’ve ever played against, and it’s been 25 years. They bark orders and duck away from my fire, and they know how to flank me, when to rush me and how to adapt to my assaults. Every time you die in this game, you come back to a slightly remixed firefight, making it endlessly replayable; I never minded going back to a checkpoint, because it never feels repetitious. In other shooters you simply memorise enemy numbers and positioning, but here you must constantly adapt your play, especially on higher Heroic or Legendary difficulty. And I’d somehow forgotten about the Hunters. The first time a pair of those spiked brutes appeared I reacted on pure decades-old muscle memory: I turned around and fled.Unfortunately, we still must contend with the Flood. After several levels of brilliant open-ended fights against intelligent foes under the strange light of a foreign sun, suddenly we are transported into a boring, claustrophobic zombie shooter. I maintain that these mid-game levels are extremely bad: shooting 400 identical parasitic baddies with a shotgun while waiting for a floating robot to open a door has never been my idea of a good time. This will be a controversial opinion, but I was grateful for the new waypoints that told me exactly where to go in the maze of zombie-filled corridors that is the Library. It meant that the worst parts of this game were over sooner.In co-op Halo becomes somewhat less challenging, atmospheric and tactical and significantly more chaotic. Especially when vehicles are involved, the game transforms completely with the addition of other players, thanks to its flexible, open level design and adaptable foes. I played through much of the game in split-screen with my partner – I maintain that playing Combat Evolved with four players just feels somehow wrong – and was reminded exactly why I spent hundreds of hours rinsing this game with friends as a teenager. Halo remains the best companionable shooting game out there.Campaign Evolved is a good remake of a brilliant game. There are things that are worse: I miss the original Warthog’s erratic handling and the early-00s sci-fi aesthetic, which is simply irreproducible with modern graphics. For all its prettiness, this remake chugs along at times – especially in split-screen it would occasionally slow to a crawl, and we never had to worry about linking various different online accounts and connecting to servers when we fancied a quick game of Halo in 2001. But the core of this game is impossible to mess up. For millions of younger players, Campaign Evolved is a perfect, modernised introduction to everything that was great about the 00s-style first-person shooter. For those of us who were there at the time, it’s a welcome return trip.Halo: Campaign Evolved is out nowExplore more on these topicsHaloGamesXboxreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cleansed review – Sarah Kane’s visions of brutal torture resonate more intensely than ever | Stage | The Guardian
description: Rebecca Frecknall pulls off this notoriously difficult 1998 play, in which appalling cruelty and violence is balanced against human yearning for love and beauty
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Rebecca Frecknall pulls off this notoriously difficult 1998 play, in which appalling cruelty and violence is balanced against human yearning for love and beauty
Content: A chilling ordinariness … Luke Cinque-White and Leo Bill in Cleansed at the Almeida theatre.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenA chilling ordinariness … Luke Cinque-White and Leo Bill in Cleansed at the Almeida theatre.Photograph: Marc BrennerStageReviewCleansed review – Sarah Kane’s visions of brutal torture resonate more intensely than everAlmeida theatre, LondonRebecca Frecknall pulls off this notoriously difficult 1998 play, in which appalling cruelty and violence is balanced against human yearning for love and beautyArifa AkbarThu 30 Jul 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Kane was much berated for the graphic violence in her plays during her lifetime. But critics beware: if you choose to scold playwrights for too much blood-letting and grotesque acts of human cruelty, you would surely have to condemn the Greeks, the Grand Guignol and Shakespeare, too.Perhaps it’s the in-yer-face nature of Kane’s gore that offends. Certainly in this 1998 play there is no flinching from horror, which comes through acts of sensational cruelty. “Death isn’t the worst thing they can do to you,” a character reflects, and his words illustrate themselves with the rapes, mutilations and beatings that follow.‘She plumbed our secret, shameful depths’: why are Sarah Kane’s plays still so shocking?Read moreIn the case of Cleansed, there are so many ways in which its revival can go wrong, not least because it is notoriously difficult to stage, with directions that require rats to walk away with amputated limbs and gigantic sunflowers to explode from the floor. It is courageous of directorRebecca Frecknallto take it on. The gamble pays off, both in its terrible resonance in our violent world and in her formidable creative accomplishment.Kane’s first play, Blasted, was a response to the conflict in Bosnia in the 1990s and this third play was part of an unrealised trilogy on war. Watching it today, in Frecknall’s potent, moving and fantastically physical production, you are reminded of all the wars before (the cutting out of a character’s tongue and his amputations are reminiscent of Titus Andronicus) and after. A scene in which the Kinks’ song Days is piped into a torture cell, though tender, holds shades of“torture lite” in Guantánamo. Again and again, you are reminded of the photos fromAbu Ghraib prison,which captured the humiliation of prisoners by American guards. Israel’s brutality and violence in Gaza echoes.View image in fullscreenOrwellian … Pearl Chanda and Jack Riddiford in Cleansed.Photograph: Marc BrennerSet in a university that seemed partly to evoke a concentration camp, Tinker (Leo Bill) is the sole “visible” torturer here (other violence is enacted by unseen agents of brutality). He is ostensibly unimposing, personifying Hannah Arendt’s banality, perhaps. He targets those deemed sexually aberrant, particularly two gay men, Rod (Parth Thakerar) and Carl (Luke Cinque-White), but also terrorises brother and sister Graham (Jack Riddiford) and Grace (Pearl Chanda), manipulates a peep show dancer (Lizzy Connolly) and another prisoner called Robin (Stuart Thompson).The cast acts out the play’s many difficult scenarios with no awkwardness or melodrama. Tinker’s cruelty is still a puzzle, especially the functionality with which he tortures. Is he motivated by power, a guiding principle or sheer sadism? It is never explained. Still, the message is clear: war and its torture is senseless, cruel and in-yer-face for those close enough to it. There is the sense of an Orwellian system tyrannising those who are deemed aberrant in their gender or sexual identities (the rats, invisible here, are reminiscent of Orwell, too). Madeleine Girling’s stage design has the grimy, institutionalised feel of a hidden hallway in a psychiatric ward or prison. Again, it evokes a chilling ordinariness.View image in fullscreenA dance of pain … Jack Riddiford and Leo Bill in Cleansed.Photograph: Marc BrennerLike the rest of Kane’s oeuvre, the play interrogates the limits of theatre and representation in its extremity and breakdown of conventional form. Exposing the theatrical construction of violence, through various techniques, does little to protect us from the horror of observing it, and Frecknall oscillates masterfully between realism and a more poetic vein. When characters are in the furthest extremity of pain, their movements become a kind of expressive dance. There is lyricism in it but not so it beautifies violence. Importantly, it never seems gratuitous, either.Sex is a kind of dance, too: bodies never make contact but intimacy and physical force are suggested through choreography. Ingrid Mackinnon’s intimacy direction brings passion and romance, never voyeurism. George Dennis’s sound design, with Angus MacRae’s compositions, combine powerfully with their blend of blazing romance and thrumming electric dread.For such a slim play, it does feel protracted, and slows in its pace. The cruelty becomes draining to watch – but in a world in which images of violence are streamed on daily feeds, it re-sensitises us, through its dissection.The poetry comes in other forms, too. There is sudden, immense beauty, declarations of love, romantic clinches and humour. Set alongside Kane’s brand of post-dramatic theatre, the play’s message is strangely romantic: the human need, maybe even demand, for love and for beauty persists, every bit as vital a force as violence – even, we are shown, for someone like Tinker.AtAlmeida theatre, London, until 29 AugustExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreAlmeida theatreSarah KaneRebecca FrecknallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Die Fledermaus review – Strauss staging has flourish and froth, but not enough fizz | Opera | The Guardian
description: Liam Steel relocates Johann Strauss’s operetta to London 1929 to create the feel of a Noël Coward-style farce. Rebecca Bottone, Olivia Carrell and Clare Presland shine amid a strong cast.
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Liam Steel relocates Johann Strauss’s operetta to London 1929 to create the feel of a Noël Coward-style farce. Rebecca Bottone, Olivia Carrell and Clare Presland shine amid a strong cast.
Content: Alison Langer   and Harry Wilson in Die Fledermaus at Opera Holland Park.Photograph: Craig FullerView image in fullscreenAlison Langer   and Harry Wilson in Die Fledermaus at Opera Holland Park.Photograph: Craig FullerOperaReviewDie Fledermaus review – Strauss staging has flourish and froth, but not enough fizzOpera Holland Park, LondonLiam Steel relocates Johann Strauss’s operetta to London 1929 to create the feel of a Noël Coward-style farce. Rebecca Bottone, Olivia Carrell and Clare Presland shine amid a strong cast.Clive PagetThu 30 Jul 2026 09.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohann Strauss’s Die Fledermaus must have done more for champagne sales than any other operetta. A good production, however, demands plenty of onstage fizz too, but the bubbles start to rise rather late in the day in Opera Holland Park’s new staging.Director and choreographer Liam Steel uses the Metropolitan Opera’s 2013 revamped English version with lyrics by Jeremy Sams and a new book by Douglas Carter Beane. His chosen setting, however, is London on New Year’s Eve 1929; cue references to the Sitwells and the Mitfords. In its determination to reflect the anything goes spirit of the age there’s even a cheeky reference to Winston Churchill’s supposed dalliance with Ivor Novello (how did he find it? “Musical,” goes the apocryphal tale.) The idea has legs, turning a 19th-century Viennese operetta into a louche Noël Coward farce with lines that are at times deliciously tart.Where it is less successful is in the playing out of this frothy saga of bourgeois infidelity and mistaken identities. With its free-standing doorframes, Neil Irish’s set for the Eisensteins’ salon feels insufficiently nouveau riche. Placed in front of the orchestra on the OHP forestage, it does at least allow the performers intimate contact with the audience. The second act’s deco ballroom with gilded Degas centrepiece has more flourish, but, confined to the rear of the stage, the company feels deflatingly distant. It’s left to act three, set in a police station complete with affable moustachioed bobby (a winning performance by Robert Burt), to raise the chuckle level to where it needs to be.View image in fullscreenAnything goers spirit … Die Fledermaus at Opera Holland Park.Photograph: Craig FullerSteel does his best, pulling off some nice bits of physical comedy, and Sams’ elegant lyrics are a treat: “Drink another drink with me, you’ve had none and I’ve had three,” sings the libidinous tenor, Alfred (a stentorian and suitably Italianate Xavier Hetherington). The acting can be inconsistent – act one starts off a little Acorn Antiques – but there are strong performances from Rebecca Bottone as the put-upon cockney chambermaid Adele and Julien Van Mellaerts as an affected Dr Falke in midnight-blue velvet and foppish earring. Matthew Siveter plays Inspector Frank as a bluff Yorkshireman with a fine line in bewildered expressions. His encounter at the ball with Thomas Atkins’ Eisenstein, where both appear as faux-Frenchmen and communicate entirely in phrases such as “coq au vin” and “menage a trois”, earns well-deserved laughter.George Jackson conducts the City of London Sinfonia stylishly, though the music is frequently too loud for the singers. Nevertheless, there are strong vocal performances from Alison Langer as Rosalinde, Clare Presland as the gender-fluid socialite Orlofsky and especially Bottone, who absolutely nails her Laughing Song. Special mention too for Olivia Carrell who sparkles in the relatively thankless role of Ida, the chorus girl from Where’s My Willie.At Opera Holland Park, London, until 8 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaOpera Holland ParkClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Marianela: Timeless review – perfect ballerina shows off a leg-whipping, frictionless mastery | Marianela Núñez | The Guardian
description: In what is officially her first solo show, the star principal marshals technically peerless performances from a tremendous company in finely chosen repertoire
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: In what is officially her first solo show, the star principal marshals technically peerless performances from a tremendous company in finely chosen repertoire
Content: Egoless self-possession … Marianela Nuñez and Vadim Muntagirov in Le Corsaire at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEgoless self-possession … Marianela Nuñez and Vadim Muntagirov in Le Corsaire at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMarianela NúñezReviewMarianela: Timeless review – perfect ballerina shows off a leg-whipping, frictionless masteryRoyal Opera House, LondonIn what is officially her first solo show, the star principal marshals technically peerless performances from a tremendous company in finely chosen repertoireLyndsey WinshipThu 30 Jul 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there such a thing as being too perfect? Marianela Nuñez is certainly one of the most perfect ballerinas around. At 44, she still has superlative technique and absolute command. She can reel off a fiendish string of fouettés (as in tonight’s extract from Le Corsaire), whipping her leg in circles, and then come to a gentle standstill, the smoothest brakes you ever saw. It is absolutely frictionless; it is beauty and capability and egoless self-possession. And this might seem an unfair ask, but do we sometimes also need a little grit?View image in fullscreenSerene … Fumi Kaneko and Lukas Brændsrød in After the Rain.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian‘The Messi of ballet’: Marianela Núñez, the Buenos Aires bombshell shaking up British danceRead moreTimeless is Nuñez’s first solo show. Not truly solo, but she’s the star, it’s her choice of repertoire, and she does everything “just right”, paying tribute to the RoyalBallet, the company she joined at 16, and its choreographers: Frederick Ashton, Kenneth MacMillan, Christopher Wheeldon, Wayne McGregor. She also offers an amazing showcase of the company’s dancers and generously allows them to shine, so much so that Matthew Ball and Mayara Magri dancing the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet is an absolute highlight, Magri giddy as she watches her Romeo swoop manfully around the stage. Akane Takada and Calvin Richardson are tender in a duet from McGregor’s Infra, and Fumi Kaneko and Lukas B Braendsrød dance Wheeldon’s serene After the Rain – although they can’t fill the long phrases in the exquisite way Nuñez once did with Thiago Soares.For herself, Nuñez chooses first Jerome Robbins’ In the Night, set to Chopin’s Nocturnes. It’s a very grownup piece for three couples, full of simple, breath-holding elegance. Nuñez dances with Ball, all super-smooth take-offs into jumps and lifts and tortuous indecision about their relationship status. It’s a subtle and gorgeous piece. Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand is the opposite, quite the melodrama, not least Nuñez’s TB-stricken courtesan, coughing on the chaise longue.But Nuñez has a level of reserve and containment that makes this a dance of resistance and surrender rather than passion and fire. Her textbook classical and neo-classical pas de deux are in some ways the most arresting; as well as Corsaire, there’s Balanchine’s Tchaikovsky Pas de Deux with the Royal’s new principal Patricio Revé, a promising partnership for the future. You could ask for more, but you can’t fault her.AtRoyal Opera House, London, until 2 AugustExplore more on these topicsMarianela NúñezBalletDancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People say I’m pouring Coca-Cola into fine malt whisky’: why is the National Theatre shaking up Sophocles? | Stage | The Guardian
description: In a bold new production starring Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss, the NT is fusing Sophocles and Ingmar Bergman. So what can two stories written 23 centuries apart tell us about how we live today?
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: In a bold new production starring Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss, the NT is fusing Sophocles and Ingmar Bergman. So what can two stories written 23 centuries apart tell us about how we live today?
Content: ‘Bergman is a north star for me’ … Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann in the film that inspired Electra/Persona.View image in fullscreen‘Bergman is a north star for me’ … Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann in the film that inspired Electra/Persona.Stage‘People say I’m pouring Coca-Cola into fine malt whisky’: why is the National Theatre shaking up Sophocles?In a bold new production starring Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss, the NT is fusing Sophocles and Ingmar Bergman. So what can two stories written 23 centuries apart tell us about how we live today?Mark LawsonThu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn around 420BC, Sophocles staged Electra, in which the title character avenges the murder of her father by her mother, Clytemnestra. In 1966, Swedish film director Ingmar Bergman premieredPersona, in which a psychiatric nurse, Alma, is caring for Elisabeth, an actor who has suffered a breakdown while playing Electra. These two dramas, written 23 centuries apart, are now sharing the stage in an alluring new National Theatre production.InElectra/Persona, director Benedict Andrews has paired the stories before and after the interval, linked by a stunning coup de theatre at the end of the first half. “Persona is a pinnacle of modernist cinema and Bergman is a north star for me,” says Andrews. “I’ve long been fascinated by the impossibility – in a good way – of staging Persona, because it is so much about the camera and the silence and the closeup: the face as a terrain. And I was always fascinated by why Bergman chose to have Elisabeth break down while playing Electra, so I wanted to put them together. I think it’s become clear in rehearsal that the whole evening is one cycle of grief.”double quotation markWe joke about having put the writer on a trawler back to IcelandEarly on, Andrews (Australian-born, Iceland-resident and identifying as “Ice-Stralian”) had the idea that Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss would alternate the roles of Electra and Clytemnestra in Electra, and Elisabeth and Alma in Persona; whoever plays Electra in the first half reappears as Elisabeth, and Clytemnestra reappears as Alma. The original plan was for Blanchett and Hoss to toss a coin on stage at the start of the evening but Tom Stoppard’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, in which a coin lands heads92 times in succession, made this strategy risky.View image in fullscreen‘They are astonishing actresses’ … Blanchett, left, and Hoss.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty Images“Also,” says Andrews, “I said to Cate and Nina, ‘To play your best game do you need to wake up in the morning and study your Electra or Persona text?’ And they said maybe. In the end, they will have a schedule and swap night by night but the audience won’t know who’s playing who until the first one walks in.” And if I say to the box office that I’ve seen one combination and want to see the other, they won’t tell me when? Andrews pauses. “No.”Although he is known for staging radical new versions of classics – including Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchardat the Donmar Warehouse in 2024, and Tennessee Williams’ A Streetcar Named Desire on a rotating setat the Young Vic in 2014– Electra/Persona is a bold project. Another writer-director, Alan Ayckbourn, once said that, while directing, he found himself cursing what the writer had given him to do. Did Andrews understand what it would be like effectively having to rehearse two plays twice each to prepare the various permutations?“Yeah. Long rehearsal days,” he sighs with a laugh. “Yesterday, unusually, we stayed in Electra all day but I still did an hour on Persona at the end. I think it’s really important to do both every day. Although they require very different energies. It’s not a double-bill; it’s onehingedwork. There are perforations from Bergman in the first half and from Sophocles in the second half.”By this stage, Andrews considers himself only a director: “We have this joke with the cast about there having been a writer. We call him Dominic. He was chained to a table for two weeks here to do rewrites but now we’ve put him on a trawler back to Iceland.”View image in fullscreen‘We are watching American imperialism fall apart’ … Andrews.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianI recently saw a hit show in which the understudy was on – they did an impersonation of the absent performer, which is standard in the circumstances. But will Blanchett and Hoss have a different interaction? “Absolutely. They are two actresses who are equally astonishing but play their instruments differently. Cate and Nina are good mates and had donethe film Tár, in which Nina plays Cate’s wife. So I thought it would be great to do something with them. They don’t look the same but there’s an echo between them: they could be sisters. In rehearsal, you see them thinking, ‘Oh, they did that in that bit? Do I take that or do my own interpretation?’ We’re searching for something in which they each play the logic of the scene, but it may come out in different ways.”When I tell him that his Donmar Warehouse Cherry Orchard was completely different the two times I saw it, he nods enthusiastically, even though some directors would greet this with a public inquiry. “Good!” he says. “I saw the [romantic rejection] scene between Lopakhin and Varya dozens of times in rehearsal and then performance – and it was different each time. And I encourage that because, in the end, you want the truth of that moment played each night. As a director, you have set up a perpetuum mobile that the actors can continue to develop.”Andrews is having an Ancient Greek period, his previous show being a version in Iceland of Aeschylus’s The Oresteia, which shares characters with Electra including Clytemnestra, Orestes and Electra herself. So is there a big overlap between his back-to-back Greek tragedies? “Huge. I moved bits across between the two shows. I spent the bulk of last year doing my text for The Oresteia. Then there was a gap before rehearsals began – for it to be translated into Icelandic – in which I wrote Electra/Persona. Which I hadn’t expected to be on so quickly. I hadn’t expected to be living with this crazy fucking family for so long!”View image in fullscreen‘I hadn’t expected to be living with this crazy family for so long!’ … Andrews’ Oresteia at the National Theatre, Reyjavik.Photograph: Owen FieneBoth shows are chamber pieces – five actors in Reykjavik, four in London – so apart from the role-swapping in Electra/Persona, there is also role-play, in which the back stories of off-stage characters are acted out: “It’s sometimes something like a Gestalttherapy game where you play your oppressor. And ‘persona’is the word for masks, for the roles we play. The king and the judge put on those robes and play those roles. How does theatre critique all these power relationships? But, in another way, how does theatre allow us to interrogate all those roles we play in our own lives, our psyche and our dream lives?”From the meeting room at the National Theatre where we talk, it’s a short walk to Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey at the BFI Southbank or to Simon Stone’sThe Oresteia at The Bridge. If the descendants of the Ancient Greek writers were on royalties, they would all have private jets. “Yes! I think they’re coming back at the moment because, in these times of big political and moral crisis, we need them. The reason we are digging in this Greek rubble and soil is that these plays were made in an imperial warring empire, that was first triumphant and then later broke apart. And we are watching that with American imperialism now.double quotation markI’ve worked a lot in Germany where radical rethinking is what the director does“We grew up with the idea that the US – our Rome, our Athens – was a military might but also a cultural might. And it’s breaking apart. So we go back to a culture that lived through wars but also gave us philosophy and theatre and gave Freud the Oedipus myth for unpacking a family. And these plays should also make us question notions of law and justice.”There is an increasingly strong Australian directorial presence in London. As well as Stone, whose Oresteia follows his Phaedra and The Lady From The Sea, Kip Williams has frequently worked in the city: recently on The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dracula, andThe Maids. Does Andrews have a WhatsApp group or reunion barbecues with his fellow expats? “Not really. But Kip was my assistant director. Simon acted in a production of mine, rotating in a glass box in Whose Afraid of Virginia Woolf? We all know each other and have collaborators that we share.”Andrews, Stone and Williams all visually or structurally disrupt classic texts – is that an Australian thing? A sort of textual anticolonialism or republicanism? “When I did my first Three Sisters in Sydney, the [Chekhov] tradition was still lace and linen. I got letters saying you’ve taken Coca-Cola and poured it into a vat of fine malt whisky. Barrie Kosky wasdoing something similarand we possibly were a battering ram against the conservatism of Australian state theatre then. But I’d worked a lot in Germany, where radical rethinking is what the director does, so it never made sense to me to be ‘faithful’ to classics. What does that even mean? I don’t think of it as disrupting classics. I’m trying to access the mythic power in the piece; X-ray the inner meaning.”Electra/Persona is atthe National Theatre, London, from 19 August to 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreCate BlanchettNational TheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was hyperventilating and sobbing’: Tomi Adeyemi says Children of Blood and Bone film ‘the worst thing I’ve ever lived through’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla Stenberg
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla Stenberg
Content: Tomi Adeyemi in 2025.Photograph: River Callaway/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTomi Adeyemi in 2025.Photograph: River Callaway/Variety/Getty ImagesMovies‘I was hyperventilating and sobbing’: Tomi Adeyemi says Children of Blood and Bone film ‘the worst thing I’ve ever lived through’Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla StenbergCatherine ShoardThu 30 Jul 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTomi Adeyemi, the author ofChildren of Blood and Bone, has spoken further on the difficult process behind adapting her novel for this big screen, calling it “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”.In a five-minute video on TikTok, the author said she left the set of the Paramount production “hyperventilating and sobbing”, adding: “I never want to hear about this project again”.Adeyemi, who co-wrote the screenplay for the film, had previously spoken about her concerns surrounding the adaptation, saying that she wasn’t intending to watch the film.The video she posted on TikTok was intended, she said, to try to put the affair to bed, although the author conceded it might prolong the story. She also said that the people involved with the film had continued to “antagonise” her.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continue“What I’m about to share is not a secret to the people involved,” she said. “It’s a reality that I’ve had to live with for about a year and a half, and everyone involved, at least at the highest level, has been made aware of this reality, and they haven’t done anything to make it better. If anything, they’ve only antagonised me, and I accept that. But I also accept if I don’t say something, I think it’s just going to be worse.”She continued: “I’m not going to speak on what I endured to make it through the young adult trilogy, and I’m not going to speak about everything that I also suffered through or endured to make the adaptation a reality.‘Attacked behind the scenes’: Children of Blood & Bone author Tomi Adeyemi distances herself from film adaptationRead more“I’m actually only going to speak about what happened after I left that set of my own film adaptation, hyperventilating and sobbing. There are many witnesses, so it’s not really a secret. I came back to America and suffered such severe somatic pain and so many panic attacks. I knew it was so bad that I would never ever be able to watch this film, and I made peace with that.”Speaking to the Los Angeles Timesearlier this week, director Gina Prince-Bythewood appeared to allude to a casting controversy involving Amandla Stenberg, who portrays Princess Amari in the film.Prince-Bythewood said the adaptation was “beautifully inspired by Nigeria and also inclusive of the whole diaspora. We wanted all of us to be able to see ourselves within this, just our complete and utter humanity, all the beautiful hues.”While the actor and novelist seemed close last spring, it looks as if a subsequent disagreement soured relations considerably. A now-deleted TikTok video posted by the writer appeared to show a group chat including Stenberg, to whom Adeyemi wrote: “Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me.”The film also stars Regina King, Damson Idris, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, Tosin Cole, Viola Davis, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Lashana Lynch and Thuso Mbedu.Prince-Bythewood was speaking at an event to mark the release of a first trailer for the film on Monday, which appears to have acted as an additional prompt to Adeyami to speak out again.“As it is being marketed,” she said on TikTok, “and as I am still being antagonised behind the scenes, which is where I hoped all of this would stay, it’s become apparent to me that reality needs to at least be made known, so that you guys can understand how this film, which I worked on to make it a little better for us to be alive, is also the worst thing I have ever had to live through.”Explore more on these topicsFilmYoung adultAction and adventure filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The crude language of Maga folks’: Joyce Carol Oates criticises Emily Wilson for criticising Nolan’s Odyssey | Movies | The Guardian
description: The novelist suggested Wilson should have been ‘a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful’ towards a film-maker who may have helped boost her book sales
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The novelist suggested Wilson should have been ‘a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful’ towards a film-maker who may have helped boost her book sales
Content: ‘Uncollegiate’ … Mia Goth and Anne Hathaway in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘Uncollegiate’ … Mia Goth and Anne Hathaway in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesMovies‘The crude language of Maga folks’: Joyce Carol Oates criticises Emily Wilson for criticising Nolan’s OdysseyThe novelist suggested Wilson should have been ‘a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful’ towards a film-maker who may have helped boost her book salesMary Beard on The Odyssey and how empires fall – Stateside with Kai and CarterCatherine ShoardThu 30 Jul 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe off-screen drama surrounding Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster version of the Odyssey stepped up a gear overnight, as the novelistJoyce Carol Oatessought to defend the film-maker from an attack by classicist Emily Wilson.Writing on X, Oates took issue with the style as well as the rhetoric of Wilson’sessay published earlier this week in the London Review of Books, in which the academic, who published a landmark translation of Homer’s epic poem in 2017, wrote that Nolan’s film lacked “psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth” and had “nothing convincing to say”.“Rather than disagreeing with interpretations of Homer in a collegial manner,” said Oates, “this person, who has benefited enormously from Nolan’s film, speaks in the crude language of Maga folks attacking someone with ideas that differ from hers.‘I would be ashamed to have written any part of this’: Odyssey translator Emily Wilson attacks Nolan blockbusterRead more“One would expect a translator, of all people, beholden to a text, in service to a text, to be just a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful of others who are acting in good faith just as (she would claim) she is.”Oates’s comments come in the wake of her own implied criticism of the film last week, when she compared it to a 1997 Hallmark Channel version and found it wanting. The authortweetedthat the TV movie made by Andrei Konchalovsky boasted a “much more interesting interpretation than Nolan” of the sexual dynamic between Circe and Odysseus.She alsopraisedits portrayal of Odysseus (“So manly, so fully human”), its hades interlude (“mesmerising”) and its comparative expansiveness (“which perhaps Nolan had not seen”).Nolan’s film has been widely applauded by critics, perhaps partly explaining why the pitch of Wilson’s objections shocked many. “I had hoped that Nolan’s affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters,” she wrote.“ButThe Odysseyfeatures his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality … the film’s vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants.”She added: “The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has a convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.”Joyce Carol Oates thinks the 90s TV adaptation of The Odyssey is the best. I beg to differ | Stuart HeritageRead moreThe classicist’s verdict was perhaps the most eagerly anticipated, as her translation had been praised by Nolan in an interview with Empire. The director told the magazine he had used the opening line of her version – “Tell me about a complicated man” – as a key reference point when constructing the character played by Odysseus.Wilson finding Nolan’s rendition of the character as relatively one-dimensional is likely to have taken the team behind the film aback. In publicity for the movie, Universal has stressed that Nolan had been linked to an adaptation long before Wilson’s translation was published, and disputed claims he had been “inspired” by it.Sales of Wilson’s translation, and those by others, have seen a significant uptick over the past month, with UK bookseller TGJones reporting a 1,560% rise in searches for the Iliad this month.However, no royalties from the film would have been paid to any writer other than Nolan himself. The Odyssey, which cost around $250m to make and about $100m to promote, has currently taken $683m at the global box office, hard on the heels of Nolan’s previous film, Oppenheimer, which made $975m.That movie, a biopic of the man behind the atomic bomb, swept the 2023 Oscars, winning seven awards. His follow-up is widely predicted to follow suit next March.The Guardian has contacted Wilson for comment.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyChristopher NolanJoyce Carol OatesClassicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCSSO/Wigglesworth / Booth review – Brett Dean’s song cycle is rich and strange  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Soprano Clare Booth, Ryan Wigglesworth and the BBC Scottish gave the world premiere of Dean’s theatrical and engaging The World’s Wife. Elgar’s 1st didn’t quite achieve lift-off but Weir’s Moon and Star had sweep and shimmer
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Soprano Clare Booth, Ryan Wigglesworth and the BBC Scottish gave the world premiere of Dean’s theatrical and engaging The World’s Wife. Elgar’s 1st didn’t quite achieve lift-off but Weir’s Moon and Star had sweep and shimmer
Content: Filmic sweep and shimmer … the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth perform Judith Weir’s Moon and Star.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenFilmic sweep and shimmer … the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth perform Judith Weir’s Moon and Star.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBBCSSO/Wigglesworth / Booth review – Brett Dean’s song cycle is rich and strangeRoyal Albert HallSoprano Clare Booth, Ryan Wigglesworth and the BBC Scottish gave the world premiere of Dean’s theatrical and engaging The World’s Wife. Elgar’s 1st didn’t quite achieve lift-off but Weir’s Moon and Star had sweep and shimmerAlexandra CoghlanThu 30 Jul 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can talk symphonic architecture, pacing and balance all day long, but when Elgar is right you just feel it. A good First Symphony lands somewhere between heart and head, each tugging you back and forth between admiration and emotion at a piece Hans Richter famously called “the greatest symphony of modern times”. In their first Prom of the season Ryan Wigglesworth and theBBC Scottish Symphony Orchestragave us a handsome account, playing up to the generous proportions of the hall, but we never quite saw “it”.Wigglesworth is a conductor who thinks in chapters, you can hear the long lines of his structures from the hyper-hushed opening Andante – whose payoff will appear nearly an hour later in the finale, when we arrive where we started and know it for the first time. But we could also hear an orchestra thinking in paragraphs. Transitions were often choppy in the first two movements, episodes in the final Allegro lacked a sense of context, balance wasn’t always perfectly voiced in the Adagio. Nothing fatal, but enough to keep us thinking rather than feeling.There was plenty of sensation in the first half, in the filmic sweep and shimmer of Judith Weir’s 1995 Moon and Star – Emily Dickinson’s poem gleaming under layers of orchestral texture, less a traditional setting than a prismatic explosion of imagery, the verse the crystal at its centre – and the theatricality of Brett Dean’s new orchestral song-cycle The World’s Wife.View image in fullscreenTheatricality: Claire Booth performs Brett Dean’s song-cycle The World’s Wife.Photograph: Mark AllanCarol Ann Duffy’s wry, confessional, irreverent verse supplies five poems for a work that looks over the shoulders of famous men – Icarus, Darwin, Perseus – at the women standing behind them in the shadows. Soprano Claire Booth is a stage animal, seizing Duffy’s text and bending it variously into love-song, satire, prayer and meditation. She’s helped by Dean, who pitches his monodrama somewhere between Pierrot Lunaire and Façade – stylised and a little arch, but so richly and strangely textured that it creates new spaces in Duffy’s tight, epigrammatic poetry, filling them with ambiguity and interest.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026PromsBBC Scottish Symphony OrchestraFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content
