title: Artists find creative haven in Côte d’Ivoire’s ‘calm and soothing’ Grand Bassam | Côte d’Ivoire | The Guardian
description: Creatives priced out of Abidjan have breathed new life into a city that was hit by a jihadist attack in 2016
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Creatives priced out of Abidjan have breathed new life into a city that was hit by a jihadist attack in 2016
Content: Artist Nuits Balnéaires in the courtyard of his studio in Grand Bassam.View image in fullscreenArtist Nuits Balnéaires in the courtyard of his studio in Grand Bassam.Côte d’IvoireArtists find creative haven in Côte d’Ivoire’s ‘calm and soothing’ Grand BassamCreatives priced out of Abidjan have breathed new life into a city that was hit by a jihadist attack in 2016Eromo Egbejulein Grand Bassam; photographs by Aïcha FallThu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the poolside of La Fourchette de Rōze hotel in Grand Bassam, aCôte d’Ivoirecity sandwiched between the Ébrié lagoon and the Atlantic Ocean, a birthday party was in progress. On the second-floor gallery, the artist Nuits Balnéaires stood by a huge painting in one corner and looked out through the window towards the billowing waves of the Atlantic Ocean.“It’s poetic … that immense energy of the ocean, which also fuels my work,” the Ivorian visual artist said. “The natural elements are the very essence and foundation of my artistic practice,” he added, as he reflected on the way in which his name, which translates as “coastal nights”, matched the ambience.Many families in Abidjan, the commercial capital of the west African country, have often drifted to Grand Bassam, just 30 miles (45km) to the east, for Sunday relaxation, including Nuits Balnéaires, whose visits from childhood gave him a strong connection to the city. In July 2019 he moved there permanently from his family home in Abidjan.View image in fullscreenNuits Balnéaires shows a print from his latest project, Eboro, winner of the Latitudes programme of the Hermès Corporate Foundation.In the last decade, it has become a road well travelled. As rents continue to rise amid a cost of living crisis in Abidjan, residents there, especially artists, have been reconsidering their lives in the city.“It [is] increasingly difficult for many artists to maintain studio spaces in the city,” said the Abidjan-based art collector Ozong Agborsangaya-Fiteu. “As a result, they are seeking more affordable alternatives in places such as Grand Bassam, Bingerville, and increasingly even farther afield in Dabou and Jacqueville. Grand Bassam itself is becoming more expensive, prompting some artists to relocate even farther out.”The biggest beneficiary of the exodus from Abidjan has undisputedly been Grand Bassam, the country’s first capital where the colonial architecture was listed as a Unesco world heritage site in 2012. With its scenic beachfronts, fresher food, cheaper markets, proximity to the airport and a sense of nostalgia even in the abandoned colonial buildings, the city represents an easier pick than Abidjan, its livelier and more chaotic cousin.View image in fullscreenThe shores of the Ouladine lagoon in Grand Bassam.Photograph: Aicha Fall/The GuardianThis, for the Guadeloupe-born artist Elladj Lincy Deloumeaux, makes it “a very calm and soothing place that’s conducive to working and finding inspiration”. Five years ago, he moved from Paris to Abidjan, and then two years ago to Grand Bassam, where he now has a studio and apartment.Once a centre of cultural trade and tourism, Grand Bassam lost some of its appeal over the years as Abidjan became more cosmopolitan and opportunities in arts and entertainment increased. A jihadist attack in 2016 that left 19 people dead also punctured the town’s reputation.View image in fullscreenGanamet House is an architectural jewel of Grand Bassam. Built around 1900, today it serves as a restaurant and a place for events such as underground parties or exhibitions.Photograph: Aicha Fall/The GuardianThese days, evidence of its renaissance abounds.Last year, the former colonial customs and post office building was reopened after a restoration project as La Maison de l’Art, a contemporary art museum with a sculpture garden and a cafe in the courtyard. At the launch, the culture minister, Françoise Remarck, said the collaboration between the private and public sector to protect local history and shine a spotlight on the country’s modern art was a “fresh breath of life” to the old city.“Today, we are doing much more than opening the doors of a space dedicated to art,” she said. “We are taking an act of recognition and appreciation of African artistic genius.”Other organisations in the vicinity are following the same route. La Fourchette de Rōze, a boutique hotel, has become a creative hub: in January 2023, it began an artist-in-residence programme that has brought in more than two dozen artists and musicians so far from all over the globe, including Nuits Balnéaires. La Cocoteraie des Arts, a creative space with an open-air art atelier and gallery in Mondoukou, only a few minutes outside the city, also offers artist residences.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGuests at the Fourchette de Roze hotel, which has become a creative hub.Photograph: Aicha Fall/The GuardianAcross Grand Bassam, dozens of new studios are popping up across the city. Later this year, the Ivorian-French photographer Aïcha Fall will add another to that number.“I grew up in the French countryside and I’ve always loved a place that is calm,” said Fall, who moved to Grand Bassam on her return from Paris in 2023, despite an attachment to Abidjan where she had spent her early years. “Bassam represents all of that. It offers you time for reverie, unlike Abidjan, which is always effervescent.”Some enthusiastic followers of the art scene are predicting that the city could eventually upstage Abidjan as an art haven in the coming years, or at least rival it.Not everyone within the industry is as optimistic. Most of Côte d’Ivoire’s galleries and art institutions remain in Abidjan, as do many of the collectors, patrons and other important elements of the ecosystem.Festivals such as Abidjan art week, for example, still bring people in from across the continent and are yet to be replicated elsewhere in the country.View image in fullscreenSculptures by Jems Koko Bi, photography by Armand Gauze and a painting by Ablade Glover exhibited at La Maison de l’Art.Photograph: Aicha Fall/The Guardian“Rather than weakening the scene, this geographical shift has created a different dynamic,” Agborsangaya-Fiteu said. “Artists benefit from more affordable and inspiring places to work while remaining close enough to the city to participate in exhibitions, openings, and other cultural activities whenever needed.”As he sipped his coffee, legs crossed, Nuits Balnéaires agreed, before pointing out that the situation was a bit like having his cake and eating it. “One of the advantages is that in Bassam, you can feel very disconnected, yet at the same time, you’re not that far removed from what’s happening in Abidjan.”Explore more on these topicsCôte d’IvoireArtAfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best cordless vacuum cleaners in the UK for a spotless home – tested | Homes | The Guardian
description: Stick vacuums are a convenient alternative to corded designs, but which model wins for overall cleaning prowess? Our expert reveals all
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: Stick vacuums are a convenient alternative to corded designs, but which model wins for overall cleaning prowess? Our expert reveals all
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterHomesReviewThe best cordless vacuum cleaners in the UK for a spotless home – testedStick vacuums are a convenient alternative to corded designs, but which model wins for overall cleaning prowess? Our expert reveals allThe best robot vacuumsHow to make your vacuum last longerAndy ShawThu 30 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Choosing a cordless vacuum isn’t a decision that should be taken lightly. You’re likely to keep a vacuum cleaner for years, relying heavily on its ability to suck up dust, crumbs, mud, pet hair and any other dry spillages or sheddings that end up on your floor. Choosing the right model can be the difference between an effective cleaner that’s a delight to pull out of the cupboard and a dud that you dread having to unblock, detangle and clean after every use.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.In this review, I took 16 of the leading cordless vacuum cleaners from a range of manufacturers and at various prices and inflicted the same cleaning tests on each one. That takes all the guesswork out of picking your next cleaner: I can tell you exactly which ones picked up the most mess.Current discountsOur favourite cordless vacuum for deep cleaning, the Dyson V15 Detect Absolute, is currently available with the Detail cleaning kit for £89 less than the vacuum on its own.£559 at DysonAt a glanceBest cordless vacuum cleaner overall:Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251£388 at AmazonBest budget cordless vacuum cleaner:Vax HomePro Pet-Design£202.12 at AmazonBestcordless vacuum for deep cleaning:Dyson V15 Detect Absolute£649 at John LewisBest cordless vacuum for clean emptying:Henry Quick Pro£399.99 at ArgosBest handheld cordless vacuum cleaner:Dyson Car+Boat£199 at John LewisWhy you should trust meI’ve been reviewing technology and home products for more than 30 years. In the past few years, I’ve specialised in testing vacuum cleaners. During that time, I’ve tested more vacuum cleaners of various shapes, sizes and types than I’d care to count, from handheld helpers to heavy-duty dirt-shifters.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach vacuum was put to the test against flour, cat litter pellets and pet hair.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianMost cordless vacuum cleaners are designed to work on carpet and hard floors, so I tested them all on both. To do this, I weighed out spillages of flour, recycled wood cat litter pellets and pet hair. Flour and cat litter are easy enough to come by, but my dog doesn’t shed enough hair to test this many vacuums. So I’m also the proud owner of a box of sweepings from a friendly (but slightly bemused) local dog groomer.I gave each of the 16 vacuum cleaners I tested a chance to pick up as much of the spillages as possible, with a single push-forward and pull-backward motion, and weighed the collection bins before and after.Most vacuums will collect more if given more chances to go over a mess, particularly from a different angle, but I wanted relatively tough tests that would truly differentiate one vacuum from another, so I allowed only a single sweep.I also tested the batteries by seeing how long it took them to run down from a full charge – at full suction and in each one’s most economical setting. I performed these tests with the floor head attached, where possible.Lastly, I tested the suction using a pressure gauge. While strong suction is useful, the cleaning tests were more important because other factors play a big part in the overall cleaning prowess. For example, a well-designed floor head can make a moderate sucker as good a cleaner as a more powerful model with an inferior brush or roller.All the vacuums I tested have been sent back to their manufacturers or donated to the British Heart Foundation.The best cordless vacuum cleaners in 2026View image in fullscreenThe lineup of test subjects.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianBest cordless vacuum cleaner overall:Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251SharkPowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKTfrom£388£399.99 at Shark£388 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent cleaner; empties into docking stationWhat we don’t loveExpensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£399.99 at Shark£388 at AmazonIf there’s one thing that makes cordless vacuum cleaners a pain, it’s the emptying: taking it to the bin and jettisoning the debris after vacuuming. And, if your family is anything like mine, you may have to do it before you clean too, because someone else didn’t bother to empty it. That won’t be the case with this Shark vacuum, though: it empties itself. It’s also very good at cleaning.Why we love itThe Shark IP3251 comes with a base station that operates as a stand and charging dock. When you rest the cordless vacuum cleaner on it, it springs into life, opening the base of the vacuum’s collection bin and sucking its contents into a larger container, leaving the cordless stick empty and ready for next time. The secondary bin has a volume of two litres, so it can take a few empties of the 0.7-litre stick.That would all be pointless if the device itself wasn’t up to snuff, but it’s an excellent cleaner. Its floor head has a fluffy roller for hard floors and a brush bar for carpet, and it works well on both surfaces, performing a literal clean sweep in my tests.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty got to work on the flour, pet hair and cat litter.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …I found it worked better if I held it lower while vacuuming on some carpets, with the fins on the base otherwise catching when I pulled it back. That may make it better for shorter than taller people.Weight:3.71kgMax suction power (measured):28kPaBattery life (measured):43minsDust capacity:0.7lAdditional filters supplied?NoSharkPowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKTfrom£388£399.99 at Shark£388 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent cleaner; empties into docking stationWhat we don’t loveExpensiveBest budget cordless vacuum cleaner:Vax HomePro Pet-DesignVaxHomePro Pet-Designfrom£202.12£319 at Argos£202.12 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, effective and easy to useWhat we don’t loveBest on carpet with no soft roller for hard floorsView image in fullscreen£319 at Argos£202.12 at AmazonThe Vax HomePro Pet-Design is good value for money, sitting at the lower end of the price spectrum but still coming with a good selection of tools for handheld use. It also performed well in all the tests.Why we love itIt’s comfortable to hold and use, and simple to operate, with just two large buttons – one to switch it on and the other to boost the power. Battery life is displayed by a light-up ring and lasted a decent 34 minutes in our rundown test.Emptying it is straightforward, too, with a button to open the collection bin, while a pump action lifts dirt off the filter, so you don’t have to poke your hands in. It’s one of the few cordless stick vacuums that can support itself when standing up, so there’s no need to find somewhere to lie it down between cleaning jobs.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Vax HomePro Pet-Design took to the floor to suck up the flour, cat litter and pet hair.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …the floor head is a basic single-brush bar, which is unsophisticated when compared with the alternatives you get on Shark and Dyson models. Still, for the price, it’s ultimately forgivable.Weight:3.5kgMax suction power (measured):19kPaBattery life (measured):34minsDust capacity:0.7lAdditional filters supplied?NoVaxHomePro Pet-Designfrom£202.12£319 at Argos£202.12 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, effective and easy to useWhat we don’t loveBest on carpet with no soft roller for hard floorsBest cordless vacuum for deep cleaning:Dyson V15 Detect AbsoluteDysonV15 Detect Absolutefrom£559.99£559.99 at Dyson£649 at John LewisWhat we loveSuperb cleaning on carpet and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and messy to emptyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£559.99 at Dyson£649 at John LewisAlthough the V15 Detect Absolute was usurped at the top of Dyson’s range by the new V16 Piston Animal, it remains widely available. That’s good news, because this older model did a much better job of cleaning up in my tests than the V16.Why we love itThe V15 Detect Absolute is as close to vacuuming perfection as we’ve seen to date. It comes with two interchangeable floor heads: one with a brush bar for carpet, the other with a fluffy roller for hard floor. They blitzed my tests, with the anti-tangle brush bar leaving only tiny fragments of cat litter and a light trace of flour on carpet after a first pass, both of which were easy to deal with on a return visit. On hard floor, the fluffy roller is king, picking up every last morsel of mess that I dropped. Its dust-detecting green glow is a genuine help, highlighting just how effective it is at collecting even tiny particles.View image in fullscreenThe Dyson V15 Detect Absolute performed fantastically in our tests.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianRemove the extension wand, and the Dyson converts into a useful handheld. The included crevice tool is good at getting into tight corners, while the combination upholstery and dusting tool copes with most other problems. Sadly, it doesn’t come with the hair screw tool, which is really effective at removing pet hair from upholstery and also handy on stairs. It’s well worth seeking outas an optional extraif you let your pets on your furniture (and suffer the consequences).It’s a shame that …Dyson hasn’t managed to solve the conundrum of messy emptying, with this model creating quite a dust cloud when you release dirt into the bin. It’s also really expensive.Weight:2.96kgMax suction power (measured):31kPaBattery life (measured):50minsDust capacity:0.77lAdditional filters supplied?NoDysonV15 Detect Absolutefrom£559.99£559.99 at Dyson£649 at John LewisWhat we loveSuperb cleaning on carpet and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and messy to emptyBest cordless vacuum for clean emptying:Henry Quick ProHenryQuick Profrom£399.99£399.99 at Argos£399.99 at JD WilliamsWhat we loveDirt collects in bags, eliminating emptying messWhat we don’t loveDisposable bags cost money and are part plasticView image in fullscreen£399.99 at Argos£399.99 at JD WilliamsMost cordless sticks create a dust cloud when you deposit the contents of their collection bins into your dustbin. The Henry Quick Pro is the only cordless vacuum we’ve reviewed here that doesn’t do that because of its disposable dirt-capturing bags.Why we love itWe can’t emphasise this enough – it’s frustrating to vacuum the floor only to have the dust billowing out of your bin and back into the air when you empty it. With the Henry Quick Pro, you push a lever on the top, and the base opens, jettisoning the bag of collected rubbish out of the bottom. It leaves no mess and has the added benefit of no filters to clean.In my tests, the Quick Pro performed decently enough, other than on hard floors with the cat litter, which it pushed ahead instead of sucking up. That job would be better tackled by removing the extension wand and using the device with a handheld attachment. It comes with a comprehensive selection of accessories, including a motorised mini head for stairs and upholstery, a flexible hose and a useful handle extension for taller users.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Henry Quick Pro tackled the flour and pet hair but left some of the cat litter behind.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …the bags have a plastic top that holds them in place inside the collection bin. Henry manufacturer Numatic claims to offset the carbon cost, but it would be better environmentally if it didn’t use any plastic at all. They also cost £1.30 per one-litre bag.Weight:3.2kgMax suction power (measured):10.75kPaBattery life (measured):1hr 11minsDust capacity:1lAdditionalbags supplied?Yes, six pods (bags)HenryQuick Profrom£399.99£399.99 at Argos£399.99 at JD WilliamsWhat we loveDirt collects in bags, eliminating emptying messWhat we don’t loveDisposable bags cost money and are part plasticBest handheld cordless vacuum cleaner:Dyson Car+BoatDysonCar+Boatfrom£199£199 at John Lewis£199 at AOWhat we loveAs powerful as a regular DysonWhat we don’t loveA fully-equipped Dyson V8 doesn’t cost much moreView image in fullscreen£199 at John Lewis£199 at AODyson doesn’t manufacture a vacuum purely for handheld use, instead opting to repackage an existing cordless stick without the extension wand. The result is a handheld device so powerful that you may wish you could also use it on the floor.Why we love itThe Dyson Car+Boat is a cunning repackage of theDyson V8. That model is now the bottom of the range of Dyson’s regular cordless stick cleaners, but it makes for a handheld unit that performs above and beyond expectations.It comes with three key attachments: a mini motorised tool for upholstery and stairs; a crevice tool for gaps; and a combination dusting brush and funnel. It’s a powerful combo that cleaned up my test messes with aplomb. I had to use the funnel rather than the motorised tool to collect cat litter, though, because there’s no way this smaller device wouldn’t just push them ahead.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Dyson Car+Boat devoured the detritus on the mat.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …you can stillbuy the V8, with the extension tube and attachments, for a similar price. It also comes with Dyson’s old mini-motorised tool. Newer models come with a better-designed tool, which has a tapering roller that doesn’t trap longer hairs. It would have been a nice addition to this repackage.Weight:1.9kgMax suction power (tested):21kPaBattery life (tested):38minsDust capacity:0.54lAdditional filters supplied?NoDysonCar+Boatfrom£199£199 at John Lewis£199 at AOWhat we loveAs powerful as a regular DysonWhat we don’t loveA fully-equipped Dyson V8 doesn’t cost much moreThe best of the restView image in fullscreenThe Shark IA3241UKT is smaller and cheaper than the Shark IP3251UKT but performed slightly better on carpet and almost as well on hard floors.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianShark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro IA3241SharkPowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro IA3241from£299.99£299.99 at Shark£299.99 at CurrysWhat we loveEffective at cleaning on carpets and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveUnclear messaging when battery was running outView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£299.99 at Shark£299.99 at CurrysBest for:smaller homesThe second self-emptying Shark in this list, the IA3241, is a smaller and cheaper version of my favourite, the IP3251, reviewed above. It performed slightly better on carpet and almost as well on hard floors, despite the fact that this model’s floor head doesn’t have the distinctive dual roller that’s typical of Shark’s best cleaners. It’s lighter and easier to push around than the IP3251, though the collection bin has a smaller capacity of 0.47l.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty got to work on the flour, pet hair and cat litter.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIn my battery tests, it appeared to last a good length of time, almost making it to the 50-minute mark. This uses a similar self-emptying base that sucks the dirt out of the collection bin and doubles up as a charging station.View image in fullscreenThe Tower VL220 Cyclone’s performance in the tests.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe vacuum cleaner is less sophisticated than Shark’s, with fewer features. It still performed reasonably well in my tests, but it only comes with a fluffy roller. That makes it ideal for homes with mostly hard floors, but it lacks the ability to dig deep into carpet.It didn’t make the final cut because …it left too much flour and pet hair behind in my carpet cleaning tests.Weight:2.6kg;suction power (tested):26.5kPa;battery life (tested):43mins;dust capacity:2l (self-emptying base);additional filters supplied?Yes, one spareTowerVL220 Cyclonefrom£113.32£249.99 at Tower£113.32 at AmazonWhat we loveMore affordable self-emptying model than the SharkWhat we don’t loveFluffy roller isn’t great on carpetDyson V16 Piston AnimalDysonV16 Piston Animalfrom£629.99£629.99 at John Lewis£639.99 at DysonWhat we loveOne head for carpets and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveNew floor head not as good as the old systemView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£629.99 at John Lewis£639.99 at DysonBest for:a Dyson that doesn’t require you to switch floor headsThe V16 Piston Animal is a significant change for Dyson, using a single floor head for both carpet and hard floor. Previously, Dyson’s top-end cordless vacuums came with two interchangeable floor heads, which needed switching over as you changed surfaces.The new floor head has several design tweaks, but basically uses a brush bar with both bristles and fluffy strips so that it works with either surface. By detecting what it’s cleaning, the vacuum adjusts its spin speed and suction to get the best performance.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Dyson V16 Piston Animal attempted to clean the mat.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianEliminating the requirement to switch makes using this Dyson less of a faff. The downside is that, in my tests, the new floor head wasn’t as effective on either carpets or hard floors as the V15 Detect Absolute above.It didn’t make the final cut because …I’m used to Dyson’s vacuums producing near-perfect results in my tests, but the redesigned floor head in the V16 fails to deliver, making the V15 a better option.Weight:3.4kg;suction power (tested):not tested;battery life (tested):1hr 11mins;dust capacity:1.3l;additional filters supplied?NoFor more, read our fullDyson V16 Piston Animal reviewDysonV16 Piston Animalfrom£629.99£629.99 at John Lewis£639.99 at DysonWhat we loveOne head for carpets and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveNew floor head not as good as the old systemGtech AirFox PlatinumGtechAirFox Platinumfrom£196.77£289.99 at Lakeland£196.77 at AmazonWhat we loveStands without support, picks up small particlesWhat we don’t loveStruggled with cat litter; uncomfortable long-termView image in fullscreen£289.99 at Lakeland£196.77 at AmazonBest for:light weight and light useA constant source of annoyance with cordless vacuum cleaners is that you have to find somewhere to lean them when you want to put them down. The AirFox is light and well-balanced enough to stand on its own, so you can leave it in the middle of the room while you do some dusting, and it won’t fall to the floor.The trigger needs to be held down to keep the vacuum running, and while there is a trigger lock to keep it in place, it’s fiddly to use. It cleaned well in my tests, though, only really struggling with the cat litter, which seemed to get stuck in the floor head.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Gtech AirFox Platinum took to the mat.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt didn’t make the final cut because …I found it uncomfortable to hold for extended periods because the back extends out over the handle, getting in the way of my wrist.Weight:2.9kg;max suction power (tested):31kPa;battery life (tested):1hr 9mins;dust capacity:0.4l;additional filters supplied?NoGtechAirFox Platinumfrom£196.77£289.99 at Lakeland£196.77 at AmazonWhat we loveStands without support, picks up small particlesWhat we don’t loveStruggled with cat litter; uncomfortable long-termMiele Duoflex HX1 Total CareMieleDuoflex HX1 Total Carefrom£499£499 at Miele£499 at John LewisWhat we loveGood performance on carpetWhat we don’t loveShort battery life, basic featuresView image in fullscreen£499 at Miele£499 at John LewisBest for:simple operationDespite being a high-end brand in most categories of domestic appliances, the Miele Duoflex HX1 sits in the middle of this gathering in terms of price. That’s largely thanks to the lack of additional features you get when compared with the likes of Shark and Dyson. It performed well in my cleaning tests but generally proved better on carpets than on hard floors.It operates in either floor or handheld mode. The floor head is basic, with a simple brush bar and no anti-tangle features. It comes with three handheld attachments – a crevice tool, a basic upholstery nozzle and a dusting brush.View image in fullscreenHow it started v how it’s going with the Miele Duoflex HX1 Total Care.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt didn’t make the final cut because …emptying relies on gravity alone, so you end up having to poke your fingers into the collection bin to clear it out. Most disappointing was the battery, which didn’t last long with the floor head attached, even on the weakest suction setting.Weight:3.1kg;max suction power (tested):12.5kPa;battery life (tested):13mins;dust capacity:0.3l;additional filters supplied?NoMieleDuoflex HX1 Total Carefrom£499£499 at Miele£499 at John LewisWhat we loveGood performance on carpetWhat we don’t loveShort battery life, basic featuresBosch Unlimited 10 BCS1051GBBoschUnlimited 10 BCS1051GBfrom£499£499 at Currys£499.99 at ArgosWhat we loveSolid build quality, good cleaning performanceWhat we don’t loveUnnecessary features drive up the priceView image in fullscreen£499 at Currys£499.99 at ArgosBest for:super-long battery lifeWith the Unlimited 10, Bosch has gone all in on the bling. It has a very flashy screen, which informs you visually when you’re changing floor surfaces, and lights up in a different colour depending on what power setting you’ve got the suction on. It’s useful, but possibly not useful enough to justify its higher-than-average cost.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) with the hair, litter and flour and how the Bosch Unlimited 10 vacuumed them up on the right.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe overall build quality is excellent, though. I loved the spring-loaded filter-clearing lever on the back, which means you can empty the collection bin in a smooth single-push motion rather than the banging and poking you have to do with most other vacuums. This lever can also compact the rubbish as you clean to reduce how often it needs emptying. The Unlimited 10 also had the best battery, which made the unit heavy but lasted an astonishing hour and a half on its Eco setting.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a bit expensive without there being enough of a cleaning benefit to justify it.Weight:3.8kg;max suction power (tested):13kPa;battery life (tested):1hr 34mins;dust capacity:0.4l;additional filters supplied?NoBoschUnlimited 10 BCS1051GBfrom£499£499 at Currys£499.99 at ArgosWhat we loveSolid build quality, good cleaning performanceWhat we don’t loveUnnecessary features drive up the priceBeldray Airgility Pet Plus+BeldrayAirgility Pet Plus+from£77.99£89.99 at Currys£77.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExtremely affordable and a fair performerWhat we don’t loveProne to getting blocked by larger particlesView image in fullscreen£89.99 at Currys£77.99 at AmazonBest for:lowest priceIf most of the other reviews left you thinking that you were going to have to take out a second mortgage to get a new cordless vacuum cleaner, the sub-£100 price tag of the Beldray Airgility Pet Plus+ should be a breath of fresh air. It’s light and petite but has small attachments, too, which aren’t large enough to pick up larger particles. It doesn’t collect dirt as well as the best vacuum cleaners here, but for a fraction of the price, it does a reasonable job.The biggest problem was cat litter, which was sucked up OK from the floor but caused a blockage after only a tiny amount had entered the collection bin. It was surprisingly proficient at removing flour from hard floors but failed to agitate my test carpet enough to replicate that success. It also left a bit of pet hair behind during testing, either on the floor or stuck to the rollers.View image in fullscreenBefore the Beldray Airgility Pet Plus+ got to work (left) and how well it picked up the mess (right).Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt didn’t make the final cut because …it didn’t perform as well as more expensive rivals, though it does still impress for the price.Weight:2.2kg;max suction power (tested):9.25kPa;battery life (tested):41mins;dust capacity:1.2l;additional filters supplied?Yes, oneBeldrayAirgility Pet Plus+from£77.99£89.99 at Currys£77.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExtremely affordable and a fair performerWhat we don’t loveProne to getting blocked by larger particlesWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenThe Dyson Car+Boat makes short work of mess.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhy choose a cordless vacuum cleanerCordless vacuum cleaners are vastly more convenient than corded models. There’s no cable to unwind and no need to find a power socket – you just take the vacuum to the mess and get started.The downside is that they run on battery power. The batteries can last anywhere between an hour or so on light settings and down to a few minutes on full blast. They should last long enough to get around an average-size housein one go, but larger spaces might need a mid-clean charge, which can take a few hours (or an expensive extra battery).What should you look for in a cordless vacuum cleaner?Suction powerGenerally speaking, a vacuum cleaner with powerful suction will be better at cleaning than a model with weak suction. However, other factors also come into play. A well-designed floor head, for example, can help a less powerful vacuum outperform a more powerful rival.I tested the suction on the models reviewed here using a vacuum gauge, which measures suction pressure in kPa (kilopascals). A suction of 25kPa or above is good. Anything less than 10kPa isn’t ideal for picking up larger debris, though it may still be good at vacuuming dust, particularly if it’s paired with a decent floor head.WeightCordless vacuum cleaners are perfect for transporting around the house, as you don’t need to worry about plugging them into a wall socket and managing a cable. It makes weight a key consideration, though, as you want a unit that’s light enough to carry around.The weights I’ve quoted are the actual weights of the vacuum cleaner in their standard configurations, including extension wand and carpet floor head.Vacuums that weigh less than 3kg are relatively light, while those approaching the 4kg mark are likely to feel quite heavy. A weighty vacuum will be less problematic in use, though, because a good portion of the weight is usually found in the floor head, which will be resting on the floor during cleaning.Vacuums will be lighter in their handheld modes without the extension wand and floor head attached, but a model that’s heavier overall is likely to be weightier in this configuration, too.Battery lifeHow long your cordless vacuum’s battery will last is important, particularly if you’re expecting to clean an entire house between charges. I test batteries by keeping the device running on a section of carpet, from a full charge until they cut out. Generally, this tends to be shorter than the battery life quoted by manufacturers, though the difference can vary from model to model.A runtime of less than 20 minutes or so may not get you all the way around a whole house clean. Longer life is a bonus, particularly if you live in a large house. If the battery life on your chosen model isn’t that long, you may still be able to buy a secondary battery that you can swap to extend cleaning sessions. You can only do this if your model has a replaceable battery, so check before you buy if you’re likely to want that feature.Bagged vsbaglessMost cordless vacuum cleaners are bagless, which means they collect all the dust and dirt directly into their collection bins, and you empty them by releasing or tipping the dirt into the bin. A few models use bags, however, which provides a cleaner emptying process, as all the dust and dirt is contained in a sack that you dispose of when you empty. If you suffer from allergies, this cleaner emptying process could make life more pleasant.Vacuum bags can vary in price, though popular models often have third-party bags available, as well as those supplied by the manufacturer. They tend to be single use only, and you dispose of the entire bag and its contents when you empty.Of more concern is what the bags are made of. While some can feel papery, most are made from synthetic plastic fibres, which often use recycled plastic but may still take a long time to break down in landfill. Bagless vacuum cleaners are significantly kinder to the environment.Carpet vs hard floorAlmost all cordless vacuum cleaners will have a good go at your carpeted areas, but most work on hard floors, too. Basic models will use the same brush bar floor head, but may spin it slower when cleaning hard floors for a gentler approach.Some models come with a soft, fluffy roller, either built into the main floor head or in a separate unit that can be swapped as required. These are even better at picking up dirt from smooth surfaces than a standard roller brush.If you don’t have much hard flooring, you probably don’t need a soft roller, as carpet vacuums work here too, or you may just prefer to do a quick sweep with a dustpan and brush.AttachmentsCordless vacuums can be broken down into a handheld device if you remove the extension wand and add an attachment. Check that the model you want comes with the attachments you need.Almost all vacuums come with a crevice tool – a narrow funnel that’s useful for getting into small spaces and nipping around skirting boards. Also useful are dusting brushes and upholstery tools with wider nozzles. Look out for motorised upholstery/pet hair tools. These look like miniature versions of a regular floor head, complete with a mini brush bar. They’re ideal for vacuuming smaller areas, such as stairs and furniture.Do cordless vacuums have good filtration systems?Yes, cordless vacuums quote high levels of filtration, with some claiming to trap even the tiniest of particles, such as pollen. However, emptying cordless vacuums that don’t use bags can create a messy dust cloud, so these may not be the models for you if you’re allergic to dirt particles. Filters also need regular cleaning, which is something you won’t be used to if you’re moving away from a vacuuming system that uses disposable bags.How to clean your cordless vacuum cleanerMaintaining your vacuum cleaner doesn’t stop at emptying the collection bin. There are a few other areas that deserve your attention if you want top performance and a long life from your vacuum.The first is keeping the filter clean. This doesn’t need doing after every use, but it’s worth keeping an eye on how dirty it’s getting and cleaning it before it gets too clogged up. Dyson recommends doing this once a month. With Dyson vacuums, you remove the filter by twisting it and lifting it out of the body of the cleaner, then rinsing it in cold water to remove the dirt. Let it air dry for at least 24 hours and check it’s completely dry before refitting.The filters on most other brands can be cleaned in a similar way, but some don’t like getting wet, so check your vacuum’s instruction manual if you’re not sure.The other problem area is the brush bar. Anti-tangle floor heads have improved things in recent years, but even these can be clogged up with hair, fluff and dirt over time. The brush bar can usually be removed from the floor head, and you can attack entangled hair with a pair of scissors. If the bristles are loaded with fluff, you can tease it out with your fingers or use an old comb.For a really deep clean, you can dismantle most vacuum cleaners and wash any non-electrical parts with a damp cloth. Make sure it’s all properly dry before putting it back together.What to do with your old vacuum cleanerWhile you might have decided to move on from your old vacuum cleaner, a working model could still hold value for others. It’s worth seeing if you can sell it locally or donate it to someone who can still get some use out of it.Alternatively, when you buy your new vacuum, ask the retailer about its WEEE (waste electrical and electronic equipment) recycling scheme. The UK’sWEEE Regulationsstate that companies selling such items must accept the device you’re replacing and responsibly recycle it.Lastly, you can always recycle it yourself. Your local recycling centre should have a section for electricals, and you can find your nearest atRecycle Your Electricals. Alternatively, check your local council’s website to find out about its recycling services and opening hours.For more cleaning inspiration from the Filter:How to make your vacuum last longerThe best robot vacuums, testedThe best steam cleaners and mopsDyson PencilVac Fluffycones vacuum reviewAndy Shaw is aconsumer journalist and technology addict. Having reviewed tech products professionally for more than 30 years, his favoured working environment is a small desk surrounded by big boxes. His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their packaging, so they rarely fit back in again when it’s time to return them.This article was originally published on 28 March 2025. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. Content: 14:08Feed with Jimi FamurewaFoodFlavour fusion in London's buzziest bakeries  – videoRestaurant critic and award-winning author Jimi Famurewa visits the best London bakeries where family food traditions  meet contemporary British baking. title: Cooking on holiday – without taking half your kitchen with you | Food | The Guardian
description: Making a meal anywhere but home can feel unnerving, but all you need is some forward planning and an essentials list
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Making a meal anywhere but home can feel unnerving, but all you need is some forward planning and an essentials list
Content: Make it your own … Georgina Hayden's roasted apricot jam and halloumi sandwiches.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMake it your own … Georgina Hayden's roasted apricot jam and halloumi sandwiches.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianFeastFoodCooking on holiday – without taking half your kitchen with youMaking a meal anywhere but home can feel unnerving, but all you need is some forward planning and an essentials listSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastMina HollandThu 30 Jul 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreetings from my parents’ kitchen in north Norfolk where, despite its familiarity, cooking takes on a less predictable dimension. By some measures their kitchen is well equipped – three toast racks, countless skewers, a three-egg poaching pan, many beer tankards, and a very noisy battery-operated pepper mill – but I’ll admit to missing my knives, my lemon juicer, and my salad spinner (my mother insists that one of the latter will never “clutter up” her cupboards, to which my riposte is, “An egg poaching pan?”). And that’s before all the ingredients that don’t make it into the hurried pre-holiday essentials shop, the indispensability of which only dawns on me in their absence – the rice wine vinegar, the maple syrup, the capers, the tahini.All this is to say that cooking anywhere but your own kitchen can feel like a paradigm shift and demands a different approach. This could mean intricate planning or, in my case, it invariably sends me running to my archive of tried-and-tested recipes, will work regardless of what shops are nearby or what equipment is in the kitchen. These have seen me through summers in various kitchens that are not my own, from this very one in Norfolk to a scattering of Airbnbs in Europe. They require little more than a knife, a couple of pans, a wooden spoon and a heat source. A box grater and a whisk are handy, too. And, as your drinks columnist, it would be disingenuous to pretend that a decent corkscrew isn’t utterly vital. (For a sound list of real kitchen essentials, which don’t include three toast racks and a battery-operated pepper mill, I have always loved referring back to Laurie Colwin’s Low-Tech Person’s Batterie de Cuisine in her book of essays,Home Cooking.)View image in fullscreen‘I tend to build holiday meals around carbs.’Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianBut what am I cookingin these hot weeks away from home? Well, there’s always pasta, and there’s alwaysRachel Roddy. Hercourgette carbonarais the silky stuff of dreams, where the summer squashes – I like a mixture of green and yellow – are cut into matchsticks and briefly fried in garlicky oil before being tossed through long pasta with beaten egg, loads of parmesan and black pepper. It is a recipe I have come back to more times than I can remember and is particularly good in summer but can, of course, be made out of season, wherever you are. Other favourites, which also put summer produce to work,include her peperonata– red peppers that have yielded to heat and fat to make a sauce as good on pasta as alongside eggs, pulses or meat – andbursting tomato pasta, one of her many iterations on tomato pasta, but which feels particularly fitting as the clammy days roll on.I tend to build holiday meals around carbs, which is perhaps not very in tune with the protein- and fibre-maxxing movements, but it suits my purposes because first, you can get pasta/rice/potatoes/rolls/ready-made pastry anywhere, and second, everyone in the family (even the noisiest and fussiest members) can get on board somehow. So atortilla de patatasis always a good shout – either hot alongside salads at supper, or for show-stopping sandwiches to have on the beach. I also love Georgina Hayden’s idea for stuffingbaps with fried halloumi and apricot jam– her recipe is for a quick homemade jam, but it also works with shop bought. I love the addition of crunchy salad or even one or two salty crisps.And then there are all the possibilities of rice. Rachel Roddy comes good again with thesestuffed peppers– a little pile of rice alongside soaks up the oily-anchovy-tomato liquor perfectly – and thesebraised green beans with tomatoes and onions, which are great with rice or bread. I recommend crowning the lot with feta.Curries can be thorny territory in a holiday rental – you never know which spices the local corner shop will carry, or what the previous guests may have left behind. I find that a holy trinity of cumin seeds, mustard seeds and turmeric goes a long way and, if I’m feeling organised, will try to take them with me (along with Marmite and breakfast tea if I’m going abroad). All that said, curries and stews are in fact brilliant for holiday cooking because they are so adaptable, much like Alison Roman’s viral“The Stew”, which uses easily found ingredients and can be adapted to as you see fit. Unless you are baking, there is rarely a right or wrong in cooking beyond whether you like it or not. I like to treat this trio of Sri Lanka-inspired Meera Sodha recipes –potato and green bean istoo,squash kiri hodiandcourgette and white bean curry– as merely an aspiration; all use ingredients that are available in supermarkets, but if any are not, you’ll still be handsomely fed by these failsafe rubrics.Speaking of adaptability, I leave you with two dishes that I come back to on holiday, year in and year out. Rosie Birkett’scheeseboard tart, a recipe she originally wrote to use up the remains of Christmas cheese, elevates any cheese. I love to add a handful of chopped jalapeños to cut through the richness. Meanwhile, Thomasina Miers’raspberry, cardamom and almond cakeis eminently versatile; I swapped the rasps for strawbs and the cardamom for black pepper. Both of these recipes call for a springform tin, which I’ll sheepishly add to the essentials list. But at least it’s not an egg poaching pan.My week in foodView image in fullscreenFill up on old recipes … favourite cookbooks.Photograph: Andreas von Einsiedel/AlamyBooksmart|A bonus of staying at my parents is their dog-eared collection of cookbooks. From a beloved pile ofRose Elliot– the OG vegetarian cookery writer, responsible for much of the food I was raised on – toJosceline Dimbleby’s series for Sainsbury’s and curiosities such as Cooking With Love by Leslie Sellers, which features seductive numbers including Kidneys Wendy, Arthur Davidson’s Stringy Meat and Carpetbag Pork Chops. Not a love language I speak.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrankenchickens|I have been gobsmacked by Project Slingshot, a campaign launched this year with the motive of ending factory farming in the UK by 2040. Founded by Veganuary co-founder Matthew Glover, the campaign is using high-impact public transport ads, social media and celebrity endorsement (including Joanna Lumley and Rutger Bregman) to raise awareness of the likes of“Frankenchickens”(hens selectively bred to grow quickly for large breast meat, but which suffer with heart, lung and mobility issues). It’s moving the debate from, “Should people eat meat?” to, “Should animals be raised in industrial conditions?” I’ll be watching closely and hoping consumers respond.Dante’s peak|I was fortunate to visit Dante, the new restaurant at Claridge’s, last week – an import from New York known for its peerless cocktails. They brought us garibaldis while we umm-ed and ahh-ed over the menu, and I am now borderline obsessed with this two-ingredient drink; 45ml Campari and 120ml fresh orange juice join to make something far greater than the sum of its parts. Zingy and bittersweet, the Dante iteration is particularly good, using “fluffy” orange juice made with a high-speed centrifugal juicer, which may now join the ranks of kitchen “essentials”.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Why catarratto is the Quincy Jones of white wine grapes | Wine | The Guardian
description: Once consigned to anonymous table wine, the unsung hero of Sicily’s vineyards is taking its place in the sun
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Once consigned to anonymous table wine, the unsung hero of Sicily’s vineyards is taking its place in the sun
Content: Catarratto grapes grow in a vineyard in the Trapani region of Sicily, Italy.Photograph: Photon-Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCatarratto grapes grow in a vineyard in the Trapani region of Sicily, Italy.Photograph: Photon-Photos/Getty ImagesWineWhy catarratto is the Quincy Jones of white wine grapesIt is often the key secret ingredient in a lot of white wines, but the unsung hero of Sicily’s vineyards is taking its place in the sunMina HollandThu 30 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Depending on where you buy and drink wine, catarratto will be very familiar or very obscure. There was a time in the 2010s when I’d have put good money on it being the house white in half of Hackney’s restaurants, and if you’ve ever picked up a sub-£15 natural white wine at an independent bottle shop, catarratto will probably have featured. If, however, you buy wine from bigger retailers and have a taste for fruity, sun-soaked whites, chances are you’ve been drinking catarratto without even knowing it.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.This is bonkers, given its prevalence. Catarratto is Sicily’s most widely planted white grape, accounting for roughly a third of the island’s vineyards; and, after sangiovese, it’s the second most planted grape in all of Italy. For decades, though, it was either destined for bulk wine, disappearing into tanks of anonymous, juicy table wines, or for use as a component of better-known Sicilian denominations such as fortified marsala or Etna bianco, where it plays a supporting role to other indigenous Sicilian grapes, such as grillo or carricante, respectively. It has about it a bit of a Quincy Jones quality: integral to the success of others before being recognised in its own right. Which it now really is, as modern producers make more complex catarrattos that really express their terroirs, be that volcanic, maritime or the rolling hills around Alcamo in the Sicilian north-west.While catarratto might not be a wine for every occasion, it is one for any occasion: ripe pear and peach, lemon and almond notes do a delicious dance to which few can object. It remains a favourite on wine lists of places that want a fun, affordable and crowdpleasing white, but it’s also being named and championed in supermarket bottles. The Purato organic catarratto/pinot grigio blend from Ocado in today’s pick might, in decades past, have been an “Italian” or “Sicilian” white, but this is a cheery drop that celebrates its component parts. Meanwhile,Vinca’s Organic White Wine(which I wrote about inmy canned wine column a fortnight ago) explicitly mentions “100% catarratto grapes” on its packaging (and is also availablein aluminium bottles from Tesco for just £8.50). And the Biddizza unfiltered amber number from Adnam’s in my pick (in a party-friendly litre bottle, too) shows yet another face of this grape. All offer excellent value, and stay true to catarratto’s roots.It’s the little guys who still get me most excited, though. I say little, but Nino Barraco, a natural winemaker based in the catarratto heartland of Marsala, overlooking the sea, is a titan of Sicilian wine. He makes single-vineyard wines with the indigenous grapes and wild yeasts of western Sicily, and I was recently seduced by his Biancomatte (see my pick), a one-off wine made in 2025, when his new bush catarratto failed to reach full ripeness. It’s light, it’s bright, it’s mineral and it’s wonderful. If you’re a sucker for a limited-edition anything, you won’t regret going in for this one.Four catarrattos to catch the eyeFazoli Gino Biddizza Catarratto£17.99 (1 litre) Adnams, 13%. The ultimate alfresco party wine: a peachy and food-versatile orange catarratto.Biancomatto Barraco 2025£22.50 Sip Wines, 9.5%. This one-off is the result of a bad year for the winemaker’s young bush catarratto – a beautiful oops.Purato Organic Catarratto Pinot Grigio£10.75 Ocado, 11%. It might be a blend, but you get bags of round, fruit-forward catarratto here.Tule Bianco Catarratto 2024£11.10 The Sourcing Table, 12%. An unfiltered, mineral number from the catarratto heartland of Alcamo: a white shirt of a wine that goes with everything.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s chicken with sweet and sour lemon and tarragon sauce – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: If it’s good enough for Prince Ottavio Gonzaga and Anna del Conte, then dare you pass up the opportunity to try this wonderfully sweet and sour way with chicken?
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: If it’s good enough for Prince Ottavio Gonzaga and Anna del Conte, then dare you pass up the opportunity to try this wonderfully sweet and sour way with chicken?
Content: Rachel Roddy's take on Anna del Conte's summer chicken in lemon sauce.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy's take on Anna del Conte's summer chicken in lemon sauce.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s chicken with sweet and sour lemon and tarragon sauce – recipeIf it’s good enough for Prince Ottavio Gonzaga and Anna del Conte, then dare you pass up the opportunity to try this wonderfully sweet and sour way with chicken?Rachel RoddyThu 30 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 01.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile I look at my copies ofJane Grigson’s Fruit Book, Anna del Conte’sAmaretto, Apple Cake and Artichokes, and Francis Bissell’sThe Scented Kitchenat home, they seem different from when they are pulled from the shelves in my parent’s kitchen in Dorset. Also, on the first morning of any stay, looking at these three with a cup of tea before anyone else is up has become a habit that may be superstitious.On the second day, I made a recipe from the inimitable Anna, who also lives in Dorset and is now 100. For her recipe of chicken breasts in a 17th-century sweet and sour sauce, Anna was inspired by Bartolomeo Stefani, chef to Prince Ottavio Gonzaga (one of the numerous members of The House of Gonzaga who ruled Mantua from 1328 to 1708) and author of the 1662 manual, L’arte di Ben Cucinare (The Art of Fine Cooking). Anna notes that Stefani was a chef of great inventiveness, and one of the first to move away from the heavily spiced recipes of the Middle Ages towards a style of cooking with a lighter touch, flavoured with herbs, citrus and flowers. And this recipe is a good example of his approach to ingredients: poached chicken (originally capon) served in thick slices with a sweet-and-sour sauce of wine, sugar, vinegar, olive oil and lemon. Once assembled, the dish is left to sit in order for the chicken slices to soak up the sauce’s flavours, and then served at room temperature. It is a lovely dish for a hot day (or evening).Bartolomeo’s recipe asks for balsamic vinegar, as does Anna’s version, but I have come to enjoy it made with a proportion of or entirely with good red-wine vinegar, also tarragon, whose mossy scent and touch of lemon and aniseed is welcome, also for the colour. When making the sauce, it is important to whisk the olive oil into the other ingredients gradually but vigorously, in much the same way you would a dressing or mayonnaise. By doing so, the oil and water molecules are forced to combine, forming a slightly thickened emulsion. Taste and taste again, then add more salt and vinegar.Just before serving, tilt the plate so you can spoon some of the sauce over the chicken slices, and add a little more tarragon and lemon slices, if you think it needs more colour. A good accompaniment is boiled or braised courgettes, new potatoes or a mix of both, while bread (which is more soft than crusty) is essential for soaking up the 17th/21st-century lemon sauce.Chicken with sweet and sour lemon and tarragon sauceWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appServes44 largeskinless chicken breasts375ml white wine300mllight vegetable stock3 tbspsoft brown sugarGratedzest of1 large unwaxed lemon,plus 2 tbsp juice1 handfulfreshtarragon leaves3 tbsp balsamic or red-wine vinegar75ml olive oilSalt andblack pepperPut the chicken breasts in a pan large enough for them to lay snugly in a single layer , then pour over 300ml wine and all of the stock, and place on a low-medium heat.Allow the wine and stock to come slowly to a lively poaching simmer (the surface should shudder) for 12 minutes, then pull from the heat and cover for three minutes. Scoop out the chicken breasts from the poaching liquid, wrap in tinfoil and leave to rest for five minutes. (If you are not using them straight away, return to the broth once it is cold until you are ready to use them.)In a small pan, warm the sugar and remaining wine and stir until the sugar has dissolved. Pull from the heat and add the lemon zest and juice, plus the tarragon leaves; leave to cool.Add the vinegar to a bowl and gradually whisk in the olive oil to form an emulsion, then taste and add salt and pepper.Lift the chicken from the broth and cut the meat into 1cm-thick slices. Arrange the slices on a plate and spoon over the dressing, then cover and set aside for at least half an hour at room temperature (and up to a few hours) before serving.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: My slow Swedish summer on the tranquil islands of Östergötland | Sweden holidays | The Guardian
description: Small boats and kayaks connect the sparse communities and flourishing wildlife living on the thousands of islets on the Baltic coast
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Small boats and kayaks connect the sparse communities and flourishing wildlife living on the thousands of islets on the Baltic coast
Content: A kayaker takes in the view during a break in paddling around the Sankt Anna archipelago.Photograph: Crelle Ekstrand/SöderköpingView image in fullscreenA kayaker takes in the view during a break in paddling around the Sankt Anna archipelago.Photograph: Crelle Ekstrand/SöderköpingSweden holidaysMy slow Swedish summer on the tranquil islands of ÖstergötlandSmall boats and kayaks connect the sparse communities and flourishing wildlife living on the thousands of islets on the Baltic coastHannah NewtonThu 30 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 5am on Arkösund bay, it is so light it could be midday. I slip out of the pretty clapboardArkösunds hotell, opened in 1895, as a small boat putters into the Baltic Sea, the sun sparkling on its calm waters. A wooden boardwalk invites me on to a string of tiny islets as geese arrow overhead and a mother swan coaxes her fluffy cygnets into a nook under a bridge.I’m on Sweden’s east coast to explore the Östergötland archipelago, a sprawl of about 9,000 islands scattered across the Baltic Sea a few hours south of Stockholm. Quieter and less crowded than the better-known isles off Stockholm or Gothenburg, it covers several pockets of coastline and smaller archipelagos: Arkösund, Sankt Anna, Gryt and Tjust. The larger islands are flecked with traditional red timber summer houses, and are home to seals, sea birds, and dense, verdant forests of alder, cedar, oak and pine.I’d arrived in a suitably slow fashion. My journey to Arkösund – a 45-minute drive from Norrköping station along a road locals call the End of the World – started 24 hours earlier, with an early morning Eurostar from London to Brussels, then on to Hamburg via Cologne, where I boarded the SJ EuroNight Train to Norrköping. I slept while we slipped across the Danish border in the early hours and crossed the Øresund Bridge into Sweden. Dawn unfolded in pink, dusky waves as we shuddered out of Malmö towards Östergötland.View image in fullscreenÖstergötland is a maze of small islands, fishing harbours and tiny villages.Photograph: Berndt-Joel Gunnarsson/AlamyVisitors navigate the region’s islands in sailboats, small motorboats or kayaks, spending elongated summer days swimming, fishing and hiking. From Arkösund jetty, I take to the water with Åsa, a local guide, in a motorboat belonging toKauko Lindstedt, a Finn who has spent 40 years living on the island of Aspöja, a four-mile crossing away. There is an unspoken rule, Åsa says, that if you spot a moored kayak or boat, move on. In the Swedish spirit ofallemansrätten– the national law to roam and sleep freely in nature – there are enough islands for everyone.double quotation markThere is an unspoken rule that if you spot a moored kayak or boat, move on. There are enough islands for everyoneAspöja is one of the few inhabited islands and Lindstedt, as with many islanders I meet, is industrious: building, hunting, smoking fish, running boating tours, and eager to share his home, where just 25 people live year-round. We land at his jetty and walk across grassy meadows dotted with lumps of granite and teeming with butterflies. There are no cars, though the jetty has a communal wheelbarrow for groceries and post. We meet Helen, who farms sheep and cattle, knits, tans sheepskins, keeps bees, grows vegetables and runs the only restaurant,Forsmans på Aspöja, with her daughter. Lunch is smoked fish and boiled potatoes heaped with fresh dill, alongside a glass of Baltic seawater, filtered through the island’s small desalination plant.View image in fullscreenThe island of Aspöja, home to just 25 year-round inhabitantsOn the trip back to the mainland, we pass an island stacked with fishing nets, buoys and wooden crates. A pair of craggy-faced men wave – brothers in their 70s, the final vestiges of a once thriving fishing industry, Åsa tells me. They are the last two fishers legally able to catch eels; the licence can only be passed on through family, and with none it ends with them.The next day, Åsa and I drive further along the coast to the Sankt Anna archipelago, stopping for lunch atMauritzberg Castle, a 400-year-old manor house rebuilt in pastel rococo splendour after the Russians burned it down in 1719. At the bay of Sankt Anna, I meet a German tourist packing his kayak for a 10-day solo adventure. He tells me he paddles for days from island to island without seeing a single soul and adores it – it’s his third trip here.Island-hopping in Sweden: an enchanted maze of tiny isles – only a bus ride from GothenburgRead moreFrom the shore I clamber into a kayak alongside Andreas, my guide, another Finn who works for outfitterKajakparadiset, and we paddle into the languid, liquid landscape. We stop for fika – hot coffee and something sweet – on one islet, stretching out on sun-scorched granite as a sea eagle soars above.double quotation markI meet a German tourist packing his kayak for a 10-day solo adventure. He tells me he paddles for days from island to island without seeing a single soul and adores itThat night I sleep atSkärgårdsbyn Mon, a hotel on the mainland shore, after a meal of buttered sea bream and potatoes eaten on the wooden balcony of the Boathouse restaurant, overlooking the marina, with the islands spilling out behind. I wonder enviously which one the German kayaker has chosen to sleep on underneath the barely darkened sky.I wake to rain. But with temperatures averaging around 23C, summer here is comfortable. Driving south with Åsa, I learn that about 70% of the country is forested, and it’s crossed by hiking and biking trails.At Fyrudden, a hamlet on the south-eastern end of a narrow peninsula in the Gryt archipelago, Magnus Lindkvist, a boat captain, is waiting in his grandfather’s wooden boat to take us across eight miles of open water to the island of Harstena. It’s where his grandparents once lived and he spent every summer of his childhood, and continues to go there today with his family.View image in fullscreenThe Gryt archipelago.Photograph: Peter Gerdehag/Imagebank SwedenA cluster of 18th-century cabins still stand. The old schoolhouse is a museum, depicting the history of these wild islands, where herring, eel fishing, seabird eggs and seal blubber were once the means of the islanders’ survival. A 1641 census registers two households, and a family tree traces local names back to their two families – including Magnus, and now his son.Back on the mainland, we drive north and inland to spend the night in Söderköping, where in 1281 King Magnus Ladulås’ wife, Helvig, was crowned in its medieval church. This tiny town is steeped in history, standing at the eastern end of the Göta Canal, which the Swedes, in a bid to avoid Danish taxes, began building in 1810, connecting Gothenburg to the Baltic Sea. I spend the next morning cycling alongside it, stopping to sample ice-cream from theSmultronställetcafe and handmade chocolates fromJolla.By evening, I am back in Norrköping, an industrial city once booming with textile and paper mills powered by water. Today, the mills have been restored into a stylish district of bars, apartments and offices. The streets are alive at night as students celebrate the end of term and city revellers gear up for a weekend of national celebrations.From the train window the following day, as I head back to the UK, I watch the fields and forests unfurl as Norrköping station slides away behind me, the summer light filtering through the trees and across the red weatherboard farmsteads. A skein of geese flies overhead in a V, and I imagine the kayaker searching for his perfect island to camp tonight, and Magnus teaching his son to fish for herring from his great-grandfather’s boat – the delicate balance of nature and visitor continuing in harmony.The trip was provided byVisit Sweden.The writer travelled by rail from Eurostar London to Brussels (from £39 one-way), then toCologne/Köln(from£16.50 one-way), and on to Hamburg (from £16.50one-way). TheSJ EuroNight trainfrom Hamburg to Nörrköping costs from£40 one-way.Elite Grand hotel Norrköpinghas doublesfrom £80 B&B;Söderköpings Brunnfrom £93 B&B;SkärgårdsbynMonfrom £100; andArkösunds hotellfrom £170 B&BExplore more on these topicsSweden holidaysScandinavia holidaysSlow travelEurope holidaysCanoeing and kayaking holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A trip down Dungeon Lane for Beatles nostalgia and coastal beauty | The Beatles | The Guardian
description: Liverpool: Paul McCartney’s latest album has brought tourists here ,but there’s so much more to see than the sign
Author: Jennifer Jones
Headline: Liverpool: Paul McCartney’s latest album has brought tourists here ,but there’s so much more to see than the sign
Content: "The southern end of Dungeon Lane is where Paul McCartney would have gone with his binoculars.’Photograph: Jen JonesView image in fullscreen"The southern end of Dungeon Lane is where Paul McCartney would have gone with his binoculars.’Photograph: Jen JonesCountry diaryThe BeatlesCountry diary: A trip down Dungeon Lane for Beatles nostalgia and coastal beautyLiverpool:Paul McCartney’s latest album has brought tourists here, but there’s so much more to see than the signJennifer JonesThu 30 Jul 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this year, Paul McCartney released an album calledThe Boys of Dungeon Lane. Among the unashamed nostalgia is a wistful track,Days We Left Behind, which evokes memories of his visits to the Mersey shore with George Harrison and friends. Young Paul was, it turns out, a keen birdwatcher.Perhaps inevitably, the album has brought crowds of tourists to photograph the sign. The Speke end of the lane where they mostly gather is uninspiring, bounded by remnants of a demolished pub, a solar farm and an electricity substation.View image in fullscreenThis section leads down to Dungeon Bay and Oglet Shore, both important sites for birds and wildlife.Photograph: Jen JonesThe southern end of Dungeon Lane is where Paul would have gone with his binoculars. This section leads down to Dungeon Bay and Oglet Shore, important sites for birds and wildlife, then as now. The coast may be more eroded, but Paul would still recognise it.The middle of the lane was cut off a few years ago by Liverpool John Lennon airport, but more curious visitors can still reach the shore via a slight detour. Here is coastal beauty. July is the quiet month for birds, but goldfinches, linnets and commonwhitethroatscall mutedly. Dense bramble guards the lane, with fecund banks of early ripeness born of this summer’s heat dome. Red soldier beetles explore wild carrot blooms, while ragwort and buddleia hostcinnabarmoth caterpillars and many butterflies.Other features point to a history before the Beatles: the second world war stone pyramids that were tank traps to repel any invading enemy, or the sandstone wall, adjacent to the shore, the only evidence of a once thriving salt industry. A salt refinery was built here in the late 17th century, and the wall may be the remains of the quay. Closer inspection shows old graffiti names and initials.Two girls are sitting on the wall gazing across the Mersey (perhaps young Paul once did the same, watching for waders). We chat briefly; they speak of its beauty, vowing to return. Walking back, a young man approaches. He reflects on when he cycled down Dungeon Lane as a child. The McCartney tourists, he says, are visiting the “wrong” part of the lane. “They should come down here instead.”View image in fullscreenPerhaps young Paul once sat on this wall, watching for waders in the Mersey.Photograph: Jen JonesUnder the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsThe BeatlesCountry diaryCoastlinesRiversLiverpoolRural affairsPaul McCartneyMerseysidefeaturesShareReuse this content

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: State department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in Brazil
Content: The map presented in Brazil on Sunday showed a landlocked Nigeria in the Sahara and placed Mozambique in the Horn of Africa.Photograph: Picture obtained by ReutersView image in fullscreenThe map presented in Brazil on Sunday showed a landlocked Nigeria in the Sahara and placed Mozambique in the Horn of Africa.Photograph: Picture obtained by ReutersUS foreign policyUS government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conferenceState department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in BrazilReutersThu 30 Jul 2026 18.48 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US government map ofAfricamislabeled every country during a state department presentation at a ⁠global conference in Brazil ⁠this week, ​causing a stir among attenders who took screenshots and posted them online.Reuters viewed a video of the presentation given at the Aids 2026 conference in ⁠Rio de Janeiro, which shows the errant map displayed halfway during a presentation about the state department’s new health agreements.A Reuters analysis found the image of the map included ⁠in the presentation contained an artificial intelligence watermark that signals it was made with OpenAI tools. The ​company said it was investigating the report.The state ‌department said it took “full responsibility” ‌for the confusion caused and that the map had been produced by a team member who hastily changed ‌the slide deck before the event.The map showed Nigeria, where the US currently has several hundred troops deployed, as landlocked in the Sahara desert. Mozambique, which is in south-eastern Africa, was relocated to the Horn of Africa, while Côte d’Ivoire in west Africa was placed on the other side of the continent.Screenshots of the map first appeared in a Substack post by the Aids expert Emily Bass and were widely ‌shared on LinkedIn, with one post garnering about 40,000 views.“Whoever created and approved this slide did not know where countries in Africa are and did not care to ​check their work,” wrote Matt Petit, who focuses on AI and geopolitics at the Atlantic Council, in the post.In a statement, the state department said: “We take full responsibility for the confusion and misrepresentation it caused for attendees, including our African partners.” The speaker at the conference was Jeff Graham, the ⁠top US health envoy who oversees the initiative known as the President’s Emergency Plan ​for Aids Relief, or Pepfar. He ​did not reply to requests for comment.The ​state department said the discussions at the conference were “substantive and constructive” despite the map ​and that it remained ‌committed to fighting Aids ​with real results. The ​Trump administration’s decision last year to pause funding pending a review disrupted aid programs worldwide, but Pepfar’s core work such as the provision of life-saving drugs has largely resumed. The US is scaling back other areas of its spending including on prevention and surveillance, and plans to fully phase out the program in South Africa.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyAfricaAids and HIVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifteen elephant deaths at Kenya park may be due to cyanide poisoning | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service
Content: A KWS investigation found 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and tests had detected a potential toxic substance.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA KWS investigation found 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and tests had detected a potential toxic substance.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockWildlifeFifteen elephant deaths at Kenya park may be due to cyanide poisoningAnalysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife ServiceCarlos Mureithiin NairobiThu 30 Jul 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe recent deaths of 15 elephants near a park in southern Kenya in the past month were likely caused by the animals ingesting pesticides used on nearby tomato farms, the KenyaWildlifeService (KWS) has said.Erustus Kanga, the agency’s director general, told Citizen TV that analysis of samples collected from the carcasses had found traces of cyanide, a chemical compound used in farming as a predator control poison and a pest fumigant, which hasalso been used by poachers.“Cyanide is a highly toxic chemical,” he said. “If elephants consume cyanide, they cannot survive a day or two.”The deaths occurred in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku Group ranch areas around Amboseli national park, an area covering 392 sq km (96,865 acres) and that, together with other neighbouring conservancies are home to more than 1,600 elephants.Kenya investigating unexpected deaths of 15 elephants in national parkRead moreKimana town is a leading tomato producer and a place where researchers at the Route to Food Initiative, a food rights programme, have previouslyreportedthe use of a cyanide substance on the crop.Isaac Lekolool, the head of veterinary and capture services at KWS, told Citizen TV that the stomach contents of one member of a herd that roamed Kimana sanctuary included “lots of tomatoes,” suggesting agrochemical poisoning.Kanga warned that the effects could reach a wider population, as livestock may also eat from farms in the area.“We have the goats, we have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this cyanide is truly the one that is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact.”On Tuesday, KWSannouncedit was investigating the deaths of the elephants from 24 June and 24 July in Amboseli. It said 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and that preliminary tests had detected a potential toxic substance.Benson Leyian, the CEO of Big Life Foundation, a conservation organisation that operates in the area surrounding Amboseli national park, said the elephant deaths were a cause for concern.“Thanks to decades of community-centred conservation, the Amboseli elephant population is one of the best protected inAfrica, and elephant poaching has been virtually eliminated here.
