Aside from losses during periods of severe drought, we haven’t seen a cluster of elephant deaths like this for some time,” he said.Ina statement, the International Fund for Animal Welfare described the deaths as “deeply alarming”, adding the incident “reinforces why we must continue investing in science, monitoring, and collaborative conservation efforts”.“Every elephant lost is significant – not only for the species, but for the health of the ecosystems they help sustain and the communities that live alongside them,” it said.Farmers and herders inKenyahave in the past poisoned wildlife in retaliation for eating their crops and livestock.In Zimbabwe, poachers have killed dozens of elephants bylacing watering holes and salt licks with the chemical compound.The Amboseli ecosystem is a major source of tourism revenue, but tensions have been building in recent months as local leaders demand the handover of the park’s management and operations to the government of Kajiado county, where it is located. Earlier this month, a court suspended the county government’s takeover.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeAnimalsKenyaAfricaFarmingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifty-three days and counting: 93-year-old leader’s record absence fuels health speculation | Cameroon | The Guardian
description: Cameroon’s Paul Biya has not made a statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 June
Author: Giovanni Wanneh
Headline: Cameroon’s Paul Biya has not made a statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 June
Content: Paul Biya giving a speech in Maroua, Cameroon, last October, with his wife, Chantal, sitting beside him.Photograph: Xinhua/AlamyView image in fullscreenPaul Biya giving a speech in Maroua, Cameroon, last October, with his wife, Chantal, sitting beside him.Photograph: Xinhua/AlamyCameroonFifty-three days and counting: 93-year-old leader’s record absence fuels health speculationCameroon’s Paul Biya has not made a statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 JuneGiovanni Wannehin Buea andEromo Egbejulein AccraThu 30 Jul 2026 08.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA record 53-day absence by the world’s oldest head of state has renewed speculation in his native Cameroon about whether he is dead or alive, even thoughdiscussing his health is illegal in the country.On 7 June, 93-year-old Paul Biya left for Switzerland for what officials described as a “brief private stay” alongside his wife, Chantal. Almost two months later, neither the president nor the first lady have addressed the country or been seen publicly.Biya, who took office in 1982 after a seven-year stint as prime minister, has taken increasingly long absences fromCameroonin recent years, spending much of his time at the five-star InterContinental hotel in Geneva.No official timetable has been announced for the president’s return from his latest trip abroad, leaving Cameroonians to rely on a succession of conflicting statements from government officials.The minister of communication, René Emmanuel Sadi, said Biya was in good health and “working from Geneva, where he currently resides”.“Reports claiming otherwise are pure fantasy and malicious manipulation aimed at destabilising opinion,” he added. Jacques Fame Ndongo, a senior official from the ruling party and the higher education minister, said Biya had been “meticulously following the files submitted to him by his aides … wherever he is”.The labour minister, Grégoire Owona, gave a different explanation, saying the president was on annual leave and comparing him to regular Cameroonian citizens. “Paul Biya, elected by the Cameroonian people and paid by them, is a worker who has the right to annual leave,” he said. “His employer is obliged to grant it. He informed his employer before leaving and will do the same upon his return.”View image in fullscreenA session of Cameroon’s national assembly this month.Photograph: Mengnjo Etienne/ReutersCameroonian authorities banned discussion of Biya’s health in October 2024, during another absence. Nevertheless, local media have published claims in recent weeks that he is critically ill, and jokes about Biya being a work-from-abroad president or a remote-work president have resurfaced on social media.Mamadou Mota, the vice-president of the opposition Cameroon Renaissance Movement party, said Biya’s latest absence had created a “glaring institutional vacuum”. “A country cannot be governed by remote control while critical socioeconomic challenges go unaddressed,” he said.Last November, Biya was sworn in for his eighth consecutive seven-year term, a month aftera presidential electionmarred by widespread allegations of irregularities and voter suppression. Although the Constitutional Council dismissed post-electoral complaints by opposition parties, many of them refused to recognise the outcome, arguing that the election had further eroded public confidence in Cameroon’s democratic institutions.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the opposition politician Issa Tchiroma protest in Douala after Biya’s re-election in October last year.Photograph: Zohra Bensemra/ReutersBiya has yet to name a government since being sworn in for his latest term. With parliamentary and municipal elections expected in early 2027, many are worried that the ripple effect of that and his prolonged absence could disrupt the electoral cycle.Cameroon has the largest economy in centralAfrica, but unemployment rates, high inflation and poor public infrastructure are stymieing the prospects of its young people, who make up about two-thirds of its estimated population of 30.6 million.“Politics should be about serving the people, but the [ruling] CPDM [party] appears more interested in holding on to power than addressing the concerns of Cameroonians,” said Kohtem Sambit, the secretary general of the opposition Movement for Patriotism and People’s Prosperity.“The minister of the economy borrowed more than 21bn [Central African francs] in the name of the Cameroonian people, saying it was approved by Mr Biya,” Sambit told the Guardian. “How do we justify this? You do not see the person who signed, nor do you know his whereabouts. That debt will be paid by the public.”Referring to Owona’s remarks, Sambit said: “If the president is on annual leave, he is still accountable to the Cameroonian people because he is paid with taxpayers’ money. His whereabouts should therefore be disclosed.”A tale of two Francks? World’s oldest leader creates deputy role – raising prospect of dynastic successionRead moreAnother opposition party, the Social Democratic Front, has argued that the issue is not whether the president has a constitutional right to travel, but rather the government’s failure to explain the extension of what had initially been described as a brief private visit. Another opposition leader, Patricia Tomaïno Ndam Njoya, of the Cameroon Democratic Union, has called for an impartial procedure to determine any “temporary or permanent incapacity of the head of state”.In April, parliament reintroduced the office of vice-president as part of a constitutional overhaul, but the position has yet to be filled, leaving Cameroon without a designated deputy should the president become incapacitated. As Biya’s son and stepsonreportedly jockey for position, public disagreements between cabinet ministers have become commonplace.Last week, the party’s secretary general, Jean Nkuete, convened a rare meeting of senior party officials. The CPDM described the gathering only as an “important working session” and did not release an agenda or further details. Attempts to obtain comment from senior party figures were unsuccessful. Several party officials have declined interview requests, citing personal reasons.For the businessman Nji Lucas, the president’s prolonged absence has become an economic concern. “I do not have confidence because it is almost as if the country is on autopilot,” he said. “No serious investor wants to commit resources in a country where there is uncertainty over political leadership. There is no trust, and investors require certainty before making long-term decisions.”Explore more on these topicsCameroonAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: A quarter of young Africans believe USAID cuts could be positive, survey finds | Global development | The Guardian
description: Losing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influence
Author: Sarah Johnson
Headline: Losing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influence
Content: Sports fans in Accra, Ghana waving the national flag. More than 40% of Ghanaians aged 18-24 were optimistic about their country’s future after USAID cuts.Photograph: Ulrich Doering/AlamyView image in fullscreenSports fans in Accra, Ghana waving the national flag. More than 40% of Ghanaians aged 18-24 were optimistic about their country’s future after USAID cuts.Photograph: Ulrich Doering/AlamyGlobal developmentA quarter of young Africans believe USAID cuts could be positive, survey findsLosing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influenceSupported byAbout this contentSarah JohnsonThu 30 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA quarter of young Africans believe aid cuts by the US could have a positive impact, saying that losing foreign money will force leaders to confront and solve their own challenges, according to a new survey.In Ghana and Nigeria, almost half (41% and 40% respectively) of young people aged 18 to 24 were optimistic, with Liberia not far behind (37%). A further one in 10 (11%) young people were uncertain about the impact, according to the African Youth Survey, which interviewed almost 5,000 people across 16 of the continent’s 54 recognised countries.The Trump administration announced in early 2025 that it waseliminating more than 90% of USAID’s foreign contractsand $60bn in overall US assistance around the world. US foreign aid had been designed to play a critical role in tackling poverty, hunger and inequality worldwide.Other countries, including Britain, France and Germany, have also been slashing aid budgets. TheUK announced in February 2025that the aid budget would be cut from 0.5% of gross national income to 0.3% in 2027, itslowest levelas a percentage of national income since records began. The UN target is 0.7%.Ivor Ichikowitz, whose South African family foundation commissioned the report, said: “The big picture [from the survey] is that the youth is concerned about governments that are overly influenced by foreign powers. What they’re saying is that African governments need to take agency and responsibility for their own reality.”View image in fullscreenA World Food Programme distribution centre in Dikwa, Borno state, Nigeria, August 2025.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersAfrica has the youngest population in the world, with 70% of sub-Saharan Africa under the age of 30,according to the UN. The median age of the continent is 19 years and six months. By 2030, Africa will behome to more than 40% of the world’s youth.The suddenUSAIDcuts were met with public outrage and pushback from development and humanitarian organisations. They caused the closure of vital services, including maternity clinics, and medicine shortages at a time when UN agencies are struggling to find money for their humanitarian work and food insecurity has been worsened by the climate crisis.According to the survey, nearly half of African youth (46%) did believe the closure of USAID would have a damaging impact on their countries, with healthcare services and disease prevention seen as the areas most affected. This anxiety is highest in Mozambique (76%), followed by Kenya (63%) and Rwanda (63%), where youth feel the cuts will disproportionately affect the most vulnerable members of society.Degan Ali, executive director ofAdeso, an African non-profitincubating ideas and enterprises to lower aid dependency, said that while the cuts were carried out in a “hugely irresponsible and inhumane” manner, she was not surprised that a significant proportion of young people saw positivity there. “I think it’s a reflection of the general feeling. A lot of people find aid very demeaning,” she said. “They didn’t feel that the aid was being used for the right things and there is a sense of ‘We can do this for ourselves’. The younger generation feel like our leaders are the duty bearers and are supposed to be handling the needs of our communities.”US ‘adapt, shrink or die’ terms for $2bn aid pot will mean UN bowing down to Washington, say expertsRead moreShe said people believed that the aid that comes into a country is not going to the right causes or the right people. “There’s all this money going into the development sector, but they’re not really seeing major changes on the ground,” she said. “The younger generation is very politically active and more savvy. They are pushing back and trying to hold their leaders accountable.”She also said that the youth was looking towards African role models on the continent, a move exemplified by the popularity of Burkina Faso’s military leader, Ibrahim Traoré, who portrays himself as a pan-Africanist figure leading his nation out of the clutches of western imperialism and neocolonialism.“He is one of the more popular leaders across the entire continent of Africa,” said Ali. “There arematatus(minibus taxis) that have his name on in Nairobi, Kenya. The youth see that he is turning around a very poor country and that he really cares about his people. That further motivates young people to protest and say, ‘We don’t need aid, we have enough resources in our country and we need our leaders to behave differently.’”Hibak Kalfan, executive director of Near, a network of civil society organisations from the global south, said the shuttering of USAID had led to the closure of initiatives and organisations across the whole continent, but had also created the opportunity to reconsider resources and sustainability. “It has put a real light on the fact that [organisations] have been highly dependent on bilateral external funding for years, and the future of aid will depend on a diversity of resources,” she said.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentAidTrump administrationUSAIDAfricaUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts | Japan | The Guardian
description: Soldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivors
Author: Gavin Blair
Headline: Soldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivors
Content: 0:43Police footage shows scale of damage inside Aeon mall after explosion cause by Japan quake – videoJapanDeath toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue effortsSoldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivorsEarthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in picturesGavin Blairin TokyoThu 30 Jul 2026 02.49 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 22.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death toll from the powerful earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday has risen to 30, as thesearch for survivorstrapped in a badly damaged shopping centre, paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country continues.‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquakeRead moreThe 6.8-magnitude quake, which struck Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu, injured at least 62 people, according to the prefectural government.Almost 5,000 Self-Defence Forces (SDF) personnel deployed to the region faced temperatures of up to 35C on Thursday, officials said, adding that a 5.8-magnitude aftershock overnight had further hampered the rescue efforts.Map of earthquake siteAbout 170 rescue workers were searching the Aeon shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake struck.The company said about 3,000 customers were evacuated to a car park before a gas explosion occurred in another part of the shopping centre. Six of the 12 people pulled from the rubble have died.All those caught in the explosion were shop workers who had returned to the building after the evacuation, Aeon said. The company’s president bowed in apology at a press conference on Wednesday, saying Aeon had failed to anticipate the explosion, the cause of which was being investigated.1:09Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – videoJapanese media footage from inside the shopping centre showed part of the ceiling had collapsed, with metal fragments and other debris scattered across the floor as helmeted, masked rescue workers searched the area.Police and SDF personnel were continuing to search for one worker in the debris at the Nippon Paper mill in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed. Of the 10 others who were trapped, eight died and two were injured.In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at the factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government.View image in fullscreenNippon Paper mill, where a chimney collapsed.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPANearly 23,000 homes had no electricity and 75,000 had no running water, Kumamoto officials said. About 15,000 people had been evacuated to 400 shelters.The defence minister said on Wednesday evening that the SDF was airlifting coolers to shelters in Kumamoto, while SDF vessels were delivering water and food.“We’re doing everything possible to make saving lives a priority, making efforts to deliver life-saving supplies, beginning with water,” Shinjiro Koizumi said.Aerial police footage showed several homes had been flattened, including some that had crumbled into a river.View image in fullscreenA collapsed house in Hikawa, Kumamoto.Photograph: Kyodo/ReutersThe earthquake registered the maximum level 7 on Japan’s seven-level shindo scale. “It was the strongest quake I have ever experienced,” Kanzo Matsumoto, 73, the operator of a luxury hot spring inn in Yatsushiro, told Agence France-Presse.The national Geospatial Information Authority said parts of the ground had shifted by 87cm during the quake.Yatsushiro town hall sustained damage to its base-isolation system, an earthquake-resistant technology designed to protect buildings by cushioning their foundations against intense shaking. The system was rebuilt after a deadly earthquake in 2016.View image in fullscreenVehicles are crushed under collapsed buildings in Yatsushiro, south-western Japan.Photograph: Hiro Komae/APSome car and semiconductor manufacturers with plants in Kyushu have halted production.Toyota said it would pause operations at three plants while it assessed the quake’s impact on suppliers and ⁠logistics. Honda suspended operations at a motorcycle plant until Friday.Taiwan’s TSMC has resumed operations at its Kumamoto facility, while Sony, Renesas Electronics and Tokyo Electron have halted production.Kyushu is ‌an important hub for Japan’s automotive and semiconductor industries, which account for about 20% of the region’s industrial output.Analysts said the shutdowns appeared to be driven largely by precaution than damage to production facilities.Kumamoto was struck by two devastatingearthquakes in 2016that killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.The archipelago, home to about 125 million people, usually experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18% of the world’s earthquakes.With Associated Press, Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsJapanEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Governor general warns of ‘growing catastrophe’ that threatens to undermine democracy in Australia  | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Sam Mostyn says there is a widespread ‘failure to understand and engage with’ civic underpinnings of our democracy
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Sam Mostyn says there is a widespread ‘failure to understand and engage with’ civic underpinnings of our democracy
Content: The Australian governor general, Sam Mostyn, at Admiralty House in Kirribilli, Sydney.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Australian governor general, Sam Mostyn, at Admiralty House in Kirribilli, Sydney.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianAustralian politicsGovernor general warns of ‘growing catastrophe’ that threatens to undermine democracy in AustraliaSam Mostyn says there is a widespread ‘failure to understand and engage with’ civic underpinnings of our democracyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorThu 30 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia faces a “growing catastrophe” from poor understanding of the country’s constitutional foundation, the governor general, Sam Mostyn, has warned as attacks on institutions and threats against elected officials undermine democratic participation.Two years after herappointment as King Charles’s representativein Canberra, and as she brings a modern touch to the role of vice regal, Mostyn said that knowledge of how the country’s system of government operates was in steady decline and better civics education was needed.“Where I see the most woeful lack of understanding … the basic understanding of the tenets of our democracy, is in the adult population,” Mostyn said.“It’s mostly people who attack our system, who say we shouldn’t have a governor general, or who ask the governor general to do things that are not within my powers, or criticise me for signing the bills that I must sign, because they think I should have a view that clearly I do not have as governor general. Certain things I must do under my constitutional requirements.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We’ve got a growing catastrophe, I think, in a failure to understand and engage with and feel proud of the very civic underpinnings of our democracy.”In an interview for Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast, released on Friday, Mostyn said schoolchildren and newly sworn Australian citizens had the best understanding of how government and institutions worked.The comments come as parliaments, the courts, the Australian Electoral Commission and officeholders around the country face mounting criticism and abuse.Since the Covid pandemic, social media and online commentary has been identified as hotbed of corrosive sentiment, coinciding withrising threats against officials.“It starts with understanding why we have a constitution, how it came to be,” Mostyn said of a potential solution.1:31Governor general takes the plunge in first Big Freeze since Neale Daniher’s death – video“It’s 125 years old this year. It was built in a particular way, to bring the states and territories together, in order to build a sense of unity around the country, and it sets up everything that then builds the strength of our democracy.”Mostyn said part of the problem was an absence of “a shared set of facts”, including in online discourse.“I think this is a moment where it’s important for everyone, particularly people like me, in these offices, to keep up the project of why it matters that we show respect for each other, we learn to understand each other.“There is a big risk that if we don’t, this is the beginning of the unraveling of social cohesion.”The former businesswoman, AFL commissioner, political adviser and community leader has prioritised civics engagement and education in the role, bringing a less formal and more down-to-earth approach to the office of governor general. When she was appointed to the role – traditionally filled by former politicians, judges and military leaders – Mostyn promisedan unstinting focuson kindness, on care and on respect.View image in fullscreenMostyn visiting Ahmed al-Ahmad in hospital, who disarmed a gunman during the Bondi Beach shooting.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesEarlier this month, she hosted a roundtable on social cohesion and civics education with the Constitution Education Fund at her official residence in Canberra, Government House, attended by educators, public service leaders and thinktanks. Former high court chief justice Robert French is the fund’s chair.Mostyn warned the types of people considering seeking political office in Australia is changing, because of sustained abuse and threats against elected representatives at all levels.She said local councillors and mayors had told her public life was becoming difficult and increasingly unappealing.“They [have] shared with me that lack of civility in their own communities, as directed to them as elected representatives, has become very very challenging, making it very difficult to seek office.“If you know that you’re putting yourself into very dangerous traffic with people who now don’t feel the need to be respectful, who make direct threats … we’ve seen this all around the world with elected representatives at all levels.“This desire to be hateful, to attack, to not enter into good, peaceful, robust but respectful discussions on things where we might not agree, and so that’s happening certainly in local government.”View image in fullscreenMostyn conducts the coin toss ahead of a netball match between Australia and Tonga at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPMostyn is the Crown’s representative in Australia, presides over the executive council, gives royal assent to legislation from parliament, appoints ministers and officials, dissolves parliament for elections and is the commander-in-chief of the Australian Defence Force.She holds the reserve powers of the constitution and attends and hosts hundreds of events every year, including for the Order of Australia.In the past two years, Mostyn has used a growing social media presence to educate the public about the function of the governor general, and has conducted dozens of interviews, including with local media outlets when visiting far-flung communities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the Bondi beach terror attack in December last year, Mostyn immediately flew to Sydney to comfort victims and members of Australia’s Jewish community. At the height of the Socceroos World Cup campaign last month, she attended a Canberra pub to watch Australia play Paraguay in the middle of the day.Speaking at Admiralty House, the governor general’s residence on Sydney Harbour, Mostyn revealed she had followed precedent from recent governors general and asked the Electoral Commissioner for an exemption from compulsory voting, preferring to be as removed as possible from political matters.Her appointment to the role was not without controversy.The Greens voted against legislation put to parliament to ensure Mostyn was paid thesame amount as her predecessor. Gen David Hurley took a lower base salarydue to his military pension.Commentators criticised Mostyn’s qualifications and said her high-profile positions on several issues including the voice to parliament referendum should have disqualified her from being appointed. One newspaper column called her “a governor-general from the Chairman’s Lounge”.View image in fullscreenSam Mostyn shakes hands with Anthony Albanese during the swearing in ceremony in the Senate chamber at Parliament House in Canberra.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPBut Mostyn has confounded some critics in her first two years on the job.In May, Chris Kenny, a columnist with The Australian newspaper lamented that too few commentators were ever prepared to admit when they were wrong about matters in public debate, acknowledging he had been mistaken in editorialising against Mostyn’s appointment on Sky News.Kenny had argued her record could be“too political for Yarralumla”. But instead, Mostyn, he said, “has been diligent, dignified, hard-working and apolitical”.The chief executive of the Constitution Education Fund, Kerry Jones, said Mostyn’s involvement could not be understated.“Probably the most important issue facing our country, our constitutional arrangements, our democracy, is that the people of Australia, the voters of Australia, seem to have lost a sense of trust in the institutions of government and the people in those institutions,” she said.“If we survive – and when we look back on this period, which is being called a lack of social cohesion, or polarisation, or the rise of populism in politics and that is resulting in racism increasing again, and resulting in antisemitism and Islamophobia – the fact that the governor general is saying it is a crisis and we need to do something about it, could be seen as one of the most significant acts ever taken, I believe, by an Australian governor general for the good of Australia.”View image in fullscreenMostyn in front of an artwork by Paddy Nyunkuny Bedford at Admiralty House.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianJones praised Mostyn’s energy and wisdom.“She cares for every single Australian citizen in every community across Australia and that radiates from everything she says.”Mostyn said one of her guiding principles comes from the memoir of one of her predecessors, the academic and writer Sir Zelman Cowen.Cowen served as governor general from 1977 until 1982, having replaced the controversial Sir John Kerr.“He says that the governor general can’t just be a functionary, ribbon-cutting, artefact of something. It’s a living job,” Mostyn said.“He says at a time when the country needs healing, the governor general needs to be present and needs to be able to play a really important role on behalf of all Australians to reflect the light and shade of the nation back to the nation, and help the nation interpret itself, in order to know where we’re going and what we could all do as citizens.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Icac revelations have left Angus Taylor’s colleagues anxious – and his factional enemies angry | Independent Commission Against Corruption | The Guardian
description: The opposition leader is the highest-profile person mentioned so far at the NSW anti-corruption commission – and the political figure with the most to lose
Author: Dan Jervis-Bardy
Headline: The opposition leader is the highest-profile person mentioned so far at the NSW anti-corruption commission – and the political figure with the most to lose
Content: The idea that Angus Taylor might have been supporting the plotters would amount to a level of treason well beyond what’s tolerated in factional politics.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe idea that Angus Taylor might have been supporting the plotters would amount to a level of treason well beyond what’s tolerated in factional politics.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesIndependent Commission Against CorruptionAnalysisIcac revelations have left Angus Taylor’s colleagues anxious – and his factional enemies angryDan Jervis-BardyThe opposition leader is the highest-profile person mentioned so far at the NSW anti-corruption commission – and the political figure with the most to loseFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 30 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 17.20 EDTShareAfter the opening days of an inquiry exposing a dark underbelly of theNew South WalesLiberals, the prevailing mood among Angus Taylor’s colleagues is one of apprehension.The federal opposition leader is not a specific target of Operation Rosny, which is investigating allegations of corruption against people associated with the NSW branch. He is not accused of wrongdoing.But Taylor is the highest-profile person mentioned so far – and the political figure with the most to lose.To briefly recap, the opposition leader was on Tuesday named as apotential donor to the Reformers, a group of hard-right Liberal operatives plotting to take over the party from the inside.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe inquiry heard that a screenshot of a message from Dallas McInerney, then the chief executive of Catholic Schools NSW, was sent to Reformers members in which McInerney said he planned to “shake down Angus for 10k” during a breakfast meeting in Canberra.Young Liberal power brokers created ‘shit sheet’ on NSW minister accusing him of extramarital affairRead moreThe message was allegedly sent in March 2021 when Taylor was energy minister in the Morrison government.Dylan Whitelaw, another Reformers associate who gave evidence on Tuesday and Wednesday, was read a later intercepted text message in which he claimed McInerney had told him he had secured a commitment from Taylor for a “15k injection and a 3k monthly donation!”Whitelaw couldn’t recall sending the message and told the inquiry he would be “very surprised” if Taylor made any contribution.After initially declining to refute the allegations,Taylor told a press conferenceon Wednesday that “no payment was made”.“I’m not going to give a running commentary on all of this. I’m not a party to the proceedings, but no payment was made,” Taylor said.If that response was supposed to put the matter to bed – and reassure his colleagues – it didn’t work.On Thursday, Taylor was asked again about any potential donations during a press conference in Logan, Queensland.“I’ve answered these questions yesterday. I’m not going to give a running commentary on it,” Taylor said.“You can ask the question 100 times,” he repeated. “I’ll give you the same answer.”Guardian Australia spoke with several Liberals on condition of anonymity, who believed Taylor must provide a more comprehensive answer, if indeed he had no role in bankrolling Reformers’ operations.Unsurprisingly, the Labor treasurer, Jim Chalmers, expressed the same view.“You know, I don’t want to interfere with the Icac process that his political allies are involved in at the moment … but there are a number of questions to be answered here, and he should front up and explain any involvement he’s had in this,” Chalmers said.There were further questions for the opposition leader after Whitelaw was asked at Wednesday’s hearing if the $3,000 monthly payments that Taylor had allegedly agreed to were connected to a similar amount that Catholic Schools NSW was paying to the Reformers-linked lobbying firm Beckington.There is no evidence that Taylor donated to the Reformers – only text messages suggesting payments would be sought or had been received.He has not yet clarified what involvement – or even knowledge – he had of the Reformers and their alleged branch-stacking operation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt Thursday’s hearing, Reformers witness Robert Assaf wasn’t sure what Taylor knew of their work but said he “definitely wasn’t opposed”.Among the troves of text messages released by Icac is one from Whitelaw in which he told Reformers that “Angus Taylor is locked-in” for an event in Goulburn in September 2020.An “Angus” is mentioned in several other text messages although the context is unclear.There are, at this stage, more questions than answers. But the evidence so far has been enough to cause anxiety among his colleagues because of Taylor’s close ties to McInerney.The pair are friends and factional allies. McInerney, one of the most powerful backroom operators in the NSW Liberal right faction, has helped Taylor with campaigns andwas influential in his overthrowing of Sussan Ley.2:01Jim Chalmers accuses Angus Taylor of trying to ‘out-One Nation One Nation’ – videoThe deeper Icac delves into McInerney’s dealings the more dangerous the inquiry becomes for Taylor, whose leadership is already tenuous given the Coalition’s dire position in the polls.Liberals are surprised Taylor has not been quicker to distance himself from McInerney, who stepped down from Catholic Schools NSW after the inquiry was announced.The opening days of evidence have elicited another emotion among Taylor’s factional enemies in NSW: anger.The Reformers’ recruitment drives targeted, among others, branches in the federal seats of Berowra, Lindsay and Farrer, with the aim of dislodging Julian Leeser, Melissa McIntosh and Sussan Ley respectively.McIntosh and Ley were only saved after an intervention from then prime minister Scott Morrison ahead of the 2022 federal election.The notion that Taylor might have been supporting the plotters – potentially even financially – would amount to a level of treason well beyond what’s tolerated in the messy blood sport of factional politics.The inquiry has more than seven weeks of hearings to go. Taylor might not be a target of Icac but he’s unlikely to emerge completely unscathed.Dan Jervis-Bardy is Guardian Australia’s chief political correspondentExplore more on these topicsIndependent Commission Against CorruptionNew South Wales politicsNew South WalesAngus TaylorLiberal partyAustralian politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Book returned to Australian library – 150 years overdue | Australia news | The Guardian
description: The book, Antiquities of Athens, was handed back to Kiama library by a man who found it bricked into a wall
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The book, Antiquities of Athens, was handed back to Kiama library by a man who found it bricked into a wall
Content: ‘We’ve never had anything that old come back’: Kiama library manager Michelle Hudson with the book Antiquities of Athens.Photograph: Jane Thompson/APView image in fullscreen‘We’ve never had anything that old come back’: Kiama library manager Michelle Hudson with the book Antiquities of Athens.Photograph: Jane Thompson/APAustralia newsBook returned to Australian library – 150 years overdueThe book, Antiquities of Athens, was handed back to Kiama library by a man who found it bricked into a wallAssociated PressThu 30 Jul 2026 06.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Australian public library has had a book returned an estimated 150 years late after being found behind a wall during a home renovation.The book, Antiquities of Athens, published in 1858, was returned to the library in the seaside town of Kiama, south ofSydney, by a man who had found it inside a tea crate bricked into a sealed fireplace“We’ve never had anything that old come back to us,” the library’s manager, Michelle Hudson, said.Australia is publishing books too quickly – and everyone is losing outRead more“I follow lots of libraries on social media and often you’ll get things that are maybe 30 or 40 years old when they’re cleaning out estates and stuff like that.”The book’s finder did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The late return fine would be around A$28,000 (US$19,500), allowing for inflation, Hudson said. That was calculated on the British three pence a week overdue fee that was printed on the inside cover of the book, along with a list of rules that applied when the library opened in 1872.View image in fullscreenThe book was marked as No 506 in the library’s original collection of about 1,000 books.Photograph: Catherine Taylor/APBut Hudson said there was no way of tracing the final borrower who had accrued the debt. The library journal from the 1870s that recorded who borrowed a book and when had been lost.“Unfortunately, we have a missing link. There’s nothing in the book that tells us who the last borrower was,” Hudson said.Library rules in the 1870s stated that a book had to be returned and an overdue debt paid before another book could be borrowed.“Maybe that’s why they never returned it to us,” Hudson said.Under the antiquated rules of the day, up to three books could be borrowed by households in which at least six members were “known to be able to read”.The book, which has some water damage from its years under a chimney, was marked as No 506 in the library’s original collection of around 1,000 books, Hudson said.She expects the book was lost within a few years of the library opening.The returned book will be displayed in the library’s local history collection.“We’re not going to allow it to go back out again. We don’t want to wait another 150 years for this book to be returned,” Hudson said.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kumanjayi Little Baby murder trial delayed until December – as it happened | Australia news | The Guardian
description: This blog is now closed
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: This blog is now closed
Content: 03.12 EDTKumanjayi Little Baby murder case delayed over ‘significant volume’ of forensic evidenceThe court process following the alleged murder ofKumanjayi Little Babywill be delayed for months, due to a “significant volume” of forensic evidence that had yet to be processed.The five-year-old Warlpiri girl was found dead in April after a five-day search following her sudden disappearance from an Alice Springs town camp. A 47-year-old man, Jefferson Lewis, was later charged with murder.On Thursday, the Alice Springs local court heard there was a “significant volume” of evidence that had not yet been fully examined or collected as part of the investigation, including 100 different forensic requests and 20 outstanding police witness statements.The court heard a “very substantial brief” of evidence had already been served in the matter, including 76 statements from different witnesses, 48 pieces of police body-worn footage, drone footage, CCTV footage, and a preliminary postmortem report. A full autopsy report was expected to be handed over in the near future.The matter returns to court on 3 December.–Samantha Jonscherin Alice SpringsShareUpdated at03.39 EDT

title: French riot police used teargas on people trying to board small boat, charity claims | Migration | The Guardian
description: CRS officers funded by UK tried to stop boarding of boat, on day four asylum seekers died trying to cross Channel
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: CRS officers funded by UK tried to stop boarding of boat, on day four asylum seekers died trying to cross Channel
Content: Footage released by Utopia 56 purports to show migrants and police clashing in CalaisMigrationFrench riot police used teargas on people trying to board small boat, charity claimsCRS officers funded by UK tried to stop boarding of boat, on day four asylum seekers died trying to cross ChannelRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 30 Jul 2026 15.20 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench riot police funded by UK taxpayers used teargas on asylum seekers in an attempt to stop them from boarding a boat in which three women were later found dead, a charity has claimed.Footage and photographs seen by the Guardian show CS gas canisters being fired towards groups of people on Plage du Braek near Dunkirk at 4am on Thursday. At 6am, three women were found dead in a boat near the same beach.According to the charity Utopia 56, which took the images, staff witnessed French riot police firing the canisters at people who were trying to board the same boat in which the bodies were discovered.As part of a £660m agreement signed by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in May, 50 officers fromCompagnies Républicaines de Sécurité (CRS)“specially trained in the use of riot and crowd control tactics” have been deployed using UK public money.In a separate development, a fourth person – a man – also died on Thursday when his dinghy got into difficulty in a separate incident off the coast of Dannes.The incidents happened hours after the busiest day for small boat crossings so far this year, which totalled 752 arrivals in the UK.View image in fullscreenPeople thought to be migrants are rescued from the sea on Thursday after they attempted to board a small boat from the beach near Dunkirk.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAClashes between riot police and asylum seekers took place on roads leading to Plage du Braek from 4am, Utopia 56 said.Angèle Vettorello, a coordinator at the charity, said: “An hour before the boat carrying the women’s bodies was found, our team was right next to the beach. Riot officers from the CRS were there and were trying to stop 80 people, including families, from trying to access the beach and those people were trying to get inside the boat.“We saw them using teargas against people and later we found at least 35 teargas canisters there. We do not know if the women whose bodies were discovered were already in the boat or were part of the group trying to reach the beach. We can see police pressure on the beach is putting more people at risk. We saw it last week and we are seeing it now and we have seen it for some time. It is terrible.”The CRS has faced allegations of brutality and racism. In February, nine officers from the force were found guilty of beating peaceful protesters who were sheltering from teargas during the “gilets jaunes” anti-government demonstrations in 2018. Two years ago, leaked WhatsApp messages showed CRS officers had exchanged an image of a sinking small boat laden with migrants.The CRS, although paid for by the UK, maintains “operational independence” inFranceand are also authorised to use water cannon, stun grenades and batons.The French interior ministry and the Home Office have been approached for comment.View image in fullscreenPeople leave the sea after failing to board a small boat from the beach near Dunkirk on Thursday.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAThe boat on which the women’s bodies were found was brought into shore at 6am. The bodies were brought ashore after the French emergency services, including firefighters, police and paramedics, mounted a rescue.Attempts to resuscitate the women failed and all three were declared dead. They were reported to be aged about 20, 30 and 50. Their nationalities are as yet unknown.The man who died was in a dinghy that capsized as people attempted to board. It had arrived from Sainte-Cécile, a beach farther south, with people already aboard. It is believed to have departed from Berck, a further 13 miles south.Six other people, including a one-year-old child, suffered minor injuries, the French authorities said. Some of those onboard were taken to hospital and a man with burns over half of his body was airlifted by a navy helicopter.Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said: “Refugees are ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances, and those who risk dangerous small boat journeys do so only out of desperation. There is no legal way for somebody escaping the Taliban in Afghanistan or brutal civil war in Sudan to reach sanctuary in the UK.“The government has even shut down family reunion for refugees, which overwhelmingly helped women and children. Fewer refugees would risk crossings if the government created safe pathways.”On Wednesday Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, insisted the government’s plan to curb Channel crossings was working, although he admitted there was “more to do”.This week French police were recorded saying they had orders not to stop people getting into their boats and setting off for the UK. One told Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, as he stood on Hardelot beach, south of Boulogne-sur-Mer: “Our order is to let them go.”More than 900 people have crossed the Channel in the past week as people smugglers take advantage of a calm sea. A total of 13,376 migrants have crossed this year, down from 24,389 at the same point last year.A government spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened to hear about these deaths. Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit.“We will continue working relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys.”Explore more on these topicsMigrationImmigration and asylumFranceWater transportEuropeRefugeesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Race to extinguish blazes across Europe as fire weather breaks records | Europe weather | The Guardian
description: Figures show hot, dry, windy conditions in EU are 43% more severe than the average over last 20 years
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Figures show hot, dry, windy conditions in EU are 43% more severe than the average over last 20 years
Content: Residents and firefighters work to extinguish an advancing wildfire near Formariz, in Zamora province, Spain, on Wednesday.Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/ReutersView image in fullscreenResidents and firefighters work to extinguish an advancing wildfire near Formariz, in Zamora province, Spain, on Wednesday.Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/ReutersEurope weatherRace to extinguish blazes across Europe as fire weather breaks recordsFigures show hot, dry, windy conditions in EU are 43% more severe than the average over last 20 yearsAjit NiranjanThu 30 Jul 2026 14.16 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFire weather in the EU has broken records for severity for this time of year, data shows, as firefighters race to extinguish blazes across the Mediterranean.Inflamed by carbon pollution, the hot, dry and windy weather across the EU from the start of the year until the end of July has been 43% more severe than the average for the same period over the last two decades, data from the European Forest Fire Information Service (Effis) shows.Three firefighters died in Greece on Tuesday, officials said, while firefighters inFrance and Spainmade overnight progress tackling monster blazes that have burned dangerously close to large cities.Fire weather severity chartThe figures, which were published on Thursday but may be revised further, showed that so far this year 435,000 hectares (1,075,000 acres) have burned, roughly triple the recent historical average. The devastation is the result of 1,400 fires, more than double the average.InFrance, where a blaze in the dense pine forests near Bordeaux grew so big it generated a rare thunderstorm that could ignite more fires, a total of 91,000 hectares have burned, according to Effis, breaking the country’s record for a full year of fires – with one month of summer still to go.Fire-ravaged south-western France experienced its “first somewhat optimistic day” on Thursday since wildfires broke out more than a week ago, said Sophie Brocas, the prefect of Gironde. “It is the first somewhat optimistic day, because we have the feeling that we are beginning to return to normal life and that things are starting to improve significantly.”Regional authorities in Gironde said the fire remained under control after a quiet night, with work continuing around its edge and in active hotspots. They said temperatures on Thursday had been expected to be “fairly favourable” after Wednesday’s 38C heat and strong winds hampered firefighting efforts.They allowed a further 84,000 people to return home on Thursday, after 60,000 people were given the green light on Tuesday.Chart showing weekly number of fires across the EU this year, compared with the 2006-25 averageInSpain, which experienced its largest wildfire on record, west of Madrid, a total of 207,000 hectares have burned across the country, according to Effis. The figure is nearly five times the average for this time of year but shy of the devastation reached by late July during the 2022 fires.Regional authorities in Madrid said the fire situation had been declared “stable” but residents of seven housing estates were unable to return home. Pedro Sánchez, the prime minister, announced the end of the national emergency in the regions of Ávila and Madrid on Thursday morning.However, a new fire near the Portuguese border prompted the evacuation of 600 people, officials said. Aemet, the Spanish meteorological agency, said temperatures above 35C were expected on Thursday in large areas of the interior, with some regions bracing for highs of 40C-42C.View image in fullscreenA wildfire approaches a building in Castellón, Spain, on 25 July.Photograph: Eva Manez/ReutersWildfires in France and Spain have forced more than 300,000 people from their homes and tourist accommodation this month, prompting both countries to request EU support in the form of firefighters, fire engines, and water-dropping planes and helicopters.Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, thanked firefighters for their “courage and commitment” on Wednesday as crews sent by Romania andGreeceextended their stays. “As the fires in France and Spain continue to ravage, European solidarity knows no limit,” she said.Further difficult weeks were expected as fires worsened inItalyand Greece, officials at the EU’s crisis management centre said on Wednesday morning. Later that day, the Greek fire department announced the deaths of two firefighters who were tackling a blaze on the island of Crete, and of another in the south of the mainland.area burned chartGreece has so far had a relatively calm fire season, Effis data up to 29 July shows, with slightly fewer fires than usual and a burned area well below the average.Meanwhile, Italy andPortugalhave had near-record breaking numbers of fires, and burned areas well above average. The countries have so far been spared the scale of destruction experienced by France and Spain, but one firefighter died in Italy last week while tackling blazes in Sicily.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWildfires on the Greek island of Crete have killed two firefighters, with another killed tackling blazes in the south of the mainland.Photograph: ReutersClimate breakdown is causing Europe to burn this summer, with a series of almost back-to-back heatwaves drying out vegetation, which then provides a vast fuel surplus that has allowed small fires to grow into raging infernos.Sánchez repeated calls to create a “national pact” to address the climate emergency during a visit to a command post on Wednesday.“These fires may or may not be caused by humans, but in any case, they increase exponentially as a result of these high temperatures, low humidity, and also the atmospheric phenomena that these fires, these large fires, cause in our forests,” he said.View image in fullscreenFirefighters in Cercosa, Portugal, battling a wildfire this month.Photograph: Paulo Cunha/EPAA study by an international team of scientists,published in the journal Scientific Reports, found that since the 1980s, the number of fires in southern Europe and the area burned had steadily declined as authorities became better at preventing and suppressing them.The study, published on Thursday, found the trend began to reverse in 2018. It found that summer days conducive to strong wildfires had more than doubled since 1981 across large parts of Portugal, Spain, France, Italy and Greece; in parts of France and Spain, the summertime fire weather index over the last decade was up to 50% higher than the 1981-2010 average.The scientists said this had resulted in European fires shifting to “fewer, but more intense and larger events”, with fires that escaped initial attacks by firefighters able to “quickly become catastrophic”.José Miguel Viñas, a meteorologist at the forecaster Meteored, who was not involved in the research, said it scientifically demonstrated a fact that southern Europe and other parts of the world had observed in recent years.“Increasingly extreme conditions of heat, dryness and wind are fuelling large forest fires,” he said. “Once started, they spread rapidly and become uncontrollable, overwhelming the firefighting efforts.”Rapid analyseshave found western Europe’s June heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” in a world without climate breakdown, while the level of soil dryness – a major factor in bigger blazes – is five times more likely than it would be in a climate 1.4C cooler. The heatwaves are estimated to have killed at least 10,000 people and cost grain farmers€2bn (£1.7bn) in lost crops.The increase in temperatures from fossil fuel pollution has come as rural regions in southern Europe have hollowed out, with farms being abandoned as populations age and young people move to cities. The resultant overgrowth in vegetation has troubled firefighters and wildfire researchers across the Mediterranean.Explore more on these topicsEurope weatherWildfiresEuropean UnionClimate crisisExtreme heatExtreme weatherFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian missile destroys US firm’s Kyiv drone factory | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Strike on Terminal Autonomy plant appears to be first time in the war that Moscow has targeted a US company
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Strike on Terminal Autonomy plant appears to be first time in the war that Moscow has targeted a US company
Content: A deep-strike drone. The plant hit by Russia made AQ-400 Scythe and AQ-100 Bayonet deep-strike drones (not pictured).Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenA deep-strike drone. The plant hit by Russia made AQ-400 Scythe and AQ-100 Bayonet deep-strike drones (not pictured).Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUkraineRussian missile destroys US firm’s Kyiv drone factoryStrike on Terminal Autonomy plant appears to be first time in the war that Moscow has targeted a US companyAram Rostonin WashingtonThu 30 Jul 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA drone factory in Kyiv destroyed by a Russian ballistic missile on Friday was owned by a US corporation registered in Delaware, in what appears to be the first time Moscow has targeted a US company in the conflict.Terminal Autonomy makes precision “deep-strike” drones with guidance systems that are resistant to Russian jamming signals, according to a person familiar with the company.The phrase “terminal autonomy” refers to the final phase of a kamikaze drone’s attack in which AI takes over control of the weapon after the defending force jams radio waves or mobile service.State records show that the corporation was registered in Delaware in 2023. The company’s website says: “We deploy AI-guided loitering munitions and precision munitions, which are already in active service against enemy assets on the frontline.”Terminal Autonomy did not reply to an emailed request for comment. The Ukrainian defence ministry also did not respond to an email.Anthony Vinci, a former senior US intelligence officer who wrote The Fourth Intelligence Revolution: The Future of Espionage and the Battle to Save America, said: “The Russians don’t care who owns the manufacturing facility. It’s still a target. They don’t care if it’s American or someone else’s.”Early in July, Donald Trump, who had previously been lukewarm to efforts to arm Ukraine, said the US would license Ukraine tomanufacture Patriot anti-aircraft missiles.Vinci said: “I do think if Patriot missiles or any American system was manufactured inUkraine, I think the Russians would target that manufacturing facility.”The Russian state news agency Tassfirst reportedon the attack on Sunday, citing the Russian defence ministry as its source. The report did not disclose that an American company owned the factory but mentioned that “specialists from a Ukrainian-American company” had worked there. Tass accurately reported that the plant made AQ-400 Scythe and AQ-100 Bayonet drones.Nobody was killed in the attack, according to a source familiar with the company.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia accused of violating Polish airspace after missile explosion near village  | Poland | The Guardian
description: Polish PM visits scene of crater thought to have occurred during deadly wave of attacks on Ukraine
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Polish PM visits scene of crater thought to have occurred during deadly wave of attacks on Ukraine
Content: Emergency crews comb the area where a missile landed near a village 50 miles from the Ukraine border.Photograph: Fot. Jakub Orzechowski/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/ReutersView image in fullscreenEmergency crews comb the area where a missile landed near a village 50 miles from the Ukraine border.Photograph: Fot. Jakub Orzechowski/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/ReutersPolandRussia accused of violating Polish airspace after missile explosion near villagePolish PM visits scene of crater thought to have occurred during deadly wave of attacks on UkrainePeter Beaumontand agenciesThu 30 Jul 2026 13.22 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 22.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has been accused of violating Polish airspace, after a missile exploded in a field in the east of the country, triggering Nato air defences, in the midst of a massive air raid that killed 13 people in neighbouringUkraine.Polish authorities said that the explosion near the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia, close to Lublin, had created a 10-metre-wide crater. Residents of Tarnawa-Kolonia reported hearing an explosion at about 4am that shook the windows of their homes, police said.Nato’s supreme ⁠allied commander forEurope, Gen Alexus Grynkewich, said: “​Nato ​will continue ​to take all necessary ​measures ‌to defend Nato ​territory.”The Polish prime minister,Donald Tusk, speaking at the scene of the explosion, in a field about 50 miles from the Ukrainian border, said the missile was most likely Russian. “From the analysis of most of the traces, the recovered fragments point to a Russian KH-101 missile,” he told journalists.He said there was no reason to think thatPolandhad been the target of the missile but said the Polish military had been prepared to shoot it down if it threatened a built-up area.As the attacks on Ukraine took place, Poland scrambled fighter jets to protect its airspace, its armed forces said.Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said in a post on X that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile had crossed into Poland.The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.View image in fullscreenPeople take shelter inside a Kyiv metro station during the Russian attack.Photograph: Alina Smutko/ReutersAntónio Costa, the president of the EU council, said on X: “Last night, Russia launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine. During the attack, Polish airspace was also violated, underlining once again that Russia’s aggression is a threat to the security of Europe as a whole.”Ursula von der ​Leyen, the European Commission president, said the ⁠Russian missile incident ⁠in ⁠Poland was ​another “unacceptable violation” of the ⁠EU’s airspace.Ukraine war briefing: F-16 crashes while chasing Russian air targetsRead moreAt least 13 people in Ukraine – including one inKyiv– died in Thursday’s attacks, which extended as far ⁠as the western city of Lviv.President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ⁠said Russia appeared to have used a North Korean missile in an attack near the central city of Kryvyi Rih, which local officials said killed ⁠six people, including two girls, aged five and 12.“In Radushne, the ​Russians ‌used a ‌missile from North ‌Korea for the first time in a long time – that is what preliminary data shows,” Zelenskyy ‌said in his nightly video address. “The alliance ​of Moscow bastards with the mad regime in North Korea – for ⁠missiles, for the ​North Korean ​contingent here ​in Europe, on our ​borders, ‌and ​for ​the killing of our Ukrainian children.”Another six people, including two children, were killed in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava.The military administration for Kyiv confirmed one death, with the mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reporting fires in several districts. Earlier, he posted: “The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!”View image in fullscreenDestruction in Kyiv after Wednesday night’s attack.Photograph: ReutersIn ‌Lviv, close to Poland, rescue workers were scrambling to clear rubble to reach those trapped after Russian missiles damaged two blocks of flats and injured 26 people, officials said.Late on Wednesday, Zelenskyy had posted: “The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago, and there is a high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight … Please, in all regions of Ukraine, pay attention to air raid alerts today and stay safe.”Zelenskyy also repeated his request to Ukraine’s allies to supply Kyiv with the missiles its air defence system lacked. “It is important that our partners fully ​understand what is happening and that the protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness, or lack of willingness, to provide air defence missiles.”View image in fullscreenThe Kyiv sky is lit up during a Russian missile attack on Wednesday night.Photograph: Gleb Garanich/ReutersRussia’s defence ministry, commenting on the strikes, said it had used land, sea and air-launched missiles, as well as strike drones, during the raid and claimed it had targeted military industrial facilities.Elsewhere on Thursday, the ⁠Ukrainian military struck four Russian ⁠tankers ​in the Black Sea ⁠and the Sea of ⁠Azov, Ukraine’s drone ​forces ‌commander, ‌Robert Brovdi, said.Brovdi said on the Telegram app that 205 tankers – ​130 in the Sea of Azov ⁠and 75 ​in the ​Black ​Sea –had ​been ‌hit in the ​past ​three weeks.Explore more on these topicsPolandRussiaUkraineKyivEuropeDonald TusknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was a big shock’: new border rules left couple stuck in Kraków after living in UK for 80 years | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Maria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to Bury
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Maria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to Bury
Content: Maria and Czeslaw Krupa with two family members  outside the Tauron Arena in Kraków.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyView image in fullscreenMaria and Czeslaw Krupa with two family members  outside the Tauron Arena in Kraków.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyBrexit‘It was a big shock’: new border rules left couple stuck in Kraków after living in UK for 80 yearsMaria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to BuryLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Polish citizens who have lived in the UK for nearly 80 years after their parents fled the second world war have spoken of their terrifying experience after being told they did not have post-Brexit rights to return to the UK.In May, while visiting Poland, they learned that although they had been welcomed as refugees after the war, they now needed special post-Brexit paperwork to return to their home in Bury,Greater Manchester.Maria Krupa, 85, and her husband, Czeslaw, 92, who met in the UK and went on to marry and settle in Bury, were issued with “aliens’ registration cards” and have travelled extensively as adults without anyone asking them for their immigration status.View image in fullscreenMaria and Czeslaw Krupa in Kraków airport.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyCzeslaw, who came from Lviv which was then part ofPoland, and Maria, who left her home town in what is now Belarus as an infant, had travelled to Poland in May to meet surviving family members.But Ryanair refused to allow them to board the flight for their return journey on the grounds that they had neither proof of the right to live in the UK nor thenew electronic travel authorisation(ETA) now required for foreign tourists entering the UK.“It was a big shock,” said Maria. “We were very, very disappointed and a bit upset because my husband takes a lot of medicine because of a stroke to his spinal cord.”They had arrived in Southampton in 1947 and 1948 as the young dependants of displaced Polish service members who had been evacuated from their homes in 1940 and later became part of Gen Władysław Anders’s Polish army that served in Persia, India, the Middle East and Africa.Anders’s army played a key role in the defeat of the Third Reich and had integrated into the British military command structure after friction with the Soviets in 1942.“We tried to explain toRyanairthat our fathers fought for Poland and England in the war, but they refused to let us on the plane because they said they would have to pay a big fine,” said Maria.“My husband was really upset,” she said, explaining that Czeslaw used a mobility scooter and was on a lot of medication after the stroke. He has difficulty getting in and out of cars and “just wanted to get home”, she said.View image in fullscreenCzeslaw Krupa, left, with his brother and cousin in Africa in 1944.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyThey are speaking out to help others who might be in the same position. “It was a big, big shock because we never heard of this and we never thought for one minute that after nearly 80 years someone would tell us we couldn’t go home,” said Maria.Kate Smart, the chief executive of Settled, who helped the Krupas, said the charity was seeing “thousands of cases” like the Krupas’. “It is a really common occurrence, almost on a daily basis,” she said.The EU settlement scheme was launched in 2019 to give EU citizens living in the UK the documentary evidence needed to travel as they had done under the pre-Brexit, free-movement rules.Many of the people seen by Settled are elderly people who have British children and grandchildren. “They have nobody in their family circle who thinks like immigrants so they don’t talk about things like ‘settled status’,” said Smart.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMaria Krupa as a child in Karachi, then part of India, where her father was stationed in 1943. Displaced Polish people were housed in refugee camps.Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa familyMaria said she had never thought to get a British passport as she had never needed it in the previous 80 years and it had never crossed her mind. “It was really important. I didn’t think of it as sort of weakening my identity. I love England. I mean, I always say, I’m very grateful to England, you know, to have taken so many people, you know thousands after the war. But I just thought it was important that we stay Polish,” she said.After being forced to leave the airport late on a Sunday night in May, they returned the next day with an ETA but the couple had to pose as tourists, claiming they lived in Poland as the online form would not accept their British address.View image in fullscreenMaria and Czeslaw Krupa celebrate Czeslaw’s 90th birthday in Bury.Photograph: Image courtesy of the Krupa familyMaria said: “When we arrived in England we were terrified. We had to be careful about what we said. We were terrified because they started asking questions and we thought we are not going to lie again and have to tell the truth.”After going to Citizens Advice in Bury, they were connected with Settled. Smart commended theHome Officeresolution centre for its swift action after the charity submitted a no-time-limit application that resulted in settled status for the Krupas last week.She appealed to the government to take note of the issues with the EU settlement scheme, arguing “a process should have kicked in at the airport” when an issue such as this one arose.A spokesperson said the Home Office would encourage people to check their immigration status before they travel, but anyone in a similar situation to the Krupas should makea no-time-limit applicationto get the paperwork they needed to travel in and out of the country.“Anyone settled in the UK without up-to-date evidence of their status is encouraged to make a no-time-limit application. This will give them access to an eVisa and facilitate seamless future travel,” they said.Explore more on these topicsBrexitHome OfficeImmigration and asylumEuropean UnionForeign policyEuropeSecond world warfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia prepares sea and possible land offensive against Houthis | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Yemeni sources say Saudis concentrating forces for what could be attack in central Yemen
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Yemeni sources say Saudis concentrating forces for what could be attack in central Yemen
Content: Saudi Arabia security forces take part in a military parade in Mecca in May. Saudi forces have been seen withdrawing from the east of Yemen in what could be preparation for a land offensive.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSaudi Arabia security forces take part in a military parade in Mecca in May. Saudi forces have been seen withdrawing from the east of Yemen in what could be preparation for a land offensive.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesSaudi ArabiaSaudi Arabia prepares sea and possible land offensive against HouthisYemeni sources say Saudis concentrating forces for what could be attack in central YemenPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorThu 30 Jul 2026 13.50 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi Arabia is preparing for a major military offensive against the Houthis by sea and possibly by land in central Yemen, Yemeni sources believe, in a move to break the chokehold on its oil exports through the southern Red Sea.Saudi forces have been seen withdrawing from the east ofYemenin what could be preparation for a land offensive. At the same time, Riyadh is trying to organise a naval coalition to protect shipping from Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait.The Saudi defence ministry said on Thursday that 14 states including Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Sudan and Djibouti had issued a joint statement supporting a multinational maritime defence coalition.The Iran-alignedHouthis, who control Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, and much of its Red Sea coastline, announced on 20 July that they were implementing a blockade against Saudi ships, but they have denied they are planning to impose tolls on all ships.US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warnRead moreThe group says it will lift the blockade once Saudi Arabia lifts its blockade on Yemen, positioning the dispute as over the future of Yemen and not directly aboutIran. Saudi Arabia intervened in the Yemeni civil war in 2015 in support of the country’s UN-recognised government against the Houthi rebels.Riyadh has also asked the US and a group of European countries including Germany, France, the UK and Italy to join a Red Sea coalition.The EU already has a naval protection mission, Aspides, operating in the Red Sea and it remains unclear if the Houthis are mounting a general blockade or one directed solely at Saudi Arabia.Houthi forces said on 25 July they had hit “sensitive” oil transport sites inside Saudi Arabia linking eastern province oilfields to a Red Sea export hub.If the Red Sea route is closed to Saudi shipping in addition to the strait of Hormuz blockade on the other side of the Arabian peninsula, the kingdom’s oil export will be severely constrained.map of Middle East conflictUp to 80% of Saudi crude exports were shipped through the strait of Hormuz before the Iran war began. The Red Sea has therefore grown in importance, with more than half of Saudi oil now transported overland to loading terminals at the port city of Yanbu.Saudi strikes in Iraqon Wednesday killed at least 20 people as it hit back at Iraqi militia for striking its oil facilities. Donald Trump said the joint US-Saudi attacks had been mounted with the agreement of the Iraqi government, a claim that Baghdad did not confirm.US joins forces with Saudis to strike Tehran-backed militias in IraqRead moreThe Saudi defence minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, held an urgent meeting with Trump and JD Vance on Wednesday to discuss the next steps. The Saudis are keen to show they will defend themselves and their industry, but are not willing to escalate the war against Iran, arguing that the disagreements between the US and Iran can still be settled by diplomacy.The troop movements inside Yemen involve concentrating forces for what could be an attack on al-Bayda, a governorate in central southern Yemen captured by the Houthis in 2020-21, the sources said.Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has erupted in the past fortnight with the Houthis mounting attacks against Saudi Aramco facilities. The strikes inside Saudi Arabia came hours after Saudi airstrikes targeted Houthi-controlled sites in the port of Hodeidah and a third Saudi commercial vessel was attacked in the Red Sea.Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have been vying for control of Yemen for more than a decade and an uneasy status quo has unravelled over the past month.The tensions inside Yemen would be reduced if the Gulf states and Iran could reach an agreement for the reopening of the strait of Hormuz. Talks between Oman and Iran are continuing, with Iran demanding that all shipping enter the strait through a northern route close to Iran’s coast.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaYemenHouthisOilIranStrait of HormuzIraqnewsShareReuse this content

title: US hits dozens of targets in Iran overnight as peace efforts under threat | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Central Command says strikes aimed at diminishing Iranian military while mediators say talks are continuing
Author: William Christou
Headline: Central Command says strikes aimed at diminishing Iranian military while mediators say talks are continuing
