Content: A US fighter jet launches amid the ongoing war on Iran, a day after joint US-Saudi strikes on Iraq.Photograph: U.S. Central Command/XView image in fullscreenA US fighter jet launches amid the ongoing war on Iran, a day after joint US-Saudi strikes on Iraq.Photograph: U.S. Central Command/XUS-Israel war on IranUS hits dozens of targets in Iran overnight as peace efforts under threatCentral Command says strikes aimed at diminishing Iranian military while mediators say talks are continuingMiddle East crisis – live updatesWilliam Christouin BeirutThu 30 Jul 2026 11.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 23.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US struckIranovernight and Tehran retaliated at US allies in the region, reigniting the low-intensity, tit-for-tat war as mediators struggled to pull the two countries back to the negotiating table.The US carried out overnight strikes on Iran – the first inmore than five days – hours afterDonald Trumpvowed to hit the country “very hard” following Tehran’s targeting of a base in Jordan that hosts American troops.The latest attacks come after adays-long pause in violence between the two sides. The resumption of fighting and the stalling of the diplomatic process has brought the war into uncharted territory and prompted concerns of a renewed regional war.US Central Command said it hit dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran as part of a “heavy wave of strikes”, including military command centres and missile and drone facilities, in a two-hour wave of strikes.Map of attacks across Middle East since 7 July“The strikes aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighbouring Gulf countries,” it said.Iranian state media said three people were injured in attacks on the island of Qeshm, in the strait of Hormuz, and that explosions were also reported in Khuzestan province, to the north-west. The IRGC said three of its members were killed by US strikes in the north-western province of Zanjan.Jordan reported incoming missiles for the second day in a row, with no reports of casualties, while Kuwait accused Iran of carrying out a strike that hit a building, killing one person. Both strikes are believed to have been part of an Iranian retaliation against the US attacks.View image in fullscreenScreengrab from a video showing rescuers clearing rubble to search for victims after a strike in Qeshm, Iran.Photograph: IRIB/ReutersMediators insisted talks were continuing despite the renewed exchange of strikes, with the Pakistani foreign ministry spokesperson, Tahir Andrabi, saying they were doing their “utmost to bring all parties back” to the negotiating table.The renewed strikescame after theUS partnered with Saudi Arabiato strike Iran-backed militias in neighbouring Iraq on Wednesday, killing at least 20 fighters and six Iranian advisers. The attacks reignited the armed conflict between Iran and the US and extinguished hopes that diplomacy would be given space to breathe.US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warnRead moreElsewhere, drone strikes led to fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian gas import hub at the port of Damietta, according to the British maritime security firm Ambrey. The Egyptian government confirmed that a drone attack ignited the blaze, but it was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes on a US-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker. No injuries were reported and the port remained operational.It was the first time Egypt has been attacked since the Iran war started in late February and signalled a potential widening of the conflict.The Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen said they were not responsible.View image in fullscreenDamietta port in Egypt, where a drone attack caused fires on two ships.Photograph: Damietta Port Authority/ReutersAsked during an Oval Office event if Iran was behind the strikes on the natural gas vessels, Trump responded: “It’s a little more of the same.”“In the meantime, we’re going to be hitting them very hard because it’s our turn to hit them,” he added.Analysts said the flare-ups on multiple fronts after several days of relative calm had pushed the region into “uncharted territory”. They also underscored the difficulty of winding down a five-month conflict that has jolted the world economy and which remains unpopular among Americans.The fighting was also likely to add to concerns that the US is further drawing down its already diminished stockpiles of sophisticated munitions needed to defend its bases and allies.Wednesday’s joint US-Saudi strikes onIraqcame after Riyadh had accused Iraqi militias of firing drones against its oil facilities. An umbrella group of Iraqi militias initially denied the allegations.10:05US-Iran strikes risk regional war in Middle East - The LatestThe Popular Mobilization Forces, a coalition of primarily Shia Iranian-backed armed groups that is officially under the command of the Iraqi military, saidat least 20 fighters were killed and 32 wounded in the overnight strikes.Iran’s deputy governor for political, security and social affairs in Markazi province told Iranian state media that four advisers from Tehran were also killed.The coalition joined the fight against the Islamic State group after it seized large sections of Iraq in 2014. The Iraqi government later designated the coalition as an “independent military formation” within the armed forces, but the militias have significant autonomy and some have attacked US facilities.Before the latest eruption, mediators had expressed optimism about bringing the US and Iran back to the negotiating table. An interim agreement collapsed in recent weeks over renewed fighting in the strait of Hormuz.The renewed hostilities sent oil prices spiking. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 7.3% to more than $88 a barrel.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows smoke coming out of an oil facility in Abqaiq, eastern Saudi Arabia, on 27 July.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus  Sentinel-2/ReutersSaudi Arabia is also locked in a renewed conflict with the Houthis. The Iran-backed militants havedeclared a blockade of Saudi shippingthat could choke off another crucial Middle East trade route, the Bab el-Mandeb strait from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden.On Wednesday, the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, met Trump and the US vice-president, JD Vance, the Associated Press reported. The Saudi decision to conduct joint strikes with the US was meant to send a message to Iran that it was displeased with strikes on its energy facilities, but the kingdom still preferred negotiations rather than a return to war, according to AP.On Monday, the Houthis said they had launched drones targeting oil facilities used to transport oil acrossSaudi Arabiato the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, a key bypass for Saudi exports blocked by Iran’s chokehold on the strait of Hormuz.The rebels said the attack was in response to a Saudi drone they said had breached Yemen’s airspace.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranSaudi ArabiaStrait of HormuzDonald TrumpIranJordanIraqnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s war with the US is not its only conflict as internal crises mount | Iran | The Guardian
description: Government fears social discontent on ‘most important battlefield’ of economy and livelihoods as war takes its toll amid anti-state dissent
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Government fears social discontent on ‘most important battlefield’ of economy and livelihoods as war takes its toll amid anti-state dissent
Content: Missiles on display at Azadi Square, Tehran, on Thursday. As war with the US escalates, a convergence of Iran’s conflicts, internal and external, becomes more likely.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/Wana/ReutersView image in fullscreenMissiles on display at Azadi Square, Tehran, on Thursday. As war with the US escalates, a convergence of Iran’s conflicts, internal and external, becomes more likely.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/Wana/ReutersIranAnalysisIran’s war with the US is not its only conflict as internal crises mountPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorGovernment fears social discontent on ‘most important battlefield’ of economy and livelihoods as war takes its toll amid anti-state dissentMiddle East crisis live – latest updatesThu 30 Jul 2026 11.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.03 EDTShareIran, in the middle of an escalating five-month war with the US, continues to stumble from one internal crisis to another – whether it is over public executions, the rising cost of living, the alleged bias of the state broadcaster or even the post-midnight destruction of pavements outside liberal-leaning Tehran cafes. Very little that happens inIran, cultural or political, momentous or trivial, does so uncontested.But there is now a growing threat of a long diplomatic deadlock, forged by mutual distrust in which neither side believes the other will stick to any agreement. That impasse has occurred as the war broadens, drawing in Yemen, Iraq and now Egypt. In Iran, at least, the advocates of escalation are winning. As a result, a convergence of Iran’s conflicts, internal and external, becomes more likely.Parts of the Trump administration and the Iranian opposition – includingReza Pahlavi, the son of the former deposed Shah – have never abandoned the belief that the Iranian government is on the brink of collapse.What is true is that the picture of cohesive if brittle society presented by themillions attending the funeralof the supreme leader Ali Khamenei earlier this month revealed only one side of the public mood.View image in fullscreenMourners gather in Mashhad to mark the burial of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei. In Tehran, millions attended the six-day funeral, but this reveals only one side of the public mood.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/Reuters‘We just practise enduring’Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, rarely tires of warning that the conditions that led tothe bloody protests in Januaryremain.At a recent meeting of the supreme judicial council he argued: “Iran is engaged in a full-scale war. Today’s war is not just a war of missiles; the enemy has come to the conclusion that it cannot force the Iranian nation to surrender through military attacks. The most important battlefield today is the economy and livelihood of the people. If economic pressures cause social discontent to form and this discontent spreads, the enormous social capital that the people have created in support of the system will be lost.”Undoubtedly dissent, in the form of despair, exists.Golshan Fathi, a Tehran human rights activist, recently wrote on her social media page: “The same sick cycle repeats … morning … the call to prayer, news of an execution … noon with power cuts, afternoon the water stops … dusk, the anxiety of war and renewed attacks on cities, and at midnight, the earth trembles.“And tomorrow, the same story again. Caught between natural disasters, management failures, and man-made crises … every day we don’t live, we just practise enduring. Repetition, repetition, repetition … until a weary land no longer asks: ‘What will tomorrow bring?’ It just waits to see: ‘When will the next crisis arrive?’”View image in fullscreenCars burn in a Tehran street during a January protest which began over the collapse of the currency’s value.Photograph: ReutersDissent in the form of political protest also exists, whether it isthose inside jailsor citizens in the squares of Isfahan protesting against the current wave ofintimidatory public executions. Many critics ask why the punishment of the accused takes place in public gallows, yet their trials are held in secret courts.On Monday the political bureau of the Nation’s Union party warned that ignoring the protests over the wave of executions could have “devastating consequences”, and urged academics and religious scholars to intervene to end this state violence.‘War has no winners’Azar Mansouri,once a close reformist ally of Pezeshkian, warned last week at the annual meeting of the Iranian reformist front about a small but vocal group that seemed determined to portray negotiated agreements with the US as retreats or defeat. War, she warned, “is not just a confrontation between military forces and armies. It is the destruction of the economy, the erosion of social capital, the spread of despair, the emigration of elites, the increase in poverty and the loss of opportunities for development. Ultimately, it threatens the future of the nation.”Similarly a “we do not want war” statement signed by 268 political activists this month said they believed the overwhelming majority opposed war, and this should be tested in a public vote. Another letter from 1,000 activists linked with the former president Mohammad Khatami warned “the contemporary experience of Iran is that war has no winners. Those who advocate negotiations should not be slandered.”What unites these initiatives is a fear that diplomats are losing, and Iran is being edged into a forever war that can be portrayed as an Iranian-Arab war, a war that would be to Israel’s advantage.Yet opposition to the whole principle of negotiation with America – fuelled by Donald Trump’s own erratic behaviour – is being voiced by hardliners, in street rallies and more recently on unofficial billboards.The sway of the hardliners lies less in their strength in parliament – many were elected on low turnouts and anyway have been deposed from key committees in parliament – but in the belief that a network of deep-state support exists in the military and in the office of the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei. The absence of Khamenei from public view makes it harder to resolve the controversy about whether the family sees any purpose in negotiations with America.View image in fullscreenAn outdoor cafe in northern Tehran. Cafes have been described by hardliners as anti-Islamic places.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APThe closure of cafes, or the destruction of the sidewalks around them, is also seen as a crude attempt to shape debate. Last year the prominent hardlinerSaeed Jalilidescribed the cafes as an anti-Islamic “third space” beyond the dormitory or the office where people go to escape loneliness. “In this concept the family loses any meaning. This stands in opposition to Islam’s philosophy of marriage.”Alleged broadcaster biasDespite being a conservative newspaper, Jomhouri-e Eslami complained “an addiction to violating the dignity of one’s political opponents is increasing every day”. That in turn is, in part, a reference to the criticism of negotiators meted out by the publicly funded national broadcaster IRIB, long seen as a preserve of those opposed to talks with the west. Many see IRIB as an exclusive platform for the hardliners rather than a mirror of a diverse society.The crisis between the government and the broadcaster is now out in the open after interventions by Pezeshkian and Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf,the chief negotiator, were censored.The government in a statement complained: “Censorship of the president’s speech, unilateral destruction of the government’s performance, and efforts to destroy the memorandum of understanding that was formed to get the country through the crisis and protect national interests are no longer media criticism; they are a stand against national cohesion, empathy, and unity.“The question is clear: is the Iranian broadcasting system with the people, government, and interests of Iran or with those who benefit from division, tension, and polarisation? The national media should be the voice of Iranian unity, not a platform for destroying the government and disrupting national understanding.”There are calls for a complete overhaul of the organisation’s accountability when a new head is appointed this September. At one level the politics of the national broadcaster should not matter, since surveys suggest less than 12% of the country watch it. The difficulty for the government is that this leaves audiences watching hostile foreign satellite channels instead.Economic toll of warThis tension over the national broadcaster coincides with a period of unprecedented economic pressure. In the next six months food rationing might become necessary, Majid-Reza Hariri, the head of the Iran-China chamber of commerce, warned this week. Gholamhossein Mohammadi, the deputy minister of labour, said more than a million jobs had been lost as a result of the war.View image in fullscreenPeople walk through Tehran’s Grand Bazaar. Food prices are increasing as inflation rises, yet the value of the minimum wage has plummeted.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APIn a way rationing – through food price inflation – has already started as Iranians are being forced to change their diets because of the cost of fruit, eggs and chicken. Year-on-year food inflation reached 134% in July, meaning the average household’s monthly food budget has more than doubled in a year. Overall inflation is at 84%. In a further sign of the long-term pressure on living standards, figures released this week showed the real value of the minimum wage had plummeted.Azadeh Mokhtari, one of the best chroniclers of the impact of the economy on everyday lives, wrote this week: “Society has reached a point where ‘I don’t have the patience’ and ‘I don’t have the energy’ have become everyday phrases. No one asks: ‘How are you?’ any more because everyone knows the answer.”The toll of the war on the economy has spread everywhere from the internet to tourism. All 400 hotels on Kish Island in the strait of Hormuz – the site of US bombing on Thursday – have shut. As many as 30,000 Iranians visited medical centres during the two wars in 2025 and 2026.Civilian facilitiessuch as the Bushehr meteorological centre have been almost destroyed and the Bushehr airport has become unusable. The Chabahar maritime watchtower has been completely destroyed; 12 bridges and two tunnel openings have been damaged. This will take decades to repair.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows airstrike damage to Bushehr airport, airbase and naval facilities after Israel-US strikes in March.Photograph: Satellite Image ©2026 Vantor/EPACrisis of trustsYet one of the biggest bombshells was detonated on national television when Zabihullah Khodayian, the head of the General Inspection Organisation, a national audit office, revealed the scale of foreign-exchange corruption among so-called trusts, highly secretive government-sponsored bodies set up to evade US sanctions.These trusts, embedded in the Iranian political system for years, are entities set up to transfer Iranian oil income outside the network of sanctions. It is self-evident that they act in a nontransparent way, and siphon off public money. Khodayian confirmed as much, saying one trust that was given $200m (£149m) had not returned the money, and had also left the country. He said a further 229 individuals owed the state a total of €23.5bn (£20.2bn), while the judiciary said cases were being opened against nearly 50 individuals.It is still unclear on what basis these trusts were selected, how much they charge, what guarantees they have provided to preserve the country’s resources, and how they are held accountable. But there is a growing chance that a major scandal is about to be revealed that could involve Iran’s elite. If so, all the talk of social cohesion across the classes will start to look very hollow.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranProtestHuman rightsMiddle East and north AfricaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Diane Abbott and Joani Reid readmitted as Labour MPs | Labour | The Guardian
description: Both MPs have had the parliamentary whip restored following separate independent disciplinary processes
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Both MPs have had the parliamentary whip restored following separate independent disciplinary processes
Content: Diane Abbott apologised after an independent investigation into her conduct concluded.Photograph: Beresford Hodge/ReutersView image in fullscreenDiane Abbott apologised after an independent investigation into her conduct concluded.Photograph: Beresford Hodge/ReutersLabourDiane Abbott and Joani Reid readmitted as Labour MPsBoth MPs have had the parliamentary whip restored following separate independent disciplinary processesAletha AduPolitical correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 18.54 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 16.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMPs Diane Abbott and Joani Reid have been readmitted into Labour and had the parliamentary whip restored, just under two weeks into Andy Burnham’s premiership.The party confirmed that this followed separate independent disciplinary processes, althoughLaboursaid the leadership played no role in either decision.Abbott, 72, the mother of the House of Commons,was suspended for a second time last summerafter saying she did not regret comments about racism that had led to her initial loss of the whip in 2023.Reid, the MP for East Kilbride and Strathaven who was elected in 2024, voluntarily relinquished the whip in March this year. Her husband had been arrested on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service in a case linked to China. Reid has never been accused of wrongdoing.The Guardian understands from Labour party sources that Reid has never been party to the police investigations into alleged Chinese spying.View image in fullscreenJoani Reid voluntarily relinquished the Labour whip in March.Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/AlamyAbbott has apologised after the investigation concluded. It is understood the disciplinary process resulted in her receiving a formal warning from the party.A Labour party spokesperson said: “The Labour party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and party members. The party assesses any alleged breaches of such standards independently of the leadership and political interference.“Following a process conducted under Labour party rules and approved by the independent review board,Diane Abbottand Joani Reid have been readmitted to the Labour party and have had the Labour whip restored in the House of Commons.“Diane Abbott has also apologised following the independent process coming to an end. All Labour elected representatives must be mindful at all times of their platform and the responsibilities that come with that privilege.”It is understood both investigations were carried out in accordance with the Labour rulebook and approved by the party’s independent review board.Abbott was first stripped of the Labour whip in April 2023after writing a letter to the Observerin which she argued that Jewish, Irish and Traveller people experienced prejudice rather than racism. She apologised and withdrew the remarks, saying an earlier draft had mistakenly been submitted for publication.Following a long investigation – which ended after dozens of MPs, Labour members and even some celebrities called for her to be reinstated because she apologised – Abbott had the whip restored just before the 2024 general election. The Hackney North and Stoke Newington MP completed antisemitism awareness training and received a formal warning.But she was suspended for a second time last July after she told the BBC: “Clearly, there must be a difference between racism which is about colour and other types of racism because you can see a Traveller or a Jewish person walking down the street, you don’t know.“I just think that it’s silly to try to claim that racism which is about skin colour is the same as other types of racism. I don’t know why people would say that.”Her second suspension last summer was seen as the latest sign that the then prime minister Keir Starmer intended to take a tougher approach to party discipline, after being forced to U-turn over controversial welfare cuts because of a massive rebellion by his MPs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReid, 39,stepped aside from the Labour party in Marchafter her husband, David Taylor, wasarrestedby counter-terrorism police.At the time, she said she was not under investigation, had done nothing wrong, and was voluntarily relinquishing the whip to avoid becoming a distraction while Labour carried out its own inquiries.Burnhamhas told Labour MPshe will change disciplinary culture and allow MPs to speak about their disagreements without fearing retribution from party whips.A government source told the Guardian that Abbott’s readmission had nothing to do with Burnham’s regime change, and that if she repeats these comments, or makes antisemitic remarks, “she’ll have to go again”.In a statement posted to her X account on Thursday, Abbott said: “Today, following a process conducted in line with party rules and approved by the independent review process, I have been readmitted to the Labour party.“I have been issued with a formal warning for a tweet I previously posted. By inadvertently referring to the Israeli Defence Force as the ‘Jewish Defence Force’, I used wording that conflates the actions of the state of Israel with the Jewish community.“I am deeply sorry for any hurt caused by that conflation and apologise for any hurt caused by it.“I have been and remain a lifelong anti-racist and remain deeply committed to opposing racism in all its forms.”Explore more on these topicsLabourDiane AbbottAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to free mayors from ‘Treasury death grip’ with new devolved powers | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Local leaders say plan will transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projects
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Local leaders say plan will transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projects
Content: Andy Burnham at the Submarine Academy for Skills and Knowledge at BAE Systems in Cumbria today. He will announce his devolution plan on Friday.Photograph: Chris Furlong/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the Submarine Academy for Skills and Knowledge at BAE Systems in Cumbria today. He will announce his devolution plan on Friday.Photograph: Chris Furlong/PADevolutionBurnham to free mayors from ‘Treasury death grip’ with new devolved powersLocal leaders say plan will transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projectsJosh HallidayNorth of England editorThu 30 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s regional mayors will be able to break out of the “death grip of the Treasury” by borrowing to invest in big projects under “transformational” plans to shift power out of Whitehall.For the first time, mayors will keep a share of income tax generated in their area from 2028, as well as business rates totalling tens of millions of pounds by April 2027.These will replace existing grants rather than being additional money, but local leaders said no longer relying on ringfenced Treasury handouts would “transform” their funding.Oliver Coppard, theLabourmayor of South Yorkshire, said: “It’s really important because it gets us out of the death grip of the Treasury and gives us that long-term certainty around income.”Andy Burnham will announce the measures on Friday as part of what he called “the biggest transfer of power from Westminster in a generation”.He said: “Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community. Soon, every local leader will have the power and resources to improve public transport, build homes and create jobs.“I know what it’s like to be ignored by politicians in Westminster. I’m not going to make that same mistake now I’m PM.”Under a new “local first” principle, Burnham will instruct ministers to justify why powers should remain in Whitehall rather than be devolved.As well asgreater control over technical education for teenagers, announced by the government this week, some of those close to the prime minister have called for mayors to oversee schools, GPs and childcare providers through health and education commissioners – a similar role to that played by police and crime commissioners.No 10 said Britain’s civil service of 520,000 would become “smaller and more strategic” as decision-making moves out of London, where one in five of these officials are based.England’s directly elected mayors, who control areas spanning three-quarters of the population, would be able to use the revenue generated from business rates and income tax as they wish, including tax breaks for important industries or rebates to residents.However, experts said one of the most significant consequences was that it would allow combined authorities to take out 30-year loans against their projected income to fund major projects that previously needed Treasury approval.Mayors said they were currently prevented from funding huge initiatives on housing and transport because they could not take out private loans on the basis of one-year funding settlements from Whitehall.Henri Murison, the chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the change “completely transforms” what combined authorities would be able to do.He said the ability for mayors to borrow against future income could unlock huge transport projects such as an underground station at Manchester Piccadilly.It is not yet clear what proportion of income tax or business rates would be retained by combined authorities, with officials still working on the numbers. John Healey, the chancellor, is expected to set out the detail in the autumn budget.Ben Houchen, the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley, suggested he would use the income tax to hand out tax rebates to local people.However, it is understood that this would be technically extremely difficult given mayors do not know how much individuals have paid in tax. Also, because the income tax revenue is not additional money for mayors but is replacing government grants, it is more likely to be spent on long-term projects than giveaways to residents.Ministers are considering ways to ensure less economically productive areas such as Humberside and north-east England are not left behind. If mayors received 2.5% of the 20p basic rate of income tax, London would get £2.3bn in 2026-27 while Hull and East Yorkshire would get £135m, according to areport last monthby the thinktank Re:State.The thinktank IPPR North described the move as “the most significant shift in how England is funded in a generation”.Policy experts previouslysaid rushing ahead with fiscal devolution risked creating a “two-tier England”, potentially leaving behind roughly a quarter of the country’s population that did not have a mayoral authority.The government is planning to encourage these areas – spanning millions of people in Dorset, Somerset, Oxfordshire, Gloucestershire, Wiltshire and parts of Kent – to form mayoral authorities in order to benefit from greater autonomy over their funding.Since 2024, only two combined authorities – Greater Manchester and West Midlands – have been able to keep all of the business rate income generated in their areas.In Greater Manchester, this amounted to £100m in 2024-25, the first year of operation. Three-quarters was retained by each of the 10 local authorities and £25m was kept by the mayoral authority and spent on projects.Explore more on these topicsDevolutionAndy BurnhamLabourTax and spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds evacuated after ‘apocalyptic’ wildfire near Suffolk nuclear power station | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: Major incident declared, with Sizewell B power station monitoring blaze and RSPB nature reserve badly hit
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Major incident declared, with Sizewell B power station monitoring blaze and RSPB nature reserve badly hit
Content: A helicopter lifts water from the sea to spread on the Dunwich Heath fire, with Sizewell B nuclear power station in the background.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA helicopter lifts water from the sea to spread on the Dunwich Heath fire, with Sizewell B nuclear power station in the background.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianSuffolkHundreds evacuated after ‘apocalyptic’ wildfire near Suffolk nuclear power stationMajor incident declared, with Sizewell B power station monitoring blaze and RSPB nature reserve badly hitPippa NeillandCaroline DaviesThu 30 Jul 2026 15.46 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 03.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of people have been evacuated and a major incident declared after a wildfire spread over more than 80 hectares (200 acres) on the coast ofSuffolk, just a few miles from the Sizewell B nuclear power station.The fire – which had been described by one witness as “apocalyptic” – was said to be stabilising on Thursday night. The statement was posted by Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service, which said at least 12 fire crews were remaining overnight in the area.Jon Lacey, the chief fire officer at Suffolk fire and rescue, said earlier in the evening: “The wind change has helped a little bit, unexpectedly, and also a helicopter [dropping water] is helping to dampen the fire down.”View image in fullscreenBathers watch the wildfire from Dunwich beach in Suffolk.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThe wildfire came a day after half of England was declared to beofficially in drought, including East Anglia and six other areas. On Thursday, Natural Resources Wales declared a drought across the whole of Wales, which is on course for itsdriest Julysince records began nearly 200 years ago.As the climate crisis supercharges “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather, the UK and Europe are seeing back-to-back heatwaves that encourage vegetation to grow but then dry it out, producing ideal fuel for fires.Firefighters have responded to 393 wildfires across England and Wales in July, making it the busiest month on record and placing significant pressure on crews and resources.Phil Garrigan, the chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council, said: “Wildfires are no longer isolated or seasonal events. They are becoming a recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities and emergency services.“As climate and environmental conditions continue to change, we must ensure our fire and rescue services are equipped to meet that challenge.”Map of the blaze showing the position of the nuclear power stationIn France, the fires around Bordeaux continued to smoulder on Thursday, while Spain and now Turkey are dealing with major blazes.In Suffolk, crews were called to reports of a fire at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, shortly after 5.30pm on Wednesday and that night a number of homes were evacuated.Rob Tucker, who has a cottage at Cliff House holiday park, said: “We were evacuated at 10pm. One of the guys that works at the holiday park came along and said we were being evacuated. Everything’s been left behind apart from my cars and the clothes that we were wearing.”A nearby caravan park was also evacuated on Thursday and residents opened up their homes to help. Andrew Turner, the chair of Westleton parish council, said: “I had two families in my house. Two families and two dogs. There are now pillows and stuff in the village hall but the objective is to get everyone into houses. The council is still taking names of people who are willing to put up rooms.“We’re a tightknit community, it’s great to see the community come together, I wouldn’t expect anything less.”View image in fullscreenEvacuees from homes and holiday parks gather at Westleton village hall in Suffolk.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianThe damage to wildlife is expected to be considerable because the fire hit the RSPB’s Minsmere nature reserve.The charity’s area manager, Adam Rowlands, said: “The heathland habitat where the main fire is is home to really special and rare species in the UK, birds like nightjars, nightingales and Dartford warblers.“It’s absolutely devastating to see this damage compared to last night when the fire started, I saw a 20ft fireball burning through the trees, with nightjars flying away from the fireball. Last night I stood on the heath and it was apocalyptic, the sky was orange, the smoke was billowing, it could be seen and smelled 20 miles to the north.”Firefighters say there is not thought to be any danger to Sizewell B, which is a few miles from the blaze. A spokesperson for EDF, which operates the site, said the wildfire was not affecting operations and was being closely monitored. It is understood Sizewell B has an emergency plan that covers a range of scenarios including a fire on site.Freddie Gulliver, from the Suffolk Joint Emergency Planning Unit, said there was currently no concern that the fire might spread towards Sizewell B. “Sizewell is not a risk, a concern, currently at this stage,” he said. “From the meetings we’ve had at the moment, that hasn’t been a concern.”View image in fullscreenA fire engine returns from the Dunwich Heath blaze.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianPeople have been urged to avoid the area where possible and keep windows and doors closed.Andy Burnham promised support to firefighters on Thursday. Speaking to reporters during a visit to Cumbria, the prime minister said: “We’ve got the situation under close monitoring, and I’m receiving regular updates. It is a very serious incident.”Dr Zakary Campbell-Lochrie, a lecturer in fire science at the University of Edinburgh, said: “This wildfire is occurring at the same time as drought conditions have officially been declared in large parts ofEngland, including Suffolk.“The hot, dry weather conditions, including the multiple heatwave events across much of the UK in recent weeks, lead to strong drying conditions for vegetation, which can subsequently be highly susceptible to ignition and can present a much greater danger when fires do occur.”The climate crisis, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, is making heatwaves more intense and more frequent. A fortnight ago, the Reform-led Suffolk county councilvoted to rescinda climate emergency declaration that had been adopted in 2019 and removed references to the climate emergency from council policies, strategies and communications “where appropriate”.On Thursday, the UK Health Security Agency saidEngland was on trackto record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer.Explore more on these topicsSuffolkFirefightersWildfiresEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Supreme court says Palestine Action co-founder can challenge ban on group | Palestine Action | The Guardian
description: UK’s highest court gives permission for Huda Ammori to challenge court of appeal ruling
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: UK’s highest court gives permission for Huda Ammori to challenge court of appeal ruling
Content: Huda Ammori has been fighting to have the ban on Palestine Action overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign.Photograph: Abdullah Bailey/AlamyView image in fullscreenHuda Ammori has been fighting to have the ban on Palestine Action overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign.Photograph: Abdullah Bailey/AlamyPalestine ActionSupreme court says Palestine Action co-founder can challenge ban on groupUK’s highest court gives permission for Huda Ammori to challenge court of appeal rulingHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 13.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe co-founder ofPalestine Actionhas won permission to challenge the ban against the group at the UK’s highest court.The direct action groupwas proscribedas a terrorist organisation in July last year but its co-founder, Huda Ammori, has been fighting to have the ban overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign.In February, the high court ruled that the ban wasdisproportionate and unlawfulbut its decision was overturned by the court of appeallast month.On Thursday, the supreme court said Ammori could appeal against the court of appeal’s decision and that the case would be heard in the final quarter of this year.It means the fate of more than 3,500 people who have been arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action since the ban remains in limbo as their cases are on hold until the legality of proscription has been definitely resolved.Ammori welcomed the supreme court’s decision, saying: “The proscription of Palestine Action has become a vehicle for a far broader crackdown on expressions of solidarity with the Palestinian people.“This unprecedented attack on free speech and the right to protest in this country is already having a chilling effect at a time when speaking out about Israel’s crimes could not be more urgent.”She appealed directly to the supreme court to hear the case after the court of appeal’s decision refused permission to appeal against its own decision within hours of the application.The court of appeal review was comprised of five judges, which is unusual as it normally consists of two or three. It included the country’s two most senior judges: the lady chief justice, Sue Carr, and the master of the rolls, Geoffrey Vos.The supreme court said it was arguable that the ban represented a disproportionate interference with articles 10 and 11 of the European convention on human rights, which protect the rights of freedom of speech and protest respectively.Ammori has pledged to challenge the ban, which has been widely condemned by civil liberties groups, as well as by UN experts and politicians from across the divide, at the European court of human rights if it is upheld by the UK courts.As the supreme court’s decision was published, dozens more people were arrested for allegedly supporting, being a member of and/or encouraging others to join Palestine Action.In a demonstration outside Westminster magistrates court in central London, protesters took turns to stand up and declare their support for or membership of Palestine Action.Many of the mainly elderly protesters lay down after speaking and were carried away by officers. Among those arrested was an 87-year-old woman in a wheelchair.Sir Jonathon Porritt was one of those arrested for showing support for Palestine Action, according to the activist group Defend Our Juries.Porritt, 76, is a former director of Friends of the Earth and was an adviser to the Prince of Wales – now King Charles – for more than 30 years.Dick Scroop, 79, from Wolverhampton, was one of those who was there to be arrested.He said: “There’s a genocide in which the British government is deeply implicated by its diplomatic efforts and the continuing supply of weapons to Israel, and the attempt to suppress legitimate protests by the wielding of anti-terrorism laws is simply unacceptable. It’s an assault on free speech.”By inviting support for Palestine Action, and expressing membership of the group, the protesters risk up to 14 years’ imprisonment in trials before a jury, a significant escalation from most of the previous arrests for holding placards which will be dealt with by magistrates and risk a maximum of six months in jail.Many arrested on Thursday had previously been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action.The Metropolitan Police said 117 people were arrested, most for “expressing support for a proscribed organisation”.Explore more on these topicsPalestine ActionUK supreme courtCourt of appealnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour says Reform ‘up to its neck in sleaze’ and demands investigation into donations | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Electoral Commission urged to look into donations made by mother of convicted fraudster
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Electoral Commission urged to look into donations made by mother of convicted fraudster
Content: Nigel Farage with George Cottrell (right, in sunglasses) in 2019.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyView image in fullscreenNigel Farage with George Cottrell (right, in sunglasses) in 2019.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyReform UKLabour says Reform ‘up to its neck in sleaze’ and demands investigation into donationsExclusive: Electoral Commission urged to look into donations made by mother of convicted fraudsterRevealed: George Cottrell transferred $2m to his mother days before her donations to Reform UKJessica ElgotDeputy political editorThu 30 Jul 2026 13.05 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour has accused Reform UK of being “up to its neck in sleaze” as it called on theElectoral Commissionto urgently investigate substantial donations made to the party by the mother of a convicted fraudster.Bridget Phillipson, Labour’s new chair, called on the commission to examine whether any rules had been broken, after revelations in the Guardian that George Cottrelltransferred more than $2m to his motherin the days before her donations to the party in 2024.ALabourspokesperson said Reform was “up to [its] neck in sleaze and dodgy money”.The commission has already made a referral to the Metropolitan police, who are looking into whether Reform may have been concealing or disguising donations derived from an “impermissible” donor.The Guardian has since reported that Cottrell’s mother, Fiona Cottrell, received several tranches of money adding up to more than $2m, which she attributed to her son, according to financial industry sources. Her son is a close ally and adviser toNigel Farage.Transfers were then made either directly to Reform or via Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle for the political party, according to sources.In her letter, Phillipson said the Guardian’s new revelations “may be relevant to the question of whether the true source of political donations made toReform UKhas been correctly identified and whether the statutory requirements governing permissible donors have been complied with”.A Labour spokesperson said it was now time for Reform to seriously address the allegations. “If these latest claims about George Cottrell are true, Reform may have taken money from a convicted fraudster who was the ultimate source of the donations,” the party said. “That would mean Reform accepted his money even though he has never shown he was legally allowed to donate to a political party at the time.“With every passing day it’s clearer that Reform think the rules don’t apply to them. They need to wake up and start treating these allegations with the seriousness they deserve and come clean about who is really bankrolling the party.”At a press conference on Thursday, Reform’s economics spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, ducked specific questions about the donations.In testy exchanges with reporters, he said the story “has been going on for a long time”, but he did not engage with the substance of the allegations.He told the BBC: “We are entirely confident that Reform followed all electoral rules at the time when the donations were made. Of course, we’ll participate with any inquiries. To the best of my knowledge, we haven’t even been contacted by the police, so I don’t think we have anything more to add to that.”Jenrick suggested that journalists should be questioning George Cottrell, and said they should return to the intended subject matter of the press conference, which was social care. “Reform is certain that all the electoral rules were followed,” he told ITV. “If you’ve got a question for Mr Cottrell then I think you have to direct that to him.”The Met’s investigation is examiningdonations to Reform, including those from Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle whose director is the party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice. The firm gave Reform two donations of £250,000 in the run-up to the 2024 general election. These were first revealed by the Guardian.Cottrell, who was convicted for fraud in the US, now lives in Montenegro but is seen often alongside Farage. He has previously been described as Farage’s chief of staff but Reform has maintained that he is only a volunteer.Asked about the transfers, lawyers for Cottrell said their client had no further comment.In previous legal correspondence, Cottrell has not denied giving his mother – who is understood to be of relatively modest means – large sums of money. Instead, he said via lawyers that “any political donations his mother has made have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”.Fiona Cottrell has not responded to several attempts by the Guardian to contact her.Asked on Wednesday for a response to the story, a Reform spokesperson said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with all donations.”Farage isfighting a byelectionafter resigning his seat of Clacton. All other mainstream parties have declined to stand a candidate against him, though there are 34 independents on the ballot paper, including novelty candidates such asCount Binface.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageParty fundingElectoral CommissionLabourBridget PhillipsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy’s husband told police children were dead, court hears | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Officers in murder trial testify of arriving at Massachusetts home after anguished 911 call from Patrick Clancy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officers in murder trial testify of arriving at Massachusetts home after anguished 911 call from Patrick Clancy
Content: Lindsay Clancy listens in court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Thursday.Photograph: CJ Gunther/Pool The Boston Herald/APView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy listens in court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Thursday.Photograph: CJ Gunther/Pool The Boston Herald/APMassachusettsLindsay Clancy’s husband told police children were dead, court hearsOfficers in murder trial testify of arriving at Massachusetts home after anguished 911 call from Patrick ClancyAssociated PressThu 30 Jul 2026 19.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 19.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe two police officers focused first on Lindsay Clancy drifting in and out of consciousness in the snow after jumping from herMassachusettshome’s second-floor window in January 2023. Within minutes, they were racing into the basement after her then husband screamed that all three of their children were dead.“I can’t wake them up – I can’t get them up!” Patrick Clancy frantically told the officers who, along with firefighters and paramedics, gave jurors first-hand accounts on Thursday of the aftermath.Themurder trialhas centered on Clancy’s mental state at the time. Her lawyers do not dispute that she strangled the children with exercise bands. But they say she was in the grip of postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth.Prosecutors say Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts general hospital, acted intentionally and is criminally responsible for the deaths.The testimony came after jurors spent two days listening totestimony fromPatrick Clancy and his anguished 911 emergency call. He was still on the phone when he discovered the bodies of three-year-old Dawson, five-year-old Cora, and eight-month-old Callan, minutes after returning home from an errand his wife had asked him to run.View image in fullscreenPatrick Clancy in court on Tuesday.Photograph: David L Ryan/Pool The Boston Globe/APPatrick Clancy has said in interviews that he forgives his ex-wife, whom he viewed as ill rather than evil. The trial marks the first time he has seen Lindsay Clancy since the killings.She remains paralyzed from the waist down after using multiple methods to try to end her life that night. She says a voice told her: “This is your last chance. Kill the children so you can kill yourself,” according to her lawyer.Officers Stephen Hall and Brian Josephine testified on Thursday that they were each dispatched separately to the house in Duxbury, a coastal town south of Boston. Hall said they arrived to find Patrick Clancy calling for help from behind the home.Patrick Clancy testified earlier this week that his injured wife told him the children were in the basement, but she did not say they were dead.When the officers followed the sound of his screams downstairs, only the baby, Callan, had a faint pulse, Josephine testified.“Based on my training experience from previous incidents, I knew it wasn’t going to be good,” Josephine said. They began rendering aid with help from firefighters.PJ Hussey, a fire department supervisor, arrived in time to glimpse through a basement window as Patrick Clancy unwrapped an exercise band from his child’s neck.View image in fullscreenDuxbury fire department captain PJ Hussey in court.Photograph: CJ Gunther/Pool The Boston Herald/AP“It turned very chaotic very quickly” as more ambulances rushed to the house, Hussey testified. Duxbury firefighter and paramedic Jennifer Stratton said the infant never regained a pulse.If convicted of murder, Lindsay Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.In opening arguments on Monday, her attorney said Lindsay Clancy had bipolar disorder, and that antidepressants prescribed after the birth of her third child worsened her condition.Patrick Clancy testified about his wife’s deteriorating mental health in the months leading up to the killings. He said she told him about intrusive thoughts of harming the children, as well as thoughts of suicide.She sought care from experts in postpartum mood disorders and was put on multiple psychiatric medications. When nothing worked, she checked into a psychiatric hospital. She killed the children 19 days after she was discharged.Clancy and her ex-husband accuse her medical providers of failing to properly diagnose, treat and monitor her, according to lawsuits filed earlier this year.In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMassachusettsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Seattle police chief resigns after deadly food festival shooting | Seattle | The Guardian
description: Mayor announces resignation of Shon Barnes after city officials faced criticism over response to Sunday shooting
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mayor announces resignation of Shon Barnes after city officials faced criticism over response to Sunday shooting
Content: A memorial for victims of the shooting at the Seattle Center in Seattle, Washington, on 28 July.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APView image in fullscreenA memorial for victims of the shooting at the Seattle Center in Seattle, Washington, on 28 July.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APSeattleSeattle police chief resigns after deadly food festival shootingMayor announces resignation of Shon Barnes after city officials faced criticism over response to Sunday shootingAssociated PressThu 30 Jul 2026 19.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 20.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeattle’s police chief has resigned amid criticism of the city’s response to a fatal shootout at a food festival last weekend, Katie Wilson, the mayor, said on Thursday.The announcement followed hours of speculation about whether Shon Barnes would step down, as some of his supporters said he had rebuffed Wilson’s request that he resign.Wilson said she was appointing deputy chief Andre Sayles, a law enforcement veteran with more than two decades of experience, as interim chief.Barnes told the Seattle Times on Thursday that whether he remained in the position was “up to the mayor”. He said he was off for the day and spending time with family. A police department spokesperson told the Associated Press he did not have any information to share about the situation.Barnes was out of town at a law enforcement conference when gunfire erupted last weekend at the Bite of Seattle, an annual three-day festival that draws hundreds of food and retail vendors and performers.Three people, including one suspect, were killed, and four people were wounded. One of the people wounded was a two-year-old boy.Dozens of officers were at the event, and at least one saw a 15-year-old suspect firing into a crowd and quickly persuaded him to surrender, according to court documents. Police are still searching for at least one other person.The Seattle police department and Wilson have faced criticism for slow and confusing communication in the shooting’s aftermath.After an initial social media post announcing that there had been a shooting with multiple victims, it took nearly five hours for police to provide any additional information to the public, including whether there was any active threat. In the meantime, Wilson announced that two people had been taken into custody, a statement she later retracted.Tyrone Davis, the assistant Seattle police chief, finally provided an update at about 11pm on Sunday night during a news conference that was also attended by the mayor, Governor Bob Ferguson and US congresswoman Pramila Jayapal.Barnes had been the second Black police chief in Seattle.Several Black community organizations, including the Seattle NAACP and the Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle, rallied to try to save his job Thursday. In an open letter to the mayor’s office, they credited him with improving relations between the department and the community, helping reduce gun violence and strengthening the department’s operations.Barnes was appointed by Seattle’s previous mayor, Bruce Harrell, in December 2024 after serving as chief of the Madison, Wisconsin, police department.When Wilson — a democratic socialist who once supported defunding police — won the mayor’s race last year, she kept Barnes on as chief. That was a signal to the city’s business establishment and community groups that she did not intend to take a radically different approach to public safety.Barnes has faced some criticism for spending time in Chicago, where his family lives. Sgt Patrick Michaud, a department spokesperson, said Thursday that Barnes has made four trips to Chicago this year and spent in total about 18 days traveling there. Barnes also has traveled to several police executive and recruitment conferences.Explore more on these topicsSeattleUS policingGun crimeWashington stateWest CoastUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mandela Barnes drops out of high-stakes Wisconsin governor’s race | Democrats | The Guardian
description: Former lieutenant governor says path to Democratic nomination no longer viable as democratic socialist rival surges ahead
Author: Lauren Gambino
Headline: Former lieutenant governor says path to Democratic nomination no longer viable as democratic socialist rival surges ahead
Content: Mandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor, at a rally in Milwaukee in October 2022.Photograph: Morry Gash/APView image in fullscreenMandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor, at a rally in Milwaukee in October 2022.Photograph: Morry Gash/APDemocratsMandela Barnes drops out of high-stakes Wisconsin governor’s raceFormer lieutenant governor says path to Democratic nomination no longer viable as democratic socialist rival surges aheadLauren GambinoThu 30 Jul 2026 18.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 19.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor ofWisconsin, dropped out of the Democratic primary for governor on Thursday, upending the high-stakes contest less than two weeks before the 11 August election.Barnes announced the decision in a video posted on social media, saying he no longer saw a viable path to the nomination, as democratic socialist Francesca Hong surged ahead with a commanding lead.“It’s become very clear who our nominee is going to be,” Barnes, 39, said.A Marquette Law School poll showed Hong significantly ahead of Barnes in a distant second place, with 38% compared to his 16%, having consolidated liberal support, especially among young voters, although about a third of primary voters remained undecided.Soon after Barnes’s withdrawal, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinelreportedit had sent questions to the candidate about past allegations of inappropriate behavior that had been anonymously submitted to the Wisconsin Democratic party, local party officials and others.According to the Journal Sentinel, the state party hired a law firm in 2025 to investigate the claims sent in a letter that Barnes had used his position in the party to pursue inappropriate relationships with “young adult women”.The party’s internal review and outside investigation found no actionable evidence because the claims were “anonymous and unspecific”, the Journal Sentinel reported, citing an unnamed person familiar with the matter.Barnes’s campaign denied any wrongdoing.“There are no allegations of misconduct or wrongdoing against Mandela,” it said in a statement.His departure adds another twist in the Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin, a perennial presidential battleground that has also been at the center of national disputes over election administration since the 2020 election.He is the third Democrat to exit the race, following lieutenant governor Sara Rodriguez, who withdrew two weeks ago amid a campaign finance scandal. After Rodriguez’s exit, Milwaukee county executive David Crowley re-entered the race with the endorsement of Governor Tony Evers, who is not seeking re-election.Earlier this summer, Missy Hughes, a former state economic development director, ended her campaign.On Wednesday, a judgerejectedan effort backed by the Democratic party to let voters who had already cast absentee ballots void their initial vote and vote again, over concerns that many early ballots had been cast for candidates who were no longer in the race.Crowley moved quickly toappealto Barnes’s supporters: “There’s a place for you in what we’re building.”Evers told reporters he was surprised by Barnes’s decision to withdraw but reiterated his support for Crowley, saying he believed Crowley was the strongest candidate “even if Mandela was in”, the Associated Press reported.The Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Wisconsin is expected to face Republican US congressman Tom Tiffany, who is backed by Donald Trump.Barnes was once viewed as a rising star in Democratic politics. In 2022, rather than seek re-election as lieutenant governor, he ran for the US Senate, narrowly losing the race to incumbent Republican Ron Johnson.Rachel Leingang contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDemocratsUS politicsWisconsinnewsShareReuse this content

title: ABC argues that early license review by FCC is ‘retaliation’ for network’s coverage | ABC | The Guardian
description: In filing, network’s lawyers urged FCC to reject petitions to deny license renewals for eight ABC-owned local stations
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: In filing, network’s lawyers urged FCC to reject petitions to deny license renewals for eight ABC-owned local stations
Content: ABC lawyers say the FCC’s actions are retaliation for the exercise of the network’s first amendment rights.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenABC lawyers say the FCC’s actions are retaliation for the exercise of the network’s first amendment rights.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersABCABC argues that early license review by FCC is ‘retaliation’ for network’s coverageIn filing, network’s lawyers urged FCC to reject petitions to deny license renewals for eight ABC-owned local stationsUS politics live – latest updatesJeremy BarrThu 30 Jul 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleABC has pushed back aggressively against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for putting the network under an expedited license renewal process for eight local television stations it owns, charging in a lengthy filing that the process is payback for the network’s editorial decision-making and coverage ofDonald Trump.“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: Accommodate the administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” lawyers representing the Disney-owned network wrote in a 109-page filing, submitted as a reply topetitionsfrom conservative media groups to deny ABC’s licenses. “The tools vary; the objective does not: a media industry too fearful of official reprisal to report the news freely.”The FCC chair, Brendan Carr, has denied that inquiries into the network relate to its editorial decision-making and instead said they stem from concerns about the company’s employment practices and compliance with statutory obligations.US media regulator Brendan Carr accuses Disney of ‘misinformation’ on investigationsRead moreABC’s lawyers pointed out how unusual it is for the FCC to demand that a group of network-owned stations apply several years early to renew their licenses. Other ABC-owned stations have licenses that run all the way until 2031.“The commission’s departure from those norms lays bare what is really going on: the administration is retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights,” ABC’s lawyers wrote. “Because this whole proceeding rests on an unconstitutional premise, the stations should never have been asked to justify license renewal years early.”Respondingto petitions to deny ABC’s licenses based on accusations of liberal bias, the network’s lawyers pointed out that the “commission has no authority to regulate the content of television programming”.“No Petitioner has established any ‘violations’ of Commission rules or regulations, let alone the ‘serious’ ones or the ‘pattern of abuse’ required to warrant denying renewal,” they added.ABC’s lawyers also argued that its eight stations had made “essential contributions to their local communities” in markets such as New York City and Philadelphia and argued that the FCC should dismiss the petitions to deny their licenses.Participants have until 5 August to reply to petitions to deny. After that time, the FCC could choose to either grant the license renewal requests – an unlikely prospect – or schedule hearings on the matter, beginning a potentially onerous and time-consuming process that could run for several years, particularly if an adverse ruling is challenged in the courts.On Tuesday, a bipartisan coalition of former FCC commissioners and staffers submitted afilingurging the commission to reject the petitions to deny ABC’s license renewals, arguing that the early renewal process ordered by Carr’s FCC in April is “a grave violation of both the Communications Act and the Constitution”.Thousands of commenters have filed on behalf of ABC in both the license renewal inquiry and another FCC investigation into the daytime talkshow The View for a potential violation of rules guarding political candidate appearances.“When given the chance to weigh in on whether to allow the FCC to continue its campaign of censorship and control, the American public showed up in a big way, and the vast majority who spoke up delivered the same message,” Anna M Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, said in a statement on Thursday. “They believe in the value of their local news, they trust those who cover their communities, and they understand that the FCC has no business deciding who is a journalist and what counts as real news.”Explore more on these topicsABCTrump administrationUS constitution and civil libertiesTelevision industryWalt Disney CompanyRegulatorsFreedom of speechnewsShareReuse this content

title: New survey reveals fears of US farm workers amid Trump’s immigration raids | US farm workers | The Guardian
description: Vast majority of farm workers say raids and deportations have affected their jobs and 61% report shopping less
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Vast majority of farm workers say raids and deportations have affected their jobs and 61% report shopping less
Content: Farm workers harvest strawberries on 31 March 2026 near Oxnard, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFarm workers harvest strawberries on 31 March 2026 near Oxnard, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesUS farm workersNew survey reveals fears of US farm workers amid Trump’s immigration raidsVast majority of farm workers say raids and deportations have affected their jobs and 61% report shopping lessSign up for the Breaking News US newsletter emailMichael SainatoThu 30 Jul 2026 15.46 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarm workersin the US are reeling from theTrump administration’s crackdown on immigration, including increased raids and deportations, according to anew surveyconducted by the United Farm Workers Foundation released on Thursday.The survey features responses from 2,250 farm workers, many of whom are undocumented, about their experiences with immigration enforcement that has intensified under the secondTrump administration.The vast majority (92%) of farm workers said that raids and deportations have affected their employment, while 90% said they worry about family separation. Fears are widespread and have affected their everyday lives: 61% said they are shopping less and 29% say they are not seeking medical attention for fear of immigration enforcement. Another 17% said they fear having to doforced laborin immigration detention if arrested.ICE agents used racial slurs during Los Angeles crackdown, court files showRead moreThese fears are prevalent despite many respondents being longtime US residents, with 80% workers saying they have been in the US for more than 10 years, while 41% said they have been in the US for more than 20 years.“When I leave to work, I’m afraid to not come home and to never see my daughters again,” said Yasmine, a farm worker, during apress conferenceabout the survey on Thursday. A mother of two daughters who are US citizens, she said: “We only go out when it’s absolutely necessary, but if we do go out, it’s for necessities like groceries.”Yasmine, who did not provide her last name, said she has been in the US for more than 20 years and is a Daca recipient, though she is experiencing delays getting her work permits renewed. Her husband is an undocumented immigrant.“I’ve even had to have conversations with our daughters about what could possibly happen. They’re small and don’t really understand what’s happening, but I try to talk to them and make sure we have a plan,” she said. “The other day was our daughter’s 11th birthday and we couldn’t celebrate it out of fear of going out. Family separation worries me a lot. I don’t know what’s going to happen. I live with stress, uncertainty and fear.”There aremore than 2.6 millionfarm workers in the US. Most (73%) are Hispanic, 66% are noncitizen immigrants and 47% report lacking work authorization, according to data from the 2022National Agricultural Workers Survey.Many hope that the US government can eventually shape up its immigration system, with 76% wanting protections from deportation and detention and 53% expressing hope for a pathway to legal status and US citizenship. Many workers are also unable to visit family in their home countries because of their immigration status, with 87% saying they would be able to visit their families if Congress passed immigration reform that gave them legal status.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThree-quarters of Americans think Trump isn’t focusing on top US issues – pollRead moreYasmine emphasized having a pathway to citizenship would be life-changing for her family.“Having a pathway to citizenship would mean a lot for me. It would change a lot for me and my family, and it would make sure that my husband and I could give a better life for our daughters,” she said. “I would finally have stability, something right now I don’t have.”The UFW Foundation noted that gathering data from undocumented farm workers is difficult, but it drew from its farm worker database to conduct the survey.“This is the first in-depth study to survey the concerns and fears of undocumented farm workers as well as their hopes and aspirations,” said Erica Lomeli Corcoran, the CEO of the UFW Foundation, in a statement. “We hope this survey will shine a light so those in power can understand the realities faced by those who are the most powerless. Then perhaps undocumented farm workers who produce the greatest abundance of food the world has ever seen will be seen and treated like the important human beings they are.”In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said: “Worksite enforcement remains a cornerstone of our efforts to protect public safety, national security, and economic stability while rescuing individuals who may be victims of labor trafficking or exploitation.”Explore more on these topicsUS farm workersUS immigrationTrump administrationUS domestic policyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US economy grows sluggish 1.5% in second quarter as inflation tops Fed target | US economy | The Guardian
description: Consumer spending remained resilient even as policymakers kept interest rates on hold
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Consumer spending remained resilient even as policymakers kept interest rates on hold
Content: The US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, speaks during a press conference at the Federal Reserve building in Washington DC on Wednesday.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAView image in fullscreenThe US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, speaks during a press conference at the Federal Reserve building in Washington DC on Wednesday.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAUS economyUS economy grows sluggish 1.5% in second quarter as inflation tops Fed targetConsumer spending remained resilient even as policymakers kept interest rates on holdGaya Guptaand agenciesThu 30 Jul 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS economyexpanded at a sluggish 1.5% pace from April through June as rising imports weighed on growth. But consumer spending rose. And theFederal Reserve’s favored measure ofinflationgrew more slowly last month despite remaining above the central bank’s 2% target.The commerce department reported on Thursday that growth in US gross domestic product (GDP) – the nation’s output of goods and services – decelerated from 2.1% in the first three months of 2026 and came in below economists’ expectations.The commerce department also said on Thursday that its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the measure of inflation favored by the Fed, rose 3.7% last month from June 2025 , down from a 4.1% year-over-year increase in May. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, so-called core consumer prices were up 3.3% from a year earlier, little changed from a 3.4% increase in May.The latest data paints a clearer picture of the effects the war in the Middle East has had on the economy after increasing energy prices and pushing inflation higher. The first GDP reading of this year captured theeffectsof just a month of war, but indicated that consumer spending was starting to slow as prices started to creep up.Fed holds interest rates steady despite Trump’s renewed calls to lower themRead moreOil prices have come down from their wartime high, and took a sharp downturn when the US and Iran announced a peace deal. But when that deal collapsed and the two countries began trading strikes again, oil prices climbed and still remain much higher than prewar levels.The pressure is growing within the Fed to raise interest rates in order to combat heightened inflation, which Kevin Warsh, the central bank’s chair, has acknowledged has remained too high for years. Though the Fed on Wednesday chose to leave its benchmark interest rateunchangedfor the fifth straight meeting, three regional Fed presidents dissented, saying they wanted to raise rates to combat elevated inflation. It was the first time in a decade so many Fed officials had dissented in the same direction over a policy vote.Higher costs have frustrated Americans ahead of November’s midterm elections, which will determine whether Donald Trump’s Republicans keep full control of Congress. Two-thirds of Americans, including 49% of Republicans, say they have little faith the federal government will address the high prices they face, according to a Harris Pollsurveyreleased earlier this month.Still, theUS economyhas proven surprisingly resilient in the face of the Iran war and the spike in energy prices it caused. The job market has bounced back this year from a lackluster 2025, giving consumers the wherewithal to spend. Employers are adding an average 92,000 jobs a month this year, compared with fewer than 10,000 a month in 2025 when high interest rates and Trump’s erratic use of tariffs discouraged businesses from hiring.Thursday’s GDP report was the first of three commerce department estimates of second quarter economic growth.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS economyEconomicsInflationFederal ReserveUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Let them eat SUVs: Trump White House orders fleet of luxury cars as Americans struggle | US news | The Guardian
description: Americans are facing a deepening affordability crisis but at least Trump and co have ... 250 new Cadillac Escalades
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: Americans are facing a deepening affordability crisis but at least Trump and co have ... 250 new Cadillac Escalades
Content: Donald Trump greets the General Motors CEO, Mary Barra, and president, Mark Reuss, during a visit to the company’s Milford proving grounds in Michigan on Monday.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump greets the General Motors CEO, Mary Barra, and president, Mark Reuss, during a visit to the company’s Milford proving grounds in Michigan on Monday.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesThis Week in TrumplandUS newsAnalysisLet them eat SUVs: Trump White House orders fleet of luxury cars as Americans struggleAdam GabbattAmericans are facing a deepening affordability crisis but at least Trump and co have ... 250 new Cadillac EscaladesThis was originally published in This Week in Trumpland.Sign up to receive it in your inbox every WednesdayThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTShareGas pricesare upalmost a dollar a gallon since the day Donald Trump took office; mortgage ratesjust hittheir highest level in nearly a year, and over the weekend a prominent economistsaidthe Iran war is costing the average US household more than $1,200.Americans are struggling through a deepening affordability crisis caused largely by Trump’s ill-fated war against Iran. They are in need of a boost, something to lift the spirits. Perhaps the president could give a speech, letting the people know that we are all in this together.Or, he could give a speech announcing that the White House has just ordered 250 brand new Cadillac Escalades, giant SUVs which have a suggested retail price of more than $90,000 each and cost significantly more to customize for secure uses.“We ordered 250 Escalades.
