That’s how we look sharp in those cavalcades, you know,” Trump said duringa rambling, hour-long addressat a General Motors facility in Michigan.“We look sharp in those Escalades. Our guys are very spoiled. They’re very spoiled. They like the Escalade. So do I.”I’d like to think I would look sharp in an Escalade. But, like most people in the US, I cannot afford one: especially if, as seems likely, the White House orders the armored version of the SUV, which can costmore than $300,000. And then, of course, I’d have to fill the 24-gallon gas tank.The symbolism of Trump’s gesture, his fiddling with car specifications while Rome burns, is consistent with hisLucille Bluth-like behavior in recent weeks. He’sdismissed “affordability”as a term concocted by Democratic political consultants to criticize his presidency,introduced a new round of tariffslikely to push up prices, andrefused to signa rare bipartisan housing bill. It’s still shocking. Even Scrooge didn’t order a new horse and cart as Tiny Tim’s health declined.Yet here we are, in 2026, with a billionaire president crowing about spending at least $22m of Americans’ money on a fleet of luxury SUVs, an act which seems extremely unlikely to boost morale.“Hey I know inflation is out of control and a lot of folks can’t afford basic necessities, but at least we’re tackling waste fra ud and abuse by buying… *checks notes* 250 Escalades for the government,” the Angry Staffer accountwrote on X, capturing much of the mood.The announcement of the car purchase was a baffling move in what was a confusing speech. Trump’s address in Michigan was supposed to be about US auto manufacturing, but instead his remarks took on transgender rights, “Marxist protesters” and how, should Democrats win control of the government: “In one year, the country will be absolutely bankrupt. You’ll live in squalor. You’ll live in fear. You won’t have police. You won’t have firemen. You won’t have anybody.”Trump also disclosed to the crowd that he was “sort of a clean freak, I like clean”, before claiming he had been awarded “man of the year” in Michigan 25 years ago. The latter was an interesting claim, because Trump has been claiming to have been awarded this Michigan man of the year title for a decade, and it never happened.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis Week in TrumplandA deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administrationPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Approaching 10 full years after Trump debuted the ‘Man of the Year’ lie, nobody has ever been able to find any evidence for it,” CNN’s Daniel Dalewrote.“The state of Michigan does not give out a ‘Man of the Year’ award, Trump has never lived in the state, and he and his team have never specified who or what entity supposedly gave him this award and when.”It’s all very well for the president: swanning about the midwest bulk-buying massive SUVs, “liking clean”, living in a fantasy world where he is handed awards left right and center.It’s hard to see, however, how this display of opulence and this dabbling in make-believe helps everyday Americans. We’ll have to see what Trump has planned next to lift the mood. Perhaps he could announce a new caviar supplier, or a wholesale purchase of top hats. Or maybe he could settle for justslathering gold all over his office.Time will tell.Explore more on these topicsUS newsThis Week in TrumplandUS politicsDonald TrumpanalysisShareReuse this content

title: US borrowing costs hit 19-year high as Fed holds interest rates | US interest rates | The Guardian
description: Bank’s chair pledges to keep up fight against inflation but decision brings fears of a failure to keep pace
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Bank’s chair pledges to keep up fight against inflation but decision brings fears of a failure to keep pace
Content: Kevin Warsh said the Federal Reserve would not waver in its commitment to tackling rising prices.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh said the Federal Reserve would not waver in its commitment to tackling rising prices.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APUS interest ratesUS borrowing costs hit 19-year high as Fed holds interest ratesBank’s chair pledges to keep up fight against inflation but decision brings fears of a failure to keep paceBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaThu 30 Jul 2026 04.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS government borrowing costs have hit their highest level since 2007 after theFederal Reservevoted to hold its key interest rate steady, feeding fears that the central bank may not move fast enough to tame a rise in inflation.The yield – or interest rate – on the 30-year US Treasury bond rose 14 basis points to nearly 5.24%, a 19-year high, after the Fed announced its decision tohold its main rate at between 3.5% and 3.75%for the fifth meeting in a row.Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, said the bank would “not waver” in its commitment to tackling rising prices. A prolonged period of high inflation meant that some Americans believed the central bank had an “implicit target” above its 2% target, he added.“There is no soft implicit target: not on this committee’s watch,” Warsh said. “There’s only a target and it’s 2%. This Fed will not waver … Our credibility rests on performing our duties and delivering on our responsibilities.”The decision to leave rates on hold has spooked investors who are worried about the US economy’s ability to absorb a rise inflation, triggered byDonald Trump’s war in Iran.US inflation cooled to an annual rate of 3.5% in June after Washington and Tehran agreed a brief ceasefire – but this has since ended, with both sides exchanging fire and sending oil prices climbing higher again.Felix Schmidt, a senior economist at the bank Berenberg, said Warsh had not “conclusively answered the question of why the Fed did not hike”.He noted that the Fed chair had implied at a press conference that an interest rate rise in the near term might not be necessary due to the rise in bond yields, which has already pushed up the cost of borrowing across theUS economy.“Perhaps Warsh hopes that higher capital market interest rates will help fight inflation in the short term, while the US central bank under new leadership decides on its approach,” Schmidt said.Before the Fed’s meeting this week, financial markets had priced in a 30% chance of a rate rise and, in the absence of such a move, nearly a 100% chance of an increase at the Fed’s September meeting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter Wednesday, however, traders put the chance of a rate rise in September at about 57%, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.US stocks also fell sharply on Wednesday, with the blue chip S&P 500 index closing down 1.5%. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 2.2% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 1.7%.Explore more on these topicsUS interest ratesFederal ReserveUS economyEconomicsInflationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% as inflation fears mount | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Split vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs close to $90 a barrel
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Split vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs close to $90 a barrel
Content: Governor of the Bank of England (BoE) Andrew Bailey addresses a press conference after today’s interest rate decisionPhotograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenGovernor of the Bank of England (BoE) Andrew Bailey addresses a press conference after today’s interest rate decisionPhotograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAInterest ratesBank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% as inflation fears mountSplit vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs close to $90 a barrelBusiness live – latest updatesOnly Middle East crisis is preventing drop in UK interest ratesRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 11.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBank of Englandhas kept UK interest rates on hold as it warned that a further escalation in the Iran war could drive inflation above 4% next year, adding to cost of living pressures on households.Against a volatile backdrop in the Middle East conflict, the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted by six to three to keep its key base rate at 3.75%.As Donald Trump’s renewed attacks on Iran drive up global energy prices, the Bank said an “adverse scenario” involving a drawn-out war and oil prices remaining above $100 a barrel could push UK inflation to a peak of 4.5% by the middle of 2027.However, on a day of fresh US strikes in the widening conflict, Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, played down suggestions among City traders that Threadneedle Street was edging closer to raising rates.In a press conference after the decision, he said there was little sign that inflationary pressures were becoming entrenched because the growth outlook for the UK economy remained weak.“Please do not leave this room thinking that the Bank of England is edging towards a [interest rate] hike because, frankly, there’s nothing in what I said, and I think any of us have said, along those lines,” Bailey said.Official figures showed inflation in the UKfell by more than expected in June to 2.6%, down from a peak of 3.8% last year. It had been on track to fall close to 2% before the outbreak of the Iran war.The Bank said a loose labour market and higher borrowing costs for households and businesses, compared with before the war, would reduce inflation over time. It added that conditions before the conflict were more “benign” than they had been before previous global shocks, including the Covid pandemic and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.The decision to keep interest rates unchanged is expected to giveAndy Burnhama boost in his push to lower the cost of living. He has announced a sweeping package of support for households in his first week as prime minister.Under his plans, electricity bills in Great Britain will be cut by an average of £45 a year from October by removing VAT from them. The Bank said it expected the policy, alongside a £2 cap on bus fares in England, to lower the headline inflation rate by 0.1 percentage point.However, the MPC said it stood “ready to act as necessary” to prevent inflationary pressures from becoming entrenched.Highlighting the risk of stubbornly high inflation, Catherine Mann, an external economist on the MPC, joined her fellow committee members Megan Greene and Huw Pill in dissenting against the majority of the panel with a vote to raise rates immediately to 4%.Greene, another external member, and Pill, the Bank’s chief economist, had previously been outvoted in pushing for a quarter-point rise at the previous MPC meeting amid concern about inflation.Financial markets had priced in a more than 90% probability of Threadneedle Street keeping borrowing costs on hold, with the outside chance of a rise. Investors expect a rise in borrowing costs to 4% before the end of the year.The news comes after the Federal Reserve held borrowing costs unchanged on Wednesday and its new chair, Kevin Warsh, unnerved some investors worried over the US central bank’s readiness to tackle high inflation – leading to a rise in US government borrowing costs to the highest level since 2007.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, briefly rose above $100 a barrel last week before falling back, amid fears that the violence across the Middle East could shatter the world economy’s earlier resilience to the Iran war. It was trading at a little below $90 on Thursday.The Bank of England said that under its central forecast – involving the oil price falling back to about $71 a barrel – it still expected UK inflation to peak at about 3.2% later this year as households came under pressure from higher energy prices.Under a milder scenario for the war, it said inflation would peak at about 3% before falling rapidly, leading the central bank to cut borrowing costs. However, economists said the situation remained highly dependent on how the conflict unfolded.Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at the consultancy CapitalEconomics, said: “Much depends on what happens to energy prices and whether or not that leads to the second-round inflation effects that could transform a temporary rise in inflation into a longer-lasting one.”While awaiting developments in the war, he said, “the BoE doesn’t seem to be moving closer to actually raising rates”.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandEconomicsEconomic policyInflationMonetary policy committeenewsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa agrees to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceed | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Uefa nations have agreed to boycott all Fifa tournaments if the global governing body continues with its plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Uefa nations have agreed to boycott all Fifa tournaments if the global governing body continues with its plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup
Content: Spain’s Dani Olmo with the World Cup after their victory over Argentina in New York.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenSpain’s Dani Olmo with the World Cup after their victory over Argentina in New York.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoUefaUefa agrees to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceedUefa agrees stance at emergency meeting on ThursdayBoycott would begin with Under-20 Women’s World CupNick AmesandMatt HughesThu 30 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean countries have agreed to boycott all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino pushes forward with his proposals to sell chunks of the World Cup toUS-based private investment.In an extraordinary development all 55 Uefa members resolved not to participate in future World Cups or other Fifa-run events, saying in a statement that they “unanimously and unequivocally reject” the proposals. An emergency meeting that lasted just short of two hours ended with a united front despite earlier fears that smaller countries, attracted by the money on offer through Infantino’s scheme, would be swayed in favour.European FAs are expected to write toFifathis week with a formal notification of their threat to boycott future tournaments unless the planned World Cup sell-off is withdrawn.Fifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s gameRead moreIt means Infantino faces an uphill battle to push his plan forward. Countries had been given until 19 September to sign up but there will now be significant pressure to drastically revise his scheme or withdraw it completely. While the majority of European FAs had submitted letters of support in favour of his re-election next March, such a decisive line in the sand fromUefaweakens his position dramatically.Uefa’s statement confirmed the decision. “As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” it read.Thursday’s meeting was introduced by the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with executive committee members and Uefa’s Fifa council representatives also addressing delegates. Those early speeches are understood to have set the tone, with around 20 further FA heads taking the floor and multiple sources describing an atmosphere of “unity”. Among those to offer their view was Debbie Hewitt, the president of the FA, who one attendee said gave a “very tough” exposition in favour of a boycott.That was backed up in a statement by an FA spokesperson that read: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”Along the lines spelled out by Uefa, at senior level the proposed boycott would begin with next year’s Women’s World Cup, while the first age-group Fifa tournament to be boycotted is likely to be the Under-20 Women’s World Cup. It is due to take place in Poland from 5 September with six of the 24 competitors, including England, due to represent Uefa countries.England’s women’s team also have a two-legged World Cup qualifying playoff tie against Greece in October, which would be a major test of the FA’s resolve if Fifa refuse to back down.The European governing body invited other confederations to follow their lead. Uefa are understood to be confident that a number of Asian countries, in particular, are similarly minded. Infantino’s strongholds traditionally lie outside Europe and a collapse in support elsewhere could have severe consequences for the Fifa president.“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences,” Uefa said. “This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.”Sources within European football believe Uefa’s decision increases the chances of a Europe-backed candidate running against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, which he had been expected to sail through without opposition.The North, Central American and Caribbean confederation, Concacaf, also unanimously rejected Fifa’s proposal after an emergency meeting chaired by the president, Victor Montagliani, who is seen as a potential successor to Infantino, but stopped short of following Uefa’s lead by announcing a boycott.Despite this, it is understood that the majority of Concacaf’s 41 members are losing confidence in Infantino’s leadership of Fifa, raising the possibility that his own position could be in serious doubt for the first time since he took office in 2016.A number of European national associations are understood to have held talks with their respective governments over the matter, many of whom have backed a boycott in private.The new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was the first politician to criticise Fifa’s plan on Tuesday evening, writing on X that the World Cup “was never anyone’s to sell”.“This is a principled decision that we strongly support. Football belongs to the fans, not billionaire investors. Enough is enough. It’s time to take a stand to protect our game.”Explore more on these topicsUefaWorld CupFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa could draw US Congress inquiry over ‘smash-and-grab scam’, top Democrat warns | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Jamie Raskin targets football body’s proposed commercial sell-off and links to Trump administration
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Jamie Raskin targets football body’s proposed commercial sell-off and links to Trump administration
Content: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, and Donald Trump during the World Cup 2026 final at New York New Jersey Stadium on 19 July in East Rutherford.Photograph: Rob Newell/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, and Donald Trump during the World Cup 2026 final at New York New Jersey Stadium on 19 July in East Rutherford.Photograph: Rob Newell/CameraSport/Getty ImagesFifaFifa could draw US Congress inquiry over ‘smash-and-grab scam’, top Democrat warnsJamie Raskin targets football body’s proposed commercial sell-off and links to Trump administrationUS politics live – latest updatesJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 30 Jul 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa could face a sweeping US congressional investigation into its expanding financial and political ties toDonald Trumpand his family if Democrats reclaim the House of Representatives in November, a senior party figure has warned.Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, accused global football’s governing body of a “smash-and-grab scam of colossal proportions” after it proposed a multibillion-dollar privatization of its commercial operations.Raskin, a Democratic representative of Maryland, would become the judiciary committee’s chair under a Democratic House majority, vowed to makeFifaan early target of scrutiny – and accused the organization of embedding itself in what he described as a pattern of corruption surrounding Trump’s second administration and the Kushner family.Uefa agrees to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceedRead more“Over the last few weeks, Fifa’s cozy relationship toDonald Trumphas been floating to the top of the swamp of quid pro quo corruption in which the Trump Administration is swimming,” Raskin said in a statement to the Guardian. “But now we see where all the bribes, kickbacks and sweetheart deals have been leading.”Raskin’s comments follow plans of the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to pursue a spin-off of the organization’s commercial business into a standalone company,reportedly valued at about $20bn. JPMorgan Chase is leading the fundraising effort, with Thrive Eternal, an investment vehicle linked to the Thrive Capital founder, Joshua Kushner, among the prospective investors. Joshua Kushner is the brother of Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a high-level White House adviser.The proposal has sparked an immediate backlash across world football, and beyond.Uefa, the European football governing body, has warned that “none of us are the owners of football”, and on Thursdayvoted to boycott the World Cupif Fifa presses ahead.The inquiry also follows a series of similarly scandalous controversies surrounding Fifa’s relationship with the Trump administration. The organization invented its first-ever “peace prize”, which theyawarded to Trumpin December, weeks after he publicly complained about missing out on the Nobel peace prize. During this summer’s World Cup, Uefa accused Fifa of undermining the tournament’s integrity after officials reversed a red card issued to the US forward Folarin Balogunfollowing a callfrom Trump to Infantino. Separately, the US Department of Justicedroppedthe long-running bribery and money-laundering cases tied to the Fifa corruption scandal after prosecutors said they no longer fit the administration’s enforcement priorities.Should Democrats – who lack the legal power to demand that witnesses appear under the current Republican House majority – win control of the chamber in November’sUS midterm elections, Raskin would have the authority to compel testimony and documents from Fifa, JPMorgan and entities connected to the Kushner family’s investment vehicles.“Fifa needs to cooperate in good faith now,” he added. “If and whenDemocratstake the House, this Committee will have the tools we need to get answers, expose corruption, protect sports fans against exorbitant and fraudulent charges and block this attempt to turn world soccer into a global financial shakedown.”The White House has previously dismissed similar allegations as politically motivated. Fifa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The judiciary committee minority under Raskin hasalready requested recordsfrom Fifa, including documents related to gifts provided to Trump, communications with the justice department, and visitor logs for Fifa’s Miami headquarters and its Trump Tower office.“Fifa appears to have struck a several hundred-billion-dollar deal orchestrated by Jared Kushner’s brother and JPMorgan to privatize Fifa’s business operations so private equity, hedge funds, autocrats, kleptocrats and large investors can come to own and control the world’s most beautiful game,” Raskin said.“The United States is set to host the Women’sWorld Cupin 2031, and we have a responsibility to ensure Fifa will not again bring its own brand of corrupt pay-to-play politics and exploitation onto our soil,” he added.Explore more on these topicsFifaWorld Cup 2026Trump administrationUS CongressDemocratsDonald TrumpWorld CupnewsShareReuse this content

title: Billy Ray Smith Jr, ex-San Diego Chargers star, dies at 64 as family cites CTE | NFL | The Guardian
description: The former Chargers standout and College Football Hall of Famer died at 64 after what his family said was a bout with CTE-caused dementia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The former Chargers standout and College Football Hall of Famer died at 64 after what his family said was a bout with CTE-caused dementia
Content: Billy Ray Smith Jr speaks at a San Diego Chargers event in 2012.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APView image in fullscreenBilly Ray Smith Jr speaks at a San Diego Chargers event in 2012.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APNFLBilly Ray Smith Jr, ex-San Diego Chargers star, dies at 64 as family cites CTEFamily says Smith faced ‘dementia caused by CTE’College Football Hall of Famer played 10 NFL seasonsAssociated PressThu 30 Jul 2026 09.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer San Diego Chargers linebacker and College Football Hall of Famer Billy Ray Smith Jr has died. He was 64.Smith’s family said in a statement Wednesday that Smith died following a bout with CTE-caused dementia.“It is with profound sadness that we share the loss of our beloved Billy Ray Smith Jr, who passed away peacefully surrounded by family,” the statement said. “Billy Ray faced his long journey with dementia caused by CTE with unmatched bravery, dignity, and strength. Billy Ray brought so much joy, light, and laughter to the world as a devoted father, husband, son, and loyal friend.”Smith played 10 seasons with the Chargers after being selected with the No 5 overall pick of the 1983NFLdraft out of Arkansas. He was named to the Chargers’ 50th anniversary team after racking up 15 career interceptions, 14 fumble recoveries and 13 forced fumbles.Smith became the sports director at the ABC affiliate in San Diego following his playing career and was co-host of a long-running radio show while covering college and professional football for national TV broadcasts.Smith was a two-time All-American at Arkansas and was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 2000. He starred at Plano Senior High School in Texas.His father, Billy Ray Smith Sr, also played at Arkansas and in the NFL from 1957 to 1970 with the Los Angeles Rams, Pittsburgh Steelers and Baltimore Colts.CTE is a degenerative brain disease that has been found in athletes in contact sports, combat veterans and others who experience repetitive head trauma. It has been known to cause violent mood swings, impulsive behavior and depression. It can be diagnosed only after death.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Eddie Howe leaves Newcastle United with Matthias Jaissle set to replace him | Newcastle United | The Guardian
description: Eddie Howe has left Newcastle and is likely to be replaced by the German coach Matthias Jaissle, who is currently in charge of the Saudi Arabian club Al-Ahli
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Eddie Howe has left Newcastle and is likely to be replaced by the German coach Matthias Jaissle, who is currently in charge of the Saudi Arabian club Al-Ahli
Content: Eddie Howe has left Newcastle United after almost five years in charge, with Al-Ahli manager Matthias Jassle in the frame to replace him.Composite: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEddie Howe has left Newcastle United after almost five years in charge, with Al-Ahli manager Matthias Jassle in the frame to replace him.Composite: AFP/Getty ImagesNewcastle UnitedEddie Howe leaves Newcastle United with Matthias Jaissle set to replace himHowe leaves after five years in charge at St James’ ParkAl-Ahli’s German coach in line to take overLouise TaylorThu 30 Jul 2026 04.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEddie Howe has left Newcastle after losing control of transfers and is likely to be replaced by the German coach Matthias Jaissle, who is in charge of the Saudi Arabian club Al-Ahli.Although the timing of Howe’s abrupt departure after almost five years in charge at St James’ Park is unexpected, his position had been uncertain for some time. He is understood to have told Newcastle’s Saudi Arabian owners he wanted to leave more than a fortnight ago and the parting is said to be “amicable”.Sources have suggested the 48-year-old told directors he was utterly drained and wanted to take a break from football after a transformative Tyneside tenure in which Newcastle won the League Cup in 2025 and twice qualified for the Champions League.In recent months, Howe has become disillusioned after seeing his previously strong powerbase and ability to dictate transfer policy diminished significantly. Already this summer Ross Wilson, the third sporting director of his managerial tenure, has presided over the sale of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively. A year ago the team’s key striker Alexander Isak departed for Liverpool.Quick GuideHowe's highs and lows at NewcastleShow2021-22: The firefighterAfter taking over from Steve Bruce in November 2021, Eddie Howe gets strong backing in the January transfer window and guides Newcastle to an 11th-place finish. A run of six straight wins at home sees the Magpies become the first team in Premier League history to avoid relegation after failing to win any of their first 14 games.2022-23: Return to EuropeAlexander Isak arrives for big money in the summer, but it is mostly existing players like Callum Wilson and Miguel Almirón who power Howe's side to the League Cup final, which ends in defeat to Manchester United. Newcastle respond well, earning a fourth-place finish to qualify for the Champions League.2023-24: Injuries biteHowe's training methods are called into doubt as Newcastle finish bottom of their Champions League group and struggle with injuries all season. They also lose £55m signing Sandro Tonali to a betting ban. A late run earns seventh spot but European hopes are dashed as Manchester United stun City in the FA Cup final.2024-25: League Cup triumphA brilliant, Dan Burn-inspired win over Liverpool at Wembley sees Howe lift the League Cup (pictured) and finally end Newcastle's long trophy drought. With Isak banging in 23 Premier League goals, the Toon secure a fifth-place finish, which is good enough to earn Champions League qualification once again.2025-26: The ghost of IsakA summer-long saga over the sale of Isak to Liverpool scuppers plans for Howe's fourth full season in charge. The fans turn on wantaway Anthony Gordon midway through a campaign that is all but ended by a humiliating 7-2 defeat at Barcelona in March. Howe's final five months in charge feature 14 defeats across all competitions as Newcastle slump to 12th in the Premier League.Tom BassamPhotograph: Danny Lawson/PAWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Not that Howe gave any indication of the events about to unfold when he spoke to reporters after Wednesday night’s 4-1 pre-season friendly defeat at Bristol City. “Every day as Newcastle manager is a great day for me,” he said. “I absolutely love the football club and that will never change. There has been a lot of change at the football club and potentially more to come. [But] I think there’s always reasons to be optimistic. I believe great things are possible every season. I see no reason for it be any different this year.”On Thursday morning the Newcastle hierarchy’s negotiations with Jaissle were said to be at an advanced stage and the club’s players had a day off interrupted by news that that there would be a change of manager. Given that Al-Ahli are also owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Jaissle’s split from his club is unlikely to prove problematic.The 38-year-old had a brief playing career as a defender with Hoffenheim and has been in charge of Al-Ahli since 2023, presiding over 90 wins, 25 draws and 23 defeats. Along the way he has won a Saudi Super Cup and two Asian Champions Leagues. In his first major head coaching role, at RB Salzburg, he won two league titles and the Austrian Cup in two seasons.After Newcastle finished a disappointing 12th in the Premier League last season some fans were calling for Howe’s dismissal but the former Bournemouth manager appeared to have convinced PIF to offer him another chance during a high level summit meeting at a Northumberland country house hotel in April.He is understood to have reiterated his commitment to the job after returning from holiday in June but subsequently became disenchanted by the events of a turbulent summer. Quite apart from the exits of Gordon and Tonali, it has featured doubt surrounding the future of the Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimarães, who is said to be closing in on an £80m move to Arsenal.At Bristol City on Wednesday night, Howe admitted he had “lost control” of transfers and did not know if Guimarães would board the team’s flight to south-east Spain before a training Camp at La Manga on Friday.While Guimarães is understood to have told Newcastle he wants to join Arsenal this summer, Howe had developed increasing reservations about a new, PIF approved, policy of signing largely young players with high resale potential priced, broadly, in the £20m-£40m bracket. With Newcastle operating under a Uefa settlement agreement, Wilson believes it is the best way to remain within football’s spending rules.View image in fullscreenEddie Howe oversaw a 4-1 friendly defeat to Bristol City on Wednesday, in what proved to be his final game in charge.Photograph: David Davies/PASo far this summer the sporting director has recruited four promising yet inexperienced players aged 20 or under in Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Touré, Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur. Howe feared expectations had been raised earlier this year when his chief executive David Hopkinson claimed he wanted Newcastle to “be in the conversation” about the identity of the best clubs in the world by 2030. Howe told friends things “no longer felt right”.Although Howe acquired a number of critics as results, increasingly, disappointed last season, he will long be remembered with affection and gratitude at St James’ Park. After succeeding Steve Bruce as manager in November 2021 he led Newcastle to two Carabao Cup finals and in winning the second – against Liverpool – last year secured the club’s first significant domestic silverware for 70 years.With his assistant, Jason Tindall, also expected to leave, the squad are likely to be placed under the caretaker charge of first team coach, Graeme Jones, for the trip to La Manga.The club hope that Jaissle will soon join them. With the former Nottingham Forest manager Vítor Pereira poised to replace him at Al-Ahli, the expectation is that the German will take the helm well before Newcastle’s training camp concludes.Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UnitedEddie HowenewsShareReuse this content

title: Double tops: Littler and Pogacar in a class of their own, but nothing lasts for ever | Sport | The Guardian
description: The champions are capable of shattering every record in a temporary aligning of the planets, the elusiveness of pure perfection
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: The champions are capable of shattering every record in a temporary aligning of the planets, the elusiveness of pure perfection
Content: Luke Littler and Tadej Pogacar looked unstoppable as they won the World Matchplay and the Tour de France.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Reuters; APView image in fullscreenLuke Littler and Tadej Pogacar looked unstoppable as they won the World Matchplay and the Tour de France.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Reuters; APSportDouble tops: Littler and Pogacar in a class of their own, but nothing lasts for everJonathan LiewThe champions are capable of shattering every record in a temporary aligning of the planets, the elusiveness of pure perfectionThu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.08 EDTShareTreble-20.“Ohh, he couldn’t.”Treble-19.“Oh, you spiteful young man.”Bull.“You spiteful person!That is ridiculous!”As ever, Wayne Mardle – commentating on the World Matchplay final for Sky Sports on Sunday night – put it most succinctly of all.The great individual champions require a vindictive streak. The ability not just to harness their own strength, but to tessellate it with their opponent’s moment of greatest vulnerability. To sense weakness, recognise doubt and pounce mercilessly upon it. To nurture and desire the very same qualities we try to extinguish and discourage in our children. To find a 167 checkout, when your opponent is sitting on double-10, in a major final.To be fair to Luke Littler, he would probably have won whatever he did, however he threw his darts, whether he did it kindly or not. Such is the gulf he enjoys over what we so euphemistically describe as “his competition”. Gerwyn Price went into Sunday’s final playing perhaps the best darts of his life; arguably better than when he won theworld championship in 2021.Of all the contenders to Littler’s crown, Price seems to have thought hardest about how to get into the teenager’s headspace, how not to be cowed, how to use the crowd and his own overwhelming self-belief to make himself the problem. Littler destroyed him 18-9 in just over an hour.View image in fullscreenLuke Littler celebrates after his victory against Gerwyn Price at the World Matchplay final.Photograph: Ben Roberts Photo/Getty ImagesLuke Littler retains World Matchplay title after crushing win against Gerwyn PriceRead moreThis was Littler’s second consecutive World Matchplay crown, to go with a second consecutive world championship in January and a second consecutive UK Open in March. There are 11 major competitions in the Professional Darts Corporation calendar and Littler has won six out of six this year, the past eight in a row, nine of the past 11. His order of merit tally of £3.1m is more than treble that of Luke Humphries in second place. A run of 36 wins in his past 37 matches in ranking tournaments stands comparison with the great Phil Taylor, who was throwing against lesser fields in a less professional era.Like many members of his terminally online generation, Littler is preoccupied by numbers and records, the clout they earn you, the tears of his beaten adversaries. Which is part of what makes him such a fascinating character to watch in big tournaments: the sense that dominance is its own end, not simply the culmination of a well-executed process. It is why he produces his best darts on the biggest stages, in the longest formats. Why he is addicted to the rush of the 170, the nine-dart finish, the TV cameras, the crowds, whether they like him or not.More than 800 miles away, on the slopes of Le Lioran, a similar phenomenon was unfolding. Yes, on an important level, I realise Littler andTadej Pogacarare very different athletes: one the perfect physical specimen honed since an early age through a strict diet and a murderous training regime, the other a five-time winner of the Tour de France. But having watched a good deal of both over the past few weeks and indeed the past few years, I’ve been struck above all by the similarities, the common sensations, the curious paradox that arises when you see someone so good at what they do that people start to accuse them of ruining it for everyone else.“It’s like watching two different sports,” the TNT Sports commentator gushed as Pogacar surged past Richard Carapaz on stage 10 on the way to stretching his lead over Jonas Vingegaard to an almost impregnable three minutes. This was the stage when the Bastille Day crowdsbegan to boo Pogacarfor the stranglehold he has begun to exert on the sport. “Haters gonna hate,” Pogacar said, and other riders would also spring to his defence. At the heart of all this lay a question: to what extent do we want to see dominant athletes dominate?View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar went solo with a little over 15km remaining of stage 10 into Le Lioran, where he was memorably beaten by Jonas Vingegaard in 2024.Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Getty ImagesFor Pogacar, these are questions loaded by road cycling’s toxic history. No matter how many doping tests he passes, no matter how much transparency he offers, there is a constituency of cycling fans for whom dominance will always equal suspicion. And – important – a suspicion that can never truly be refuted. You don’t trust the anti-doping protocols and you don’t truly believe the Tour can be won clean. In which case, how is anyone meant to exhibit transcendence? What is the point of a three-week sporting event in which nobody can ever truly be allowed to be exceptional? Why are you even watching this sport in the first place?For Littler, by contrast, the fascination lies in the very absence of exegesis, the sheer inadequacy of the darting vocabulary to contextualise what it is he does. There are numbers and palmarès, of course, but really the Littler supremacy consists of a vibe, an implication, a terror, the sense he can win a game however he wants. He can destroy you in minutes or hours; from the front or coming from behind, with a smile or a snarl. The result may never be in contention, but virtually everything else is.As with Pogacar, Littler’s dominance has drawn as much negative as positive comment in recent months, not so much in the form of personal criticism but a lament for an age when the sport was more capricious and open. Part of the moral panic is that they are still young – Pogacar 27, Littler 19, both still capable of shattering every record in the game, demoralising an entire generation of challengers.Relentless Tadej Pogacar wins fifth Tour de France to equal recordRead moreEven the very greatest dominate only fleetingly. Eddy Merckx, perhaps Pogacar’s only remaining rival as the greatest cyclist of all time, won pretty much everything he won in an eight-year stretch from 1967 to 1975. Roger Federer’s imperial phase basically lasted for six years; Usain Bolt’s and Steffi Graf’s roughly eight. Even Taylor’s two decades of dominance require a little context: only from around 2005 onwards was darts a genuinely year-round sport.The weekend before last, I went to the London Stadium to watch another seemingly invincible athlete do their thing. Mondo Duplantis had broken the men’s pole vault world record 13 times in four years and would inevitably break it again. Except, he didn’t. He got injured and had to make do with second place with a still-unfathomable height of 5.95m.Far from feeling short-changed, I left feeling strangely melancholy, reminded that what felt inexorable at the time was not a new normal, but a brief anomaly. Perhaps we underestimate the ephemerality of true dominance, the extent to which it is not a permanent state of affairs, but a temporary aligning of the planets, the elusiveness of pure perfection.Pogacar, Littler, Duplantis, Jannik Sinner, Barcelona Women, Australia Women: hate them if you must. But know too that it could all be gone tomorrow.Explore more on these topicsSportLuke LittlerTadej PogacarcommentShareReuse this content

title: Experimental Liverpool down Wrexham thanks to Rio Ngumoha’s winner | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The substitute’s 75th-minute effort gave Liverpool a 1-0 win in a pre-season game of few chances at Yankee Stadium
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: The substitute’s 75th-minute effort gave Liverpool a 1-0 win in a pre-season game of few chances at Yankee Stadium
Content: Rio Ngumoha celebrates with Dominic Szoboszlai after scoring Liverpool’s winner against Wrexham at Yankee Stadium.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRio Ngumoha celebrates with Dominic Szoboszlai after scoring Liverpool’s winner against Wrexham at Yankee Stadium.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesSoccerExperimental Liverpool down Wrexham thanks to Rio Ngumoha’s winnerSubstitute’s deflected strike earns 1-0 win in New YorkChances few and far between in pre-season friendlyAndy Hunterat Yankee StadiumWed 29 Jul 2026 21.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 04.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool turned the Empire State Building red when launching a new away kit on Tuesday but neither they nor Wrexham could illuminate Yankee Stadium 24 hours later. It was rough in the diamond, although Rio Ngumoha’s deflected goal made it two wins out of two for Andoni Iraola on his first pre-season tour asLiverpoolhead coach.Ngumoha, a second half substitute who Iraola deployed on the right, satisfied the majority of a 42,204 crowd with a 75th-minute shot that looped in offWrexhamdefender Lewis Brunt. Wrexham’s Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney (now simply Rob Mac) were in attendance for what the former had labelled a “punch-me moment” but in truth few blows were traded at the iconic baseball stadium.Liverpool prepare opening offer for Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley BarcolaRead moreLiverpool’s preparations for the second game of pre-season were not exactly smooth, in fairness to Iraola’s team. Their flight from Chicago was cancelled on Tuesday night with players and staff on the tarmac ready to take off. Poor weather conditions in the New York area delayed their arrival until the day of the game, and Liverpool only checked into their Midtown hotel around midday. They were flying back to Chicago straight after the match too.Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch did not make the trip from Liverpool’s training base despite joining up with the squad following their post-World Cup holidays. The game came too early in their pre-season preparations to be considered. With Joe Gomez injured and Federico Chiesa also absent through illness, Iraola had little choice but to select another young and experimental side. Six of Liverpool’s starting line-up had no Premier League experience whatsoever but at least the emphasis on youth offered the crowd a glimpse of the highly-rated Joshua Abe.View image in fullscreenJoshua Abe reacts after failing to score at Yankee Stadium.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesAbe, a pacy and prolific right winger, is regarded as one of the brightest prospects in the country and was inundated with offers before committing his future to Liverpool when turning 16 earlier this month. Manchester City, Manchester United and Chelsea were all interested in the Warrington-born England youth international, with deals worth £40,000-a-week reportedly on his table. There was understandable relief inside Anfield when he agreed scholarship terms in June with a three-year professional contract to follow on his 17th birthday next July.Abe could have marked his first senior Liverpool start with an early goal when released clear of the Wrexham defence by Harvey Elliott. A heavy first touch gave the Wrexham and former Liverpool goalkeeper Danny Ward opportunity to save at the feet of the teenager. Iraola started with a front line of Calum Scanlon, Lewis Koumas and Abe. Koumas went close from distance and had a penalty shout waved away but, aside from a few surging midfield runs by Dominik Szoboszlai, it was a quiet friendly.Wrexham are further along in their pre-season work – their first competitive game is a week on Friday against Middlesbrough in the Carabao Cup – and it showed as the first half progressed and Phil Parkinson’s team gained a physical edge. Sam Smith and Callum Doyle were unable to trouble Giorgi Mamardashvili with the chances that fell their way.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAbe, Scanlon, Milos Kerkez and Trey Nyoni were replaced at half-time by Ngumoha, Kieran Morrison, Kostas Tsimikas and Curtis Jones respectively. Elliott was presented with a sight of the Wrexham goal by Koumas minutes after the restart but his first-time shot from 20 yards was well saved by Ward. The Wales international also denied Szoboszlai from distance but this was a Liverpool performance – and pre-season friendly – that failed to ignite.Wrexham substitute Nathan Broadhead almost succeeded with a powerful drive from 25 yards that was pushed away by Mamardashvili. Brunt and Kieffer Moore both had good late chances to equalise but miscued from close range.Explore more on these topicsFootballLiverpoolWrexhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Not so black and white: how Eddie Howe lost control at Newcastle in one summer | Newcastle United | The Guardian
description: Everything was looking rosy for Howe at St James’ Park until Alexander Isak’s departure led to rushed signings and a messy season
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Everything was looking rosy for Howe at St James’ Park until Alexander Isak’s departure led to rushed signings and a messy season
Content: Eddie Howe was popular during five years on Tyneside in which he delivered the club’s first domestic trophy since 1955.Photograph: Scott Heppell/PAView image in fullscreenEddie Howe was popular during five years on Tyneside in which he delivered the club’s first domestic trophy since 1955.Photograph: Scott Heppell/PANewcastle UnitedAnalysisNot so black and white: how Eddie Howe lost control at Newcastle in one summerLouise TaylorEverything was looking rosy for Howe at St James’ Park until Alexander Isak’s departure led to rushed signings and a messy seasonThu 30 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTShareLast September, David Hopkinson, just installed as Newcastle’s chief executive, perched on a stool at a downstairs corner table in Shearer’s Bar at St James’ Park and between sips of zero alcohol lager, likenedEddie Howeto Bruce Springsteen. According to Hopkinson, Newcastle’s manager was “the Boss” and “the talent”. He conjured up an imaginary scene involving Springsteen asking for M&M’s before a concert and being duly supplied with a dressing room overflowing with the brightly coloured confectionery. The same principle, he said, would apply to “Eddie”, who would e furnished with “whatever he wants”.Six months later, things had changed. In late March, Hopkinson sat around a heavy wooden table in a St James’ Park boardroom and, between sips of coffee, said he did not “have a stance on the manager’s future”. What he could tell assembled reporters was that arecent home defeatby Sunderland “hurt”. It “resonated” and was being taken “seriously”. Given that Newcastle had just lost aChampions League tie 8-3 to Barcelona on aggregateand were en route to finishing 12th in the Premier League, Howe admitted to “sleepless nights” before a summit with the club’s majority Saudi Arabian ownership at Matfen Hall hotel in Northumberland the following month.Football Daily | Thought leader Eddie Howe runs out of time and ideas at NewcastleRead moreThe 48-year-old, who only a year earlier had choreographedNewcastle’s Carabao Cup triumph, securing their first domestic trophy since 1955, would win that particular battle. Thanks to a convincing, typically articulate presentation detailing his future tactical plans, Howe was allowed by the visitors from Riyadh to remain in the job he had occupied since November 2021. Even then, however, he suspected he was losing a war that had begun long before Hopkinson’s installation.It was an often subliminal conflict about power and control that started when Amanda Staveley, the club’s former co-owner, was ousted in the summer of 2024. Howe had been very much Staveley’s appointment and, given that she was then responsible for running the club on a daily basis, he was permitted considerable say in buying and selling players.During his time in charge of Bournemouth, Howe exerted significant control over all spheres of the organisation, his unwillingness to delegate even extending to proof reading the match programme. In an era when sporting directors rather than managers invariably call the ultimate shots in the Premier League Howe, unusually, enjoyed similar authority at Newcastle. With Andy Howe, his nephew, occupying a senior recruitment role and invitations to visit the team’s training ground issued at Eddie’s discretion, Howe’s word was law.That regimen initially served him well. When Paul Mitchell, who succeeded Dan Ashworth as sporting director, suggested alterations to transfer policy and playing style, Howe made his displeasure plain. Within a year Mitchell left. It was June 2025 and with the League Cup won three months earlier the manager had never seemed more secure. Yet that exit of a second sporting director arguably prefaced Howe’s ownfall.View image in fullscreenAlexander Isak celebrates scoring the second goal in the Carabao Cup final against Liverpool at Wembley in March 2025. Three months later he asked to leave the club.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersAdmittedly, it was not his fault Alexander Isak forced a £125m move to Liverpool last summer, but Howe was heavily involved in Newcastle signing £240m of largely underachieving talent in a forlorn attempt to compensate for the Sweden striker’s defection. If neither the £69m Nick Woltemade nor the £55m Yoane Wissa were suitable replacements for Isak, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga often underwhelmed. Only the central defender Malick Thiaw impressed.Moreover, it had not gone unnoticed in Riyadh that Howe’s unwillingness to sell players exacerbated the ownership’s financial problems at a time when Newcastle’s comparatively low commercial revenues made it a struggle to remain within football’s spending rules. In May, the club entered a Uefa settlement agreement after breaching European investment rules last season. It dictates they must balance the books very carefully for the next three years and explains why their latest sporting director, Ross Wilson,sold Anthony Gordonand Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively this summer. Howe was reluctant to lose the pair and became dismayed at the prospect of seeing another key individual in Bruno Guimarães depart for Arsenal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionToon turnover: the stats behind Eddie Howe’s highs and lows at NewcastleRead moreWilson, who arrived from Nottingham Forest in October, has presided over a marked policy pivot involving signing young players possessing high resale potential. So far this close season Newcastle have acquired four promising yet inexperienced newcomers aged 20 or under in Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Touré, Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur. Hopkinson has boasted that Newcastle are aiming to be one “of the best clubs in the world” by 2030 but Howe is not the only one to have detected a disconnect between such lofty expectations and a bold experiment with youth that could easily go badly wrong. Well aware he had remained at Bournemouth a season too long before being sacked in 2020, it seems Howe decided it would be better to jump rather than be pushed, and leave on amicable terms.In five years on Tyneside, he improved some players almost beyond recognition – Joelinton and Jacob Murphy in particular – and choreographed an often thrilling brand of football during two Champions League campaigns. At their high tempo, hard-pressing best, Newcastle were gloriously entertaining, but Howe’s team became frequently poor in possession and adept at forfeiting leads. Pace and athleticism seemed prioritised ahead of vision and incision. Like their workaholic manager, Newcastle increasingly resembled a team that had forgotten how to relax and read the game’s nuances.Howe is gifted enough, intelligent enough and young enough to reach the highest echelons of coaching but first he needs to rest, reassess and, perhaps, remember why he once fell in love with Arsenal’s football during their Cesc Fàbregas-inspired tiki-taka phase. The irony of his Newcastle tenure is that a manager obsessed with off-field control came undone partly by its absence on the pitch.It is a paradox Howe may reflect on as he sits at his treasured piano and creates some new mood music of his own.Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UnitedEddie HoweanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Maxence Lacroix joins ‘beautiful club’ Chelsea as John Stones seals Inter deal | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Maxence Lacroix has joined Chelsea from Crystal Palace to become the club’s fifth signing of the summer so far
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Maxence Lacroix has joined Chelsea from Crystal Palace to become the club’s fifth signing of the summer so far
Content: Chelsea have secured their main defensive target after Maxence Lacroix signed a six-year deal.Photograph: Chris Lee/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChelsea have secured their main defensive target after Maxence Lacroix signed a six-year deal.Photograph: Chris Lee/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesChelseaMaxence Lacroix joins ‘beautiful club’ Chelsea as John Stones seals Inter dealFrance centre-back moves to Blues in £52m transferStones signs two-year contract with Serie A clubPA MediaThu 30 Jul 2026 14.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaxence Lacroix has joined Chelsea fromCrystal Palaceto become the club’s fifth signing of the summer. The France international, who won the FA Cup and Conference League with Palace, was the Blues’ main defensive target of the window.Lacroix, 26, signs a six-year deal with Xabi Alonso’s side. “I am really happy to be part of this beautiful club,” said Lacroix, who played three times for France at the World Cup, including in their 6-4 bronze medal match defeat by England.Where all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the seasonRead more“Everyone knows the legend ofChelsea, its tradition of winning, and to be a part of that is a proud moment. I think it’s the best move for me because it’s the best club in the world. When I spoke with the manager, I saw that we have the same direction and desire for this club.“We want to win. When you see the quality of the players here, everything we have around the club, it’s something that we can achieve. The ambition is to lift trophies, and I can’t wait to contribute.”Chelsea had been looking to add experience to their back line havingmissed out on Rennes’ Jérémy Jacquetin January, with the player opting to join Liverpool. Levi Colwill, who is considered to be a key part of the club’s long-term plans, missed almost all of last season with an anterior cruciate ligament injury, with Wesley Fofana and Trevoh Chalobah forming the central-defensive partnership for much of the campaign.After a dismal season that saw the club finish 10th, the club’s hierarchy has acknowledged a change in recruitment policy is needed, with a refocusing away from young, inexperienced players towards ones that can help the team compete for the title.Lacroix, who made 55 appearances last season for Palace, has been one of the league’s most consistent defenders since moving to Selhurst Park from Wolfsburg in 2024.The Blues confirmed theclub-record arrival of Aston Villa forward Morgan Rogerslast week, and have also added Atalanta defender Marco Palestra, striker Emmanuel Emegha from Strasbourg and Sporting Lisbon’s Geovany Quenda.Chelsea also look set to signBrighton’s Danny Welbeck and Jordan Hendersonafter his contract with Brentford was terminated.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJohn Stoneshas joined Inter on a two-year contract, the Serie A club have announced.The England centre-back was a free agent after leaving Manchester City and had attracted interest from clubs across Europe.The 32-year-old ended his 10-year stay at City in June. He made 295 appearances for the club after joining from Everton for £47.5m in 2016 and won six Premier League titles, three FA Cups and a Champions League title.Explore more on these topicsChelseaTransfer windowCrystal PalaceJohn StonesInternazionalenewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubs | Football politics | The Guardian
description: The Premier League has proposed a deal that would result in an extra £1.5bn being shared with EFL clubs over the next decade
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: The Premier League has proposed a deal that would result in an extra £1.5bn being shared with EFL clubs over the next decade
Content: The Premier League could raise the transfer levy to pay for the scheme.Photograph: Valerio Rosati/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Premier League could raise the transfer levy to pay for the scheme.Photograph: Valerio Rosati/AlamyFootball politicsPremier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubsClubs vote unanimously for ‘new deal for football’‘Lifeboat’ fund for clubs in crisis would be set upPaul MacInnesThu 30 Jul 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThePremier Leaguehas agreed on a proposal to reset financial distribution within English football’s top four divisions, one that would lead to an extra £1.5bn being shared across the pyramid over the next decade.Clubs voted unanimously to support the so-called “new deal for football” at a meeting on Thursday, after discussions with the EFL. The offer will now be presented to the EFL’s board for consideration.According to details originally published by Sky News, the Premier League’s offer would run for 10 years and result in an additional £1.5bn being shared with EFL clubs on top of the £1.6bn currently distributed to clubs and communities every three years. Some of the money would be put into discrete funds – a “lifeboat” fund for clubs in immediate crisis and one that is directed exclusively at infrastructure.To cover the extra costs, Premier League clubs have reportedly agreed to raise the transfer levy applied to all top-flight deals from 4% to 6%. The Guardian reported this week thatManchester City were initially opposed to increasing the levy.The Premier League said in a statement that its clubs had “unanimously voted to approve a funded proposal for a new strategic partnership with the EFL”. It said it would now “look forward to continuing discussions with the EFL on progressing this proposal” and remain “committed to finding a football-led solution”.The EFL has yet to officially receive the offer but acknowledged “constructive” discussions with the Premier League and said its board would “review the full detail of the proposal, including its potential benefits, implications and alignment with the long-term interests of our 72 clubs, ahead of further dialogue with the Premier League”.This is the first time that Premier League clubs have officially agreed a proposal that could be put to the EFL since they were first asked to give more money to the rest of the  pyramid five years ago. The Covid pandemic had revealed the precarious nature of finances at many EFL clubs and in 2022 the then sports minister Nigel Huddleston said the British public were  already “out of patience” over a failure to reach an improved settlement.The belief that the Premier League’s riches could be shared more effectively across the game helped lead in part to the creation of the Independent Football Regulator, which came into being last year. The regulator has played no direct part in the negotiations, but has a “backstop” power to force a settlement if none is agreed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile there is cautious optimism that a deal can now finally be agreed, it is not a guarantee that the EFL will accept the Premier League’s offer, with sources suggesting it sees the proposal as being very similar to one that was mooted in 2023 but ultimately never approved by Premier League clubs. Both sides say they remain committed to ongoing dialogue.Explore more on these topicsFootball politicsPremier LeagueFootball LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches | The FA | The Guardian
description: The minimum ban for discriminatory behaviour is to be raised to 10 matches by the Football Association
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: The minimum ban for discriminatory behaviour is to be raised to 10 matches by the Football Association
Content: Preston’s Milutin Osmajic was banned for nine matches after he was found to have made racist remarks.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenPreston’s Milutin Osmajic was banned for nine matches after he was found to have made racist remarks.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersThe FAFA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matchesDiscrimination ‘continues to be challenge’Current minimum ban is six matchesPaul MacInnesThu 30 Jul 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.Premier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubsRead moreAcross the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted. If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.Explore more on these topicsThe FAFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership returns with McInnes adding new twist to Old Firm rivalry | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Derek McInnes has a score to settle with Celtic after swapping Hearts for Rangers, while Motherwell could impress again
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Derek McInnes has a score to settle with Celtic after swapping Hearts for Rangers, while Motherwell could impress again
Content: Derek McInnes has landed the Rangers job he has always wanted, after so nearly leading Hearts to a historic title last term.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenDerek McInnes has landed the Rangers job he has always wanted, after so nearly leading Hearts to a historic title last term.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership returns with McInnes adding new twist to Old Firm rivalryDerek McInnes has a score to settle with Celtic after swapping Hearts for Rangers, while Motherwell could impress againEwan MurrayThu 30 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly residents of cloud cuckoo land can hold the firm belief that Scottish football will emerge promptly from a summer of discontent. The onset of a new domestic season, ordinarily a cause for excitement, instead gives reason to ponder the grim realities of what came before.That it is unsurprising there has been no detailed explanation or plan from the Scottish Football Associationfollowing a lamentable World Cupdoes not prevent the scenario from being so deflating.Mike Mulraney, the president, was last seen peeking out from the crowd behind Gianni Infantino and the US president at Trump Tower. Ian Maxwell, the Scottish FA’s chief executive, bemoaned “hysterical commentary” around his country’s World Cup performance during a brief media appearance after Steve Clarke had resigned. These executives had all but spurted with laughter when it was suggested handing Clarke a four-year contract immediately before Scotland set sail for the United States was perhaps a needless dalliance with risk.Football transfer rumours: Jack Grealish to make Saudi switch to Al-Hilal?Read morePerhaps Mulraney and Maxwell are too engrossed in the sourcing of Clarke’s replacement to speak out on the overall state of the national sport. It is only fair to give them the opportunity to appoint a coach who can oversee much-needed transition in a geriatric Scotland squad.The nation’s leading clubs have been moot on a big picture they wilfully ignore but that was exposed at a World Cup. The problem is that lingering and legitimate anger over Scotland’s showing on the biggest stage – despite all rationale behind it – mirrors so much broader sentiment as the Premiership returns. This has scope to be a troublesome, toxic campaign.Celtic’s supporters remain irate at the custodians of their club, whom they perceive as complacent and out of touch. In Derek McInnes, Rangers have a new manager who is deeply unpopular on the other side of the city. Nobody should underestimate the lingering resentment that exists among followers of Hearts overthe way the campaign of 2025-26 concluded.The most reprehensible element of that arrived on 11 June, when the Scottish Professional Football League published the outcome of a disciplinary process into the pitch invasion that forced the ending of Celtic’stitle-clinching clashagainst the Edinburgh club.View image in fullscreenCeltic fans run on to the pitch after their team went 3-1 up against Hearts in the title-deciding game.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PASnuggled in alongside wrist tickles for Hamilton Academical, Inverness and Stenhousemuir was a meagre fine for Celtic and a suspended, paltry ticket reduction. Rangers fans, who need little encouragement to rail against officialdom, were subdued untilMcInnes was slapped with a touchline banfor comments made against a refereeing decision.Rangers have criticised elements of an independent report intothe chaos which followedtheir March Scottish Cup loss to Celtic. Motherwell are speaking with lawyers due to objection to a Scottish FA fine for a video posted on social media.A 2-0 European qualifying first-leg defeat in Kosovo last week was rightly sufficient to send Hibs fanatics into the internet’s version of orbit. Such results stopped being a shock long ago.Certain clubs do actually have reasons to be cheerful. Celtic’s signing of Kasper Høgh for a club record fee not only demonstrated the kind of fiscal muscle-flexing that supporters wish happened more often but provided the most intriguing transfer arrival of the close season. Scepticism exists over the ability of players to perform outside the perennially successful environment of Bodø/Glimt.Without such doubts and at a fee which even many Championship clubs would think little of, Høgh would have moved long ago. The 25-year-old, though, has a physical profile and direct style that should succeed in Scotland.Celtic’s challenge is to replace existing first-team performers – Arne Engels and Alistair Johnston the prime examples – should irresistible bids arrive without posting the kind of net profit that makes balance sheets look more important than trophies. Fans have rightly welcomed the Høgh signing but need more.Rangers, in contrast to their oldest foes, have burned through extraordinary amounts of cash in recent years while generally watching others lift trophies. This has fuelled rage in and reputational damage from the stands, which an American ownership has curiously opted not to challenge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn McInnes, Rangers – who kick off the season at Dundee United on Friday – have a manager whose knowledge of club and culture looks better placed than most before him in recent years to lay gloves on Celtic. Vanja Dragojevic looks a smart midfield signing from Partizan Belgrade. Rangers need attacking spark yet it should be no surprise that McInnes’s first act was to implement a stronger core. He lacks nothing in motivation or work ethic in the job he has always craved. This version of Rangers should be much improved. Yet on the simple basis of course and distance specialism, Celtic remain the title favourites.View image in fullscreenMotherwell’s recent success offers a template for other top-flight clubs to follow.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PANobody linked to Hearts should have been expected by now to fully process the circumstances in which they came within minutes of a first title win in 66 years, only forthat dream to be snatched away. McInnes’s departure for Rangers, the completely new style implemented by Wouter Vrancken and a palpable raising of expectations all contribute to a period of upheaval.Hearts’ tilt at glory came earlier than anyone could anticipate. The club remains on the minds of people who previously had no interest in the Scottish game. A comprehensive Champions League qualifying defeat by Sturm Graz showed the scale of work Vrancken has ahead of him. Patience, however, would be wise.Motherwell’s work with and post the management of Jens Berthel Askou proved those below the Premiership’s biggest fish needn’t only cling on for dear life. The football was superb, the attendance figures boosted and a broader market was impressed. Motherwell’s sales of Elijah Just and Elliot Watt for multimillion pound fees completely justify a club model that thinks outside the box.St Mirren have clear aspirations of introducing more young players and a more alluring brand of football. Kilmarnock displayed that at the end of last season under Neil McCann. Aberdeen will surely be a stronger force this time under Stephen Robinson.Only one artificial pitch remains in Scotland’s top flight, which provides cause for celebration.Football remains a Scottish obsession. It is also undeniably a sick patient. The dawning of a fresh season should appeal only if there is a glimpse of fresh thinking.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipCelticRangersHeartsMotherwellfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s game | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Fifa’s pitch to persuade members to approve sale of World Cup’s commercial rights includes more tournaments, higher ticket prices and debt financing
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa’s pitch to persuade members to approve sale of World Cup’s commercial rights includes more tournaments, higher ticket prices and debt financing
Content: Gianni Infantino proposed making the World Cup a biennial tournament five years ago.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino proposed making the World Cup a biennial tournament five years ago.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersFifaFifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s gameFifa’s 25-page sales deck produced by JP MorganReference made to doubling global tournamentsExclusive byMatt HughesThu 30 Jul 2026 10.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa’s sales pitch to persuade members to approvethe sale of the World Cup’s commercial rightsclearly states that its plans for financial growth will be achieved by staging more tournaments, having higher ticket prices and debt financing.A 25-page sales deck titled “Fifa Forward Enterprise Member Materials”, that has been seen by the Guardian, makes the case for the creation of a new company to run Fifa’s commercial operations, 20% of which would be sold to Joshua Kushner, a US investor who is the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.Fifa’s sale of the century: how Kushners and Trump are at centre of a tangled webRead moreThe prospectus has been produced by JP Morgan, the US bank that was also behind the failed European Super League breakaway five years ago.In addition to the previously reported $20m (£15m) sign-up payment Fifa has offered to all 211 member associations, which could be made available as soon as January, the document projects that the four-year Fifa Forward payments would increase to $24m for each member by the 2035-39 cycle.JP Morgan makes clear in the sales deck that such growth will come from “a growing tournament portfolio”, “third party sources of capital and debt financing”, and prioritising “high yield” partnerships and events.There is also a reference to more than doubling the number of global tournaments held each year, from 200 to 450, which if followed through would put a huge strain on player workload.Staging the World Cup more frequently would be the most obvious way of raising revenue, withGianni Infantinohaving previously proposed making it a biennial tournament five years ago.The bank also raises the prospect of TV coverage of the biggest events such as theWorld Cupbeing sold to subscription channels or streamers, by referring to a lan to “expand and optimize media rights monetization”.JP Morgan claims that Fifa is “undermonetized” but significantly makes comparisons with other sports leagues with the revenue figures based on club or franchise earnings, rather than with comparable governing bodies.Fifa’s stated annual revenue of $3.6bn therefore compares unfavourably with the NFL’s compared revenue of $21.2bn, Major
