League Baseball’s $13.1bn and the NBA’s $12.5bn.The document was sent to all 211 member associations on Wednesday night and immediately provoked a strong reaction.One senior figure queried why Fifa, which has cash reserves of around $4bn and accumulated revenues of $15bn over the current four-year cycle, would need to take on debt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnother highlighted the odd comparison of a world governing body with private, member-run leagues, while JP Morgan’s proposed timeline for completing the deal was also questioned.According to the document “Investors will be given access to a term sheet and select materials” in August before a vote of Fifa members has taken place.Significantly there is little mention of the investor group elsewhere in the prospectus, with no reference to its identity, projected returns or exit terms.There is one more major omission in the document, as there is not a single mention of women’s football anywhere across the 25 pages.Fifa was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsFifaWorld Cup 2026World CupFootball politicsGianni InfantinonewsShareReuse this content

title: Harvey Elliott revels in ‘second chance’ at Liverpool and has no regrets over Aston Villa loan | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Harvey Elliott believes he has been given “a second chance” at Liverpool and denied his ill-fated loan to Aston Villa was a lost year in his career
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Harvey Elliott believes he has been given “a second chance” at Liverpool and denied his ill-fated loan to Aston Villa was a lost year in his career
Content: Harvey Elliot salutes the crowd at Yankee Stadium after playing for Liverpool in their pre-season victory over Wrexham in New York.Photograph: Rebekah Wynkoop/SPP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHarvey Elliot salutes the crowd at Yankee Stadium after playing for Liverpool in their pre-season victory over Wrexham in New York.Photograph: Rebekah Wynkoop/SPP/ShutterstockLiverpoolHarvey Elliott revels in ‘second chance’ at Liverpool and has no regrets over Aston Villa loanMidfielder grateful to be back with boyhood clubHardly played at Villa but won the Europa LeagueAndy Hunterin New YorkThu 30 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarvey Elliott believes he has been given “a second chance” atLiverpooland denied his ill-fated loan to Aston Villa was a lost year in his career.Elliott joined Villa on aseason-long loan last Septemberwith an obligation for them to buy the midfielder for £35m once he made 10 appearances for the club. However, Elliott featured only nine times, playing 277 minutes in total, with Unai Emery and Villa unconvinced over completing the deal. Having made an 89th-minute substitute appearance for Liverpool at Newcastle in August, the 23-year-old was unable to sign for a third club in a single season.Experimental Liverpool down Wrexham thanks to Rio Ngumoha’s winnerRead moreElliott has featured in both of Liverpool’s pre-season wins under Andoni Iraola in the United States. While non-committal about his long-term future – Sunday’s opponents Leeds have been linked – Elliott spoke positively about his time at Villa, the first time he has discussed last season’s issues, and claimed he could yet feature in Iraola’s plans.“Everyone knows how much I love the club so the feeling never goes of putting the shirt back on, representing the club, and fulfilling your childhood dream,” said Elliott, a boyhood Liverpool fan. “But truthfully, yes [I felt it would never happen again], because I wanted a new challenge. I wanted to explore something, come out of my comfort zone, and I thought that would take me on as a player. Unfortunately, it didn’t work out, but the way I see it is it’s kind of a second chance, especially with the gaffer and new coaching staff coming in.“It’s another chance to impress and hopefully get in their good books. But whatever happened last season, I wish Villa nothing but the very best. I had a lot of love for them and they treated me very well. I’m here now, and I’m trying to cement my spot in the team or within the squad.”Quick GuideJoe Gomez facing month on sidelinesShowLiverpool defender Joe Gomez is expected to miss the start of the new Premier League season with a muscle injury, Andoni Iraola has confirmed.Gomez went down injured after only eight minutes of Liverpool’s first pre-season friendly against Sunderland in Nashville on Saturday. The defender is facing a month on the sidelines – and Liverpool open their league campaign at Newcastle on 23 August – increasing Iraola's concerns about the depth of his defensive options.“Joe has a muscle injury,” said the new Liverpool head coach on Thursday. “It was quite clear since he complained straight away so he will be some weeks off. It’s difficult to say [how long] – normally one month. If it goes very good, then a little bit less. If it goes bad then a bit more but it’s a muscle injury. It’s not massive. I think it will be impossible to have him for the start of the season because we are not so far but it shouldn’t be a lot more.”With Virgil van Dijk starting pre-season training back on Merseyside this week, Giovanni Leoni recovering from an ACL injury and new signing Jérémy Jacquet yet to feature in the US after a shoulder problem, Iraola has been forced to field young and makeshift central defensive partnerships against Sunderland and Wrexham. Two 18-year-olds, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, and full-back Luke Chambers occupied the positions in the wins in Nashville and New York.Iraola said: “You’ve seen in these games that we are pretty thin in the centre-back position. The only centre-backs we have are Mor and Ifeanyi who are 18, just arrived at the club, and are doing incredibly well. I’m happy that the team has shown composure and solidity at the back and it speaks very well about them."Jacquet could make his first Liverpool appearance against Leeds in Chicago on Sunday, the final game of the club’s US tour. Florian Wirtz may also feature and Iraola has confirmed where he wants to deploy the £116m signing next season.“I see Flo probably more in that position behind the striker,” Iraola said. “I know he has played on the left sometimes but we're going to start with him as the No 10. He's quite complete as a player and I'd like to add a few more things. In the first days of training it's clear that he's in a good place mentally.”Andy HunterWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Elliott insists he harbours “no hard feelings” towards Villa. The Liverpool player was named player of the tournament at the European Under-21s Championship in the summer of 2025 and was touted as a possible member of Thomas Tuchel’s World Cup squad before his career stalled in the Midlands. But he insists: “I wouldn’t say it was a lost year because, at the end of it, I won the Europa League. To have that on my CV is incredible, especially with Villa. I saw with my own eyes how much it meant for them and I wouldn’t say it’s a lost year when you achieved something like that, because that’s selfish.“It was a situation I couldn’t control. It was just a case of accepting it, and just trying to get my head clear and get myself in the best position to come back here, and I tried as hard as I could. I still feel like I can get better and I’m working as hard as I can to do that.”Elliott admits Emery discussed his reasoning several times and that enabled him to handle the frustration of being sidelined for the majority of the season. “He explained very, very clearly and a fair few times. The whole club were very apologetic about the situation and, ultimately, it was a situation that I couldn’t control,” Elliott said. “But I knew 100% what the case was. It was like, ‘Ok, I can get over it, I know what the situation is now’.“It was just about me handling it and showing my professionalism. I’m not that kind of guy who wanted to kick up a fuss and cause problems, because no one really deserves that. It’s just part of football and it was a learning curve for me and an opportunity that I hope I don’t experience again. But it’s a situation where I know I’ve been able to get through it.“I’m really happy to be back and putting a Liverpool shirt on again. Playing at Liverpool, there’s no better feeling.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s golden sprinters speak out on cycling defector: ‘Good riddance’ | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Gold in the men’s team sprint on day one of Commonwealth Games track cycling prompted Matt Richardson’s former teammates to make their feelings clear
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gold in the men’s team sprint on day one of Commonwealth Games track cycling prompted Matt Richardson’s former teammates to make their feelings clear
Content: Australia’s sprint team of Daniel Barber, Ryan Elliott and Leigh Hoffman celebrate after winning gold at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenAustralia’s sprint team of Daniel Barber, Ryan Elliott and Leigh Hoffman celebrate after winning gold at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PACommonwealth Games 2026Australia’s golden sprinters speak out on cycling defector: ‘Good riddance’Views on Matt Richardson aired after gold in team sprintOne of three Australian cycling gold medals won on day sevenAustralian Associated PressThu 30 Jul 2026 19.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeigh Hoffman has bid Matt Richardson good riddance after Australia’s gold medal in the team sprint on day one of the Commonwealth Games track cycling program.Teammate Ryan Elliott also joked they had cleared Hoffman as their leader, checking his passport to make sure he will stay in the Australian program. While expressing sympathy for Richardson after a recent nasty race crash in Japan, his former teammates finally spoke freely about the shock defection.Their big win over England was one of Australia’s three cycling gold medals at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, along with the women’s team pursuit and para-cyclist Tara Neyland.Rose Davies makes history in Australian 5,000m one-two at Commonwealth GamesRead moreBut England gained some revenge for the Paris Olympics, beating Australia in the men’s team pursuit final. Two years ago, Australia narrowly downed Great Britain in a pulsating ride-off for gold. Soon after Paris, Richardson stunned the sport by switching allegiances to Great Britain.The ex-Australian was to be one of the biggest stories of the Glasgow Games, taking on former teammates in the match sprint. But there was more drama on the eve of the track program when Richardson pulled out because of injuries from the Japan crash, when a rival cyclist sideswiped him.Hoffman was sympathetic, to an extent. After largely keeping their counsel over the past two years, the Australians made their feelings about the defection clear.“It was horrible, I’ve seen video of the crash, it’s pretty serious. I would have loved for him to come here and race and see how Danny [teammate Danny Barber] and I stack up,” Hoffman said.“It would have been great if he stayed in Australia, but his heart was obviously never always in it – so good riddance.”Elliott was also asked about Hoffman stepping up since Paris as the leader of the sprint squad.“We checked his passport for his lineage, so he’s good,” Elliott joked, in reference to Richardson’s dual citizenship. “It [the rivalry with the British] has definitely grown a lot since the ... defection. Definitely it’s there [with] the defector himself. This one is sweet.”England were only 0.045 of a second behind in qualifying, but Elliott, Hoffman and Danny Barber beat them by more than half a second in the final.There was drama in the men’s team sprint ride-off for bronze when Wales did not start because one of their riders was unwell on the start line, handing third place to Trinidad and Tobago.Australia won three of the seven gold medals on offer during day one at the velodrome.View image in fullscreenFelicity Wilson-Haffenden leads Australia in the team pursuit.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPThe Australian women successfully defended their team pursuit Games title, overhauling New Zealand and breaking their own Commonwealth Games record.Sophie Edwards came out of the pursuit quartet who qualified fastest, with three-time Games gold medallist Georgia Baker taking her place.Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, Claudia Marcks and Alyssa Polites joined Baker in comfortably beating New Zealand for the gold medal. Australia rode 4:10.658, while New Zealand clocked 4:12.775.“Bloody awesome – I couldn’t ask for much more. We came in here wanting to win gold, but it’s easier said than done,” said women’s coach Ash Ankudinoff, a former team pursuit world champion.“It’s an exciting bunch. I never cracked an Olympic medal, but we have a good bunch. It’s just a step in the right direction – look out LA.”Kane Perris and his pilot Luke Zaccaria won bronze in the men’s tandem B 1km time trial, while Scotland delighted the crowd by winning the first gold of the track program in the event ahead of Wales.Para-sport veteran Jess Gallagher, with Jacqui Mengler-Mohr piloting, took silver behind New Zealand in the women’s tandem B sprint.Molly McGill, Kristina Clonan and Alessia McCaig were fourth-fastest qualifiers in the women’s team sprint and lost their bronze ride-off to Scotland, as Wales beat England for gold.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026CyclingAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rose Davies makes history in Australian 5,000m one-two at Commonwealth Games  | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Rose Davies added gold to her 10,000m triumph at the Glasgow Games as Jessica Hull won silver
Author: Jack Snape
Headline: Rose Davies added gold to her 10,000m triumph at the Glasgow Games as Jessica Hull won silver
Content: 1:57Australia's Rose Davies wins historic second Commonwealth Games gold medal – videoCommonwealth Games 2026Rose Davies makes history in Australian 5,000m one-two at Commonwealth GamesDavies adds gold to her 10,000m triumph at Glasgow GamesCompatriot Jessica Hull comes in second to claim silverJack SnapeThu 30 Jul 2026 18.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the fading Glasgow light, the two fluorescent yellow figures powered around the final bend of the 5,000m at theCommonwealth Games, leaving the rest of the field behind.Megan Keith, the young Scot who had broken the field apart with a mile to go, could not keep up. Behind her was Kenya’s last hope of making it six 5,000m women’s golds in a row, Caroline Nyaga, as well as Ugandan Esther Chebet and England’s Hannah Nuttall. All of them, now irrelevant.Australia’s men lose Commonwealth cycling pursuit to England but women triumphRead moreAustralian Rose Davies had stayed within this leading group for the entire race, before surging past Keith with 200m to go. History was in her grasp: a woman had never done the 10,000m-5,000m double at the Commonwealth Games.The 26-year-old had company, however. A stride behind was Jessica Hull, the formidable Olympic and world champion medallist in the 1,500m who also became the first Australian woman to qualify for a World Championships 800m final last year. The imposing figure is the pioneer in Australia’s track resurgence in recent years, proving domestic prominence can turn into global medals.Hull has spent the past two years building her focus beyond the 800m and 1,500m towards the 5,000m, as she hopes to extend her career to Brisbane 2032. Her race in Glasgow had unfolded perfectly to plan, as an untroubled passenger in the train led by Davies that had just pulled out of its final station.And so there they were. Two Australians and daylight. Two Novocastrians, striding down the straight.“I knew I might have been in trouble leading with Jess on my shoulder with 150 metres to go. She’s so fast, and I just thought, give it everything,” Davies told Channel Seven.View image in fullscreenRose Davies drapes herself in the Australian flag after winning her second gold medal of these Games.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPJust 12 days ago, in the final lap of the 3,000m at the prestigious London Diamond League meet, Hull’s surge arrived at exactly this moment, leaving Davies languishing in second place in a prophetic Australian one-two. That memory of London was in Davies’ mind, as her countrywoman pulled alongside with 100m to go.For Hull, equally, this was not easy. “It was very tricky racing a countrywoman with 150 to go,” she said. “It’s pretty special to have another Aussie out there with me, but to be battling home for the gold against an Aussie was a bit of a mind flip.”The 29-year-old had already run a heat in her preferred distance of the mile earlier in the day. In this longer race format, she is still finding her way. “Closing out a 5k is a different beast and I think I found myself quite tactically raw out there,” she said.“I didn’t really know what to do a lot, I was looking for dad [her coach, Simon Hull] in the crowd. I was like, ‘Do I stay here? Do I move up? So with three laps to go when Rose went around I was like, ‘OK, Rose knows what to do here so just follow her’.”With 70m to go, Hull dragged herself up alongside Davies, and the lead looked hers. But she could never break her teammate, who lifted in turn.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDavies found another level, and suddenly, the closing gap was now opening again. The double was on. “I just gave it everything,” Davies said. “I was running as hard as I could and I just wanted it so bad.”Fifty metres. Thirty metres. Then 10 metres. By then a full stride ahead. Davies realised and threw her arms out to the side as if she was an aeroplane. Like a child might do, soaring around an imaginary sky.Davies was once a child prodigy, Australia’s best in her age group by age 14. But her development was not linear, and she would not set another personal best for five years. Her teenage years were spent as a part-time runner as she battled inflammation issues in her hip. As an adult with a more forgiving body, she rediscovered her passion for the sport thanks to the patient encouragement of her coach Scott Westcott.It was to him, watching at home on television, that her mind turned in the immediate aftermath. “He’s worked so hard with me in the past, I don’t know, 10 years or so,” she said. “I’m just so happy that he can celebrate this win, too.”One of Australia’s steady improvers in recent years, Davies is now one of the country’s greats, her achievements cemented by this unforgettable evening. The last time two Australians finished first and second on the Commonwealth Games track was in 1974 when Raelene Boyle beat Denise Robertson over 200m.This one-two delivered the enduring image of these games, Davies crossing the line first in wonderment. And Hull just behind, her grimace turning to a smile.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Australia sportAthleticsCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

Africa.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PACommonwealth Games 2026Perfect Pearson fires England into netball semi-final showdown with New ZealandEngland 58-54 South AfricaLois Pearson scores 17 goals from 17 shotsPA MediaThu 30 Jul 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland stormed back from a six-goal deficit at the end of the first quarter to book title: Charley Hull refuses to apologise after £100,000 scratchcard prank on caddie | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: Charley Hull, who was two under after her first round, said: ‘I think people need to lighten up,’ while Atthaya Thitikul leads on -7
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Charley Hull, who was two under after her first round, said: ‘I think people need to lighten up,’ while Atthaya Thitikul leads on -7
Content: Charley Hull said her caddy, Adam Woodward, took the prank well.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenCharley Hull said her caddy, Adam Woodward, took the prank well.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAWomen's OpenCharley Hull refuses to apologise after £100,000 scratchcard prank on caddieHull: ‘I think people need to lighten up’Thitikul leads on -7; double major winner Ryu on -5Ewan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesThu 30 Jul 2026 15.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharley Hull has delivered an emphatic, unapologetic response towards those who criticised a prank on the eve of the Women’s Open.Hull used pre-tournament media duties to reveal she bought fake scratchcards in a Blackpool joke shop, before using one to trick her caddie, Adam Woodward, into believing he had won £100,000. Hull filmed Woodward’s initially euphoric and subsequently despondent reaction to the incident.While some onlookers saw the funny side of the stunt, Hull also drew harsh words for her treatment of Woodward. Many perceived it as unduly cruel. The caddie has worked for Hull for the vast majority of her professional career. Hull’s carefree, playful nature is well known within her sport.Charley Hull shooting for Open glory after multiple near misses at majorsRead moreIn this instance, Hull cares little about splitting opinion. “People that have complaints about it, I would say loosen up,” Hull said after a two-under-par 69 to start her challenge at Royal Lytham & St Annes. “I don’t have my social media on my phone on tournament weeks. I delete it and when I go home I’ll add it again. I don’t really like people seeing me and tagging me and stuff. I like to keep in the present moment. But I think people need to lighten up if they’re taking that too seriously because it was pretty funny.”Hull added she would “100%” participate in a similar scenario again. “He thought it was funny after, he is not uptight,” she said of Woodward. “It’s a joke. If people don’t like it they can lump it, do you know what I mean?“I felt bad for Adam but at the end of the day I have just got to have a good week. At the end of the week I’ll buy him 100 scratchcards.” A peculiar business.Hull trails the early leader, Atthaya “Jeeno” Thitikul, by five shots. The Thai player has been astonishingly consistent in majors – posting 11 top-10 finishes since 2021 – but is yet to win. Perhaps Lytham will be key – Thitikul won top amateur honours as a 15-year-old when the Women’s Open was staged here in 2018. Thitikul’s close shaves on the biggest stage are worthy of comparisons with Hull. Her 64 was the lowest score in a Lytham Women’s Open.Ryu Hae-ran’s ambition is not only to extinguish the hopes of her rivals but secure a little piece of history. Until Thitikul’s surge, Ryu topped the leaderboard. Victories at this year’s PGA and Evian Championships mean she is in the incredible position of seeking a third major win in a row. Only four female golfers have achieved the feat yet Ryu’s position is unique. She has not played in any other tournaments outside the majors in question.Unsurprisingly perhaps, the South Korean responded with a firm no when asked whether she has contemplated three from three. Fifty-four holes in a links environment provide the epitome of a long way to go. Still, her five-under-par 66 – which included half a dozen birdies and an outward half of 31 – felt significant.View image in fullscreenRyu Hae-ran has won the past two majors on the women’s tour and is going for a hat-trick at Lytham.Photograph: Jon Super/AP“I felt so hard on this type of course that I cannot focus on the win,” Ryu said. “I have to just enjoy my golf and not stress too much. Today’s score is pretty good but we have three more days and this is a major. I just keep thinking about myself, not winning, and keep enjoying myself on the golf course.”Ryu has always been an elite ball striker, with her greens in regulation statistics remarkable. Improvement in putting has elevated her game in 2026. “These days my golf is pretty good,” said the 25-year-old with more than a whiff of understatement. Shiho Kuwaki later matched Ryu’s first-round total.Lottie Woad’s 69 enhanced hopes of a home winner, eight years after England’s Georgia Hall prevailed at Lytham. Woad has quietly risen to fifth in the world rankings, little over a year since she turned professional. Her round owed much to avoiding every one of Lytham’s 174, highly penal bunkers. Woad’s approach is an aggressive one. “I think I hit the most drivers out of anyone in my group,” she said. “It’s one of my strengths, so I didn’t see the point in laying back.“Some of the par fives are pretty tight off the tee but they’re probably the only birdie opportunities you’re really going to get round here so I was just always trying to play driver for those.”Minjee Lee made birdie at the par-three 1st and bagged an eagle at the 6th but still slumped to a 75. The former champion Sophia Popov was 10 shots worse than that. The English duo of Mimi Rhodes and Annabell Fuller both signed for 71. Lydia Ko is also even par. Nelly Korda is far from out of this tournament but has significant work to do after opening with a two-over-par 73.Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Raids across UK in crackdown on nuisance car finance texts | Spam | The Guardian
description: Laptops, phones and documents seized as information commissioner acts on messages about mis-selling scandal
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Laptops, phones and documents seized as information commissioner acts on messages about mis-selling scandal
Content: Phones seized during raids by the Information Commissioner's Office on nuisance phone calls.Photograph: Information Commissioner's OfficeView image in fullscreenPhones seized during raids by the Information Commissioner's Office on nuisance phone calls.Photograph: Information Commissioner's OfficeSpamRaids across UK in crackdown on nuisance car finance textsLaptops, phones and documents seized as information commissioner acts on messages about mis-selling scandalRupert JonesThu 30 Jul 2026 09.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaptops, mobile phones and documents have been seized after officials carried out search warrants in a crackdown on claims companies plaguing people with spam text messages about the car finance mis-selling scandal.The UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO)executed warrants at homes and businesseslinked to five companies in London, Liverpool, Bolton, Burnley and Swansea on Wednesday.More than 12m complaints about nuisance marketing text messages have been submitted by the public since September 2025 as claims management companies (CMCs) and other firms attempt to grab a share of the billions of pounds in compensation expected to be paid out to motorists who were mis-sold car loans.The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced a£7.5bn industry-wide compensation schemefor the millions of victims of the scandal in March.Legal challenges, however, forced the regulatorto partly suspend the scheme.The FCA had expected to start paying out £829 on average this year to those affected by the scandal – in which drivers were overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers between 2007 and 2024 – but a court ordered the regulator to suspend parts of the scheme until a hearing in December or February next year.The head of investigations at the ICO, Andy Curry, said: “People are fed up with being bombarded by unwanted calls, texts and emails about car finance claims, and we’re taking action.”This week’s raids “send a clear message to the claims management sector: comply with the law or expect to hear from us”, he said.The companies linked to the searches are subject to continuing investigation. They are believed to be responsible for sending a combined 170m texts to members of the public between September 2025 and May this year.The ICO is working with the FCA, the Advertising Standards Authority and the Solicitors Regulation Authority to tackle poor practices relating to motor finance claims by some CMCs, law firms and lead generation companies.The raids represent an escalation of the crackdown on rogue CMCs and other businesses. As a result of the FCA’s work, more than 1,200 misleading adverts have been removed or amended since January 2024.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome firms face enforcement investigations, while others have had to reduce their “unreasonable” fees or allow consumers to walk away from contracts free of charge.The ICO has the power to apply to the courts for a warrant to search premises as part of investigations under the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, where evidence may be seized. This can include mobile phones, laptops and sim farms: collections of devices that house hundreds or thousands of mobile phone sim cards.The FCA has said there is no need to use a CMC or law firm because people can complain for free using atemplate letteron its website. This week itlaunched a nationwide advertising campaignto direct people to the letter. It will run across TV, radio, print, billboards and social media until 6 September.Explore more on these topicsSpamMotor financeInformation commissionerFinancial Conduct AuthorityRegulatorsConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Elon Musk’s xAI sues Minnesota over law banning ‘nudification’ technology | Elon Musk | The Guardian
description: First-in-nation law sets up test on states’ power to regulate use of AI as it tries to outlaw fake nude images of real people
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: First-in-nation law sets up test on states’ power to regulate use of AI as it tries to outlaw fake nude images of real people
Content: Elon Musk at the Viva Technology conference at the Porte de Versailles exhibition centre in Paris, France, in 2023.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersView image in fullscreenElon Musk at the Viva Technology conference at the Porte de Versailles exhibition centre in Paris, France, in 2023.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersElon MuskElon Musk’s xAI sues Minnesota over law banning ‘nudification’ technologyFirst-in-nation law sets up test on states’ power to regulate use of AI as it tries to outlaw fake nude images of real peopleAssociated PressWed 29 Jul 2026 20.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElon Musk’s company xAI has suedMinnesotaover the state’s first-in-the-nation law banning “nudification” technology on websites and apps, potentially providing a test for how far states can go in constitutionally regulating the use of artificial intelligence.Musk’s company sued on Monday in federal court, days before the law is set to take effect on Saturday and make Minnesota the first state to try to outlaw the increasingly proliferating technology that lets people use AI to create fake nude images of real people. The law was signed in May.In the 38-page lawsuit, xAI – whose AI model chatbot and image generator Grok is available on the social media platform known as X, formerly Twitter, and elsewhere – said it does not contest the state’s interest in banning the distribution of AI-generated nude images of real people without their consent. But it said Minnesota’s law “extends far beyond that goal”, banning many constitutionally protected images and video and subjecting the company to a penalty of $500,000 for each violation.The lawsuit argues there is no “safe harbor” provision for companies that make good-faith efforts to prevent such images from being created by users and that it covers images that were consented to by the depicted person, or even created by that person.It also says the law’s definition of “intimate part” is overly broad, covering body parts that are routinely displayed in public.In a statement, Keith Ellison, the Minnesota attorney general, said his office had not been served with the lawsuit yet or seen it.“But I know that using AI to generate nude images of people against their will is appalling. There are plenty of worthy debates to have about AI policy. This is not one of them. AI nudification robs the target of their dignity and can cause immense harm on an emotional, personal and professional level,” Ellison said.State laws over election deepfakes have had mixed results in courts. California’s law was blocked over first amendment speech protections. Minnesota’s law has thus far survived a 2025 court challenge by Musk’s company.The law is distinct from state and federal laws that outlaw deepfakes and AI-generated sexually explicit images of people without their consent. Those laws typically penalize the people who use the tools to make these images, not the makers of the tools themselves. The federal Take It Down Act, passed last year, also requires websites and apps to implement a process to remove those images.Texas last year took on nudification in a slightly different way. It made a website or app owner liable for civil damages from a person depicted in a nudified image – and potentially criminal penalties – if the website or app owner knew the person hadn’t given consent to its creation or failed to take it down promptly when told about it.In the lawsuit, xAI said the terms of service for using Grok prohibit using it for “any illegal, harmful, or abusive activities” that violate someone’s privacy, including altering their image to nudify them or depict them in a sexually explicit image. It said it enforces those rules against violators through account suspensions or terminations, and by reporting suspected child sexual abuse content.xAI also said earlier this year that it has “zero tolerance for any forms of child sexual exploitation, non-consensual nudity, and unwanted sexual content”.After a global backlash over sexualized images of women and children, Grok said in January it will geo-block content if it violates laws in a particular place, preventing people from editing photos of real people in revealing clothing in places where that is illegal. Grok’s “spicy mode” had allowed users to create explicit content, leading to a backlash from governments worldwide.“We have implemented technological measures to prevent the Grok account from allowing the editing of images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis, underwear and other revealing attire,” xAI said in a January statement.Explore more on these topicsElon MuskAI (artificial intelligence)MinnesotanewsShareReuse this content

title: German chancellor chooses pope’s AI encyclical over pacy potboiler as holiday read | Germany | The Guardian
description: With his popularity at a record low, Friedrich Merz packs the papal guide Magifica humanitas
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: With his popularity at a record low, Friedrich Merz packs the papal guide Magifica humanitas
Content: Friedrich Merz has faced a string of setbacks since becoming Germany’s chancellor 14 months ago.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APView image in fullscreenFriedrich Merz has faced a string of setbacks since becoming Germany’s chancellor 14 months ago.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APGermanyGerman chancellor chooses pope’s AI encyclical over pacy potboiler as holiday readWith his popularity at a record low, Friedrich Merz packs the papal guide Magifica humanitasEurope live – latest updatesDeborah Colein BerlinThu 30 Jul 2026 08.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSummer is normally thought of as the time for pacy potboilers and brain-soothing page-turners – airport reads that wind up sandy and sunscreen-stained. Not so forFriedrich Merz’s holiday reading list.Germany’s embattled chancellor, who has faced one rough patch after another since taking office 14 months ago, seems to be seeking spiritual guidance this year while putting his feet up.According tothe conservative broadsheet Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, the Christian Democratic Union leader is taking Pope Leo’s encyclical on artificial intelligence, Magnifica humanitas (Magnificent humanity), on his break.Introduced bythe Guardian in Mayas “the first major text on safeguarding humankind of his papacy”, the encyclical makes the case for the “most rigorous” ethical constraints on the march of technology, calling AI the biggest threat to humanity.View image in fullscreenPope Leo XIV, right, at the presentation of his first encyclical, Magnifica humanitas.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APOne of the world’s 1.4 billion Roman Catholics, Merz tends to beprivate about matters of belief, so his beach reading speaks volumes.Thehistorically unpopular70-year-old politician has described AI as a challenge and a chance for Europe’s top economy after seven years of stagnation, just as he has demanded streamlined EU rules to prevent red tape from snuffing out its potential.In aspeechin April, he said Germany was one of the world’s leading nations in the use of AI, particularly in industry. Merz said he was banking on its power to boost productivity and prosperity as he faces asurge in support for the far right.Despite the “euphoria” in some circles about how machines can alter the way we live, Merz said many Germans feared AI’s power to eliminate jobs and upend lives.“The question, however, is not whether we want AI or not,” he said. “AI is here and is already being put to practical use. It is now up to us to decide what happens in this transformation.”It is perhaps fitting that Merz would choose to wrestle with life’s great moral questions while on his holiday, reportedly to be spent largely inGermany.His latest woes were touched off two weeks ago when the ambitious head of his CDU parliamentary group, Jens Spahn, announced he and his husband had welcomeda baby born to a surrogate in the US.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe movesmacked of hypocrisygiven the CDU’s firm opposition to surrogacy, which is illegal in Germany, and Spahn resigned within days. His departure prompted Germany’s biggest cabinet reshuffle since the early 1960s.The shake-up orchestrated by Merz was chaotic, with one designated minister pulling out at the last minute, leaving the sitting official he was to replace hung out to dry until he finally stepped down to preserve his own “dignity”.The shambolic proceedings have led to intrigue worthy of a political thriller, with talk of a“palace revolt” against Merz and speculation over whether he would make it in office until Christmas. After his return to Berlin, Merz will face three state elections in September, in which the far-right AfD could see record results.With the impression of disarray taking hold, theFrankfurter Allgemeine Zeitungcould not resist noting that Merz’s other title for the book pile was a novel called Ship of Fools.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzEuropePope Leo XIVAI (artificial intelligence)The papacynewsShareReuse this content

title: Flock surveillance cameras can pose a crash risk for drivers, US experts say | Ohio | The Guardian
description: Roadside safety advocates say some automated license plate readers may not meet highway safety standards
Author: Stephen Starr
Headline: Roadside safety advocates say some automated license plate readers may not meet highway safety standards
Content: The city of Toledo approved a three-year $846,000 contract with Flock Group Inc in November 2025, $282,000 annually.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe city of Toledo approved a three-year $846,000 contract with Flock Group Inc in November 2025, $282,000 annually.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesOhioFlock surveillance cameras can pose a crash risk for drivers, US experts sayRoadside safety advocates say some automated license plate readers may not meet highway safety standardsStephen Starrin Beavercreek, OhioThu 30 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlock Safety cameras have been pilloried for facilitating theAI-powered surveillance of private citizens and fortargeting immigrantsfor years. But now safety advocates are also claiming that their physical location can pose potential roadside hazards.At the bottom of a tree-lined hill on a narrow, two lane rural road in Greene county,Ohio, stands a black metal rod with a camera and solar panel attached at the top.The camera, an automated license plate reader (ALPR), is owned by Flock Safety and is painted black, making it difficult to see.Its dark color isn’t the only thing that makes it a potential hazard for drivers.The metal rod has no breakaway plate – a safety feature close to the ground that, in the case of a collision with a vehicle, sees the pole snap, reducing the resistance and impact experienced by the vehicle and the people inside it.It has no obvious stickers indicating it’s been inspected by safety authorities and is placed about two feet from the edge of the asphalt road.According tothe Ohio department of transportation (ODOT), however, “On uncurbed facilities, [license plate readers must be] at least 8 [feet] from the nearest edge of a travel lane.”The Beavercreek police department, Flock’s customer in this case, says that Flock is responsible for all instalments and that all cameras in its jurisdiction “received the appropriate approval”.ALPRs record license plate details, as well as the make, model, color and any other notable features of a vehicle. Flock has an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 cameras deployed in more than6,000 communitiesacross the US. (Flock told the Guardian it wouldn’t share the exact number orlocationof its surveillance devices.)This potential physical danger is one that Tennessee-based Steve Eimers, known online as theGuardrail Guy, has found himself increasingly documenting in recent months. Following the death of his 17-year-old daughter after the vehicle in which she was traveling crashed into a roadside structure on Interstate 75 a decade ago, Eimers has toured the country to highlight the failure of various authorities to meet their own legal requirements. His videos, posted across social media, have garnered millions of views.“There are a billion different people looking into the top part of the cameras [but] nobody’s been looking at the bottom, and the crashworthy elements,” he says.“The guardrail had to go through a heavy vetting process – they had to do a whole series of crash tests, they had to submit the crash test results in full with photos [which] are reviewed by state [department of transportation] engineers,” he says.In 2024, crashes between a motor vehicle and a fixed barrier accounted for26% of vehicle deathsnationwide, according to the National Safety Council, a non-profit.According tothe Federal Highway Administration, sign poles and rods can become a deadly hazard for motorists, which has led to the establishment of astandard“that requires all roadside sign supports in the clear zone … to be breakaway, yielding, or shielded by a barrier or crash cushion”.Roadside safety hardware includescrash cushions, breakaway supports, transitions and other structures and spaces that help to prevent catastrophe for motorists who leave the road.“Permits are required when working within ODOT’s right-of-way, including the installation of license plate reader cameras,” says David Rose, of Ohio’s department of transportation, who notes that state authorities are not involved in the installation of ALPRs, even when located on the state’s right-of-way.“All work performed within corporation limits must be approved through the appropriate city or village, as ODOT does not have jurisdiction within corporation limits.”Eimers says he has only ever found one Flock pole, in Erie county, Ohio, installed with the required breakaway plate.But even in that case, he says the breakaway plate was positioned higher off the ground than the Federal Highway Administration permits, meaning the metal pole could catch the underside of a low-lying vehicle and potentially ignite a battery- or gas-fueled fire.“Flock is not a sophisticated user of roadside safety hardware. They are nowhere near doing what they are supposed to be, what should be done,” Eimers says.Flock and police departments say the cameras are an effective crime reduction tool, having played a key role in recovering stolen property and missing persons across the country.The company says it follows all state and local requirements when it comes to the safe location of its hardware.“We do not agree with the premise that Flock regularly installs poles in violation of federal, state, or local safety requirements. The appropriate pole type and installation specifications depend on the roadway, speed, location, jurisdiction, and requirements of the relevant transportation or permitting authority,” says Paris Lewbel, a Flock Safety spokesperson, who noted that the company planned to undergo a review of camera pole installations across its network.“Customers generally determine camera locations based on their public safety priorities. Flock then works with the customer.”Flock isn’t alone. ALPR companies such asMotorola Solutions,Redflex Traffic Systemsand others are apparently routinely failing to meet roadside structure requirements, including often using other structures to place their monitoring devices on, in violation of state requirements.While in urban areas Flock cameras are oftentimes attached high up on traffic lights or other larger structures, reducing the crash risk, in suburban and rural areas – where traffic speeds are typically higher – they are regularly erected as stand-alone structures where they add to the number of objects drivers can collide with.What Eimers and others have found is that Flock and other ALPR camera structures, for the most part, are not being inspected by municipal authorities for meeting safety requirements as other roadside structures such as municipal signs are. What’s more, that they are painted black, with no reflecting surfaces, can make them difficult for drivers to see at night.“Without that, what can happen is that metal pipe can act like a spear; that’s hollow pipe, it’ll core out your brain,’ warns Eimers, a registered nurse who says he has spent tens of thousands of hours inspecting and researching roadside safety requirements and manuals since his daughter’s death.“We know that a lot of people leave the road, so we want a forgiving roadside.”Explore more on these topicsOhioAI (artificial intelligence)Road safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: Lloyds Bank to cut £2bn in costs as part of AI-powered strategy | Lloyds Banking Group | The Guardian
description: Chief executive says the four-year plan will lead to greater efficiency but gives no details of potential job losses
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Chief executive says the four-year plan will lead to greater efficiency but gives no details of potential job losses
Content: Lloyds reported a rise in second-quarter profits to £2.3bn.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverView image in fullscreenLloyds reported a rise in second-quarter profits to £2.3bn.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverLloyds Banking GroupLloyds Bank to cut £2bn in costs as part of AI-powered strategyChief executive says the four-year plan will lead to greater efficiency but gives no details of potential job lossesBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 06.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLloyds Banking Group will cut another £2bn of costs as part of a four-year plan under which its chief executive will use new tech and AI to drive growth.Charlie Nunn said the strategy, which the UK’s largest high street lender will launch in January, would involve investing £13bn into the business by 2030, including for “pioneering technology” to lure new business, improve efficiency and increase payouts for shareholders.That will involve rolling out “AI-powered advice” for wealth and workplace pensions, and using it to offer personalised offers based on customer behaviour, and give “support and guidance” to relationship managers, who are assigned to specific accounts.While Nunn praised colleagues for guiding customers through “increasingly complex services, he said “we can make it even better, and even simpler, because we’re not good enough today, relative to our ambition”.When asked how staff would be affected by £2bn in planned cuts, Nunn said he would consider all the same business areas that were in the bank’s crosshairs over the past five years, including better technology, reviewing physical office space and “improving our ability to increase productivity”, without giving details of any potential job losses.“So, when we look to this next stage, those kind of levers will continue in front of us,” he told journalists on Thursday. “And we do think that there are new opportunities for agentic AI to both differentiate our services and grow more efficiently: IE provide services we’ve never been able to provide.“That is going to impact work. It is going to require us to continue to re-skill peopleand hire new people, but that’s been my history for 30-odd years in financial services.”As for the future of Lloyds’s 550 branches, Nunn said: “It will be important part of our proposition, but we’re going to follow the customers and our customer data around our branches.”The strategy also pointed to international expansion, with Lloyds aiming to grow its corporate and institutional bank in the US and Europe, marking a big shift from the retrenchment that followed the lender’s bailout at the height of the 2008 financial crisis.Nunn said he was also betting on AI and blockchain technology to cut waiting times for mortgage approvals to about three days; the bank would also boost rewards and loan discounts to retain loyal customers.Lloyds will double down on its car loan division, which is still waiting to settle thelong-running motor finance commission scandal, by creating a one-stop-shop app for drivers wanting to buy, insure and set up charging points for electric vehicles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Nunn’s strategy to move away from the traditional lending business continues to deliver for Lloyds, though it is still a work in progress.“The push towards the US and more corporate banking is understandable, but Lloyds would hardly be the first UK name to follow this demanding path – success here is far from guaranteed. Lloyds has the heft in its home market, but a move to a bigger global player is a significant undertaking.”It came as the bank reported better-than-expected second-quarter profits, which rose to £2.3bn between April and June, a 14% jump from the same period last year. It meant bosses could increase payouts for shareholders, with a 1.58p a share dividend and the first ever share buyback announced at half-year, worth £1bn.Lloyds’s share price rose 1.7% in response to the news on Thursday morning.Explore more on these topicsLloyds Banking GroupBankingAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: The best cordless vacuum cleaners in the UK for a spotless home – tested | Homes | The Guardian
description: Stick vacuums are a convenient alternative to corded designs, but which model wins for overall cleaning prowess? Our expert reveals all
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: Stick vacuums are a convenient alternative to corded designs, but which model wins for overall cleaning prowess? Our expert reveals all
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterHomesReviewThe best cordless vacuum cleaners in the UK for a spotless home – testedStick vacuums are a convenient alternative to corded designs, but which model wins for overall cleaning prowess? Our expert reveals allThe best robot vacuumsHow to make your vacuum last longerAndy ShawThu 30 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Choosing a cordless vacuum isn’t a decision that should be taken lightly. You’re likely to keep a vacuum cleaner for years, relying heavily on its ability to suck up dust, crumbs, mud, pet hair and any other dry spillages or sheddings that end up on your floor. Choosing the right model can be the difference between an effective cleaner that’s a delight to pull out of the cupboard and a dud that you dread having to unblock, detangle and clean after every use.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.In this review, I took 16 of the leading cordless vacuum cleaners from a range of manufacturers and at various prices and inflicted the same cleaning tests on each one. That takes all the guesswork out of picking your next cleaner: I can tell you exactly which ones picked up the most mess.Current discountsOur favourite cordless vacuum for deep cleaning, the Dyson V15 Detect Absolute, is currently available with the Detail cleaning kit for £89 less than the vacuum on its own.£559 at DysonAt a glanceBest cordless vacuum cleaner overall:Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251£388 at AmazonBest budget cordless vacuum cleaner:Vax HomePro Pet-Design£202.12 at AmazonBestcordless vacuum for deep cleaning:Dyson V15 Detect Absolute£649 at John LewisBest cordless vacuum for clean emptying:Henry Quick Pro£399.99 at ArgosBest handheld cordless vacuum cleaner:Dyson Car+Boat£199 at John LewisWhy you should trust meI’ve been reviewing technology and home products for more than 30 years. In the past few years, I’ve specialised in testing vacuum cleaners. During that time, I’ve tested more vacuum cleaners of various shapes, sizes and types than I’d care to count, from handheld helpers to heavy-duty dirt-shifters.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach vacuum was put to the test against flour, cat litter pellets and pet hair.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianMost cordless vacuum cleaners are designed to work on carpet and hard floors, so I tested them all on both. To do this, I weighed out spillages of flour, recycled wood cat litter pellets and pet hair. Flour and cat litter are easy enough to come by, but my dog doesn’t shed enough hair to test this many vacuums. So I’m also the proud owner of a box of sweepings from a friendly (but slightly bemused) local dog groomer.I gave each of the 16 vacuum cleaners I tested a chance to pick up as much of the spillages as possible, with a single push-forward and pull-backward motion, and weighed the collection bins before and after.Most vacuums will collect more if given more chances to go over a mess, particularly from a different angle, but I wanted relatively tough tests that would truly differentiate one vacuum from another, so I allowed only a single sweep.I also tested the batteries by seeing how long it took them to run down from a full charge – at full suction and in each one’s most economical setting. I performed these tests with the floor head attached, where possible.Lastly, I tested the suction using a pressure gauge. While strong suction is useful, the cleaning tests were more important because other factors play a big part in the overall cleaning prowess. For example, a well-designed floor head can make a moderate sucker as good a cleaner as a more powerful model with an inferior brush or roller.All the vacuums I tested have been sent back to their manufacturers or donated to the British Heart Foundation.The best cordless vacuum cleaners in 2026View image in fullscreenThe lineup of test subjects.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianBest cordless vacuum cleaner overall:Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251SharkPowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKTfrom£388£399.99 at Shark£388 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent cleaner; empties into docking stationWhat we don’t loveExpensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£399.99 at Shark£388 at AmazonIf there’s one thing that makes cordless vacuum cleaners a pain, it’s the emptying: taking it to the bin and jettisoning the debris after vacuuming. And, if your family is anything like mine, you may have to do it before you clean too, because someone else didn’t bother to empty it. That won’t be the case with this Shark vacuum, though: it empties itself. It’s also very good at cleaning.Why we love itThe Shark IP3251 comes with a base station that operates as a stand and charging dock. When you rest the cordless vacuum cleaner on it, it springs into life, opening the base of the vacuum’s collection bin and sucking its contents into a larger container, leaving the cordless stick empty and ready for next time. The secondary bin has a volume of two litres, so it can take a few empties of the 0.7-litre stick.That would all be pointless if the device itself wasn’t up to snuff, but it’s an excellent cleaner. Its floor head has a fluffy roller for hard floors and a brush bar for carpet, and it works well on both surfaces, performing a literal clean sweep in my tests.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty got to work on the flour, pet hair and cat litter.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …I found it worked better if I held it lower while vacuuming on some carpets, with the fins on the base otherwise catching when I pulled it back. That may make it better for shorter than taller people.Weight:3.71kgMax suction power (measured):28kPaBattery life (measured):43minsDust capacity:0.7lAdditional filters supplied?NoSharkPowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKTfrom£388£399.99 at Shark£388 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent cleaner; empties into docking stationWhat we don’t loveExpensiveBest budget cordless vacuum cleaner:Vax HomePro Pet-DesignVaxHomePro Pet-Designfrom£202.12£319 at Argos£202.12 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, effective and easy to useWhat we don’t loveBest on carpet with no soft roller for hard floorsView image in fullscreen£319 at Argos£202.12 at AmazonThe Vax HomePro Pet-Design is good value for money, sitting at the lower end of the price spectrum but still coming with a good selection of tools for handheld use. It also performed well in all the tests.Why we love itIt’s comfortable to hold and use, and simple to operate, with just two large buttons – one to switch it on and the other to boost the power. Battery life is displayed by a light-up ring and lasted a decent 34 minutes in our rundown test.Emptying it is straightforward, too, with a button to open the collection bin, while a pump action lifts dirt off the filter, so you don’t have to poke your hands in. It’s one of the few cordless stick vacuums that can support itself when standing up, so there’s no need to find somewhere to lie it down between cleaning jobs.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Vax HomePro Pet-Design took to the floor to suck up the flour, cat litter and pet hair.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …the floor head is a basic single-brush bar, which is unsophisticated when compared with the alternatives you get on Shark and Dyson models. Still, for the price, it’s ultimately forgivable.Weight:3.5kgMax suction power (measured):19kPaBattery life (measured):34minsDust capacity:0.7lAdditional filters supplied?NoVaxHomePro Pet-Designfrom£202.12£319 at Argos£202.12 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable, effective and easy to useWhat we don’t loveBest on carpet with no soft roller for hard floorsBest cordless vacuum for deep cleaning:Dyson V15 Detect AbsoluteDysonV15 Detect Absolutefrom£559.99£559.99 at Dyson£649 at John LewisWhat we loveSuperb cleaning on carpet and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and messy to emptyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£559.99 at Dyson£649 at John LewisAlthough the V15 Detect Absolute was usurped at the top of Dyson’s range by the new V16 Piston Animal, it remains widely available. That’s good news, because this older model did a much better job of cleaning up in my tests than the V16.Why we love itThe V15 Detect Absolute is as close to vacuuming perfection as we’ve seen to date. It comes with two interchangeable floor heads: one with a brush bar for carpet, the other with a fluffy roller for hard floor. They blitzed my tests, with the anti-tangle brush bar leaving only tiny fragments of cat litter and a light trace of flour on carpet after a first pass, both of which were easy to deal with on a return visit. On hard floor, the fluffy roller is king, picking up every last morsel of mess that I dropped. Its dust-detecting green glow is a genuine help, highlighting just how effective it is at collecting even tiny particles.View image in fullscreenThe Dyson V15 Detect Absolute performed fantastically in our tests.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianRemove the extension wand, and the Dyson converts into a useful handheld. The included crevice tool is good at getting into tight corners, while the combination upholstery and dusting tool copes with most other problems. Sadly, it doesn’t come with the hair screw tool, which is really effective at removing pet hair from upholstery and also handy on stairs. It’s well worth seeking outas an optional extraif you let your pets on your furniture (and suffer the consequences).It’s a shame that …Dyson hasn’t managed to solve the conundrum of messy emptying, with this model creating quite a dust cloud when you release dirt into the bin. It’s also really expensive.Weight:2.96kgMax suction power (measured):31kPaBattery life (measured):50minsDust capacity:0.77lAdditional filters supplied?NoDysonV15 Detect Absolutefrom£559.99£559.99 at Dyson£649 at John LewisWhat we loveSuperb cleaning on carpet and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveExpensive and messy to emptyBest cordless vacuum for clean emptying:Henry Quick ProHenryQuick Profrom£399.99£399.99 at Argos£399.99 at JD WilliamsWhat we loveDirt collects in bags, eliminating emptying messWhat we don’t loveDisposable bags cost money and are part plasticView image in fullscreen£399.99 at Argos£399.99 at JD WilliamsMost cordless sticks create a dust cloud when you deposit the contents of their collection bins into your dustbin. The Henry Quick Pro is the only cordless vacuum we’ve reviewed here that doesn’t do that because of its disposable dirt-capturing bags.Why we love itWe can’t emphasise this enough – it’s frustrating to vacuum the floor only to have the dust billowing out of your bin and back into the air when you empty it. With the Henry Quick Pro, you push a lever on the top, and the base opens, jettisoning the bag of collected rubbish out of the bottom. It leaves no mess and has the added benefit of no filters to clean.In my tests, the Quick Pro performed decently enough, other than on hard floors with the cat litter, which it pushed ahead instead of sucking up. That job would be better tackled by removing the extension wand and using the device with a handheld attachment. It comes with a comprehensive selection of accessories, including a motorised mini head for stairs and upholstery, a flexible hose and a useful handle extension for taller users.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Henry Quick Pro tackled the flour and pet hair but left some of the cat litter behind.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …the bags have a plastic top that holds them in place inside the collection bin. Henry manufacturer Numatic claims to offset the carbon cost, but it would be better environmentally if it didn’t use any plastic at all. They also cost £1.30 per one-litre bag.Weight:3.2kgMax suction power (measured):10.75kPaBattery life (measured):1hr 11minsDust capacity:1lAdditionalbags supplied?Yes, six pods (bags)HenryQuick Profrom£399.99£399.99 at Argos£399.99 at JD WilliamsWhat we loveDirt collects in bags, eliminating emptying messWhat we don’t loveDisposable bags cost money and are part plasticBest handheld cordless vacuum cleaner:Dyson Car+BoatDysonCar+Boatfrom£199£199 at John Lewis£199 at AOWhat we loveAs powerful as a regular DysonWhat we don’t loveA fully-equipped Dyson V8 doesn’t cost much moreView image in fullscreen£199 at John Lewis£199 at AODyson doesn’t manufacture a vacuum purely for handheld use, instead opting to repackage an existing cordless stick without the extension wand. The result is a handheld device so powerful that you may wish you could also use it on the floor.Why we love itThe Dyson Car+Boat is a cunning repackage of theDyson V8. That model is now the bottom of the range of Dyson’s regular cordless stick cleaners, but it makes for a handheld unit that performs above and beyond expectations.It comes with three key attachments: a mini motorised tool for upholstery and stairs; a crevice tool for gaps; and a combination dusting brush and funnel. It’s a powerful combo that cleaned up my test messes with aplomb. I had to use the funnel rather than the motorised tool to collect cat litter, though, because there’s no way this smaller device wouldn’t just push them ahead.View image in fullscreenBefore (left) and after (right) the Dyson Car+Boat devoured the detritus on the mat.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt’s a shame that …you can stillbuy the V8, with the extension tube and attachments, for a similar price. It also comes with Dyson’s old mini-motorised tool. Newer models come with a better-designed tool, which has a tapering roller that doesn’t trap longer hairs. It would have been a nice addition to this repackage.Weight:1.9kgMax suction power (tested):21kPaBattery life (tested):38minsDust capacity:0.54lAdditional filters supplied?NoDysonCar+Boatfrom£199£199 at John Lewis£199 at AOWhat we loveAs powerful as a regular DysonWhat we don’t loveA fully-equipped Dyson V8 doesn’t cost much moreThe best of the restView image in fullscreenThe Shark IA3241UKT is smaller and cheaper than the Shark IP3251UKT but performed slightly better on carpet and almost as well on hard floors.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianShark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro IA3241SharkPowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro IA3241from£299.99£299.99 at Shark£299.99 at CurrysWhat we loveEffective at cleaning on carpets and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveUnclear messaging when battery was running outView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£299.99 at Shark£299.99 at CurrysBest for:smaller homesThe second self-emptying Shark in this list, the IA3241, is a smaller and cheaper version of my favourite, the IP3251, reviewed above. It performed slightly better on carpet and almost as well on hard floors, despite the fact that this model’s floor head doesn’t have the distinctive dual roller that’s typical of Shark’s best cleaners. It performed well in my cleaning tests but generally proved better on carpets than on hard floors.It operates in either floor or handheld mode. The floor head is basic, with a simple brush bar and no anti-tangle features. Most disappointing was the battery, which didn’t last long with the floor head attached, even on the weakest suction setting.Weight:3.1kg;max suction power (tested):12.5kPa;battery life (tested):13mins;dust capacity:0.3l;additional filters supplied?NoMieleDuoflex HX1 Total Carefrom£499£499 at Miele£499 at John LewisWhat we loveGood performance on carpetWhat we don’t loveShort battery life, basic featuresBosch Unlimited 10 BCS1051GBBoschUnlimited 10 BCS1051GBfrom£499£499 at Currys£499.99 at ArgosWhat we loveSolid build quality, good cleaning performanceWhat we don’t loveUnnecessary features drive up the priceView image in fullscreen£499 at Currys£499.99 at ArgosBest for:super-long battery lifeWith the Unlimited 10, Bosch has gone all in on the bling.
