The Unlimited 10 also had the best battery, which made the unit heavy but lasted an astonishing hour and a half on its Eco setting.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a bit expensive without there being enough of a cleaning benefit to justify it.Weight:3.8kg;max suction power (tested):13kPa;battery life (tested):1hr 34mins;dust capacity:0.4l;additional filters supplied?NoBoschUnlimited 10 BCS1051GBfrom£499£499 at Currys£499.99 at ArgosWhat we loveSolid build quality, good cleaning performanceWhat we don’t loveUnnecessary features drive up the priceBeldray Airgility Pet Plus+BeldrayAirgility Pet Plus+from£77.99£89.99 at Currys£77.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExtremely affordable and a fair performerWhat we don’t loveProne to getting blocked by larger particlesView image in fullscreen£89.99 at Currys£77.99 at AmazonBest for:lowest priceIf most of the other reviews left you thinking that you were going to have to take out a second mortgage to get a new cordless vacuum cleaner, the sub-£100 price tag of the Beldray Airgility Pet Plus+ should be a breath of fresh air. It’s light and petite but has small attachments, too, which aren’t large enough to pick up larger particles. It doesn’t collect dirt as well as the best vacuum cleaners here, but for a fraction of the price, it does a reasonable job.The biggest problem was cat litter, which was sucked up OK from the floor but caused a blockage after only a tiny amount had entered the collection bin. It was surprisingly proficient at removing flour from hard floors but failed to agitate my test carpet enough to replicate that success. It also left a bit of pet hair behind during testing, either on the floor or stuck to the rollers.View image in fullscreenBefore the Beldray Airgility Pet Plus+ got to work (left) and how well it picked up the mess (right).Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt didn’t make the final cut because …it didn’t perform as well as more expensive rivals, though it does still impress for the price.Weight:2.2kg;max suction power (tested):9.25kPa;battery life (tested):41mins;dust capacity:1.2l;additional filters supplied?Yes, oneBeldrayAirgility Pet Plus+from£77.99£89.99 at Currys£77.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExtremely affordable and a fair performerWhat we don’t loveProne to getting blocked by larger particlesWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenThe Dyson Car+Boat makes short work of mess.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhy choose a cordless vacuum cleanerCordless vacuum cleaners are vastly more convenient than corded models. There’s no cable to unwind and no need to find a power socket – you just take the vacuum to the mess and get started.The downside is that they run on battery power. The batteries can last anywhere between an hour or so on light settings and down to a few minutes on full blast. They should last long enough to get around an average-size housein one go, but larger spaces might need a mid-clean charge, which can take a few hours (or an expensive extra battery).What should you look for in a cordless vacuum cleaner?Suction powerGenerally speaking, a vacuum cleaner with powerful suction will be better at cleaning than a model with weak suction. However, other factors also come into play. A well-designed floor head, for example, can help a less powerful vacuum outperform a more powerful rival.I tested the suction on the models reviewed here using a vacuum gauge, which measures suction pressure in kPa (kilopascals). A suction of 25kPa or above is good. Anything less than 10kPa isn’t ideal for picking up larger debris, though it may still be good at vacuuming dust, particularly if it’s paired with a decent floor head.WeightCordless vacuum cleaners are perfect for transporting around the house, as you don’t need to worry about plugging them into a wall socket and managing a cable. It makes weight a key consideration, though, as you want a unit that’s light enough to carry around.The weights I’ve quoted are the actual weights of the vacuum cleaner in their standard configurations, including extension wand and carpet floor head.Vacuums that weigh less than 3kg are relatively light, while those approaching the 4kg mark are likely to feel quite heavy. A weighty vacuum will be less problematic in use, though, because a good portion of the weight is usually found in the floor head, which will be resting on the floor during cleaning.Vacuums will be lighter in their handheld modes without the extension wand and floor head attached, but a model that’s heavier overall is likely to be weightier in this configuration, too.Battery lifeHow long your cordless vacuum’s battery will last is important, particularly if you’re expecting to clean an entire house between charges. I test batteries by keeping the device running on a section of carpet, from a full charge until they cut out. Generally, this tends to be shorter than the battery life quoted by manufacturers, though the difference can vary from model to model.A runtime of less than 20 minutes or so may not get you all the way around a whole house clean. Longer life is a bonus, particularly if you live in a large house. If the battery life on your chosen model isn’t that long, you may still be able to buy a secondary battery that you can swap to extend cleaning sessions. You can only do this if your model has a replaceable battery, so check before you buy if you’re likely to want that feature.Bagged vsbaglessMost cordless vacuum cleaners are bagless, which means they collect all the dust and dirt directly into their collection bins, and you empty them by releasing or tipping the dirt into the bin. A few models use bags, however, which provides a cleaner emptying process, as all the dust and dirt is contained in a sack that you dispose of when you empty. If you suffer from allergies, this cleaner emptying process could make life more pleasant.Vacuum bags can vary in price, though popular models often have third-party bags available, as well as those supplied by the manufacturer. They tend to be single use only, and you dispose of the entire bag and its contents when you empty.Of more concern is what the bags are made of. While some can feel papery, most are made from synthetic plastic fibres, which often use recycled plastic but may still take a long time to break down in landfill. Bagless vacuum cleaners are significantly kinder to the environment.Carpet vs hard floorAlmost all cordless vacuum cleaners will have a good go at your carpeted areas, but most work on hard floors, too. Basic models will use the same brush bar floor head, but may spin it slower when cleaning hard floors for a gentler approach.Some models come with a soft, fluffy roller, either built into the main floor head or in a separate unit that can be swapped as required. These are even better at picking up dirt from smooth surfaces than a standard roller brush.If you don’t have much hard flooring, you probably don’t need a soft roller, as carpet vacuums work here too, or you may just prefer to do a quick sweep with a dustpan and brush.AttachmentsCordless vacuums can be broken down into a handheld device if you remove the extension wand and add an attachment. Check that the model you want comes with the attachments you need.Almost all vacuums come with a crevice tool – a narrow funnel that’s useful for getting into small spaces and nipping around skirting boards. Also useful are dusting brushes and upholstery tools with wider nozzles. Look out for motorised upholstery/pet hair tools. These look like miniature versions of a regular floor head, complete with a mini brush bar. They’re ideal for vacuuming smaller areas, such as stairs and furniture.Do cordless vacuums have good filtration systems?Yes, cordless vacuums quote high levels of filtration, with some claiming to trap even the tiniest of particles, such as pollen. However, emptying cordless vacuums that don’t use bags can create a messy dust cloud, so these may not be the models for you if you’re allergic to dirt particles. Filters also need regular cleaning, which is something you won’t be used to if you’re moving away from a vacuuming system that uses disposable bags.How to clean your cordless vacuum cleanerMaintaining your vacuum cleaner doesn’t stop at emptying the collection bin. There are a few other areas that deserve your attention if you want top performance and a long life from your vacuum.The first is keeping the filter clean. This doesn’t need doing after every use, but it’s worth keeping an eye on how dirty it’s getting and cleaning it before it gets too clogged up. Dyson recommends doing this once a month. With Dyson vacuums, you remove the filter by twisting it and lifting it out of the body of the cleaner, then rinsing it in cold water to remove the dirt. Let it air dry for at least 24 hours and check it’s completely dry before refitting.The filters on most other brands can be cleaned in a similar way, but some don’t like getting wet, so check your vacuum’s instruction manual if you’re not sure.The other problem area is the brush bar. Anti-tangle floor heads have improved things in recent years, but even these can be clogged up with hair, fluff and dirt over time. The brush bar can usually be removed from the floor head, and you can attack entangled hair with a pair of scissors. If the bristles are loaded with fluff, you can tease it out with your fingers or use an old comb.For a really deep clean, you can dismantle most vacuum cleaners and wash any non-electrical parts with a damp cloth. Make sure it’s all properly dry before putting it back together.What to do with your old vacuum cleanerWhile you might have decided to move on from your old vacuum cleaner, a working model could still hold value for others. It’s worth seeing if you can sell it locally or donate it to someone who can still get some use out of it.Alternatively, when you buy your new vacuum, ask the retailer about its WEEE (waste electrical and electronic equipment) recycling scheme. The UK’sWEEE Regulationsstate that companies selling such items must accept the device you’re replacing and responsibly recycle it.Lastly, you can always recycle it yourself. Your local recycling centre should have a section for electricals, and you can find your nearest atRecycle Your Electricals. Alternatively, check your local council’s website to find out about its recycling services and opening hours.For more cleaning inspiration from the Filter:How to make your vacuum last longerThe best robot vacuums, testedThe best steam cleaners and mopsDyson PencilVac Fluffycones vacuum reviewAndy Shaw is aconsumer journalist and technology addict. Having reviewed tech products professionally for more than 30 years, his favoured working environment is a small desk surrounded by big boxes. His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their packaging, so they rarely fit back in again when it’s time to return them.This article was originally published on 28 March 2025. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. This article was last updated on 30 July 2026; the Shark PowerDetect IA3241 was added after testing, two vacuums were removed, and prices were updated throughout.Explore more on these topicsHomesThe FilterFamilyInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Line Held Tight – miners, mechs and mismanagement on a distant planet | Games | The Guardian
description: Deep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on you
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Deep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on you
Content: Dark and satanic … A Line Held Tight.Photograph: Humble GroveView image in fullscreenDark and satanic … A Line Held Tight.Photograph: Humble GroveSummer games previewsGamesA Line Held Tight – miners, mechs and mismanagement on a distant planetDeep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on youKeith StuartThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is rare for video games to feature industrial action as a key theme, but it does happen. There’s the shady Dockworker’s Union in Disco Elysium and the Orbital Workers Union in space adventure Tacoma; then there is Lynx, the evil union-bashing corp in Hardspace: Shipbreaker. Soon we can add A Line Held Tight, a visual novel that puts workers’ rights – and workers’ lives – at the very centre of the narrative.In the distant future, a colony of miners digs far beneath the surface of an isolated planet, searching for veins of some exotic ore, protected from the poisonous atmosphere within giant mech suits. But the working conditions are woeful and as a strike looms, an unpopular employee named the Canary must decide whether or not to stand with colleagues and fight against suppression. The player, of course, takes on the role of the Canary, navigating personal as well as political struggles in a world rendered in stark monochrome.View image in fullscreenStark choices … A Line Held Tight.Illustration: Humble GroveAlthough there are clear parallels with the miners’ strike in 80s Britain, Humble Grove’s three-person team was inspired by a situation closer to home. “My interest in telling a story about a trade union comes from our own industry’s burgeoning union interest in the face of mass layoffs,” says co-founder Cel Davison. “People who write sci-fi generally speaking fall into one of two camps: those who are interested in writing speculative futures and those who use futuristic settings to tell stories that are reflections of our present. We tend to fall into the latter end of that spectrum.”Using the highly adaptable narrative game engineNarrat, the game provides a dynamic story guided by player choices. The Canary has a complicated personal connection with the mine, the union and its leaders, which the player has to make sense of. “We’re very interested in the internal workings and conflicts within a collective, how they can make or break a political movement. Our protagonist the Canary starts off as someone quite disinterested in politics, but finds themself in situations where they have to decide what and who they really care about. There’s a lot of variables behind the scenes tracking how the mine’s inhabitants feel about the Canary and the decisions they make.”Although the game is set in the distant future on an alien planet, elements of it are very grounded in British history. It has a traditional folk soundtrack, recorded by two of Humble Grove, Davison and Beck Michalak, who both play at folk sessions in Yorkshire where mining and union-related songs are common. The game’s visuals resemble charcoal sketches providing a stark, almost Victorian feel. “We first got the idea from some wonderful charcoal drawings at the Wakefield Coal Mining Museum,” says Davison. “Charcoal gives a great coal-like feel, and being a traditional medium gives it a grounded textural feel, but conversely when we worked with it we found it can create some very gauzy, ghostly imagery. This really mirrors the way the Canary processes the world as someone trapped in their own head, especially at the beginning of the game.”Humble Grove’s debut game No Longer Home was a thoughtful meditation on moving house and leaving a life behind; it looks like A Line Held Tight will take a similarly meditative approach. This time however, the themes are more prescient than Humble Grove may have intended. “I hope it helps people consider how their everyday actions can have political consequences,” says Davison. “If I’m being really honest I hope it convinces more people to join a union.”A Line Held Tighter is released onPCand Mac in late 2026Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Halo: Campaign Evolved review – they don’t make ‘em like this any more | Halo | The Guardian
description:
PC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game Studios
Halo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the time
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: PC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game StudiosHalo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the time
Content: Once more unto the breach … Halo: Campaign Evolved.Photograph: Halo StudiosView image in fullscreenOnce more unto the breach … Halo: Campaign Evolved.Photograph: Halo StudiosHaloReviewHalo: Campaign Evolved review – they don’t make ‘em like this any morePC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game StudiosHalo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the timeKeza MacDonaldThu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis 25th-anniversary remake of Xbox’s most iconic shooter comes loaded with symbolism. It arrives at a time when Xbox’s whole gaming division (and indeed the games business as a whole)is in turmoil. It’s been made by Halo Studios, an outfit that has arguably never quite recaptured the magic conjured by Halo: Combat Evolved’s original developer Bungie, a studio now owned by rival Sony. It has been polished and prettified using Unreal Engine 5, making it look and feel more modern at the expense of visual uniqueness: Halo now looks similar to hundreds of other games made with those same tools, where Bungie’s 2001 original, made with a bespoke engine, still looks austerely distinctive. I never wanted to become this person, but: perhaps thingswerebetter in the old days?I had my misgivings after the opening level, in which freshly defrosted supersoldier Master Chief fends off an alien attack on a disintegrating spaceship. Originally this was a masterclass in explosive action: you wake up, you look around (once a clever way to determine whether you needed to invert the controls), and you get right into it, firing gaming’s best pistol at chittering alien grunts who scatter from your bullets. Now it’s wrapped in needlessly expanded cutscenes and explanations. WhereHaloStudios has made changes to Combat Evolved’s pacing, it really feels noticeable.After that, however, I spent much less time thinking about what has been changed, and much more thinking about what hasn’t. Nobody really makes single-player shooters like Halo any more: tense, adaptable, challenging. In 2026, we have multiplayer shooters of every imaginable kind; there is little reason for computer-controlled enemies to be intelligent and unpredictable, because we mostly play against other humans, and they provide infinite variation. What we don’t have in abundance in 2026 is atmospheric single-player shooters like this, or Half-Life, or System Shock 2. Solo campaigns in shooters such as Call of Duty have been reduced to flashy “cinematic” shooting galleries. Halo: Campaign Evolved reminded me what we’ve been missing.The imposing Elites are still the probably cleverest foes I’ve ever played against, and it’s been 25 years. They bark orders and duck away from my fire, and they know how to flank me, when to rush me and how to adapt to my assaults. Every time you die in this game, you come back to a slightly remixed firefight, making it endlessly replayable; I never minded going back to a checkpoint, because it never feels repetitious. In other shooters you simply memorise enemy numbers and positioning, but here you must constantly adapt your play, especially on higher Heroic or Legendary difficulty. And I’d somehow forgotten about the Hunters. The first time a pair of those spiked brutes appeared I reacted on pure decades-old muscle memory: I turned around and fled.Unfortunately, we still must contend with the Flood. After several levels of brilliant open-ended fights against intelligent foes under the strange light of a foreign sun, suddenly we are transported into a boring, claustrophobic zombie shooter. I maintain that these mid-game levels are extremely bad: shooting 400 identical parasitic baddies with a shotgun while waiting for a floating robot to open a door has never been my idea of a good time. This will be a controversial opinion, but I was grateful for the new waypoints that told me exactly where to go in the maze of zombie-filled corridors that is the Library. It meant that the worst parts of this game were over sooner.In co-op Halo becomes somewhat less challenging, atmospheric and tactical and significantly more chaotic. Especially when vehicles are involved, the game transforms completely with the addition of other players, thanks to its flexible, open level design and adaptable foes. I played through much of the game in split-screen with my partner – I maintain that playing Combat Evolved with four players just feels somehow wrong – and was reminded exactly why I spent hundreds of hours rinsing this game with friends as a teenager. Halo remains the best companionable shooting game out there.Campaign Evolved is a good remake of a brilliant game. There are things that are worse: I miss the original Warthog’s erratic handling and the early-00s sci-fi aesthetic, which is simply irreproducible with modern graphics. For all its prettiness, this remake chugs along at times – especially in split-screen it would occasionally slow to a crawl, and we never had to worry about linking various different online accounts and connecting to servers when we fancied a quick game of Halo in 2001. But the core of this game is impossible to mess up. For millions of younger players, Campaign Evolved is a perfect, modernised introduction to everything that was great about the 00s-style first-person shooter. For those of us who were there at the time, it’s a welcome return trip.Halo: Campaign Evolved is out nowExplore more on these topicsHaloGamesXboxreviewsShareReuse this content

title: No TV experience? At CBS News, that’s no problem | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: The conservative columnist Ross Douthat is the network’s latest perplexing hire – but the move is in line with the new leadership
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: The conservative columnist Ross Douthat is the network’s latest perplexing hire – but the move is in line with the new leadership
Content: ‘It all began when CBS News’s new ownership – led by the billionaire scion David Ellison – appointed Bari Weiss as editor in chief last October.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘It all began when CBS News’s new ownership – led by the billionaire scion David Ellison – appointed Bari Weiss as editor in chief last October.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersOpinionCBSNo TV experience? At CBS News, that’s no problemMargaret SullivanThe conservative columnist Ross Douthat is the network’s latest perplexing hire – but the move is in line with the new leadershipThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.04 EDTShareIn media circles, this week’shireof a prominent New York Times columnist as a correspondent for CBS’s 60 Minutes was greeted with disbelief.The collective response went something like this: “What?!”Ross Douthat would not have been high on anyone’s list to replace the likes of Scott Pelley, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi, all experienced reporters who were let go in recent weeks from the venerable news show. Or the likes of Anderson Cooper, who left of his own accord amid the months-long tumult and internal complaints that political bias was being injected into 60 Minutes news reports.Yes, it seemed downright odd. After all, Douthat has no broadcast television experience and he is – in the journalistic vernacular – an opinion guy, not a news guy. He’s certainly not a practitioner of investigative journalism, the longtime calling card of 60 Minutes.60 Minutes adds new correspondents and contributors after key departuresRead moreDouthat is known for his lofty takes on national politics and religion – not for the usual reporting skills of grilling reluctant sources with tough questions and digging out information that somebody important doesn’t want you to have.His Times boss, the top opinion editor, Katie Kingsbury, had kind words for Douthat in a staff memo, according to a Timesarticle.As a columnist, Douthat argued for “a religiously serious, intellectually restless conservatism”, Kingsbury wrote. “He was right about things early, wrong about things honestly and never, not once, boring.”Terrific qualities in an opinion writer, certainly, but not exactly a great fit for a job defined decades ago by the bulldog tenacity of the investigative reporter Mike Wallace.But at the all-new 60 Minutes, the hire is being positioned as a coup. And, in fact, it lines up surprisingly well with the new leadership.It all began when CBS News’s new ownership – led by the billionaire scion David Ellison –appointed Bari Weiss as editor in chieflast October.Like Douthat’s hire, it didn’t seem to make much sense on the surface.She too lacked television experience, and she too had made her name on the opinion side of journalism, where she leaned right. She founded the Free Press, a successful digital media company that concentrates on opinion journalism, especially with an “anti-woke” flavor. Before that, she’d been an opinion editor at the New York Times, where she and Douthat had overlapped. Weissquit the Times, complaining about its internal culture.Her conservative profile, and her disagreements with legacy media, was just what Ellison wanted, as he tried to cozy up to Donald Trump and others in the administration. After all, Ellison was trying to get big corporate mergers approved and needed federal approval.When it came time for Weiss to appoint a new executive producer for 60 Minutes, she chose Nick Bilton – another surprising hire who had no TV news experience and who shared roots at the New York Times.If broadcast networks are judged by ratings, things aren’t going well so far. Theyhave plummetedat CBS News,including atits evening news show, where Weiss had quickly installed a new anchor, Tony Dokoupil, to great fanfare.Morley Safer of 60 Minutes was my father. He would be disgusted by what Bari Weiss is doing to CBS Is doing to CBS | Sarah SaferRead moreWith big-name talent departing and longtime viewers feeling angry and betrayed, Weiss and company are in serious rebuilding mode. 60 Minutes is perhaps the highest priority, in part because the controversies there attracted so much negative publicity.Pelley went so far as to accuse Weiss of “murdering” the legendary program. “She was brought in to kill it and she’s been doing exactly that,” hechargedin a staff meeting. His comments soon went viral and, despite his decades at CBS and his many awards and accolades, he was quickly shown the door.In addition to Douthat, theCBSstar Norah O’Donnell will join the show as a correspondent. Other new contributors include Sebastian Junger, the prominent author and former ABC News correspondent; Gianna Toboni, formerly of Vice; and CBS’s Trevor Phillips.In announcing Douthat’s move, Nick Bilton waxed poetic. He is “a thinker of uncommon rigor and a journalist of deep empathy”.But perhaps more than all that, elevated as it sounds, Douthat’s hire sends a clear message.He may not be a TV guy, an investigative guy, or even a news guy – but heisone of America’s best-known conservative opinion journalists.And at the CBS News ofBari Weissand David Ellison, that’s the credential that seems to matter most.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsCBSOpinionBari WeissUS press and publishingUS television industryUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Money has strangled sports. Now Fifa is putting soccer up for sale | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino’s plan for a Fifa subsidiary is odious – but it’s hard to feel surprised
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Gianni Infantino’s plan for a Fifa subsidiary is odious – but it’s hard to feel surprised
Content: ‘What’s the goal here? To have a World Cup on Mars? To clone Lionel Messi?’Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘What’s the goal here? To have a World Cup on Mars? To clone Lionel Messi?’Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersOpinionFifaMoney has strangled sports. Now Fifa is putting soccer up for saleDave SchillingGianni Infantino’s plan for a Fifa subsidiary is odious – but it’s hard to feel surprisedThu 30 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.09 EDTShareJust when you thought global soccer couldn’t get more odiously capitalistic,Gianni Infantinosaid: “Hold my beer” (as long as that beer you’re holding is a Michelob Ultra, one of the official sponsors of the 2026World Cup).The World Cup, one of the largest and most prestigious sporting competitions on the planet, is for sale. Infantino, the president of the soccer governing body Fifa, is thearchitect of a planto sellup to 20%of a new subsidiary that would administer tournaments such as the World Cup and Club World Cup. The subsidiary, which would oversee Fifa’s commercial activities, would be called “Fifa Forward Enterprises”. If I see the word “forward” in a corporate initiative, I assume it’s either a diversity program that’ll get dropped after a couple years, a training video on how to exit a building during an emergency evacuation, or a blatant cash grab. Take a guess which one I think this is.The Guardian view on selling off the World Cup: a red-card offence by Gianni Infantino | EditorialRead moreIf you were waiting for a six-degrees-of-separation connection toDonald Trumpin this story, here it is: the head of the potential investment group is Thrive Eternal – which sounds like the name of an obscure Star Wars villain or a nu-metal band from 2003. Thrive is the handiwork of Josh Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. The scheme could rain down profits on anyone lucky enough to be able to invest in one of the surest bets in live entertainment. I’m not sure I’ll be able to grab a piece of the action, but if I could, I’d be in line to buy a private island, a private plane, and maybe even theStanley Kubrick Criterion Collection box setif I’m lucky.As it stands now, Fifa is registered as anon-profit entityin Switzerland. Infantino’s plan would preserve this, while creating a new company under Fifa control that wouldtheoretically distributemoney into the member nations. While this sounds like a great deal, in the way that anAmway salespersoncan convince you it’s possible to make millions hawking vitamin supplements to your cousins, the backlash to the proposal has been swift and fierce. Uefa, Europe’s soccer governing body,lashed out almost immediately. The English Football Association and North and Central America’s Concacafsaythey are “deeply concerned” by the plan, which is far from a done deal.The deal has to be approved by a majority of the 211 countries in Fifa, with each country given an equal vote. There’s no version of the UN security council for Fifa. The Democratic Republic of Congo has the same power as the new World Cup champion, Spain. If Infantino can cobble together enough support from smaller countries that could use the influx of cash immediately, the soccer superpowers can’t do much to stop it. And Infantino made it very clear in his letter to the member nations that if they don’t approve the deal, they’lllose access to $40m worth of fundingand have tosettle for a far smaller figure.It all sounds pretty icky to my ear, with Uefa stating plainly that it believes Fifa is “[using the] sport to enrich themselves and their friends”. But, I guess, you know … that’s pretty much all sports? The amateurist spirit of the Olympics went out the window decades ago, as TV rights and sponsorships made the International Olympic Committee a non-profitworth nearly $5bn.As suspicious as the English Football Association is about Fifa’s proposal, pretty much every soccer jersey in the top English league (and most other major leagues, including the US and Canada’s Major League Soccer) has sponsorships and corporate logos slathered on it. Stadium naming rights are sold to companies such as Etihad and Emirates Airlines, and American Express. The very formation of the English Premier League was deemed controversial when it launched in 1992, because it gave the top clubs more freedom to negotiate lucrative TV deals or sell naming rights for theleague to Barclays Bankfor 15 years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWho dares ridicule Gianni Infantino as the World Cup boss creates global peace? Not me: is it you? | Marina HydeRead moreI’m not saying we should just let Fifa sell the World Cup to the highest bidder. I’m no cynic. But I can’t pretend money isn’t the primary reason professional sports exist, especially soccer. Why else would Donald Trump have any interest in soccer all of the sudden, considering most of his supporters probably look at it as a game only for snobby coastal elites and infants? Trump’s other sports pal, UFC head Dana White, said soccer was the “least-talented sport on Earth” back in 2021. “There’s a reason three-year-olds can play soccer,” he continued, as though he was a bit jealous he couldn’t figure out a way to get toddlers into the Octagon to juice pay-per-view buy rates.Soccer is the most popular sport in the world, regardless of what Dana White thinks. But the rhetoric from Gianni Infantino describes his proposal as the “next stage of growth” for a game that dwarfs all others in participation and interest. I don’t even know why it would need to grow any larger. At some point, you’re just growing for the sake of saying you can. What’s the goal here? To have a World Cup on Mars? To clone Lionel Messi? If every nation in Fifa gets the same payout, do lesser soccer countries get any sort of tangible advantage? Do world-class systems in England, France, Germany or Brazil need this money? How can Fifa blame anyone for thinking the whole thing is a grift?All I see for the future of the World Cup is more branding, more commercial advertising masquerading as “hydration breaks”, and higher ticket prices. The World Cup is under siege, with the very real risk of it turning into the sports equivalent of a local restaurant chainswallowed up by private equity. The relentless drive for profit has strangled the purity out of sports, but it’s only gotten that way because we, the fans, have allowed it. Perhaps now, we can all finally agree that it’s bad enough.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsFifaOpinionGianni InfantinoFootball politicsWorld CupcommentShareReuse this content

title: Don’t call them ICE detention centers. Call them camps | John Washington | The Guardian
description: I’ve spent a decade reporting on immigration enforcement. The word ‘camp’ best captures the political function of these facilities
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I’ve spent a decade reporting on immigration enforcement. The word ‘camp’ best captures the political function of these facilities
Content: ‘Calling such facilities “detention centers” sanitizes their brutal and increasingly deadly reality. Calling them “Alligator Alcatraz” or the “Cornhole Clink” sensationalizes them.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Calling such facilities “detention centers” sanitizes their brutal and increasingly deadly reality. Calling them “Alligator Alcatraz” or the “Cornhole Clink” sensationalizes them.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAOpinionUS immigrationDon’t call them ICE detention centers. Call them campsJohn WashingtonI’ve spent a decade reporting on immigration enforcement. The word ‘camp’ best captures the political function of these facilitiesThu 30 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTShareWe don’t have concentration camps today in the United States, but we have something close. More than 65,000 people are currently confined in demeaning, often dangerous, sometimes torturous and increasingly deadly conditions not because they have committed a crime, but because they have committed the civil infraction ofbeing on the wrong side of a border. They are ripped from their homes, their families, their jobs and are shipped hundreds of miles away where they languish in squalid, freezing cold and punishing conditions with limited and sometimes no access to lawyers, loved ones, nutritious food, sunlight or medical care. At least 52 peoplehave died in ICE custodysince the second Trump administration came into office.Tens of thousandshave been held in solitary confinement.Oversight mechanisms of these facilities have been gutted, members of Congress have been turned away, and ICE hasstopped reportingbasic and legally mandated data about who is inside and what happens to them. The rapid expansion of the detention system, the inherent inhumanity of policing human mobility, and lack of oversight is partly whya womanin Arizona, who has been detained for 16 months without proper medical care to treat her leukemia, has reportedly lost more than 70lb and is regularly vomiting blood. It’s why people in a now shuttered camp in Florida wereallegedly subjectedto a two-by-two-foot outdoor punishment cage. The stories that leak out of these camps should terrify not only the migrants directly targeted, but should alarm the conscience of us all.Life inside the Delaney Hall ICE detention camp is a travesty | Moira DoneganRead moreCalling such facilities “detention centers” sanitizes their brutal and increasingly deadly reality. Calling them “Alligator Alcatraz” or the “Cornhole Clink” sensationalizes them.As a journalist who has spent a decade reporting on immigration and border enforcement, I’ve dedicated much of my career to trying to expose a reality glossed over and concealed by whitewashing official designations. Which is why I’ve started to call themcamps, not only because of the accurate historical resonance of the term, but as a warning. The word camp best captures the political function they serve: concentrating, immobilizing and excluding populations deemed unwanted.Concentration camps under the Third Reich began not with the extermination camps of Auschwitz or Treblinka, but as holding centers that incarcerated alleged subversives. They followed a model first developed in Cuba and South Africa by the Spanish and British respectively at the end of the 19th century, and later mirrored in the United States with Japanese American “internment camps”. This is the history that we must invoke to help us understand, and ultimately close, today’s immigration camps. The Italian philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls the variations of camps a “progression”, suggesting that there is slippage among them.A definitional aspect of detention camps is that they strip people of, or at least diminish, their legal personhood. And while people held in immigration camps are not completely outside the sphere of law, they are mocked by the law. As the scholar Dan Stone writes of people held in immigration camps: “They are very close to falling into [philosopher Hannah] Arendt’s category of the superfluous stateless person from whom the ‘right to have rights’ has been removed.”A concentration camp, in its most basic definition, is a place where a targeted civilian population, not necessarily accused of a crime, is detained and at least some of their basic rights are suspended. That’s precisely what’s happening in the United States today. We don’t need to stretch history or force an analogy to see how the term applies to immigration detention: US officials have long used the term themselves. FDR called for concentration camps to detain Japanese Americanseven beforethe second world war, and then built them to lock away more than 120,000 people during the war. Ina 1981 memo, released as the Reagan administration began caging tens of thousands of Cuban and Haitian refugees, an immigration taskforce worried that “the appearance of ‘concentration camps’ which, at the present time, would be filled largely by blacks, may be publicly unacceptable”. They used scare quotes, but successive administrations have only expanded the immigration camp system in the United States.While the prison system is also rife with suffering and injustice, there is at least a semblance of court regulation and due process. People suffering inside prisons or jails are there, the logic goes, because of something they allegedly did. In immigration camps, along with concentration camps, people are locked up because of who they are or where they are from. That is an even more penetrating attack on their personhood.ICE holds people in disgusting conditions. Now it’s turning warehouses into camps | Moira DoneganRead moreNot only is the current administration spending billions to try to rapidly grow the camp system, they are trying to make it more painful and permanent. Last fall, the Board of Immigration Appealsruledthat no undocumented migrants who entered the country without inspection would be eligible for release on bond. The camp became mandatory: indefinite detention without the benefit of trial by jury. And while the fifth circuitrecently ruledthat people held under that mandatory detention statute must get a bond hearing within 90 days, that ruling merely claws back a modicum of rule of law. Nobody gets released because of the ruling. They just, for now, get to make their case for freedom every 90 days instead of never. An appeal from the government is expected.Meanwhile, despite some rollbacks of the spectacular violence seen in the streets of Minneapolis and elsewhere, more immigrantsthan ever beforeare being arrested in this country, and tens of thousands of them – abducted off the streets – will suffer for weeks, months, or longer in the camps. Recent reportingdetailedjust how cramped some of these facilities can be, with 86 people at one point held in a small room – a “closet of humanity that smelled of sweat, urine and feces”. In one notoriously abusive Texas camp, one person said hewas told: “You’re only getting out deported or dead.”Immigration camps in the United States today disappear people politically before, all too frequently, they disappear them physically. To combat the suffering we should use language that reveals the inhumanity rather than conceals it. The word camp does just that.John Washington is the author ofHow to Close a Camp: Dispatches from the Fight against Immigrant Detention, released this month from Haymarket Books. He is also a staff writer atLookoutExplore more on these topicsUS immigrationOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US CongressLaw (US)commentShareReuse this content

title: I’ve spent years researching what it means to be alive. This is what I’ve learned | Melanie Challenger | The Guardian
description: To understand the experience of life, don’t look to the mind. Look to the body
Author: Melanie Challenger
Headline: To understand the experience of life, don’t look to the mind. Look to the body
Content: ‘By the digital age, Marvin Minsky was declaring the body a “meat machine”.’Photograph: kieferpix/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘By the digital age, Marvin Minsky was declaring the body a “meat machine”.’Photograph: kieferpix/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionLife and styleI’ve spent years researching what it means to be alive. This is what I’ve learnedMelanie ChallengerTo understand the experience of life, don’t look to the mind. Look to the bodyThu 30 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.06 EDTShareIn a 1982 article, the American feminist scholar Elizabeth Spelman coined the term “somatophobia” to describe the strange human delusion that we are minds rather than bodies.Forty years later, artificial intelligence is everywhere, offering the most powerful illusion yet that intelligence can exist without flesh. Two-thirds of people surveyed in a recentstudybelieve that tools like ChatGPT possess some consciousness and feeling. We are living in the age of somatophobia. Now is the moment to resist it.Our machine-takeover fantasy is the outcome of an ancient delusion that the mind is a separate substance, a “thinking thing” that might somehow live beyond death. It arises ultimately from our fears about the fragility of embodied life. “The body is a source of endless trouble to us,” Plato complained more than 2,000 years ago.By the digital age, Marvin Minsky was declaring the body a “meat machine”. Today, the techno-philosopher Ray Kurzweil promises “a backup version of ourselves” in the cloud. The immortal soul has been rebranded as the digital self.For the past six years, I have been researching the latest evidence for how life and intelligence actually work. Far from being marginal, our bodies are essential to who we are, because life and intelligence require a unique form of physical holism and integration.What would our lives look like if we no longer had to work? As a thought experiment I tried to imagine | Brigid DelaneyRead moreWhat’s more, research into the origins of life, including Nick Lane and William Martin’s work onmembrane bioenergetics, suggests that these capabilities may depend on particular elements and conditions, rather than an abstract formula of some sort.These unique qualities enable biological beings to do something remarkable in the cosmos. Our bodies both generate and direct energy to preserve our own organisation. In this sense, it is the body that is synonymous with selfhood.This is no longer a philosophical claim. In cognitive science, Lawrence Barsalou’s influential account of “grounded cognition” argues that thought depends on perception, bodily states and situation. In neuroscience, Antonio Damasio’s “somatic marker” hypothesis, tested through theIowa Gambling Task, shows how bodily feeling helps guide decision-making before explicit reasoning catches up. More recent workshowsthat the brain is constantly predicting and regulating signals from the heart, gut, lungs and viscera.The intelligent actions of organisms, then, arise from the imperatives of whole bodies that must preserve their own conditions for existence. Holistic processes like homeostasis are more decisive than minds, and the body drives many critical state changes, including aspects of gene regulation.Ultimately, little of intelligence can meaningfully be said to be controlled by a separable thinking part that you might identify as who you are. Instead, intelligence is the sum of minute reformations across the associated regions of our bodies. In fact, mind often enters late, receiving and integrating acts the body has already begun.Wanting a cup of coffee, for instance, isn’t an abstract decision but the body in full spate – molecules accumulating, cells signalling and chemical cascades translating into action. In other words, we are not brains in vats. We are embodied creatures fully immersed in the world.Yet today, the body’s intelligence is being systematically disrupted. We are living through the rapid translation of a biological life in nature into a technologically mediated life. This represents a refusal of our remarkable living bodies on a global scale.For Spelman, somatophobia isn’t simply fear of one’s body. It is a structure of devaluation manifesting in misogyny, racism and class hierarchy. AI is an expensive form of mimicry, copying the patterns of our thought while lacking the bodies that bring real meaning and intelligence. Meanwhile, information devices are co-opting our physical experiences. We are passing into a virtual realm, and with this comes the narrowing of human agency.Where does body-refusal take us? We are burnt out by hyper-connectivity and the expectation that our “deliverables” will be available 24 hours a day. Onestudylinked working 55 hours or more a week to a 35% higher risk of stroke and a 17% higher risk of dying from heart disease.At the same time, we have become increasingly sedentary, changed like unwitting cyborgs by the machines that drive this productivity. In 2024, the World Health Organizationreportedthat nearly one-third of adults worldwide did not meet recommended physical activity levels. We are living as though cognition can be separated from movement, circulation, muscles and the wider environment.We boast that our machines have enabled global connectivity. But another 2025reporton social connection found that one in six people worldwide is affected by loneliness, linked to about 100 deaths every hour. Humans aren’t just minds exchanging information. We are whole beings that regulate one another through touch, voice, smell, gesture and shared time.Meanwhile, we continue to encode a social hierarchy in which some people get to be minds and others are reduced to bodies. In western society, white people have too often been permitted to be thinkers and leaders, while brown bodies are fixed in roles of labour or dependency. Only those with power have the privilege of forgetting their bodies. The powerless are rarely allowed to be anything else.In my research, I argue that being alive is first and foremost a way of being a body. Being genuinely intelligent depends on the complete system of body and energy flow that we find only in biological organisms.double quotation markMeaning is not produced by raw information; it begins wherever a living body has something at stakeAs such, neither information nor mind – nor AI – are alive or intelligent in any meaningful sense. The body-denying impulse is therefore also a form of life-denial. Should we be surprised that we are destroying life on Earth to unprecedented degrees?When the self is imagined as mind or information, the living body becomes an inconvenience, a disposable support system. This is not just a philosophical mistake. It alters how we approach medicine, mental health and other species. But we are not machines. We are precious bodies – dynamic, perceptive and determined.Pain matters because a body can be damaged. Love matters because embodied beings are dependent, social and mortal. Grief matters because living bodies can be irreversibly lost. This is the thrilling intelligence of life. Meaning is not produced by raw information; it begins wherever a living body has something at stake.Ironically, most AI models do not share our confusion. Recently, I asked ChatGPT about the endpoint of the machine metaphor. The reply: “In truth, I am only an artifact of statistical patterns.” Well, indeed. That so many of us have been drawn away from embodied reality into physically sedentary lives is the endpoint of an obsession with mental life as the essence of who we are. It is time to recall the body.Melanie Challenger is a researcher and writer on history of ideas and history and philosophy of science. Her newest bookAlive: The Hidden Intelligence of the Living Worldwill be released on 11 AugustExplore more on these topicsLife and styleOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)HealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why would I waste my precious holiday time going to a zoo in another country? | James Colley | The Guardian
description: I can hear the howls of disagreement now but we’ve got zoos – complete with giraffes and elephants – at home. Seen one, you’ve seen them all
Author: James Colley
Headline: I can hear the howls of disagreement now but we’ve got zoos – complete with giraffes and elephants – at home. Seen one, you’ve seen them all
Content: Taronga zoo, Sydney. ‘Perhaps I am speaking from a point of privilege. My local zoo happens to sit directly on Sydney Harbour with one of the most glorious views of the city possible.’Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTaronga zoo, Sydney. ‘Perhaps I am speaking from a point of privilege. My local zoo happens to sit directly on Sydney Harbour with one of the most glorious views of the city possible.’Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianOpinionZoosWhy would I waste my precious holiday time going to a zoo in another country?James ColleyI can hear the howls of disagreement now but we’ve got zoos – complete with giraffes and elephants – at home. Seen one, you’ve seen them allThu 30 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 19.34 EDTShareWhen I first took my toddler to the zoo, I realised that here were her celebrities. To see a giraffe in real life is the three-year-old’s equivalent of seeing Tom Hanks strolling through your local shopping centre. After all, every night we lie in bed and read stories about the exploits of shy turtles or bossy rhinos or the occasional lion who didn’t want to go to bed. Then, one day, these heroes are right in front of you, ambling about in a pen, being gawked at by the paparazzi.All of a sudden, I felt my own childlike excitement reinvigorated, getting to surprise her with the next animal and the next animal. A visit to your local zoo is truly one of the greatest experiences you can have as a parent.But we will not be visiting any other zoos.Recently, in an act of masochism, my wife and I took both of our children along for a working holiday in Europe. During our first week in London, while my wife attended a conference, I had the joyful experience of taking my kids around a new city in a new country, knowing that even though they might not remember it, I would. One morning, as we discussed the itinerary for the coming days, my wife said offhandedly that, obviously, we would be taking them to the zoo. I said that I surely wouldn’t. And we were off. From such small sparks, bonfires are born.The simple fact of the matter is there is no point visiting a zoo in another city, or another country.Tasmanian devil Mary found 2km from her Gold Coast theme park home after two weeks on the runRead moreLet’s start here: there are no exclusive animals. Oh, you’d like to see an elephant? We’ve got elephants at home. Better elephants, probably. Who cares? Seen one, you’ve seen them all. If, say, the London zoo could promise me that this was the only place on Earth where I’d be able to see a real-life grumpt in the flesh, then we’d have a reason to go! What’s a grumpt? When are they feeding the grumpt? This is worth the price of admission.Don’t try to tell me that the animals at this zoo are different or special. This is not true. It is also not the point of the zoo. Never before have I heard someone return from the zoo and tell me that the ibex had a stunning personality.Plus, we all know deep in our hearts that every zoo has a section of filler animals. Yes, every animal on this Earth is precious and dignified and potentially delicious but we can admit that in the back corner of every zoo there are a series of horned-and-hoofed creatures that are in all practicality the same animal with different hairstyles. You are already testing my patience when we get to the third South African variant of a curly horned whatever on home soil, let alone wasting precious holiday time.Also, it is a little humiliating to see your own native animals playing an away game in a foreign zoo. When I see the wombat waddling about, it’s hard to resist the urge to whisper like I’m conspiring on a prison break.We’re going to get you out of here, brother.If I’m being entirely honest, when on holidays I do my best to avoid other Australians in general. Don’t be offended, you do it too. We don’t need to see other Australians. We’ve got them at home. So why do I need to see a kangaroo lounging about on a little pile of mulch sandwiched between an aviary and a canteen filled with suspicious meats?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI am certain there are some passionate zoo fans out there that are already flooding the comments section with incendiary remarks about how I am ignorant of the beauty of the foreign zoo and how you haven’t lived until you’ve seen an orangutan in a French zoo enjoy a pain au chocolat and a cigarette. For the record, I have visited zoos in other nations at different times in my life and yes, they were entirely fine. They were zoos. All I would say is that if you are, for example, a London resident aghast that I have snubbed your zoo, I would beg you to have a little more confidence in your city. It’s not that the zoo is bad per se, it’s that there are other things to do and, as every parent knows, the zoo is a last resort. It’s a parachute you pull deep into the school holidays when you’ve exhausted every bit of play equipment inside the air-conditioned shopping centres in your local area.Perhaps I am speaking from a point of privilege. My local zoo happens to sit directly onSydneyHarbour with one of the most glorious views of the city possible. Maybe once you have seen it, no other zoo could possibly compare. I wouldn’t know. I only visit that zoo because the ibex has a stunning personality.James Colley is a comedy writer from Sydney. title: The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together | Zheng Zeguang | The Guardian
description: There is no point competing in isolation. There are so many benefits to be had, in manufacturing, healthcare, research and governance, says Zheng Zeguang, Chinese ambassador to the UK
Author: Zheng Zeguang
Headline: There is no point competing in isolation. There are so many benefits to be had, in manufacturing, healthcare, research and governance, says Zheng Zeguang, Chinese ambassador to the UK
Content: A visitor high-fives a humanoid robot at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, Shanghai, 18 July 2026.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersView image in fullscreenA visitor high-fives a humanoid robot at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, Shanghai, 18 July 2026.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working togetherZheng ZeguangThere is no point competing in isolation. There are so many benefits to be had, in manufacturing, healthcare, research and governanceZheng Zeguang is the Chinese ambassador to the UKThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.11 EDTShareArtificial intelligence is widely regarded as one of the defining technologies of our time. Like the steam engine, the harnessing of electricity and the internet before it, it has the potential to transform how we work, live and interact.But every technological revolution brings challenges as well as opportunities. As AI systems become more capable, people are asking legitimate questions. How can AI remain safe, accountable andunder human control? How should its development be governed? How can itsbenefits be sharedmore widely?These questions were at the heart of the 2026 World AI Conference, held last week in Shanghai. Representatives from more than 100 countries and international organisations gathered to discuss how AI could better serve humanity, and how a more inclusive and effective global governance framework could be built. I am glad the UK also sent a delegation to the conference.China’s president, Xi Jinping, delivered an important address calling on all countries to “boost innovation-driven development”, in a spirit of openness and mutual benefit, to strengthen risk-awareness and ensure that AI is secure and controllable. We must, he said, encourage inclusiveness and promote mutual learning between civilisations. He also stressed the importance of improving global AI governance together.Things are moving quickly. To further support global AI development, China has announced that in the next five years it will provide developing countries with 5,000 opportunities in AI training and seminar programmes. We will also develop international AI-application cooperation centres with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the League of Arab States, the African Union, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and our fellow Bric countries. Thirty nations will also be able to use the AI-powered, early-warning weather system,Mazu.View image in fullscreenXi Jinping delivering the keynote speech at the World AI Conference, Shanghai, China, 17 July 2026.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockTo ensure that AI is a trustworthy tool for humanity, legitimate concerns over data security, privacy protection and responsible use must be taken seriously. These challenges transcend national borders. They obviously require international collaboration, especially in areas such as developing common standards and practical governance. At the same time, security considerations should not become a blanket justification for restricting normal technological cooperation or fragmenting global innovation.China’s own experience reflects this approach. Through the AI Plus Initiative, AI is being integrated into manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, energy and consumer services, helping to build one of the world’s most dynamic AI ecosystems. In 2025, China’s core AI industry exceeded 1.2tn yuan (about £130bn) and a large number of AI companies are growing rapidly.Another notable feature of China’s AI development is its emphasis onopen-source and open-weightmodels. The success of models such as Qwen,DeepSeekand Kimi demonstrates that advanced AI capabilities can be developed at lower cost and made accessible to a much wider community of developers and users. Lowering the barriers to innovation allows more countries, researchers and smaller enterprises to participate in the AI revolution instead of being left behind.It is important to say that no country has a monopoly on innovation. Different nations bring different strengths to AI development, and lasting progress will depend on how well those strengths complement one another rather than compete in isolation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath RaghavanRead moreThis is where China and the UK have much to gain from working together. The UK has a competitive edge in frontier research, life sciences, financial services and AI innovation. China has well-recognised strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering and large-scale industrial deployment, plus one of the world’s largest markets for AI applications. These advantages are highly complementary.In healthcare, combining British strengths in biomedical research with China’s capacity to deploy AI at scale can acceleratedrug discovery, improve medical imaging and enhance healthcare delivery. In manufacturing, pairing British innovation with China’s industrial capabilities can speed up the adoption of smarter, cleaner and more efficient production. Joint research can also contribute to internationally applicable standards for AI safety, testing and evaluation, supporting innovation while strengthening public trust. Such cooperation would not only benefit our two countries but also generate solutions with wider global value.Policymakers, researchers and business leaders from China and the UK need to increase exchanges and translate dialogue into joint research, commercial partnerships and closer cooperation on AI governance.For China, for Britain and for the wider world, cooperation is not simply desirable. It is the right way forward to ensure that AI develops in a way that benefits us all.Zheng Zeguang is the Chinese ambassador to the UKDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
