title: Europe is burning – and if Trump’s war on the climate is not met with sanctions, things will only get worse | Alexander Hurst | The Guardian
description: The White House seems committed to ecocide. The EU should harness the power of the single market to force it to change course, says Guardian Europe writer Alexander Hurst
Author: Alexander Hurst
Headline: The White House seems committed to ecocide. The EU should harness the power of the single market to force it to change course, says Guardian Europe writer Alexander Hurst
Content: Fire erupts in Galicia, Spain, on 14 June 2026.Photograph: Brais Lorenzo/EPAView image in fullscreenFire erupts in Galicia, Spain, on 14 June 2026.Photograph: Brais Lorenzo/EPAOpinionWildfiresEurope is burning – and if Trump’s war on the climate is not met with sanctions, things will only get worseAlexander HurstThe White House seems committed to ecocide. The EU should harness the power of the single market to force it to change courseThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.15 EDTShareAre we understanding it yet? AsEuropeburns in the west, the south and the north, are we grasping the fact that our economies, food systems, political stability and even our ability to plan for the future, will all be charred in a world on fire?Paris got a taste of what is in store for us Europeans when, weeks ago,fire ripped through Fontainebleau forest, a bouldering paradise and one of the world’sfirst natural reserves. But the wildfires currently threatening Bordeaux and Madrid, which experts are calling themost extremeseen in Europe, are apocalyptic in comparison. In the Gironde region around Bordeaux, tens of thousands of hectares have burned, creating an unpredictable “thunderstorm of fire” as the region’s chief administrator called it. More than 200,000 people have been displaced in the largest peacetime evacuations in France’s history. Only the bravery of firefighters, dozens of whom have been injured, is keeping the fires within mere kilometres of Bordeaux and its more than a million inhabitants.In Spain, multiple fires have merged on the outskirts of Madrid, creating “the largest fire in Spain’s history”, burning more than triple the hectares of an average July as yet another heatwave menaces the country. Scientists blame “weather whiplash” due to the accelerating climate crisis for bringing the fires this close to the ancient streets and squares of Madrid and Bordeaux. As far south as Sicily, as far north as Norway, the story is much the same: a summer of almost unendurable heat has erupted into tempests of flame.Across the Atlantic, thicksmoke drifting southwardsfrom fires across Canada’s 270m hectares of boreal forest obscured, once again, the skies in cities in the United States. Certain Maga-affiliated politicians reacted notwith offers of firefighting assistance, as Canada has so consistently sent to US states in need, but byproposing sanctionson Canada, or tariffs. As if the problem, to minds obscured long before the skies ever were, isinsufficient raking.A catastrophe of this scale will necessarily be politicised. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez,condemned disinformationand conspiracy theories around the fires; French opposition figureshave criticisedthe government for delaying the acquisition of two additional Canadair firefighting planes, and the government isaccusing the oppositionof using tragedy for political point-scoring. But why should the blame game stop at borders, when the carbon that we have collectively emitted is drifting in our shared atmosphere?To adapt a phrase from Animal Farm, we are all responsible, but some are more responsible than others. In this case, the US is the beast more responsible than all the rest: it has emitted more than one-fifth of all historical emissions, and remains by far the highestper-capita major emitteralongside Saudi Arabia. To be fair, Canada is not far behind, and the smaller Gulf states like Qatar deserve a special mention of shame too.It would be one thing if the US was guilty of historic emissions while making a concerted effort to change. China, for all its ownproblematic emissions, is at least fosteringbreathtaking growthin renewables and now dominates the world’s green industries as a result. Instead, the US has almost always been recalcitrant – or worse – about the crisis. US fossil fuel, energy and auto companieshid evidence and blocked actionfor decades, while the US government undermined and withdrew from the Kyoto protocol under George W Bush, promoted a fracking boom under Barack Obama, and withdrew from the Paris agreement during Donald Trump’s first presidential term.The US has flipped so far beyond recalcitrance during Trump’s second stint in the White House that it can only be described as waging ecological warfare. The phallic mantra of “drill, baby, drill” is guiding an administration for which the faintest speck of care for the Earth is already too woke. Green policies are not merelydismantled, but increased fossil fuel use is beingpursued with heinous glee. Such a conflict effectively pits the US against the rest of the world. So let’s take the US’s Maga senators and congresspeople seriously: as the skies fill with smoke and forests turn to ash, shouldn’t the United States, the guiltiest of guilty parties, be made to pay?As the Guardianrecently reported, countries individually responsible for less than 2% of global emissions are nevertheless the largest plurality, collectively responsible for 33% of the world’s emissions. There is no individual country that can address the catastrophe under way on its own; but there is no collective solution without each individual country making cuts.And when it comes to Europe, there is something additional of consequence that we can do: use the power of the single market to make the world’s worst ecological actor change course, or at least make it pay to fund the global effort to adapt to the climate crisis.For most of the past year, European industry and Europe’s rightwing parties have been pushing toroll back or slow walkregulation, thinking that the way to remain economically competitive is to race Trump’s America to the bottom. It is not. It is economic doom to race to a future where nothing is insurable, where crops fail en masse, where hundreds of thousands of evacuees have become millions of internally displaced climate refugees and where the combination of these calamities has pushed public finances to breaking point.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo safeguard its political and economic future, Europe needs to accept that the US’s environmental war must be met with an economic response – coordinated with other actors, including China. Let’s extend the EU’semissions trading system (ETS) carbon marketto all sectors, beef up the “carbon border tax” to protect against retaliation, slap tariffs on finished goods and services from the US that have easy substitutes and place export taxes on materials and intermediate components used in US-located production. All that cash could then be pooled, shared and earmarked for decarbonisation and adaptation.This might sound ludicrous. But what is truly ludicrous is that this is only the beginning. This is what three decades of inaction and insufficient action have produced. Ludicrous would be allowing the US, under the grasp of a handful of villainous, ecocide billionaires and ideologues, to drag us all into the abyss of even more years of catastrophic inaction.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoirGeneration Desperationis out nowExplore more on these topicsWildfiresOpinionClimate crisisFranceSpainEuropeExtreme weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m torn by the hard hat v graduation cap debate. Is it wrong that I want my kids to go to university? | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: As Andy Burnham intervenes, it’s clear that the shine is coming off higher education. But is society ready for this mindshift? Am I? asks Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: As Andy Burnham intervenes, it’s clear that the shine is coming off higher education. But is society ready for this mindshift? Am I? asks Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: Andy Burnham has said this country should ‘value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap’.Photograph: Joerg Sarbach/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has said this country should ‘value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap’.Photograph: Joerg Sarbach/APOpinionHigher educationI’m torn by the hard hat v graduation cap debate. Is it wrong that I want my kids to go to university?Emma BrockesAs Andy Burnham intervenes, it’s clear that the shine is coming off higher education. But is society ready for this mindshift? Am I?Thu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.55 EDTShareFor a while now I’ve been having a conversation with friends that a few years ago would’ve been largely unthinkable. Partly, this is because of how sheltered we all tend to be when trying to imagine our kids’ lives running on different tracks to our own. But it’s also about the world changing. A brilliant young person I know left school, took up an internship, turned it into a job and now she’s in her early 20s with no debt and a great position at a big fashion house. “Maybe I won’t go to university, either,” said one of my kids, eyeing me for a reaction, while I nodded thoughtfully and tried to ride out the panic.Andy Burnham’sannouncementthis week that university shouldn’t be the single, aspirational goal of all young people is perfectly timed and sensibly presented and shouldn’t sound as radical as it does. It is, of course, a correction to existing norms that university-for-all is a proper national goal and the only personal determinant of ambition and success. By contrast, Burnham said on Tuesday, this country should “value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap” as he spoke about tailoring technical and vocational training to meet local job needs and tackle youth unemployment.The evidence on the ground suggests that a culture shift is already under way and that Burnham is simply validating an existing trend. I’m in the US at the moment, where the cost-reward ratio of going to college is so out of whack that student numbers have beendropping for years. Smart people on podcasts direct young people towards their in-state universities, which charge a fraction of the cost of the prestigious private ones (not the Ivy Leagues, so much, which can afford to subsidise any family making less than $400,000 a year, but the smaller, boutique liberal arts colleges that charge as much as $80,000 in annual tuition and have been closing due to dwindling student numbers).In the UK, too, for the last two years, university numbers havedippedslightly. This is partly a result of changing demographics – smaller families mean a smaller supply of school-leaving 18-year-olds – and partly to do with the cost, as increasing numbers of universities charge the highest tariff rate, even those that, a few years ago, were middle to low fee-charging.View image in fullscreenA young apprentice working in construction gets stuck in on a site.Photograph: Andrew Sparkes/AlamyThe question is what this is doing to perceptions about the usefulness or otherwise of going to college, which, as we know, isn’t just about earning potential. In both theUSand theUK, being a graduate still delivers average median earnings that are higher than the earnings of non-graduates. But while middle-class people make jokes about how their plumbers probably earn more than they do, the fact remains that it is the other stuff – the cultural and social capital of going to college – that underscores this particular bias.So it is that, while “low-value” degrees have been the target of derision for decades – ever since media studies became a thing in the 90s – when you dig down into why people want their kids to go to university, it has as much to do with social benefitsas academic attainment. When will they meet the friends who will stay with them and godparent their children if not while sitting around watching mid-morning telly for three years as they slowly mature into adults? Are those friendships worth 10 grand a year? How, exactly, do you put a value on the non-academic stuff? I always think of a thing Don DeLillo said once about honouring a need to “drink coffee and look at the world” for a space of years, something that in the current economic climate sounds like a preposterous indulgence. And yet, for lots of 18-year-olds, it remains a valuable exercise.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI thought my life would feel sorted when I turned 40. It doesn’t – and that’s OK | Carolin WürfelRead moreBut not all of them. The problem with current thinking about university is that it’s so uniform, and the main takeaway from Burnham’s speech is a reminder that there is more than one way of doing things. You can go to college, or not go to college, or go at 35 not 18, and all those things should be regarded as equal. Meanwhile the whole conversation around college is just part of a larger one about changing work patterns in which, on the evidence so far, gen Z are proving reluctant torepeat the experienceof their parents’ generation by taking up office jobs – with additionalpushback from gen X, who feel they came of age in office structures that taught them all sorts of useful things, such as how to work alongside people they found basically unbearable.We all bring such biases to these questions of how to live life. I went to university and want my kids to do the same. My mum would’ve loved to have gone to university but had to leave school at 16 and I’m sure that’s in the mix, too. But when the question of college education came up in our house, I tried hard to take myself off generational autopilot, stop being so hidebound by precedent, and properly consider the alternative.Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist. She is the author of She Left Me The Gun: My Mother’s Life Before MeExplore more on these topicsHigher educationOpinionParents and parentingUniversitiesCareerscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’ve seen what can confound Farage on his home turf: optimism. People need a politics that offers them that | Owen Jones in Clacton | The Guardian
description: You can’t blame his constituents in Clacton for their pessimism – because they have been let down for years, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: You can’t blame his constituents in Clacton for their pessimism – because they have been let down for years, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Clacton-on-Sea, on 7 July, the day Nigel Farage announced his resignation as MP.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClacton-on-Sea, on 7 July, the day Nigel Farage announced his resignation as MP.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOpinionNigel FarageI’ve seen what can confound Farage on his home turf: optimism. People need a politics that offers them thatOwen Jonesin ClactonYou can’t blame his constituents in Clacton for their pessimism – because they have been let down for yearsThu 30 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 06.39 EDTShareUnder battered England flags, cynicism, pessimism and exhaustion stalk the streets of Clacton.As the byelection called byNigel Farageapproaches, one young couple do not know which candidates are standing. Neither has ever voted. Living in Britain is “depressing”, says the woman in a black floral dress. “The cost of living these days is stupid,” says her partner, wearing a black and grey mechanic’s shirt and a black and red cap. They both work 40 or 50 hours a week, he says, yet “we’re still struggling to pay rent, food, electric, everything else”. They rarely get a day off, and time spent together is rarer still.No wonder they are not agonising over the£5m personal giftFarage received from a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, or thedonations in kindfrom a convicted fraudster. Life is already taking up all their time.Communities across Britain have endured stagnation and decline since the financial crash of 2008, but Clacton has more problems than most. Families still descend on the flashing arcades and fairground rides of Clacton pier, but nothing has replaced the economic world swept away by the decline of the English seaside holiday. Clacton is among thetop 10% of deprived English constituencies. One neighbourhood is ranked the most deprived in England.Yet the scandal over Farage’s income provokes precious little anger here. “I know how corrupt everything is,” says a former soldier, who served 22 years. “It’s just part and parcel of politics.” The belief that all politicians are on the take – and that Farage is therefore no different – is everywhere. Tell people that other politicians are not receiving £5m lump sums from foreign billionaires and many simply shrug. Contempt for politicians has become Farage’s protection.Some come up with their own comforting explanations. A flat cap-wearing man in a wheelchair, who arrived here from Cyprus six decades ago, assumes Farage might invest the £5m in the local community.There is concern, but it is crowded out by other grievances. “That’s the bit that bothers me,” says one elderly man, before adding something more revealing. “Do you want him as a prime minister? Probably not, but what choice do we have?”Farage continues to profit from the belief that both Labour and the Conservatives have failed in office. A middle-aged man in a navy polo shirt says he will vote Reform because “the others have just given me a load of rubbish”. The deceit of the toppled prime minister has left its mark. “That Keir Starmer was a complete liar,” he says.One thought on the Clacton contenders: the ‘establishment’ looks a bit different these days, doesn’t it? | Marina HydeRead moreFarage also benefits from what voters project on to him. When I approach one elderly couple, the man is promptly abandoned by his wife, who correctly anticipates that he will answer at length. He regrets voting for Boris Johnson’s Conservatives – and, before that, Margaret Thatcher. “She sold us off,” he says. “Water, telecoms.”Why, then, I ask, supportsomeone who regards Thatcheras a political hero? “You’ve got to give them a chance,” he replies, apparently without noticing that he has repeatedly regretted doing exactly that.Only around one in 20 residents herewas born abroad, and 96% are white, yet migration and race loom over the constituency. Economic grievance inevitably plays a part. When I suggest to one affable young man covered in tattoos that migrants are blamed for the country’s problems, he agrees. “It’s an easy route out, isn’t it?”He still intends to vote for Farage, because “I believe he does what he says he’s going to do”. Unfortunately, he cannot say what that is.But economics cannot explain everything. Disinformation about migrants and refugees – promoted by sections of the media and spread online – has cut through. One middle-aged couple told me they would have voted for the far-right Restore party, had it fielded a candidate. They grow increasingly agitated as we speak.“Eighty-five per cent of Muslim women can’t even speak English, and that’s a fact,” says the man. Where did he get this statistic? Annoyed at being asked for evidence, he eventually says it came “from news” and tells me to “go and look it up”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter they leave, I do. According to recentcensus data, two-thirds of Muslim women have English as their main language, with 87.7% speaking the language proficiently. Among British-born women, nearly all have English as their main language.This is what happens when real anger at a country in crisis collides with lies about who has caused it. “This country’s in a right mess,” says a bald, weather-beaten, middle-aged man, his sleeveless shirt open at the chest. When I ask what is wrong, he answers pithily: “Everything about it, everything.”Unless there is a secret army of shy Count Binface voters, the comedy writer turned “independent space warrior” – popular on social media – will not triumph here. I find only a couple of people intending to plump for him.The Guardian view on Nigel Farage’s byelection stunt: spectacle is not scrutiny | EditorialRead moreThat’s not to say there isn’t dissent. Outside a cafe, an elderly man with a wispy grey ponytail and sunglasses pushed back on his head nurses a drink from a white mug, an England flag hanging in the window behind him. He tells me he has Asperger’s and has “always known from a young age that we’re all the same”.Farage, he argues, is riding in “on a white charger to rescue them from the refugees”, even though “I don’t believe Nigel Farage is for the working man”. Politicians roll up their sleeves and affect the common touch, but “they’re a different class. They’re the ruling class, and it’s the same fucking ruling class all the time”.He has lost his soulmate and says he rarely leaves home. In a town where so many are resigned to cynicism, he has a simple prescription: “We’ve got one world,” he says. “Let’s look after it and let’s look after each other.”Clacton is not uniquely prejudiced, nor is it afflicted by mass stupidity. You can’t blame the people here for their prevailing pessimism. Neither the Tories nor Labour haverescued coastal townslike this from their pronounced decline – nor Britain as a whole from a generation of stagnation. The anger is real: work that doesn’t pay, public services that have been stripped back, communities not invested in. The people of Clacton have concluded that if the main parties have no answers, why not bet on something else?But acrypto billionaire-funded multimillionairewith multiple jobs who blames migrants for their ills is hardly the solution. Indeed, Farage wants to double down on the very economic policies that have caused so much pain. One young man intending to vote for Farage complains about Labour attacking disability benefits. “Yeah, but they’re all trying to do that,” he says bleakly. “Everyone’s trying to do it.” The only way out is surely a politics which ends people’s resignation to decline – and offers some optimism.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Burnham the crowd-pleaser knows how to make friends, but he’ll be defined by how he makes enemies | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The prime minister’s instinct to not upset people is set against a lifelong desire to effect transformative change. The two may not sit together easily, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The prime minister’s instinct to not upset people is set against a lifelong desire to effect transformative change. The two may not sit together easily, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Andy Burnham on a visit to Alstom Transport in Derby on Tuesday, as the government launches new technical educational routes for young people.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham on a visit to Alstom Transport in Derby on Tuesday, as the government launches new technical educational routes for young people.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/PAOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham the crowd-pleaser knows how to make friends, but he’ll be defined by how he makes enemiesAndy BeckettThe prime minister’s instinct to not upset people is set against a lifelong desire to effect transformative change. The two may not sit together easilyThu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.50 EDTShareAndy Burnham has always liked to be liked. Studying at secondary school near Liverpool in the 1980s, he writes in his autobiography and manifesto,Head North, “involved me walking something of a tightrope. Because of my mum and dad’s insistence that I should aim for university, I would largely try to keep up to date with my work. But … I realised I could often make the class laugh and that won me credit with the in-crowd. It was hard to be both a good student and one of the lads.”As the new leader of a divided country, he is still trying to appeal to opposing interests while establishing his own, upbeat brand. “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity,” he said in hisfirst speech outside 10 Downing Street. After a post-Brexit decade dominated by angry rightwing politics, Labour infighting, never-ending culture wars and online acrimony, Burnham’s affable, seemingly inclusive politics has a strong initial appeal. This week, for the first time in 18 months,Labour is ahead of Reform UKin the polls. It’s possible that some voters have finally had enough of divisive politics and would like to try something different.As an insecure party, temperamentally and electorally,Labouris periodically drawn towards a politics of national unity. “New Labour is the political arm of none other than the British people as a whole,” claimed its general election manifesto in 1997, managing to sound both wildly over-confident and anxiously self-justifying. Lacking the Tories’ right to rule aura and association with deep Englishness – even though those politically priceless qualities depend on a deliberately partial reading of history – Labour tries to make its governments seem more legitimate by using patriotic, non-partisan language. Yet only its most articulate and assured leaders, such as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and perhaps now Burnham, successfully pull this off.Yet unlike Blair in 1997 and Wilson in 1964, Burnham is not launching a fresh Labour project in relatively benign economic and political times, and aiming to keep the status quo broadly intact. Instead, he is trying to rescue a two-year-old administration by promising “a new political model and a new economic model”, and “the biggest changes [in Britain] in the last 40 years”. None of these can be done, it seems reasonable to assume, without challenging many of the old order’s beneficiaries. So how is his politics of unity likely to fare once he starts making lots of enemies?Those may include shareholders of privatised utilities, wealthy owners of under-taxed homes, people who like London’s national dominance, leaders of other parties who don’t want Burnham’s “more collaborative” politics, and journalists who prefer reporting on Westminster plots and rivalries rather than the progress of reforms in the rest of the country. The instantly hostile, sometimes hysterical reaction from much of the press and most other parties to his initial, relatively modest and non-partisan policy proposals gives a hint of the fury coming his way. As Gordon Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer all painfully learned, any Labour leadership even fractionally to the left of Blair’s in any policy areawill be widely presented as areturn to the supposedly bleak 1970sor the beginning of a socialist dictatorship – even though such comparisons are dependent on crude caricatures and huge exaggerations. Many voters, across multiple parties, from Labour to the Greens to Reform UK, have been saying for years that they want Britain to be governed in a new way; but heaven help any government that dares to try.Yet Burnham’s positivity may be less naive than it seems. As mayor of Greater Manchester and a candidate in Makerfield, his can-do air attracted support far beyond Labour’s shrunken strongholds. Many voters don’t pay close attention to government policies, to all their practical implications and precisely how they will be funded. If they did, Starmer would have got more credit for the painstaking and important improvements his government made toemployment rights, for instance.But voters do notice politicians with zest. “I think this might be the best day of my life,” said Burnhamat the opening of No 10 Northin Manchester. The apparent unguardedness, and the risk that it will come back to haunt him, both break the cautious rules of British politics as they have accumulated since the 1990s. The opening paragraphs of future articles about the rise and fall of the Burnham administration already write themselves. Yet successful governments put an appealing emotional and rhetorical frame around their unavoidably diffuse and incompleteactivities, which makes these activities resonate and seem part of a bigger story. These governments, in short, are greater than the sum of their parts.Burnham saw some of the pervasive impact of Margaret Thatcher’s premiership as a politically conscious teenager. His school bus passed the entrance to a local colliery, where striking miners were slowly but surely being defeated. As a junior minister, he served in the equally pivotal Blair government. As mayor, Burnham spent nine years away from Westminster, watching from a distance as several of Blair and Thatcher’s successors quickly failed. So it’s not surprising that Burnham gives the impression of having thought quite a lot about how to be an effective prime minister. “I am under no illusions about how hard this is all going to be,”he wrote last week, “but I have a clear plan and I know how to get things done.”We’ll see. So far, his plan includes several elements – a 10-year time span, tight immigration restrictions, increased defence spending and a focus on working class and non-metropolitan Britain – familiar from Starmer’s premiership and other failed governments since Brexit. Burnham also appears to believe that less-than-revolutionary figures such as his new chancellor, John Healey, can help achieve his ambitious goal of “ending neoliberalism” in Britain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch appointments could be a cunning ploy: seeking radical ends by deceptively moderate, reassuring means. Or they could show that Burnham’s bolder ideas, developed relatively recently, are still outweighed by his instinct not to upset people. But as his year-long, often dismissed, but precisely executed leadership coup has just demonstrated, his capacity to surprise should not be underestimated.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourManchestercommentShareReuse this content

title: Dedicated followers of passion: the Kinks’ 40 greatest songs – ranked! | The Kinks | The Guardian
description: To coincide with a new exhibition in London about the Davies brothers, we rate the best of a band who brought a sociologist’s eye to hard rock, gentle pastoralia and so much in between
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: To coincide with a new exhibition in London about the Davies brothers, we rate the best of a band who brought a sociologist’s eye to hard rock, gentle pastoralia and so much in between
Content: Peter Quaife, Dave Davies, Mick Amory and Ray Davies of the Kinks in a promotional image for Sunny Afternoon, painted by BEV (Douglas Binder, Dudley Edwards and David Vaughan) in 1967.View image in fullscreenPeter Quaife, Dave Davies, Mick Amory and Ray Davies of the Kinks in a promotional image for Sunny Afternoon, painted by BEV (Douglas Binder, Dudley Edwards and David Vaughan) in 1967.RankedThe KinksDedicated followers of passion: the Kinks’ 40 greatest songs – ranked!To coincide with a new exhibition in London about the Davies brothers, we rate the best of a band who brought a sociologist’s eye to hard rock, gentle pastoralia and so much in betweenAlexis PetridisThu 30 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google40. Scattered (1993)The quality of Kinks albums declined precipitously from the late 80s: you sensed their hearts weren’t really in it. Even so,Ray Daviescouldn’t stop himself writing the occasional gem: from their final studio album Phobia, Scattered is a sweet, sad reflection on the Davies family’s complexities, powered by jangling guitars.39. Rosy Won’t You Please Come Home (1966)The decision of Davies’s older sister Rose to emigrate to Australia “devastated” him: it lurked in the background of Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire) but took centre stage on this track from Face to Face: evidently heartfelt, it twists and turns, deploying everything from pleading to mockery to secure her return.38. You Can’t Stop the Music (1975)Originally the soundtrack to a Ray Davies TV special, Soap Opera nearly broke the Kinks: some members assumed it would be their last album. There’s certainly a sense of finality to its closing track, impressive though it is: despite the title, it sounds like a eulogy for rock’n’roll, spiked with personal bitterness.View image in fullscreenRay Davies, Pete Quaife, Dave Davies and Mick Avory of the Kinks in 1965.Photograph: Chris Walter/WireImage37. Two Sisters (1967)As an example of how out of step the Kinks were with the burgeoning counterculture in 1967, the harpsichord-led Two Sisters is hard to beat. Loving domesticity and parenthood trumps free-spirited bohemia: formerly jealous of her unencumbered sibling, the married sister ends the song delightedly running “round the house with her curlers on”.36. I Go to Sleep (1965)Never released by the Kinks – a demo version is on the deluxe version of Kinda Kinks – the fraught ballad I Go to Sleep was the most sophisticated song Ray Davies had written by this time. The most famous cover is by the Pretenders, but the best is the 1967 version byGerman singer Marion Maerz: lushly orchestrated, echo-laden, girl group-adjacent, magnificent.35. Lavender Lane (1971)Belatedly excavated for the 2013 deluxe edition of Muswell Hillbillies, Lavender Lane’s failure to make the cut in 1971 seems baffling. It’s fantastic, a broadside against what would now be called gentrification that pivots between nostalgic sadness and fury, aimed at “the old school tie and all the la-di-do-dahs”.34. I’m Not Like Everybody Else (1966)In the hands of the Chocolate Watchband, who covered it in 1968, I’m Not Like Everybody Else is a classic screw-you garage band sneer. The Kinks’ original has a menacing power, but feels more complicated and personal, its emotional temperature shifting from defiant to faintly distraught.33. Living on a Thin Line (1984)From the largely ho-hum Word of Mouth, this is an atmospheric, ominous and pessimistic survey of Thatcher’s Britain from the pen of Dave Davies – “there’s no England now,” he dolefully concludes – subsequently rescued from obscurity and brought to the wider audience it deserved by its inclusion on the soundtrack of The Sopranos.32. (Wish I Could Fly Like) Superman (1979)At their height of Britpop, it was common to compare Damon Albarn’s brand of social satire to that of Ray Davies, a fairly obvious influence. More bizarre is how much this impressive single from 1979’s Low Budget sounded like Blur’s Girls and Boys: disco beat, slashing guitars, mannered Cockney vocals.View image in fullscreenThe Kinks on British TV in 1967.Photograph: ITV/Rex Features31. Too Much on My Mind (1966)Easy to overlook amid the waspish character studies and social satires of Face to Face – the Kinks’ first entirely superb album – Too Much on My Mind feels like Ray Davies’s most personal song of the era: a plaintive depiction of a man teetering on the verge of a breakdown. Understated, but quietly devastating.30. Till the End of the Day (1965)The last of the Kinks’ riff-heavy garage rock anthems – although the fantastic She’s Got Everything belatedly slipped out as a B-side in 1968 – is more sophisticated than its predecessors: check the harmony vocals. But it’s just as thrilling, and – curiously for the Kinks – snottily optimistic in tone. But if you flipped the single over …29. Where Have All the Good Times Gone? (1965)… you got the first – but definitely not the last – example of Ray Davies in contrarian mode. The 60s are fully swinging, the Kinks are at the centre of the action, and yet he’s riven with angst, complaining that things ain’t what they used to be, suggesting his parents had it better.28. This Time Tomorrow (1970)Not all of Davies’s scabrous music business satire Lola Vs Powerman and the Moneygoround Pt 1 has aged well, but This Time Tomorrow still rings out: detached from the album’s concept, it ceases to be a song about touring, and instead becomes a hugely affecting study of a life turned aimless.27. Death of a Clown (1967)Dave Davies’s aborted late 60s solo album was doomed by the Kinks’ gradually declining commercial fortunes rather than a lack of strong material, evidenced by Death of a Clown, rhythmically jaunty but hauntingly eerie: a compelling solo hit that wound up on 1967’s Something Else By the Kinks.26. Sitting in My Hotel (1972)Songs in which rock stars complain about life on the road seldom elicit much sympathy from the listener – there are, far, far worse jobs, after all – but Sitting in My Hotel is among the few exceptions: a heartbreaking piano ballad that perfectly expresses a sense of homesick dislocation.25. Mr Pleasant (1967)Sometimes, Ray Davies could sound like a grumpy reactionary, sometimes like a revolutionary, seething with class rage. It isn’t entirely clear what Mr Pleasant has done to incur Davies’s wrath, beyond being middle class, but his downfall is brilliantly, wittily depicted, to a jolly music hall-inspired backing. The evident delight in Davies’s voice is quite unsettling.24. Sweet Lady Genevieve (1973)As Ray Davies’s theatrical ambitions got more elaborate, his songwriting genius seemed to flicker more fitfully: the Kinks’ 70s concept albums can be a longwinded slog. But persevere and you’re occasionally rewarded with a song like the gorgeous Sweet Lady Genevieve, entirely up to the standards he’d set himself. Perhaps the Kinks’ great lost classic.23. 20th Century Man (1971)It isn’t entirely clear if the character in 20th Century Man is a character, or an expression of Ray Davies’s increasing alienation and the precarious state of his mental health. “I don’t want to be here,” it offers. He would attempt suicide two years later. Ironically, the music that misery is set to is utterly charming.22. Victoria (1969)Victoria deals in the sort of ambiguity that had become one of Davies’s most striking trademarks. Is it a nostalgic celebration of a bygone era, or a biting satire on empire? Probably both. Whatever it is, it’s a great song, blessed with a wonderful middle eight and an exultant brass arrangement.21. See My Friends (1965)Depending on who you believe, the sound ofSee My Friendswas either inspired by a brief stopover in Mumbai, or the raga-influenced playing of folk guitarist Jon Mark. Either way, it was a hugely innovative pop single, both for its droning sound and its (admittedly oblique) lyrical treatment of homosexuality.20. Come Dancing (1983)The Kinks’ only UK hit in the final22 yearsof their career concerned their fraught origin story – the death of Ray Davies’s sister Rene in a dancehall, the same day she gave him his first guitar – and featured a sound that recalled their mid-60s hits: the synth hasn’t dated well, but the song itself is sweet, sad nostalgia.View image in fullscreenRay Davies in 1965.Photograph: David Magnus/Rex Features19. Big Black Smoke (1966)Sixties London not as the swinging epicentre of the world, but a dark, forbidding nightmare, ready to swallow the unwary, including the song’s increasingly speed-addled protagonist. Ferociously performed and emotionally complex, as empathy for the girl’s frantic mother battles it out with a certain native Londoner’s relish at her grim fate.18. Better Things (1981)The Kinks’ unexpected early 80s elevation into hard-rocking, arena-packing stars in the US sailed over British audiences’ heads. If their albums from that era aren’t up to 60s standards, they have their moments, of which Better Things’ unexpectedly optimistic – and richly melodic – reflection on a collapsing marriage is the most stellar.17. Celluloid Heroes (1972)Kinks fans can argue all night over whether 1972’s Everybody’s in Show-Biz represents their last soup-to-nuts classic album. Less contentious is how great its highlights are, as evidenced by Celluloid Heroes, an impossibly weary rumination on celebrity and posthumous reputation, provoked by a visit to Hollywood Boulevard’s Walk of Fame.16. Dead End Street (1966)Outside of the world of folk, mid-60s British pop wasn’t big on social realism or protest, which made Dead End Street’s depiction of working-class poverty, complete with mournful french horn and shouted chorus, all the more striking. It had more in common with contemporary TV dramas than it did the rest of the charts.15. Shangri-La (1969)Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire) was a much thornier exploration of Britishness than the preceding year’s The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society. The lengthy, episodic Shangri-La’s melody barely conceals a lyric livid about conformity, limited aspirations and social mobility, a country “too scared to complain”.14. Picture Book (1968)It’s hard to pick out individual tracks from The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society – it works best taken as a whole – but Picture Book’s interrogation of memory (“those days when you were happy, a long time ago”) is particularly great: sentimental but irreverent, and genuinely affecting.13. Oklahoma USA (1971)Muswell Hillbillies is a curious, fascinating album, packed with great songs drenched in Americana but lyrically rooted in north London. Oklahoma USA is its highlight: its tune among Ray Davies’s prettiest, the lyrics both wistful and sharp – its dreams of a more glamorous existence in Oklahoma are fuelled by the Hollywood musical rather than reality of life there.12. Lola (1970)The subject of some controversy in recent years, Lola’s depiction of a brief, confused dalliance with a trans woman was more or less uncharted territory for pop in 1970, a topic no one other than Lou Reed had ventured to touch. It seemed to energise Ray Davies, pulling one of his greatest tunes out of him.11. David Watts (1967)Partly inspired by the Kinks’ encounter with a gay Midlands promoter, this story of schoolboy rivalry is liberally sprinkled with homoeroticism. Does the narrator envy Watts’s wealth and accomplishments or is his fascination sparked more by Watts’s lack of interest in girls? The music fits perfectly: relentless, agitated, but deliberately mannered.10. Dedicated Follower of Fashion (1966)The Kinks, Marianne Faithfull subsequently opined, were “creepy and silent” and seemed “fearful of everyone”. Perhaps Ray Davies was taking notes, which would explain how perfectly he skewered the affectations of 60s hipsters here. Best moment: when the lyric slips into contemporary journalese: “This pleasure-seeking individual always looks his best.”View image in fullscreenThe Davies brothers on stage in the US in 1975.Photograph: Stephen Morley/Redferns9. God’s Children (1971)If you want an example of Ray Davies’s contrarian nature, consider God’s Children. Easily one of his finest early 70s songs – spellbinding melody, intriguing lyrics about the advance of technology – and he stuck it on the soundtrack to a sex comedy about a man rendered irresistible to women after a penis transplant.8. A Well Respected Man (1965)The song that introduced a sharp brand of social satire into 60s British pop and inspired a legion of contemporary imitators – Semi-Detatched Suburban Mr James, et al. But no one else was as nuanced a lyricist as Ray Davies: listen to the verse about the protagonist’s ghastly mother, and you can virtuallyseeher.7. You Really Got Me (1964)After 60 plus years, You Really Got Me is so familiar, it’s hard to picture the jolt it must have delivered in the summer of 1964, its distorted riff, unhinged guitar solo and Ray Davies’s vocal – alternately impassioned and slightly camp – sounding nothing like anything British pop had thus far produced. It still rocks.6. All Day and All of the Night (1964)That rarest of things: an attempt to follow up a huge hit with something similar that improves on the original. Cut from the same cloth as You Really Got Me, it succeeds by dialling everything up: it’s tougher, heavier, more exhilarating, and the mid-chorus key change is a masterstroke.5. The Village Green Preservation Society (1968)The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society flopped on release: perhaps a rock band singing in praise of the George cross and virginity was too confusing amid 1968’s revolutionary tumult. It was correctly reassessed as their masterpiece. The opening track demonstrates Davies’s songwriting firing on all cylinders: funny, sharp, provocative, warm.4. Sunny Afternoon (1966)How good a writer was Ray Davies at his zenith? Good enough to draw a pen portrait of a dissipated, abusive aristocrat and somehow manage to elicit a sense of empathy from the listener, helped by the irresistible melody and the song’s timelessness: its story could have been written in the 1920s but it’s not a nostalgic pastiche.3. Autumn Almanac (1967)At the close of the summer of love, Ray Davies was to be found lovingly hymning the mundane life of a suburban gardener. Far more than a mere dry run for The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society, Autumn Almanac is a lovely song: no snark or cynicism, just warmth and empathy.2. Days (1968)That Days failed to make the UK Top 10 tells you everything about the Kinks’ waning commercial fortunes and nothing about the song itself. In a just world, anything blessed with a tune this beautiful, so suffused with equal part sadness and reflective warmth, would have been No 1 for weeks. A masterpiece.1. Waterloo Sunset (1967)Critic Robert Christgau called Waterloo Sunset “the most beautiful song in the English language”: certainly it’s among the greatest singles of the 60s, quite possibly one of the greatest pop songs of all time and a remarkable example of the songwriter’s art. On top of an extraordinarily beautiful melody, the lyrics are perfectly balanced between love for London, affection for the lovers meeting outside Waterloo Station and aching sadness: ever the outsider, Davies looks on at it all from a distance, and complains about the cold. It’s his best song, but it isn’t head-and-shoulders over everything else he wrote, which says a great deal about his brilliance.The Kinks: Brothers, by Ray Davies, Dave Davies and Christian Furr, is at the Gibson Garage, London, until 6 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsThe KinksRankedPop and rockRay DaviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I had a really crippling break’: how author Michael Thomas lost 20 years to mania, depression and more | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: In 2006 the novel Man Gone Down made Thomas famous and won him a €100,000 prize. He expected to produce a follow-up within a year – but life had other plans
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: In 2006 the novel Man Gone Down made Thomas famous and won him a €100,000 prize. He expected to produce a follow-up within a year – but life had other plans
Content: ‘I could be living in my car’ … Michael Thomas.Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I could be living in my car’ … Michael Thomas.Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianAutobiography and memoirInterview‘I had a really crippling break’: how author Michael Thomas lost 20 years to mania, depression and moreSteve RoseIn 2006 the novel Man Gone Down made Thomas famous and won him a €100,000 prize. He expected to produce a follow-up within a year – but life had other plansThu 30 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt should be some kind of happy ending when, after years of poverty and graft, an aspiring writer publishes their debut novel and it is greeted with acclaim and awards – but that’s not how it happened for Michael Thomas. His 2006 novel Man Gone Down seemed to augur the arrival of a powerful new literary voice, the beginning of a brilliant career. He featured on the cover of the New York Times Book Review, hewon the €100,000 Dublin literary award– one of the most generous prizes in the book world – and he was promoted to assistant professor at Hunter College, New York, where he taught creative writing. But a follow-up would not arrive until now, 20 years later. Thomas’s new memoir, The Broken King, goes some way to explaining what happened in between. It also confirms his formidable talent.The Broken King is an extraordinary read – deeply personal and intimate, but also expansive and free-ranging, taking in everything from TS Eliot (the title comes from Eliot’s poemLittle Gidding) to James Baldwin, Brazilian football and the Rolling Stones. Thomas’s story runs through what he describes as a “perfect storm of conditions”: poverty, parental abandonment, racism, alcoholism, sexual violence, self-sabotage and mental illness. It would be tempting to classify it as some kind of misery memoir, but it is neither bleak nor generic – Thomas is simply too good a writer for that. Reviews in the US have been glowing: “Thomas has rendered beautifully an excruciating existence from which it is impossible to turn away,” raved the author Thomas Chatterton Williamsin the New York Times.Thomas did not “enjoy” literary success first time round. In fact, it contributed to his breakdown. Receiving the Dublin literary award did not make him think, “I am a great author,” he tells me via video call. His reaction was more relief that he could pay off some of his debts: “We were two months behind on our mortgage.” Nor did he revel in the attention: “When I started getting critical acclaim and showing up on the cover of things, I couldn’t feel it. And I kept trying to tell people that I couldn’t feel it, and they thought it was being smug or humble. I was really in a year-long descent.”View image in fullscreenThomas after winning the Impac Dublin literary award in 2009.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyHe’s sitting in his office at Hunter College. Behind him are books, artefacts, an acoustic guitar and a commanding view over Manhattan. “It’s in a state of construction. I’m making a floating birch wall over here,” he apologises, pointing off-camera. He speaks gently, with a musical lilt, and he looks much younger than his 58 years – partly because he’s as athletic as he is artistic. He enjoys exercise and physical labour, such as house-building and carpentry, as much as he does teaching and writing. To him, there’s nothing contradictory about “thinking of the poetry I want to write while doing an intense set of deadlifts”.In late 2007, less than a year after Man Gone Down was published, Thomas was planning his next step. “I had a proposal, six pages, and it was neat and clean and tidy. I gave it to my editor; I had a meeting with the publisher. They said: ‘Great, go off and do your thing.’ I was glib about it, like: ‘Yeah, I’ll knock this out in six months to a year. I can write about mental illness’ – not mine.” He pauses to laugh at the irony. “My father’s, and my brother’s. And then I had a break, a really crippling break.”double quotation markI hope this doesn’t seem insensitive: the book is autistic. It’s really just a study of someone with level-one autismPromoting his book, travelling, doing talks; trying to write, teach, read, parent; procrastinating, not sleeping well, drinking too much coffee, he became what he now characterises as “short-cycling manic depressive”. “I would have an ‘illumination’ for two hours, and then I wouldn’t have time to record it and I’d tumble into a depressive state. And I could have multiple states within a few days, and so the brilliant idea would become mundane or esoteric or fragmented, almost as though I was getting a narrative from a stranger.”Events came to a head when he was alone in Kansas City on his book tour, “seeing dragons and demons and all kinds of things”. Waiting to board a flight home, he had a breakdown at the airport. “I knew I was insane,” he writes. When his wife takes him to a psychiatric hospital back in New York, he tells the doctor: “It’s a curious thing, the phrase ‘out of your mind’ … My trouble now is that I’m in a way, in part, deep in it. More than I’ve ever been. It’s not a good environment, doctor.”As with the rest of the book, Thomas catalogues these events and experiences in uncanny, almost photographic detail, but the narrative also pans out across his memories and anxieties, and his vast cultural hinterland. He almost apologises for The Broken King’s expansiveness: “Part of it was realising how personal it was going to be, and trying to make it more intricate to really distance myself from the work.”Man Gone Down was a loosely fictionalised account of a small section of Thomas’s life, when he was in his 30s, desperately trying to keep his head above water, financially and psychically, and hold on to his marriage and his three young children. The Broken King expands on that narrative considerably, particularly Thomas’s male relationships: with his father (who abandoned the family when Thomas was eight, struggled with depression, drank heavily, and at times lived in his car); his older brother (who steals from his family and others, and is in and out of prison); and his two sons (he also has a daughter), whom he worries are destined to extend the lineage of troubled men.View image in fullscreenAs a kid Thomas struggled to fit in.Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianThere’s a moment halfway through the book when the penny almost drops: an occupational therapist diagnoses his second son, Miles, with a “non-specific cognitive disorder”, and even suggests: “Like father, like son.” That took him by “complete surprise”, Thomas says, but he did not act on it until much later. Until that point he had attributed his difficulties in life to all manner of factors – “race, class, artistic temperament, and just so many other things. Models from books and films and music, and just this kind of alienation and estrangement … but no, not neurodivergence.” As a child he was diagnosed with dyslexia, ADHD and other conditions, but it wasn’t until adulthood that it was defined as level 1 autism. As such, The Broken King is, among other things, a chronicle of neurodivergence from the inside. “I hope this doesn’t seem insensitive: the book is autistic,” Thomas says. “It’s really just a study of someone with level-one autism trying to tell a story.”double quotation markWe grew up in public housing with a single mom believing education was the great equaliser, and she just busted her assThomas’s story raises all kinds of questions about the relationship between neurodivergence and artistic talent, not to mention nature and nurture. How to square his diagnosis with other traumatic elements of his upbringing: the poverty, the alcoholism, the abandonment? Racism also plays a part. His great-grandfather was born enslaved, in Virginia, he tells me. He remembers his great-grandmother when he was a child – a living connection to that time. He shows me a photograph of his mother in Virginia, in 1951. She is looking at a burnt cross that was put up outside her high school. She migrated north to Boston, where she met his father, but largely raised him and his two older siblings singlehandedly. “We grew up in public housing with a single mom believing education was the great equaliser, and she just busted her ass.”As a kid Thomas struggled to fit in, socially as well as racially (he also has Irish and Native American ancestry). “I could read at an early age and could do my brother’s homework, but I couldn’t tie my shoes.” He connected with Black role models – Malcolm X, Martin Luther King, Stokely Carmichael, Frederick Douglass – but he also loved the Beatles and Bob Dylan and Greek mythology. “I was called an Oreo [Black on the outside, white on the inside, like the cookie], or a ‘honky nigger’ or ‘not really Black’.”At the same time, Thomas writes, “white people were dangerous because they were extreme. They tried to either aid or block my passage into their segregated world.Benevolentwhites didn’t think I was Black. Whatever native intelligence I possessed had nothing to do with my race. Blackness was something they were helping me overcome.” Meanwhile, he was “subject to most of the chronic and systemic, acute and arbitrary violence the republic or the individual believed I deserved”.View image in fullscreen‘I don’t want the things that happened to me to happen to my kids.’Photograph: Kacey Jeffers/The GuardianThomas’s marriage to a relatively wealthy white woman complicates matters further, in terms of both fitting in with his white in-laws and raising mixed-race children. Their experience of the world will certainly be different from his, he says. “Just as my mother didn’t want her experience to be mine, I don’t want the things that happened to me to happen to my kids. I’m not worried about them ‘losing their Blackness’, though. They get to define who they are.” All of Black culture is theirs, he says, as is all of every other culture – as it was for him, as it should be for everyone.There is another challenging, complicating element to Thomas’s story: early on in the book he discloses that he was raped when he was seven years old. He doesn’t go into detail about the incident – except to say it happened when he was at a day camp in Boston. He didn’t tell anyone at the time; in fact, he strove to hide the incident from his parents, even burning his clothes afterwards. “I knew my pain would kill them,” he writes. He is open about how the incident warped his life. “Growing into a young man I was distant, wayward, wild, drunk. I could be cruel. I’d lie to everyone I knew.” He struggled with self-harm, alcoholism, depression, physical and emotional intimacy – “I lived in a perpetual post-trauma.” He told his future wife in his 20s after he was re-traumatised reading a passage about rape in a Baldwin novel. As soon as he finished reading it he went into a fever, was trapped in his apartment for days hallucinating, and was eventually hospitalised with pneumonia. As soon as he recovered, a dinner party conversation about sex caused him to shut down and not speak for three days.In this context, I hesitate to even bring the incident up. Thomas is comfortable talking about it right now, he says, but when he has told friends about it, he has often regretted it.“It didn’t bring any clarity to me and it hurt them,” he explains. “Like it was giving them too much to deal with. And watching people over the years or just over the weeks, wondering how to be with me and be with that information, they had to treat me differently.” These things can become a lens through which to judge others’ actions and behaviours, he suggests. You could say the same of race, or neurodivergence, or gender, or any number of factors.double quotation markI’m becoming acutely aware of my strangeness, but not self-conscious about it, or apologetic or aggressiveI was feeling apprehensive about interviewing Thomas, I tell him, given how honestly and openly he has written about his life. He felt the same, he admits, having not been in the public eye for decades, though he has been relaxed and talkative throughout our 90-minute conversation, which digresses at times into chat about sports teams or our favourite Beatles albums. Is there a worry, though, given how his last experience of literary success contributed to his breakdown, that the same thing could happen this time around?He seems less worried about it. A lot has happened in the intervening two decades. He got divorced in 2014, which inevitably affected his children. His mother died from Covid in 2020 (his next book will be about her life, he says). His eldest son, Alex, is now 30, and a social worker. His other son, Miles, is 27 and handling his own neurodivergence very differently from how Thomas did. “He doesn’t have as much invested in controlling the conventional world. He’s not angry.” Thomas also has an eight-year-old son with a new partner. He has no idea how he has been as a father, he says: “Sometimes I think I intensified some of the suffering … sometimes I feel like I gave them a lot … sometimes I just think I became my father with privilege and safety nets. Without growing up privilege-adjacent, and then having literary and academic success and a tenured position, and people saving my bacon over the years, I could be living in my car right now.”Lena Dunham on going to rehab: ‘It was like the first day of college, except many of the people had a problem with heroin’Read moreIn general, at present, it feels as if he has found some stability. “I’m trying to figure it out through Bowie right now,” he says, jokingly, quoting lines from Changes: “‘I turned myself to face me, but I never caught a glimpse …’ I’m becoming acutely aware of my strangeness, but not self-conscious about it, or apologetic or aggressive.”Is that liberating? “It calms some of the noise,” he replies. “This might sound cheesy: I don’t know if I’m OK with myself, but I think I’m starting to accept myself. I’m also about to turn 59, so I don’t have that younger man’s piss and vinegar. I think I’m a little more reflective and less impulsive. I don’t have the anger I used to have. I don’t have the fear I used to have – at least in this moment. I know it can come again. I feel incredibly lucid. There’s been a lot of loss in the last decade, so … today I feel OK.”The Broken King by Michael Thomas is published by Summit (£16.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com.
