title: ‘People say I’m pouring Coca-Cola into fine malt whisky’: why is the National Theatre shaking up Sophocles? | Stage | The Guardian
description: In a bold new production starring Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss, the NT is fusing Sophocles and Ingmar Bergman. So what can two stories written 23 centuries apart tell us about how we live today?
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: In a bold new production starring Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss, the NT is fusing Sophocles and Ingmar Bergman. So what can two stories written 23 centuries apart tell us about how we live today?
Content: ‘Bergman is a north star for me’ … Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann in the film that inspired Electra/Persona.View image in fullscreen‘Bergman is a north star for me’ … Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann in the film that inspired Electra/Persona.Stage‘People say I’m pouring Coca-Cola into fine malt whisky’: why is the National Theatre shaking up Sophocles?In a bold new production starring Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss, the NT is fusing Sophocles and Ingmar Bergman. So what can two stories written 23 centuries apart tell us about how we live today?Mark LawsonThu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn around 420BC, Sophocles staged Electra, in which the title character avenges the murder of her father by her mother, Clytemnestra. In 1966, Swedish film director Ingmar Bergman premieredPersona, in which a psychiatric nurse, Alma, is caring for Elisabeth, an actor who has suffered a breakdown while playing Electra. These two dramas, written 23 centuries apart, are now sharing the stage in an alluring new National Theatre production.InElectra/Persona, director Benedict Andrews has paired the stories before and after the interval, linked by a stunning coup de theatre at the end of the first half. “Persona is a pinnacle of modernist cinema and Bergman is a north star for me,” says Andrews. “I’ve long been fascinated by the impossibility – in a good way – of staging Persona, because it is so much about the camera and the silence and the closeup: the face as a terrain. And I was always fascinated by why Bergman chose to have Elisabeth break down while playing Electra, so I wanted to put them together. I think it’s become clear in rehearsal that the whole evening is one cycle of grief.”double quotation markWe joke about having put the writer on a trawler back to IcelandEarly on, Andrews (Australian-born, Iceland-resident and identifying as “Ice-Stralian”) had the idea that Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss would alternate the roles of Electra and Clytemnestra in Electra, and Elisabeth and Alma in Persona; whoever plays Electra in the first half reappears as Elisabeth, and Clytemnestra reappears as Alma. The original plan was for Blanchett and Hoss to toss a coin on stage at the start of the evening but Tom Stoppard’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, in which a coin lands heads92 times in succession, made this strategy risky.View image in fullscreen‘They are astonishing actresses’ … Blanchett, left, and Hoss.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty Images“Also,” says Andrews, “I said to Cate and Nina, ‘To play your best game do you need to wake up in the morning and study your Electra or Persona text?’ And they said maybe. In the end, they will have a schedule and swap night by night but the audience won’t know who’s playing who until the first one walks in.” And if I say to the box office that I’ve seen one combination and want to see the other, they won’t tell me when? Andrews pauses. “No.”Although he is known for staging radical new versions of classics – including Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchardat the Donmar Warehouse in 2024, and Tennessee Williams’ A Streetcar Named Desire on a rotating setat the Young Vic in 2014– Electra/Persona is a bold project. Another writer-director, Alan Ayckbourn, once said that, while directing, he found himself cursing what the writer had given him to do. Did Andrews understand what it would be like effectively having to rehearse two plays twice each to prepare the various permutations?“Yeah. Long rehearsal days,” he sighs with a laugh. “Yesterday, unusually, we stayed in Electra all day but I still did an hour on Persona at the end. I think it’s really important to do both every day. Although they require very different energies. It’s not a double-bill; it’s onehingedwork. There are perforations from Bergman in the first half and from Sophocles in the second half.”By this stage, Andrews considers himself only a director: “We have this joke with the cast about there having been a writer. We call him Dominic. He was chained to a table for two weeks here to do rewrites but now we’ve put him on a trawler back to Iceland.”View image in fullscreen‘We are watching American imperialism fall apart’ … Andrews.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianI recently saw a hit show in which the understudy was on – they did an impersonation of the absent performer, which is standard in the circumstances. But will Blanchett and Hoss have a different interaction? “Absolutely. They are two actresses who are equally astonishing but play their instruments differently. Cate and Nina are good mates and had donethe film Tár, in which Nina plays Cate’s wife. So I thought it would be great to do something with them. They don’t look the same but there’s an echo between them: they could be sisters. In rehearsal, you see them thinking, ‘Oh, they did that in that bit? Do I take that or do my own interpretation?’ We’re searching for something in which they each play the logic of the scene, but it may come out in different ways.”When I tell him that his Donmar Warehouse Cherry Orchard was completely different the two times I saw it, he nods enthusiastically, even though some directors would greet this with a public inquiry. “Good!” he says. “I saw the [romantic rejection] scene between Lopakhin and Varya dozens of times in rehearsal and then performance – and it was different each time. And I encourage that because, in the end, you want the truth of that moment played each night. As a director, you have set up a perpetuum mobile that the actors can continue to develop.”Andrews is having an Ancient Greek period, his previous show being a version in Iceland of Aeschylus’s The Oresteia, which shares characters with Electra including Clytemnestra, Orestes and Electra herself. So is there a big overlap between his back-to-back Greek tragedies? “Huge. I moved bits across between the two shows. I spent the bulk of last year doing my text for The Oresteia. Then there was a gap before rehearsals began – for it to be translated into Icelandic – in which I wrote Electra/Persona. Which I hadn’t expected to be on so quickly. I hadn’t expected to be living with this crazy fucking family for so long!”View image in fullscreen‘I hadn’t expected to be living with this crazy family for so long!’ … Andrews’ Oresteia at the National Theatre, Reyjavik.Photograph: Owen FieneBoth shows are chamber pieces – five actors in Reykjavik, four in London – so apart from the role-swapping in Electra/Persona, there is also role-play, in which the back stories of off-stage characters are acted out: “It’s sometimes something like a Gestalttherapy game where you play your oppressor. And ‘persona’is the word for masks, for the roles we play. The king and the judge put on those robes and play those roles. How does theatre critique all these power relationships? But, in another way, how does theatre allow us to interrogate all those roles we play in our own lives, our psyche and our dream lives?”From the meeting room at the National Theatre where we talk, it’s a short walk to Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey at the BFI Southbank or to Simon Stone’sThe Oresteia at The Bridge. If the descendants of the Ancient Greek writers were on royalties, they would all have private jets. “Yes! I think they’re coming back at the moment because, in these times of big political and moral crisis, we need them. The reason we are digging in this Greek rubble and soil is that these plays were made in an imperial warring empire, that was first triumphant and then later broke apart. And we are watching that with American imperialism now.double quotation markI’ve worked a lot in Germany where radical rethinking is what the director does“We grew up with the idea that the US – our Rome, our Athens – was a military might but also a cultural might. And it’s breaking apart. So we go back to a culture that lived through wars but also gave us philosophy and theatre and gave Freud the Oedipus myth for unpacking a family. And these plays should also make us question notions of law and justice.”There is an increasingly strong Australian directorial presence in London. As well as Stone, whose Oresteia follows his Phaedra and The Lady From The Sea, Kip Williams has frequently worked in the city: recently on The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dracula, andThe Maids. Does Andrews have a WhatsApp group or reunion barbecues with his fellow expats? “Not really. But Kip was my assistant director. Simon acted in a production of mine, rotating in a glass box in Whose Afraid of Virginia Woolf? We all know each other and have collaborators that we share.”Andrews, Stone and Williams all visually or structurally disrupt classic texts – is that an Australian thing? A sort of textual anticolonialism or republicanism? “When I did my first Three Sisters in Sydney, the [Chekhov] tradition was still lace and linen. I got letters saying you’ve taken Coca-Cola and poured it into a vat of fine malt whisky. Barrie Kosky wasdoing something similarand we possibly were a battering ram against the conservatism of Australian state theatre then. But I’d worked a lot in Germany, where radical rethinking is what the director does, so it never made sense to me to be ‘faithful’ to classics. What does that even mean? I don’t think of it as disrupting classics. I’m trying to access the mythic power in the piece; X-ray the inner meaning.”Electra/Persona is atthe National Theatre, London, from 19 August to 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreCate BlanchettNational TheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra’: why cinema loves the cello | Movies | The Guardian
description: From Audrey Hepburn to Pedro Pascal, cellists have become a movie shorthand for sensitivity, intensity and emotional depth. But why has Hollywood turned one orchestral instrument into a character in its own right?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Audrey Hepburn to Pedro Pascal, cellists have become a movie shorthand for sensitivity, intensity and emotional depth. But why has Hollywood turned one orchestral instrument into a character in its own right?
Content: Take a bow … Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenTake a bow … Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!Photograph: Album/AlamyMovies‘It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra’: why cinema loves the celloFrom Audrey Hepburn to Pedro Pascal, cellists have become a movie shorthand for sensitivity, intensity and emotional depth. But why has Hollywood turned one orchestral instrument into a character in its own right?Jonathan WellsThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a throwaway line in 2012’s The Avengers, after a character’s death, when his partner is alluded to. “There was a cellist, I think,” muses Robert Downey Jr’s Tony Stark. It’s a spot of pathos amid the punch-ups – but also rather telling. Because when even a superhero blockbuster reaches for the cello, you know the instrument is carrying more than just a melody.Earlier this month,a trailer droppedfor the upcoming Pedro Pascal drama Behemoth!, in which he plays a celebrated cellist returning to Hollywood to score films. Real-life cellist and film composer Hildur Guðnadóttir says the instrument “is definitely having a moment right now. But it’s always been present.”View image in fullscreenAudrey Hepburn in Love in the Afternoon.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIt’s true. And this cinematic love affair first found its rhythm almost 70 years ago, whenAudrey Hepburnplayed a witty young cellist in Love in the Afternoon. In the decades since, the instrument has become a marker for a certain type of character: cultured, intense, romantic, haunted. Think Alan Rickman in Truly, Madly, Deeply – or the titular cellist in the 1996 Czech drama Kolya, which won the Academy Award for best foreign language film. Even Woody Allen toyed with the stereotype; in Annie Hall, Carol Kane’s leftwing, liberal intellectual played the cello in a deleted scene.But why, out of every option in the orchestra, did the cello become the instrument of introspection? “It’s the cliche, but it’s probably because the cello comes closest to the human vocal range,” says Guðnadóttir. “It has this ability to play around with notes, too, like human intonation. Press a note on a keyboard and it’s straightforward, definitive. The cello – like our voices – can play with this intonation for expression.”Put an actor in a scene playing the cello, then, and they can deliver dialogue without words. Guðnadóttir says the only other instrument with this human timbre and “fluidity of intonation” is the bass clarinet. But you’re unlikely to see a protagonist reaching for one – nor a prestige biopic being made of a famous bass clarinettist. In fact, the cello has cornered the market on tragic orchestral stories – perhaps most notably in the Emily Watson-starring Hilary and Jackie.“That film, the story of cellist Jacqueline du Pré, is the cello film that has stuck with me most,” says Guðnadóttir. And it’s not the only cellist biopic to reach the screen. In 2009’s The Soloist,Jamie Foxxwas cast as musician Nathaniel Ayers, but the narrative was restrung, swapping his primary instrument – the double bass – for the cello.View image in fullscreenSuite soul … Emily Watson as Jacqueline du Pré in Hilary and Jackie.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyYou can see why. Not only does the cello have that uncannily human register, it’s also visually dynamic. A cellist’s bow strokes are physical and expressive, and the performer’s face is rarely obscured – making it a perfect screen partner.It’s probably why cellists tend to be the beating heart of musical dramas. Guðnadóttir also scored Cate Blanchett’s tour-de-force Tár, in which a cellist becomes the catalyst for the drama. Christopher Walken’s cellist, struggling with Parkinson’s, is the centrepiece of 2012’s A Late Quartet, and Dermot Mulroney (a real-life cellist who played on the scores of multiple Mission: Impossible films) frequently guest-starred in Prime Video series Mozart in the Jungle.View image in fullscreenHeartstrings … Jamie Foxx in The Soloist (2009).Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarBut cellist characters are not confined to musical dramas. The cello’s emotional shorthand has been transcribed across almost every genre: from Chloë Grace Moretz in sci-fi romance If I Stay, to Maryam d’Abo in 007 adventure The Living Daylights, to cellist love interests in sitcoms from Frasier to New Girl. And then there’s the darker side of the cello, whether channelled by Michelle Pfeiffer in supernatural thriller What Lies Beneath, Uma Thurman in neo-noir Jennifer 8 or Jenna Ortega in Netflix’s smash series Wednesday.“There is a gothic connection to the cello,” says Guðnadóttir, who won her Oscar for scoring Joker, a soundtrack that features the instrument prominently, with its neck being “choked”. “When it’s played in an ugly way – because we yearn for it to be this beautiful instrument – it feels uncomfortable.”Director Richard Shepard took that darker side one step further in 2018 with The Perfection, a horror set inside a prestigious music academy. When choosing the instrument his two leads would play, he wanted something both sinister and sensual.“I remember growing up on the Upper West Side of New York City, near Lincoln Center,” he says, “and seeing these young cellists on the subway, lugging these huge cases. It stuck with me. How big it is. How much effort it takes to not only play it, but just move it. When writing The Perfection, we felt that physicality could make a statement. It’s sexy. It’s a sexy instrument.”The film-makers behind the Allison Williams-starring horror film were determined to make the cello playing as convincing as the scares. “It was really hard work,” says Shepard, “but I’m proud there are only two shots of musicians’ hands rather than actors’ hands in the entire film.”View image in fullscreenHigh-toned … Alan Rickman in Truly, Madly, Deeply (1990).Photograph: BBC/AllstarThe cello is an instrument actors can’t bluff their way through – it’s harder to fake than hiding your hands behind a piano or overdubbing a singing voice. Ortega trained for Wednesday and earned Golden Globe and Emmy nominations. Watson trained for Hilary and Jackie and got an Oscar nod. Pascal recently told Vanity Fair that taking on the cello was “literally the hardest, hardest, hardest thing I’ve ever had to learn to do.” If he’s angling for awards, there are few better bets than a deep, introspective stringsman.And that perception extends beyond the screen. David Cohen, the principal cellist of the London Symphony Orchestra, says that “there’s definitely a stereotype that cellists are the orchestra’s empaths – warm, thoughtful and just a little bit intense. I’m not sure it’s entirely true, but it’s amusing that film-makers so often cast cellists as the emotionally intelligent ones. You rarely see the villain saying: ‘Just let me finish my Bach Suite …’”Cohen adds that the cello’s versatility often shapes the characters written around it. “It can sound noble, lonely, hopeful or quietly heroic – often within the same phrase,” he says. “It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra. And, because it has the depth to suggest sadness without wallowing in it, the cello is also film music’s favourite therapist.”Catherine Warner is a music therapy practitioner who has long watched the cello play its introspective, insular part on film. But she also points to the instrument’s role in memorable cinematic dialogues. In The Witches of Eastwick, a devilish Jack Nicholson seduces Susan Sarandon’s cellist during a duet, which Warner says “seemed to symbolise Sarandon’s character’s sexual awakening, as well as her discovery of authentic emotional expression – she had previously struggled to bring that into her playing”.In Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World, Paul Bettany plays a cello bass line under Russell Crowe’s virtuosic violin flourishes. Warner says this “symbolises a close supportive working relationship whereby the soloist can be freer to express their brilliance”. The cello, then, is a literal baseline: a “straight man” that performs whatever emotional function the story needs.View image in fullscreenDevilish … Jack Nicholson and Susan Sarandon in The Witches of Eastwick (1987).Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyWarner also returns to something she once wrote in a collection of essays: “Symbolically, the cello can evoke the sense of the instrument being rather like a person.” And this gets closest to explaining Hollywood’s obsession with the instrument. More than any other member of the orchestra, introducing a cello is like casting another actor in a scene. Guðnadóttir even says that “there’s something about the size of it being quite close to the human body – not to mention the shape of the cello almost looking like a torso.”Pair its resemblance to the human body with its similarity to our vocal range, and it’s no wonder cinema loves the instrument. It’s a character actor in and of itself. It can be embraced, fought, comforted or strangled. Now we just need to wait for the inevitable Oscar category: best bowed string instrument in a leading role. It’s either that, or Pascal runs the risk of having his cello nominated ahead of him.Explore more on these topicsFilmClassical musicPedro PascalAudrey HepburnJamie FoxxEmily WatsonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The crude language of Maga folks’: Joyce Carol Oates criticises Emily Wilson for criticising Nolan’s Odyssey | Movies | The Guardian
description: The novelist suggested Wilson should have been ‘a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful’ towards a film-maker who may have helped boost her book sales
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The novelist suggested Wilson should have been ‘a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful’ towards a film-maker who may have helped boost her book sales
Content: ‘Uncollegiate’ … Mia Goth and Anne Hathaway in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘Uncollegiate’ … Mia Goth and Anne Hathaway in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesMovies‘The crude language of Maga folks’: Joyce Carol Oates criticises Emily Wilson for criticising Nolan’s OdysseyThe novelist suggested Wilson should have been ‘a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful’ towards a film-maker who may have helped boost her book salesMary Beard on The Odyssey and how empires fall – Stateside with Kai and CarterCatherine ShoardThu 30 Jul 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe off-screen drama surrounding Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster version of the Odyssey stepped up a gear overnight, as the novelistJoyce Carol Oatessought to defend the film-maker from an attack by classicist Emily Wilson.Writing on X, Oates took issue with the style as well as the rhetoric of Wilson’sessay published earlier this week in the London Review of Books, in which the academic, who published a landmark translation of Homer’s epic poem in 2017, wrote that Nolan’s film lacked “psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth” and had “nothing convincing to say”.“Rather than disagreeing with interpretations of Homer in a collegial manner,” said Oates, “this person, who has benefited enormously from Nolan’s film, speaks in the crude language of Maga folks attacking someone with ideas that differ from hers.‘I would be ashamed to have written any part of this’: Odyssey translator Emily Wilson attacks Nolan blockbusterRead more“One would expect a translator, of all people, beholden to a text, in service to a text, to be just a wee bit more thoughtful and respectful of others who are acting in good faith just as (she would claim) she is.”Oates’s comments come in the wake of her own implied criticism of the film last week, when she compared it to a 1997 Hallmark Channel version and found it wanting. The authortweetedthat the TV movie made by Andrei Konchalovsky boasted a “much more interesting interpretation than Nolan” of the sexual dynamic between Circe and Odysseus.She alsopraisedits portrayal of Odysseus (“So manly, so fully human”), its hades interlude (“mesmerising”) and its comparative expansiveness (“which perhaps Nolan had not seen”).Nolan’s film has been widely applauded by critics, perhaps partly explaining why the pitch of Wilson’s objections shocked many. “I had hoped that Nolan’s affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters,” she wrote.“ButThe Odysseyfeatures his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality … the film’s vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants.”She added: “The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has a convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.”Joyce Carol Oates thinks the 90s TV adaptation of The Odyssey is the best. I beg to differ | Stuart HeritageRead moreThe classicist’s verdict was perhaps the most eagerly anticipated, as her translation had been praised by Nolan in an interview with Empire. The director told the magazine he had used the opening line of her version – “Tell me about a complicated man” – as a key reference point when constructing the character played by Odysseus.Wilson finding Nolan’s rendition of the character as relatively one-dimensional is likely to have taken the team behind the film aback. In publicity for the movie, Universal has stressed that Nolan had been linked to an adaptation long before Wilson’s translation was published, and disputed claims he had been “inspired” by it.Sales of Wilson’s translation, and those by others, have seen a significant uptick over the past month, with UK bookseller TGJones reporting a 1,560% rise in searches for the Iliad this month.However, no royalties from the film would have been paid to any writer other than Nolan himself. The Odyssey, which cost around $250m to make and about $100m to promote, has currently taken $683m at the global box office, hard on the heels of Nolan’s previous film, Oppenheimer, which made $975m.That movie, a biopic of the man behind the atomic bomb, swept the 2023 Oscars, winning seven awards. His follow-up is widely predicted to follow suit next March.The Guardian has contacted Wilson for comment.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyChristopher NolanJoyce Carol OatesClassicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shaboozey: The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales review – a striking addition to the rich canon of country concept albums | Music | The Guardian
description: Beneath the Hollywood narrators, Pink Floyd-y interludes and accompanying comic books lies songwriting that proves the Tipsy singer’s breakout success was no fluke
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Beneath the Hollywood narrators, Pink Floyd-y interludes and accompanying comic books lies songwriting that proves the Tipsy singer’s breakout success was no fluke
Content: Darkly atmospheric and powerful … Shaboozey.View image in fullscreenDarkly atmospheric and powerful … Shaboozey.Alexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewShaboozey: The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales review – a striking addition to the rich canon of country concept albums(American Dogwood/Empire)Beneath the Hollywood narrators, Pink Floyd-y interludes and accompanying comic books lies songwriting that proves the Tipsy singer’s breakout success was no flukeAlexis PetridisThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s fair to say that if Shaboozey never released another note of music, his place in history would still be assured.He wasn’t the only Black country-leaning artist brought to a wider audience by a guest appearance on Beyoncé’s 2024 album Cowboy Carter, but no one else capitalised on the exposure quite so remarkably. Released two weeks after his guest appearance on that album’s Spaghettii, his single A Bar Song (Tipsy) unexpectedly eclipsed Beyoncé’s success, becoming the biggest-selling country single of the year – more than 1.75bn streams and counting on Spotify – and for a time, the joint longest-running US No 1 of all time. He’s received three nominations at theCountryMusic awards, an event traditionally resistant to artists of colour. The accompanying album, Where I’ve Been, Isn’t Where I’m Going, was by far the most successful sustained attempt to fuse hip-hop and country, two genres that have been warily circling each other for some time, spawning the occasional novelty hit such as Nelly and Tim McGraw’s Over and Over Again, the Ludacris-featuring 2010 remix of Jason Aldean’s Dirt Road, and Lil Nas X’s Old Town Road; the baleful, rap-influenced spectre of bro country; and the deep underground sub-genre of hick-hop, a hidden world of Maga politics, confederate flags and festivals held at Georgia mud holes. The album is still on the US chart, 112 weeks after its release.View image in fullscreenShaboozey: The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales.Understandably, its success has led Shaboozey to swing for the fences two years on. The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales is a 20-track concept album, accompanied by a three-issue comic of the same name. It features scene-setting interstitial tracks: cinematic and orchestral, ambient and Pink Floyd-y, with weeping pedal steel subbing for David Gilmour’s trademark mournful string-bends. There’s narration by actors Jamie Foxx, Teyana Taylor and Sam Elliott, the latter going some way to ameliorate the traditional problem with concept albums: that the listener quickly loses the thread of the narrative and spends most of the album listening without a clue what’s supposed to be going on.Country got to concept albums long before rock did. Marty Robbins’ thematically linked Gunfighter Ballads and Trail Songs were released in 1959, Johnny Cash’s Bitter Tears in 1964 – and they loom large in the genre’s history. Willie Nelson’s Red Headed Stranger, the 1975 saga of a murderer on the run, is regularly voted the greatest country album of all time; many major artists, including Emmylou Harris, Kenny Rogers and Dolly Parton, have at least one in their catalogue. You could thus view The Outlaw Cherie Lee as a concerted effort to pivot away from pop into country’s heartlands, albeit while still featuring a heavily Auto-Tuned guest appearance by rapper Gunna on High Noon (“spent a hundred thou on clothes / I got bad hoes,” he offers, presumably not referencing farming equipment). Cowgirl and Born to Die are two obvious – and, it has to be said, remarkably charming – attempts to replicate the success of Shaboozey’s biggest hit: “Got another bar song for you,” he notes by way of introduction to the former. Bullets and Blades, meanwhile, is a big and strikingly beautiful ballad with Shaboozey duetting with R&B star Kehlani.Elsewhere, The Outlaw Cherie Lee is more purely country: If I Was an Outlaw has saloon-bar piano, Sweet Revenge goes country rock, while the closing track is a burst of the traditional cowboy ballad Streets of Laredo sung by Orville Peck. The album’s predominant mode is stark and brooding, driven by fingerpicked acoustic guitar and decorated with fiddle. At their best, these tracks are darkly atmospheric and powerful – as on Drunk – although it’s occasionally hard not to feel that part of Shaboozey’s USP has gone with his decision to dial down the rap influence in his vocals. He can certainly croon with a glowering power, but there’s a distinct leap in excitement when he reverts to a hip-hop-inspired delivery, the better to inhabit the character of a swaggering outlaw on Til Sunday.How gen Z women are conquering country music: ‘Fans are speaking louder than gatekeepers’Read moreStill, as a demonstration of his eclecticism – or, if you prefer, a desire to be all things to all people – The Outlaw Cherie Lee works well. The pop-facing tracks hit, the strike rate when he diversifies is higher than his naysayers would suggest, and there’s an impressive boldness about his evident desire to draw R&B, soul and hip-hop artists into his world – aside from Gunna and Kehlani, there’s an impressive turn from Leon Bridges on Burn It Down. The overarching storyline is tight and well handled. Perhaps most importantly, the album never feels like the work of an artist whose career has been destabilised by a huge, unexpected and unrepeatable hit, but rather the work of an artist digging in for the long haul.What Alexis listened to this weekMr Wa7t – Secrets (Richard Norris Fitness Mix)The original is great soulful, deep pop, but Richard Norris’s remix turns it into delightfully smooth, hot-afternoon Balearic: very much what is needed at the moment.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekCountryRapPop and rockHip-hopalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have to become warriors’: the fight to save the world’s only women’s sculpture park | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With most monuments in London made by men, Claire Mander envisaged the Artist’s Garden as a way to redress the balance. Now, she says, it could be turned into a generic space for VIP events and cocktails
Author: Anita Chaudhuri
Headline: With most monuments in London made by men, Claire Mander envisaged the Artist’s Garden as a way to redress the balance. Now, she says, it could be turned into a generic space for VIP events and cocktails
Content: ‘It has never occurred to me not to work on a large scale’ …  Lakwena Maciver with her installation at the Artist’s Garden at Temple in London in 2021.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreen‘It has never occurred to me not to work on a large scale’ …  Lakwena Maciver with her installation at the Artist’s Garden at Temple in London in 2021.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAArt and design‘We have to become warriors’: the fight to save the world’s only women’s sculpture parkWith most monuments in London made by men, Claire Mander envisaged the Artist’s Garden as a way to redress the balance. Now, she says, it could be turned into a generic space for VIP events and cocktailsAnita ChaudhuriThu 30 Jul 2026 06.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years ago, when Claire Mander was studying for an art history MA at the Courtauld Institute inLondon, she stumbled upon the neglected roof terrace of nearby Temple underground station. She found herself strangely drawn to the overgrown expanse with its stunning views of the Thames and the London Eye.“It was dirty, abandoned and a magnet for antisocial behaviour,” recalls Mander, now director and curator of theColab, an arts charity and incubator specialising in large-scale outdoor sculptures. She researched the history of the abandoned space, which was built as part of the Victoria Embankment in 1870. Before that, the ground beneath the site housed a 17th-century sculpture garden created by the Countess of Arundel.“It inspired me to visualise how the roof terrace could become a really special women’s sculpture garden,” says Mander. “The ‘hidden in plain sight’ nature of the location felt to me like the perfect place to redress some of the gender disparity that we see in public artworks.”View image in fullscreen‘Hidden in plain sight’ … view over the the Artist’s Garden in central London.Photograph: theCOLABA survey byArtUK revealed that of almost 1,500 monuments in London, more than a fifth were dedicated to named men and only 4% were dedicated to women, half as many as those that celebrated animals. And of all the public sculptures in London, only 13% were created by women.Mander kept badgering Westminster council until eventually they gave her the go-ahead. With funding from donations and over £500,000 to date from the council, the Artist’s Garden opened in October 2021. It is the world’s first and only public sculpture garden devoted to the work of female artists. Since then they have attracted 100,000 visitors a year, commissioned 18 major works, and collaborated with 24 different emerging and established artists.But now, theColab has been informed by Places for London, Transport for London’s property arm, that their licence to occupy the site will not be renewed on 1 October and they must clear the garden.View image in fullscreenTechnicolor forest … Alice Wilson’s Savoy on show at the Artist’s Garden.Photograph: theCOLABA Places for London spokesperson said: “The terrace and station roof may now require essential repair and safety works, and the space needs to be cleared for the assessment of the extent of the works required. We are working with Westminster city council and local stakeholders to explore alternative locations nearby for the Artist’s Garden, while also developing future plans for the terrace at Temple. As a legally protected space, it will always remain accessible to the public.”Mander disputes this, stating that the repairs relate to upgrading the commercial property below the terrace, and that according to the scope of works, no large-scale overhaul of the roof is mentioned. She believes the space is at risk of being handed over to a private developer. “It’s a prime location with incredible views of the river, ideal for VIP events selling overpriced cocktails. They don’t understand that this is a landmark project. Their perception seems to be that we’re a small, pathetic female-led charity that’s doing some sort of nice little sculptural things. But we are prepared to take this to court if it comes to it.” They have launched a campaign and petition to save the garden.Alexandra Hodby, head of programmes at YorkshireSculpturePark and a trustee of the gardens, points out that such spaces are of vital cultural and economic value, both to artists and to the cities they inhabit. “Look at the High Line in New York. It wasn’t even a public space, then it was made public through art. Artists activated it. Now it’s one of the most visited places in the city.”Hodby believes that sculpture has a particular power to engage the public in a way that art on gallery walls does not. “There’s an immediacy about it, there’s no separation between the work and the world.” This is true. On the day I visit, London is in the grip of a heatwave. Office workers, builders on an early lunch, bemused tourists, all throng the space. A toddler crawls towards Mexican artist Adeline de Monseignat’s pebbled Croissant, no doubt spying a potential see-saw. In the distance, I spot people posing for selfies beside Alice Wilson’s Savoy, a giant forest of technicolor timbers.View image in fullscreenAdeline de Monseignat’s Up-Up showing at the Artist’s Garden.Photograph: theCOLAB“Obviously, seeing art made by women inspires other women who want to make art themselves. But it goes far beyond that,” says Hodby. “Representation is about being part of a public space and being seen. Visibility allows visitors to see themselves, be it the Artist’s Garden or Yorkshire Sculpture Park where we endeavour to show a broad range of artists including non-binary, queer practice and younger artists.”Lakwena Maciver created the site’s opening exhibit, a kaleidoscopic mural titled Back in the Air: A Meditation on Higher Ground. It unfurled across the entire 140 sq-metre space. For the British-Ugandan artist, the site holds particular emotional significance. “When I was a teenager, we would get the train up to town and I remember sitting in Embankment Gardens eating Skittles with my sister. I’d be thinking about my future but also feeling that, as a minority, London didn’t belong to me. To be asked to do the mural was very special because I was being invited to contribute something so monumental. It was like, I do belong! It has never occurred to me not to work on a large scale but I had so many positive interactions with visitors at that site, it gave me a lot of confidence.”View image in fullscreen‘A place to reflect’ … the Artist’s Shed at the Artist’s Garden.Photograph: theColabArtist Florence Peake created work for the site’s current show Sculpture in Three Acts. “It’s rare these days in London to find a public space that is free and doesn’t have a commercial agenda. It’s a place to reflect, take a breath and be with artworks that may draw you in, and hold space for a state of reflection.”She believes the garden has provided a much-needed space. “It allows visitors to see that women can make huge monolithic work. Of course we can! It’s just that so often we’re not trusted to be ambitious and do things to scale. Our visions are often rejected and considered naive. This is what I’ve encountered in my 30 years of being an artist anyway. A man comes along and says ‘I want to build a big steel thing sticking 18 metres up in the air’ and he’s hailed as a genius. A woman suggesting the same thing, there are anxious sideways glances.”At the heart of the garden is the artist’s hut, currently featuring a wraparound photomontage created by feminist artist Linder Sterling. “The Artist’s Garden is situated in Temple, once the province of the Knights Templar,” she says. “It seems that women have to become warriors now and defend our right to take up space there.”Presiding over the back wall of the montage is a portrait of the Countess of Arundel, reminding us of the lineage of women who have gone before. “On one of the walls of the hut, you can see the phrase ‘She Is Here’, the title of the work, writ large,” adds Sterling. “Now that the site is under threat, She Is Here has become a rallying cry - we’re not going anywhere.”Explore more on these topicsArt and designSculptureWomenArtLondonTfLfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Freudian trip: how psychoanalysis and skydiving are helping Aurora orchestra open up Mahler’s First | Classical music | The Guardian
description: When Mahler premiered his first symphony, it left audiences baffled. For their latest Prom, Aurora are bringing it to life – with the help of Sigmund Freud
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When Mahler premiered his first symphony, it left audiences baffled. For their latest Prom, Aurora are bringing it to life – with the help of Sigmund Freud
Content: Flautist (and artistic director) Jane Mitchell is airborne in Aurora Orchestra’s Shostakovich’s Fifth by Heart at the BBC Proms in August 2025.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenFlautist (and artistic director) Jane Mitchell is airborne in Aurora Orchestra’s Shostakovich’s Fifth by Heart at the BBC Proms in August 2025.Photograph: Andy ParadiseClassical musicFreudian trip: how psychoanalysis and skydiving are helping Aurora orchestra open up Mahler’s FirstWhen Mahler premiered his first symphony, it left audiences baffled. For their latest Prom, Aurora are bringing it to life – with the help of Sigmund FreudJane MitchellThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2014, Aurora Orchestra did something that had never been done at the Proms before. We played Mozart’s 40th symphony – that has been done,many times– but from memory.It was terrifying. Orchestral musicians usually start getting out their instruments 10 minutes before they go on stage, but people started warming up nearly an hour before – endless repetitions of fragments of music as players tested what they thought they might forget. We didn’t know if we would get on stage and freeze or fall off. Thankfully, we did neither and fear turned into excitement. Ourbassoonist Amy Harmandescribed the feeling as “like skydiving without a parachute. But in a good way.”Even so, if someone had told me then that 12 years later we would be performing from memory Mahler’s First Symphony – a piece almost twice as long as the Mozart that uses more than double the number of musicians – I would have been surprised. And if I’d then been told that in the first half of the concert we’d be presenting a new play about Mahler, featuring choreography involving the entire orchestra alongside two actors and a complicated sound design (and written by me!), I’d have laughed. Butthis weekendwe will do exactly this.View image in fullscreenRehearsals earlier this week for Mahler’s First By Heart.Photograph: Aurora OrchestraAfter the Mozart, our performances from memory became a regular Proms feature. Then, three years ago, we upped the ante when we took on Stravinsky’sThe Rite of Spring. Memorising that enormously complex work was a challenge, but what felt especially scary was the fact we were dedicating the concert to a single piece.The second half would feature the performance; the first would introduce the work to the audience … somehow. It was my job to figure out what this actually meant – and it took a really long time.What emerged was a 40-minute first half that told the story of how the Rite was written and premiered, combining text, musical analysis, orchestral excerpts, choreography for the whole orchestra and video projection, and featuring performances by the actors Charlotte Ritchie and Karl Queensborough.It felt as if we had hit on something, so we have continued in this vein. At the following year’s Proms, we presented a first half dedicated to the creation ofBeethoven’s Ninth Symphonybefore performing the work itself; last year, we turned toShostakovich’s Fifth.It’s hard to know what to call these first halves. We used to use the word “presentation”, but it has become more than that. “Play” or “orchestral theatre” feel closer, but all suggestions are welcome.View image in fullscreenKarl Queensborough and Charlotte Ritchie with  Aurora Orchestra’s 2023 The Rite by Heart at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Andy ParadiseOur choice of repertoire tends to be as simple as what would be fun to perform from memory and which pieces have an interesting story to explore. The first question is especially important, as we are asking players to spend hours and hours with this music. Everyone will have their own process of memorising – some go for runs with the music on headphones, some play it over and over – and some get out highlighter pens.My own creative process always begins with reading. I’ll know the music from playing it (I’m Aurora’s principal flautist), but I’ll want to learn more about the composer and the historical context. It’s always the words that come directly from the composers and their contemporaries that tell me what we should do.When I researched The Rite of Spring, I was struck by the many collaborative voices clamouring to give their accounts of how they created the premiere production. For Beethoven’s Ninth, I read the composer’s conversation books: notebooks in which he asked friends to write down what they were saying, as an aide for his profound hearing loss, and realised we didn’t need any other words. With Shostakovich’s Fifth, I realised how few words exist from the composer himself – however much I read, he remained elusive.I work closely with our conductor, Nicholas Collon, to untangle the score and decide which passages to focus on and how to present the music in a way that shows physically what the score is doing. James Bonas co-directs – we often refer to him as our “bad audience member”, as he tells us what is working, what is not and what is too academic or music-jargony. I used to find this part of the process excruciating, but I’ve learned to enjoy it.I love the fact that every year I get to be completely immersed in a different composer’s world and music. This year has all been about Mahler. The first time I performed his music as a student flautist, I felt as if I had stepped inside a world I didn’t quite understand, but which was oddly familiar. I remember clinging on to the other more experienced instrumentalists and their phrasing and timing. Everything seemed exaggerated. Every melody carried so much emotion, with dynamics lurching from the quietest, highest held chord to the loudest eruption of the full orchestra. Daunting stuff when you’re just starting out, but also the adrenaline high orchestral players live for.Mahler, in stark contrast to Shostakovich, left us many words, and they reveal an artist constantly analysing his own feelings and emotions.double quotation mark…for as long as I can remember –my need to express myself musically begins at the point where the dark feelings hold sway, at the door which leads to the other world – the world in which things are no longer separated by time and space … For those that listen closely, everything about me is explained in my music.This is particularly the case with his First Symphony, into which he poured his lived experience: memories of soldiers in the forests of his childhood home, the sound of cuckoos outside his composing room, songs about problematic love affairs and children’s nursery rhymes.Little surprise, then, that when Mahler presented his First Symphony to the world, in Budapest in 1889, he felt as if he was baring his soul. But audiences were baffled. Reviewers described the music as “offensively trivial”, “a disaster” and “ridiculous”. In the months that followed, his friends described him as looking sick and feeling misunderstood. “For goodness sake, where do people put their ears and their hearts if they can’t understand this music?” he said.View image in fullscreenMax Revell (centre) as a silent Shostakovich in Aurora Orchestra’s Proms performance in 2025.Photograph: Andy ParadiseI began wondering what Mahler might have thought ofSigmund Freudand the groundbreaking work he was doing around this same time. I was fascinated to learn that the two had met: the composer made an appointment to talk to Freud in 1910. The accounts of their meeting tell us that they discussed exactly these ideas, why he felt he needed to write particular kinds of music and why he felt the public couldn’t understand him. I began to wonder if this meeting could become a framework through which to explore the symphony.And so my script follows Mahler’s journey, from conceiving and composing the symphony to premiering it to widespread bewilderment and then trying to get people to understand it.The programme notes he provided for the second performance read hilariously like someone overexplaining themselves. I love his attempts to describe his third movement, with which people had a particular problem:double quotation markI want you to imagineThe Hunter’s Funeral Procession, a picture from an old book of children’s fairytales: in this picture – the beasts of the forest accompany the dead woodsman’s coffin to the grave, with hares carrying a small banner, with a band of Bohemian musiciansin front, and the procession escorted by music-making cats, toads, crows etc …There’s plenty more. We have a script and we have a brilliant singer (Natalie Lewis) and two wonderful actors (Jack Bardoe and Sarah Twomey) who have been rehearsing with me, James and Nicholas this past week. But the orchestra will have only a day and a half to rehearse the first half, in which they are required to remember terribly confusing versions of bits of the symphony and lots of strictly choreographed moves around the stage.The only way this works is if we have a military plan mapped out. We call this flat-packing. The players need to trust us – which has taken time, I admit. Each year, I do wonder: perhaps this will be the year where we’ve pushed them too far? That thought is certainly in my head this week.View image in fullscreenAurora Orchestra, conducted by Nicholas Collon, perform Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring from memory at the 2023 Proms.Photograph: Andy ParadiseYou might ask: “Why bother?”For me, there are two main reasons. First, I am so aware of how lucky I am to have the best seat in the house at orchestral concerts. Flutes sit right in the middle of the orchestra and I can hear all the conversations between instruments and the shifting textures surrounding me. The aural experience is visceral and immersive. I want to find ways to give audiences the same breathtaking experience I have.Second, I am in a very small minority of people who have spent a lot of time studying music: at university, then music college, then for 20 years as a professional musician. Yet I still don’t feel I know much. Whenever a conductor or colleague talks to me about how a bit of a score works, or breaks apart a texture, or gives some historical context, it always enhances my understanding of the music and makes me listen more closely.Our plays are about giving audiences ways to feel closer to the music. Someone once described it to me as “giving the keys to the kingdom”, which I love. You may listen to the music differently because you know more about the composer, or the social context, or because you’ve seen musical textures brought to life; the players choreographed across the stage reflect this. We want to communicate the music to everyone, whether this is your first orchestral concert or you know and love the work. Come and see if we’ve got it right at the Royal Albert Hall in London this Saturday and Sunday.Jane Mitchell is Aurora Orchestra’s artistic director. Mahler’s First By Heart is at the BBC Proms at7pm on 1 Augustand at11am on 2 August. All Proms are live on BBC Radio 3 and available on BBC Sounds until 12 OctoberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicAurora OrchestraProms 2026Sigmund FreudShareReuse this content

title: Netflix sued for $105m over stolen Nicolas Cage war thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: Makers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles office
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Makers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles office
Content: Nicolas Cage.Photograph: Jeff Vespa/@portraits/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNicolas Cage.Photograph: Jeff Vespa/@portraits/ShutterstockMoviesNetflix sued for $105m over stolen Nicolas Cage war thrillerMakers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles officeBenjamin LeeThu 30 Jul 2026 15.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflixis being sued for $105m over the theft of a hard drive including an unreleasedNicolas Cagewar movie.The streamer’s Los Angeles office was the target of a theft involving a number of hard drives, one of which contained a copy of second world war spy thriller Fortitude.The makers of the $45m-budgeted film are now suingNetflixover the loss.“Netflix disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards,” a spokesperson said in a statement shared with theHollywood Reporter. “While we do not own the rights to Fortitude, we take content security seriously and have taken extra measures to support the film-maker and his team. This includes conducting a thorough investigation and offering to monitor known piracy sites for any unauthorized distribution or sale.”Netflix reportedly received a copy of the film in June after expressing interest in promotional materials at the end of last year. A digital copy was then sent so the film could be screened internally with the film’s producers instructing Netflix to delete the files afterward.Sean Berney, head of Netflix film acquisitions, wrote in an email that it was a first for the company to be the subject of such a theft. “We’ve been working through this with our security teams to no luck,” he added. “Our piracy teams are on high alert with the breach and will monitor.”Netflix is accused of failing to disclose details of whether a police report was initially filed as well as later declining a request by the film-makers to involve the LAPD after they filed their own report.The lawsuit claims that any future sale of the film has now been put in jeopardy with any international release strategy and awards campaign paused.“The resulting damage to plaintiffs is profound,” the lawsuit said, according toPage Six. “Through its mishandling of the film and subsequent dismissiveness, Netflix has jeopardized plaintiffs’ investment of over $45m and the significant value of the film itself. Netflix has also deprived the film, its cast and its creators of the opportunity to bring their work to market and receive recognition that a properly marketed worldwide release likely would have generated.”Fortitude is a London-set espionage thriller focused on British intelligence operatives changing the course of the second world war. Cage stars alongside Matthew Goode, Michael Sheen and Ben Kingsley. The film is directed by Simon West, whose previous credits include Tomb Raider and The General’s Daughter.Martin Scorsese was at one point attached to the project but was then the subject of alawsuitclaiming he took $500,000 from first-time screenwriter Simon Afram to help develop the film but failed to do so. Scorsese’s lawyers called it a “classic example of the novice film-maker who refuses to appreciate the stark difference between expectation and reality in the film-making business”. It was later settled.“I spent seven years of my life bringing this incredible true story to the screen,” Afram said in a statement. “But this film was never mine alone. It belongs to the extraordinary cast and their performances of a lifetime that deserve to be seen and recognized. It represents the moment these artists have earned.”Explore more on these topicsFilmNetflixNicolas CageUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was hyperventilating and sobbing’: Tomi Adeyemi says Children of Blood and Bone film ‘the worst thing I’ve ever lived through’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla Stenberg
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla Stenberg
Content: Tomi Adeyemi in 2025.Photograph: River Callaway/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTomi Adeyemi in 2025.Photograph: River Callaway/Variety/Getty ImagesMovies‘I was hyperventilating and sobbing’: Tomi Adeyemi says Children of Blood and Bone film ‘the worst thing I’ve ever lived through’Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla StenbergCatherine ShoardThu 30 Jul 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTomi Adeyemi, the author ofChildren of Blood and Bone, has spoken further on the difficult process behind adapting her novel for this big screen, calling it “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”.In a five-minute video on TikTok, the author said she left the set of the Paramount production “hyperventilating and sobbing”, adding: “I never want to hear about this project again”.Adeyemi, who co-wrote the screenplay for the film, had previously spoken about her concerns surrounding the adaptation, saying that she wasn’t intending to watch the film.The video she posted on TikTok was intended, she said, to try to put the affair to bed, although the author conceded it might prolong the story. She also said that the people involved with the film had continued to “antagonise” her.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continue“What I’m about to share is not a secret to the people involved,” she said. “It’s a reality that I’ve had to live with for about a year and a half, and everyone involved, at least at the highest level, has been made aware of this reality, and they haven’t done anything to make it better. If anything, they’ve only antagonised me, and I accept that. But I also accept if I don’t say something, I think it’s just going to be worse.”She continued: “I’m not going to speak on what I endured to make it through the young adult trilogy, and I’m not going to speak about everything that I also suffered through or endured to make the adaptation a reality.‘Attacked behind the scenes’: Children of Blood & Bone author Tomi Adeyemi distances herself from film adaptationRead more“I’m actually only going to speak about what happened after I left that set of my own film adaptation, hyperventilating and sobbing. There are many witnesses, so it’s not really a secret. I came back to America and suffered such severe somatic pain and so many panic attacks. I knew it was so bad that I would never ever be able to watch this film, and I made peace with that.”Speaking to the Los Angeles Timesearlier this week, director Gina Prince-Bythewood appeared to allude to a casting controversy involving Amandla Stenberg, who portrays Princess Amari in the film.Prince-Bythewood said the adaptation was “beautifully inspired by Nigeria and also inclusive of the whole diaspora. We wanted all of us to be able to see ourselves within this, just our complete and utter humanity, all the beautiful hues.”While the actor and novelist seemed close last spring, it looks as if a subsequent disagreement soured relations considerably. A now-deleted TikTok video posted by the writer appeared to show a group chat including Stenberg, to whom Adeyemi wrote: “Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me.”The film also stars Regina King, Damson Idris, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, Tosin Cole, Viola Davis, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Lashana Lynch and Thuso Mbedu.Prince-Bythewood was speaking at an event to mark the release of a first trailer for the film on Monday, which appears to have acted as an additional prompt to Adeyami to speak out again.“As it is being marketed,” she said on TikTok, “and as I am still being antagonised behind the scenes, which is where I hoped all of this would stay, it’s become apparent to me that reality needs to at least be made known, so that you guys can understand how this film, which I worked on to make it a little better for us to be alive, is also the worst thing I have ever had to live through.”Explore more on these topicsFilmYoung adultAction and adventure filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Paul McCartney becomes first-time nominee for Mercury prize, up against Olivia Dean, Dave and more | Mercury prize | The Guardian
description: Big names including Raye and Suede go up against smaller artists such as Knats and Nia Archives for prestigious album award
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Big names including Raye and Suede go up against smaller artists such as Knats and Nia Archives for prestigious album award
Content: Decent pedigree … Paul McCartney pictured in 2022.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/ReutersView image in fullscreenDecent pedigree … Paul McCartney pictured in 2022.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/ReutersMercury prizePaul McCartney becomes first-time nominee for Mercury prize, up against Olivia Dean, Dave and moreBig names including Raye and Suede face off against smaller artists such as Knats and Nia Archives for prestigious album awardBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 30 Jul 2026 05.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA formidable array of chart-topping A-listers feature in a competitive shortlist for the 2026Mercury prize, the prestigious award that honours the best album of the year by a British or Irish artist.Despite the prize’s history stretching back to 1992, Paul McCartney gets his first ever nomination this year, for his albumThe Boys of Dungeon Lane, a hugely affecting look back at his Liverpool childhood and his burgeoning friendships with his Beatles bandmates.Speaking to the Guardian as the album was released in May, McCartney said he felt the presence of John Lennon when writing it. “My collaborator was probably one of the best writers of the century, so, yeah, you’re going to miss him. But when I write [about a specific place], I kind of know he would’ve known it. I can gauge his reaction:that’s good, stick that in.”He may have the greatest pedigree of anyone on the shortlist, but McCartney is up against one of the most sensational British success stories of recent years: Olivia Dean, whose albumThe Art of Lovingswept the board at the Brit awards this year and could do the same at next year’s Grammys. It has spent all but one of its 43 weeks since release in the UK Top 5, eight of them at No 1.View image in fullscreenRaye performing at the BET awards in Los Angeles in June.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersHer British pop peer Raye is alongside her, for the ambitious, symphonic-scaleThis Music May Contain Hope, her second album in a row to be nominated after her debut, My 21st Century Blues.Another big hitter is rapper Dave, nominated forThe Boy Who Played the Harp, containing the global smash Raindance. The album was awarded five stars in the Guardian, with Dave described as “a fantastically smart, sharp lyricist”. Dave won the Mercury prize with his debut album Psychodrama in 2019, though didn’t make the shortlist for its follow-up We’re All in This Together.Florence + the Machine earns her fourth Mercury nomination, for her sixth albumEverybody Scream, which was also strongly acclaimed in the Guardian and described as “rounded musically and emotionally”. If she was to lose, only Radiohead would have been nominated more times without winning.There is a panoply of other big names on a rare compilation album to be nominated for the Mercury: Help(2), a charity album recorded at Abbey Road to raise money for War Child. It features new recordings by artists including former Mercury winners Arctic Monkeys, Pulp, Sampha, English Teacher, Ezra Collective, Young Fathers and Beth Gibbons (who won with Portishead), plus a host of other top UK and US talent. It is the sequel to 1995’s The Help Album, the only other compilation to be nominated in Mercury history.All of the aforementioned albums reached No 1 in the UK, while another reached No 3:That’s Showbiz Baby!by Jade, whose post-Little Mix career continues to win acclaim. Goth-tinged Britpoppers Suede are nominated for another commercial success,Antidepressants, which reached No 2; the band won the Mercury for their self-titled 1993 debut, but haven’t been nominated since 1997’s Coming Up.There is space for some less well-known artists, including an album that could be seen as the dark horse:Blizzard, by Irish singer-songwriter Dove Ellis, which received some of 2025’s most rapturous reviews across the music press, including a five-star Guardian rave. He also appears on Help(2).View image in fullscreenKnats pictured recording their Mercury-nominated album.Photograph: Ellie SlorickJazz outfitKnatsare nominated for A Great Day in Newcastle, which features a huge cast of musicians, including spoken word artists, combining for a grand, groove-driven listen. As natives of Newcastle where the award ceremony is now held, they’ll be hoping for a repeat of last year when local boy Sam Fender was given the prize.Stalwart UK rapper Kojey Radical, celebrated for his cerebral, socially conscious yet commercially minded tracks, earns his second Mercury nomination, while Nia Archives – a producer and DJ who cleverly combines junglist rhythms with indie rock and R&B – also earns her second nomination, forEmotional Junglist, released only last week, on the last day of the eligibility period.It adds up to a diverse list where eight of the 12 albums feature artists of colour. There are of course some snubs, most notably Lily Allen’s West End Girl, which was a huge part of 2025’s cultural conversation.Other artists missing out include Harry Styles, Boards of Canada, Gorillaz, Sienna Spiro, Lola Young, Ed Sheeran, Kneecap, James Blake, the Cribs, Celeste, Cat Burns, the Last Dinner Party, Robert Plant, Joy Crookes, Fakemink, Dry Cleaning and My New Band Believe. Charli xcx’s Wuthering Heights soundtrack wasn’t nominated, though her new album Music, Fashion, Film was just outside the eligibility period. Blood Orange’s massively acclaimed Essex Honey was outside the eligibility period by one day.The prize will be awarded at Newcastle’s Utilita Arena on 22 October, and the winner will be decided by an 11-strong panel of experts from across the music industry.The 2026 Mercury prize nomineesDave: The Boy Who Played the HarpDove Ellis: BlizzardFlorence + the Machine: Everybody ScreamJade: That’s Showbiz BabyKnats: A Great Day in NewcastleKojey Radical: Don’t Look DownNia Archives: Emotional JunglistOlivia Dean: The Art of LovingPaul McCartney: The Boys of Dungeon LaneRaye: This Music May Contain HopeSuede: AntidepressantsWar Child Records: Help(2)Explore more on these topicsMercury prizePop and rockAwards and prizesPaul McCartneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Staff at V&A site in London vote to strike over toilet and water breaks | V&A | The Guardian
description: Union calling for two paid breaks a day in what it says is punishing schedule for Storehouse ‘order an object’ workers
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Union calling for two paid breaks a day in what it says is punishing schedule for Storehouse ‘order an object’ workers
Content: The V&A Storehouse’s ‘order an object’ service requires staff members to retrieve items requested by members of the public from around the building.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe V&A Storehouse’s ‘order an object’ service requires staff members to retrieve items requested by members of the public from around the building.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianV&AStaff at V&A site in London vote to strike over toilet and water breaksUnion calling for two paid breaks a day in what it says is punishing schedule for Storehouse ‘order an object’ workersNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentThu 30 Jul 2026 10.11 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStaff at the V&A’s Storehouse site in eastLondonhave voted overwhelmingly to strike in a dispute over what they say are inadequate toilet and hydration breaks.They will join staff across V&A sites in London who on Wednesday also voted to strike in a wider dispute over pay, working conditions, andthe museum having declined to seek living wage accreditation.The trade union Prospect said members at V&A Storehouse, which opened in May 2025, are denied enough time during the day for toilet breaks or hydration.The dispute centres on collections access officers who facilitate the “order an object” service, a central part of the Storehouse’s offering of public access to its vast collection.The union is calling for two paid breaks a day, saying staff need time to use the toilet and hydrate during what it describes as a punishing schedule. It said a collective grievance had failed to secure an “extremely reasonable request for customary paid breaks”, which workers elsewhere in the organisation receive.Prospect said many of the staff had been recruited from the local community, something the V&A had highlighted publicly, but that they were treated worse than colleagues at other sites.One Prospect member told the Guardian: “We get just one unpaid lunch hour, even though we’re on our feet for long hours, interacting with the public and doing a lot of manual labour.“Breaks are a welfare issue. The Storehouse is purpose-built for storing objects, but they haven’t really thought about the human aspect – how far we have to travel around the building or where the bathrooms are.“We’ve experienced a lot of dehydration, and sometimes people don’t even go to the bathroom for the whole day.”They added: “We’ve tried every internal procedure possible. We’ve brought the issue up in one-to-one meetings, we did a petition, we went through a formal grievance, and we’ve never got proper answers.”V&A East Storehouse and Norwich Castle among finalists for museum of the yearRead moreAnother Prospect member said: “Every day we go into work, there’s someone who has a headache because they’re dehydrated. Management says we always have time to take breaks and drink water. But we need someone to relieve us because we can’t leave trolleys of collection objects unattended. We need breaks scheduled fixed into our calendars.“We are the newest department at the V&A. We are the most diverse back-of-house department. It’s not lost on us that we were hired to represent the east London community, but our welfare is being neglected.”At V&A Storehouse, 100% of those voting backed strike action on a turnout of nearly 88%, while 92% supported action short of a strike.As part of the wider dispute, Prospect is seeking a minimum 4% pay rise for staff earning above the living wage, time-and-a-half for bank holiday working, accreditation as a London living wage employer within 12 months and improved food provision at V&A East sites.Across the V&A, 83% voted for strike action on an 82% turnout, and 95% voted for action short of a strike. The timing of any industrial action has yet to be decided.Mike Clancy, Prospect’s general secretary, said: “This incredible new way of showing off our heritage is being delivered by workers who are denied adequate break time to use the toilet or have a drink of water.“Visitors will be appalled to learn that the kinds of working practices unions campaign against in companies like Amazon also exist in an internationally renowned heritage institution.”He said the dispute reflected “a shocking lack of respect” for staff across the museum.A V&A spokesperson said: “The V&A has been in negotiations with the trade union side since February and those negotiations are ongoing. Our offer sees a 3.6% increase in the overall pay bill, an above-inflation pay award as a minimum, and 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues. As always, we have maintained our longstanding commitment to paying at least the London living wage.“The safety and wellbeing of our staff is of utmost importance to the V&A – all our staff have access to water and toilet facilities and regular breaks while at work. At V&A East Storehouse we have water fountains on every floor to ensure both staff and visitors in front-of-house areas have access to drinking water throughout the building. To ensure the safety and security of national collections, during visits to V&A East Storehouse, food and drink are not permitted for visitors or staff in the main collections hall or storage areas.“Extensive measures were implemented to support our staff during the heatwave, ranging from additional rest breaks, increasing staff rotations across gallery spaces, closing several galleries at V&A South Kensington and closing Young V&A altogether on 11 days during the peak of the heatwave.”Responding previously toa separate strike ballot by the Public and Commercial Services union, the V&A said all staff had access to water, toilet facilities and regular breaks, and pointed to additional measures introduced during this summer’s heatwave, including extra rest breaks, staff rotations and temporary gallery closures.The London living wage is£14.80 an hour. While the V&A has said all its staff are paid at least this rate, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors are not in receipt of the living wage and V&A has not so far become an accredited living wage employer, although it says this will be reviewed this year. V&A Dundee is an accredited living wage employer.Explore more on these topicsV&ALondonEnglandIndustrial actionTrade unionsMuseumsnewsShareReuse this content

title: George and Amal Clooney evacuate from French house: ‘We do not know whether our beautiful home will survive’ | George Clooney | The Guardian
description: In a letter to the local mayor, the actor added that ‘whatever happens, they remain fully part of this community’ and will ‘contribute to its rebuilding’
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: In a letter to the local mayor, the actor added that ‘whatever happens, they remain fully part of this community’ and will ‘contribute to its rebuilding’
Content: Chez Clooney … Domaine du Canadel, in Brignoles.Photograph: FRAT/BEST IMAGE/BACKGRIDView image in fullscreenChez Clooney … Domaine du Canadel, in Brignoles.Photograph: FRAT/BEST IMAGE/BACKGRIDGeorge ClooneyGeorge and Amal Clooney evacuate from French house: ‘We do not know whether our beautiful home will survive’In a letter to the local mayor, the actor added that ‘whatever happens, they remain fully part of this community’ and will ‘contribute to its rebuilding’Catherine ShoardThu 30 Jul 2026 11.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge and Amal Clooneyhave been forced to evacuate their home in south-eastern France as a wildfire burned nearby, his agent confirmed to Associated Press on Thursday.The Clooneys bought their hilltop estate, Domaine du Canadel, in Brignoles in the Var in 2021 and it has since become their primary residence. Last December, the French government awarded the whole family – including the couple’s nine-year-old twins –French citizenship.In a letter to Didier Bremond, the mayor of Brignoles, the actor wrote that while “at this point we have no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment and as we evacuate Brignoles”, he wanted to “emphasise two things”.‘Suspension of entry into the US’, paparazzi – and wine: three other reasons George Clooney moved to FranceRead more“First we hope you and the people of our city are safe and second that Amal and I are determined to ensure that, whatever happens to our village, we remain fully part of this community and [will] contribute to its rebuilding. We love Brignoles and the friends we have there.”The fire near Brignoles broke out on Wednesday afternoon and burned some 130 hectares (321 acres), local officials said. Some 600 residents were evacuated and four firefighters injured.Speaking to Esquire magazine earlier in the year about his rationale for relocating from the US, Clooney said he and his wife, a highly respected human rights lawyer, did not want their children either observed by paparazzi or being raised with an urban myopia.“A good portion of my life growing up was on a farm, and as a kid I hated the whole idea of it,” he said. “But now, for them, it’s like – they’re not on their iPads, you know? They have dinner with grownups and have to take their dishes in. They have a much better life.”Explore more on these topicsGeorge ClooneyAmal ClooneyFranceWildfiresnewsShareReuse this content
