title: Don’t Date Brandon review – this lazy true-crime show doesn’t start to do justice to these women’s horrors | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The tale of the women who came together to unpick the destructive swathe that one man cut through his local dating pool is woefully lacking in the detail you need to understand their plight. It feels voyeuristic and misguided
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The tale of the women who came together to unpick the destructive swathe that one man cut through his local dating pool is woefully lacking in the detail you need to understand their plight. It feels voyeuristic and misguided
Content: Going public … Brandon’s first and second wives, Amber (left) and Athena.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenGoing public … Brandon’s first and second wives, Amber (left) and Athena.Photograph: Channel 4TV reviewTelevision & radioReviewDon’t Date Brandon review – this lazy true-crime show doesn’t start to do justice to these women’s horrorsThe tale of the women who came together to unpick the destructive swathe that one man cut through his local dating pool is woefully lacking in the detail you need to understand their plight. It feels voyeuristic and misguidedLucy ManganThu 30 Jul 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m beginning to suspect that the feminist movement is operating a covert psyops wing. I like to think that this is the motive force behind the slew of true-crime documentaries that show us, time and again, what bad men do and how they go about it. Perhaps the repeated stories of women – often unhappy with parts of their lives, or otherwise emotionally vulnerable – being love-bombed by apparent male saviours then finding themselves isolated, controlled, coerced, destabilised and battered into submission and sometimes killed that form the predominant subject of this popular modern genre are a way of teaching the young (especially) what is out there. Maybe it’s a way to help them spot the earliest signs of a predator’s approach and arm the innocent against them.Otherwise, you know, it’s just voyeuristic filler for the ever-gaping schedule maw.So, then, to the latest possibly instructive tool, possibly a piece of mindless rubbish: Don’t Date Brandon. It’s a strange title – both lazy and misguided, more suggestive of a 90s sitcom (ditzy roommates! Wild situations! One hot guy!) than an account of one man’s cutting of a destructive swathe through his local dating pool, which is what it is.But that is all of a piece with what is – at least on the basis of the one episode of the three that was made available for review – a lazy and misguided programme. It is based on the podcast Ex-Wives Undercover, which tells survivors’ stories about toxic relationships (gaslighters, catfishers, romance scammers, men leading double lives, those who threaten harm and those who carry it out). It is hosted by the two women around whose experiences with a man called Brandon Johnson the documentary is built.Amber Rasmussen met him online when she was 35 and became his second wife. He warned her to stay away from his ex-wife Athena Klingerman, with whom he had a four-year-old daughter Sydney, and – after he showed Amber the messages that proved Athena to be the “psycho” he said she was – Amber was happy to do so.That was until the red flags around her own relationship with Brandon – the woman claiming to be his girlfriend, the mystery job that required so much travel, the cancer diagnosis just as she was planning on moving out of the marital home, inexplicable bills and parking tickets – made her contact Athena. Whereupon they began unpicking the web of lies Brandon had been telling them both. He had of course been lying about his job, which was mostly the cover for an affair he was having with a woman called Avery (Sydney had a bedroom at her house and was told to keep everything secret from her mother and Amber), and his cancer claims (he had pretended to be ill while he was with Athena too), and about Athena’s nature. She had never run up $100,000 on his credit card, as he had told Amber, and the message threads he had shown his second wife had been completely fabricated by him over an entire year.Most of this information, however, is crammed into the last few minutes of the first episode. The rest of it is spent largely marking time. Amber outlines at length the facts of their relationship, but there is very little emphasis on the psychological effects of Brandon’s actions. Without that, the manipulation looks – to the outsider – so obvious, so blatant that you begin not to sympathise with Brandon’s victim but rather to roll your eyes at a naivety so profound.I am not saying Amber is in any way to blame, you understand. I’m saying that the programme’s pacing, and its lack of granular detail for so long, means that it does not even start to do justice to the gradual erosion of mind and spirit, the inexorable normalisation of the unacceptable, upon which perpetrators like Brandon depend. I imagine that the next two episodes concentrate on the escalation of Brandon’s behaviour (he was eventually charged with assault and attempted kidnapping with intention to commit rape, and accepted a plea agreement that means he is serving a 10-year sentence in a state prison and is eligible for parole next year) and on Amber and Athena going public with their stories. That in turn leads to the uniting of many other victims of Brandon, a man the women discover was served his first restraining order in 1997 at the age of 19. But those episodes will come on top of a shaky foundation that puts Amber (especially) and Athena in the position of effectively having something to prove about themselves, rather than about the man who hurt them.Don’t Date Brandon is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How Harlan Coben became the king of potboiler TV | Television | The Guardian
description: The prolific crime author’s latest Netflix thriller I Will Find You has become one of the streamer’s most-watched shows of all time – but what’s his secret?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The prolific crime author’s latest Netflix thriller I Will Find You has become one of the streamer’s most-watched shows of all time – but what’s his secret?
Content: Sam Worthington and Britt Lower in I Will Find You.Photograph: Christos Kalohoridis/Netflix © 2025View image in fullscreenSam Worthington and Britt Lower in I Will Find You.Photograph: Christos Kalohoridis/Netflix © 2025TelevisionHow Harlan Coben became the king of potboiler TVThe prolific crime author’s latest Netflix thriller I Will Find You has become one of the streamer’s most-watched shows of all time – but what’s his secret?Stuart HeritageThu 30 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix’s all-time top 10 English languageseries chartis starting to look like a stale old thing. It is topped by Wednesday, which is four years old, and includes dusty old hits including Stranger Things season four (four years old), Monster: The Jeffrey Dahmer Story (four years old), The Queen’s Gambit (six years old), and Bridgerton season one (six years old).I Will Find You review – seen one maddeningly watchable Harlan Coben adaptation? You’ve seen them allRead moreBut wait. Just before you write off Netflix as a platform half a decade past its peak, a plucky new entryhas entered the all-time top10 to liven things up. That show is I Will Find You, the latest belched out from the glistening ovipositor of Harlan Coben. If you’re a fan of Coben’s work – and we’ll get into that in due course – then I Will Find You will be instantly recognisable, since it bears many of the author’s hallmarks.Does it have a cast so confusing that your brain needs to take a few moments to adjust to it? Yes. Does it have a title that appears to be picked at random from a tombola barrel filled with the world’s least descriptive words? Absolutely. Do you have a sense when you’re watching it that your television has deliberately leftNetflixand put ITV3 on just to see if you’re paying attention? Oh heavens yes. But it is so popular that you end up worrying that you’re the only person alive who doesn’t actively enjoy it? The numbers speak for themselves.Functionally, there is not much separating I Will Find You from any of the previous 12 Netflix Coben adaptations, like Hold Tight or Fool Me Once or Stay Close or Run Away or Missing You (or even any of the shows he made with other platforms, like Sky’s The Five or Prime’s Harlan Coben’s Shelter). And, indeed, these were all extremely popular too. While the newest show leads with 101.9m worldwide views, 2024’s Fool Me Once gained 98.2m, with 2025’s Missing You and this year’s Run Away both getting over 50m views.This isn’t surprising, given that Coben is a phenomenally successful writer, who has sold more than 90m books in his 30-year career. What might be more surprising, though, is the fact that almost nobody professes to be a fan of his. Compare the reaction to his work to that of George RR Martin, or Lee Child, or even Anne Rice during her lifetime – authors who inspire fervent, noisy support in their fans – and you’ll see the difference.This might be Coben’s appeal, in fact. Rather than develop a cult of personality, he just unfussily gets on with the job of churning out one potboiler after another, and is presumably rewarded with riches beyond his wildest dreams. But this does nothing to change the assumption that people consume his shows without ever fully loving them.Part of this, I’m convinced, is down to the scattershot casting of his adaptations, which seem to hoover up whichever actor happens to be at a loose end at any given point in time. I Will Find You is a perfect case in point. It stars Britt Lower, brilliant in Severance, who until recently had been curating a career playing spiky oddballs in work that went out of its way to confound viewers. But here she is, playing a flat plot device in the sort of show that feels like it was designed to be the fourth thing you watch on a long haul flight.View image in fullscreenHarlan Coben.Photograph: Arnold Jerocki/WireImageThe glut of Netflix adaptations has made Coben extremely wealthy – in 2018 he signed a multimillion-dollar deal to see 14 of his novels developed into content – but he cannot write quickly enough to keep up with the pace of adaptation. He still has some unadapted books in the tank, like Play Dead and Miracle Cure and last year’s Gone Before Goodbye (although since that last one was apparently co-written with Reese Witherspoon, it has to be a matter of time). However, this all might be about to change with the news that an adaptation of his Myron Bolitar bookshas just started filming.This is potentially the lodestar. Despite having a name that sounds like someone choking on some fish, Myron Bolitar is Coben’s best-loved character. A hotheaded basketball player turned agent, who finds himself investigating murders on the side, Bolitar has been the subject of 12 books (along with a handful of young adult books about Myron’s nephew Mickey), and is essentially Coben’s Jack Reacher.If Bolitar lands with anything like the impact of I Will Find You, its recurring premise and cast (including Colin Woodell from Pulse, Chloe Fineman from Saturday Night Live and Griffin Dunne from being Griffin Dunne) will probably help it grow over the course of several years. In other words, don’t be surprised if it becomes Harlan Coben’s biggest hit yet. Just don’t be surprised if you can’t find anyone who will actually admit liking it.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionHarlan CobenUS televisionNetflixThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Helm by Sarah Hall audiobook review – a breath of fresh air from the Pennines  | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Louise Brealey teases out the playful and poetic moments of these shapeshifting stories, told from the perspective of the northeasterly wind and those it has wreaked chaos on through the ages
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Louise Brealey teases out the playful and poetic moments of these shapeshifting stories, told from the perspective of the northeasterly wind and those it has wreaked chaos on through the ages
Content: Lyrical prose … Sarah Hall.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/The ObserverView image in fullscreenLyrical prose … Sarah Hall.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/The ObserverAudiobook of the weekFictionReviewHelm by Sarah Hall audiobook review – a breath of fresh air from the PenninesLouise Brealey teases out the playful and poetic moments of these shapeshifting stories, told from the perspective of the northeasterly wind and those it has wreaked chaos on through the agesFiona SturgesThu 30 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe only named wind in the British Isles, Helm is a strong northeasterly gale that blows down the slopes of Cross Fell in the Pennines and is known for its unusual cloud formations. Helm has been known to dislodge roofs, haystacks, trees and riders from their horses.Twenty years in the writing, Sarah Hall’s Helm is an ambitious novel that tells stories from the perspective of the wind, and from the people on whom, through the ages, Helm has wreaked chaos. Those figures include a Neolithic tribeswoman and seer called NaNay who is building a stone circle; an astrologer and exorcist known as a “wizard priest”; a Victorian meteorologist who travels across the Pennines by train and later by carriage into Helm’s “onslaught”; and a climatologist measuring microplastics in the atmosphere from her observation hut in the fells. Separated by centuries, their stories are nonetheless woven together, each of them bonded by weather.Helm is a book of vast scope, lyrical prose and sharp shifts in style and tone, all of which makes it a tricky job for a narrator. Fortunately, the actor Louise Brealey – who has already read two of Hall’s books: The Wolf Border and Burntcoat – proves more than able, teasing out its playful and poetic moments and revelling in the flashes of coarseness.Helm is a slippery, shapeshifting phenomenon that Hall notes can be hard to visualise and explain, though that doesn’t stop her from trying. “Imagine a skater launching off a quarter pipe two-thousand feet high, then somersaulting. Again. And again. And again.”Available via Faber, 13hr 3minFurther listeningWhistlerAnn Patchett, Bloomsbury, 10hr 43minA fiftysomething English teacher notices an older man following her around New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and eventually recognises him as her former stepfather, Eddie. As they reconnect, old memories come to the surface. Read by the author.London FallingPatrick Radden Keefe, Picador, 12hr 59minBlending true crime and social history, the Empire of Pain author unravels the knotty story of a troubled teenager’s death by falling from a building into the River Thames.Explore more on these topicsFictionAudiobook of the weekreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin review – the Peruvian leftist who fell in love with Margaret Thatcher | Mario Vargas Llosa | The Guardian
description: This stylish biography of the author traces his journey from left to right, and from ‘posh Lima’ to Cricklewood
Author: Pratinav Anil
Headline: This stylish biography of the author traces his journey from left to right, and from ‘posh Lima’ to Cricklewood
Content: Mario Vargas Llosa in 1986.Photograph: Christopher Pillitz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMario Vargas Llosa in 1986.Photograph: Christopher Pillitz/Getty ImagesBook of the dayMario Vargas LlosaReviewMario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin review – the Peruvian leftist who fell in love with Margaret ThatcherThis stylish biography of the author traces his journey from left to right, and from ‘posh Lima’ to CricklewoodPratinav AnilThu 30 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Those words on the opening page of Conversation in the Cathedralannounced the arrival of a writer who understood that national history could become the organising principle of fiction. At precisely the moment when Latin America was discovering the intoxicating possibilities of magical realism – a form whose exuberance had an elective affinity with revolutionary politics, collapsing the distinction between the marvellous and the possible – Mario Vargas Llosa plumped for old-fashioned realism instead.It was a question of sensibility as much as politics, Gerald Martin suggests in this chatty yet coolly analytical biography. He traces the path of a novelist who began by dissecting oligarchy with surgical precision and ended happily dining among its ranks, completing one of literary history’s most spectacular political migrations – from the hard left to the hard right, over the course of half a century.Yet Martin’s revisionist point is that Vargas Llosa crossed a shorter ideological distance than is often imagined. He never truly belonged to the left. His brief flirtation was not with socialism so much as with a socialist: the dazzling, unattainable Lea Barba, whom he met at San Marcos University. Their undergraduate comradeship unfolded between bookshops and the smoky tables of a bohemian nightclub managed by Lea’s communist father. Beneath the guerrilla chic, Martin finds in Vargas Llosa an old patrician confidence in hierarchy. The “factory defect”, as one university contemporary put it, was congenital: Vargas Llosa never ceased to be a “Lima posh boy”.double quotation markHe wrote up the encounter with Thatcher in a piece titled The Lady Among the Wild BeastsVargas Llosa’s greatest novels were written under Jean-Paul Sartre’s spell, before the French philosopher’s indulgence towards revolutionary regimes finally alienated him. The break with Sartre in particular and the left in general came in 1971 with the “Padilla affair”, when the Cuban poet Heberto Padilla was arrested and compelled to perform a grotesque public confession renouncing his “counter-revolutionary” work and denouncing fellow dissidents. Vargas Llosa led an international campaign against Castro’s treatment of writers. Martin is strikingly unsentimental about this celebrated moment of liberal courage. He argues that Vargas Llosa’s comparison of Castro with Stalin was wildly overdrawn and that the campaign against Havana helped isolate the regime at precisely the moment the Latin American left most needed it.Many biographies are now exercises in rehabilitation. Happily, Martin has written a genuinely critical life. The occasional overworked oedipal reading of his subject’s affairs and an inexplicable fondness for the word “sexy” are minor irritants in a searching, stylish account whose real subject is not merely Vargas Llosa but the intellectual and political milieux that made and unmade him.Martin restores the women whom Vargas Llosa reduced to literary raw material. His scandalous marriage at 19 to his aunt-by-marriage, Julia Urquidi, 10 years his senior, became Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter – the sunniest, and by some distance the best loved, of his novels. Her own memoir, What Varguitas Didn’t Say exposes the gap between Vargas Llosa’s breezy romance and the less charming reality of adultery and abandonment. Alas, it never troubled the bestseller lists.Julia was discarded for Patricia Llosa, his first cousin, nine years his junior, with whom he had three children. Like so many writers’ wives of her generation, she was forever taking one for the team, quietly spiriting away the offending pram whenever he bellowed: “Patriiiicia! Take this baby away, I can’t woooork!”Half a century later, she too was replaced, this time by the Spanish society doyenne Isabel Preysler, the mother of the singer Enrique Iglesias, with whom the octogenarian finally exchanged the republic of letters for the pages of ¡Hola!.His move to England proved unexpectedly formative. Vargas Llosa settled in unswinging Cricklewood, which suited a pre-existing taste for suburban conservatism. The historian Hugh Thomas, another distinguished émigré from the left, played Virgil to Vargas Llosa’s Dante, escorting him into the circles of Tory respectability and, eventually, to Margaret Thatcher herself. He wrote up the encounter with fanboy adoration in a piece titled The Lady Among the Wild Beasts.The novelist who spent decades exposing the seductions of ideology proved remarkably susceptible to a new one. After Peru rejected his presidential ambitions when he ran on a neoliberal ticket against Alberto Fujimori in 1990, he increasingly revelled in precisely those circles where power congratulates itself upon its realism. Utopias, sources of aspiration on the left, became mere pathologies in his later fictions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the 2010 Nobel prize, Vargas Llosa increasingly lent his prestige to the hard right, backing Peru’s trigger-happy unelected ruler Dina Boluarte and Chile’s anti-gay, anti-abortion crusader José Antonio Kast; denouncing feminism as literature’s “staunchest enemy,” and treating every leftward electoral twitch as a “return tocaudillismo.”Gabriel García Márquez is the book’s foil: the magician to Vargas Llosa’s realist, the man who stayed with the leftist tribe while his lesser rival abandoned it. Martin, now thebiographer of both, is uniquely placed to reconstruct the most famous right hook in literary history. In 1976, Vargas Llosa floored García Márquez with a punch after allegedly accusing him of overstepping the mark by comforting Patricia during the collapse of their marriage.The punch marked more than a personal rupture. It sealed an ideological one. García Márquez later remarked that there were only “two soups on the menu”: capitalism and socialism. Vargas Llosa turned up his nose at one and spent the rest of his life gorging himself on the other.Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life by Gerald Martinis published by Bloomsbury (£35).Explore more on these topicsMario Vargas LlosaBook of the dayBiography booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Kind of like a fairytale’: documentary tells the unusual tale of Flaco the Owl | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Wild Inside looks back on the incredible year when an escaped zoo owl managed to bring New Yorkers together
Author: Vivian Ho
Headline: Wild Inside looks back on the incredible year when an escaped zoo owl managed to bring New Yorkers together
Content: ‘There are certain places in New York City that will forever be changed for me by his existence in those places’ … a still from Wild Inside.Photograph: Image courtesy of Sandbox Films Photographer  Benny PolatseckView image in fullscreen‘There are certain places in New York City that will forever be changed for me by his existence in those places’ … a still from Wild Inside.Photograph: Image courtesy of Sandbox Films Photographer  Benny PolatseckDocumentary films‘Kind of like a fairytale’: documentary tells the unusual tale of Flaco the OwlWild Inside looks back on the incredible year when an escaped zoo owl managed to bring New Yorkers togetherVivian HoThu 30 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlaco the Eurasian eagle-owl gained a cult following after leaving his life in captivity at the Central Park zoo in 2023 and surviving, against all odds, for more than a year as a free bird in Manhattan.Birdwatcherstracked his every move, capturing his vast wingspan and luminous orange eyes with their cameras. His fansgot tattoosin his honor. And now, Wild Inside, a new documentary chronicling Flaco’s year about town, is set to premiere this week.‘It’s a tragic loss’: New Yorkers mourn Flaco, the owl the city took to its heartRead morePenny Lane, who directed the documentary, said she felt compelled to tell the story of Flaco because, like so many other New Yorkers, she too found herself swept up in his magic. “Owls are uniquely magical creatures,” she said. “They’re associated with other worlds, these mystical realms. So the appearance of a creature like that inNew YorkCity … it feels like kind of a fairytale.”Flaco escaped from the zoo in February 2023, after someone deliberately cut the mesh of the enclosure where he lived for 13 years. Zoo staff and birdwatchers alike feared for his wellbeing. Flaco did not know how to hunt on his own. Observers noticed he had trouble flying. Attempts to lure him back with live lab rats were unsuccessful.But eventually, he figured it out. Local birders documented him successfully hunting and eating some of the city’s many rats. And after two weeks, zoo officials suspended their efforts to recapture him. Flaco had done the impossible: he had learned to be wild again, in perhaps one of the wildest environments of all – the concrete jungle of New York City. “As the saying goes, if you can make it here, you’ll make it anywhere,” one news anchor quipped in a news segment about the owl.Lane sought to capture Flaco’s wild fairytale magic in the film, interspersing interviews with awestruck New Yorkers celebrating each Flaco sighting with whimsical background music and dreamy visuals. She spoke to New Yorkers from all walks of life who projected their own experiences on to the owl that triumphed, calling him a survivor and hailing him as another immigrant success story (Eurasian eagle-owls are a non-native species). “Every New Yorker dreams of moving out of their tiny shitty apartment into a nicer neighborhood and Flaco did it,” Seth Meyers joked ina Late Show monologue.“New Yorkers, we love an underdog,” Lane laughed. But for the local birding community, Flaco’s story went beyond that. “We were watching a zoo animal transform into a wild animal before our eyes,” Lane said. Flaco’s ability to revert back to instincts he never had to use in his life were raising questions over the true nature of wildness – and if it exists within all of us like it did for Flaco.“He was born in captivity. His parents were born in captivity. His grandparents were born in captivity. As far back as I could trace, he was as close to a domesticated wild animal you could get in the sense that he was of a captive lineage,” Lane said. “But he showed pretty quickly that he was not a domesticated animal.”But Flaco’s story doesn’t have a fairytale ending. Just over a year after his escape, Flaco crashed into a building on West 89th Street and died from the impact. A necropsy conducted on his body found that he had been weakened by pigeon herpes virus, which he caught from eating the pigeons that he hunted, as well as four kinds of anticoagulants that are common in the rodenticide used to kill rats – a common cause of death and illness for all wild birds that hunt rats in New York City.View image in fullscreenStreet art mural honoring Flaco in New York’s Freemans Alley.Photograph: Bing Guan/Reuters“I was devastated,” Lane said. She had planned to film Flaco for the entirety of his life, thinking it would be for at least 10 more years. The birdwatchers and naturalists interviewed in the film grappled with questions of if Flaco would have been better off if he had never escaped the zoo at all – no longer free, but alive and safe. “You can’t help but feel guilty and implicated,” Lane said. “You loved seeing him so much, but you knew in the back of your mind all the while that this was not a safe place for him.”A few months after his death, the city councilapproved “Flaco’s law”, an initiative that established a pilot schemes to deploy rat contraceptives rather than poison in an effort to curb the population.The year Flaco spent hooting from water towers and peeking into apartment windows was brief, yes – but it was extraordinary in how it brought the natural world into the hustle and bustle of Manhattan, a reminder to city dwellers of the magic that exists alongside them, Lane said. “There are certain places in New York City that will forever be changed for me by his existence in those places,” Lane said. “I’ll walk down certain blocks and be like, ‘Oh, this is where I heard him hooting on the Upper West Side for the first time and I couldn’t believe how loud it was.’“Everywhere he went, he left that place like a little more magical, and that magic is still there.”Wild Inside opens on 31 July in New York and at over 40 theaters nationwideExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsAnimalsBirdsNew YorkWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cleansed review – Sarah Kane’s visions of brutal torture resonate more intensely than ever | Stage | The Guardian
description: Rebecca Frecknall pulls off this notoriously difficult 1998 play, in which appalling cruelty and violence is balanced against human yearning for love and beauty
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Rebecca Frecknall pulls off this notoriously difficult 1998 play, in which appalling cruelty and violence is balanced against human yearning for love and beauty
Content: A chilling ordinariness … Luke Cinque-White and Leo Bill in Cleansed at the Almeida theatre.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenA chilling ordinariness … Luke Cinque-White and Leo Bill in Cleansed at the Almeida theatre.Photograph: Marc BrennerStageReviewCleansed review – Sarah Kane’s visions of brutal torture resonate more intensely than everAlmeida theatre, LondonRebecca Frecknall pulls off this notoriously difficult 1998 play, in which appalling cruelty and violence is balanced against human yearning for love and beautyArifa AkbarThu 30 Jul 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Kane was much berated for the graphic violence in her plays during her lifetime. But critics beware: if you choose to scold playwrights for too much blood-letting and grotesque acts of human cruelty, you would surely have to condemn the Greeks, the Grand Guignol and Shakespeare, too.Perhaps it’s the in-yer-face nature of Kane’s gore that offends. Certainly in this 1998 play there is no flinching from horror, which comes through acts of sensational cruelty. “Death isn’t the worst thing they can do to you,” a character reflects, and his words illustrate themselves with the rapes, mutilations and beatings that follow.‘She plumbed our secret, shameful depths’: why are Sarah Kane’s plays still so shocking?Read moreIn the case of Cleansed, there are so many ways in which its revival can go wrong, not least because it is notoriously difficult to stage, with directions that require rats to walk away with amputated limbs and gigantic sunflowers to explode from the floor. It is courageous of directorRebecca Frecknallto take it on. The gamble pays off, both in its terrible resonance in our violent world and in her formidable creative accomplishment.Kane’s first play, Blasted, was a response to the conflict in Bosnia in the 1990s and this third play was part of an unrealised trilogy on war. Watching it today, in Frecknall’s potent, moving and fantastically physical production, you are reminded of all the wars before (the cutting out of a character’s tongue and his amputations are reminiscent of Titus Andronicus) and after. A scene in which the Kinks’ song Days is piped into a torture cell, though tender, holds shades of“torture lite” in Guantánamo. Again and again, you are reminded of the photos fromAbu Ghraib prison,which captured the humiliation of prisoners by American guards. Israel’s brutality and violence in Gaza echoes.View image in fullscreenOrwellian … Pearl Chanda and Jack Riddiford in Cleansed.Photograph: Marc BrennerSet in a university that seemed partly to evoke a concentration camp, Tinker (Leo Bill) is the sole “visible” torturer here (other violence is enacted by unseen agents of brutality). He is ostensibly unimposing, personifying Hannah Arendt’s banality, perhaps. He targets those deemed sexually aberrant, particularly two gay men, Rod (Parth Thakerar) and Carl (Luke Cinque-White), but also terrorises brother and sister Graham (Jack Riddiford) and Grace (Pearl Chanda), manipulates a peep show dancer (Lizzy Connolly) and another prisoner called Robin (Stuart Thompson).The cast acts out the play’s many difficult scenarios with no awkwardness or melodrama. Tinker’s cruelty is still a puzzle, especially the functionality with which he tortures. Is he motivated by power, a guiding principle or sheer sadism? It is never explained. Still, the message is clear: war and its torture is senseless, cruel and in-yer-face for those close enough to it. There is the sense of an Orwellian system tyrannising those who are deemed aberrant in their gender or sexual identities (the rats, invisible here, are reminiscent of Orwell, too). Madeleine Girling’s stage design has the grimy, institutionalised feel of a hidden hallway in a psychiatric ward or prison. Again, it evokes a chilling ordinariness.View image in fullscreenA dance of pain … Jack Riddiford and Leo Bill in Cleansed.Photograph: Marc BrennerLike the rest of Kane’s oeuvre, the play interrogates the limits of theatre and representation in its extremity and breakdown of conventional form. Exposing the theatrical construction of violence, through various techniques, does little to protect us from the horror of observing it, and Frecknall oscillates masterfully between realism and a more poetic vein. When characters are in the furthest extremity of pain, their movements become a kind of expressive dance. There is lyricism in it but not so it beautifies violence. Importantly, it never seems gratuitous, either.Sex is a kind of dance, too: bodies never make contact but intimacy and physical force are suggested through choreography. Ingrid Mackinnon’s intimacy direction brings passion and romance, never voyeurism. George Dennis’s sound design, with Angus MacRae’s compositions, combine powerfully with their blend of blazing romance and thrumming electric dread.For such a slim play, it does feel protracted, and slows in its pace. The cruelty becomes draining to watch – but in a world in which images of violence are streamed on daily feeds, it re-sensitises us, through its dissection.The poetry comes in other forms, too. There is sudden, immense beauty, declarations of love, romantic clinches and humour. Set alongside Kane’s brand of post-dramatic theatre, the play’s message is strangely romantic: the human need, maybe even demand, for love and for beauty persists, every bit as vital a force as violence – even, we are shown, for someone like Tinker.AtAlmeida theatre, London, until 29 AugustExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreAlmeida theatreSarah KaneRebecca FrecknallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Marianela: Timeless review – perfect ballerina shows off a leg-whipping, frictionless mastery | Marianela Núñez | The Guardian
description: In what is officially her first solo show, the star principal marshals technically peerless performances from a tremendous company in finely chosen repertoire
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: In what is officially her first solo show, the star principal marshals technically peerless performances from a tremendous company in finely chosen repertoire
Content: Egoless self-possession … Marianela Nuñez and Vadim Muntagirov in Le Corsaire at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEgoless self-possession … Marianela Nuñez and Vadim Muntagirov in Le Corsaire at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMarianela NúñezReviewMarianela: Timeless review – perfect ballerina shows off a leg-whipping, frictionless masteryRoyal Opera House, LondonIn what is officially her first solo show, the star principal marshals technically peerless performances from a tremendous company in finely chosen repertoireLyndsey WinshipThu 30 Jul 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there such a thing as being too perfect? Marianela Nuñez is certainly one of the most perfect ballerinas around. At 44, she still has superlative technique and absolute command. She can reel off a fiendish string of fouettés (as in tonight’s extract from Le Corsaire), whipping her leg in circles, and then come to a gentle standstill, the smoothest brakes you ever saw. It is absolutely frictionless; it is beauty and capability and egoless self-possession. And this might seem an unfair ask, but do we sometimes also need a little grit?View image in fullscreenSerene … Fumi Kaneko and Lukas Brændsrød in After the Rain.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian‘The Messi of ballet’: Marianela Núñez, the Buenos Aires bombshell shaking up British danceRead moreTimeless is Nuñez’s first solo show. Not truly solo, but she’s the star, it’s her choice of repertoire, and she does everything “just right”, paying tribute to the RoyalBallet, the company she joined at 16, and its choreographers: Frederick Ashton, Kenneth MacMillan, Christopher Wheeldon, Wayne McGregor. She also offers an amazing showcase of the company’s dancers and generously allows them to shine, so much so that Matthew Ball and Mayara Magri dancing the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet is an absolute highlight, Magri giddy as she watches her Romeo swoop manfully around the stage. Akane Takada and Calvin Richardson are tender in a duet from McGregor’s Infra, and Fumi Kaneko and Lukas B Braendsrød dance Wheeldon’s serene After the Rain – although they can’t fill the long phrases in the exquisite way Nuñez once did with Thiago Soares.For herself, Nuñez chooses first Jerome Robbins’ In the Night, set to Chopin’s Nocturnes. It’s a very grownup piece for three couples, full of simple, breath-holding elegance. Nuñez dances with Ball, all super-smooth take-offs into jumps and lifts and tortuous indecision about their relationship status. It’s a subtle and gorgeous piece. Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand is the opposite, quite the melodrama, not least Nuñez’s TB-stricken courtesan, coughing on the chaise longue.But Nuñez has a level of reserve and containment that makes this a dance of resistance and surrender rather than passion and fire. Her textbook classical and neo-classical pas de deux are in some ways the most arresting; as well as Corsaire, there’s Balanchine’s Tchaikovsky Pas de Deux with the Royal’s new principal Patricio Revé, a promising partnership for the future. You could ask for more, but you can’t fault her.AtRoyal Opera House, London, until 2 AugustExplore more on these topicsMarianela NúñezBalletDancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They played noughts and crosses on the PM’s huge forehead!’ An Indian standup picks his favourite gen Z protest memes | Comedy | The Guardian
description: They turned the news into a Funny or Die video. They cooked up a romcom between PM Modi and Giorgia Meloni. And they fought the police with Lana del Rey memes. Our writer observes the Cockroach party’s bold new strategy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: They turned the news into a Funny or Die video. They cooked up a romcom between PM Modi and Giorgia Meloni. And they fought the police with Lana del Rey memes. Our writer observes the Cockroach party’s bold new strategy
Content: ‘Rather than delivering another grave protest, gen Z began to entertain’ … a poster depicting Narendra Modi and Donald Trump at a protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Rather than delivering another grave protest, gen Z began to entertain’ … a poster depicting Narendra Modi and Donald Trump at a protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersComedy‘They played noughts and crosses on the PM’s huge forehead!’ An Indian standup picks his favourite gen Z protest memesThey turned the news into a Funny or Die video. They cooked up a romcom between PM Modi and Giorgia Meloni. And they fought the police with Lana del Rey memes. Our writer observes the Cockroach party’s bold new strategyAnuvab PalThu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 03.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve spent 16 years doing standup in India, 10 of them under prime minister Narendra Modi’s government. I’ve learned – especially at corporate events, private shows and turns at various associations, universities and business schools among the English-speaking urban elite – that people are most thrilled when politics doesn’t come up, as if it doesn’t exist. I’m often told: “Anuvab, you can joke about anything – just don’t mention any specific names, places, incidents or events.”You might read that and think I live in some humourless, semi-monarchic stasis. That isn’t true either. Many comedians and influencers joke about the government. Some get into trouble and some don’t, the overall assessment being that it is not worth the risk. InIndia, whatever is true, the opposite is often true as well.double quotation markOverwhelmed by memes, the education minister resignedProtests in India have a playbook, dating from the Raj era. There’s often a hunger strike by a prominent person (Gandhi first, the OG). Some injustice is done, demands are made, people gather, police beat people with sticks, things are broken, a compromise is reached, the prominent person breaks their fast, the cause eventually sells out and a small faction becomes a political party. None of it is funny.View image in fullscreen‘We were taught to always worry about what people will say about you’ … Anuvab Pal.Photograph: Karla GowlettSo I was quite cynical when thegen Z protestsstarted. And what I was definitely not expecting was that comedy would create governmental change. A key medical exam paper was leaked (bribery, that good old tool in India), the education minister Dharmendra Pradhan was accused of lapses, prominent educator Sonam Wangchuk went on hunger strike, a satirical collective calling themselves the Cockroach Janata party rallied behind him, a flood of students poured into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar area, the police started beating them up, the government were open for talks and … I thought I’d seen this movie before.But what the Cockroach party’s gen Z army did in response surprised everyone. Rather than sticking to the usual political sloganeering, where Marxist catchphrases blend with street theatre, or resisting the police by throwing things at them, they targeted the government and the media ecosystem that supports it with witty, profane, often downright abusive and sometimes very funny memes, doctored videos, AI-generated nonsense, posters and protest art – all of it going viral across Indian social media.One video showed hundreds of students at a train station chanting in unison: “The prime minister is a thief.” One cartoon featured Modi being kissed by two billionaires on either side of him – and the artist, defiantly, signed his name. Something had begun. Rather than delivering another grave protest, gen Z began to entertain.double quotation markIndia has never seen anything like thisTech and India’s young are as synonymous as sheep and New Zealand. Tech’s been our biggest export. Yet none of the great tech gods – not Zuckerberg, not Musk, nor, for that matter, the Indian government or oligarchs – foresaw a situation in which this huge young population, rich and poor, all armed with smartphones, would get angry and decide to use their editing talent to unleash madness on Insta and X.One of my favourite themes links Modi and Italian PM Giorgia Meloni. One gen Z-er appealed to Meloni, saying she should not date Modi because he’s all red flags and ghosting. Another piece of AI slop showed Kim Jong Un, a supposed rival for Meloni’s affections, hurling profanities at Modi in Hindi and charging at him.Modi has done many decisive things. Yet in the face of thousands of Meloni/Modi romcom meme mashups, he stalled.View image in fullscreenA toxic relationship? … protesters wearing masks of Modi and Giorgia Meloni.Photograph: Gabrielle Fonseca Johnson/ReutersElsewhere, young people at the protest site have been uploading reels next to policemen, soundtracked by the Lana Del Rey line “everyone knows I’m a good girl, officer” and holding posters that read: “Arrest me daddy.” India has never seen anything like this.Modi did his best to respond, releasing a selfie video talking about legitimate steps being taken. The gen Z-ers weren’t listening. Within minutes, there were AI parodies showing Modi swearing, directing rhyming obscenities at the education minister. Many believed it was real. Soon, they had taken a screenshot of him and started to play noughts and crosses on his disproportionately large forehead! Another viral smash. Modi responded with another video, but with his head further away from the camera, more stylised. They mocked that as well, showing him getting further and further away from camera until he vanishes. They were unstoppable. Modi was trying to communicate. They were having fun.Government folks and their media channels tried all the usual narratives. It’s all politically motivated, backed by George Soros, with China playing some role in destabilising things, they said. But the students, who don’t watch TV, made viral comedy clips in response, taking a few seconds of a news anchor and adding in their own split-screen commentaries. It turned a sombre evening show by eminent pro-government news anchor Arnab Goswami on Republic TV, railing against the terrorist youth, into a Funny or Die video, with a touch of British satiristMichael Spicer’s The Room Next Door.View image in fullscreenUnstoppable … protesters at Jantar Mantar.Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty ImagesMy two favourite clips were a fake Soros saying, in a local Indian language, that he’s isn’t involved, and a protester pretending to call Chinese premier Xi Jinping from Delhi to report that the plan was going well. Eventually, overwhelmed by memes,the education minister resigned.Like many post-empire Indians who grew up under socialism, we were taught to always worry about what people will say about you. We did comedy with that in mind. It was stifling but possible. India’s gen Z has proved they do not care – so they’re much funnier. I have no idea whether they’re actually interested in straight debates with the government … but they’re definitely having a laugh.A new education minister was appointed, Pralhad Joshi. Before he’d said anything, the first comment under the announcement on X read: “Resign Pralhad Joshi.”Explore more on these topicsComedyIndiaProtestNarendra ModiInternetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Love’s Labour’s Lost review – paella, bullfighting and flamenco make Shakespeare’s farce a fiesta | Stage | The Guardian
description: Choreographer Carmen Igarza deserves to take a bow as spectacular dance and movement add passion to the seemingly unfinished play
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Choreographer Carmen Igarza deserves to take a bow as spectacular dance and movement add passion to the seemingly unfinished play
Content: Show-stopping … Norah Lopez Holden and Pablo Egea in Love’s Labour’s Lost at Shakespeare’s Globe.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreenShow-stopping … Norah Lopez Holden and Pablo Egea in Love’s Labour’s Lost at Shakespeare’s Globe.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianStageReviewLove’s Labour’s Lost review – paella, bullfighting and flamenco make Shakespeare’s farce a fiestaShakespeare’s Globe, LondonChoreographer Carmen Igarza deserves to take a bow as spectacular dance and movement add passion to the seemingly unfinished playMark LawsonThu 30 Jul 2026 07.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fact that Love’s Labour’s Lost is relatively unloved by Shakespeare producers and scholars is due to this mid-16th-century comedy being an early example of his dramatic craft – anRSC online timelinelists it ninth in the 38 main attributed plays – and an unusually inconclusive ending: the typical act five marry-go-round is suddenly deferred for a year.These problems mean that even purists object less than usual to a solving directorial concept. Tom Littler, inalfresco stagingsplaying this summer in Guildford and Richmond, pairs the seemingly incomplete piece with Much Ado About Nothing (which some believe to be an otherwise lost Shakespeare piece called Love’s Labour’s Won), unifying the characters and plot lines.‘I just knew it would sound incredible!’: why the Globe is giving Shakespeare some flamenco fireRead moreApart from also being outdoors, Indiana Lown-Collins’s revival for Shakespeare’s Globe is an equally but differently radical revision. Shakespeare has the Spanish kingdom of Navarre – where three young men have signed up to an early detox scheme, renouncing sex and food for meditation – visited by a princess of France and her retinue, who threaten their pledges.In this version, everyone is Spanish – a translation helped, in the summer of 26, by there being as many fans flapping in the audience as in a high-season Madrid street cafe. On stage, adieu becomes adios with some other English words translated – a repast is specified to be paella – and the action punctuated and inflected by sequences of flamenco dance and song.The hunting of a deer in the original here becomes a choreographed bullfight, spectacularly danced by Pablo Egea as the tauran prey. Dance and movement routines – the romantic longing and underlying violence of flamenco reasonably reflecting the themes of the play – regularly stop the show. The programme bills Carmen Igarza as choreographer and Vanessa Guevara as pre-hispanic movement consultant; however this duet worked, they deserve to take a bow at the end of each performance.Less happily, substantial rewriting introduces the figure of Queen Elizabeth I to the masque staged amid the climactic anti-romantic interactions, including jokes about her sex life and vagina. Shakespeare’s play is filled with bawdy that this production always stands up: in the scene in which the three would-be abstinent men are disguised as Muscovites, they sport golden penile codpieces and nippled shoulder pads. However, had Shakespeare pricked his patron in the way this production adds, Love’s Labour’s Lost would have been his final play, the other 29 lost to us.Love’s Labour’s Lost / Much Ado About Nothing review – breezy double bill brings out the best in bothRead moreI would be concerned about students and tourists leaving the Globe admiring Shakespeare’s Elizabethan lèse-majesté, and such is the power of Littler’s double bill that Love’s Labour’s Lost played alone now feels even more half-hearted. But this production is, within its concept, generally a joy.The cast is multi-national, sometimes within a single performer. The Swiss-British-Turkish-Italian Philip Arditti also inflects his cocky reluctant-abstinent Berowne with libidinous dons from culture, and spars nicely with Bea Segura’s sparky Rosaline. Another Spanish actor, Andro Crespo, is an unusually authentic Don Adriano de Armado, while also beautifully leading Michael McMahon and Adrián Solá’s setting of the final song, “When daisies pied and violets blue”. Alongside those responsible for movement and music, casting director Becky Paris should also win applause.AtShakespeare’s Globe, London, until 13 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageShakespeare's GlobeWilliam ShakespearereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Give respect to Africa and the bush people’: Mulatu Astatke on pioneering Ethio-jazz and honouring his roots  | Music | The Guardian
description: The musician faced resistance when he premiered his sound in the 60s, but audiences have fallen in love with it since. At 82, he’s still finding new directions – and wants more recognition for Africa’s indigenous artists
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: The musician faced resistance when he premiered his sound in the 60s, but audiences have fallen in love with it since. At 82, he’s still finding new directions – and wants more recognition for Africa’s indigenous artists
Content: ‘Ethio-jazz is a beautiful science’ … Mulatu Astatke.Photograph: Alexis MaryonView image in fullscreen‘Ethio-jazz is a beautiful science’ … Mulatu Astatke.Photograph: Alexis MaryonMusic‘Give respect to Africa and the bush people’: Mulatu Astatke on pioneering Ethio-jazz and honouring his rootsThe multi-instrumentalist faced resistance when he premiered his sound in the 60s but audiences have fallen in love with it since. Now aged 82, he’s still finding new directions – and wants recognition for Africa’s indigenous artistsGeneva AbdulThu 30 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Do you know the Metro club?” I feign recognition to the 82-year-old father of Ethio-jazz, Mulatu Astatke, who knows the UK capital’s vanished haunts better than I do (the Soho venue closed down decades ago). By then, he had immersed himself in the city’s 60s jazz scene, befriending Ronnie Scott and the saxophonist Joe Harriott, with whom he occasionally jammed across Soho’s clubs, as well as musicians from Africa and the Caribbean.But when he returned to “Swinging Addis” years later with the new genre he’d innovated in England and the United States, the audience at one of his first performances weren’t so taken by his fusion of jazz riffs with the harp-likebegena. “Stop,” Astatke was told. “No more!” He didn’t say a word. Instead, he bowed, said his thanks and walked off. “I said: ‘I’ll show you,’” recalls Astatke in his smoky voice. “‘One day, I’ll come back and show you.’”True to his word, audiences around the world have since fallen under the spell of his otherworldly music. We meet days after Astatke’s performance at London’s Royal Festival Hall in June, which is expected to be his last performance in the UK. Like much of his music, he’s difficult to place at first. Dressed in all black, he blends into an armchair in the almost empty lounge of a north London hotel with art deco flourishes. It was beautiful to see the packed audience appreciating Ethiopian jazz, he tells me.But it wasn’t easy trying to do something new. The jazz he has built across more than a dozen albums is mesmeric, layering the distinct pentatonic scales of traditional Ethiopian music with western-style jazz and funk, and infectious Afro-Latin rhythms. He weaves in traditional instruments – thekrar,masenqoandkebero– as well as religious chants dating back to the fourth century. “Ethio-jazz is a beautiful science,” he says, leaning back into his chair. “You can hear jazz, you can hear 12th notes, you can hear the 5th notes and everything all combined together.”View image in fullscreenBig cheese in the Big Apple … Mulatu in Time Square in 1972.Photograph: Courtesy of Mulatu AstatkeLong before the Ethiopian giant honed his sound, he was sent by his parents to aboarding school in Wrexham, north Wales, at 16, set on studying aeronautical engineering. It was there he picked up the trumpet and was encouraged toward a career in music. Subsequent spells at London’s Trinity College of Music and Boston’s Berklee College of Music, as its first ever African student, followed.Throughout the late 60s, Astatke shuttled between New York – where his group, the Ethiopian Quintet, recorded the albums Afro-Latin Soul 1 & 2 – and Addis Ababa, where he began recording singles for Amha Records, the country’s first independent label, in 1969. “I really wanted to be different, I wanted to be myself, I wanted to be Mulatu,” he says of the years spent honing his sound. “Then once I created Ethio-jazz, I became myself.”double quotation markPromoting Ethiopia, promoting our cultural people to the world, that’s what makes me so great and happyHis Ethio-jazz is rooted within the musical culture of a country that, unlike many of its neighbours, has enjoyed independence for most of the last 2,000 years (with the exception of a brief Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941). Astatke had returned to Addis with his own vibraphone and electric keyboards, to a golden age of nightlife and music under Emperor Haile Selassie’s reign (think saxophonist Getatchew Mekurya, singer Mahmoud Ahmed and keyboardist Hailu Mergia, to name a few), which served as fertile ground for experimentation.With his reputation growing, in 1973 Astatke performed in Addis with Duke Ellington, who was touring Ethiopia and Zambia on a state-sponsored trip. He “never expected this from an African”, the US jazz legend told Astatke, as the saxophone section played Ethio-jazz. “He loved it,” he recalls today, wistfully. “It was so good, so beautiful.”View image in fullscreenGood vibes … Astatke in the late 1960s.Photograph: Courtesy of Mulatu AstatkeThe era of a famously wild nightlife under Selassie came to an end when the emperor was deposed by a Marxist regime in 1974, and a repressive period followed for nearly two decades in which hundreds of thousands of Ethiopians were killed, jailed or exiled.My questions about Astatke’s performances for Selassie and life under Ethiopia’s Communist junta are, however, met with reticence. “I have no involvement with the military, I have no involvement with politics, I have no involvement with nobody. I live peacefully. That’s how I survive,” he says firmly. Why the lack of interest in politics? “I don’t love it. You don’t respect politicians. I love my country, I love my culture, I love the people. That’s all. Nothing else.”Astatke wants to ensure that Ethiopia’s cultural contributions don’t go unnoticed. Speak with the musician long enough and each conversation will inevitably bend to the country’s “bush people”, who he feels have yet to receive credit for their musical contributions. Take, for example, the diminished scales used by American saxophonist Charlie Parker (imagine leaps or half-steps in sound); the Derashe tribe in southern Ethiopia, he says, play the same scale. “Who is first? Is it Charlie Parker or this tribe?” he says. “We never give respect to these people.”As he lists off other examples that speak to the forgotten African influence in western music, it feels like I’ve stumbled on to a gameshow. Which came first, themasenqoor the cello? The energised cha-cha and mambo music he heard in a visit to Cuba when he met Fidel Castro, or the similar sounds found in Nigerian, Ghanaian and Tanzanian rhythms?View image in fullscreenBass pleasures … a Mulatu of Ethiopia session in 1972.Photograph: Mulatu AstatkeAstatke jumps then to Japan, a country whose traditional music uses the same five-note scale as Ethiopia. (“Who was first? Who created? Where did this come from?”) Then he compares Beethoven and Tchaikovsky, who famously had distinct musical notations, to St Yared, a sixth-century Aksumite composer credited with creating his own musical notations (“How much respect do you give to him?”). Astatke recalls being invited to lecture at a university in Ethiopia, where students couldn’t name the mountain beyond the classroom but knew the German and Russian composers. “We don’t do any research, we go more to Europe instead of doing research on African people,” he says. “I feel sorry for the educational system in the world, culturally.”Mulatu Astatke review – father of Ethio-jazz still innovating during farewell tourRead moreIn the 1990s, Astatke visited various Ethiopian indigenous communities – the Derashe in the south and Gambella, home to the Nilotic Anuak people – where he was immediately welcomed. There he would have long discussions and, on occasion, stay in small huts. The high respect he holds for them is palpable: “The bush people created Mulatu, because I became a musician by listening to themasenqo.”His manager, sitting at the table with us, gets out his laptop and pulls up a joyous performance by Astatke with members of the Derashe tribe, one of the several communities he brought to the studio in the 1990s. A second video,from the 1970s, shows him performing with traditional musicians playing thekrar. “I became a musician by listening to these people,” he says, “they created me.”Astatke will soon return to Addis Ababa where he’s expecting an audience at the AfricanJazzVillage he opened in 2013, now run by his son. The venue still draws international visitors and spotlights local musicians today.What’s next? He toys with the idea of playing new music at the club in Addis. His most recent album, Mulatu Plays Mulatu, was a new arrangement of hisclassics with his UK band, but his next will feature musicians from “the bush” as well as those in Addis. But there is no name for the project yet, he insists – it is still a work in progress.“Promoting Ethiopia, promoting our cultural people to the world, that’s what makes me so great and happy,” he says. “It took me years and years, but finally we made it.” Only then, do I see a smile beneath Astatke’s serious demeanour. “Give respect to Africa,” he says again, “and the bush people.”Mulatu Astatke’s album Mulatu Plays Mulatu is out now on Strut Records.Explore more on these topicsMusicJazzEthiopiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: BBCSSO/Wigglesworth / Booth review – Brett Dean’s song cycle is rich and strange  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Soprano Clare Booth, Ryan Wigglesworth and the BBC Scottish gave the world premiere of Dean’s theatrical and engaging The World’s Wife. Elgar’s 1st didn’t quite achieve lift-off but Weir’s Moon and Star had sweep and shimmer
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Soprano Clare Booth, Ryan Wigglesworth and the BBC Scottish gave the world premiere of Dean’s theatrical and engaging The World’s Wife. Elgar’s 1st didn’t quite achieve lift-off but Weir’s Moon and Star had sweep and shimmer
Content: Filmic sweep and shimmer … the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth perform Judith Weir’s Moon and Star.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenFilmic sweep and shimmer … the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth perform Judith Weir’s Moon and Star.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBBCSSO/Wigglesworth / Booth review – Brett Dean’s song cycle is rich and strangeRoyal Albert HallSoprano Clare Booth, Ryan Wigglesworth and the BBC Scottish gave the world premiere of Dean’s theatrical and engaging The World’s Wife. Elgar’s 1st didn’t quite achieve lift-off but Weir’s Moon and Star had sweep and shimmerAlexandra CoghlanThu 30 Jul 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can talk symphonic architecture, pacing and balance all day long, but when Elgar is right you just feel it. A good First Symphony lands somewhere between heart and head, each tugging you back and forth between admiration and emotion at a piece Hans Richter famously called “the greatest symphony of modern times”. In their first Prom of the season Ryan Wigglesworth and theBBC Scottish Symphony Orchestragave us a handsome account, playing up to the generous proportions of the hall, but we never quite saw “it”.Wigglesworth is a conductor who thinks in chapters, you can hear the long lines of his structures from the hyper-hushed opening Andante – whose payoff will appear nearly an hour later in the finale, when we arrive where we started and know it for the first time. But we could also hear an orchestra thinking in paragraphs. Transitions were often choppy in the first two movements, episodes in the final Allegro lacked a sense of context, balance wasn’t always perfectly voiced in the Adagio. Nothing fatal, but enough to keep us thinking rather than feeling.There was plenty of sensation in the first half, in the filmic sweep and shimmer of Judith Weir’s 1995 Moon and Star – Emily Dickinson’s poem gleaming under layers of orchestral texture, less a traditional setting than a prismatic explosion of imagery, the verse the crystal at its centre – and the theatricality of Brett Dean’s new orchestral song-cycle The World’s Wife.View image in fullscreenTheatricality: Claire Booth performs Brett Dean’s song-cycle The World’s Wife.Photograph: Mark AllanCarol Ann Duffy’s wry, confessional, irreverent verse supplies five poems for a work that looks over the shoulders of famous men – Icarus, Darwin, Perseus – at the women standing behind them in the shadows. Soprano Claire Booth is a stage animal, seizing Duffy’s text and bending it variously into love-song, satire, prayer and meditation. She’s helped by Dean, who pitches his monodrama somewhere between Pierrot Lunaire and Façade – stylised and a little arch, but so richly and strangely textured that it creates new spaces in Duffy’s tight, epigrammatic poetry, filling them with ambiguity and interest.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. title: Die Fledermaus review – Strauss staging has flourish and froth, but not enough fizz | Opera | The Guardian
description: Liam Steel relocates Johann Strauss’s operetta to London 1929 to create the feel of a Noël Coward-style farce. Rebecca Bottone, Olivia Carrell and Clare Presland shine amid a strong cast.
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Liam Steel relocates Johann Strauss’s operetta to London 1929 to create the feel of a Noël Coward-style farce. Rebecca Bottone, Olivia Carrell and Clare Presland shine amid a strong cast.
Content: Alison Langer   and Harry Wilson in Die Fledermaus at Opera Holland Park.Photograph: Craig FullerView image in fullscreenAlison Langer   and Harry Wilson in Die Fledermaus at Opera Holland Park.Photograph: Craig FullerOperaReviewDie Fledermaus review – Strauss staging has flourish and froth, but not enough fizzOpera Holland Park, LondonLiam Steel relocates Johann Strauss’s operetta to London 1929 to create the feel of a Noël Coward-style farce. Rebecca Bottone, Olivia Carrell and Clare Presland shine amid a strong cast.Clive PagetThu 30 Jul 2026 09.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohann Strauss’s Die Fledermaus must have done more for champagne sales than any other operetta. A good production, however, demands plenty of onstage fizz too, but the bubbles start to rise rather late in the day in Opera Holland Park’s new staging.Director and choreographer Liam Steel uses the Metropolitan Opera’s 2013 revamped English version with lyrics by Jeremy Sams and a new book by Douglas Carter Beane. His chosen setting, however, is London on New Year’s Eve 1929; cue references to the Sitwells and the Mitfords. In its determination to reflect the anything goes spirit of the age there’s even a cheeky reference to Winston Churchill’s supposed dalliance with Ivor Novello (how did he find it? “Musical,” goes the apocryphal tale.) The idea has legs, turning a 19th-century Viennese operetta into a louche Noël Coward farce with lines that are at times deliciously tart.Where it is less successful is in the playing out of this frothy saga of bourgeois infidelity and mistaken identities. With its free-standing doorframes, Neil Irish’s set for the Eisensteins’ salon feels insufficiently nouveau riche. Placed in front of the orchestra on the OHP forestage, it does at least allow the performers intimate contact with the audience. The second act’s deco ballroom with gilded Degas centrepiece has more flourish, but, confined to the rear of the stage, the company feels deflatingly distant. It’s left to act three, set in a police station complete with affable moustachioed bobby (a winning performance by Robert Burt), to raise the chuckle level to where it needs to be.View image in fullscreenAnything goers spirit … Die Fledermaus at Opera Holland Park.Photograph: Craig FullerSteel does his best, pulling off some nice bits of physical comedy, and Sams’ elegant lyrics are a treat: “Drink another drink with me, you’ve had none and I’ve had three,” sings the libidinous tenor, Alfred (a stentorian and suitably Italianate Xavier Hetherington). The acting can be inconsistent – act one starts off a little Acorn Antiques – but there are strong performances from Rebecca Bottone as the put-upon cockney chambermaid Adele and Julien Van Mellaerts as an affected Dr Falke in midnight-blue velvet and foppish earring. Matthew Siveter plays Inspector Frank as a bluff Yorkshireman with a fine line in bewildered expressions. His encounter at the ball with Thomas Atkins’ Eisenstein, where both appear as faux-Frenchmen and communicate entirely in phrases such as “coq au vin” and “menage a trois”, earns well-deserved laughter.George Jackson conducts the City of London Sinfonia stylishly, though the music is frequently too loud for the singers. Nevertheless, there are strong vocal performances from Alison Langer as Rosalinde, Clare Presland as the gender-fluid socialite Orlofsky and especially Bottone, who absolutely nails her Laughing Song. Special mention too for Olivia Carrell who sparkles in the relatively thankless role of Ida, the chorus girl from Where’s My Willie.At Opera Holland Park, London, until 8 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaOpera Holland ParkClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Giordano: Marina album review – a fascinating resurrection of an unsung early opera | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The long-lost score, finally premiered 138 years after it was written, brims with melodic promise despite its dramatic shortcomings
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The long-lost score, finally premiered 138 years after it was written, brims with melodic promise despite its dramatic shortcomings
Content: Treasurable, thrilling … Eleonora Buratto at the world premiere of Umberto Giordano’s Marina in 2026.Photograph: Lorenza DaverioView image in fullscreenTreasurable, thrilling … Eleonora Buratto at the world premiere of Umberto Giordano’s Marina in 2026.Photograph: Lorenza DaverioClassical musicReviewGiordano: Marina album review – a fascinating resurrection of an unsung early operaBuratto/De Tommaso/Orchestra I Pomeriggi Musicali/Milletarì(Decca)The long-lost score, finally premiered 138 years after it was written, brims with melodic promise despite its dramatic shortcomingsClive PagetThu 30 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a bold move by the 21-year-old Umberto Giordano to enter the 1888 one-act opera competition won by Mascagni’s Cavalleria Rusticana. Marina, set in Montenegro during an unspecified conflict with Serbia, came sixth, the score languishing until 2026, when it received its belated premiere at Milan’s Teatro dal Verme. This recording reveals a composer with a keen ear for musical colour even if the opera is no masterpiece.View image in fullscreenGiordano: Marina.Photograph: DeccaWhen Marina, a Montenegrin, takes in Giorgio, a wounded Serb, the inevitable conflict with her brother and her bullish suitor precipitates a typical verismo catastrophe. After a militaristic opening, Marina takes centre stage with an aching ballad of lost opportunity. Her scene with the injured Giorgio follows abruptly, redeemed by Giordano’s knack for trotting out appealing melodies. It’s not the most sophisticated writing but it comes straight from the heart.There’s a drinking song that sounds like a crib from Verdi’s Otello and a patriotic Montenegrin ditty which, alongside a brief aria for Giorgio, is the show’s hit. The scene between Marina and her brother is decently judged, even if the one-act format prevents the kind of character development a longer work would permit.Eleonora Buratto is treasurable as Marina, her bright soprano thrilling at the top. As Giorgio, Freddie De Tommaso proves a classy verismo hero, his voice dark yet suitably Italianate. The Orchestra I Pomeriggi Musicali is supple and secure under the idiomatic baton of Vincenzo Milletarì.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
